summary: Rome captured Cales in Campania and established a Roman colony there.
text: Cales (modern Calvi), a city in Campania, is taken by the Romans and a Roman colony is established there.

summary: Syracusan mathematician and philosopher Hicetas died.
text: Hicetas of Syracuse, Greek mathematician and philosopher (b. c. 400 BC)

summary: Alexander I of Epirus crossed into Italy to aid Tarentum and defeated Lucanian, Bruttian, and Samnite forces.
text: Alexander of Epirus, at the request of the colony of Taras (Tarentum) crosses over into Italy, to aid them against the Lucanians and Bruttii. He wins victories over the Italian Samnite tribes.

summary: Alexander I of Epirus defeated the Samnites and Lucanians near Paestum and concluded a treaty with Rome.
text: After a victory over the Samnites and Lucanians near Paestum, Alexander of Epirus makes a treaty with the Romans.

summary: Alexander I of Epirus took Heraclea from the Lucanians and Terina and Sipontum from the Bruttians.
text: Alexander of Epirus takes Heraclea from the Lucanians, and Terina and Sipontum from the Bruttii.

summary: Tarentum turned against Alexander I of Epirus, who was then defeated and killed at the Battle of Pandosia.
text: Tarentum turns against Alexander of Epirus when they realize that he intends to create a kingdom of his own in southern Italy. Alexander is defeated and killed in the Battle of Pandosia on the banks of the Acheron.

summary: The Senones and the Romans concluded a peace treaty establishing friendly relations.
text: The Gallic tribe of the Senones and the Romans conclude a peace and enter upon a period of friendly relations which lasts the rest of the century.

summary: Alexander I of Epirus died after being defeated in battle in southern Italy.
text: Alexander I of Epirus, Aeacid dynasty king of Epirus (b. c. 370 BC)

summary: Vitruvius Vaccus led Fondi and Privernum in an unsuccessful rebellion against Rome.
text: The Italian cities of Fondi and Privernum, led by Vitruvius Vaccus, launch a failed revolt against Rome.

summary: Rome declared war on the Samnites after they failed to stop raids on Fregellae.
text: Samnite Wars: Rome declared war on the Samnites after their failure to prevent their subjects raiding Fregellae.

summary: The Romans besieged Neapolis, expelled the occupying Samnite garrison, and allied with the city.
text: The Samnite army captures Neapolis (present-day Naples). The Romans, who are meanwhile moving south while the Samnites are occupied with Tarentum, take the opportunity to recover Neapolis and, after a long siege, evict the Samnite garrison from the city and make it an ally of Rome.

summary: The Samnites declared war on Rome, beginning the Second Samnite War.
text: Following their defeat by the Roman forces in Naples, the Samnites declare war on Rome starting the Second Samnite War. To help defeat the Samnites, the Romans make alliances with the peoples of Central Italy to the north of Samnium and with the Apulians to the southeast.

summary: The oligarchic government of Syracuse exiled Agathocles after he attempted to overthrow them.
text: Agathocles, a rich and ambitious citizen of Syracuse, is exiled for attempting to overthrow the oligarchic party in the city.

summary: The Samnites sued for peace after Roman victories, but rejected the harsh terms offered by Rome.
text: Continuing successes by Rome's armies against the Samnites forces the Samnites to sue for peace. However, the terms offered by Rome are so stringent that they are rejected by the Samnites and the war goes on.

summary: Samnite general Gaius Pontius trapped Roman consuls Spurius Postumius Albinus and Titus Veturius Calvinus at the Caudine Forks, forcing them to agree to a humiliating treaty.
text: Two Roman consuls, Spurius Postumius Albinus and Titus Veturius Calvinus, leading an invading force into Samnium, are trapped in a mountain pass known as the Caudine Forks (Caudium) near Beneventum, where they can neither advance nor retire, and after a desperate struggle, they are forced to submit to the humiliating terms imposed by the Samnite victor, Gaius Pontius. The captured consuls pledge themselves to a five-year treaty on terms most favourable for the Samnites.

summary: Pyrrhus, future king of Epirus and adversary of Rome, was born.
text: Pyrrhus of Epirus, King of the Molossians, Epirus and Macedonia (d. 272 BC)

summary: Polyperchon fled to Epirus and formed an alliance with Olympias and King Aeacides of Epirus.
text: Polyperchon flees to Epirus, where he joins Alexander the Great's mother Olympias, Alexander's widow Roxana, and Alexander's infant son Alexander IV. He forms an alliance with Olympias, who is acting as regent for Alexander IV, and King Aeacides of Epirus.

summary: The citizens of Syracuse appointed Acestorides of Corinth as their supreme commander.
text: Acestorides, a native of Corinth, is made supreme commander by the citizens of Syracuse.

summary: Agathocles returned to Syracuse with an army, banished or murdered thousands of citizens, and made himself tyrant.
text: After twice being banished for attempting to overthrow the oligarchical party, Agathocles returns with an army and banishes or murders about 10,000 citizens (including the oligarchs), and sets himself up as tyrant of Syracuse. Acestorides is banished from the city.

summary: Agathocles, tyrant of Syracuse, extended his control over eastern Sicily.
text: Agathocles, the new tyrant of Syracuse, extends his rule over the eastern part of the island.

summary: The Samnites defeated the Romans under Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus at the Battle of Lautulae and advanced toward Rome.
text: The Romans, with an eye to capturing Apulia, send an army (led by dictator Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus) to seize the town of Lucera from the Samnites. They are badly beaten in the Battle of Lautulae and the Samnites go on to reach within 32 kilometres of Rome.

summary: Cassander took control of Epirus after King Aeacides was deposed by his people and the young Pyrrhus was rescued.
text: The King of Epirus, Aeacides, faces a revolt from his people and they drive him from the kingdom. His son, Phyrrhus, who is then only two years old, is saved from being killed by some faithful servants. Cassander takes control of Epirus.

summary: Agathocles, tyrant of Syracuse, seized the city of Messina.
text: Agathocles, the tyrant of Syracuse, seizes the city of Messina.

summary: The Romans captured the Apulian city of Ferentum, prompting the citizens of Nuceria to end their alliance with Rome.
text: The Romans take Ferentum, a city of Apulia, and this pushes the citizens of Nuceria to end their friendship with Rome.

summary: The Samnites defeated a Roman army led by dictator Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus at the Battle of Lautulae.
text: The Samnites defeat a Roman army led by dictator Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus at the Battle of Lautulae.

summary: Samnite military successes brought Campania to the verge of defection and prompted several Samnite towns to make peace with Rome.
text: Success seems to be going the Samnites' way in their ongoing battles against the Romans. Campania is on the verge of deserting Rome. Peace is established between Rome and some Samnite towns.

summary: Roman consuls marched to Tarracina and decisively defeated a Samnite army, killing ten thousand enemy troops.
text: The Roman consuls march their combined army to Tarracina and defeat a Samnite army there; killing 10,000 Samnites in the battle and the subsequent pursuit.

summary: Rome appointed Gaius Maenius as dictator to secure Campania, prompting the Campanians near Capua to surrender rebels and renew their Roman alliance.
text: While the consuls are fighting the Samnites at Tarracina, the Romans elect Gaius Maenius as Dictator with Marcus Foslius Flaccinator as his Magister Equitum (Master-of-Horse, Second-in-Command) and send them into Campania at the head of a large army. When Maenius and Foslius arrive near Capua, the Campanians, hearing about the defeat of the Samnites at Tarracina, start negotiating terms with the Romans; they surrender those who are guilty of the uprising and in turn are reinstated in their alliance with Rome.

summary: Roman dictator Gaius Poetelius Libo Visolus marched on Fregellae and placed a Roman garrison there after the Samnites fled.
text: The Samnites take Fregellae in Latium, the Roman dictator Gaius Poetelius Libo Visolus marches his army from Rome and moves to retake it, but the Samnites leave at night; Visolus places a garrison in the city.

summary: Consul Gaius Junius Bubulcus Brutus captured Nola, Atina, and Calatia.
text: The consul Gaius Junius Bubulcus Brutus is credited with the capture of Nola, Atina, and Calatia by some sources.

summary: Rome established colonies at Pontiae, Interamna Sucasina, and Suessa Aurunca.
text: The Romans establish colonies at the Volscian island of Pontiae, the Volscian town of Interamna Sucasina and at Suessa Aurunca.

summary: Carthage sent a large military force to Sicily in response to an appeal from Syracusan exiles led by Deinocrates against Agathocles.
text: Deinocrates, the leader of the Syracusan exiles, sends envoys to the Carthaginians to ask them for help against Agathocles, the tyrant of Syracuse. The Carthaginians, fearing for their own possessions in Sicily, send a large force to the island.

summary: Following a failed attempt by Syracusan exiles to seize Centoripini, Agathocles executed everyone in the city suspected of sedition.
text: The exiles send Nymphodorus (a friend of Deinocrates) with some soldiers to take Centoripini (some of whose elite had promised to assist the exiles in taking the city). Nymphodorus is killed in the failed attempt to capture the city. Agathocles executes everyone he suspects of sedition in the city.

summary: King Aeacides of Epirus died.
text: Aeacides, King of Epirus.

summary: The people of Epirus elevated Alcetas II to the kingship following the death of Aeacides.
text: The people of Epirus elevate Aeacides' brother, Alcetas, to the kingship.

summary: Cassander marched his army into Epirus after Alcetas attacked Acarnania, compelling Alcetas to accept an alliance.
text: Alcetas advances on the Macedonian garrison of Acarnania under Lyciscus, a general of Cassander. Three battles are fought and a defeated Alcetas flees to a fortress in Epirus. Cassander marches the main Macedonian field army into Epirus and forces Alcetas to ally with him.

summary: The people of Epirus revolted against the harsh rule of Alcetas II and murdered him and his sons.
text: The people of Epirus, tired of Alcetas (who ruled Epirus harshly), rose up and murdered him and his sons.

summary: Agathocles enlarged his armed forces in Syracuse until they exceeded the Carthaginian garrison forces stationed on Sicily.
text: Agathocles, tyrant of Syracuse, increased the size of his forces until they surpassed the Carthaginian garrison forces on the island.

summary: Carthage dispatched a large fleet and army under Hamilcar to Sicily to check the growing power of Agathocles.
text: Carthage, concerned with Agathocles' increasing powers, decided to send 130 warships and 14,200 soldiers under the command of a general named Hamilcar (son of Gisco, grandson of Hanno the Great).

summary: Severe storms sank sixty Carthaginian warships and destroyed two hundred transports from Hamilcar's expeditionary fleet.
text: Hamilcar's fleet was caught by several storms which sank 60 warships and destroyed 200 transports.

summary: After landing in Sicily, Hamilcar gathered the survivors of the storm, hired mercenaries, and recruited local forces to rebuild a large army.
text: After landing on Sicily, Hamilcar gathered the remnants of his army, he also started to hire mercenaries, enlist those Sicilians opposed to Agathocles and enroll soldiers from the Carthaginian garrisons already on Sicily. In this way he was able to muster a large army.

summary: Agathocles seized Gela, executed four thousand citizens on suspicion of treason, and confiscated their property.
text: Agathocles, fearing Gela would turn against him, took over the city, executed 4,000 leading Geloans he suspected of treason, and confiscated their property.

summary: The Romans appointed Gaius Sulpicius Longus as dictator to counter an anticipated Etruscan invasion that did not materialize.
text: The Second Samnite War continues: there are rumours of a mobilisation of the Etruscans; since the consul Marcus Valerius Maximus Corvus is campaigning in Samnium and his consular colleague Publius Decius Mus is to ill to lead an army, the people appoint Gaius Sulpicius Longus as dictator. Sulpicius appoints Gaius Junius Bubulcus Brutus as his Magister Equitum (Second-in-command). Sulpicius ' mission is to defend against the Etruscan invasion which never materialize; Sulpicius and Brutus remain in camp at Rome until the end of the campaigning season.

summary: Appius Claudius Caecus took office as censor, began construction of the Appian Way, and enacted wide-ranging political reforms in Rome.
text: The Roman censor, Appius Claudius Caecus, a patrician, enters office and begins construction of the Appian Way (the Via Appia) between Rome and Capua. He also embarks on a program of political reform, including the distribution of the landless citizens of Rome among the tribes, which at this time constitute basic political units. Appius also admits sons of freedmen into the Roman Senate. He also asserts the right of freed slaves to hold office.

summary: Roman engineers completed construction of the Aqua Appia, bringing the city of Rome its first aqueduct.
text: Rome gets its first pure drinking water as engineers complete the first aqueduct into the city, the Aqua Appia.

summary: Roman consuls Gaius Junius Bubulcus Brutus and Quintus Aemilius Barbula divided their command during the Second Samnite War.
text: The Second Samnite War continues, the Roman consuls Gaius Junius Bubulcus Brutus and Quintus Aemilius Barbula divide their command.

summary: Gaius Junius Bubulcus Brutus retook Cluviae, sacked Bovianum, and repelled a Samnite ambush.
text: The Samnites take the Roman garrison of Cluviae and scourge their prisoners. Junius liberates the city and then moves on Bovianum and sacks it. The Samnites try to ambush the Romans, but the Romans are able to overcome their assailants.

summary: Quintus Aemilius Barbula marched to relieve the Roman ally Sutrium from an Etruscan siege, fighting an indecisive battle.
text: The Etruscans are besieging Sutrium, an ally which the Romans see as their key to Etruria. Barbula marches to their aid, and a battle is fought; the Romans start to gain the upper hand, but darkness stops the battle. Barbula's campaign ends indecisive.

summary: Hamilcar crossed from Carthage to Sicily and defeated Agathocles of Syracuse at the Battle of the Himera River.
text: The Carthaginian general Hamilcar crosses the Mediterranean with an army and wins the Battle of Himera against Agathocles, the tyrant of Syracuse.
names: Battle of the Himera River (311 BC)

summary: Hamilcar laid siege to Syracuse after Agathocles retreated into the city.
text: Hamilcar then proceeds with laying siege to Syracuse, where Agathocles had retreated.

summary: Agathocles escaped the Carthaginian siege of Syracuse and defeated the Carthaginians at the Battle of White Tunis in North Africa.
text: The tyrant of Syracuse, Agathocles, escapes from the siege of the city by the Carthaginians with a fleet and carries the war with the Carthaginians back into his enemy's territory. He defeats the Carthaginians in the Battle of White Tunis.

summary: Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus led the Romans to victory over the Etruscans at the Battle of Lake Vadimo.
text: Rome deals with renewed trouble from the Etruscans, who are persuaded by the Samnites to cease their alliance with the Romans. In the Battle of Lake Vadimo, the Romans under Fabius Maximus Rullianus defeat the Etruscans.

summary: Bomilcar's attempted coup to restore absolute monarchy in Carthage failed, cementing the Carthaginian republic.
text: Since 480 BC, an aristocratic Council of Elders has effectively ruled Carthage. The titular king of Carthage, Bomilcar, attempts a coup to restore the monarchy to full power. His attempt fails, which leads to Carthage becoming, in name as well as in fact, a republic.

summary: Agathocles landed in North Africa, allied with Ophellas of Cyrenaica, and nearly captured Carthage during internal unrest.
text: Leaving his brother Antander to continue the defence of Syracuse, Agathocles lands in North Africa with the aim of distracting the Carthaginians from their siege of Syracuse. Agathocles concludes a treaty with Ophellas, ruler of Cyrenaica. He then takes advantage of the civil unrest in Carthage and nearly succeeds in conquering the city.

summary: Roman dictator Lucius Papirius Cursor won a decisive victory over the Samnites at Longula.
text: The Samnites again rise against Rome. Lucius Papirius Cursor is appointed dictator for the second time and wins a great victory at Longula over the Samnites.

summary: Ptolemy II Philadelphus was born on the island of Kos.
text: Ptolemy II Philadelphus, King of Egypt (d. 246 BC)

summary: Rome suppressed an uprising by the Umbrians, Picentes, and Marsians during the Second Samnite War.
text: The Second Samnite War escalates when the tribes of the central Apennines, the Umbrians, Picentes, and Marsians join the war against Rome. However, Rome is able to control the uprising.

summary: The Etruscans sued for peace with Rome and accepted harsh terms.
text: The Etruscans sue for peace with Rome, which is granted by the Romans on severe terms.

summary: Carthage dispatched an army and forced the Zuphones back into alliance.
text: The Carthaginians send out an army to coerce the Zuphones, a Numidian tribe, back into their alliance with Carthage; they are successful in their endeavour.

summary: Agathocles marched after the Carthaginian army, leaving Archagathus in command of the camp before Tunis.
text: Agathocles leaves his main army under the command of his son Archagathus encamped before Tunis while he, with a strikeforce of 8,000 infantry, 800 cavalry and 50 chariots, marches after the Carthaginian army.

summary: Agathocles defeated Carthaginian forces and their Numidian allies after escalating skirmishes.
text: The Carthaginians send the Numidians to harass Agathocles' strike force, the skirmishing draws in more and more troops until it eventually leads to a battle which is won by Agathocles.

summary: Agathocles returned to his camp following a Numidian raid, divided the remaining plunder, and erected a victory trophy.
text: While Agathocles was in pursuit of the defeated Carthaginian army, the Numidians (who had retreated from the battle earlier on) attack his camp and ride off with a part of his army's booty. Agathocles returns to his camp, divides what is left of the booty (so no one can complain) and sets up a victory trophy.

summary: Agathocles sent an envoy to Cyrene to request military assistance from Ophellas against Carthage.
text: Agathocles sends Orthon the Syracusan to Cyrene to request aid in subduing Carthage from Ophellas (Ptolemy's governor of Cyrenaica).

summary: Ophellas recruited an army of over ten thousand men to campaign alongside Agathocles against Carthage.
text: Ophellas recruits an army of 10,000 infantry, 600 cavalry and 100 chariots for his campaign in support of Agathocles.

summary: Ophellas completed an arduous march across the desert to join Agathocles' forces in Carthaginian territory.
text: After an arduous march from Cyrenaica to Carthaginian Libya Ophellas' forces link up with Agathocles' army.

summary: Agathocles launched a surprise attack on Ophellas' camp, killed him, and absorbed his army.
text: Agathocles lures Ophellas into a false sense of security and launches a surprise attack on his camp. Ophellas is killed in the fighting and Agathocles takes over Ophellas' army, adding its numbers to his own.

summary: Bomilcar attempted a coup to become tyrant of Carthage but failed and was executed.
text: While the Carthaginian army is away from the city, Bomilcar tries to make himself tyrant of Carthage. He fails and is executed.

summary: Hiero II of Syracuse was born.
text: Hiero II, Greek Sicilian tyrant and king of Syracuse

summary: Ophellas, governor of Cyrenaica, died after being betrayed and killed by Agathocles.
text: Ophellas, ruler of Cyrenaica (governor for Ptolemy).

summary: Upon becoming ruler of Epirus, Pyrrhus allied himself with Demetrius and Antigonus.
text: Upon becoming ruler of Epirus, Pyrrhus allies himself with his brother-in-law, Demetrius and through him with Antigonus.

summary: Agathocles surprised Utica and tied captured citizens to his siege engines when the city refused to surrender.
text: Agathocles, the tyrant of Syracuse, (who has been campaigning in North Africa for several years) launches a surprise attack on Utica. He captures around 300 citizens outside the walls and tries to negotiate a surrender of the city; Utica refuses. Agathocles then uses the prisoners as human shields by binding them to his siege engines.

summary: Agathocles assaulted and sacked Utica after breaching its defenses, leaving behind a garrison.
text: Agathocles assaults the walls of Utica. The Uticans, despite having to inflict death and injury on their fellow citizens, fiercely defend their city. Eventually, Agathocles' army is able to break into the city, they sacked the city and left behind a garrison.

summary: Agathocles captured Hippu Acra, prompting regional towns and Numidian tribes to join his side.
text: Agathocles besieges and takes a town called Hippu Acra. After capturing Hippu Acra several towns and cities come over to his side; even some Numidian tribes start sending their warriors to join Agathocles.

summary: Agathocles left Archagathus in charge of the African campaign and sailed with his fleet back to Sicily.
text: With his expeditionary army now superior in numbers to the Carthaginians, Agathocles decides to leave his son Archagathus in command of the African campaign and return to Sicily. He starts constructing transports and when enough ships have been built sets sail for Sicily.

summary: Archagathus dispatched Eumachus on two successful inland campaigns in North Africa, securing substantial war booty.
text: Archagathus sends Eumachus, one of his father's generals, on two successful inland campaigns. On both occasions Eumachus gained a lot of war booty.

summary: Carthage mustered thirty thousand soldiers and dispatched three separate armies across North Africa.
text: Carthage musters (30,000 soldiers in total) and sends out three armies; one inland, one into the midlands, and one against the cities along the coast.

summary: Carthaginian forces defeated the Greek detachments and blockaded Archagathus in Tunis.
text: Archagathus counters by dividing his army in three and sending them against the Carthaginian armies. Unfortunately for the Greeks, one army (commanded by Aeschrion) gets ambushed and another (commanded by Eumachus) is defeated in battle. Archagathus retreats to Tunis, regroups his army and sends messengers to his father in Sicily to inform him on the situation. The Carthaginians concentrate their forces at Tunis as well and start a blockade of the city.

summary: Agathocles returned to his army in Africa and suffered a costly defeat against the Carthaginians outside Tunis.
text: Agathocles returns to his expeditionary army. Trying to restore his army's moral, he fights a battle under less than ideal conditions and suffers a bloody defeat (losing 3,000 soldiers).

summary: A fire during a sacrificial ceremony caused panic in the Carthaginian camp, leading the army to flee back to Carthage.
text: During a victory ceremony involving human sacrifice (the Carthaginians sacrificed prisoners of war by burning them alive) the Carthaginian camp catches fire, in the ensuing panic the Carthaginian army breaks and flees back to Carthage.

summary: Five thousand fleeing Libyan deserters caused panic in Agathocles' camp, scattering the Greek army.
text: 5,000 Libyans deserters, who came fleeing back to Agathocles' camp, cause panic in the Greek camp, scattering the army.

summary: Agathocles decided to return to Sicily after his Libyan allies deserted and his forces fell into disarray.
text: After the lost battle and the night-time panic, all his Libyan allies desert. With his army in no condition to fight on, Agathocles decides to return to Sicily.

summary: Agathocles secretly abandoned his army and his sons in Africa and sailed back to Sicily, prompting his mutinous troops to murder his sons.
text: Agathocles abandons his army and his sons and secretly sails back to Sicily. His soldiers kill his sons in anger.

summary: Leptines and Demophilus defeated the Agrigentine general Xenodocus, forcing Acragas to abandon its war against Agathocles.
text: Xenodocus, a general from Acragas, leads an army of 10,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry against Agathocles' generals on Sicily. Leptines and Demophilus, two of Agathocles' generals, oppose Xenoducus with 8,200 infantry and 1,200 cavalry. Xenoducus is defeated and retreats to Acragas. As a result of this defeat the people of Acragas give up the fight against Agathocles.

summary: Agathocles landed at Selinus, forced Heraclea Minoa to submit, made a treaty with Therma, expelled its Carthaginian garrison, and seized Cephaloedium and Centuripa.
text: Agathocles puts in at Selinus, marches on Heraclea (probably Heraclea Minoa) and forces its people to submit once more. He then marches across the island on the city of Therma, makes a treaty with its people and removes its Carthaginian garrison. After taking Cephaloedium (near Therma), he marches back south taking the cities of Centuripa and Sicily.

summary: Deinocrates rallied the enemies of Agathocles into a large army and marched against him, compelling Agathocles to retreat to Syracuse.
text: Deinocrates, the leader of the exiles, proclaims himself the champion of common liberty and uses this to gather the bulk of Agathocles' enemies into one army. After mustering an army of 20,000 infantry and 1,500 cavalry, he marches on Agathocles, who refuses to do battle and retreats to Syracuse.

summary: Agathocles broke through the Carthaginian blockade off Syracuse with seventeen warships, defeating the opposing fleet to relieve his forces in Africa.
text: Receiving word of the losses that had been inflicted on his expeditionary army (commanded by his son Archagathus) in Africa, Agathocles equips 17 warships to go to his son's aid. While breaking through the Carthaginian blockade, he is able to defeat his opponents' fleet.

summary: Leptines defeated the Agrigentine general Xenodocus for the second time in Sicily.
text: Leptines, one of Agathocles' generals, defeats Xenodocus for the second time.

summary: Agathocles executed five hundred political opponents in Syracuse before setting sail for Africa.
text: Agathocles purges Syracuse of his opponents; 500 citizens are executed. With the city secure in his loyalty he sets sail for Africa.

summary: Agathocles returned to Sicily following his defeat in Africa and razed the city of Segesta to plunder its wealth.
text: After meeting disaster in Africa (losing his army and two of his sons), Agathocles returns to Sicily. In dire need of cash, he razes the city of Segesta.

summary: Archagathus, son of Agathocles of Syracuse, was killed by mutinous soldiers in North Africa.
text: Archagathus, son of Agathocles the tyrant of Syracuse.

summary: Heracleides, son of Agathocles of Syracuse, was killed by mutinous soldiers in North Africa.
text: Heracleides, son of Agathocles the tyrant of Syracuse.

summary: The Samnites captured the Roman-allied towns of Sora and Calatia and enslaved their inhabitants.
text: The Samnites take Sora and Calatia, cities allied to the Romans, and enslave their inhabitants.

summary: The Romans stormed the Samnite-held town of Silvium in Iapygia and subsequently ravaged Samnium for five months.
text: The Romans invade Iapygia and begin a siege of Silvium (garrisoned by the Samnites). Eventually, they take the city by storm, taking 5,000 prisoners. After the Siege of Silvium they invade Samnium itself, pillaging the countryside for five months.

summary: Agathocles attempted to negotiate a settlement with Deinocrates, who rejected the proposal and prolonged the war in eastern Sicily.
text: Agathocles tries to negotiate a settlement with Deinocrates, the leader of the exiles, but the latter refuses, forcing Agathocles to continue the war for dominance over eastern Sicily.

summary: Syracuse and Carthage concluded a peace treaty restricting Carthaginian authority in Sicily to the west of the Platani River.
text: A peace agreement is reached between Syracuse and Carthage. The peace restricts Carthaginian power in Sicily to the area west of the Halycus (Platani) River. This agreement allows the tyrant of Syracuse, Agathocles, to strengthen his rule over the Greek cities in the east of Sicily.

summary: The Hernici declared their independence from the Roman Republic.
text: The Hernici declared their independence from Rome.

summary: The Romans defeated the Paeligni, confiscated their land, and granted Roman citizenship to those deemed friendly to Rome.
text: The Romans defeat the Paeligni and take their land, some (those who look well disposed towards Rome) they grant citizenship.

summary: Roman consuls Marcus Fulvius Curvus Paetinus and Lucius Postumius Megellus decisively defeated the Samnites at the Battle of Bovianum, concluding the Second Samnite War.
text: The Roman consuls, Marcus Fulvius Curvus Paetinus and Lucius Postumius Megellus, decisively defeat the Samnites in the Battle of Bovianum to end the Second Samnite War.

summary: Agathocles defeated the larger army of Deinocrates and the Syracusan exiles at the Battle of Thorgium.
text: Agathocles, unable to come to terms with Deinocrates and the exiles, takes to the field with the remnants of his forces; at the Battle of Thorgium Agathocles defeats the much larger army of the exiles.

summary: Agathocles concluded an agreement with Deinocrates and appointed him a general over a detachment of his army.
text: Deinocrates comes to terms with Agathocles who appoints him a general over a part of his army.

summary: The Roman Republic concluded a peace agreement with the Samnites, formally ending the Second Samnite War and removing Samnite hegemony over Campania.
text: The second Samnite war formally ends with a peace agreement in which the Samnites obtain peace on terms that are severe but not as crushing as those agreed by the Romans with the Etruscans four years earlier. Under the peace, Rome gains no territory, but the Samnites renounce their hegemony over Campania. Rome is also successful in ending the revolts amongst the tribes surrounding Roman territory.

summary: Agathocles of Syracuse assumed the title of King of Sicily and expanded his influence into southern Italy.
text: The tyrant Agathocles of Syracuse takes on the title of King of Sicily. He extends his influence into southern Italy and the Adriatic.

summary: The Roman Republic conquered the Aequi.
text: Rome conquered the Aequi.

summary: Cleonymus of Sparta assisted Tarentum and pacified the Lucanians with the agreement of the Romans.
text: The citizens of Tarentum seek the help of the Spartan general, Cleonymus. He is able to pacify the Lucanians with the agreement of the Romans.

summary: The Lex Ogulnia was passed in Rome, opening priesthoods to plebeians.
text: The Lex Ogulnia was passed, allowing plebeians to become priests.

summary: Consul Marcus Fulvius Paetinus sacked the Umbrian city of Nequinum after a Roman siege.
text: The consul Marcus Fulvius Paetinus sacks the Umbrian city of Nequinum, which Rome had been besieging since the previous year, and he possibly also fights with success against the Sabines.

summary: Roman consul Titus Manlius Torquatus died.
text: Titus Manlius Torquatus, Roman consul

summary: Agathocles, king of Syracuse, assisted the Italiotes against the Bruttians and Romans.
text: Agathocles, king of Syracuse, assists the Italian Greeks against the Bruttians and supports the Greeks against the Romans.

summary: Ptolemy gave his stepdaughter Theoxena in marriage to Agathocles of Syracuse.
text: Ptolemy gives his stepdaughter Theoxena in marriage to Agathocles, the tyrant of Syracuse (in south-eastern Sicily).

summary: Rome declared war on the Samnites following an appeal from the Lucanians.
text: Samnite Wars: Rome declared war on the Samnites after an appeal by the Lucani.

summary: Rome captured the Samnite cities of Bojano and Castel di Sangro.
text: Samnite Wars: Rome captured the Samnite cities of Bojano and Castel di Sangro.

summary: Pyrrhus of Epirus was restored to his kingdom with Ptolemy's aid and subsequently assassinated his co-ruler Neoptolemus II.
text: Ptolemy decides to support Pyrrhus of Epirus and restores him to his kingdom. At first, Pyrrhus reigns with a kinsman, Neoptolemus II of Epirus (who is a son of Cleopatra of Macedonia and a nephew of Alexander the Great), but soon he has him assassinated.

summary: A Roman army defeated a numerically superior Samnite force at Città di Castello.
text: Battle of Tifernum: A Roman army defeated a numerically superior Samnite force at Città di Castello.

summary: The temple to Bellona was erected at the prata Flaminia in Rome.
text: The temple to Bellona is erected at the south end of the prata Flaminia, later the Circus Flaminius, in Rome.

summary: Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges dedicated the first Roman temple to Venus.
text: The first temple to Venus, the Roman goddess of love, beauty and fertility, is dedicated by Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges.

summary: Ptolemy, the son of King Pyrrhus of Epirus, was born.
text: Ptolemy, son of Pyrrhus of Epirus (d. 272 BC)

summary: Samnite military leader Gellius Egnatius was killed at the Battle of Sentinum.
text: Gellius Egnatius, Roman military leader of the Samnites

summary: Roman consul Publius Decius Mus was killed in the Battle of Sentinum.
text: Publius Decius Mus, Roman consul (killed in the Battle of Sentinum)

object: coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbri, and Senones
summary: A Roman army decisively defeated a coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbri, and Senones at Sentinum.
text: Battle of Sentinum: A Roman army decisively defeated a numerically superior force of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbri and Senones in coalition at Sentinum. The consul Publius Decius Mus (consul 312 BC) was killed.
names: coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbri, and Senones

object: Parauaea, Tymphaea, Acarnania, Amphilochia, and Ambracia
summary: Pyrrhus of Epirus took control of Parauaea, Tymphaea, Acarnania, Amphilochia, and Ambracia amid Macedonian dynastic conflicts.
text: Pyrrhus of Epirus exploits the dynastic quarrel in Macedonia involving Alexander V of Macedon, his brother, Antipater II and Demetrius Poliorcetes to take over the frontier areas of Parauaea and Tymphaea, along with Acarnania, Ampholochia, and Ambracia.
names: Parauaea, Tymphaea, Acarnania, Amphilochia, and Ambracia

summary: Roman and Samnite forces fought a battle at Lucera.
text: Samnite Wars: Roman and Samnite forces battled at Lucera.

summary: The Roman Republic introduced the worship of Aesculapius from Epidaurus to Rome to combat an ongoing plague.
text: The worship of Aesculapius is introduced from Epidaurus to Rome in the hope of ending a plague.

summary: A Roman army destroyed the majority of the Samnite forces at the Battle of Aquilonia.
text: Battle of Aquilonia: A Roman army destroyed the majority of Samnite forces, probably in modern Agnone.

summary: A Roman census recorded approximately 270,000 citizens in Rome.
text: A census counted about 270,000 residents of Rome.

summary: Samnite general Gaius Pontius died.
text: Gavius Pontius, Samnite general

summary: Rome conquered and established a Latin colony at the Samnite city of Venosa.
text: Samnite Wars: Rome conquered and colonized the Samnite city of Venosa.

summary: Lucius Caecilius Metellus, future Roman consul and Pontifex Maximus, was born.
text: Lucius Caecilius Metellus, Roman consul and Pontifex Maximus (d. 221 BC)

summary: The Roman Republic crushed the last effective Samnite resistance, bringing an end to the Third Samnite War.
text: Samnite Wars: The last effective Samnite resistance was eliminated.

summary: Agathocles of Syracuse died after restoring democracy on his deathbed, sparking succession disputes that renewed Carthaginian power in Sicily.
text: The tyrant of Syracuse, Agathocles, dies after restoring the Syracusan democracy on his death bed by stating that he does not want his sons to succeed him as king. However, the resulting dissension among his family about the succession leads to a renewal of Carthaginian power in Sicily.

summary: Agathocles, ruler and king of Syracuse, died.
text: Agathocles, tyrant of Syracuse, Sicily from 317 BC and self-styled king of Sicily after 304 BC (b. 361 BC)

summary: Disbanded mercenaries calling themselves Mamertines seized Messana following the death of Agathocles.
text: Following the death of Agathocles, some of his disbanded mercenaries seize Messana in northeast Sicily and set up a society, calling themselves Mamertines (Sons of Mars). The city becomes a base from which they will ravage the Sicilian countryside.

summary: Dictator Quintus Hortensius enacted the Lex Hortensia following a plebeian secession threat, making plebiscites binding on all citizens.
text: A new law, Lex Hortensia, gives much greater power to the ' (Plebeian Council) compared to the Senate. This law is passed following a threat from plebeian soldiers to secede. In the face of this threat, the Senate yields to plebeian concerns over their lack of political power and over their level of debt to the aristocracy. The law is named after Quintus Hortensius, a plebeian, who is made dictator to settle the controversy.

summary: The Lex Hortensia theoretically erased political distinctions between patricians and plebeians, though an oligarchic elite retained power.
text: With the Lex Hortensia in place, in theory the political distinctions in Rome between the patricians and the plebeians disappear. However, in practice, the coalition of leading plebeian families keep control which means that the patricians are able to largely nullify the power of the assemblies. So Roman government continues to be oligarchic in character.

summary: Pyrrhus of Epirus was proclaimed king of Macedonia.
text: Pyrrhus is proclaimed King of Macedonia.

summary: Archimedes was born in Syracuse.
text: Archimedes of Syracuse, Greek mathematician, physicist, engineer, astronomer and philosopher (d. c. 212 BC)

summary: The Roman plebeians seceded to the Janiculum in the final secessio plebis.
text: Conflict of the Orders: A secessio plebis took place.

summary: Lysimachus expelled Pyrrhus of Epirus from Macedonia and declared himself its king.
text: After allowing Pyrrhus of Epirus to remain in possession of Macedonia with the title of king, he is expelled by Lysimachus who declares himself its king in the place of Pyrrhus.

summary: The Roman Republic enacted the Lex Aquilia to compensate property owners for wrongful damage.
text: The new law, Lex Aquilia, is enacted. This is a Roman law which provides compensation to the owners of property injured as a result of someone's fault.

summary: The Senones defeated the Romans at the Battle of Arretium before being expelled from Italy by Manius Curius Dentatus.
text: The Gallic tribe called the Senones, who have settled on the Adriatic coast north of Picenum, attack Arretium in Etruria. While attempting to relieve this allied city, the Romans under the command of Lucius Caecilius Metellus Denter suffer a costly defeat in the Battle of Arretium. Aroused by this disaster, a Roman army under Manius Curius Dentatus invades the Senones' territory, defeating them and driving them out of the Italian peninsula.

summary: Roman consul Lucius Caecilius Metellus Denter was killed in the Battle of Arretium.
text: Lucius Caecilius Metellus Denter, Roman consul and general (killed in the Battle of Arretium) (b. c. 320 BC)

summary: Publius Cornelius Dolabella and Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus Maximus served as Roman consuls.
text: Consuls: Publius Cornelius Dolabella and Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus Maximus.

summary: Publius Cornelius Dolabella led Roman forces to defeat allied Etruscans and Gauls at the Battle of Lake Vadimo.
text: At the Battle of Lake Vadimo, Roman forces finally quell the allied Etruscans and Gauls. The Roman army is led by consul Publius Cornelius Dolabella. Rome is at last undisputed master of northern and central Italy.

summary: Rome defeated the Etruscans at the Battle of Populonia.
text: The Battle of Populonia is fought between Rome and the Etruscans. The Romans are victorious and, as a result, the Etruscan threat to Rome is sharply diminished.

summary: Tarentum attacked Roman ships and mistreated Roman envoys after Rome came to the aid of Thurii.
text: The Magna Graecia city of Thurii appeals to Rome for help against the native Italian tribes. Though the Roman Senate hesitates, the plebeian Assembly decides to respond. Thurii is saved, but Tarentum, jealous of Rome's interference, attacks and sinks some Roman ships entering its harbour. Roman envoys, sent to protest, are mistreated.

summary: Rome declared war on Tarentum, prompting King Pyrrhus of Epirus to offer assistance.
text: Rome declares war on Tarentum. King Pyrrhus of Epirus declares his willingness to come to the aid of Tarentum. Tarentum also looks for support from the Samnites and other Italian tribes in southern Italy.

summary: Cineas attempted without success to dissuade King Pyrrhus of Epirus from invading southern Italy.
text: Cineas, a Thessalian serving as chief adviser to King Pyrrhus of Epirus, after visiting Rome attempts, without success, to dissuade Pyrrhus from invading southern Italy.

summary: Taranto appealed to Epirus for military assistance against the Roman Republic.
text: Taranto appealed to Epirus for aid against Rome.

summary: Pyrrhus of Epirus formed an alliance with King Ptolemy Ceraunus of Macedon prior to invading southern Italy.
text: Pyrrhus makes an alliance with Ptolemy Keraunos, King of Macedon. This allows him to go to southern Italy with his army.

summary: King Pyrrhus of Epirus defeated the Roman army under consul Publius Valerius Laevinus at the Battle of Heraclea.
text: Responding to an appeal from Tarentum, King Pyrrhus of Epirus uses his army of over 20,000 men against the Romans. In the Battle of Heraclea he defeats a Roman army led by consul Publius Valerius Laevinus. Pyrrhus's judicious use of his elephants plays a large part in his victory. Several tribes including the Lucani, Bruttii and the Messapians as well as the Greek cities of Crotone and Locri join Pyrrhus.

summary: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus negotiated with King Pyrrhus of Epirus, who released Roman prisoners without ransom.
text: Roman commander and statesman, Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, is sent to negotiate the ransom and exchange of prisoners. Pyrrhus is so impressed by Fabricius refusing to accept a bribe, that Pyrrhus releases the prisoners without the requirement of a ransom. Following his victory, Pyrrhus advances as far north as Latium.

summary: An Epirote army of approximately 25,000 men landed at Taranto to begin the Pyrrhic War.
text: Pyrrhic War: An Epirote army of some 25,000 landed at Taranto.

summary: Carthage and the Roman Republic concluded a defensive alliance against King Pyrrhus of Epirus.
text: The Carthaginians and the Romans agree to support each other against a common foe. The Carthaginians give Rome money and ships in their fight against Pyrrhus, the king of Epirus.

summary: The Roman Republic rejected peace proposals delivered by Cineas on behalf of King Pyrrhus of Epirus.
text: Pyrrhus realizes that he cannot capture Rome and suggests peace terms to the Romans. Pyrrhus sends his chief advisor, Cineas, to Rome to negotiate a peace. Cineas demands that the Romans halt their aggression against the Greeks of southern Italy and restore the lands the Romans have taken from the Bruttii, the Apulians, and the Samnites. The Romans reject his demands, largely at the instigation of the former Roman censor, Appius Claudius Caecus.

summary: Pyrrhus of Epirus won a costly victory over the Roman forces of Publius Decius Mus at the Battle of Asculum.
text: In renewed fighting, Pyrrhus of Epirus, leading the combined Tarantine, Oscan, Samnite, and Greek forces, wins a 'Pyrrhic victory' against the Romans led by consul Publius Decius Mus at the Battle of Asculum, called such because his victory comes at a great cost to his own forces. Pyrrhus is reported to have said afterwards, "One more victory against the Romans and we shall be utterly ruined!" Disheartened, Pyrrhus retires to Tarentum and sends Cineas to make renewed peace overtures to Rome. These talks are inconclusive.

summary: Carthage intervened in Sicily and besieged Syracuse, prompting the Syracusans to summon Pyrrhus of Epirus for assistance.
text: The Carthaginians seize an opportunity to interfere in a quarrel between Syracuse and Agrigentum and besiege Syracuse. The Syracusans ask for help from Pyrrhus and Pyrrhus transfers his army there.

summary: Pyrrhus of Epirus defeated the Carthaginians across Sicily, capturing almost the entire island except Lilybaeum.
text: On his arrival in Sicily, Pyrrhus' forces win battles against the Carthaginians across Sicily. Pyrrhus conquers almost all of Sicily except for Lilybaeum (Marsala).

summary: Pyrrhus of Epirus was proclaimed king of Sicily and made plans for his sons to inherit his western domains.
text: Pyrrhus is proclaimed king of Sicily. He plans for his son Helenus to inherit the kingdom of Sicily and his other son Alexander to inherit Italy.

summary: Pyrrhus of Epirus captured the Carthaginian fortress of Eryx, prompting other Carthaginian-held cities in Sicily to defect to him.
text: Pyrrhus captures Eryx, the strongest Carthaginian fortress in Sicily. This prompts the rest of the Carthaginian-controlled cities in Sicily to defect to Pyrrhus.

summary: The Samnites defeated Roman forces at the Battle of the Cranita Hills during the Pyrrhic War.
text: Battle of the Cranita Hills: Roman forces are defeated by the Samnites at the Cranita Hills during the Pyrrhic War.

summary: Roman consul Publius Cornelius Rufinus campaigned against the Lucanians and Bruttians and captured Crotone.
text: Consul Publius Cornelius Rufinus campaigns against the Lucanians and the Bruttians and captures Crotone.

summary: Pyrrhus of Epirus abandoned Sicily and returned to mainland Italy after alienating the Sicilian Greeks and failing to conclude a treaty with Carthage.
text: Pyrrhus negotiates with the Carthaginians to end the fighting between them in Sicily. The Carthaginians are inclined to come to terms with Pyrrhus, but he demands that Carthage abandon all of Sicily and make the Libyan Sea the boundary between Carthage and the Greeks. Meanwhile, he begins to display despotic behaviour towards the Sicilian Greeks and soon Sicilian opinion moves against him. Therefore, fearing that his successes in Sicily may lead him to become the despot of their country, the Syracusans ask Pyrrhus to leave Sicily. He does so, and returns to the Italian mainland, noting that he expects Sicily to be a "fair wrestling ring" for Carthage and Rome.

summary: Roman forces under consul Manius Curius Dentatus fought Pyrrhus of Epirus at Beneventum, after which Pyrrhus negotiated peace and withdrew to Epirus.
text: When Pyrrhus returns from Sicily, he finds himself vastly outnumbered by a superior Roman army under the command of consul Manius Curius Dentatus. After the inconclusive Battle of Beneventum, Roman commander and statesman, Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, negotiates a peace with Pyrrhus, after which Pyrrhus decides to end his campaign in Italy and return to Epirus, which results in the loss of all his Italian holdings.

summary: The citizens and army of Syracuse appointed Hiero II as military commander following the departure of Pyrrhus.
text: Following the departure of Pyrrhus from Sicily, the Syracusan army and the city's citizens appoint Hiero II as the commander of their slaves. He strengthens his position by marrying the daughter of Leptines, the city's leading citizen.

summary: Carthaginian general and statesman Hamilcar Barca was born.
text: Hamilcar Barca, Carthaginian general, statesman and father of Hannibal

summary: Roman general and statesman Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus was born.
text: Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus, Roman dictator, politician and leader

summary: Pyrrhus of Epirus invaded Macedonia, defeated Antigonus II Gonatas at the Battle of the Aous, and was proclaimed King of Macedonia.
text: Pyrrhus returns from Italy and Sicily and invades Macedonia defeating Antigonus II Gonatas at the Battle of the Aous and conquering Upper Macedonia and Thessaly while Antigonus holds onto the coastal Macedonian towns. Antigonus' troops desert him and Pyrrhus is declared King of Macedonia.

summary: Roman forces under Manius Curius Dentatus conquered the Lucanians.
text: The Romans under Manius Curius Dentatus conquer the Lucanians.

summary: Ptolemy II Philadelphus of Egypt sent a diplomatic embassy to Rome following the Roman defeat of Pyrrhus.
text: Impressed by Rome's defeat of Pyrrhus of Epirus, Pharaoh Ptolemy II Philadelphus sends a friendly embassy. The visit is reciprocated.

summary: Roman statesman and former consul Appius Claudius Caecus died.
text: Appius Claudius Caecus, Roman politician and consul

summary: Tarentum made peace and surrendered to the Romans.
text: Tarentum, a Greek city in Italy, makes peace with the Romans.

summary: Rome built the Anio Vetus aqueduct leading to the Esquiline Hill.
text: Rome builds the aqueduct Anio Vetus on the Esquiline hill.

summary: The Romans finally conquered the Samnites and brought Magna Graecia under Roman domination following the surrender of Tarentum.
text: Pyrrhus' departure from southern Italy three years earlier leads to the Samnites finally being conquered by the Romans. With the surrender of Tarentum, the cities of Magna Graecia in southern Italy come under Roman influence and become Roman allies. Rome now effectively dominates all of the Italian peninsula.

summary: Pyrrhus invaded Laconia to attack Sparta on behalf of Cleonymus, but Spartan resistance and reinforcements forced him to break off the siege.
text: Cleonymus, a Spartan of royal blood who has been outcast by his fellow Spartans, asks the King of Macedonia and Epirus, Pyrrhus, to attack Sparta and place him in power. Pyrrhus agrees to the plan, but intends to win control of the Peloponnese for himself. As a large part of the Spartan army led by king Areus I is in Crete at the time, Pyrrhus has great hopes of taking the city easily, but the citizens organise stout resistance, allowing one of Antigonus II's commanders, Aminias the Phocian, to reach the city with a force of mercenaries from Corinth. Soon after this, the Spartan king, Areus, returns from Crete with 2,000 men. These reinforcements stiffen Spartan resistance and Pyrrhus, finding that he is losing men to desertion every day, breaks off the attack and starts to plunder the country.

summary: Pyrrhus was stunned by a thrown roof tile and killed in street fighting at Argos.
text: As they plunder the countryside, Pyrrhus and his troops move onto Argos. Entering the city with his army by stealth, Pyrrhus finds himself caught in a confused battle with the Argives (who are supported by Antigonus' forces and a detachment from Sparta) in the narrow city streets. During the confusion an old woman watching from a rooftop throws a roof tile at Pyrrhus which stuns him, allowing an Argive soldier to kill him.

summary: Alexander II succeeded his father Pyrrhus as king of Epirus while Antigonus II Gonatas recovered the Macedonian throne.
text: Following his death in Argos, Pyrrhus is succeeded as king of Epirus by his son Alexander II while Antigonus II Gonatas regains his Macedonian throne which he has lost to Pyrrhus two years earlier.

summary: Ptolemy, son of Pyrrhus of Epirus, was killed during the campaign against Sparta.
text: Ptolemy, son of Pyrrhus of Epirus (b. 295 BC)

summary: Pyrrhus of Epirus, king of Epirus and Macedon, died in Argos.
text: Pyrrhus of Epirus, king of the Molossians (from c. 297 BC), Epirus (306–301 and 297–272 BC) and Macedon (288–284 and 273–272 BC); involved in disputes in southern Italy against Rome and in Sicily (b. 318 BC)

summary: Pyrrhus withdrew with his army to Epirus, concluding his campaigns in southern Italy.
text: Pyrrhic War: Pyrrhus withdrew with his army to Epirus.

summary: Rome recaptured Rhegium from the Mamertines and defeated the Brutians, Lucanians, Calabrians, and Samnites, completing its subjugation of southern Italy.
text: Rome's subjugation of Italy is completed by the recapture of Rhegium (southern Italy) from the Mamertines and the defeat of the Brutians, the Lucanians, the Calabrians and the Samnites. The town of Rhegium is then restored by the Romans to its Greek inhabitants.

summary: Carthage, ruled by merchant oligarchs and suffetes, maintained control over Sardinia, southern Spain, and Numidia using mercenary forces.
text: Carthage, already in control of Sardinia, southern Spain and Numidia, is ruled by an oligarchy of merchants under two Suffetes or chief magistrates. While Carthage's military commanders are strong, the state relies on mercenaries (including Spanish ones) for its soldiers.

summary: Hamilcar Barca, Carthaginian general and father of Hannibal, was born.
text: Hamilcar Barca, founder of Barcid Spain and leading Carthaginian general who will fight against Rome in Sicily and Italy, against the Libyans and the mercenary revolt in Africa, and against the Iberians and Celti-Iberians in Spain (d. 228 BC)

summary: Roman epic poet and playwright Gnaeus Naevius was born.
text: Gnaeus Naevius, was a Roman epic poet and dramatist of the Old Latin period. (d. 201 BC)

summary: Roman military hero Marcus Valerius Corvus died.
text: Marcus Valerius Corvus, Roman hero (b. c. 370 BC)

summary: Roman consul and general Manius Curius Dentatus died.
text: Manius Curius Dentatus, Roman general, conqueror of the Samnites and victor against Pyrrhus, King of Epirus

summary: Hieron defeated the Mamertines at the Longanus River, but Carthaginian intervention prevented the capture of Messana, and Hieron was proclaimed tyrant of Syracuse.
text: The Mamertines, a body of Campanian mercenaries who have been employed by Agathocles, the former tyrant of Syracuse, capture the stronghold of Messana (Messina in north-eastern Sicily), from which they harass the Syracusans. The Syracusan military leader, Hieron, defeats them in a pitched battle at the Longanus River near Mylae, but Carthaginian forces intervene to prevent him from capturing Messana. His grateful countrymen then choose Hieron as their king and tyrant, to be known as Hieron II.

summary: The Romans founded a Latin colony at Malventum, renaming it Beneventum.
text: The Romans found a colony at Malventum which they, for superstitious reasons, call Beneventum (since male means bad and bene means good in Latin).

summary: The Romans founded a colony at Ariminum.
text: The Romans found a colony at Ariminum.

summary: The Roman Republic raised the number of quaestors from four to ten.
text: The number of quaestors was raised from four to ten.

summary: Marcus Atilius Regulus and Lucius Julius Libo celebrated triumphs over the Salentini in Rome.
text: Marcus Atilius Regulus and Lucius Julius Libo celebrate triumphs over the Salentini.

summary: The Roman Republic annexed Calabria and Messapia.
text: Calabria and Messapia are annexed by the Roman Republic.

summary: Caparronia, a Roman Vestal virgin, died by hanging after being convicted of unchastity.
text: Caparronia, an ancient Roman Vestal virgin died by hanging after being convicted of unchastity.

summary: The Mamertines appealed to Carthage and Rome for protection against Hiero II of Syracuse.
text: Hiero II threatens to renew his attack on the Mamertines. They appeal to Carthage and receive the support of a Carthaginian garrison. The Mamertines also appeal to the Romans who are also willing to help.

summary: Roman and Carthaginian forces clashed in the Battle of Messana.
text: The Battle of Messana (265-264 BCE) takes place as the first military clash between the Roman Republic and Carthage.

summary: Roman forces captured the Etruscan city of Volsinii during a siege that claimed the life of consul Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges.
text: The Etruscan city of Volsinii is brought under Roman control. During a siege, the consul Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges is killed.

summary: Roman consul Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges was killed during the siege of Volsinii.
text: Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges, Roman consul

summary: Rome concluded an alliance with the Mamertines of Messina, initiating the First Punic War against Carthage.
text: The tyrant of Syracuse, Hiero II, once more attacks the Mamertines. They ally themselves with a nearby Carthaginian fleet and hold off the Syracusans. However, when the Carthaginians do not leave, the Mamertines appeal to Rome for an alliance, hoping for more reliable protection. Although initially reluctant to assist, lest it encourage other mercenary groups to mutiny, Rome is unwilling to see Carthaginian power spread further over Sicily and encroach on Italy. Rome therefore enters into an alliance with the Mamertines. By this action, the First Punic War begins and will embroil Rome in a conflict with Carthage that will continue for 23 years.

summary: Appius Claudius Caudex deployed Roman legions to Sicily in Rome's first military operation outside peninsular Italy.
text: The Roman consul Appius Claudius Caudex and his two legions are deployed to Sicily, the first time a Roman army has gone into action outside the Italian peninsula.

summary: Appius Claudius Caudex occupied Messina after receiving the city from the Mamertines.
text: Appius Claudius Caudex leads his forces to Messina, and as the Mamertines have convinced the Carthaginians to withdraw, he meets with only minimal resistance. The Mamertines hand the city over to Appius Claudius, but the Carthaginians return to set up a blockade. The Syracusans, meanwhile, are also stationed outside the city.

summary: Appius Claudius Caudex defeated Syracusan and Carthaginian forces outside Messina.
text: Appius Claudius leads his troops outside the city of Messina to defeat the Syracusans in battle forcing Hiero to retreat back to Syracuse. The next day Claudius defeats the Carthaginians.

summary: A temple to Vertumnus was erected on the Aventine Hill in Rome.
text: The temple to Vertumnus is built on the Aventine Hill in Rome.

summary: Three pairs of gladiators fought in the first recorded Roman gladiatorial combat at the funeral games of Junius Brutus Pera.
text: Three pairs of gladiators face off in the first recorded gladiatorial combat, held at the funeral games in honour of aristocrat Junius Brutus Pera in the Forum Boarium.

summary: Manius Valerius Messalla secured a treaty of alliance between Rome and Hiero II of Syracuse.
text: The Romans under the consul Manius Valerius Messalla secure the alliance of Hiero II of Syracuse. The treaty with Rome restricts Hiero's kingdom to southeast Sicily and the eastern coast of Sicily as far as Tauromenium. From this date until his death, Hiero remains loyal to the Romans.

summary: Roman forces under Manius Valerius Messalla captured Catania and took a sundial to Rome.
text: The Romans capture Catania in Sicily under Messalla. A sundial is part of the booty, which is placed in the Comitium in Rome and will be significant in Roman timekeeping.

summary: The Roman Republic defeated a Carthaginian relief force and captured Agrigentum after a prolonged siege.
text: Rome besieges the city of Agrigentum which is held by Carthage under the command of Hannibal Gisco. Rome's siege involves both consular armies – a total of four Roman legions – and takes several months to resolve. The garrison of Agrigentum manages to call for reinforcements and a Carthaginian relief force commanded by Hanno comes to the rescue and destroys the Roman supply base at Erbessus. Nevertheless, after a few skirmishes, the battle of Agrigentum is fought and won by Rome, and the city falls. Gisco manages to escape to Carthage in the late stages of the battle.

summary: Roman forces sacked Agrigentum and enslaved its Greek inhabitants.
text: After the loss of Agrigentum, the Carthaginians retire to organise their fleet. In the meantime, the Romans sack Agrigentum and enslave its Greek inhabitants. The Romans are now determined to drive the Carthaginians out of Sicily.

summary: The Romans built a naval fleet modelled after a captured Carthaginian quinquereme to challenge Carthage for Sicily.
text: The Romans, determined to win control of Sicily from Carthage, build a fleet based on the model of a captured Carthaginian quinquereme.

summary: Roman forces relieved the besieged Sicilian cities of Segesta and Macella from Carthaginian attacks.
text: The Roman advance continues westward from Agrigentum with their forces relieving the besieged cities of Segesta and Macella. These cities have sided with the Roman cause, and have come under Carthaginian attack for doing so.

summary: Hannibal Gisco defeated a Roman naval detachment and captured consul Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Asina near Lipari.
text: Hannibal Gisco returns to fight in Sicily as the admiral in charge of the Carthaginian fleet in the Strait of Messina. With the Romans about to launch their first ever navy, Carthage is determined that this innovation be thwarted. Gisco defeats part of the Roman fleet and captures the Roman consul Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Asina in an encounter near Lipari; the consul's nickname Asina (which means donkey) is earned in this encounter. However, this Carthaginian victory is of limited practical value as the bulk of the Roman fleet continues to manoeuvre in the surrounding waters.

summary: Roman consul Gaius Duilius heavily defeated the Carthaginian fleet under Hannibal Gisco at the Battle of Mylae.
text: Confident in Carthage's superiority at sea, Hannibal Gisco deploys his ships for the Battle of Mylae in the traditional long line arrangement. Although inexperienced in sea battles, the Romans, led by consul Gaius Duilius Nepos, heavily defeat the Carthaginian fleet, mainly due to the innovative use of land tactics in naval warfare (including the use of the grappling irons and the corvus boarding bridge).

summary: Carthage executed Hannibal Gisco and other commanders for incompetence after their naval defeats.
text: Having lost the confidence of his peers, Hannibal Gisco is subsequently executed for incompetence shortly afterwards, together with other defeated Punic generals.

summary: Carthaginian forces under Hamilcar defeated advancing Roman troops at Thermae in northern Sicily.
text: In the north of Sicily, the Romans, with their northern sea flank secured by their naval victory in the Battle of Mylae, advance toward Thermae. They are defeated there by the Carthaginians under Hamilcar.

summary: Carthaginian commander Hannibal Gisco was executed following his defeat at Mylae.
text: Hannibal Gisco, Carthaginian military commander in charge of both land armies and naval fleets (b. c. 300 BC)

summary: Carthaginian forces under Hamilcar counterattacked Roman positions in Sicily, capturing Enna and advancing toward Camarina.
text: The Carthaginians under Hamilcar take advantage of their victory at Thermae in Sicily by counterattacking the Romans and seizing Enna. Hamilcar continues south to Camarina, in Syracusan territory, to try to convince the Syracusans to rejoin the Carthaginian side.

summary: The Romans regained the initiative in Sicily by retaking Enna and Camarina and capturing Mytistraton, but were halted at Panormus.
text: The Romans are able to regain the initiative in Sicily against Carthage by retaking Enna and Camarina. In central Sicily, they take the town of Mytistraton, which they have attacked twice previously. The Romans also move in the north by marching across the northern coast toward Panormus, but are not able to take the city due to the city's heavily fortified walls.

summary: Gaius Duilius was elected Roman censor alongside Lucius Cornelius Scipio.
text: Gaius Duilius Nepos, the Roman commander who has won a major naval victory over the Carthaginians is made censor with Lucius Cornelius Scipio. The election of a novus homo (i.e. the first in his family to serve in the Roman Senate or be elected as consul) to the censorship is a very rare honor.

summary: The Roman Republic attacked Sardinia in an attempt to capture it from Carthage.
text: The Romans attack Sardinia and try to capture it from the Carthaginians.

summary: Roman naval forces defeated the Carthaginian fleet at the Battle of Tyndaris and captured the town.
text: The Battle of Tyndaris is fought between the Roman fleet (with Gaius Atilius Regulus in command) and the Carthaginian fleet off Tyndaris (modern Tindari) in Sicily. Hiero II, tyrant of Syracuse, has allowed Tyndaris to be a base for the Carthaginians. However, after this battle, the town falls to Roman forces.

summary: Roman consuls Marcus Atilius Regulus and Lucius Manlius Vulso Longus defeated the Carthaginian fleet at the Battle of Cape Ecnomus.
text: Rome aims for a quick end to hostilities in the First Punic War and decides to invade the Carthaginian colonies in Northern Africa to force the enemy to accept terms. A major fleet is built, including transports for the army and its equipment, and warships for their protection. Carthage under Hamilcar tries to intervene but a force under the Roman general and consul Marcus Atilius Regulus and his colleague Lucius Manlius Vulso Longus defeat the Carthaginian fleet in the Battle of Cape Ecnomus off the southern coast of Sicily.

summary: The Roman army landed in North Africa and forced the capitulation of Clupea.
text: Following the Battle of Cape Ecnomus, the Romans land an army near Carthage (Tunesia, North Africa) and begin ravaging the Carthaginian countryside. The Roman army soon forces the capitulation of Clupea, a town east of Carthage. After setting up Roman defenses for the city, the two consuls receive instructions from Rome that Vulso is to set sail for Rome, taking most of the fleet with him. Regulus, on the other hand, is to stay with the infantry and cavalry to finish the war.

summary: Marcus Atilius Regulus captured Aspis after a short siege.
text: Marcus Atilius Regulus marches to Aspis and takes the town after a short siege.

summary: Roman forces defeated the Carthaginian army at the Battle of Adys.
text: From their new base at Aspis the Romans march on towards Carthage; they encounter and defeat the Carthaginian army at the Battle of Adys.

summary: Marcus Atilius Regulus defeated the Carthaginians at Adys, but Carthage rejected his harsh peace terms.
text: The Battle of Adis (or Adys) is fought near the city of that name, southeast of Carthage, between Carthaginian forces and a Roman army led by Marcus Atilius Regulus. The Romans inflict a crushing defeat upon the Carthaginians, and the latter then sue for peace. The ensuing negotiations between the parties lead to Regulus demanding Carthage agree to an unconditional surrender, cede Sicily, Corsica and Sardinia to Rome, renounce the use of their navy, pay an indemnity, and sign a vassal-like treaty. These terms are so harsh that the people of Carthage resolve to keep fighting.

summary: Carthaginian forces led by Xanthippus decisively defeated the Romans at the Battle of Tunis and captured Marcus Atilius Regulus.
text: The Carthaginians, angered by Regulus' demands, hire Xanthippus, a Spartan mercenary, to reorganize the army. The revitalised Carthaginian army, led by Xanthippus, decisively defeat the Romans in the Battle of Tunis and capture their commander Marcus Atilius Regulus. A Roman fleet, sent to rescue Regulus and his troops, is wrecked in a storm off Sicily.

place.title: Battle of the Bagradas River (255 BC)

names: Battle of the Bagradas River (255 BC)
Sinking of the Roman fleet (255 BC)

summary: Consuls Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Asina and Aulus Atilius Calatinus captured Panormus.
text: A Roman army led by consuls Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Asina and Aulus Atilius Calatinus capture Panormus in Sicily.

summary: Carthage regained control of the Sicilian city of Agrigentum from the Romans.
text: The Romans lose control of the Sicilian city of Agrigentum to the Carthaginians.

summary: Roman commander Marcus Livius Salinator was born.
text: Marcus Livius Salinator, Roman consul and commander during the Second Punic War

summary: Roman playwright Plautus was born in Sarsina.
text: Titus Macchius Plautus, Roman playwright who is credited with forming the foundations of modern comedy (d. 184 BC)

summary: A Roman war fleet was wrecked in a storm on the voyage from Lilybaeum to Rome.
text: A second Roman war fleet of 150 ships is wrecked on the voyage from Lilybaeum (in Sicily) to Rome.

summary: Tiberius Coruncanius became the first plebeian elected pontifex maximus of Rome.
text: Tiberius Coruncanius is the first plebeian to be elected pontifex maximus of Rome.

summary: Roman forces under Lucius Caecilius Metellus defeated the Carthaginians at the Battle of Panormus and captured the city.
text: The Romans, led by Lucius Caecilius Metellus, attack the Carthaginian held port city of Panormus after taking Kephalodon. After fierce fighting in the Battle of Panormus, the Carthaginians, led by Hasdrubal (the Fair), are defeated and the city falls.

summary: Much of western inland Sicily submitted to the Roman Republic following the fall of Panormus, effectively ending major Carthaginian land campaigns on the island.
text: With Panormus captured, much of western inland Sicily falls with it. The cities of Ieta, Solous, Petra and Tyndaris agree to peace with the Romans in the same year. This defeat marks the end of significant Carthaginian land-based campaigning in Sicily.

summary: The Roman Republic burned Selinous and Heraclea Minoa and began the siege of Lilybaeum.
text: In the Punic War, the Romans shift their attention to the southwest of Sicily. They send a naval expedition toward the Carthaginian city of Lilybaeum. En route, the Romans seize and burn the Carthaginian held cities of Selinous and Heraclea Minoa. The Romans then begin the siege of Lilybaeum.

summary: Marcus Atilius Regulus urged the Roman Senate to reject Carthaginian peace terms before returning to Carthage to face execution.
text: According to tradition (Horace, Odes, iii. 5), after the defeat of the Carthaginians at the Battle of Panormus, the Carthaginians release Marcus Atilius Regulus from prison and he is sent to Rome on parole to negotiate a peace or an exchange of prisoners. However, on his arrival, he strongly urges the Roman Senate to refuse both proposals and continue fighting. After this he then honours his parole by returning to Carthage where he is executed by being placed in a spiked barrel, which is then let roll down a hill.

summary: Agron, future king of the Ardiaean Kingdom in Illyria, was born.
text: Agron, king of the Ardiaean Kingdom

summary: Roman general and former consul Marcus Atilius Regulus was executed in Carthage.
text: Marcus Atilius Regulus, Roman general and consul (executed)

summary: Greek historian Timaeus died in Syracuse.
text: Timaeus, Greek historian who has studied rhetoric under a pupil of Socrates (b. c. 345 BC)

summary: Carthaginian naval forces under Adherbal severely defeated the Roman fleet under Publius Claudius Pulcher at the Battle of Drepana.
text: The Battle of Drepana involves the Romans, under the command of the Roman consul Publius Claudius Pulcher, attacking the Carthaginian fleet, under the command of Adherbal, in the harbour of Drepanum (modern Trapani, Sicily). The Romans are badly defeated and lose 93 of their 123 vessels.

summary: The Roman Republic appointed Aulus Atilius Caiatinus dictator, relieved Lilybaeum, and captured Eryx.
text: Following the disastrous defeat of Roman forces at the Battle of Drepana, Publius Claudius Pulcher is fined 120,000 asses and his colleague, Lucius Junius Pullus, commits suicide. Aulus Atilius Calatinus is then elected dictator and leads an army into Sicily, becoming the first dictator to lead a Roman army outside Italy. The Roman forces at Lilybaeum are relieved, and Eryx, near Drapana, is seized. Its idol of Astarte is transported to Rome, where it becomes the Erycine Venus.

summary: Carthaginian general Hanno conquered Theveste and settled peace terms concluding the war with the Numidians.
text: In Numidia Carthaginian general Hanno conquered the city of Theveste (nicknamed: Hekatompylos) after which he negotiated a peace settlement with the Numidians ending Carthage's war with the Numidians. He was praised by both parties for the fairness of the treaty.

summary: Hamilcar Barca took command of Carthaginian forces in Sicily, secured Mount Ercte near Palermo, and launched raids against southern Italy.
text: By this stage in the Punic War, Carthage has lost to Rome all its Sicilian possessions except Lilybaeum (now Marsala) and Drepanum (now Trapani). In the winter of 248/7, Hamilcar Barca takes over the chief command of the Carthaginian forces in Sicily at a time when the island is almost completely in the hands of the Romans. Landing on the north-west of the island with a small mercenary force, he seizes a strong position on Mount Ercte (Monte Pellegrino, near Palermo), and not only successfully defends himself against all attacks, but also carries his raids as far as the coast of southern Italy.

summary: Hannibal Barca was born in Carthage.
text: Hannibal Barca, Carthaginian military commander (d. c. 183 BC)

summary: Ptolemy III succeeded his father Ptolemy II as ruler of Egypt.
text: Egypt's Ptolemy II dies and is succeeded by his son, Ptolemy III. At the time of Ptolemy II's death, Egypt comprises the ancient kingdom of Egypt in the Nile Valley, Cyrene, Judea and the coast of southern Syria, Cyprus and a number of cities on the shores and islands of the Aegean Sea. The Macedonian Ptolemies maintain their authority over their territories with a small mercenary army made up of Macedonians and other Greeks.

summary: Ptolemy III invaded Syria to avenge his sister's murder, initiating the Third Syrian War.
text: Berenice's brother, Ptolemy III, sets about to avenge his sister's murder by invading Syria which begins the Third Syrian War (also known as the Laodicean War). Ptolemy III's navy, perhaps with the aid of rebels in the cities, advances against Seleucus II's forces as far as Thrace, across the Hellespont, and also captures some islands off the Anatolian coast.

summary: Ptolemy III defeated Seleucus II across Syria and Anatolia and briefly occupied Antioch.
text: Ptolemy III wins major victories over Seleucus II in Syria and Anatolia and briefly occupies Antioch. These victories are marred by the loss of the Cyclades to Antigonus II Gonatas in the Battle of Andros.

summary: The Roman Republic funded a new fleet by private subscription to contest Carthaginian naval dominance.
text: With Hamilcar Barca wearing the Romans down in Sicily, the Romans, by private subscription, build another fleet with the aim of regaining command of the sea.

summary: The Roman Republic increased the number of praetors from one to two to handle foreign legal affairs and military commands.
text: In Rome, the number of praetors is increased from one to two. The second praetor is appointed to relieve the backlog of judicial business and to give the Republic a magistrate with Imperium who can field an army in an emergency when both consuls are away fighting a war.

summary: Claudia was convicted of treason in Rome and fined.
text: Claudia is convicted of treason and forced to pay a fine.

summary: Arsinoe III was born in Egypt to Ptolemy III and Berenice II.
text: Arsinoe III, queen of Egypt from 220 BC, daughter of Ptolemy III and Berenice II (d. 204 BC)

summary: Ptolemy II Philadelphus died in Alexandria.
text: Ptolemy II Philadelphus, king of Egypt from 285 BC, second king of the Ptolemaic dynasty, who has extended his power by skillful diplomacy, developed agriculture and commerce, and made Alexandria a leading centre of the arts and sciences (b. 308 BC)

summary: Ptolemy III captured the cities of Babylon and Susa from the Seleucid Empire.
text: Babylon and Susa fall to the Ptolemaic armies of Ptolemy III.

summary: Ptolemy III married Berenice II of Cyrene, reuniting Egypt and Cyrenaica.
text: Following a long engagement, Ptolemy III marries Berenice II, the daughter of Magas, king of Cyrene; thereby reuniting Egypt and Cyrenaica.

summary: Callimachus produced the Pinakes, a bibliographic catalogue for the Library of Alexandria.
text: Approximate date – Callimachus produces the Pinakes, a subject index to the Library of Alexandria.

summary: Hasdrubal Barca was born in Carthage.
text: Hasdrubal Barca, Carthaginian general and Younger brother of Hannibal (d. 207 BC)

summary: The Achaean League allied with Ptolemy III against the Seleucid Empire during the Third Syrian War.
text: The war in Asia Minor and the Aegean Sea intensifies as the Achaean League allies itself to Ptolemy III Euergetes of Egypt, while Seleucus II secures two allies in the Black Sea region. Ptolemy III's armies reach as far as Bactria and the borders of India in their attacks on the Seleucid Empire.

summary: Antigonus II defeated the Egyptian navy at Andros, maintaining his naval hegemony in the Aegean Sea.
text: By defeating the Egyptian fleet at Andros, Antigonus II is able to maintain his control over the Aegean Sea.

summary: Hamilcar Barca shifted his army to Mount Eryx to support the besieged garrison at Drepanum.
text: Hamilcar Barca transfers his army to the slopes of Mount Eryx, from which he is able to lend support to the besieged garrison in the neighbouring town of Drepanum (Trapani).

summary: Carthaginian general Mago Barca, brother of Hannibal, was born.
text: Mago Barca, Carthaginian general and brother of Hannibal (d. 203 BC)

summary: Roman consul Gaius Lutatius Catulus blockaded the Sicilian strongholds of Lilybaeum and Drepanum with a fleet of two hundred ships.
text: The Roman consul and commander, Gaius Lutatius Catulus, blockades the Sicilian cities of Lilybaeum and Drepanum with a fleet of 200 ships.

summary: The Roman Republic created the magistracy of the praetor peregrinus to administer justice in disputes involving non-citizens.
text: The office of the praetor qui inter peregrinos ius dicit, a Praetor with jurisdiction over foreigners, was created.

summary: The Roman fleet commanded by Gaius Lutatius Catulus decisively defeated the Carthaginian fleet at the Battle of the Aegates.
text: Battle of the Aegates: The Carthaginian fleet sent to relieve the Roman blockade of the Sicilian cities of Lilybaeum and Drepanum is totally defeated near the Aegates Islands off western Sicily by the Roman fleet led by Roman consul and commander Gaius Lutatius Catulus.
