The result is a decisive Roman victory which forces an end to the protracted First Punic War, to Rome's distinct advantage.

summary: Carthage accepted the Treaty of Lutatius, evacuating Sicily, paying Rome an indemnity of 3,200 talents, and agreeing to keep warships out of Italian waters.
text: The Carthaginians under Hamilcar Barca are forced to accept severe peace terms and agree to evacuate Sicily. As part of the treaty with Rome, Carthage agrees to abandon all its claims on Sicily, to refrain from sailing her warships in Italian waters and to pay an indemnity of 3,200 talents. However, the Carthaginian army is allowed to return home with its arms. Rome is now the dominant power in the Western Mediterranean basin.

summary: The Roman Republic crushed the revolt of the Falisci, destroyed Falerii Veteres, and relocated the survivors to Falerii Novi.
text: The Falisci people of Falerii Veteres revolt against Rome, but is crushed in six days. Falerii Veteres is destroyed and the people resettled to the less defensible Falerii Novi.

summary: Unpaid mercenaries transported from Sicily rejected Hanno the Great's reduced payment offers and occupied Tunis, threatening Carthage directly.
text: A mercenary army of some 20,000 is transported from Sicily to Carthaginian territory, by Carthaginian commander, Gisco. Upon arrival in Carthaginian territory, the mercenaries submit a demand to Hanno the Great for payment of their contracts. Hanno attempts, unsuccessfully, to convince the mercenaries to accept smaller payments due to Carthage's impoverished post-war conditions. Negotiations break down. The mercenaries take up arms, march on Tunis, occupy it, and threaten Carthage directly.

summary: Mercenaries at Tunis captured Carthaginian negotiator Gisco after negotiations broke down, triggering the Mercenary War.
text: Given their strong position, the mercenaries inflate their demands and request payment for the non-mercenary Libyan conscripts in the army as well. Gesco is sent to negotiate with the mercenaries at Tunis. Negotiations break down, Gisco is captured, and the Mercenary War commences.

summary: Former Roman consul and commander Tiberius Coruncanius died.
text: Tiberius Coruncanius, Roman consul and military commander for the battles against Pyrrhus of Epirus

summary: The Roman Republic organized Sicily as the province of Sicilia following the First Punic War.
text: First Punic War: Sicily was organized as the province of Sicilia.

summary: Spendius and Mathos led the Libyan troops and mercenaries at Tunis into a general rebellion against Carthage, taking Gisco hostage.
text: Two of Carthage's mercenary commanders – Spendius and Mathos – convince the Libyan conscripts of the mercenary army occupying the Carthaginian city of Tunis to accept their leadership. They persuade the native Libyans that Carthage will take revenge against them for their part in the conflict once the foreign mercenaries are paid and sent home. They then convince the combined mercenary armies to revolt against Carthage and convince the various native Libyan towns and cities to back the revolt. Spendius and Mathos then take the Carthaginian commander Gesco as a hostage. What has started as an argument over pay owed to soldiers by the Carthaginian Government, explodes into a full-scale revolt, known as the Mercenary War.

summary: Rebel forces loyal to the mercenaries besieged Utica and Hippacritae after both cities refused to defect from Carthage.
text: The Libyan forces loyal to the mercenaries besiege the towns of Utica and Hippacritae, which refuse to defect to the mercenaries.

summary: Mercenary forces defeated a Carthaginian army commanded by Hanno the Great at the Battle of Utica.
text: Hanno the Great is given command of the Carthaginian forces. However, the mercenaries defeat the Carthaginian armies in the Battle of Utica.

summary: Hamilcar Barca ended the mercenary siege of Utica and defeated the rebel mercenary forces at the Battle of the Bagradas River.
text: Carthage decides to give Hamilcar Barca joint command with Hanno the Great. Hamilcar Barca is able to end the siege of Utica by the mercenaries. He is then placed in complete command of the Carthaginian forces and defeats the mercenaries in the Battle of the Bagradas River.

place.title: Battle of the Bagradas River (240 BC)

names: Battle of the Bagradas River (240 BC)

summary: Reinforced by the defecting Numidian leader Narawas, Hamilcar Barca defeated the mercenaries again and pardoned prisoners willing to serve Carthage.
text: After the Numidian mercenary leader Narawas defects to Hamilcar Barca, Numidian reinforcements (about 2,000 men) help him defeat the mercenaries again. Hamilcar pardons his captured prisoners, accepting into his army anyone who will fight for Carthage, and exiling anyone who will not.

summary: Rome assumed full control of Sicily and permanently stationed a Roman legion on the island.
text: Rome takes over full control of Sicily and stations a legion there.

summary: Livius Andronicus staged the first Latin tragedy, Achilles, in Rome.
text: The first Latin tragedy by Livius Andronicus, Achilles, is first produced.

summary: Mathos and Spendius ordered the mutilation and execution of about seven hundred Carthaginian prisoners, including Gesco, to bind the rebel mercenaries together.
text: Concerned that Hamilcar Barca's leniency in pardoning those who he has captured who have participated in the Mercenary War will encourage others to defect, Mathos and Spendius order the mutilation and execution of "about seven hundred" Carthaginian prisoners, including Gesco. With the mercenaries jointly guilty of these atrocities, defectors dare not face Carthaginian justice under Hamilcar.

summary: Besieged by mercenaries while Utica revolted, Carthage appealed to Rome and Hiero II of Syracuse for aid.
text: Carthage is besieged by the mercenary armies, while the city of Utica revolts and attempts to secede from Carthage. Carthage appeals to Hiero II of Syracuse and to Rome for aid against the mercenaries. However, the mercenary leaders reject the efforts of Roman mediators.

summary: Rome took advantage of an anti-Carthaginian revolt by mercenaries to annex Sardinia.
text: Sardinia revolts against Carthage and Rome takes the opportunity to annex the island.

summary: Quintus Ennius, the father of Roman poetry, was born in Rudiae.
text: Quintus Ennius, Latin poet and writer, considered the father of Roman poetry

summary: Rome seized Corsica and Sardinia.
text: Rome captures Corsica and Sardinia

summary: Hamilcar Barca severed the supply lines of the mercenary army besieging Carthage and trapped them in the Battle of the Saw.
text: Hamilcar Barca strikes at the supply lines of the mercenary army besieging Carthage, forcing them to cease the siege of the city. He then fights a series of running engagements with the mercenary armies, keeping them off balance. Hamilcar manages to force the mercenary armies into a box canyon in the Battle of "The Saw". The mercenaries are besieged in the canyon.

summary: Hamilcar Barca defeated the mercenary breakout force under Spendius at the Battle of the Saw and executed roughly forty thousand prisoners.
text: The mercenary army, under the leadership of Spendius, attempts to fight its way out of the siege but is totally defeated by the Carthaginian forces led by Hamilcar Barca. After the battle, Hamilcar executes some 40,000 rebel mercenaries.

summary: Hamilcar Barca captured several rebel Libyan cities, prompting most Libyan settlements except Utica and Hippacritae to surrender to Carthage.
text: Hamilcar's armies capture a number of rebel Libyan cities. The Libyan settlements that have rebelled surrender to Carthage, with the exception of Utica and Hippacritae.

summary: Hamilcar Barca and Hannibal besieged Mathos at Tunis and crucified captured mercenary leaders in view of the city.
text: Hamilcar and another Carthaginian general, Hannibal, besiege Mathos' mercenary army at Tunis and crucify the captured mercenary leaders in sight of the mercenary battlements.

summary: Mathos assaulted Hannibal's camp outside Tunis, capturing and crucifying Hannibal along with several high-ranking Carthaginians.
text: Mathos exploits a weakness in Hannibal's defenses and launches an attack against his army, capturing Hannibal and several other high ranking Carthaginians. The mercenaries then crucify the captured Carthaginian leaders.

summary: Hanno the Great reinforced Carthaginian forces to defeat the rebel army and capture Mathos.
text: Carthaginian reinforcements led by Hanno the Great join the battle. They defeat Mathos' mercenary forces and Mathos is captured.

summary: Carthaginian armies besieged and captured Utica and Hippacritae, ending the Mercenary War.
text: The Carthaginian armies besiege and capture Utica and Hippacritae. This ends the Carthaginian civil war.

summary: Rome declared war on Carthage over Sardinia, compelling Carthage to surrender all claims to the island.
text: The Romans declare war on the Carthaginians over which state controls Sardinia. However, Carthage defers to Rome rather than enter yet another war and gives up any claim to Sardinia.

summary: Masinissa, the future king of Numidia, was born.
text: Masinissa, king of Numidia

summary: Philip V, future king of Macedonia, was born.
text: Philip V, king (basileus) of Macedonia (d. 179 BC)

summary: Autaritus, a Gallic mercenary leader, died.
text: Autaritus, Gallic mercenary leader

summary: Hannibal, a Carthaginian general in the Mercenary War, died.
text: Hannibal, Carthaginian general

summary: Hanno the Great opposed Hamilcar Barca's proposed Carthaginian conquest of the Iberian Peninsula.
text: Hamilcar Barca's success in defeating the rebels results in a growth in his strength as leader of Carthage's popular party and support for his proposed invasion of the Iberian Peninsula. However, as spokesman for the landed nobility, Hanno opposes the policy of foreign conquest pursued by Hamilcar Barca.

summary: Hamilcar Barca led a Carthaginian invasion of the Iberian Peninsula to build a base for future conflict with Rome.
text: Nevertheless, Hamilcar Barca leads a Carthaginian army in an invasion of the Iberian Peninsula with the aim of building a base from which war with Rome can be renewed. By skillful generalship and able diplomacy, Hamilcar extends Carthaginian dominion over many Spanish tribes.

summary: Istolatios, warlord of the Turdetani, was crucified by Hamilcar Barca.
text: Istolatios, warlord of the Turdetani (Iberian Peninsula), crucified by Hamilcar Barca (father of Hannibal)

summary: King Ptolemy III Euergetes appointed Eratosthenes as head librarian of the Library of Alexandria.
text: Eratosthenes is appointed by King Ptolemy III Euergetes as head and third librarian of the Alexandrian library.

summary: Scipio Africanus, Roman general and statesman, was born.
text: Scipio Africanus, Roman general in the Second Punic War and statesman of the Roman Republic (d. 183 BC)

summary: Consul Titus Manlius Torquatus presided over the first closing of the gates of the Temple of Janus in Rome, signifying peace.
text: In Rome, the consul Titus Manlius Torquatus presides over the first ever closing of the gates of the Temple of Janus, signifying peace.

summary: A dramatic work by the Latin epic poet and dramatist Gnaeus Naevius was performed for the first time.
text: A work by the Latin epic poet and dramatist Gnaeus Naevius is performed for the first time.

summary: The Epirote Alliance was replaced by the Epirote League as a federal state.
text: The Epirote Alliance is replaced by the Epirote League, which is a federal state with its own parliament (or synedrion).

summary: Corsica, Sardinia, and Liguria rebelled unsuccessfully against Rome.
text: Corsica, Sardinia and Liguria rebel unsuccessfully against Rome.

summary: Marcus Porcius Cato, Roman statesman and orator, was born in Tusculum.
text: Marcus Porcius Cato (Cato the Elder), Roman statesman, (d. 149 BC)

summary: Zenodotus of Ephesus, first librarian of the Library of Alexandria, died.
text: Zenodotus of Ephesus, first librarian of the Library of Alexandria

summary: Princess Deidamia II of Epirus died.
text: Deidamia II is the Greek princess and daughter of Pyrrhus II of Epirus

summary: Gaius Flaminius passed a measure distributing plots in the Ager Gallicus to poor plebeian citizens.
text: Despite the opposition of the Roman Senate and of his own father, the Roman political leader Gaius Flaminius wins the passage of a measure to distribute land among the plebeians. The Romans decide to parcel out land north of Rome (the Ager Gallicus) into small holdings for its poorer citizens whose farms have fallen into ruin during the First Punic War.

summary: King Agron of Illyria routed the invading Aetolian army on behalf of King Demetrius II of Macedonia.
text: Demetrius II, king of Macedonia, seeks military help from Agron, king of Illyria, a loosely organized state on the Adriatic coast north of Epirus, against the advancing Aetolians. The Illyrian army routs the Aetolians and returns home as the victor.

summary: The Romans sent envoys to Massilia to negotiate with the Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca.
text: The Romans send envoys to Massilia (modern Marseille, France) to negotiate with the Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca who is based there.

summary: Hieronymus, future tyrant of Syracuse, was born.
text: Hieronymus, tyrant of Syracuse (d. 214 BC)

summary: King Agron of the Ardiaean Kingdom died.
text: Agron, king of the Ardiaean Kingdom (Western Balkans)

summary: Queen Teuta assumed regency over Illyria and launched piratical attacks against Roman and Greek shipping.
text: King Agron of Illyria dies. Pinnes, the son of Agron and Agron's first wife Triteuta, officially succeeds his father as king, but the kingdom is effectively ruled by Agron's second wife, Queen Teuta (Tefta), who expels the Greeks from the Illyrian coast and then launches Illyrian pirate ships into the Ionian Sea, preying on Roman shipping. She continues her husband's policy of attacking cities on the west coast of Greece and practising large-scale piracy in the Adriatic and Ionian Seas.

summary: Rome occupied Corcyra after Illyrian forces murdered Roman and Issaean ambassadors at sea.
text: With Roman merchants being killed by the Illyrian pirates, envoys are sent by Rome to Illyria. After the Roman ambassador Lucius Coruncanius and the Issaean ambassador Cleemporus are murdered at sea by Illyrian soldiers after causing offence to Queen Teuta, Roman forces occupy the island of Corcyra with the aim of humbling Teuta.

summary: Carthaginian admiral Adherbal died.
text: Adherbal, admiral of the Carthaginian fleet who has battled for domination of the Mediterranean Sea for Carthage in the First Punic War against Rome

summary: King Agron of Illyria died.
text: Agron of Illyria as aforementioned (vid. supra)

summary: Roman consuls landed in Illyria, lifting Illyrian sieges and establishing protectorates over Epidamnus, Apollonia, Corcyra, and Pharos.
text: The First Illyrian War started when the Roman Senate dispatched an army under the command of the consuls Lucius Postumius Albinus and Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus to Illyria. Rome forced the withdrawal of Illyrian garrisons in the Greek cities of Epidamnus, Apollonia, Corcyra and Pharos and establishes a protectorate over these Greek towns.

summary: The Illyrian tribe of the Ardiaei was subdued by the Romans.
text: The Illyrian tribe of the Ardiaei is subdued by the Romans.

summary: Antigonus III became regent of Macedonia following the death of Demetrius II, ruling on behalf of young Philip V.
text: The King of Macedonia, Demetrius II, dies. His nephew, Antigonus III comes to the Macedonian throne as regent for his half-cousin and the future king Philip V, who is only ten years old.

summary: Antigonus III pursued friendly relations with the Illyrians to counter Roman expansion in the Adriatic region.
text: Concerned at Rome's expansion, Antigonus III pursues a policy of befriending the Illyrians, even though the Greeks in the region support Rome in quelling the Illyrian pirates.

summary: Rome established friendly ties with the Aetolian League and the Achaean League following its intervention in Illyria.
text: The involvement of Rome in Illyria led to the establishment of friendly relations between Rome and the enemies of Macedonia: the Aetolian League and Achaean League, which approve the suppression of Illyrian piracy.

summary: Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus, Roman general and future consul, was born.
text: Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus, Roman consul and general (d. 160 BC)

summary: Titus Quinctius Flamininus, Roman general and future consul, was born.
text: Titus Quinctius Flaminius, Roman consul and general (d. 174 BC)

summary: King Demetrius II of Macedonia died.
text: Demetrius II, Macedonian king from 239 BC (b. c. 276 BC)

summary: Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca was killed in battle in Hispania, and command of Carthaginian forces passed to Hasdrubal the Fair.
text: The Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca is killed in a battle in Hispania, ending his lengthy campaign to conquer the Iberian Peninsula for Carthage. In eight years, by force of arms and diplomacy, he has secured an extensive territory in the Iberian Peninsula, but his death in battle prevents him from completing the conquest. Command of his army in the Iberian Peninsula passes to his son-in-law Hasdrubal.

summary: Hasdrubal the Fair founded Carthago Nova as his capital in Hispania.
text: Hasdrubal makes immediate policy changes, emphasizing the use of diplomatic rather than military methods for expanding Carthaginian Hispania and dealing with Rome. He founds Carthago Nova or New Carthage (modern Cartagena) as his capital city.

summary: Roman forces accepted the surrender of Demetrius of Pharos, landed at Apollonia, and advanced north to besiege the Illyrian capital Shkodra.
text: The Illyrian queen Teuta's governor, Demetrius of Pharos has little alternative but to surrender to the overwhelming Roman force. In return, the Romans award him a considerable part of Teuta's holdings to counter-balance the power of Teuta. Meanwhile, the Roman army lands further north at Apollonia. The combined Roman army and fleet proceed northward together, subduing one town after another and besieging Shkodra, the Illyrian capital.

summary: Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca died in battle in the Iberian Peninsula.
text: Hamilcar Barca, Carthaginian general who has assumed command of the Carthaginian forces in Sicily during the last years of the First Punic War with Rome, helped Carthage win the Mercenary War and brought extensive territory in the Iberian Peninsula under Carthaginian control (b. c. 270 BC)

summary: The Ardiaei surrendered territory and ports to the Roman Republic, ending the First Illyrian War.
text: Illyrian Wars: The Ardiaei surrendered some territory, including strategically significant ports, to Rome, ending the war.

summary: Queen Teuta of Illyria surrendered to the Roman Republic and accepted peace terms restricting her territory and imposing annual tribute.
text: Queen Teuta of Illyria finally surrenders to Roman forces and is forced by the Romans to accept an ignominious peace. The Romans allow her to continue her reign but restrict her to a narrow region around the Illyrian capital, Shkodra, deprive her of all her other territory, and forbid her to sail an armed ship below Lissus just south of the capital. They also require her to pay an annual tribute and to acknowledge the final authority of Rome.

summary: The Roman Republic organized Sardinia and Corsica into a single province and provided for the annual election of two praetors.
text: Sardinia and Corsica are made a combined province. Rome appoints, and in the future annually elects, two praetors (with autocratic consular powers) for this province and for Sicily.

summary: Gaius Flaminius became the Roman Republic's first governor of Sicily.
text: Gaius Flaminius becomes Rome's first governor of Sicily.

summary: Future Roman consul and general Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica was born.
text: Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica, Roman consul and general

summary: A large host of Cisalpine and Transalpine Gauls advanced southward to threaten Rome.
text: A formidable host of Gauls, some of them from across the Alps, threaten Rome.

summary: The Roman Republic formed an alliance with the Iberian city of Saguntum following appeals from merchants in Massilia.
text: The Greek merchants of Massilia, frightened by Carthaginian successes in Spain (including their exploitation of the Spanish silver mines), appeal to Rome. Rome makes an alliance with the independent Spanish port city of Saguntum south of the Ebro River.

summary: The Roman Republic concluded the Ebro Treaty with Hasdrubal the Fair, barring Carthaginian military expansion north of the Ebro River.
text: The Romans send an embassy to Hasdrubal and conclude the Ebro Treaty which prohibits him from waging war north of the river Ebro, but allowing him a free hand to the south even at the expense of the interests of the town of Massilia.

summary: A coalition of Cisalpine and Transalpine Gauls invaded Italy, crossed the Apennines, and plundered Etruria.
text: A coalition of Cisalpine Gallic tribes (Taurini, Taurisces, Insubres, Lingones, Salasses, Agones, and Boii), reinforced by large numbers of Transalpine adventurers called Gaesatae (Gaesati), invade Italy. Avoiding the Romans at Ariminum, the Gauls cross the Apennines into Etruria and plunder the country.

summary: Roman armies led by consuls Lucius Aemilius Papus and Gaius Atilius Regulus trapped invading Gallic forces along the coast of Etruria near Telamon.
text: To meet this invasion, the Romans call on the Insubres' enemies, the Adriatic Veneti, the Patavini, and the Cenomani, who rapidly mobilise defensive forces. These armies are placed under the command of consuls Lucius Aemilius Papus and Gaius Atilius Regulus. After the Battle of Faesulae (near Montepulciano) between the Gauls and a Roman army in which the Romans lose many men, the combined Roman forces succeed in outmaneuvering the Gauls and force the invaders towards the coast of Tuscany. Papus pursued and harassed their rear but did not risk a pitched battle. The other Consul, Regulus, had crossed from Sardinia, landed at Pisa, and was marching towards Rome. His scouts met the Celts' advance guard head on near Telamon (modern Talamone), in an area called Campo Regio.

summary: Roman consul Gaius Atilius Regulus was killed at the Battle of Telamon.
text: Gaius Atilius Regulus, consul of the Roman Republic (Battle of Telamon).

summary: Roman forces led by consuls Gaius Atilius Regulus and Lucius Aemilius Papus decisively defeated a coalition of Cisalpine Gallic tribes at the Battle of Telamon.
text: The Romans, led by Consuls Gaius Atilius Regulus and Lucius Aemilius Papus, decisively defeat the coalition of Cisalpine Gallic tribes at the Battle of Telamon thus extending Roman influence over northern Italy. On the Roman side Gaius Atilius Regulus, commander of the Roman cavalry, is killed in the battle. On the Gallic side, one of the leaders, Concolitanus, is captured in battle, while the leader of the Gaesatae, Aneroëstes, kills himself when the battle is lost.

summary: Aneroëstes, chieftain of the Gaesatae, committed suicide following his defeat at the Battle of Telamon.
text: Aneroëstes, leader of the Gallic Gaesatae (suicide)

summary: Consuls Gaius Flaminius and Publius Furius Philus forced the Gauls south of the Alps to submit to Rome, creating the province of Cisalpine Gaul.
text: Gaius Flaminius is elected consul for the first time and, with his co-consul Publius Furius Philus, he forces the Gauls south of the Alps to submit to Rome, creating the province of Cisalpine Gaul.

summary: Roman consuls Marcus Claudius Marcellus and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus besieged the Insubrian stronghold of Acerrae.
text: The Roman consuls Marcus Claudius Marcellus and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus march into Insubres territory and besiege Acerrae, an Insubre fortification on the right bank of the River Adda between Cremona and Laus Pompeia. The Insubres are unable to relieve Acerrae because the Romans control all the strategic points around it. Therefore, they hire 30,000 Gaesatae mercenaries, led by Viridomarus (or Britomartus), who march to Clastidium, an important and strategically situated town, owned by the Marici, a Ligurian tribe allied to the Romans, they start a siege hoping that this will force the Romans to lift their siege of Acerrae to come to Clastidium's aid.

summary: Marcus Claudius Marcellus defeated the Gaesatae at the Battle of Clastidium and personally slew King Viridomarus to claim the spolia opima.
text: The Romans split their forces. Marcus Claudius Marcellus heads for Clastidium while his colleague Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus continues the siege of Acerrae. At the Battle of Clastidium Marcellus defeats the Gaesatae. Marcellus personally slays Viridomarus. This victory removes the Gallic threat to Rome. Marcellus is awarded the spolia opima for the third and last time in Roman history.

summary: Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus captured Mediolanum, forcing the unconditional surrender of the Insubres and securing Roman control over the Po Valley.
text: After taking Acerrae Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus marches on Mediolanum (modern Milan), another stronghold of the Insubres, which also falls into Roman hands, upon which the chieftains of the Insubres lose all hope and surrendered unconditionally. Thus the Romans succeeded in conquering the largest independent Celtic tribe in Italy and firmly established their hegemony over the Po Valley, then the most productive agricultural region in the peninsula.

summary: Viridomarus, chieftain of the Gaesatae, was slain at the Battle of Clastidium.
text: Viridomarus, military leader of the Gaesatae (Gaul)

summary: Following the assassination of Hasdrubal the Fair, Hannibal was proclaimed commander-in-chief of Carthaginian forces in Iberia.
text: The Carthaginian general Hasdrubal is murdered by a Celtic assassin while campaigning to increase the Carthaginian hold on Spain. Following the assassination of Hasdrubal, Hannibal, the son of the Carthaginian general, Hamilcar Barca, is proclaimed commander-in-chief by the army and his appointment is confirmed by the Carthaginian government.

summary: Hannibal campaigned from Cartago Nova to consolidate Carthaginian power in Spain, defeating the Olcades, Vaccaei, and Carpetani.
text: Hannibal immediately moves to consolidate Carthage's control of Spain. He marries a Spanish princess, Imilce, then begins to conquer various Spanish tribes. He fights against the Olcades and captures their capital, Althaea; quells the Vaccaei in the northwest; and, making the seaport of Cartagena (Carthago Nova, the capital of Carthaginian Spain) his base, wins a resounding victory over the Carpetani in the region of the Tagus River.

summary: Ptolemy IV Philopator succeeded Ptolemy III Euergetes as ruler of Egypt, appointing Sosibius as his chief minister.
text: Egypt's Ptolemy III dies and is succeeded by his son, Ptolemy IV. Sosibius is appointed by Ptolemy IV as his chief minister and immediately has a great influence over the young king, directing all of the affairs of state.

summary: Ptolemy IV Philopator executed his uncle Lysimachus, his brother Magas, and his mother Berenice II.
text: At Sosibius' direction, Ptolemy IV puts to death in succession his uncle, Lysimachus, his brother Magas, and his mother Berenice II.

summary: Ptolemy IV Philopator imprisoned the exiled Spartan king Cleomenes III on conspiracy charges.
text: King Cleomenes III of Sparta, who is in exile in Egypt, is imprisoned by Ptolemy IV on a charge of conspiracy.

summary: Philip V of Macedon succeeded Antigonus III Doson as king of Macedonia after Antigonus died in battle against the Illyrians.
text: Antigonus III dies during a battle against the Illyrians and is succeeded by his young cousin Philip V as King of Macedonia.

summary: Gaius Flaminius constructed the Circus Flaminius race track in Rome.
text: Gaius Flaminius builds a second race track for Rome, the Circus Flaminius.

summary: Antigonus III Doson, king of Macedonia, died during a battle against the Illyrians.
text: Antigonus III Doson, king of Macedon from 227 BC (b. 263 BC)

summary: Berenice II, queen of Egypt, was murdered on the orders of her son Ptolemy IV Philopator.
text: Berenice II, queen of Egypt, daughter of Magas, king of Cyrenaica (in modern Libya), whose marriage to Ptolemy III Euergetes has reunited her country with Egypt (b. c. 267 BC)

summary: Hasdrubal the Fair, Carthaginian commander in Hispania, was assassinated.
text: Hasdrubal, Carthaginian general and son-in-law of Hamilcar Barca (assassinated) (b. c. 270 BC)

summary: Lucius Caecilius Metellus, Roman consul and general of the First Punic War, died.
text: Lucius Caecilius Metellus, Roman consul and general during the First Punic War (b. c. 290 BC)

summary: Ptolemy III Euergetes, king of Egypt, died.
text: Ptolemy III, king of Egypt, who has reunited Egypt and Cyrenaica and successfully waged the Third Syrian War against the Seleucid Empire

summary: Demetrius of Pharos and Scerdilaidas attacked Roman-protected Illyrian cities and launched a piratical raid on Pylos.
text: Together with fellow Illyrian, Scerdilaidas, Demetrius of Pharos attacks Illyrian cities under Roman protection and leads a piratical squadron into Greek waters. They unsuccessfully attack Pylos, an Achaean town on the Messenian coast, in the Peloponnesus of Greece.

summary: Scerdilaidas and the Aetolians invaded Achaea, seizing and burning the Arcadian town of Cynaetha.
text: Scerdilaidas and the Aetolians invade Achaea. With the help of Cynaethan traitors, they attack, seize and burn Cynaetha, a town in the north of Arcadia.

summary: Rome launched military action against Illyrian pirates, precipitating the Second Illyrian War.
text: Rome strikes again against the Illyrian pirates precipitating the Second Illyrian War.

summary: Rome occupied Pharos and Dimillos, compelling Demetrius of Pharos to seek refuge with Philip V of Macedon.
text: Demetrius seeks refuge with Philip V of Macedon, who is very resentful of the Roman interference. Rome occupies Demetrius' chief fortresses, Pharos and Dimillos.

summary: Philip V of Macedon assembled the Hellenic League at Corinth to wage the Social War against Aetolia, Sparta, and Elis.
text: Aratus of Sicyon counters Aetolian aggression by obtaining the assistance of the Hellenic League now under the leadership of Philip V of Macedon. In the resulting Social War, the Hellenic League of Greek states is assembled in Corinth at Philip V's instigation. He then leads the Hellenic League in battles against Aetolia, Sparta and Elis.

summary: Arsinoe III married her brother Ptolemy IV Philopator of Egypt.
text: Arsinoe III marries her brother, King Ptolemy IV of Egypt.

summary: Gaius Flaminius built the Circus Flaminius on the Campus Martius and constructed the Via Flaminia from Rome to Ariminum.
text: During his censorship, the Roman political leader, Gaius Flaminius, builds the Circus Flaminius on the Campus Martius and constructs the Via Flaminia from Rome to Ariminum (Rimini).

summary: Hannibal campaigned against the Vaccaei, storming their strongholds of Helmantice and Arbucala.
text: Hannibal campaigns against the Vaccaei, he storms the Vaccaen strongholds of Helmantice and Arbucala.

summary: Hannibal defeated a coalition of Iberian tribes led by the Carpetani at the Tagus river.
text: On his return home, laden with many spoils, a coalition of Hispanic tribes, led by the Carpetani, attack his army at the river Tagus, here Hannibal wins his first independent victory.

summary: Attalus II Philadelphus, future king of Pergamon, was born.
text: Attalus II Philadelphus, king of Pergamon (d. 138 BC)

summary: Roman tragic poet Pacuvius was born in Brundisium.
text: Pacuvius, Roman tragic poet and writer (d. c. 130 BC)

summary: Roman statesman and general Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus the Elder was born.
text: Tiberius Gracchus the Elder, father of the Roman political reformer Tiberius Gracchus (d. 154 BC)

summary: Antiochus III the Great initiated the Fourth Syrian War by capturing Seleucia Pieria, Tyre, and Ptolemais while Sosibius conducted delaying negotiations.
text: Following the defection of one of Ptolemy IV's leading commanders, Egypt's Syrian territories are seriously threatened by Antiochus III, thus initiating the Fourth Syrian War. When the Seleucid ruler captures the important eastern Mediterranean sea ports of Seleucia-in-Pieria, Tyre, and Ptolemais, Ptolemy IV's advisor, Sosibius, and the Ptolemaic court enter into delaying negotiations with the enemy, while the Ptolemaic army is reorganized and intensively drilled.

summary: Exiled Spartan king Cleomenes III escaped from an Egyptian prison and committed suicide after failing to incite a revolt in Alexandria.
text: The former King of Sparta, Cleomenes III, escapes from his Egyptian prison and, after failing to raise a revolt in Alexandria, takes his own life.

summary: The Romans extended their control around the northern Adriatic Sea to Istria by conquering tribes east of the Veneti.
text: The Romans extend their area of domination around the head of the Adriatic Sea as far as the peninsula of Histria by the conquest of peoples who dwell to the east of the Veneti. Thus, with the exception of Liguria and the upper valley of the Po River, all Italy south of the Alps is brought within the Roman sphere.

summary: Hannibal laid siege to Saguntum, triggering the outbreak of the Second Punic War between Rome and Carthage.
text: Hannibal lays siege to Saguntum thus initiating the Second Punic War between Carthage and Rome. Saguntum is an independent Iberian Peninsula city south of the Ebro River. In the treaty between Rome and Carthage concluded in 226 BC, the Ebro had been set as the northern limit of Carthaginian influence in the Iberian Peninsula. Saguntum is south of the Ebro, but the Romans have "friendship" with the city and regard the Carthaginian attack on it as an act of war. The siege of Saguntum lasts eight months, and in it Hannibal is severely wounded. The Romans, who send envoys to Carthage in protest, demand the surrender of Hannibal.

summary: Lucius Aemilius Paullus led a Roman army to Illyria, capturing Dimale and driving Demetrius of Pharos into flight.
text: The Roman Senate sends the consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus to Illyria with an army. On discovering Rome's intent, the Illyrian leader Demetrius of Pharos puts to death those Illyrians who oppose his rule, fortifies Dimale and goes to Pharos. After a seven-day siege by the Roman fleet under Lucius Aemilius Paulus, Dimale is taken by direct assault. From Dimale, the Roman navy heads to Pharos, where the Roman forces rout the Illyrians. Demetrius flees to Macedonia, where he becomes a trusted councilor at the court of King Philip V.

summary: Cleomenes III, former king of Sparta who had overhauled its political system, died in Egypt.
text: Cleomenes III, Spartan king from 235 BC to 222 BC, who reorganized Sparta's political structure and struggled unsuccessfully to destroy the Achaean League.

summary: The Second Punic War began between the Roman Republic and Carthage.
text: Second Punic War

summary: A Carthaginian army under Hannibal departed Cartagena to begin their march toward Italy.
text: Second Punic War: A Carthaginian army departed Cartagena.

summary: Demetrius of Pharos fled to the court of Philip V in Macedonia following his defeat by Rome.
text: Illyrian Wars: Demetrius of Pharos fled to Macedonia.

summary: Gaius Flaminius was re-elected Roman consul alongside Gnaeus Servilius Geminus and raised new legions to confront Hannibal.
text: Gaius Flaminius is re-elected consul with Gnaeus Servilius Geminus, in what is considered to be a rebuke of the Senate's prosecution of the war. Flaminius raises new legions and marches north to meet the Carthaginian general Hannibal.

summary: Hannibal advanced to the Arno River, bypassed Gaius Flaminius at Arretium, and reached Faesulae and Perugia.
text: Hannibal advances to the Arno River and then outmanoeuvres the army of Gaius Flaminius at Arretium and reaches Faesulae (modern Fiesole) and Perugia.

summary: Hannibal annihilated the Roman army under Gaius Flaminius at the Battle of Lake Trasimene and destroyed Roman cavalry reinforcements.
text: On the northern shore of Lake Trasimene, in Umbria, Hannibal's troops all but annihilate Gaius Flaminius' army in the Battle of Lake Trasimene, killing thousands (including Flaminius) and driving others to drown in the lake. Reinforcements of about 4,000 cavalry from Ariminum under the praetor, Gaius Centenius, are intercepted before they arrive and are also destroyed. The Carthaginian troops then march on Rome.

summary: The Roman Senate appointed Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus as dictator amid fears of an attack by Hannibal.
text: Gaius Flaminius' supporters in the Senate begin to lose power to the more aristocratic factions as the Romans fear Hannibal is about to besiege their city. The Senate appoint Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus as dictator.

summary: Quintus Fabius Maximus implemented his strategy of delay, avoiding pitched battle while cutting off Carthaginian supplies.
text: Quintus Fabius Maximus begins his strategy of "delay". This involves avoiding a set battle with the Carthaginians and creating a "scorched earth" area around Hannibal's army. Manoeuvring among the hills, where Hannibal's cavalry is ineffective, Fabius cuts off his enemy's supplies and harasses Hannibal's forces incessantly. Fabius gains the name Cunctator (The Delayer) for this strategy.

summary: Hannibal ravaged Apulia and Campania while Quintus Fabius Maximus limited the Roman army to skirmishes.
text: Hannibal ravages Apulia and Campania; meanwhile the delaying tactics of Quintus Fabius Maximus' army allows only skirmishes to occur between the two armies.

summary: After Marcus Minucius Rufus achieved a minor success near Geronium, the Romans elevated him to equal rank as dictator alongside Fabius.
text: Fabius' delaying policy becomes increasingly unpopular in Rome, and Fabius is compelled to return to Rome to defend his actions under the guise of observing some religious obligations. Marcus Minucius Rufus, the master of horse, is left in command and manages to catch the Carthaginians off guard near their camp in Geronium and inflicts severe losses on them in a large skirmish. This "victory" causes the Romans, disgruntled with Fabius, to elevate Minucius to the equal rank of dictator with Fabius.

summary: Quintus Fabius Maximus arrived just in time to save Marcus Minucius Rufus from an ambush set by Hannibal near Geronium.
text: Minucius takes command of half the army and camps separately from Fabius near Geronium. Hannibal, informed of this development, lays an elaborate trap, which draws out Minucius and his army and then Hannibal attacks it from all sides. The timely arrival of Fabius with the other half of the army enables Minucius to escape after a severe mauling. After the battle, Minucius turns over his army to Fabius and resumes the duties of Master of Horse.

summary: Carthaginian forces under Hannibal defeated the Romans at Lake Trasimene, the Trebia River, and the Ticinus River.
text: Carthaginians defeat the Romans at Lake Trasimene; at the Trebia River and at the Ticinus River

summary: Advised by Demetrius of Pharos, Philip V negotiated peace with the Aetolian League at Naupactus to end the Social War.
text: Learning of Hannibal's victory over the Romans at Lake Trasimene and seeing a chance to recover his Illyrian kingdom from the Romans, Demetrius of Pharos immediately advises Philip V to make peace with the Aetolians, and turn his attentions toward Illyria and Italy. Philip, at once begins negotiations with the Aetolians. At a conference on the coast near Naupactus, Philip meets the Aetolian leaders and a peace treaty is concluded, ending the three-year-long "Social War".

summary: Publius Cornelius Scipio and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus defeated Hasdrubal's fleet in a naval battle at the Ebro River near Tarraco.
text: Publius Cornelius Scipio is sent with reinforcements by Rome to Spain as proconsul. In a naval battle on the Ebro River at Tarraco, the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal's fleet is largely destroyed by a daring surprise Roman attack led by Publius Cornelius Scipio and his brother Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus. As a result, the Romans are able to strengthen their hold on the Ebro River region.

summary: Roman consul Gaius Flaminius was killed in the Battle of Lake Trasimene.
text: Gaius Flaminius, Roman consul and general

summary: Pinnes, king of Illyria and son of Agron, died.
text: Pinnes (also Pinneus or Pineus), son of Agron, king of Illyria, and Agron's first wife Triteuta

summary: Hannibal marched south through Italy and captured the Roman army supply depot at Cannae.
text: The Carthaginian general, Hannibal, moves his forces southward through Italy and seizes the large army supply depot at Cannae on the Aufidus River.

summary: Hannibal won an overwhelming victory over the Roman army at the Battle of Cannae, killing Lucius Aemilius Paullus and tens of thousands of Romans.
text: The Battle of Cannae (east of Naples) ends in victory for Hannibal whose 50,000-man army defeats a Roman force of 86,000 led by consuls Lucius Aemilius Paullus (who is killed in the battle) and Gaius Terentius Varro. 50,000-70,000 Roman troops are killed, making this perhaps the deadliest one-day battle in all history.

summary: Hiero II of Syracuse provided money and supplies on loan to support the Roman army in Sicily.
text: A loan of money and supplies for the Roman army in Sicily is sought and obtained from Hiero II of Syracuse.

summary: The Roman historian Quintus Fabius Pictor visited Delphi to consult the oracle after Rome's defeat at Cannae.
text: The Roman historian Quintus Fabius Pictor is sent to Delphi in Greece to consult the Oracle for advice about what Rome should do after its defeat in the Battle of Cannae.

summary: Following Hannibal's triumph at Cannae, communities in Apulia, Lucania, Samnium, and Bruttium defected from Rome to join Carthage.
text: Following Hannibal's victory, many regions begin to defect from Rome, while others are conquered by Hannibal's forces. In Apulia, Lucania, Samnium and in Bruttium, Hannibal finds many supporters.

summary: The city of Capua defected from Rome to ally with Hannibal, who quartered his army there for the winter.
text: The city of Capua switches sides to join Hannibal and the Carthaginian army winters there.

summary: Marcus Claudius Marcellus rallied the Roman remnants at Canusium and prevented Hannibal from capturing Nola and southern Campania.
text: After the defeat at Cannae, Roman general, Marcus Claudius Marcellus, commands the remnants of the Roman army at Canusium and saves the city of Nola and southern Campania from occupation by Hannibal.

summary: Gauls ambushed and virtually wiped out a Roman force under Lucius Postumius Albinus near Litana.
text: A Roman force of 25,000 led by Lucius Postumius Albinus is ambushed by Gauls near Litana and almost completely wiped out.

summary: The Carthaginian senate ordered Hasdrubal Barca to march from Spain to Italy to reinforce Hannibal.
text: Hasdrubal is ordered by the Carthaginian government to march to Italy.

summary: Roman commanders Gnaeus and Publius Cornelius Scipio successfully prevented Hasdrubal Barca from marching from Spain to Italy.
text: Roman forces in Spain led by Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus and Publius Cornelius Scipio successfully thwart Hasdrubal's attempt to march to Italy.

summary: A Carthaginian fleet ravaged the coastal territories of the Kingdom of Syracuse.
text: The Carthaginian fleet ravages the territory of The Kingdom of Syracuse.

summary: Philip V of Macedon invaded Illyria and sent ambassadors to Hannibal in Italy, starting the First Macedonian War.
text: Philip V of Macedon, still resenting Rome's interference in Illyrian politics, seizes his opportunity to invade Illyria. Ambassadors from Philip V visit Hannibal at his headquarters in Italy. These actions mark the beginning of the First Macedonian War between Rome and Macedonia.

summary: Heavy Roman casualties occurred on August 2 during the Battle of Cannae.
text: August 2

summary: Roman consul and general Lucius Aemilius Paullus was killed in the Battle of Cannae.
text: Lucius Aemilius Paullus, Roman consul and general (killed in the Battle of Cannae)

summary: Roman consul Gnaeus Servilius Geminus was killed in the Battle of Cannae.
text: Gnaeus Servilius Geminus, Roman consul 217 BC (killed in the Battle of Cannae)

summary: Roman consul and former Master of the Horse Marcus Minucius Rufus was killed in the Battle of Cannae.
text: Marcus Minucius Rufus, Roman consul 221 BC, Master of the Horse 217 BC (killed in the Battle of Cannae)

summary: Gelo, co-ruler and son of King Hiero II of Syracuse, died.
text: Gelo, son of Hiero II

summary: Roman consul and augur Marcus Aemilius Lepidus died.
text: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, Roman consul 232 BC and priest (augur)

summary: The Roman Republic sent Titus Manlius Torquatus with an army to Sardinia after bad weather delayed a Carthaginian invasion fleet.
text: A Carthaginian invasion fleet bound for Sardinia is delayed by bad weather giving the Romans the time to organize an intervention; the Roman general Titus Manlius Torquatus, one of it original conquerors, is sent to Sardinia with an army.

summary: Roman forces led by Titus Manlius Torquatus defeated a combined Sardinian and Carthaginian army at the Battle of Decimomannu, ending the Sardinian rebellion.
text: Battle of Decimomannu, the Romans led by Torquatus defeat a combined Sardinian/Carthaginian army ending the Sardinian rebellion and driving off the Carthaginians.

summary: Roman naval squadrons operating from Sicily harassed the retreating Carthaginian invasion fleet.
text: On its return journey the Carthaginian invasion fleet is harassed by Roman squadrons operating from Sicily.

summary: Publius Cornelius Scipio and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus defeated Hasdrubal Barca at the Battle of Dertosa, preventing Carthaginian reinforcements from reaching Italy.
text: The Carthaginian general, Hannibal, is denied any reinforcements from Spain for his forces now based in Italy by the activities of the Roman general Publius Cornelius Scipio and his brother Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus, who, in a battle at Dertosa near the Ebro River effectively stop the Carthaginian general, Hasdrubal's attempt to break through to Italy.

summary: Tribune Gaius Oppius instituted the Lex Oppia, restricting women's wealth and public display of luxury in Rome.
text: The Roman law, Lex Oppia, is instituted by Gaius Oppius, a tribune of the plebs during the consulship of Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus and Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus. The Lex Oppia is the first of a series of sumptuary laws introduced in Rome. It not only restricts women's wealth, but also their displaying it.

summary: Marcus Claudius Marcellus repulsed an attack by Hannibal on the city of Nola.
text: The Roman general, Marcus Claudius Marcellus, again repulses an attack by Hannibal on the city of Nola.

summary: Hannibal occupied the cities of Heraclea and Thurii, but was unable to prevent the Romans from besieging Capua.
text: Hannibal's forces occupy the cities of Heraclea and Thurii. However, Hannibal is unable to prevent the Romans from besieging Capua.

summary: Philip V of Macedon and Hannibal negotiated an anti-Roman alliance pledging mutual support and defense.
text: Philip V of Macedon and Hannibal negotiate an alliance under which they pledge mutual support and defence. Specifically, they agree to support each other against Rome, and that Hannibal shall have the right to make peace with Rome, but that any peace would include Philip and that Rome would be forced to give up control of Corcyra, Apollonia, Epidamnus, Pharos, Dimale, Parthini and Atintania and to restore to Demetrius of Pharos all his lands currently controlled by Rome.
names: List of ancient tribes in Illyria

summary: Hiero II, longtime tyrant of Syracuse and ally of Rome, died.
text: Hiero II, tyrant of Syracuse from 270 BC (b. c. 308 BC)

summary: Hieronymus, tyrant of Syracuse and grandson of Hiero II, was assassinated.
text: Hieronymus, grandson of Hiero II of Syracuse and tyrant (assassinated) (b. c. 231 BC)

summary: Carthage persuaded Syracuse to revolt against Rome and ally with Carthage.
text: Carthage persuades Syracuse to revolt against Rome and ally itself with Carthage instead.

summary: Roman legions led by Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus defeated Carthaginian forces under Hanno near Beneventum.
text: Roman legions led by Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus defeat Hanno's Carthaginian forces in a battle near Beneventum, thus denying Hannibal much needed reinforcements.

summary: Marcus Claudius Marcellus stormed Leontini and besieged Syracuse, but Syracusans repelled his naval attacks with the help of Archimedes' inventions.
text: The Roman general, Marcus Claudius Marcellus, who is in Sicily at the time of the revolt of Syracuse, leads an army which storms Leontini and besieges Syracuse. With the help of Archimedes' ideas and inventions, the Syracusans repel his attacks by sea.

summary: Roman censors Publius Furius Philus and Marcus Atilius Regulus degraded senators and equestrians who refused to return to Carthaginian captivity or advocated surrender after Cannae.
text: The censors Publius Furius Philus and Marcus Atilius Regulus condemn and degrade (i.e. cause to lose rank in Roman society and politics) two groups of Romans of high rank, including senators and equestrians. The first group are those Roman officers captured by Hannibal's forces in the Battle of Cannae who have come as Carthaginian hostages to Rome to plead for their ransom (and those of their fellow prisoners), and who then refuse to return to Carthaginian captivity when the Senate refuses to ransom any prisoners. The second group are those Romans who have advocated surrender to Carthage after the Battle of Cannae, or who have made plans to flee Rome and offer their services in Greece, Egypt, or Asia Minor.

summary: The Romans retook Samnium.
text: Romans retake Samnium

summary: Philip V of Macedon invaded Illyria, capturing Oricum and besieging Apollonia.
text: Philip V of Macedon attempts an invasion of Illyria by sea with a fleet of 120 craft. He captures Oricum and, sailing up the Aous (modern Vjosë) river, he besieges Apollonia.

summary: Roman propraetor Marcus Valerius Laevinus crossed the Adriatic and retook Oricum from Philip V.
text: Upon receiving word from Oricum of Philip V's actions in Illyria, Roman propraetor Marcus Valerius Laevinus crosses the Adriatic with his fleet and army. Landing at Oricum, Laevinus is able to retake the town with little fighting.

summary: Quintus Naevius Crista launched a surprise attack on Philip V's camp at Apollonia, routing Macedonian forces and forcing Philip to burn his fleet.
text: Laevinus sends 2,000 men under the command of Quintus Naevius Crista, to Apollonia. Catching Philip's forces by surprise, Quintus Naevius Crista attacks and routs their camp. Philip V is able to escape back to Macedonia, after burning his fleet and leaving many thousands of his men dead or as prisoners of the Romans.

summary: Illyrian ruler Demetrius of Pharos died while attacking Messene.
text: Demetrius of Pharos, Illyrian ruler

summary: Hieronymus, tyrant of Syracuse, died.
text: Hieronymus, tyrant of Syracuse (b. 231 BC)

summary: The Romans recovered Casilinum and Arpi from Hannibal.
text: Casilinum and Arpi are recovered by the Romans from Hannibal.

summary: Archimedes's war machines repelled the Roman army that was besieging Syracuse.
text: Archimedes's war machines repel the Roman army that is invading Syracuse.

summary: Aratus of Sicyon, long-serving leader of the Achaean League, died.
text: Aratus of Sicyon, Greek statesman, general and advocate of Greek unity, who, for many years, has been the leader of the Achaean League (b. 271 BC)

summary: Philip V of Macedon took inland areas of Illyria, including Dimale, while avoiding the Roman fleet.
text: After being stopped twice by the Romans in his attempts to invade Illyria by sea, and constrained by the Roman commander Marcus Valerius Laevinus' fleet in the Adriatic, Philip V of Macedon keeps his activities in Illyria land based. Keeping clear of the coast, he takes Dassaretis, Atintani and Parthini, and the town of Dimale.

summary: Syphax of the Masaesyli allied with Rome and attacked the Massylii, prompting Hasdrubal to return to Africa.
text: Syphax, king of the western Numidian tribe, the Masaesyli, concludes an alliance with the Romans and they send military advisers to help Syphax train his soldiers. He then attacks the eastern Numidians (the Massylii) ruled by Gala, who is an ally of the Carthaginians. The Carthaginian general Hasdrubal travels to northern Africa from Spain to stamp out the uprising by the Numidians.

summary: Publius Cornelius Scipio and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus captured Saguntum from the Carthaginians.
text: The Roman generals Publius Cornelius Scipio and his elder brother, Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus, capture Saguntum (modern Sagunto) from the Carthaginians.

summary: Publius Licinius Crassus Dives was elected pontifex maximus despite never having held major political office.
text: Publius Licinius Crassus Dives is elected "pontifex maximus" over more distinguished candidates, despite never having held any major offices. He will hold this position until his death.

summary: Hannibal was admitted into Tarentum by conspirators and captured the city, though the citadel remained in Roman hands.
text: The Roman soldiers billeted in Tarentum so alienate the citizens of the city that conspirators admit the Carthaginian general Hannibal to the city. The conspirators then defeat the Roman contingent in it. Hannibal keeps control of his troops so that looting is limited to Roman houses. The citadel in Tarentum remains under Roman control, which denies Hannibal the use of the harbour.

summary: Roman consuls Appius Claudius Pulcher and Quintus Fulvius Flaccus besieged Capua and defeated Hanno near Beneventum.
text: The Roman consuls, Appius Claudius Pulcher and Quintus Fulvius Flaccus, besiege Capua with eight legions. Hanno moves to Beneventum to try to help the inhabitants of Capua, but he is defeated by the Romans.

summary: Hannibal sent Numidian cavalry to Capua, defeating the besieging Roman army under Flaccus and Pulcher.
text: The Capuans then send an appeal for help to Hannibal. In response, Hannibal sends 2,000 Numidian cavalry as reinforcements to Capua. The combined Carthaginian forces defeat the Roman force led by Flaccus and Pulcher, the latter of whom will soon die of wounds he has sustained.

summary: Hannibal destroyed a Roman force led by Marcus Centenius Penula at the Battle of the Silarus.
text: The Battle of the Silarus is fought between Hannibal's army and a Roman force led by praetor Marcus Centenius Penula. The Carthaginians are victorious, effectively destroying Centenius Penula's army.

summary: Hannibal destroyed a Roman army under Gnaeus Fulvius Flaccus at the Battle of Herdonia.
text: The Battle of Herdonia is fought between Hannibal's Carthaginian army and Roman forces who are laying siege to Herdonia led by praetor Gnaeus Fulvius Flaccus, brother of the consul, Quintus Fulvius Flaccus. The Roman army is destroyed, leaving Apulia free of Romans for the year.

summary: Marcus Claudius Marcellus took Syracuse after a two-year siege.
text: After a two year siege, Roman general, Marcus Claudius Marcellus, gradually forces his way into Syracuse and takes it in the face of strong Carthaginian reinforcements and despite the use of engines of war designed by the Greek mathematician and scientist Archimedes (such as the Claw of Archimedes).

summary: Marcus Claudius Marcellus sacked Syracuse, leading to Archimedes's death, and carried off its art treasures to Rome.
text: Although Marcellus wishes to spare the lives of the Syracusans, he is unable to prevent the sack of the city by his soldiers, which includes the killing of Archimedes. Marcellus carries off the art treasures of Syracuse to Rome, the first recorded instance of a practice which is to become common.

summary: Archimedes, the Syracusan mathematician, scientist, and inventor, was killed during the Roman capture of Syracuse.
text: Archimedes of Syracuse, Greek mathematician and scientist, who has calculated formulae for the areas and volumes of spheres, cylinders, parabolas and other plane and solid figures. He has also founded the science of hydrostatics, including the principle of the upthrust on a floating body which has led to his cry, "Eureka". Thirdly, he has invented siege-engines for use against the Romans and the Archimedean screw to raise water (b. c. 287 BC)

summary: Roman general and former consul Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus died.
text: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, Roman consul from 215 to 213 BC

summary: Hannibal continued his military operations across Italy.
text: SpringHannibal invades Italy.

summary: Hasdrubal Barca defeated the Romans in Spain, killing Publius and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio and retaking land south of the Ebro.
text: The Carthaginian general Hasdrubal Barca returns to Spain after his victory over the rebellious Numidians. He then manages to turn the tide against the Romans in Spain, with the Roman generals Publius Cornelius Scipio and his brother Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus killed in separate battles—Publius on the upper Baetis (Guadalquivir) and Gnaeus in the hinterland of Carthago Nova (Cartagena). The Carthaginians recover all their territory south of the Ebro.

summary: The Romans completed the pacification of all Sicily after capturing Syracuse.
text: With the capture of Syracuse, the Romans are able to pacify all of Sicily.

summary: The Romans captured Capua, executed its nobility, confiscated its lands, and dissolved its municipal government.
text: The Romans besiege the town of Capua (which is allied with Hannibal). The town eventually falls to the Romans and its citizens are punished by them. The town's nobility are put to the sword, its territory is confiscated and its municipal organisation is dissolved.

summary: Hannibal marched on the city of Rome in an unsuccessful attempt to take it.
text: Hannibal marches northwards on the city of Rome in a belated and unsuccessful effort to capture the city.

summary: Rome relieved widespread famine and inflation by purchasing grain from King Ptolemy IV of Egypt.
text: Rome faces the burdens of inflation and the danger of famine, caused by the disturbed conditions in Italy and Sicily and the withdrawal of so many men from farming. The situation is only relieved by an urgent appeal by the Romans to the King of Egypt, Ptolemy IV, from whom grain is purchased at three times the usual price.

summary: Rome concluded an alliance with the Aetolian League against Philip V of Macedon.
text: The Roman commander Marcus Valerius Laevinus explores the possibility of an alliance with the Aetolian League as the Aetolians are once again ready to consider taking up arms against their traditional enemy, Macedonia. A treaty is signed to counter Philip V of Macedon who is allied to Hannibal. Under the treaty, the Aetolians are to conduct operations on land, the Romans at sea. Also, Rome will keep any slaves and other booty taken and Aetolia will receive control of any territory acquired.

summary: Roman general Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus was killed in battle in Spain.
text: Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus, Roman general, statesman and brother of Publius Cornelius Scipio

summary: Roman general and former consul Manius Pomponius Matho died.
text: Manius Pomponius Matho, Roman general, consul and maternal grandfather of Scipio Africanus

summary: Roman general and proconsul Publius Cornelius Scipio was killed in battle on the upper Baetis.
text: Publius Cornelius Scipio, Roman general, consul and proconsul during the Second Punic War

summary: Publius Cornelius Scipio assumed command of Roman forces in Spain following the deaths of his father and uncle.
text: Following the death of his father, Publius Cornelius Scipio, and his uncle, Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus, at the hands of the Carthaginians, the young Publius Cornelius Scipio takes over command of the Roman troops in Spain. His appointment reflects the Roman Senate's dissatisfaction with the cautious strategy of the propraetor, Gaius Claudius Nero, then commander in Spain north of the Ebro.

summary: The Roman pacification of Sicily eased famine and inflation in Rome.
text: The famine and inflation facing Rome is eased with the pacification, by the Romans, of Sicily.

summary: Hannibal defeated a Roman proconsular army at Herdonia, killing Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus Maximus.
text: The Carthaginian general Hannibal proves his superiority in tactics by inflicting a severe defeat at Herdonia in Apulia upon a proconsular army, slaying the consul Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus Maximus.

summary: Marcus Claudius Marcellus was elected consul for the fourth time and recaptured Salapia in Apulia from Hannibal's allies.
text: The Roman general Marcus Claudius Marcellus is elected consul for the fourth time and takes Salapia in Apulia, which has revolted and joined forces with Hannibal.

summary: Vulgar Latin brought to the Iberian Peninsula by the Romans during the Second Punic War began developing into the Spanish language.
text: The Spanish language evolves from Vulgar Latin, which was brought to the Iberian Peninsula by the Romans during the Second Punic War.

summary: Philip V of Macedon attacked Roman positions in Illyria but failed to capture Corcyra or Apollonia due to the Roman fleet and a hostile coalition.
text: After allying with Hannibal, Philip V of Macedon attacks the Roman positions in Illyria, but fails to take Corcyra or Apollonia, which are protected by the Roman fleet. Rome's command of the sea prevents his lending any effective aid to his Carthaginian ally in Italy. The Aetolians, Sparta and King Attalus of Pergamum join the Romans in the war against Philip V. This coalition is so strong that Philip V has to stop attacking Roman territory.

summary: Roman consul Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus Maximus was killed in battle against Hannibal at Herdonia.
text: Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus Maximus, Roman consul and general

summary: Roman general and former consul Tiberius Sempronius Longus died.
text: Tiberius Sempronius Longus, Roman consul and general

summary: Roman forces under Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus captured Tarentum from Carthaginian control.
text: The Romans under Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus capture Tarentum (modern Taranto), which the Carthaginian general Hannibal has held for three years.

summary: Marcus Claudius Marcellus fought an indecisive battle against Hannibal at Canusium.
text: The Battle of Canusium is fought between Hannibal's Carthaginian army and a Roman force led by Marcus Claudius Marcellus. The battle is indecisive.

summary: Scipio Africanus launched an assault from Tarraco and captured the Carthaginian stronghold of Carthago Nova.
text: From his headquarters at Tarraco (Tarragona), Publius Cornelius Scipio, the Roman commander in Spain, launches a combined military and naval assault on the Carthaginian headquarters at Carthago Nova (modern-day Cartagena). He successfully besieges and captures the city. In capturing this city, Scipio gains access to copious stores and supplies, Spanish hostages, the local silver mines, a splendid harbour and a base for an advance further south.

summary: Philopoemen reorganized the military of the Achaean League and defeated the Aetolians on the Elean frontier.
text: As strategos of the Achaeans, the Greek general Philopoemen is responsible for turning the Achaean League into an aggressive military power. He builds up the League's military capability. The Achaean League's army and cavalry under Philopoemen then defeat the Aetolians on the Elean frontier.

summary: Scipio Africanus defeated Hasdrubal Barca at Baecula, prompting Hasdrubal to retreat across the Pyrenees toward Italy.
text: The Romans under Publius Cornelius Scipio defeat the Carthaginians under their commander Hasdrubal Barca at Baecula (Bailen) in Baetica. As a result, Hasdrubal Barca decides to cross the Pyrenees with his remaining troops into Transalpine Gaul, with the intention of joining his brother Hannibal in Italy.

summary: Roman general and consul Marcus Claudius Marcellus was ambushed and killed by Hannibal's forces near Venusia.
text: The Roman general Marcus Claudius Marcellus is killed in battle while fighting Hannibal near Venusia, Apulia.

summary: Hannibal destroyed a Roman force at the Battle of Petelia.
text: Hannibal destroys a Roman force at the Battle of Petelia.

summary: Polybius, Greek historian of Rome's rise to dominance, was born in Megalopolis.
text: Polybius, Greek historian, famous for his book called "The Histories" or "The Rise of the Roman Empire", covering in detail the period between 220 and 146 BC (d. 120 BC)

summary: Roman general Marcus Claudius Marcellus died in an ambush near Venusia.
text: Marcus Claudius Marcellus, Roman general who has captured Syracuse during the Second Punic War and has become known as "the sword of Rome" (b. 268 BC)

summary: Gaius Claudius Nero fought an indecisive battle against Hannibal at Grumentum before marching north to reinforce Marcus Livius Salinator.
text: The Roman consul Gaius Claudius Nero fights an indecisive battle with the Carthaginian general Hannibal at Grumentum. Nero is unable to stop Hannibal's advance into Canusium. Nevertheless, he rapidly marches the elite parts of his army some one hundred kilometres north to reinforce the army of Marcus Livius Salinator.

summary: Roman armies led by Marcus Livius Salinator and Gaius Claudius Nero defeated the Carthaginians at the Battle of the Metaurus, killing Hasdrubal Barca.
text: The Battle of the Metaurus, fought near the Metaurus River in Umbria, is a pivotal battle during the Second Punic War between Rome and Carthage. The Carthaginians are led by Hannibal's brother Hasdrubal Barca, and the Roman armies are led by the consuls Marcus Livius Salinator and Gaius Claudius Nero. The Carthaginian army is defeated by the Romans and Hasdrubal is killed in the battle. This major loss by the Carthaginians ends Hannibal's hopes of success in Italy.

summary: Philopoemen led the Achaean League to victory over the Spartans at the Battle of Mantinea, killing the Spartan regent Machanidas.
text: The general leading the Achaean League, Philopoemen, introduces heavier Macedonian armour and phalanx tactics. His army then crushes the Spartans under the Spartan regent and general, Machanidas, in the battle of Mantinea. Machanidas is killed by Philopoemen during the battle.

summary: Nabis took power in Sparta by overthrowing King Pelops and initiated major social reforms.
text: Nabis, a Syrian sold into slavery, rises to power in Sparta and becomes regent of the young Spartan king, Pelops, following the death of Machanidas. Nabis soon overthrows Pelops, claiming to be a descendant of the Eurypontid Spartan king Demaratus. Nabis then starts a social revolution which will lead to the freeing of all the helots, the destruction of the ruling oligarchy, the redistribution of land and the cancelling of debts.

summary: Greek Stoic philosopher Chrysippus died in Athens.
text: Chrysippus, Greek philosopher from Soloi who was the principal systematiser of Stoic philosophy (b. c. 280 BC)

summary: Carthaginian general Hasdrubal Barca died at the Battle of the Metaurus.
text: Hasdrubal Barca, Carthaginian general who has unsuccessfully attempted to sustain Carthage's military ascendancy on the Spanish peninsula in the face of Roman attacks (b. 245 BC)

summary: Spartan general and regent Machanidas was killed in the Battle of Mantinea.
text: Machanidas, Spartan general and regent (killed in the battle of Mantinea)

summary: Publius Cornelius Scipio defeated Carthaginian generals Mago Barca and Hasdrubal Gisco at the Battle of Ilipa.
text: In the Battle of Ilipa (Alcalá del Río, near Seville) in Spain, the Carthaginian generals, Mago Barca and Hasdrubal Gisco, are defeated by the Roman general Publius Cornelius Scipio. Mago retreats to Gades (modern Cádiz) and then sails for the Balearic Islands.

summary: Publius Cornelius Scipio secured Gades, ending Carthaginian rule and establishing Roman control over Hispania.
text: The Roman general Publius Cornelius Scipio secures Gades, thus making Roman control of Spain complete. With the effective withdrawal of the Carthaginians from Spain, Hispania becomes a Roman province.

summary: Publius Cornelius Scipio founded the city of Italica to settle Roman soldiers wounded at the Battle of Ilipa.
text: The city of Italica (northwest of modern Seville, Spain) is founded by Scipio as a place to settle for the Roman soldiers wounded in the Battle of Ilipa.

summary: Publius Cornelius Scipio returned in triumph to Rome from Spain and was elected consul.
text: After having successfully driven the Carthaginians out of Spain, Scipio returns in triumph to Rome and is elected consul. He then prepares to carry the war into Carthage's territory in North Africa.

summary: Hasdrubal Gisco crossed to North Africa and allied with Syphax, king of the Masaesyli, by giving his daughter in marriage.
text: Hasdrubal Gisco retreats to the coast and then crosses to North Africa, where he gives his daughter in marriage to Syphax, king of the Numidian Masaesyli tribe, to formalize their military alliance.

summary: Numidian chieftain Masinissa defected to Rome, while Syphax expelled him and claimed the throne of Numidia.
text: After being an ally of Carthage and fighting with them, Numidian chieftain, Masinissa switches sides when the Carthaginians are driven from Spain and offers to assist Rome. Syphax expels his rival Masinissa and claims himself to be King of Numidia. The Romans support Masinissa's claim to the Numidian throne against Syphax, the pro-Carthaginian ruler of the Masaesyli tribe.

summary: The war between Rome and Macedonia continued inconclusively in Greece.
text: The war between Macedonia and Rome drags on with no decisive advantage on either side. Rome's interest lies not in conquest, but in keeping Macedon, the Greek city-states and Greek political leagues continually divided and non-threatening.

summary: Philip V of Macedon sacked Thermum and forced the Aetolians to accept a peace treaty on his terms.
text: Philip V of Macedon is able to take advantage of Roman inactivity. After sacking Thermum, the religious and political centre of Aetolia, Philip is able to force the Aetolians to accept a peace treaty based on his terms.

summary: Greek Stoic philosopher Chrysippus died in Athens.
text: Chrysippus, Greek Stoic philosopher

summary: Scerdilaidas, king of the Ardiaean Kingdom in Illyria, died.
text: Scerdilaidas, Illyrian king of the Ardiaean Kingdom

summary: Philip V of Macedon concluded the Peace of Phoenice with Rome, ending the First Macedonian War.
text: Philip V of Macedon makes a temporary peace (the Peace of Phoenice) with Rome on favourable terms for Macedonia ending the First Macedonian War. The treaty formally acknowledges the favourable position of Macedonia, including their capture of Illyria, but in return Philip effectively repudiates his alliance with Hannibal.

summary: Philopoemen expelled Nabis of Sparta from Messene after Sparta renewed war against the Achaean League.
text: After the peace, the Spartan king, Nabis, goes to war with the Achaean League. The Achaean general Philopoemen expels Nabis of Sparta from Messene.

summary: Philip V of Macedon formed an alliance against Rhodes and allied pirate fleets, igniting the Cretan War.
text: The Peace of Phoenice prohibits Philip from expanding westward into Illyria or the Adriatic Sea, so the king turns his attentions eastwards to the Aegean Sea, where he starts to build a large fleet. After concluding the First Macedonian War, Philip of Macedon, seeing his chance to defeat Rhodes, forms an alliance with Aetolian and Spartan pirates who begin raiding Rhodian ships. The Cretan War begins between Philips' Macedonians, the Aetolian League, several Cretan cities (of which Olous and Hierapytna are the most important) and Spartan pirates against the forces of Rhodes and later Attalus I of Pergamum, Byzantium, Cyzicus, Athens and Knossos.

summary: Philip V of Macedon attacked territories belonging to allies of Rhodes in Thrace and around the Sea of Marmara.
text: With the Rhodian fleet and economy suffering from the depredations of the pirates, Philip begins attacking the lands of Rhodes' allies in Thrace and around the Sea of Marmara.

summary: Scipio crossed to Sicily with a volunteer force in preparation for an invasion of North Africa.
text: Publius Cornelius Scipio boldly determines to disregard Hannibal in Italy and political opposition in the Roman Senate and rather decides to strike at the Carthaginian holdings in North Africa. Scipio crosses to Sicily with an army consisting partly of volunteers as the Roman Senate would not provide him with an army.

summary: Quintus Pleminius captured Epizephyrian Locris from the Carthaginians and repelled Hannibal's relief attempt.
text: The Roman propraetor Quintus Pleminius captures the town of Epizephyrian Locris from the Carthaginians. Hannibal's attempt to recapture the town is foiled by the appearance of Scipio's army.

summary: Scipio sent Gaius Laelius on an advance expedition to North Africa to prepare for the Roman invasion.
text: Scipio sends the Roman general Gaius Laelius to North Africa to prepare the way for his later invasion.

summary: Mago Barca landed in Liguria and captured Genoa and Savona.
text: A Carthaginian army under Mago Barca lands in Liguria, capturing Genoa and Savona.

summary: Hannibal erected a bilingual Punic and Greek inscription detailing his achievements at the temple of Juno Lacinia near Crotone.
text: Hannibal erects a bilingual Punic/Greek inscription describing his accomplishments in the temple of Juno Lacinia near Crotone.

summary: Hasdrubal Gisco secured an alliance with the Numidian king Syphax through his marriage to Sophonisba.
text: Having lost his alliance with the Numidian chief Masinissa, the Carthaginian general, Hasdrubal Gisco, finds a new ally in the Numidian king Syphax, who marries Sophonisba, Hasdrubal's daughter, who, until his defection to Rome, has been betrothed to Masinissa.

summary: Scipio besieged Utica but was forced to withdraw before the combined forces of Hasdrubal Gisco and Syphax.
text: Roman forces under Publius Cornelius Scipio besiege Utica in Carthaginia. Scipio is unable to stop the combined forces of the Carthaginians under Hasdrubal Gisco and the Numidians under their chief, Syphax, and he is forced to lift his siege of Utica.

summary: Publius Sempronius Tuditanus fought an indecisive battle against Hannibal near Crotona.
text: The Battle of Crotona is fought between Hannibal's Carthaginian army, and a Roman force led by Publius Sempronius Tuditanus, with no decisive outcome for either side.

summary: Philip V of Macedon and Antiochus III agreed to partition the overseas possessions of the Ptolemaic Kingdom.
text: Philip V of Macedon and Antiochus III of the Syrian-based Seleucid kingdom realize Egypt's weakness and agree to partition Egypt's Anatolian and Aegean possessions. Antiochus' share is to be southern Syria, Lycia, Cilicia and Cyprus, while Philip is to gain western Anatolia and the Cyclades.

summary: Scipio Africanus executed the Carthaginian general Hanno the Elder.
text: Hanno the Elder, Carthaginian general executed by Scipio Africanus

summary: Ptolemy IV Philopator, Pharaoh of Ptolemaic Egypt, died.
text: Ptolemy IV Philopator, king (Pharaoh) of Egypt

summary: Publius Cornelius Scipio destroyed the Carthaginian camp near Utica and defeated Carthaginian and Numidian forces at the Battle of the Great Plains.
text: The Roman general, Publius Cornelius Scipio, while undertaking peace negotiations with the Carthaginians at Utica, makes a surprise attack on the Carthaginian camp and destroys it. Then, sweeping down on the forces that the Carthaginians and their allies, the Numidians, are trying to muster on the Great Plains near the upper Bagradas River (in modern Tunisia), he smashes that army in the Battle of the Great Plains. The Numidian king, Syphax, and the Carthaginian leader, Hasdrubal Gisco, manage to escape separately.

summary: Gaius Laelius and Masinissa pursued and captured King Syphax of Numidia near Cirta.
text: The Roman general, Gaius Laelius, and Rome's Numidian ally, Masinissa, follow Syphax towards Cirta, the Numidian capital. In the pursuit, Syphax is captured after his badly wounded horse throws him off. He is delivered to Scipio and is made a prisoner of the Romans, dying in the Italian town of Alba Fucens later in the year.

summary: Masinissa became king of unified Numidia as an ally of the Roman Republic.
text: Masinissa becomes king of both the Massyli and the Massaesyli tribes in Numidia and remains a loyal ally to the Romans.

summary: Hannibal departed Italy and returned to Carthage to defend against the Roman invasion.
text: Hasdrubal Gisco persuades the Carthaginians to raise a new army and to send for Hannibal to return home from Italy. Hannibal finally leaves Italy and returns to Carthage.

summary: Roman forces defeated and mortally wounded Carthaginian general Mago Barca at the Battle of Insubria.
text: The Carthaginian general, Mago Barca, is defeated and wounded by the Romans in the Battle of Insubria. He dies of his wounds on the return voyage to Carthage.

summary: Hannibal concentrated the remnants of Carthaginian forces at Hadrumetum to prepare for battle.
text: A preliminary armistice between Carthage and Rome is declared and the Carthaginian armies accept Scipio's severe terms. However, on his return to Carthage, Hannibal concentrates the remnants of the Carthaginian forces at Hadrumetum (modern Sousse, Tunisia) and prepares them for battle.

summary: Carthaginian general Mago Barca died of wounds while sailing back to Carthage.
text: Mago Barca, Carthaginian general during the Second Punic War against Rome who has accompanied his brother Hannibal on the invasion of Italy (b. 243 BC)

summary: Roman general and statesman Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus died in Rome.
text: Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus, Roman general and statesman whose cautious delaying tactics (which have led to his surname Cunctator, meaning "delayer") during the early stages of the Second Punic War have given Rome time to recover its strength and take the offensive against the invading Carthaginian army of Hannibal (b. c. 275 BC)

summary: Former Numidian king Syphax died in Roman captivity at Alba Fucens.
text: Syphax, Numidian king allied with the Carthaginians during the Second Punic War against Rome

summary: Hasdrubal Gisco committed suicide in Carthage to escape a lynching by an angry mob.
