text: Accused of treason by the Carthaginians after being defeated by the Romans at the Battle of the Great Plains, Hasdrubal Gisco commits suicide to avoid being lynched by a Carthaginian mob.

summary: Roman and Numidian forces led by Scipio Africanus and Masinissa decisively defeated Hannibal at the Battle of Zama.
text: The Battle of Zama (130 kilometers south-west of Carthage) ends the Second Punic War and largely destroys the power of Carthage. Roman and Numidian forces under the leadership of the Roman general Publius Cornelius Scipio and his Numidian ally, Masinissa, defeat a combined army of Carthaginians and their Numidian allies under the command of Hannibal and force Carthage to capitulate. Hannibal loses 20,000 men in the defeat, but he is able to escape Masinissa's pursuit.

summary: Publius Cornelius Scipio received the cognomen Africanus to celebrate his defeat of Carthage.
text: Following the Battle of Zama, the Roman general Publius Cornelius Scipio gains the cognomen "Africanus" in honour of his feats in North Africa against Carthage.

summary: Agathocles became the guardian of the young Ptolemy V upon the retirement of Sosibius.
text: The Egyptian regent and chief minister, Sosibius, retires and Agathocles, another member of the ruling clique, becomes Ptolemy V's guardian.

summary: Tlepolemus marched on Alexandria and incited a mob that compelled Agathocles to resign as regent.
text: Agathocles rule provokes Tlepolemus, the governor of Pelusium (Egypt's eastern frontier city), into action. Tlepolemus marches on Alexandria, where his supporters rouse a mob, compelling Agathocles to resign.

summary: Tlepolemus became regent for Ptolemy V after an Alexandrian mob lynched Agathocles and his family.
text: The Egyptian boy king, Ptolemy V, is encouraged by a mob clamouring for revenge against the murderers of his mother Arsinoe III to agree to Agathocles being killed. As a result, the mob searches out and butchers Agathocles and his family. Tlepolemus takes Agathocles' place as regent. However, he soon proves to be incompetent and is removed.

summary: Carthaginian general Hasdrubal Gisco committed suicide in Carthage.
text: Hasdrubal Gisco, Carthaginian general who has fought against Rome in Iberia and North Africa during the Second Punic War, customarily identified as the son of Gisco (suicide)

summary: Carthage accepted Rome's harsh peace terms, surrendering overseas territories and ending the Second Punic War.
text: On Hannibal's advice, Carthage sues for peace with the Romans, ending the Second Punic War. Carthage is reduced to a client state of Rome. In the peace treaty between Carthage and Rome, Carthage surrenders all her Mediterranean possessions to Rome, including her Iberian territories. The Carthaginians agree to pay Rome 200 talents per year for 50 years, allow Masinissa to rule Numidia as an independent kingdom, make no war without Rome's permission, and destroy all but 10 of the Carthaginian warships.

summary: Hannibal was elected suffet of Carthage and enacted major administrative and financial reforms.
text: Following the conclusion of the peace with Rome, Hannibal is elected as suffet, or chief magistrate, of Carthage. The office has over the years become insignificant in Carthaginian politics, but Hannibal restores its power and authority. He sets out to reform the administration and finances of Carthage and reduce the power of the oligarchy which has ruled Carthage before and during the Second Punic War.

summary: Roman forces expelled the Carthaginians from Malta.
text: The Romans oust the Carthaginians from Malta.

summary: The Roman Republic distributed land to veterans of the Second Punic War in Rome.
text: In Rome, according to the Roman historian Livy, land is distributed to veterans of the Second Punic War. This is the first documented instance of a practice that later becomes commonplace.

summary: Philip V of Macedon captured Samos and the Egyptian fleet stationed there before besieging Chios.
text: Philip V of Macedon captures Samos and the Egyptian fleet stationed there. He then besieges Chios to the north.

summary: Rhodes and allied fleets from Pergamon, Cyzicus, and Byzantium defeated Philip V of Macedon at the Battle of Chios.
text: Rhodes and its allies Pergamum, Cyzicus, and Byzantium combine their fleets and defeat Philip V in the Battle of Chios. His flagship is trapped and rammed by two enemy ships.

summary: Philopoemen and the Achaean League defeated the Spartan forces of Nabis at Tegea after Nabis invaded Messene.
text: The Spartan king, Nabis, once more invades and captures Messene. However, the Spartans are forced to retreat when the Achaean League army of Philopoemen intervenes. Nabis' forces are decisively defeated at Tegea by Philopoemen and Nabis is forced to check his expansionist ambitions for the time being.

summary: Latin epic poet and dramatist Gnaeus Naevius died.
text: Gnaeus Naevius, Latin epic poet and dramatist of the Old Latin period, who invented a new genre of written historical plays called fabulae praetextae, which are based on Roman historical or legendary figures and events (b. c. 264 BC).

summary: Philip V of Macedon defeated the Rhodians at Lade and advanced into Pergamum and Caria.
text: Philip V of Macedon's fleet defeat the Rhodians at Lade. His forces then advance into Pergamum, plundering Pergamese territory and attacking cities in Caria.

summary: Attalus I of Pergamum traveled to Athens to meet with Athenian leaders and Roman ambassadors after an Acarnanian invasion of Attica.
text: The Acarnanians, with Macedonian support, invade Attica, causing Athens, which has previously maintained its neutrality, to seek help from the enemies of Philip. Attalus I of Pergamum, who is with his fleet at Aegina, receives an embassy from Athens asking him to come to the city for consultations. After he is told that Roman ambassadors are also in Athens, Attalus goes there in haste.

summary: The Roman Republic declared war on Macedon after Philip V rejected an ultimatum delivered by Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, initiating the Second Macedonian War.
text: The Roman ambassador to Greece, Syria, and Egypt, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus delivers an ultimatum to Philip V warning Macedonia not to make war on any Greek state. Philip decides to reject the Roman ultimatum and the Romans declare war on Macedon, thus starting the Second Macedonian War.

summary: Publius Sulpicius Galba Maximus and Attalus I conducted a joint naval campaign against Macedonian possessions in the Aegean Sea.
text: The Roman consul, Publius Sulpicius Galba Maximus, asks Attalus I and his fleet to meet up with the Roman fleet off the Greek Aegean coast and they conduct a naval campaign against Philip V, harassing Macedonian possessions in and along the Aegean.

summary: Roman artists began producing faux-marble wall paintings in private residences.
text: Roman artists begin attempting to produce the illusion of thin slabs of colored marble covering the walls, which are set off by actual architectural moldings and columns, in private houses. These attempts last for 120 years.

summary: A Roman fleet arrived in Illyria attempting to relieve a Macedonian siege of Abydos.
text: Second Macedonian War: A Roman fleet arrived in Illyria to relieve a Macedonian siege of Abydos.

summary: The Insubres defeated the Roman general Gnaeus Baebius Tamphilus in Cisalpine Gaul, inflicting over 6,700 casualties.
text: The Roman general Gnaeus Baebius Tamphilus attacks the Insubres in Gaul, but loses over 6,700 soldiers in the process.

summary: Scipio Africanus was elected censor and named princeps senatus.
text: Scipio Africanus becomes censor and princeps Senatus (the titular head of the Roman Senate).

summary: Tribune Publius Porcius Laeca proposed the Lex Porcia to give Roman citizens the right of appeal in capital cases.
text: The Roman law, Lex Porcia, is proposed by the tribune P. Porcius Laeca to give Roman citizens in Italy and provinces the right of appeal in capital cases.

summary: Titus Quinctius Flamininus took command of the Roman forces in Macedonia, secured the backing of the Achaean League, and opened negotiations with Philip V.
text: After his election to the consulship, Titus Quinctius Flamininus is chosen to replace Publius Sulpicius Galba Maximus as the leading Roman general in Macedonia. He then crosses into Macedonia with his army. Flamininus realizes that future peace depends on breaking the power of king Philip V of Macedon, not merely humbling him. He secures the backing of the Achaean League and then opens peace negotiations with Philip at Nicaea in Locris. Though peace proposals are submitted to the Roman Senate, the talks break down, and fighting resumes.

summary: Titus Quinctius Flamininus drove Philip V out of most of Greece and defeated him at the Battle of the Aous.
text: Titus Quinctius Flamininus' forces manage to push Philip V out of most of Greece, except for a few fortresses. He then defeats Philip V in the Battle of the Aous, near modern Tepelenë in Albania.

summary: Antiochus III defeated Ptolemaic forces at the Battle of Panium, seizing Palestine and Coele-Syria from Ptolemy V.
text: The Battle of Panium is fought between Seleucid forces led by Antiochus III and Ptolemaic forces led by Scopas of Aetolia. The Seleucids win the battle which allows Antiochus III to obtain entire possession of Palestine and Coele-Syria from King Ptolemy V of Egypt. Though the Romans send ambassadors to Ptolemy V, they are unable to lend him any serious assistance against Antiochus III.

summary: Antiochus III agreed to marry his daughter Cleopatra to Ptolemy V as part of their peace settlement.
text: In the resulting peace, Antiochus III agrees to give his daughter Cleopatra in marriage to Ptolemy V.

summary: Eumenes II became king of Pergamum following the death of his father Attalus I Soter.
text: Eumenes II becomes King of Pergamum following the death of his father Attalus I Soter.

summary: Antiochus III occupied portions of the Kingdom of Pergamum and Greek cities in Anatolia.
text: Antiochus III occupies parts of the kingdom of Pergamum and a number of Greek cities in Anatolia.

summary: Ptolemy V suppressed rebel forces in the Nile Delta, dealing cruelly with capitulating leaders.
text: The Egyptian King, Ptolemy V, fights rebels in the Nile Delta, exhibiting great cruelty toward those of their leaders who capitulate.

summary: Nabis of Sparta acquired Argos from Philip V of Macedon and then defected to the Romans.
text: The Spartan ruler, Nabis, acquires the important city of Argos from Philip V of Macedon, as the price of his alliance with the Macedonians. Nabis then defects to the Romans in the expectation of being able to hold on to his conquest.

summary: Titus Quinctius Flamininus decisively defeated Philip V of Macedon at the Battle of Cynoscephalae in Thessaly, ending the war through the Treaty of Tempe.
text: The Battle of Cynoscephalae in Thessaly gives a Roman army under proconsul Titus Quinctius Flamininus a decisive victory over Philip V of Macedon. In the Treaty of Tempe, the terms of the peace proposed by the Roman general and adopted by the Roman Senate specify that Philip V can retain his throne and control of Macedonia, but he has to abandon all the Greek cities he has conquered. Philip also has to provide to the Romans 1,000 talents as indemnity, surrender most of his fleet and provide hostages, including his younger son, Demetrius, who is to be held in Rome. The Aetolians propose that Philip V be ejected from his throne but Flamininus opposes this.

summary: The Roman Republic divided Hispania into the provinces of Hispania Citerior and Hispania Ulterior.
text: Hispania is divided into Hispania Ulterior and Hispania Citerior.

summary: The Iberian revolt broke out in Hispania Citerior and Hispania Ulterior against Roman domination.
text: The Iberian revolt breaks out in Citerior and Ulterior against Roman domination.

summary: King Attalus I of Pergamon died.
text: Attalus I Soter, ruler of Pergamum from 241 BC, who has taken on the title of king after about 230 BC. Through his military and diplomatic skills, he has created a powerful kingdom in Anatolia (b. 269 BC)

summary: The Roman Republic increased the number of quaestors to twelve.
text: The number of quaestors was increased to twelve.

summary: The Roman Republic increased the number of praetors to six.
text: The number of Praetors was increased to six.

summary: The Roman Republic defeated the Insubres in the Po Valley.
text: The Insubres, Gauls of the Po Valley, believed by the Romans to have been incited to revolt by Carthage, are finally defeated.

summary: A new priesthood, the tresviri epulones, was created at Rome to oversee sacred banquets for the gods.
text: A new category of Roman priests, the tresviri epulones, are elected to supervise the feasts of the gods; the first three men selected are Gaius Licinius Lucullus, Publius Manlius, and Publius Porcius Laeca.

summary: Titus Quinctius Flamininus proclaimed the freedom and self-government of the Greek cities at the Isthmian Games in Corinth.
text: At the Isthmian Games at Corinth, the Roman proconsul Titus Quinctius Flamininus proclaims that all Greeks are to be free and governed by their own laws. For this deed he is hailed in many Greek cities as a saviour and accorded homage alongside the gods.

summary: Titus Quinctius Flamininus captured Gythium and compelled Nabis of Sparta to surrender Argos.
text: Flamininus accuses the Spartan ruler, Nabis, of tyranny, takes Gythium in Laconia and forces Nabis to surrender Argos.

summary: The first triumphal arch was constructed in Rome.
text: The first triumphal arch built in Rome.

summary: Eumenes II founded a library at Pergamon, spurring the development of parchment due to an Egyptian papyrus embargo.
text: According to the Roman scholar and writer Marcus Terentius Varro, the foundation of a library at Pergamum around this time by Eumenes II of Pergamum, combined with an embargo on papyrus by Ptolemy V, leads to the invention of parchment.

summary: Ptolemy V Epiphanes issued a trilingual royal edict that was inscribed on the Rosetta Stone.
text: The Rosetta Stone is created. This stone is a Ptolemaic era stele written with the same text in two Egyptian language scripts (hieroglyphic and demotic) and in classical Greek. The translation of the Greek passage reveals that the inscription is a royal edict recording the benefits conferred on Egypt by the pharaoh Ptolemy V Epiphanes at the time of his coronation. This stone will provide the key to the hieroglyphic, or pictographic writing, of ancient Egypt and the decree on it reveals the increasing influence of Egyptian natives, remitted debts and taxes, released prisoners, pardoned rebels who have surrendered, and granted increased benefactions to the temples.

summary: Antiochus III the Great crossed into Thrace and rejected Roman demands to withdraw from Europe and Anatolia.
text: Antiochus III's army crosses the Hellespont into Thrace, where he claims sovereignty over territory that has been won by Seleucus I in 281 BC. A war of harassment and diplomacy with Rome ensues. The Romans send ambassadors demanding that Antiochus stay out of Greece and set free all the autonomous communities in Anatolia. To meet these demands would mean Antiochus III giving up the western part of his Seleucid Empire. Thus Antiochus refuses the Romans' demands.

summary: Marcus Cornelius Cethegus, former Roman consul and censor, died.
text: Marcus Cornelius Cethegus, Roman consul and censor

summary: Macedonia surrendered its Greek possessions and agreed to pay an indemnity, concluding the Second Macedonian War.
text: Second Macedonian War: Macedonia surrendered its conquests in Greece and agreed to pay a war indemnity, ending the war.

summary: Hannibal went into voluntary exile from Carthage after political rivals denounced him to the Romans.
text: Because of his administrative and constitutional reforms in Carthage, Hannibal becomes unpopular with an important faction of the Carthaginian nobility and he is denounced to the Romans for inciting the Seleucid king Antiochus III to take up arms against the Romans. Rome demands that Carthage surrender Hannibal. However, Hannibal voluntarily goes into exile.

summary: Antiochus III the Great gave refuge to Hannibal at Ephesus, worsening tensions with Rome.
text: Tensions between Antiochus III and Rome increase when Hannibal is given refuge by Antiochus III at Ephesus and becomes his adviser.

summary: Antiochus III the Great made peace with Ptolemaic Egypt at Lysimachia, securing southern Syria and territories in Anatolia.
text: After Roman diplomatic intervention, Antiochus III finally halts his war with Egypt. In the peace agreement (the Peace of Lysimachia), Antiochus III formally takes possession of southern Syria, which has been fought over for 100 years by the Ptolemies and Seleucids, and also takes possession of the Egyptian territories in Anatolia.

summary: Marcus Porcius Cato suppressed an Iberian revolt in Spain before being succeeded by Lucius Aemilius Paullus.
text: A Spanish revolt against Roman consolidation of the ex-Carthaginian colonies is effectively put down by Marcus Porcius Cato ("the Censor"). He avoids one defeat by paying the Celtiberians 200 talents (around 120,000 denarii), a much-criticised tactic. On Cato's return to Rome, Aemilius Paulus succeeds him as Roman governor in Spain.

summary: The Roman Republic repealed the Lex Oppia despite strong opposition from consul Marcus Porcius Cato.
text: The Roman sumptuary law, the Lex Oppia, which restricts not only a woman's wealth, but also her display of wealth, is repealed despite consul Marcus Porcius Cato's strong opposition.

summary: An allied coalition led by Rome, Rhodes, the Achaean League, and Pergamon captured Gythium and forced Sparta to surrender.
text: The Battle of Gythium is fought between Sparta and a coalition of Rome, Rhodes, the Achaean League and Pergamum. As the port of Gythium is an important Spartan base, the allies decide to capture it before they advance inland to Sparta. The Romans and the Acheans are joined outside the city by the Pergamese and Rhodian fleets. The Spartans hold out; however, the proconsul Titus Quinctius Flamininus arrives with 4,000 extra men. Facing too great an army, the Spartans decide to surrender the city on the condition that the garrison can leave unharmed. As a result, Nabis, the tyrant of Sparta, is forced to abandon the surrounding land and withdraw to the city of Sparta. Later that year, Sparta capitulates to the allies.

summary: Aristophanes of Byzantium became the chief librarian at Alexandria.
text: Aristophanes of Byzantium, Greek scholar, critic and grammarian, becomes the chief librarian at Alexandria.

summary: Roman comic playwright Terence was born in Carthage.
text: Terence or Publius Terentius Afer, Roman comic playwright (d. 159 BC)

summary: Roman forces under Titus Quinctius Flamininus withdrew from Greece after curbing the power of Nabis of Sparta.
text: After checking the ambitions of Nabis, the tyrant of Sparta, the Roman forces under proconsul Titus Quinctius Flamininus finally withdraw from Greece.

summary: The Aetolians incited Nabis of Sparta to retake his lost territories following the Roman departure from Greece.
text: With the Roman legions under Flaminius returning to Italy, the Greek states are once again on their own. The Romans leave the dominant powers in the region; the kingdom of Macedonia, the Aetolians, the strengthened Achaean League and the weakened Sparta. The Aetolians, who have opposed the Roman intervention in Greek affairs, incite the Spartan leader, Nabis, to retake his former territories and regain his influence in Greek affairs.

summary: Hannibal encouraged Antiochus III the Great to challenge Roman influence in Greece.
text: With his peace agreement with the Egyptians in place, Antiochus III now turns his attention to the West. He is encouraged to challenge Rome's protection of the Greeks by his advisor, the former Carthaginian general Hannibal.

summary: Philip V of Macedon, Rhodes, Pergamon, and the Achaean League allied with Rome against Antiochus III the Great.
text: Philip V of Macedon, along with Rhodes, Pergamum, and the Achaean League, join Rome against Antiochus III.

summary: The Romans defeated the Boii at the Battle of Mutina, effectively eliminating the Gallic threat in Italy.
text: The Battle of Mutina is fought between the Romans and the Boii (a Gallic tribe). The Romans are victorious in the battle which effectively ends the threat of the Gauls in Italy.

summary: Liternum and Puteoli were established as Roman colonies.
text: The Italian towns of Liternum and Puteoli become Roman colonies.

summary: Greek mathematician and geographer Eratosthenes died in Alexandria.
text: Eratosthenes, Greek mathematician, geographer and astronomer (b. 276 BC)

summary: Eumenes II of Pergamon appealed to Rome for assistance against Antiochus III the Great.
text: Eumenes II of Pergamum appeals to Rome for help against the Seleucid king Antiochus III who is threatening to conquer Greece. The Roman proconsul Titus Quinctius Flamininus supports the Roman championship of Greek autonomy in Anatolia.

summary: Titus Quinctius Flamininus warned Antiochus III the Great not to interfere with the Greek states.
text: Flamininus is sent to negotiate with Antiochus III and warns him not to interfere with the Greek states. Antiochus does not accept that Flamininus has the authority to speak for the Greeks and promises to leave Greece alone only if the Romans do the same.

summary: Titus Quinctius Flamininus persuaded the Achaean League to declare war on Antiochus III the Great and the Aetolians.
text: Flamininus attempts to rally the Greeks against Antiochus III and to counter the pro-Seleucid policy of the Aetolians. When the Aetolians call on Antiochus III for aid, Flamininus persuades the Achaean League to declare war on both parties. He also prevents Philopoemen from taking Sparta.

summary: Nabis of Sparta moved to recover lost Laconian territory, including Gythium.
text: In the meantime, the Spartan ruler, Nabis, moves to recover lost territory, including Gythium.

summary: The first public porticoes were constructed in Rome.
text: The first porticos were built in Rome.

summary: Cleopatra I Syra married King Ptolemy V Epiphanes of Egypt at Raphia.
text: Cleopatra I Syra, daughter of Antiochus III and Laodice, marries the Egyptian King Ptolemy V Epiphanes.

summary: The Achaean League requested Roman military aid against Sparta, prompting Rome to send a fleet and envoys.
text: The Achaeans respond to Sparta's renewed interest in recovering lost territory by sending an envoy to Rome with a request for help. In response, the Roman Senate sends the praetor Atilius with a navy, as well as an embassy headed by Titus Quinctius Flamininus.

summary: Spartan forces defeated the Achaean fleet and repelled Philopoemen at Gythium.
text: Not waiting for the Roman fleet to arrive, the Achaean army and navy head towards Gythium under the command of Philopoemen. The Achaean fleet under Tiso is defeated by the Spartan fleet. On land, the Achaeans are unable to defeat the Spartan forces outside Gythium and Philopoemen retreats to Tegea.

summary: Philopoemen overcame an ambush by Nabis of Sparta and defeated the Spartan army in Laconia.
text: When Philopoemen reenters Laconia for a second attempt, his forces are ambushed by the Spartan tyrant, Nabis, but nevertheless Philopoemen manages to gain a victory over the Spartan forces.

summary: Titus Quinctius Flamininus persuaded Philopoemen to halt his planned assault on Sparta.
text: Philopoemen's plans for capturing Sparta itself are put on hold at the request of the Roman envoy Flaminius after his arrival in Greece. In return, Nabis decides, for the moment, to accept the status quo.

summary: Philopoemen entered Sparta following the assassination of Nabis and forced the city into the Achaean League.
text: Nabis then appeals to the Aetolians for help. They send 1,000 cavalry under the command of Alexamenus to Sparta. However, the Aetolians murder Nabis and temporarily occupy Sparta. The Aetolian troops seize the palace and set about looting the city, but the inhabitants of Sparta are able to rally and force them leave the city. Philopoemen, however, takes advantage of the Aetolian treachery and enters Sparta with his Achaean army. Now in full control of Sparta, Philopoemen forces Sparta to become a member state of the Achaean League.

summary: Antiochus III the Great invaded Greece at the invitation of the Aetolian League, landing at Demetrias and taking Euboea.
text: Seleucid forces under their king, Antiochus III, invade Greece at the invitation of the Aetolian League, who are revolting against the Romans. The Aetolians appoint him commander in chief of their league. Antiochus lands in Demetrias, Thessaly with only 10,500 men and occupies Euboea. However, he finds little support for his cause in central Greece.

summary: Nabis, the tyrant and last independent ruler of Sparta, was assassinated by Aetolian troops.
text: Nabis, tyrant and last independent ruler (from 207 BC) of Sparta

summary: Roman forces defeated Antiochus III the Great at the Battle of Thermopylae, compelling his retreat from Greece.
text: The Romans under Manius Acilius Glabrio and Cato the Elder cut the Seleucid king Antiochus III off from his reinforcements in Thrace and outflank his position at the pass of Thermopylae in the Battle of Thermopylae. With the remainder of his troops, Antiochus flees to Chalcis on Euboea and from there he retreats by sea to Ephesus.

summary: Manius Acilius Glabrio campaigned against the Aetolian League until restrained by Titus Quinctius Flamininus.
text: Manius Acilius Glabrio then turns his attention to the Aetolian League, which has persuaded Antiochus to declare war against Rome, and is only prevented from crushing them by the intercession of Titus Quinctius Flamininus.

summary: Scipio Africanus persuaded the Roman Senate to mount an expedition against Antiochus III the Great in Anatolia.
text: Scipio Africanus persuades the Roman Senate to continue the war against Antiochus III by making him the chief commander and allowing him and his brother, Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus, to follow Antiochus into Anatolia.

summary: Rome adjusted its calendar via the Lex Acilia de intercalando to align with the seasons.
text: The Roman calendar, which is four months ahead of the seasons, is adjusted (by Lex Acilia de intercalando).

summary: Cisalpine Gaul was constituted as a Roman province.
text: Cisalpine Gaul becomes a Roman province.

summary: Rome rejected Carthage's early full payment of its war indemnity to retain influence over the city.
text: The Carthaginians manage to collect the indemnity due to Rome (through the peace treaty signed between them ten years earlier) but not payable in full for 50 years. The Romans, in order to keep their hold on Carthage, refuse to accept the early payment of the indemnity.

summary: A Rhodian fleet allied with Rome and Pergamon defeated a Seleucid fleet commanded by Hannibal at the Battle of the Eurymedon.
text: The Battle of the Eurymedon is fought between a Seleucid fleet and ships from Rhodes and Pergamum, who are allied with the Roman Republic. The Seleucids are led by the famous Carthaginian general Hannibal. The Rhodians and their allies are victorious and Hannibal's fleet is forced to flee.

summary: A Roman and Rhodian fleet defeated the Seleucid fleet at the naval Battle of Myonessus.
text: Subsequently, the naval Battle of Myonessus is fought between a Seleucid fleet and a Roman fleet with the help of Rhodian ships. The Romans and their allies are victorious.

summary: Rome remitted the tribute of Philip V of Macedon and restored his hostage son Demetrius in gratitude for his aid against enemies in Greece.
text: As Philip V of Macedon has aided Rome against her enemies on the Greek peninsula, his tribute to Rome is remitted and his son, Demetrius, is restored to him after being held hostage in Rome for a number of years.

summary: A Roman army under Scipio Africanus and Lucius Scipio crossed the Hellespont into Anatolia alongside King Eumenes II of Pergamon.
text: Meeting no further resistance from the Seleucids and their allies, the Roman army under general Scipio Africanus and his brother Lucius, along with King Eumenes II of Pergamum and other allies, cross the Hellespont into Anatolia.

summary: Roman and Pergamene forces defeated Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire at the Battle of Magnesia.
text: With the increasingly real threat to his Empire from the Romans, Antiochus III is eager to negotiate on the basis of Rome's previous demands, but the Romans insist that he first give up the region west of the Taurus Mountains. When Antiochus refuses, the Battle of Magnesia is fought near Magnesia ad Sipylum, on the plains of Lydia in Anatolia, between the Romans, led by the consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio and his brother, Scipio Africanus, with their ally Eumenes II of Pergamum, and the army of Antiochus III the Great of the Seleucid Empire. The resulting decisive Roman victory ends the conflict with the Seleucids for the control of Greece.

summary: Artaxias and Zariadres declared independence from the Seleucid Empire, establishing the Kingdom of Armenia and Sophene with Roman approval.
text: Following Antiochus III's defeat by the Romans, two of Antiochus III's Armenian satraps, Artaxias and Zariadres, declare themselves independent of the Seleucids. With Roman consent, they establish themselves as kings of the Kingdom of Armenia and the district of Sophene (Armenia Minor), respectively. Artaxias builds his capital, Artaxata, on the Araxes River (now the Aras River) near Lake Sevan.

summary: Rome rewarded Eumenes II of Pergamon with the Thracian Chersonese and former Seleucid lands in Anatolia.
text: For assisting the Romans in defeating Antiochus III, Eumenes II of Pergamum is rewarded with a great increase in territory. He is given control over the Thracian Chersonese (the modern Gallipoli peninsula) and over most of the former Seleucid possessions in Anatolia.

summary: The Appian Way was extended to Benevento and Venosa in Roman Italy.
text: One of the main highways in Roman Italy, the Via Appia, is extended to Benevento and Venosa.

summary: Cornelia, the second daughter of Scipio Africanus and later mother of the Gracchi, was born.
text: Cornelia, second daughter of Scipio Africanus. She will be considered by Roman society to be the perfect example of a virtuous Roman woman (d. 100 BC)

summary: Cato the Elder criticized consul Marcus Fulvius Nobilior for granting military awards for routine tasks.
text: Cato the Elder criticizes the consul Marcus Fulvius Nobilior for giving awards to Roman soldiers for doing ordinary tasks, such as digging wells.

summary: Deprived of Seleucid support after the Battle of Magnesia, the Aetolian League signed a peace treaty making it a subject ally of Rome.
text: The defeat of Antiochus III by the Romans in the Battle of Magnesia robs the Aetolian League of its principal foreign ally and makes it impossible for them to stand alone in continued opposition to Rome. The League is forced to sign a peace treaty with Rome that makes it a subject ally of the Republic. Although the League continues to exist in name, the power of the League is broken by the treaty and it never again constitutes a significant political or military force.

summary: Consul Gnaeus Manlius Vulso and King Eumenes II defeated the Galatians in Anatolia and subjected them to Pergamon.
text: The Romans under consul Gnaeus Manlius Vulso, along with a Pergamene army under Eumenes II, defeat the Galatians in Anatolia and make them subjects of Pergamum.

summary: Philopoemen led the Achaean League into Laconia, demolished Sparta's defensive wall, abolished Spartan laws, and made the League dominant in the Peloponnese.
text: The leader of the Achaean League, Philopoemen, enters northern Laconia with his army and a group of Spartan exiles. His army demolishes the wall that the former tyrant of Sparta, Nabis, has built around Sparta. Philopoemen then restores Spartan citizenship to the exiles and abolishes Spartan law, introducing Achaean law in its place. Sparta's role as a major power in Greece ends, while the Achaean League becomes the dominant power throughout the Peloponnese.

summary: Persistent conflicts among Greek cities and leagues reinforced Rome's conviction that regional peace required full Roman control.
text: The continuing quarrels among the Greek cities and leagues increases the conviction in Rome that there will be no peace in Greece until Rome takes full control.

summary: The Treaty of Apamea forced Antiochus III to cede his Anatolian possessions west of the Taurus, pay 15,000 talents, and hand over hostages.
text: Through the peace treaty of Apamea (in Phrygia), the Romans force the Seleucid king, Antiochus III, to surrender all his Greek and Anatolian possessions as far east as the Taurus Mountains, to pay 15,000 talents over a period of 12 years and to surrender to Rome the former Carthaginian general Hannibal, his elephants and his fleet, and furnish hostages, including the king's eldest son, Demetrius. Rome is now the master of the eastern Mediterranean while Antiochus III's empire is reduced to Syria, Mesopotamia, and western Iran.

summary: Hannibal escaped via Crete to Bithynia, taking refuge at the court of King Prusias I.
text: Hannibal flees via Crete to the court of King Prusias I of Bithynia who is engaged in warfare with Rome's ally, King Eumenes II of Pergamum.

summary: Under the Treaty of Apamea, Rome granted Phrygia, Lydia, Lycia, Pisidia, and Pamphylia to Eumenes II of Pergamon to serve as a buffer against the Seleucids.
text: Following the peace of Apamea, Eumenes II receives the provinces of Phrygia, Lydia, Lycia, Pisidia, and Pamphylia from his Roman allies, as the Romans have no desire to actually administer territory in Hellenistic Anatolia but want to see a strong, friendly state in Anatolia as a buffer zone against any possible Seleucid expansion in the future.

summary: Antiochus III was killed while pillaging a temple near Susa and was succeeded by his son Seleucus IV Philopator.
text: The Seleucid king, Antiochus III, attempts to collect tribute from a temple near Susa, Persia, where he was killed. He is succeeded by his son, Seleucus IV, who inherits an empire consisting of Syria, Mesopotamia, Babylonia, western Iran.

summary: Tribune Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus vetoed the prosecution of Scipio Africanus and was subsequently betrothed to Scipio's daughter Cornelia.
text: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus is elected tribune of the plebs, in which capacity he is recorded as having saved Scipio Africanus from prosecution by interposing his veto. Tiberius is no friend nor political ally of Scipio's, but feels that the general's services to Rome merit his release from the threat of trial like any common criminal. Supposedly, in gratitude for this action, Scipio betrothes his youngest daughter, Cornelia, to him.

summary: The construction of the Via Aemilia was completed from Ariminum to Placentia across northern Italy.
text: The construction of the Via Aemilia, a trunk road in the north Italian plains, running from Ariminum (Rimini), on the Adriatic coast, to Placentia (Piacenza) on the river Padus (Po), is completed.

summary: Ptolemy V appointed Queen Cleopatra I as his vizier.
text: Queen Cleopatra I is appointed Vizier (Chief Minister) to the King Ptolemy V Epiphanes.

summary: Seleucid ruler Antiochus III the Great died near Susa.
text: Antiochus III the Great, Seleucid king of the Hellenistic Syrian Empire from 223 BC (b. c. 241 BC)

summary: The Roman Senate issued a decree severely restricting the Bacchanalia cult across Italy.
text: The rapid spread of the Bacchanalia cult throughout the Roman Republic, which, it is claimed, indulges in all kinds of crimes and political conspiracies at its nocturnal meetings, leads to the Roman Senate issuing a decree, the Senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus, by which the Bacchanalia are prohibited throughout all Italy except in certain special cases which must be approved specifically by the Senate.

summary: King Eumenes II of Pergamon defeated King Prusias I of Bithynia in battle.
text: Eumenes II of Pergamum defeats Prusias I of Bithynia.

summary: Future Ptolemaic king of Egypt Ptolemy VI Philometor was born.
text: Ptolemy VI Philometor, king of Egypt, who will reign from 180 BC (d. 145 BC)

summary: Cato the Elder accused Scipio Africanus and Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus of bribery, prompting Scipio Africanus to retire to Liternum.
text: The Roman general Scipio Africanus and his brother Lucius are accused by Cato the Elder and his supporters of having received bribes from the late Seleucid king Antiochus III. Scipio defies his accusers, reminds the Romans of their debt to him, and retires to his country house at Liternum in Campania. However, Cato is successful in breaking the political influence of Lucius Scipio and Scipio Africanus.

summary: The Roman general and statesman Publius Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus was born.
text: Publius Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus, leading general and politician of the Roman Republic. As consul he will be the commander of the final siege and destruction of Carthage and will be the leader of the senators opposed to the Gracchi (d. 129 BC)

summary: Cato the Elder and Lucius Valerius Flaccus were elected censors at Rome and launched a campaign to preserve traditional Roman customs.
text: Cato the Elder, along with his colleague, Lucius Valerius Flaccus, are elected censors in Rome. Already the champion of the ancient, austere Roman way of life, Cato inaugurates a puritanical campaign. He aims at preserving the mos maiorum ("ancestral custom") and combating all Greek influences, which he believes are undermining the older Roman standards of morality. He passes measures taxing luxury and strictly revises the list of persons eligible for the Senate. Abuses by tax gatherers are brought under control, and public building is promoted as a worthy cause.

states.value: Cato the Elder and Lucius Valerius Flaccus

summary: Rome sent an embassy led by Appius Claudius Pulcher to Greece and Macedonia to observe Philip V.
text: With concerns rising in Rome over whether Philip V of Macedon is preparing for a new war with the Romans, Appius Claudius Pulcher is sent at the head of an embassy into Macedonia and Greece to observe Philip's activities.

summary: The Romans established the colony of Pisaurum in the territory of the Picentes.
text: The town of Pisaurum is established by the Romans as a colony in the territory of the Picentes, a tribe living in the Marche on the Adriatic.

summary: Cato the Elder completed the Basilica Porcia in Rome during his censorship.
text: The oldest known basilica, the Basilica Porcia, is completed in Rome by Cato the Elder during the time he is censor. The building is used by the Romans for transacting business and disposing of legal matters.

summary: The Roman comic playwright Plautus died.
text: Titus Macchius Plautus, Roman comic dramatist, whose works, loosely adapted from Greek plays, established a truly Roman drama in the Latin language (b. c. 254 BC)

summary: Rome established colonies at Mutina, Pisa, and Parma in northern and central Italy.
text: Roman colonies are established at Mutina (later Modena), Pisa and Parma in northern and central Italy.

summary: The Roman general Scipio Africanus died at Liternum in Campania.
text: The Roman general Scipio Africanus dies at Liternum in Campania.

summary: Hannibal poisoned himself at Libyssa in Bithynia to avoid being surrendered to Rome by King Prusias I.
text: The Roman statesman Titus Quinctius Flamininus is sent to the court of Prusias I, king of Bithynia, to demand the surrender of the former Carthaginian statesman and general Hannibal. When Hannibal finds out that Prusias is about to agree to the Roman demands and thus betray him, he poisons himself in the village of Libyssa in Bithynia.

summary: Philopoemen, general of the Achaean League, was captured during a rebellion at Messene and forced to drink poison.
text: The town of Messene rebels against the Achaean League. When the Achaean League's general, Philopoemen, intervenes to try to control the rebellion, he is captured during a skirmish and imprisoned. He is then given poison to take so that he can die honourably.

summary: Roman politician Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Serapio was born.
text: Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Serapio, consul in 138 BC, who will have a prominent part in the murder of Tiberius Gracchus by leading a group of conservative senators and other knights in opposition to Gracchus and his supporters (d. 132 BC).

summary: The Roman general and statesman Scipio Africanus died.
text: Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus Major, Roman statesman and general, famous for his victory over the Carthaginian leader Hannibal in the Battle of Zama in 202 BC, which ended the Second Punic War and gave him the surname Africanus (b. 236 BC)

summary: The Greek statesman and general Philopoemen died at Messene.
text: Philopoemen, Greek general and statesman, strategos of the Achaean League on eight occasions and a major figure in the demise of Sparta as a Greek power (b. 253 BC)

summary: The Carthaginian general Hannibal died in Bithynia.
text: Hannibal, Carthaginian statesman, military commander and tactician, one of history's great military leaders, who has commanded the Carthaginian forces against Rome in the Second Punic War (b. 247 BC)

summary: Prusias II succeeded his father Prusias I as king of Bithynia.
text: The king of Bithynia, Prusias I Chlorus dies and is succeeded by his son, who rules as Prusias II.

summary: Future Ptolemaic king Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II was born.
text: Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II, king of the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt (d. 116 BC)

summary: King Prusias I of Bithynia died.
text: Prusias I Chlorus, king of Bithynia (b. c. 228 BC)

summary: Ptolemy VI Philometor succeeded his poisoned father Ptolemy V under the regency of Cleopatra I.
text: Ptolemy V is poisoned after a reign of 24 years in which the Egyptian kingdom has declined in power and influence and has lost most of its empire outside Egypt other than Cyprus and Cyrenaica. The elder of his two sons, Ptolemy VI Philometor succeeds him, but since he is an infant, he rules under the regency of his mother Cleopatra the Syrian.

summary: Rome founded a frontier colony at Aquileia to check the Illyrians.
text: Rome founds a colony at Aquileia, on the narrow strip of land between the mountains and the lagoons, as a frontier fortress to check the advance of the Illyrians.

summary: Pharnaces I invaded Galatia against Eumenes II and Ariarathes IV, but negotiations mediated by Roman deputies broke down.
text: Pharnaces I of Pontus decides to attack both Eumenes II of Pergamum and Ariarathes IV of Cappadocia and therefore invades Galatia with a large force. Eumenes leads an army to oppose him, however, hostilities are soon suspended following the arrival of Roman deputies, who have been appointed by the Roman Senate to inquire into the matters in dispute. Negotiations take place at Pergamum but are inconclusive, with Pharnaces' demands being rejected by the Romans as unreasonable. As a consequence, the war between Pontus and Pergamum and Cappadocia is renewed.

summary: King Philip V of Macedon had his son Demetrius executed after Perseus accused him of treason and an alliance with Rome.
text: After three years of intriguing against his younger brother Demetrius, including accusing him of coveting the succession to the Macedonian throne and being allied to Rome, Perseus persuades his father King Philip V of Macedon to have Demetrius executed.

summary: Rome defeated the Ligurians near Genoa and deported 40,000 of them, completing the subjugation of Italy.
text: Rome completes its subjugation of all of Italy with the defeat of the Ligurians in a battle near modern Genoa. Rome deports 40,000 Ligurians to other areas of the Republic.

summary: Lucca was established as a Roman colony.
text: Lucca becomes a Roman colony.

summary: Cleopatra I ruled as co-regent with her young son Ptolemy VI Philometor while maintaining friendly relations with Rome.
text: Ptolemy VI Philometor, aged 6, rules as co-regent with his mother, Cleopatra I, who, although a daughter of a Seleucid king, does not take King Seleucus IV's side and remains on friendly terms with Rome.

summary: Apollodorus of Athens, the Greek scholar and grammarian, was born.
text: Apollodorus of Athens, Greek scholar and grammarian (d. c. 120 BC)

summary: Future Roman consul and general Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus was born.
text: Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus, Roman consul (d. 113 BC)

summary: Viriathus, the Lusitanian chieftain and general, was born.
text: Viriathus, Lusitanian chieftain and general (d. 139 BC)

summary: Aristophanes of Byzantium, Greek scholar and head librarian of Alexandria, died.
text: Aristophanes of Byzantium, Greek scholar, critic and grammarian, particularly renowned for his work in Homeric scholarship, but also for work on other classical authors such as Pindar and Hesiod. After early studies under leading scholars in Alexandria, he has been chief librarian since about 195 BC (b. 257 BC)

summary: Lucius Valerius Flaccus, Roman statesman, former consul, and censor, died.
text: Lucius Valerius Flaccus, Roman statesman, consul in 195 BC, censor in 183 BC and colleague of Cato the Elder

summary: Ptolemy V Epiphanes, King of Egypt, died.
text: Ptolemy V Epiphanes, king of Egypt (b. 210 BC)

summary: The Roman Republic passed the Lex Villia Annalis, establishing minimum age limits and career requirements for public office.
text: The Lex Villia annalis, which established minimum ages for high office and required a minimum of two years in private life between offices, was passed.

summary: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus arrived in Hispania as Roman governor to quell uprisings.
text: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus goes to Hispania as Roman governor to deal with uprisings there.

summary: The Pons Aemilius, regarded as the world's first stone bridge, was completed across the Tiber in Rome.
text: The Pons Aemilius is completed across the Tiber River in Rome. It is regarded as the world's first stone bridge.

summary: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus was appointed censor and princeps senatus in Rome.
text: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus is appointed both censor and princeps senatus.

summary: Philip V of Macedon died at Amphipolis and was succeeded by his son Perseus.
text: Philip V of Macedon dies at Amphipolis in Macedonia, remorseful for having put his younger son Demetrius to death, at the instigation of his older son Perseus. Nevertheless, he is succeeded by his son Perseus.

summary: Eumenes II of Pergamum defeated Pharnaces I of Pontus, compelling Pharnaces to cede conquests in Galatia and Paphlagonia.
text: Eumenes II of Pergamum defeats Pharnaces I of Pontus in a major battle. Finding himself unable to cope with the combined forces of Eumenes and Ariarathes IV of Cappadocia, Pharnaces is compelled to purchase peace by ceding all his conquests in Galatia and Paphlagonia, with the exception of Sinope.

summary: Philip V, King of Macedonia who fought multiple wars against Rome, died.
text: Philip V, king of Macedonia from 221 BC, whose attempt to extend Macedonian influence throughout Greece has occurred at a time of growing Roman involvement in Greek affairs and resulted in his military defeat by Rome (b. 238 BC)

summary: Lucius Postumius Albinus celebrated a triumph in Rome after conquering the Vaccaei and Lusitani in Hispania Ulterior.
text: In Rome, the praetor Lucius Postumius Albinus celebrates a triumph after conquering the Vaccaei and Lusitani during his time as Roman commander in the province of Hispania Ulterior.

summary: Perseus renewed Macedonia's treaty with Rome while expanding his army and diplomatic alliances.
text: One of Perseus' first acts on becoming king of Macedonia is to renew the treaty between Macedonia and Rome. In the meantime, Perseus builds up the Macedonian army and puts out feelers for creating an alliance with the Greek leagues, with his northern barbarian neighbours, and also with the Seleucid king Seleucus IV.

summary: Perseus of Macedon married Laodice, the daughter of Seleucid king Seleucus IV.
text: Perseus of Macedonia marries Laodice, the daughter of the Seleucid king Seleucus IV.

summary: The Roman Republic subdued the Illyrian tribe of the Histri after two military campaigns.
text: After two military campaigns, the Romans finally subdue the Illyrian tribe of the Histri.

summary: The Roman Republic founded the colony of Luna at the mouth of the Magra River in northern Italy.
text: Luni in northern Italy is founded by the Romans with the name Luna at the mouth of the Magra River.

summary: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus subdued Sardinia and enslaved a portion of the local population.
text: The Roman general, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, subdues Sardinia, enslaving some of the population.

summary: Cleopatra I Syra died, leaving her son Ptolemy VI Philometor to rule Egypt alone.
text: Cleopatra I Syra dies leaving her son, Ptolemy VI, to rule Egypt alone.

summary: Cleopatra I Syra, Queen of Egypt and regent for Ptolemy VI Philometor, died.
text: Cleopatra I Syra, queen of Egypt from 193 BC, wife of Ptolemy V Epiphanes and regent for her young son, Ptolemy VI Philometor (b. c. 204 BC)

summary: Heliodorus assassinated Seleucus IV Philopator and seized the throne of the Seleucid Empire.
text: King Seleucus IV of Syria arranges for the exchange of his brother Antiochus for Demetrius, the son of Seleucus IV, who has been a hostage in Rome following the Treaty of Apamea in 188 BC. However, Seleucus IV is assassinated by his chief minister Heliodorus, who then seizes the Syrian throne.

summary: Antiochus IV Epiphanes ousted Heliodorus and seized the Seleucid throne for himself.
text: Antiochus manages to oust Heliodorus and takes advantage of Demetrius' captivity in Rome to seize the throne for himself under the name Antiochus IV Epiphanes.

summary: The Roman Senate refused to take sides when Ptolemy VI claimed Coele-Syria and both Egypt and Syria appealed to Rome.
text: During this period of uncertainty in Syria, the Egyptian ruler, Ptolemy VI, lays claim to Coele Syria, Palestine, and Phoenicia, which the Seleucid king Antiochus III has previously conquered. Both the Syrian and Egyptian parties appeal to Rome for help, but the Roman Senate refuses to take sides.

summary: Antiochus IV Epiphanes appointed Timarchus as governor of Media to counter the Parthian threat and named Heracleides minister of royal finances.
text: Timarchus is appointed governor of Media in western Persia by Antiochus IV to deal with the growing threat from the Parthians. At the same time, Timarchus' brother, Heracleides, becomes minister of the royal finances.

summary: Pergamon began construction of the western front of the Pergamon Altar.
text: The construction of the western front of the altar in Pergamum, Turkey, begins and is finished in 156 BC. A reconstruction of it is now kept at the Pergamon Museum in Berlin.

summary: Quintus Caecilius Metellus, Roman consul and dictator, died.
text: Quintus Caecilius Metellus, Roman consul and dictator (b. c. 250 BC)

summary: Seleucid king Seleucus IV Philopator died.
text: Seleucus IV Philopator, king of the Seleucid dynasty, who has ruled since 187 BC (b. c. 217 BC)

summary: Queen Cleopatra I of Egypt died.
text: Cleopatra I of Egypt, mother of Ptolemy VI.

summary: The first street pavements were laid in Rome.
text: The first street pavements were laid in Rome.

summary: Roman consul and censor Publius Aelius Paetus died.
text: Publius Aelius Paetus, Roman consul and censor

summary: Roman general and statesman Titus Quinctius Flamininus died.
text: Titus Quinctius Flamininus, Roman general and statesman whose skillful diplomacy has enabled him to establish a Roman protectorate over Greece (b. c. 227 BC)

summary: Ptolemy VI Philometor married his sister Cleopatra II.
text: Ptolemy VI Philometor marries his sister, Cleopatra II.

summary: The Temple of Fortuna Equestris was dedicated in Rome.
text: Dedication of the Temple of Fortuna Equestris.

summary: Antiochus IV Epiphanes paid the Roman Republic the remaining indemnity from the Treaty of Apamea.
text: Antiochus IV pays the remainder of the war indemnity that has been imposed by the Romans on Antiochus III in the Treaty of Apamea (188 BC).

summary: Future Seleucid ruler Antiochus V Eupator was born.
text: Antiochus V Eupator, ruler of the Seleucid Empire from 164 BC (d. 162 BC)

summary: Roman consul and general Lucius Cornelius Lentulus died.
text: Lucius Cornelius Lentulus, Roman consul and general

summary: Eumenes II of Pergamon warned the Roman Senate about Perseus of Macedon and was later ambushed near Delphi.
text: Eumenes II of Pergamum travels to Rome to warn the Roman Senate of the danger from Perseus of Macedon. On his return from Rome, Eumenes II is nearly killed at Delphi and Perseus is suspected of being the instigator.

summary: The Roman Senate arbitrated a border dispute between Carthage and Numidia in Numidia's favor.
text: The peace treaty at the end of the Second Punic War requires that all border disputes involving Carthage be arbitrated by the Roman Senate and requires Carthage to get explicit Roman approval before going to war. As a result, envoys from Carthage appear before the Roman Senate to request resolution of a boundary dispute with Numidia. The dispute is decided in Numidia's favour.

summary: Roman consul and general Quintus Fulvius Flaccus died.
text: Quintus Fulvius Flaccus, Roman consul and general

summary: The Roman Republic declared war on Macedonia, initiating the Third Macedonian War.
text: Third Macedonian War: Rome declared war on Macedonia.

summary: Epirus joined Macedonia in its war against Rome.
text: Epirus joins Macedonia in the latter's fight against Rome. However, the leagues of southern Greece remain neutral.

summary: Perseus of Macedon defeated a Roman army led by consul Publius Licinius Crassus at the Battle of Callicinus.
text: Thanks to the efforts of Eumenes II of Pergamum while in Rome, the Romans declare war on Macedonia and send troops to Thessaly, thus beginning the Third Macedonian War. In the resulting Battle of Callicinus the Macedonians, led by their king, Perseus, are victorious over a Roman force led by consul Publius Licinius Crassus.

summary: The Roman Republic dissolved the Boeotian League.
text: Boiotian League dissolved by the Romans.

summary: The Roman Senate founded Colonia Libertinorum Carteia in Hispania as the first Roman colony outside Italy.
text: The first Roman colony outside Italy is founded at Carteia in southern Hispania after Iberian-born descendants of Roman soldiers appear before the Roman Senate to request a town to live in and are given Carteia, which is named Colonia Libertinorum Carteia.

summary: Rome sent Lucius Postumius Albinus as ambassador to Masinissa of Numidia and to Carthage to recruit troops against Macedonia.
text: Lucius Postumius Albinus is sent by Rome as an ambassador to King Masinissa of Numidia, and to the Carthaginians in order to raise troops for the war against Perseus of Macedonia.

summary: King Perseus of Macedon repulsed a Roman army under Aulus Hostilius Mancinus in Thessaly while Roman and Pergamene troops sacked Abdera.
text: In Thessaly, King Perseus of Macedon repulses a Roman army which is commanded by Aulus Hostilius Mancinus. Meanwhile, the Thracian city of Abdera is sacked by Roman and Pergamese troops.

summary: Antiochus IV Epiphanes invaded Egypt, captured Ptolemy VI Philometor, and conquered all but Alexandria.
text: With the guardians of the young king Ptolemy VI Philometor demanding the return of Coele-Syria to Egyptian control, the Seleucid king, Antiochus IV Epiphanes, decides on a preemptive strike against Egypt and invades the country, conquering all but the city of Alexandria. He is also able to capture Ptolemy VI.

summary: Antiochus IV Epiphanes left Ptolemy VI on the Egyptian throne as a puppet and garrisoned Pelusium.
text: Antiochus IV decides to let Ptolemy VI continue as king of Egypt, but as his puppet. He does this to minimise any reaction from Rome towards his invasion. Antiochus IV then departs Egypt to deal with disturbances in Palestine, but he safeguards his access to Egypt with a strong garrison in Pelusium.

summary: The citizens of Alexandria acclaimed Ptolemy VIII Physcon as king, after which the Ptolemaic siblings agreed to rule Egypt jointly.
text: With Antiochus IV now absent from the country, the citizens of Alexandria choose Ptolemy VI's brother Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II as their king. The two Ptolemy brothers agree to rule Egypt jointly with their sister Cleopatra II and Coele Syria is invaded by the Egyptian forces.

summary: Hellenistic grammarian Dionysius Thrax was born.
text: Dionysios Thrax, a Hellenic grammarian who will live and work in Alexandria and later on Rhodes (d. 90 BC)

summary: Roman tragic poet Lucius Accius was born in Pisaurum.
text: Lucius Accius (or Lucius Attius), Roman tragic poet and literary scholar (d. c. 86 BC)

summary: Greek-Egyptian businesswoman Apollonia Senmothis was born.
text: Apollonia Senmothis, Greek-Egyptian businesswoman.

summary: Perseus of Macedon trapped a Roman army under Quintus Marcius Philippus near the Vale of Tempe, but failed to exploit the tactical advantage.
text: Macedonian forces led by Perseus of Macedon trap a Roman army led by Consul Quintus Marcius Phillipus near Tempe, but the Macedonians fail to take advantage of their resulting superior tactical position.

summary: King Perseus of Macedon asked Antiochus IV Epiphanes to join forces against Rome, but received no response.
text: King Perseus asks the Seleucid King Antiochus IV to join forces with him against the danger that Rome presents to all of the Hellenic monarchs. Antiochus IV does not respond.

summary: Tribune Quintus Voconius Saxa introduced the Lex Voconia in Rome, prohibiting wealthy citizens from naming women as heirs.
text: Lex Voconia (The Voconian Law) is introduced in Rome by the tribune, Quintus Voconius Saxa, with the support of Cato the Elder. This law prohibits those who own property valued at 100,000 sesterces from making a woman their heir.

summary: Roman epic poet and dramatist Quintus Ennius died.
text: Quintus Ennius, Roman epic poet, dramatist, and satirist, the most influential of the early Latin poets – and often called the founder of Roman literature or the father of Roman poetry. His epic Annales, a poem telling the story of Rome from the wanderings of Aeneas to Ennius' own time, remains the national epic until it is later eclipsed by Virgil's Aeneid.

summary: Lucius Anicius Gallus defeated King Gentius of Illyria at Scodra and captured him, knocking Illyria out of the war against Rome.
text: The king of Illyria, Gentius, is defeated at Scodra by a Roman force under Lucius Anicius Gallus and then brought to Rome as a captive to be interned in Iguvium. This loss removes Illyria as an important ally for Macedonia and effectively weakens Perseus of Macedon in his battle with Rome.

summary: Consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus arrived in Thessaly to assume command of the trapped Roman army.
text: The Roman general, Lucius Aemilius Paulus, is elected consul and arrives in Thessaly to lead the Roman army which has been trapped by Perseus' forces.

summary: Lucius Aemilius Paullus decisively defeated and captured Perseus of Macedon at the Battle of Pydna, ending the Third Macedonian War.
text: The Battle of Pydna (in southern Macedonia) gives Roman forces under Lucius Aemilius Paulus a crushing victory over Perseus and his Macedonian forces, thus ending the Third Macedonian War. Perseus is captured by the Romans and will spend the rest of his life in captivity at Alba Fucens, near Rome.

summary: The Roman Republic dissolved the Macedonian kingdom into four client republics and deported hundreds of leading Greeks to Rome.
text: The Macedonian kingdom is broken up by the Romans into four smaller states, and all the Greek cities which have offered aid to Macedonia, even just in words, are punished. The Romans take hundreds of prisoners from the leading families of Macedonia, including the historian Polybius.

summary: Ptolemy VI, Ptolemy VIII, and Cleopatra II sent a renewed request to Rome for aid against the Seleucids.
text: The joint rulers of Egypt, Ptolemy VI, Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II and their sister Cleopatra II send a renewed request to Rome for aid.

summary: The fleet of Antiochus IV Epiphanes won a victory off Cyprus and took control of the island.
text: The fleet of the Seleucid king Antiochus IV wins a victory off Cyprus, whose governor then surrenders the island to him.

summary: Roman ambassador Gaius Popillius Laenas drew a circle around Antiochus IV outside Alexandria, forcing him to withdraw from Egypt and Cyprus.
text: Antiochus IV then invades Egypt again and occupies Lower Egypt and his forces camp outside Alexandria. However, the Roman ambassador in Alexandria, Gaius Popillius Laenas, intervenes. He presents Antiochus IV with an ultimatum that he evacuate Egypt and Cyprus immediately. Antiochus, taken by surprise, asks for time to consider. Popillius, however, draws a circle in the earth (i.e. "a line in the sand") around the king with his walking stick and demands an unequivocal answer before Antiochus leaves the circle. Fearing the consequences of a war with Rome, the king agrees to comply with the ambassador's demands. In return, the Romans agree that Antiochus IV can retain southern Syria, to which Egypt has laid claim, thus enabling Antiochus IV to preserve the territorial integrity of his realm.

summary: Roman politician and agrarian reformer Tiberius Gracchus was born.
text: Tiberius Gracchus, Roman politician who would create turmoil in the Republic through his attempts to legislate agrarian reforms in the Roman Republic (d. 133 BC)

summary: Roman comic poet Caecilius Statius died.
text: Caecilius Statius, Roman comic poet, admirer and imitator of the Greek playwright Menander (b. c. 219 BC)

summary: Roman authorities used captured documents to incriminate leaders of the Achaean League and deported many influential Greeks to Rome.
text: Private documents collected by the Romans when they capture Perseus of Macedon incriminate political leaders of the Achaean League. Many influential Greeks are deported to Rome.

summary: Lucius Aemilius Paullus destroyed seventy towns across Epirus and enslaved over 100,000 citizens on orders from the Roman Senate.
text: On his way back to Rome, the Roman general Lucius Aemilius Paulus is ordered by the Roman Senate to inflict a brutal revenge on Epirus for being an ally of Macedonia. Seventy towns in Epirus are destroyed, and at least 100,000 citizens are sold into slavery. These actions take place despite the fact that Epirus has not aided Perseus in his war with Rome.

summary: Lucius Aemilius Paullus celebrated a triumph in Rome with Perseus as his captive, bringing vast wealth that ended direct taxation for Roman citizens.
text: Lucius Aemilius Paulus returns to Italy with the King of Macedonia, Perseus, as his prisoner for his triumphal procession in Rome, where the Macedonians captured are sold into slavery. The huge amount of booty brought home after the battle enriches Rome allowing the Government to relieve her citizens of direct taxation. As a gesture of acknowledgment for his achievements in Macedonia, the senate awards Lucius Aemilius Paulus the surname Macedonicus.

summary: Former Roman consul Gaius Claudius Pulcher died.
text: Gaius Claudius Pulcher, Roman consul in 177 BC

summary: Rome captured King Perseus and partitioned Macedonia into four subject districts.
text: Third Macedonian War: The Macedonian king Perseus of Macedon was captured. Macedonia was divided into four districts subject to Rome.

summary: Antiochus IV Epiphanes mounted a campaign against the Parthians, leaving Lysias in charge of southern Syria.
text: The Seleucid king Antiochus IV mounts a campaign against the Parthians who are threatening his empire in the east. He leaves his chancellor, Lysias, with responsibility for the government of southern Syria and the guardianship of his son.

summary: Terence's play Andria was performed for the first time.
text: The Roman playwright Terence's Andria (The Girl from Andros) is first performed.

summary: Perseus, the last Antigonid king of Macedonia, died in Roman captivity.
text: Perseus, the last Macedonian king of the Antigonid dynasty (b. c. 212 BC)

summary: Terence's play Hecyra was performed for the first time.
text: The Roman playwright Terence's play Hecyra (The Mother-in-Law) is first performed.

summary: Ptolemy VIII expelled his brother Ptolemy VI Philometor from Alexandria, forcing him to flee to Rome.
text: The Egyptian King Ptolemy VI Philometor is expelled from Alexandria by his brother Ptolemy VIII Euergetes and flees to Rome to seek support.

summary: Antiochus IV Epiphanes died in Persia and was succeeded by his young son Antiochus V Eupator under the regency of Lysias.
text: The Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes died while on a campaign in Tabae (or Gabae, now Isfahan) in Persia. He is succeeded by his son Antiochus V Eupator who is only nine years old. The regent for the boy is the late king's chancellor, Lysias, who was left in charge of Syria when Antiochus IV departed for his campaign in Persia. Lysias is, however, seriously challenged by other Syrian generals and finds himself with a precarious hold on power. To make matters worse for him, the Roman Senate is holding Demetrius, the son of the former king Seleucus IV and, therefore, the rightful heir to the Seleucid throne, as a hostage. By threatening to release him, the Senate can influence events in the Seleucid kingdom.

summary: Rhodes concluded a treaty of alliance with Rome.
text: Rhodes signs a treaty with Rome and becomes its ally.

summary: Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus was elected censor in Rome.
text: Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus is elected censor in Rome.

summary: Construction began on the Gigantomachy frieze of the Pergamon Altar depicting Athena attacking the Giants.
text: Construction of the detail of the frieze from the east front of the altar in Pergamon, Athena Attacking the Giants, begins and is finished eight years later. It is now kept at the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, Antikensammlung, Pergamonmuseum in Berlin, Germany.

summary: Cleopatra Thea, future queen of the Seleucid Empire, was born.
text: Cleopatra Thea Euergetis ("Benefactress"), ruler of the Seleucid kingdom from 125 BC, a daughter of Ptolemy VI of Egypt and his sister/wife Cleopatra II (d. 121 BC)

summary: Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes died and was succeeded by Antiochus V Eupator.
text: Antiochus IV Epiphanes ("God Manifest"), Seleucid king of the Syrian kingdom who has reigned since 175 BC, and has encouraged Greek culture and institutions but also attempted to suppress Judaism, which has led to the uprisings in Judea towards the end of his reign (b. c. 215 BC)

summary: Roman intervention partitioned the Ptolemaic realm, granting Cyrenaica to Ptolemy VIII and Egypt and Cyprus to Ptolemy VI Philometor.
text: The Ptolemaic king Ptolemy VI Philometor is restored to his throne through the intervention of the citizens of Alexandria. However, the Romans intervene and partition the kingdom, giving Ptolemy VIII Euergetes Cyrenaica and Ptolemy VI Cyprus and Egypt. The two brothers accept the Roman partition.

summary: Terence's play Heauton Timorumenos was first performed in Rome.
text: The Roman playwright Terence's play Heauton Timorumenos ("The Self-Tormentor") is first performed.

summary: Roman politician Marcus Aemilius Scaurus was born.
text: Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, Roman politician and ambassador (d. 89 BC)

summary: Roman plebeian tribune and agrarian reformer Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus was born.
text: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, Roman politician, who, as a plebeian tribune, will cause political turmoil in the Republic through his attempts to legislate agrarian reforms; his political ideals will eventually lead to his death at the hands of supporters of the conservative faction (Optimates) of the Roman Senate (d. 132 BC)

summary: Roman consul Manius Juventius Thalna died.
text: Manius Juventius Thalna, Roman consul (b. before 206 BC)

summary: Demetrius I Soter escaped Rome, returned to Syria, executed Antiochus V Eupator and Lysias, and claimed the Seleucid throne.
text: With the aid of the Greek statesman and historian Polybius, the son of the former Seleucid king Seleucus IV Philopator, Demetrius escapes from Rome, where he has been held as a hostage for many years, and returns to Syria to claim the throne from his cousin Antiochus V. In the resulting dispute, Antiochus V and his regent, Lysias, are overthrown and put to death. Demetrius then establishes himself on the Seleucid throne.

summary: Young Seleucid king Antiochus V Eupator was overthrown and put to death by Demetrius I Soter.
text: Antiochus V Eupator, ruler of the Seleucid Empire, who has reigned since 164 BC (b. c. 173 BC)

summary: Seleucid general and regent Lysias was overthrown and executed.
text: Lysias or Lusias, Seleucid general and governor of Syria and regent for Antiochus V Eupator

summary: Roman statesman and general Gnaeus Octavius was assassinated in Syria.
text: Gnaeus Octavius, Roman statesman and general

summary: The Roman Senate backed Ptolemy VIII's claim to Cyprus but disengaged after his attempt to conquer the island failed.
text: Ptolemy VIII Euergetes, now king of Cyrenaica, convinces the Roman Senate to back his claim for control of Cyprus, but the Egyptian king Ptolemy VI Philometor ignores this threat, and after Ptolemy VIII Euergetes' attempt to conquer the island fails, the Roman Senate disengages from the dispute.

summary: Terence's plays Eunuchus and Phormio were first performed in Rome.
text: The Roman playwright Terence's plays Eunuchus (The Eunuch) and Phormio are first performed.

summary: Envoys of Judas Maccabeus concluded a treaty of friendship with the Roman Senate.
text: Envoys of Judas Maccabeus conclude a treaty of friendship with the Roman Senate.

summary: Praetor Marcus Pomponius secured a senatorial decree expelling philosophers and rhetoricians from Rome.
text: Marcus Pomponius, praetor in 161 BC, obtains a decree of the senate, forbidding philosophers and rhetoricians from living in Rome.

summary: Cleopatra III, future queen of Egypt, was born.
text: Cleopatra III, queen of Egypt from 142 BC (d. 101 BC)

summary: Demetrius II Nicator, future king of the Seleucid Empire, was born.
text: Demetrius II Nicator, king of the Seleucid Empire from 145 BC and 129 BC (d. 125 BC)

summary: Seleucid king Demetrius I Soter defeated a Jewish rebellion in Palestine.
text: The Seleucid king, Demetrius I Soter defeats a Jewish rebellion at Palestine.

summary: Seleucid forces defeated the Maccabees at the Battle of Elasa, where Judas Maccabeus was killed.
text: Judas Maccabeus and many of his supporters regroup to face the Seleucid forces in the Battle of Elasa (near modern day Ramallah). Greatly outnumbered, the Maccabees are defeated and Judas Maccabeus is killed during the battle.

summary: Jonathan Maccabeus succeeded his brother Judas Maccabeus as army commander and leader of the Maccabees.
text: Judas Maccabeus is succeeded as army commander and leader of the Maccabees by his younger brother, Jonathan Maccabeus.

summary: Demetrius I defeated and killed the rebel Timarchus and was recognized as Seleucid king by the Roman Senate.
text: Demetrius I defeats and kills the rebel general Timarchus and is recognized as king of the Seleucid empire by the Roman Senate. Demetrius acquires his surname of Soter (meaning Saviour) from the Babylonians, for delivering them from the tyranny of Timarchus. The Seleucid empire is temporarily united again.

summary: Mithridates I of Parthia seized Media from the Seleucid Empire following the death of Timarchus.
text: The Parthian King, Mithradates I, seizes Media from the Seleucids following the death of Timarchus.

summary: Artavasdes I succeeded his father Artaxias I as king of Armenia.
text: Artavasdes I succeeds his father Artaxias I as king of Armenia.

summary: Terence's comedy Adelphoe was first performed at the funeral games of Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus.
text: The Roman playwright Terence's play Adelphoe (The Brothers) is first performed at the funeral of the Roman general, Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus.

summary: Future king of Numidia Jugurtha was born.
text: Jugurtha, King of Numidia (d. 104 BC)

summary: Greek astronomer and mathematician Theodosius of Bithynia was born.
text: Theodosius of Bithynia, Greek astronomer and mathematician who will write Spherics, a book on the geometry of the sphere (d. c. 100 BC), later translated from Arabic back into Latin to help restore knowledge of Euclidean geometry to the West.

summary: Roman statesman and general Quintus Caecilius Metellus Numidicus was born.
text: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Numidicus, Roman statesman and general

summary: Artaxias I, founder of the Artaxiad dynasty and king of Armenia, died.
text: Artaxias I, king of Armenia who has ruled since 190 BC and the founder of the Artaxiad dynasty, whose members would rule the Kingdom of Armenia for nearly two centuries

summary: Roman general and politician Gaius Laelius died.
text: Gaius Laelius, Roman general and politician who was involved in Rome's victory during the Second Punic War between Rome and Carthage

summary: Judas Maccabeus, leader of the Maccabean revolt against the Seleucid Empire, died.
text: Judas Maccabeus, third son of the Jewish priest Mattathias, who led the Maccabean revolt against the Seleucid Empire until his death

summary: Roman general and victor of Pydna Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus died.
text: Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus, Roman consul, politician and general whose victory over the Macedonians in the Battle of Pydna ended the Third Macedonian War (b. c. 229 BC)

summary: Timarchus, rebel governor of Media, was killed in battle by Seleucid forces under Demetrius I Soter.
text: Timarchus, Seleucid nobleman, possibly from Miletus in Anatolia, appointed governor of Media in western Iran by the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes and who has rebelled against his successor, Demetrius I Soter, until he is killed in a battle with Demetrius' forces

summary: Attalus II Philadelphus succeeded his brother Eumenes II as king of Pergamon.
text: Attalus II Philadelphus succeeds his brother Eumenes II as king of Pergamon.

summary: The Seleucids re-established Alcimus as High Priest in Jerusalem following their victory in Judea.
text: With the Seleucid victory in Judea over the Maccabees, Alcimus is re-established as the High Priest of Israel, and a strong force is left in Jerusalem to support him. However, he does not enjoy his triumph for long, as he dies soon after from a paralytic stroke.

summary: Roman jurist and politician Quintus Mucius Scaevola Augur was born.
text: Quintus Mucius Scaevola Augur, politician of the Roman Republic and an early authority on Roman law (d. 88 BC)

summary: Charops of Epirus, ruler of Epirus, died.
text: Charops of Epirus, ruler of Epirus.

summary: Alcimus, High Priest of Judea, died of a stroke.
text: Alcimus, high priest of Judea.

summary: King Eumenes II of Pergamon died.
text: Eumenes II, king of Pergamon.

summary: Roman comic playwright Terence died.
text: Publius Terentius Afer (Terence), Roman comic dramatist, the author of six verse comedies that are long regarded as models of pure Latin (b. c. 195 BC) .

summary: Demetrius I Soter attacked Cappadocia, ousted Ariarathes V, and replaced him with Orophernes.
text: At the request of the Romans, Ariarathes V, king of Cappadocia, rejects a proposal from the Seleucid king, Demetrius I, for him to marry the sister of Demetrius I. In response, Seleucid forces attack Cappadocia and remove Ariarathes V from the Cappadocian throne. Demetrius I then replaces him with Orophernes Nicephorus, a supposed son of the late king, Ariarathes IV. With Ariarathes V deprived of his kingdom, he flees to Rome.

summary: Roman consul, statesman, and historian Publius Rutilius Rufus was born.
text: Publius Rutilius Rufus, Roman consul, statesman, orator and historian (d. c. 78 BC).

summary: Marcus Porcius Cato led a Roman senatorial commission to arbitrate a truce between Carthage and Masinissa of Numidia.
text: The Carthaginians, prevented by their treaty with Rome from engaging in armed resistance, but equally guaranteed against any loss of territory, appeal to Rome against the depredations of King Masinissa of Numidia. The Roman censor Marcus Porcius Cato heads a commission which arbitrates a truce between Carthage and her former ally, Masinissa.

summary: Alarmed by Carthage's prosperity, Cato the Elder began ending all his Senate speeches demanding the destruction of Carthage.
text: During his time in Carthage, Cato is so struck by the evidence of Carthaginian prosperity that he is convinced that the security of Rome now depends on the annihilation of Carthage. From this time on, Cato keeps repeating the cry "Ceterum censeo Carthaginem esse delendam" ("Moreover, I advise that Carthage must be destroyed") at the end of all his speeches, no matter what subject they concern.

summary: The Roman Senate restored Ariarathes V to the Cappadocian throne to reign jointly with Orophernes.
text: After Ariarathes V has been deposed from the Cappadocian throne by the Seleucid king Demetrius I Soter and has fled to Rome, the new king of Cappadocia, Orophernes, sends two ambassadors to Rome to join the Seleucid emissaries of Demetrius in opposing Ariarathes V's return to power. Despite their efforts, Ariarathes V is restored to his throne by the Romans. However, Rome allows Orophernes to reign jointly with him. The joint government, however, does not last long, as Ariarathes V becomes sole king of Cappadocia shortly afterwards.

summary: The Seleucid Empire recognized Jonathan Maccabeus as a ruler within Judea.
text: Jonathan Maccabeus is recognised by the Seleucids as a minor king within their dominions.

summary: Roman general and seven-time consul Gaius Marius was born.
text: Gaius Marius, Roman general, consul (approximate year) (d. 86 BC)

summary: The First Dalmatian War began between the Roman Republic and the Dalmatians.
text: The first Dalmatian war begins.

summary: Roman praetor Lucius Mummius defeated the Lusitani near Gibraltar.
text: Under the command of Punicus and then Caesarus, the Lusitani, a Hispanic tribe, reach a point near modern day Gibraltar. Here they are defeated by the Roman praetor Lucius Mummius.

summary: Consul Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum conquered Delminium, forcing the Dalmatians to pay tribute and ending the First Dalmatian War.
text: As part of the Roman efforts to fully conquer and occupy the whole of Illyria, a Roman army under consul Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum attacks the Dalmatians for the first time and conquers the Dalmatian capital of Delminium.
