summary: Galerius gathered an army with Danubian veterans, Goths, and Armenians in preparation for campaigning against Persia.
text: Diocletian watches over the Syrian provinces while Caesar Galerius makes preparations for a campaign against the Persian king Narseh. He recruits veterans from Illyria and Moesia, recruits new soldiers, and strengthens his army with Gothic mercenaries and the Armenian units of Tiridates III.

summary: Domitius Domitianus launched a rebellion against Diocletian in Egypt.
text: August: Domitius Domitianus launches a usurpation against Diocletian in Egypt. He is perhaps aided by popular discontent with Diocletian's taxation reform.

summary: Aurelius Achilleus took over leadership of the rebellion in Egypt following the death of Domitius Domitianus.
text: December: Domitianus dies, but his corrector Aurelius Achilleus takes over as the leader of the rebellion.

summary: Galerius surprised and sacked King Narseh's camp in western Armenia at the Battle of Satala.
text: Battle of Satala: Galerius launches a surprise attack against Narseh's camp in western Armenia. The Romans sack the camp and capture Narseh's wives, sisters and daughters, including his Queen of Queens Arsane. Narseh is wounded and escapes to his empire.

summary: Diocletian laid siege to the rebels in Alexandria.
text: Autumn: Diocletian besieges the rebels in Alexandria, Egypt.

summary: Emperor Diocletian retook Alexandria and crushed the usurpation of Aurelius Achilleus.
text: Spring: Emperor Diocletian retakes Alexandria and crushes the usurpation of Aurelius Achilleus.

summary: Emperor Diocletian ceded the Dodekaschoinos to the Nubians and concluded treaties with the Nubians and Blemmyes.
text: Diocletian then travels into Upper Egypt and possibly campaigns on the Nubian frontier. In either this year or in 300/301, he makes agreements with the Meroitic Nubians and the Blemmyes. He agrees to pay subsidies to both peoples, and he cedes the Dodecashoenos to the Nubians on the understanding that the Nubians will defend the region against the Blemmyes.

summary: Caesar Galerius restored Tiridates III to Armenia, invaded the Sasanian Empire, and captured Nisibis.
text: Caesar Galerius restores Tiridates III to the throne of Armenia and invades the Sassanid Empire. His army marches through Adiabene, Atropatene, Susiana and Lower Mesopotamia. He then retakes the strategically important city of Nisibis in Upper Mesopotamia.

summary: Athanasius of Alexandria, future Christian patriarch, was born in Alexandria.
text: Athanasius of Alexandria, Egyptian patriarch (d. 373)

summary: Roman usurper Aurelius Achilleus died after Diocletian retook Alexandria.
text: Aurelius Achilleus, Roman usurper

summary: Christian martyr Cassian of Tangier was executed.
text: Cassian of Tangier, Christian martyr

summary: Christian martyr Marcellus of Tangier was executed.
text: Marcellus of Tangier, Christian martyr

summary: Emperor Diocletian and Persian King Narseh concluded the Peace of Nisibis, establishing Roman hegemony over Armenia and Upper Mesopotamia.
text: Peace of Nisibis: Emperor Diocletian signs a treaty with the Persian king Narseh that will last for 40 years. The Persians accept Roman dominion over Armenia, the Caucasus, and Upper Mesopotamia. The pro-Roman ruler Tiridates III receives all of Armenia as far as the border with Atropatene. Mirian III of the Kingdom of Iberia is made a Roman client, and at some point in time, as a result of the treaty, Caucasian Albania will follow suit. Rome also gains five satrapies beyond the Tigris, which are perhaps given to Tiridates to administer.

summary: Caesar Galerius commissioned the Arch of Galerius in Thessaloniki to celebrate his Persian victory.
text: To celebrate his victory over the Persians, Galerius commissions the Arch of Galerius in Thessaloniki (modern Greece).

summary: Caesar Galerius defeated a Sarmatian army through a swamp and campaigned against the Marcomanni.
text: In this or the following year, Galerius campaigns with success against Sarmatians and the Marcomanni, attacking through a swamp to defeat a Sarmatian army.

summary: Emperor Maximian concluded his North African campaign against the Quinquegentiani and other Berbers.
text: Having first crossed into Africa in 296, Emperor Maximian concludes his campaigns against the Quinquegentiani and other Berbers. His campaigns had ranged as far as Mauretania in the west and Tripolitania in the east. Julianus, a rebel leader in Africa, throws himself into a fire after the Romans breach the walls of his stronghold.

summary: Returning to Rome in triumph, Emperor Maximian commissioned the Baths of Diocletian.
text: Returning to Rome in triumph, Maximian commissions the Baths of Diocletian in honour of his 'brother' Diocletian.

summary: Emperor Diocletian expelled Christians from the Roman army.
text: Diocletian expels Christians from the Roman army.

summary: Emperor Diocletian began construction of his retirement palace at Split.
text: Emperor Diocletian begins construction of a palace that will become the city of Split . Diocletian, who plans on abdicating, intends to use this palace as his place of retirement.

summary: Caesar Constantius Chlorus won a victory over the Franks.
text: Caesar Constantius I wins a victory over the Franks .

summary: The lion became extinct in Armenia.
text: The lion becomes extinct from Armenia .

summary: The elephant became extinct in North Africa.
text: The elephant becomes extinct in North Africa .

summary: The porphyry sculpture of the Tetrarchs was produced in Egypt.
text: The Tetrarchs are probably made in Egypt. After 330 they are moved to Constantinople and in 1204 they are installed at the corner of the facade of the St Mark's Basilica, Venice .

summary: Peter of Alexandria became Patriarch of Alexandria.
text: Peter of Alexandria becomes Patriarch of Alexandria.

summary: Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus, early Greek manuscripts of the Bible, were possibly produced around this time.
text: Possible date of the Codex Vaticanus Graecus 1209 and Codex Sinaiticus, manuscripts of the Bible written in Greek.

summary: The Synod of Elvira convened in Hispania, prohibiting Christian interaction with Jews, pagans, and heretics.
text: Approximate date of the Synod of Elvira in Elvira, Spain, which prohibits interaction with Jews, pagans, and heretics.

summary: Gallo-Roman physician Aemilia Hilaria was born.
text: Aemilia Hilaria, Gallo-Roman physician

summary: Roman prefect and politician Flavius Hermogenes was born.
text: Flavius Hermogenes, Roman prefect and politician (d. 361)

summary: Syrian Christian missionary and future bishop Frumentius was born.
text: Frumentius, Syrian missionary and bishop

summary: Gallo-Roman bishop Hilary of Poitiers was born.
text: Hilary of Poitiers, Gallo-Roman bishop

summary: Coptic Christian monk and hermit Macarius of Egypt was born.
text: Macarius of Egypt, Coptic Christian monk and hermit (d. 391)

summary: Christian bishop and martyr Zeno of Verona was born.
text: Zeno of Verona, Christian bishop and martyr

summary: Greek mathematician Sporus of Nicaea died.
text: Sporus of Nicaea, Greek mathematician

summary: Caesar Galerius began a major campaign against the Carpi and Bastarnae, winning the first of several victories.
text: Caesar Galerius begins a major war against the Carpi and Bastarnae and wins the first of several victories.

summary: Emperor Diocletian issued a monetary reform revaluing the Roman currency.
text: September: Emperor Diocletian issues a reform that revalues the Roman currency.

summary: Emperor Diocletian issued the Edict on Maximum Prices to curb inflation, but it caused panic and was quickly abandoned.
text: November: Diocletian issues his Edict on Maximum Prices, which, rather than halting rampant inflation, causes widespread panic and an increase in inflation. The measure is quickly abandoned.

summary: King Tiridates III proclaimed Christianity as the official state religion of Armenia, and construction of Etchmiadzin Cathedral began.
text: King Tiridates III (the Great) proclaims Christianity as the official state religion, making Armenia the first nation to adopt Christianity as its official religion (traditional date). Construction of the original Etchmiadzin Cathedral by Gregory the Illuminator begins.

summary: The republic of San Marino was traditionally established on Mount Titano.
text: The republic of San Marino is established .

summary: Emperor Diocletian persecuted the Manichaeans after accusing them of being a Persian fifth column.
text: Emperor Diocletian persecutes the Manichaeans, accusing them of being a Persian fifth column.

summary: Caesar Galerius won his second victory over the Carpi.
text: Caesar Galerius wins his second victory over the Carpi.

summary: Caesar Constantius I was trapped by Alemannic invaders at Langres but sallied out the same day to defeat them.
text: An invasion of Gaul by the Alemannic Lingones almost traps Caesar Constantius I between the enemy and the walls of a town. Constantius himself is carried onto the wall via a crane. However, within the same day, Constantius sallies forth from the walls and defeats the enemy in a major battle.

summary: Hormizd II succeeded his father Narseh as shahanshah of the Sasanian Empire.
text: Narseh, ruler (Shahanshah) of the Sassanid Empire, dies after a 9-year reign. He is succeeded by his son Hormizd II.
names: List of monarchs of the Sasanian Empire

summary: Neoplatonist philosopher Iamblichus of Chalcis wrote a treatise on magic and the occult.
text: Iamblichus of Chalcis writes a treatise on magic and the occult.

summary: Leontius of Caesarea consecrated Gregory the Illuminator as Patriarch of Armenia.
text: Gregory the Illuminator is consecrated as Patriarch of Armenia by Leontius of Caesarea.

summary: Narseh, ruler of the Sasanian Empire, died.
text: Narseh (or Narses), ruler of the Sassanid Empire

summary: Emperor Diocletian launched the Great Persecution against Christians across the Roman Empire.
text: Great Persecution: Emperor Diocletian launches the last and largest major persecution of Christians in the Empire. Caesar Galerius and Hierocles are said to have been the instigators. In a series of four edicts published from February 23, 303, to 304, the Christians are forbidden to worship in groups, are made to perform sacrifices, and must surrender sacred texts. Churches are destroyed, and the clergy are arrested en masse. The persecution lasts in some parts of the empire until 313, and thousands of Christians are killed. Those put to death include Agnes of Rome, a 12-year-old Christian girl who has refused marriage and consecrated her virginity to God. Hailed as a martyr, she will be honored as the patron saint of chastity, gardeners, rape victims and virgins.

summary: Fermin was beheaded by Roman authorities while preaching in Amiens.
text: On a voyage preaching the gospel, Saint Fermin of Pamplona is beheaded in Amiens (Modern day France).

summary: Diocletian and Maximian reunited in Rome to celebrate their joint vicennalia and agreed on a plan of abdication.
text: The Augusti Diocletian and Maximian reunite in Rome to celebrate the 20th anniversary of Diocletian's accession, which is now treated as a joint anniversary for both emperors. A series of columns in the Roman Forum and a triumphal arch are dedicated to the emperors. The two emperors also agree on a plan of abdication.

summary: Galerius defeated the Carpi for the third time and dedicated the Arch of Galerius in Thessaloniki.
text: Galerius wins his third victory over the Carpi and is perhaps joined on campaign by Diocletian. The Arch of Galerius is dedicated in Thessaloniki.

summary: Constantius Chlorus defeated Germanic invaders at the Battle of Vindonissa.
text: Caesar Constantius I wins a victory over Germanic invaders in the battle of Vindonissa.

summary: Gregory the Illuminator and King Tiridates III completed the construction of Etchmiadzin Cathedral.
text: Etchmiadzin Cathedral is completed by Gregory the Illuminator and Tiridates III, king of Armenia.

summary: King Tiridates III of Armenia was baptized into Christianity.
text: Baptism of Tiridates III of Armenia.

summary: Adrian and Natalia were martyred for their Christian faith at Nicomedia.
text: Adrian and Natalia of Nicomedia are martyred.

summary: Magnentius, future Roman usurper, was born.
text: Magnentius, Roman usurper (d. 353)

summary: Saint George, Roman soldier and Christian martyr, died.
text: George of Lydda, Roman soldier and martyr

summary: Agathius, Roman centurion and Christian martyr, died.
text: Acacius of Byzantium, Roman centurion and martyr

summary: Anthimus of Rome, Christian priest and martyr, died.
text: Anthimus of Rome, Christian priest and martyr

summary: Cessianus, Christian child martyr, died.
text: Cessianus, Christian child martyr

summary: Crescentinus, Roman soldier and Christian martyr, died.
text: Crescentinus, Roman soldier and martyr

summary: Cyriacus, Roman nobleman and Christian martyr, died.
text: Cyriacus, Roman nobleman and martyr

summary: Devota, Corsican Christian martyr, died.
text: Devota, Corsican woman and martyr

summary: Erasmus of Formia, Christian bishop and martyr, died.
text: Erasmus of Formiae, Christian martyr

summary: Expeditus, Roman centurion and Christian martyr, died.
text: Expeditus, Roman centurion and martyr

summary: Felix and Adauctus, Christian martyrs, died at Rome.
text: Felix and Adauctus, Christian martyrs

summary: Fermin, Christian bishop and martyr, died.
text: Fermin, Christian bishop and martyr

summary: Pantaleon, Christian wonderworker and martyr, died.
text: Pantaleon, Christian wonderworker and martyr

summary: Romanus of Caesarea, Christian martyr, died at Antioch.
text: Romanus of Caesarea, Christian martyr

summary: Victor Maurus, Christian martyr, died at Milan.
text: Victor Maurus ("the Moor"), Christian martyr

summary: Saint Vitus, Christian martyr, died.
text: Vitus (or Guido), Christian martyr

summary: Galerius defeated the Carpi and resettled surviving Carpi and Bastarnae within the Roman Empire.
text: Caesar Galerius, perhaps accompanied by Emperor Diocletian, wins his fourth and final victory over the Carpi. Many of the surviving Carpi and Bastarnae are resettled in the Roman Empire, where they are split up. The Bastarnae are not attested after this time, and the Carpi are attested only once more in the 310s.

summary: Diocletian became seriously ill while inspecting the Roman border along the Danube.
text: Diocletian, while inspecting the Danube border, becomes seriously ill.

summary: Constantius Chlorus besieged a Germanic raiding force on an island in the Rhine and forced their surrender.
text: Caesar Constantius I besieges a Germanic raiding force on an island in the Rhine and forces their surrender.

summary: Pope Marcellinus died in Rome after an eight-year pontificate.
text: Pope Marcellinus dies at Rome after an 8-year reign. The papal throne will remain vacant until 308.

summary: Saint Agnes of Rome was martyred by fire.
text: Saint Agnes of Rome (martyred by fire) (b. c. 291)

summary: Saint Pancras of Rome was martyred by beheading.
text: May 12 (or 303?) – Saint Pancras of Rome (martyred by beheading) (b. c. 289)

summary: Saint Philomena was martyred by beheading.
text: c. August 10 – Saint Philomena (martyred by beheading)

summary: Pope Marcellinus died.
text: Pope Marcellinus

summary: Saint Anastasia of Sirmium was martyred by beheading.
text: Saint Anastasia of Sirmium (martyred by beheading)

summary: Saint Afra was martyred by fire.
text: Saint Afra (martyred by fire)

summary: Saints Agape, Chionia, and Irene were martyred by fire and sword in Thessalonica.
text: Saints Agape, Chionia, and Irene (martyred by fire and sword)

summary: Saint Alban was martyred by beheading.
text: Saint Alban (martyred by beheading) (possibly 309)

summary: Saint Florian was martyred by drowning in the Enns River.
text: Saint Florian (martyred by drowning)

summary: Saint Gorgonius of Nicomedia was martyred.
text: Saint Gorgonius of Nicomedia (martyred)

summary: Saint Juliana of Nicomedia was martyred.
text: Saint Juliana of Nicomedia (martyred)

summary: Saint Lucy of Syracuse was martyred by fire and sword.
text: Saint Lucy of Syracuse (martyred by fire and sword)

summary: Saint Margaret the Virgin was martyred by beheading.
text: Saint Margaret the Virgin (martyred by beheading)

summary: Saints Theodora and Didymus were martyred by beheading at Alexandria.
text: Saints Theodora and Didymus (martyred by beheading)

summary: Saint Vincent of Saragossa was martyred at Valencia.
text: Saint Vincent of Saragossa (martyred)

summary: Emperor Diocletian abdicated and retired to his palace at Salona.
text: Emperor Diocletian abdicates and retires to his palace at Salona (modern Split) on the Adriatic coast, after a reign of nearly 21 years, in which the last vestiges of republican government have disappeared.

summary: Maximian retired from office and left for his villas in southern Italy.
text: Maximian retires from office, and leaves for Campania or Lucania (southern Italy), to live a life of ease in his luxury villas.

summary: Galerius allowed Constantine to leave his court and join Constantius in the west.
text: Constantius requests leave for his son Constantine I to join him in the west, who has been living at the courts of Diocletian and Galerius as a hostage. Galerius allows Constantine to return.

summary: Constantine joined Constantius in Gaul, crossed to Britain, and successfully campaigned against the Picts.
text: Summer – Constantine joins his father at Bononia (Boulogne) in Gaul; they cross the Channel to Britain and make their way to Eboracum (York), capital of Britannia Secunda and home to a large military base. They campaign with success against the Picts.

summary: Galerius began campaigning against the Sarmatians, winning a victory before the end of the year.
text: Galerius begins a series of campaigns against the Sarmatians, winning his first victory before the end of the year.

summary: Maximinus Daza persecuted the Christians of Egypt, driving many into the desert where monasticism and Coptic writing developed.
text: Maximinus Daza persecutes the Christians of Egypt, many of whom take refuge in the desert. In time, this refuge leads to the monastic life. In these monasteries, Coptic writing develops, supporting the propagation of Christian texts.

summary: Saint Proculus and Saint Januarius were thrown to wild beasts in the Flavian Amphitheater at Pozzuoli and then beheaded at Solfatara.
text: Patron of Pozzuoli, Saint Proculus, and patron of Naples, Saint Januarius are thrown to wild beasts in Pozzuoli's Flavian Amphitheater, then beheaded at Solfatara.

summary: The Baths of Diocletian were dedicated in Rome, becoming the largest imperial baths in the city.
text: In this or the following year, the Baths of Diocletian are dedicated; the thermae become the largest imperial baths in Rome.

summary: The Daysan River flooded Edessa.
text: The Daysan River floods Edessa.

summary: Senatorial landowners dominated the Roman Empire exempt from crushing taxes, while municipal curiales were burdened with tax collection.
text: Landowners dominate the Roman Empire, and enjoy the title of senator, which exempts them from the crushing taxes imposed on the rest of the population. The Senate has lost all its power and the landowners almost never attend Senate sessions. Members of municipal senates (curiales or decuriones) are charged with the responsibility of collecting taxes and paying arrears; smaller landowners are held responsible for providing recruits for the Roman army, and with keeping wastelands under cultivation.

summary: Catherine confessed Christianity at Alexandria and was tortured on a spiked wheel and beheaded on the orders of Maximinus Daza.
text: Catherine makes a public confession of the Christian gospel at a sacrificial feast ordered by Maximinus Daza at Alexandria. A virgin of royal descent, she is tortured on a spiked wheel (later called the "Catherine Wheel") and beheaded; her remains are spirited to Mount Sinai.

summary: The Council of Illiberis decreed clerical celibacy and prohibited Christians from associating with or marrying Jews.
text: The Council of Illiberis decrees that priests must be celibate. Additionally, it condemns visiting the homes of Jews and prohibits Christian women from marrying Jews, unless they have converted.

summary: Bishop Januarius died as a martyr.
text: Januarius I of Benevento, Roman bishop and martyr

summary: Catherine of Alexandria died as a Christian martyr.
text: Catherine of Alexandria, Christian martyr and virgin

summary: Neoplatonist philosopher and writer Porphyry of Tyre died.
text: Porphyry of Tyre, Neoplatonist philosopher and writer

summary: Proculus of Pozzuoli died as a Christian martyr.
text: Proculus of Pozzuoli (or Proclus), Christian martyr

summary: Roman proconsul and aristocrat Sossianus Hierocles died.
text: Sossianus Hierocles, Roman proconsul and aristocrat

summary: Vincent, Orontius, and Victor were martyred.
text: Vincent, Orontius, and Victor, Christian martyrs

summary: Diocletian and Maximian abdicated, making Constantius and Galerius augusti, while Severus and Maximinus Daza were appointed caesars.
text: Diocletian and Maximian abdicated. Constantius and Galerius were elevated to augusti in the west and east. Galerius appointed Flavius Valerius Severus Caesar in the west and Maximinus II Caesar in the east.

summary: Constantius died at Eboracum, whereupon Constantine was proclaimed emperor by his troops and Galerius recognized Severus as western augustus and Constantine as caesar.
text: Constantius I dies outside Eboracum (modern-day York). Constantine, aged 23 or 24, is declared emperor by his troops. Emperor Galerius grants Constantine the title of Caesar, and elevates Flavius Valerius Severus to emperor in the Western part of the Roman Empire.

summary: Constantine instituted religious toleration for Christians across his territories.
text: Constantine institutes toleration of the Christians in his territories.

summary: Constantine established his capital at Augusta Treverorum and began a major expansion of the city.
text: Constantine establishes his capital in Augusta Treverorum (Trier). He begins a major expansion of the city, strengthening the walls, expanding the palace complex and building the Imperial Baths.

summary: Galerius introduced the poll tax to central and southern Italy and reduced the size of the Praetorian Guard.
text: Building on the efforts of Diocletian, Galerius introduces the poll tax to central and southern Italy and truncates the size of the Praetorian Guard, with plans to disband the Guard altogether.

summary: Maxentius led a revolt in Rome, was proclaimed emperor, and recalled his father Maximian from retirement.
text: Maxentius, son of former Western Emperor Maximian, leads a revolt by the Praetorian Guard and members of the Senate in Rome, and is proclaimed Emperor. Southern Italy supports Maxentius, as do Africa, Corsica, Sardinia and Sicily. Maxentius recalls Maximian from retirement, who joins his son in Rome.

summary: Constantine campaigned successfully against the Franks along the Rhine frontier.
text: Winter: Constantine fights with success against the Franks.

summary: Galerius commissioned the construction of the Rotunda in Thessaloniki.
text: Galerius has the Rotunda of Galerius built in Thessaloniki (Macedonia).

summary: The Synod of Elvira concluded and issued several canons of church law.
text: The Synod of Elvira concludes with the issue of various canons, including one declaring that killing through a magic spell is a sin and the work of the devil.

summary: Metrophanes became the bishop of Byzantium.
text: Metrophanes becomes bishop of Byzantium.

summary: The Diocese of Lisbon was established.
text: The Patriarchate of Lisbon is established.

summary: Christianity became established in Roman Britain.
text: Christianity is established in Roman Britain. British bishops participate in the councils of Arles (314), Nicaea (325) and Arminum (349).

summary: Syriac theologian and hymnodist Ephrem the Syrian was born.
text: Ephrem the Syrian, Syriac theologian and hymnodist (d. 373)

summary: Roman soldier and Christian martyr Theodore of Amasea died.
text: Theodore of Amasea, Roman soldier and martyr

summary: Christian martyrs Adrian and Natalia died at Nicomedia.
text: Adrian and Natalia of Nicomedia, Christian martyrs

summary: Roman emperor Constantius Chlorus died at Eboracum.
text: Constantius Chlorus, Roman emperor (b. c. 250)

summary: Christian hermit and martyr Saint Maginus died.
text: Maginus, Christian hermit and martyr

summary: Roman soldier and Christian martyr Demetrius of Thessaloniki died.
text: Demetrius of Thessaloniki, Roman soldier and martyr

summary: Galerius won his second victory over the Sarmatians along the Danube.
text: Winter: Emperor Galerius wins his second victory over the Sarmatians.

summary: Maximian besieged Severus II at Ravenna and forced his surrender after his soldiers deserted.
text: Galerius sends Valerius Severus with the army of northern Italy, to suppress the rebellion in Rome. However, faced with their former emperor Maximian, the soldiers desert him, and Severus flees to Ravenna. Maximian besieges Severus in Ravenna, who then surrenders. Maxentius makes Severus a hostage, in an attempt to keep Galerius at bay.

summary: Maximian travelled to Gaul to forge an alliance with Constantine.
text: Summer: Anticipating an offensive by Galerius, Maximian travels to Gaul to make an alliance with Constantine I.

summary: Galerius invaded Italy but failed to capture Rome, withdrawing while Maxentius executed Severus II.
text: Late summer or autumn: Galerius invades Italy but Maxentius remains behind the walls of Rome. Galerius finds he cannot besiege the city, and the image of an emperor making efforts against Rome hurts Galerius' image among the troops. The fact that Maxentius is his son-in-law does not help, and Maxentius makes an effort to bribe Galerius' troops. Galerius unsuccessfully attempts to negotiate, and recognizing Maxentius' attempts at bribery and the danger of being trapped in Italy by Maximian and Constantine, Galerius chooses to withdraw from Italy. To satiate his troops during the withdrawal, he pillages the Italian countryside. Meanwhile, Maxentius executes Severus.

summary: Galerius elevated Licinius to the rank of Augustus following the death of Severus II.
text: Following the murder of Severus, Galerius promotes Licinius to Augustus.

summary: Constantine married Maximian's daughter Fausta and was promoted to Augustus by Maximian.
text: December: Constantine marries Maximian's daughter Fausta, and is promoted to Augustus by Maximian.

summary: Galerius bestowed the title of Augusta upon his wife Galeria Valeria.
text: Near the end of the year, Galerius gives his wife (Diocletian's daughter) Galeria Valeria the title of Augusta.

summary: Deposed Roman emperor Severus II was murdered in captivity.
text: Severus II, Roman emperor (murdered)

summary: Bishop and Christian martyr Septimius of Iesi died.
text: Septimius of Iesi, German bishop, martyr and saint

summary: Galerius achieved his third and final victory over the Sarmatians.
text: Winter: Emperor Galerius wins his third and final victory over the Sarmatians.

summary: Maximian attempted to depose Maxentius in Rome but was forced by loyal troops to flee to Constantine.
text: April: In Rome, Emperor Maximian attempts to depose his son Maxentius, but the soldiers in Rome side with Maxentius and force Maximian to flee to the court of Constantine I.

summary: Soldiers in Roman Africa proclaimed the vicarius Domitius Alexander as emperor against Maxentius.
text: The overthrow of Maximian prompts the soldiers of Roman Africa to prop up the vicarius of Africa, Domitius Alexander, as a usurper.

summary: Constantine raided the Bructeri and constructed a bridge across the Rhine at Cologne.
text: Constantine raids the territory of the Bructeri and builds a bridge across the Rhine at Cologne.

summary: Galerius, Diocletian, and Maximian convened at Carnuntum, appointing Licinius as Augustus and declaring Maxentius a public enemy.
text: The Conference of Carnuntum: Attempting to keep peace within the Roman Empire, Galerius recalls Diocletian briefly from retirement, and they convene with Maximian. Diocletian persuades Maximian to return to retirement, and he and Galerius declare Maxentius a public enemy. Licinius is proclaimed Augustus of the west, while rival contender Constantine I is again declared Caesar.

summary: Maxentius began construction of the Basilica of Maxentius in the Roman Forum.
text: Bereft of his father's support, Maxentius increasingly presents himself as the Conservator Urbis Suae (Preserver of His Own City). Construction of the Basilica of Maxentius (or Basilica Nova), the largest building in the Roman Forum, is begun.

summary: Maxentius instituted religious toleration for Christians across his territories.
text: Maxentius institutes toleration of the Christians in his territories.

summary: Pope Marcellus I succeeded Pope Marcellinus as bishop of Rome.
text: May 27 or June 26 – Pope Marcellus I succeeds Pope Marcellinus as the 30th pope.

summary: The Christian martyr Adrian of Batanea was martyred.
text: Adrian of Batanea (or Eubulus), Christian martyr

summary: Gaius Ceionius Rufius Volusianus defeated the usurper Domitius Alexander and purged Africa of his supporters.
text: Gaius Ceionius Rufius Volusianus, the Praetorian Prefect of Emperor Maxentius, defeats the usurper Domitius Alexander and purges Africa of his supporters.

summary: King Hormizd II invaded Ghassanid territory and killed their king, but was then ambushed and mortally wounded by Ghassanid forces.
text: King Hormizd II, ruler of the Sassanid Empire, demands that the king of the Ghassanids pays tribute. After the king refuses, Hormizd invades Ghassanid territory. The Ghassanids seek aid from Maximinus Daza, but before a Roman army can arrive, Hormizd defeats the Ghassanid army and kills their king. A Ghassanid force then ambushes Hormizd's small retinue while the latter is on a hunting trip, and the Sasanian king is mortally wounded. He dies after a 7-year reign.

summary: Shapur II succeeded Adur Narseh as king of the Sasanian Empire following Adur Narseh's brief reign and murder.
text: Hormizd is succeeded by his infant son Shapur II following the brief reign and murder of Adur Narseh.

summary: Emperor Maxentius banished Pope Marcellus I from Rome.
text: Pope Marcellus I is banished from Rome by Emperor Maxentius.

summary: Eusebius succeeded Marcellus I as pope before being banished to Sicily.
text: Eusebius succeeds Marcellus I as the 31st pope, but is himself banished on August 17 to Sicily (these events may have also taken place in 310).

summary: Shapur II, king of the Sasanian Empire, was born.
text: Shapur II (the Great), king of the Sassanid Empire (d. 379)

summary: Pope Marcellus I died.
text: Marcellus I, bishop of Rome (b. 255)

summary: Adur Narseh, king of the Sasanian Empire, was murdered.
text: Adur Narseh, king of the Sassanid Empire

summary: Elias and his companions were martyred for their Christian faith.
text: Elias and companions, Christian martyrs

summary: Hormizd II, king of the Sasanian Empire, died from mortal wounds.
text: Hormizd II, king of the Sassanid Empire

summary: Maximian rebelled against Constantine the Great in Arles while Constantine was campaigning against the Franks.
text: Maximian, retired emperor, rebels against Constantine I in Arles while the latter is campaigning against the Franks.

summary: Maximinus Daza was acclaimed augustus by his troops, forcing Galerius to recognize him as co-ruler in the East.
text: Maximinus Daza, caesar under Emperor Galerius, is acclaimed augustus by his troops. Galerius is forced to recognize him as co-ruler of the East. The Roman Empire is thus divided between seven simultaneous emperors: Galerius (East), Maximinus II (East), Licinius (Middle), Constantine I (West), Maximian (West), Maxentius (Italy), and Domitius Alexander (Africa).

summary: Maximian surrendered at Marseille and was compelled by Constantine to hang himself.
text: July – Maximian flees to Marseille where he is besieged and surrenders. Constantine encourages his suicide and Maximian, age 60, hangs himself. Emperor Maxentius condemns the killing of his father.

summary: Licinius campaigned successfully against the Carpi.
text: Licinius campaigns with success against the Carpi.

summary: Constantine ordered the minting of the solidus at Trier to establish a stable gold standard.
text: At Trier, Constantine orders the minting of a new coin, the solidus, in an effort to offset the declining value of the denarius and bring stability to the imperial currency by restoring a gold standard. The solidus (later known as the bezant) will be minted in the Byzantine Empire without change in weight or purity until the 10th century.

summary: Emperor Maxentius banished Pope Eusebius to Sicily, where he died.
text: Pope Eusebius succeeds Pope Marcellus I as the 31st pope, but is banished on August 17 by the Emperor Maxentius to Sicily, where he dies, perhaps from a hunger strike.

summary: The Roman poet and rhetorician Ausonius was born.
text: Ausonius, Roman poet and rhetorician (d. 395)

summary: Epiphanius of Salamis, Church Father, was born.
text: Epiphanius of Salamis, Church Father (d. 403)

summary: The Gothic bishop and missionary Ulfilas was born.
text: Wulfila, Gothic bishop and missionary (d. 383)

summary: Pope Eusebius died in exile in Sicily.
text: Eusebius, bishop of Rome

summary: Retired Roman emperor Maximian died by suicide at Marseille.
text: July – Maximian, Roman emperor (b. c. 250)

summary: The Christian martyrs Domnina, Berenice, and Prosdoce died.
text: Domnina, Berenice, and Prosdoce, Christian martyrs

summary: Emperor Galerius issued the Edict of Serdica, granting Christians religious freedom and ending the Diocletianic Persecution in the east.
text: On his deathbed, Emperor Galerius declares religious freedom and issues the Edict of Serdica, ending the Diocletianic Persecution of Christians in the eastern half of the Roman Empire.

summary: Emperor Galerius died from a gruesome disease at age 51.
text: Galerius dies at age 51 from a gruesome disease, possibly colorectal cancer or Fournier gangrene.

summary: Maximinus Daza resumed the persecution of Christians in his territories.
text: Maximinus recommences the persecution of Christians, having encouraged his subjects to petition him to do so.

summary: Maximinus Daza formed a secret alliance with Maxentius against Licinius and Constantine.
text: Fearing an alliance between Licinius and Constantine I, Maximinus forges a secret alliance with Emperor Maxentius.

summary: Miltiades succeeded Eusebius as the pope in Rome.
text: Pope Miltiades succeeds Eusebius as the 32nd pope of Rome.

object: Christianity in the Roman Africa province
summary: The Donatist schism began within the Church of Roman Africa.
text: The Donatist schism begins in the African Church.
names: Christianity in the Roman Africa province

summary: Roman emperor Galerius died.
text: May 5: Galerius, Roman emperor (b. c.258)

summary: Patriarch Peter I of Alexandria died.
text: Peter I, patriarch of Alexandria

summary: Roman usurper Domitius Alexander died in Africa.
text: Domitius Alexander, Roman emperor and usuper

summary: Following the death of Galerius, Licinius and Maximinus Daza agreed to divide the Eastern Roman Empire between themselves.
text: Galerius died. Licinius and Maximinus agreed to divide the eastern Empire between themselves.

summary: Constantine the Great concluded an alliance with Licinius and offered his half-sister Flavia Julia Constantia in marriage.
text: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy: Constantine the Great concluded an alliance with Licinius, offering his half-sister Flavia Julia Constantia to him in marriage.

summary: Former Roman emperor Diocletian died, possibly from suicide.
text: Diocletian died, possibly from suicide.

summary: Constantine the Great crossed the Cottian Alps and defeated the forces of Maxentius at Turin, Brescia, and Verona.
text: Constantine I crosses the Cottian Alps with an army (40,000 men) and defeats Maxentius's generals in three battles at Turin, Brescia and Verona. Maxentius's Praetorian Prefect Ruricius Pompeianus is killed in the fighting outside Verona.

summary: Constantine the Great defeated Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, becoming the sole Roman emperor in the West.
text: Battle of the Milvian Bridge: Constantine defeats Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge, becoming the only Roman emperor in the West. Prior to the battle, he reportedly has a vision of a cross (labarum) with the phrase "in hoc signo vinces" ("In this sign you shall conquer"). This encourages him to convert to Christianity.

summary: Constantine the Great entered Rome in a grand adventus after the decapitated body of Maxentius was retrieved from the Tiber.
text: Constantine enters Rome; he stages a grand adventus in the city, and is met with popular jubilation. Maxentius' body is fished out of the Tiber and decapitated.

summary: Constantine the Great allied with Licinius and disbanded the Praetorian Guard and the Imperial Horse Guard in Rome.
text: Constantine forges an alliance with co-emperor Licinius, and offers him his half-sister, Constantia, in marriage. The Praetorian Guard and Imperial Horse Guard (equites singulares Augusti) are disbanded.
names: List of political groups by country

summary: Emperor Maximinus Daza campaigned unsuccessfully against the Kingdom of Armenia.
text: Emperor Maximinus Daza campaigns unsuccessfully against the Armenians.

summary: Constantine the Great adopted the motto "in hoc signo vinces" and had the Chi-Rho monogram emblazoned on his soldiers' shields.
text: Constantine I adopts the words "in hoc signo vinces" as a motto, and has the letters X and P (the first letters of the Greek word Christ) emblazoned on the shields of his soldiers.

summary: The Council of Carthage supported Donatism, endorsing a rigorous interpretation of the sacraments.
text: The Council of Carthage supports Donatism, which espouses a rigorous application and interpretation of the sacraments. These doctrines will be condemned by the Council of Arles (314).

summary: Constantine the Great promoted a policy of state sponsorship of Christianity.
text: Constantine I promotes a policy of state sponsorship of Christianity, perhaps even becoming a Christian himself (see Constantine the Great and Christianity).

summary: Roman emperor Maxentius died at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge.
text: Maxentius, Roman emperor (b. 283)

summary: Christian bishop and martyr Clement of Ancyra was martyred.
text: Clement of Ancyra, Christian bishop and martyr

summary: Roman praetorian prefect Ruricius Pompeianus died fighting outside Verona.
text: Ruricius Pompeianus, Roman praetorian prefect

summary: Retired emperor Diocletian died in his palace in Split, likely from natural causes.
text: At the end of 312 or in early 313, the retired Emperor Diocletian dies in his palace in Split, most likely from natural causes.

summary: Constantine the Great and Licinius convened in Milan and issued the Edict of Milan, decreeing freedom of religion.
text: February: Emperors Constantine I and Licinius convene in Mediolanum (modern Milan). Licinius marries Constantine's half-sister Constantia, and they issue the Edict of Milan. This edict ends the Great Persecution against the Christians and is the first piece of legislation in western history to decree freedom of religion. It also returns property confiscated from Christians. The edict is posted in Nicomedia on June 13.

summary: Maximinus Daza crossed the Bosporus and captured Heraclea in Thrace after an eight-day siege.
text: Emperor Maximinus Daza crosses the Bosphorus with an army of 70,000 men and lays siege to Heraclea in Thrace. He captures the city after eight days.

summary: Licinius defeated Maximinus Daza at the Battle of Tzirallum, after which Maximinus fled to Cilicia and committed suicide.
text: Battle of Tzirallum: Licinius defeats his rival Maximinus in Thrace, who then flees to Cilicia. After losing the Cilician Gates to Licinius' forces, Maximinus commits suicide.

summary: Licinius conducted a purge of the wider Tetrarchic dynasty, executing relatives of Galerius, Valerius Severus, and Maximinus Daza.
text: Licinius conducts a purge of the wider Tetrarchic dynasty. He executes Galerius' son Candidianus, Valerius Severus' son Severianus (whom he accuses of conspiracy), and Maximinus' wife, son and daughter. Diocletian's wife Prisca and daughter Galeria Valeria go into hiding.

summary: The Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine in Rome was completed.
text: Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine (or Basilica Nova), in Rome, is finished.

summary: The Lateran Synod declared Donatism to be a heresy.
text: Lateran Synod: Donatism is declared a heresy.

summary: Arius preached regarding the human nature of Jesus.
text: Arius preaches of the human nature of Jesus.

summary: Christian bishop and theologian Cyril of Jerusalem was born.
text: Cyril of Jerusalem, Christian bishop and theologian (d. 386)

summary: Alexandrian theologian Didymus the Blind was born.
text: Didymus the Blind, Alexandrian theologian (d. 398)

summary: Pope Achillas of Alexandria died.
text: Achillas (the Great), pope and patriarch of Alexandria

summary: Flavius Severianus, son of former emperor Severus, was executed by Licinius.
text: Severianus, son of Valerius Severus

summary: Roman emperor Maximinus Daza died at Tarsus.
text: Maximinus died at Tarsus.

summary: The Picts attempted a large raid southwards into Roman Britain.
text: A large Pictish raid southwards in Roman Britain is attempted.

summary: Pope Miltiades ended his pontificate as bishop of Rome.
text: Pope Miltiades' reign ends.

summary: Pope Sylvester I succeeded Pope Miltiades as bishop of Rome.
text: Pope Sylvester I succeeds Pope Miltiades as the 33rd pope.

summary: The Council of Arles confirmed the condemnation of Donatism as a schism and passed new canons.
text: Council of Arles: Confirms the pronouncement of Donatism as a schism, and passes other canons.

summary: The Synod of Ancyra declared that consulting a magician was a sin requiring five years of penance.
text: Synod of Ancyra: Consulting a magician is declared a sin earning five years of penance.

summary: Alexander became bishop of Byzantium.
text: Alexander becomes Bishop of Byzantium.
names: List of bishops and Ecumenical Patriarchs of Constantinople

summary: Greek rhetorician and sophist Libanius was born in Antioch.
text: Libanius, Greek rhetorician and sophist

summary: Pope Miltiades died in Rome.
text: Miltiades (or Melchiades), bishop of Rome

summary: Constantine the Great defeated the forces of Licinius at the Battle of Cibalae near modern Vinkovci.
text: Battle of Cibalae: Constantine the Great dealt a bloody defeat to Licinius's forces at modern Vinkovci.

summary: Constantine the Great and Licinius campaigned against the Sarmatians, Goths, and Carpi along the Danube, and Constantine led an expedition into Dacia.
text: Constantine the Great and co-emperor Licinius battle the Sarmates, the Goths and the Carpians along the Danube. Constantine leads a punitive expedition into Dacia and reestablishes the Roman fortifications of the frontier.

summary: The Arch of Constantine was completed near the Colosseum in Rome to commemorate Constantine the Great's victory over Maxentius.
text: The Arch of Constantine is completed near the Colosseum at Rome to commemorate Constantine's victory over Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge. As part of the ceremony Constantine is expected to make a sacrifice to Rome's traditional gods, but he refuses to do so.

summary: Constantine I dedicated the Basilica of Maxentius in Rome and installed a colossal statue of himself inside it.
text: Constantine I dedicates the Basilica of Maxentius and installs a large statue of himself inside it.

summary: Crucifixion was abolished as a legal punishment throughout the Roman Empire.
text: Crucifixion is abolished as punishment in the Roman Empire.

summary: A program of assistance to the poor was established in the Roman Empire.
text: A program of assistance to the poor is established in the Roman Empire.

summary: Large imperial baths were constructed in Augusta Treverorum.
text: Immense baths are constructed in Augusta Treverorum (modern-day Trier).

summary: Eusebius became bishop of Caesarea Maritima.
text: Eusebius becomes bishop of Caesarea .

summary: The lamb became adopted as a symbol of Jesus in Christian art.
text: The lamb becomes the symbol of Jesus in Christian art.

summary: Roman prince Hannibalianus, later ruler of Armenia and Pontus, was born.
text: Flavius Hannibalianus, ruler of Armenia and Pontus (d. 337)

summary: Hilary of Poitiers, future bishop and Doctor of the Church, was born in Poitiers.
text: Hilary of Poitiers, Christian bishop and Doctor of the Church

summary: Greek sophist and rhetorician Himerius was born in Prusa.
text: Himerius, Greek sophist and rhetorician

summary: Roman politician Vettius Agorius Praetextatus was born in Rome.
text: Vettius Agorius Praetextatus, Roman politician (d. 384)

summary: Bishop Maternus of Cologne died in Trier.
text: Maternus of Cologne, bishop of Trier

summary: Former Roman empress Galeria Valeria was executed in Thessalonica.
text: Galeria Valeria, Roman empress and wife of Galerius

summary: Former Roman empress Prisca was executed in Thessalonica.
text: Prisca, Roman empress and wife of Diocletian (b. 247)

summary: Bishop Valerius of Saragossa died in exile.
text: Valerius of Saragossa, Christian bishop and martyr

summary: Constantine the Great issued an edict prohibiting the punishment of slaves by crucifixion and facial branding.
text: Emperor Constantine the Great issues an edict, prohibiting the punishment of slaves by crucifixion and facial branding.

summary: Constantine I sent Julius Constantius to Licinius at Sirmium proposing Bassianus as Caesar, which Licinius rejected.
text: Constantine I sends his half-brother Julius Constantius to Licinius at Sirmium (Pannonia), with the proposal to accept Bassianus as Caesar and give him power over Italy. Licinius refuses, and forces a conspiracy against Constantine.

summary: Licinius elevated Valerius Valens to Augustus, while Bassianus was executed for conspiracy.
text: Licinius elevates Valerius Valens to Augustus, and mobilises an army against Constantine. Bassianus is accused of conspiracy and executed.

summary: Constantine the Great defeated Licinius at the Battle of Cibalae, forcing Licinius to flee to Sirmium and cede most of the Balkans.
text: Battle of Cibalae: Constantine the Great defeats his rival Licinius near the town of Colonia Aurelia Cibalae (modern-day Vinkovci, Croatia). Licinius is forced to flee to Sirmium and loses all of the Balkans except for Thrace. Peace negotiations are initiated between the two Augusti, but they are unsuccessful.

summary: Constantine I defeated Licinius and Valerius Valens at the Battle of Mardia near modern Harmanli.
text: December – Battle of Mardia: Constantine I defeats his rival Licinius and senior officer Valerius Valens, near the town of Harmanli (Bulgaria).

summary: Constantine I intervened at the request of Christians to attempt to resolve the Donatist schism.
text: At the request of the Christians, Constantine I attempts to end the schism with the Donatist sect.

summary: Constantine II, future Roman emperor, was born at Arles.
text: Constantine II, Roman emperor (d. 340)

summary: Martin of Tours, future bishop of Tours, was born in Savaria.
text: Martin of Tours, bishop of Tours (d. 397)

summary: Former Roman emperor Diocletian died at his palace near Salona.
text: Diocletian, Roman emperor, commits suicide (b. 244) (most historians date his death to 311 or 312)

summary: Saint Blaise, bishop of Sebastea, was martyred.
text: Blaise, bishop of Sebastea (martyred)

summary: Bassianus, a Roman politician and advisor, was executed.
text: Bassianus, Roman advisor and politician

object: Crispus, Constantine II, and Licinius II
summary: Constantine the Great and Licinius elevated Crispus, Constantine II, and Licinius II to the rank of Caesar, and Constantine took control of Pannonia and Macedonia.
text: Emperor Constantine the Great and co-emperor Licinius elevate their sons Crispus, Constantine II and Licinius II to Caesars. After this arrangement Constantine rules the dioceses Pannonia and Macedonia, and establishes his residence at Sirmium, from where he prepares a campaign against the Goths and Sarmatians.
names: Crispus, Constantine II, and Licinius II

summary: Constantius II, future Roman emperor, was born at Sirmium.
text: Constantius II, Roman emperor (d. 361)

summary: Junius Bassus Theotecnius, a Roman politician and future urban prefect of Rome, was born.
text: Junius Bassus Theotecnius, Roman politician (d. 359)

summary: Themistius, a statesman and philosopher, was born in Paphlagonia.
text: Themistius, Byzantine statesman and philosopher

summary: Valerius Valens, co-emperor of Licinius, was executed.
text: Valerius Valens, Roman emperor

summary: Licinius retreated from Constantine the Great after fighting the indecisive Battle of Mardia.
text: Battle of Mardia: After a bloody battle, probably at modern Harmanli, Licinius retreated from contact with Constantine the Great.

summary: Licinius recognized Constantine the Great as his superior, ceded all European territories except Thrace, and agreed to execute Valerius Valens.
text: Licinius recognized Constantine the Great as his superior, ceded all his territories outside of Thrace, and agreed to depose and execute Valerius Valens, whom he had raised to augustus.

summary: Constantine the Great renamed Drepana to Helenopolis in honour of his mother Helena and built a church there.
text: Emperor Constantine the Great gives the ancient Roman town Drepana (Asia Minor) the name Helenopolis, after his mother Helena, and builds a church in honour of the martyr St. Lucian.

summary: Constantine the Great received the victory title Britannicus Maximus following successful operations in Britain.
text: Constantine the Great is given the title Brittanicus Maximus, for successful engagements in Britain.

summary: Gregory the Illuminator appointed his son Aristakes as successor in the patriarchate of Armenia.
text: Gregory the Illuminator appoints his son Aristax as successor in the patriarchate of Armenia.

summary: Theodota of Philippi was martyred.
text: Theodota of Philippi, Greek harlot and martyr

summary: Constantine the Great issued a law prohibiting the separation of slave families during changes in ownership.
text: Emperor Constantine the Great prohibits the separation of the families of slaves, during a change in ownership.

summary: Christianity was introduced to Colchis.
text: Christianity is introduced in Colchis, present-day Georgia.

summary: Arius travelled to Nicomedia after being condemned for heresy in Alexandria.
text: Arius travels to Nicomedia at the invitation of Bishop Eusebius, after having been accused of heresy and condemned by Alexander, the Patriarch of Alexandria. This gives rise to the Arian Controversy.

summary: Theodore Stratelates, a Roman general and Christian martyr, was executed.
text: Theodore Stratelates, Greek general and martyr (b. 281)

summary: Crispus defeated the Franks along the Rhine and took up residence at Augusta Treverorum.
text: Crispus, eldest son of Constantine I, leads a victorious campaign against the Franks, assuring twenty years of peace along the Rhine frontier. He establishes his residence in Augusta Treverorum (modern Trier), capital of Germania.

summary: Licinius reneged on the Edict of Milan and launched a new persecution of Christians in the Eastern Roman Empire.
text: Licinius reneges on the religious freedom promised by the Edict of Milan, and begins a new persecution of Christians in the Eastern Roman Empire. He imprisons Christians, confiscates their properties and destroys churches.

summary: Construction began on the Old Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome.
text: Construction begins on the Old St. Peter's Basilica, Rome .

summary: Pappus of Alexandria observed a solar eclipse and wrote a commentary on Ptolemy's Almagest.
text: Pappus of Alexandria, Greek philosopher, observes an eclipse of the sun and writes a commentary on The Great Astronomer (Almagest).

summary: Historian and politician Aurelius Victor was born.
text: Aurelius Victor, Roman historian and politician

summary: Future Roman emperor Constans was born.
text: Constans I, Roman emperor (d. 350)

summary: Future Patriarch Flavian I of Antioch was born.
text: Flavian I, Patriarch of Antioch (d. 404)

summary: Greek physician Oribasius was born.
text: Oribasius, Greek physician

summary: Martyrs Narcissus, Argeus, and Marcellinus died at Tomis.
text: Narcissus, Argeus, and Marcellinus, Roman Catholic martyrs and saints

summary: Bishop Valerius of Trèves died.
text: Valerius of Trèves, Roman Catholic priest and saint

summary: Dorothea of Alexandria was martyred.
text: Dorothea of Alexandria, Roman Catholic virgin, martyr and saint

summary: The Forty Martyrs of Sebaste were killed for their Christian faith.
text: 40 Martyrs of Sebaste

summary: Christian martyrs Cyrion and Candidus died at Sebaste.
text: Cyrion and Candidus, Armenian Orthodox priest and saints

summary: Christian martyrs Januarius and Pelagia died.
text: Januarius and Pelagia, Roman Catholic priests, martyrs and saints

summary: Saint Illuminata died in Umbria.
text: Saint Illuminata, Roman Catholic religious sister and saint

summary: Proculus, Bishop of Verona, died.
text: Proculus of Verona, Roman Catholic priest and saint

summary: Christian author and imperial advisor Lactantius died.
text: Lactantius, Christian writer

summary: Emperor Constantine I expelled the Goths from the Danube frontier, repaired Trajan's Bridge, and campaigned in Dacia.
text: Emperor Constantine I expels the Goths from the Danube frontier and repairs Trajan's Bridge. He leads an expedition into the old province Dacia (modern Romania) and makes peace with the barbarians.

summary: Emperor Constantine I decreed Sunday as a day of rest for urban residents and businesses throughout the empire.
text: Constantine I signs legislation directing urban residents to refrain from work, and businesses to be closed, on the "venerable day of the Sun". An exception is made for agriculture.

summary: Calcidius translated Plato's Timaeus into Latin.
text: Calcidius translates Plato into Latin.

summary: Constantine I assigned convicts to grind flour in Rome to curb rising food prices.
text: Constantine I assigns convicts to grind Rome's flour, in a move to hold back the rising price of food in an empire whose population has shrunk as a result of plague.

summary: Emperor Constantine I granted the Christian Church the legal right to hold property and receive bequests.
text: The Christian Church is allowed to hold property.

summary: A synod held in Alexandria condemned the doctrine of Arianism.
text: A synod held in Alexandria condemns Arianism.

summary: Constantine I issued an edict confirming Jewish civic duties in Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, marking the earliest documentation of Jews in Germany.
text: History of the Jews in Germany: Jews in modern-day Germany are documented for the first time, in Colonia Agrippinensium (modern-day Cologne).
names: History of the Jews in Germany

summary: Future Roman emperor Valentinian I was born at Cibalae.
text: Valentinian I ("the Great"), Roman emperor (d. 375)

summary: Philogonius, Bishop of Antioch, died.
text: Philogonius (or Filogonius), bishop of Antioch

summary: Constantine the Great defeated the invading Goths and Sarmatians north of the Danube in Dacia.
text: Emperor Constantine the Great defeats the invading Goths and Sarmatians north of the Danube in Dacia, and claims the title of Sarmaticus Maximus.
names: List of Roman imperial victory titles

summary: Arius promulgated his theological doctrine in the Banquet, leading to his condemnation and subsequent vindication at a synod in Bithynia.
text: The poetic work Banquet (Thalia) by the Libyan-born Egyptian Christian priest Arius, age 73, expresses the doctrine that Jesus of Nazareth was not of the same substance as God but rather had a finite nature. As an ascetic, he leads a Christian community near Alexandria, and comes under suspicion of heresy. Arius writes to his former schoolmate Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, asking for support. Eusebius writes to other bishops, and when Arius is condemned in September, Eusebius gives him safe haven, and sponsors a synod at Bithynia in October, which nullifies Arius's excommunication (see Council of Nicaea).

summary: Future Roman emperor Constans was born.
text: Constans I, Roman consul and emperor (d. 350)

summary: Bosporan client king Tiberius Julius Rhadamsades died.
text: Tiberius Julius Rhadamsades, Roman prince and client king

summary: Crispus and Constantine II took office as Roman consuls.
text: Flavius Julius Crispus Caesar, the sons of the Emperor Constantine and his expected heir, and Flavius Claudius Constantinus begin their one year terms as the new Roman consuls.

summary: Aurelius Isidorus of Karanis used the Greek word monachos in an Egyptian petition, marking its earliest known recorded use for a monk.
text: June – The earliest known use of the Greek word monachós to refer to a monk is made in a petition filed in Egypt by a man named Aurelius Isidorus, a man from the town of Karanis in Egypt.

summary: Constantine the Great defeated Licinius at the Battle of Adrianople, forcing him to retreat to Byzantium.
text: Battle of Adrianople: Emperor Constantine the Great defeats his rival Licinius near Adrianople, forcing him to retreat to Byzantium. Constantine then invades Thrace with a Visigothic force and raids the countryside.

summary: Crispus destroyed the fleet of Licinius at the Battle of the Hellespont, opening the crossing into Asia for Constantine.
text: July – Battle of the Hellespont: Flavius Julius Crispus, the designated heir of his father Constantine, destroys the naval fleet of Licinius in the Dardanelles, allowing Constantine to cross over the Bosphorus into Asian provinces. Byzantium is besieged and Licinius assembles a second military force, under his newly elevated co-emperor Martinian at Lampsacus (modern-day Lapseki).

summary: Constantine I definitively defeated Licinius at the Battle of Chrysopolis and became the sole Roman emperor, ending the Tetrarchy.
text: Battle of Chrysopolis: Constantine I definitively defeats Licinius at Chrysopolis, and becomes sole Emperor, thus ending the period of the Tetrarchy. Licinius escapes and gathers around 30,000 of his surviving troops at Nicomedia. Thus, the Civil wars of the Tetrarchy, which began in 306, end with Constantine ruling as sole Emperor.

summary: Constantine declared his son Constantius II to the rank of caesar.
text: Emperor Constantine declares his son, Flavius Julius Constantius, to the rank of caesar, designating Flavius as his successor. Flavius will ascend the throne as Constantine the Second in 337 AD.

summary: The Lateran Basilica was dedicated in Rome.
text: Dedication of the Lateran Basilica in Rome.

summary: Licinius abdicated as emperor and was banished to Thessalonica after being pardoned by Constantine I.
text: Licinius abdicates his position as Emperor. He is pardoned by Constantine I as a result of the supplication of his wife Constantia (who is Constantine's halfsister), and banished to Thessalonica as a private citizen.

summary: Constantine I seized Byzantium and began rebuilding the city to serve as the new imperial capital.
text: (Date unknown) The Roman Emperor Constantine I seizes the Byzantine Empire's capital, Byzantium, and commences work on rebuilding the city as the Eastern Empire's capital, which he will inaugurate as Constantinople in 330.

summary: Constantine reorganized the Roman army into three grades: palatini, comitatenses, and limitanei.
text: Constantine reorganises the Roman army in smaller units classified into three grades: palatini, (imperial escort armies); comitatenses, (forces based in frontier provinces) and limitanei (auxilia border troops).

summary: Constantine I secured the Danube frontier by defeating the Goths, Vandals, and Sarmatians.
text: German and Sarmatian campaigns of Constantine: Emperor Constantine I personally assures the security of the Danube frontier by defeating the Goths, the Vandals and the Sarmatians.
names: German and Sarmatian campaigns of Constantine

summary: Constantine ordered the execution of deposed emperors Licinius and Martinian for conspiracy.
text: Constantine has deposed Emperors Licinius and Martinian executed in Thessalonica and Cappadocia respectively for conspiring and raising troops against him.

summary: Constantine prohibited criminals from being forced to fight to the death as gladiators.
text: Constantine forbids criminals being forced to fight to the death as gladiators.

summary: The Colossus of Constantine in the Basilica of Maxentius was remodeled.
text: The Colossus of Constantine in the Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine, Rome, is perhaps remodelled at about this date. (The remains are moved to the Palazzo dei Conservatori, Rome, in the 15th century).

summary: Constantine summoned the First Council of Nicaea, which adopted the Nicene Creed, resolved the calculation of Easter, and exiled Arius.
text: First Council of Nicaea: Constantine summons an ecumenical council of bishops in Nicaea (Turkey). The Nicene Creed, adopted on June 19, declares that the members of the Trinity (the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit) are equal. The council decides that Easter is celebrated on the first Sunday after the first full moon after the vernal equinox. Arius is exiled to Illyria; his works are confiscated and consigned to the flames.

summary: Deposed Roman emperor Licinius was executed.
text: Licinius, deposed Roman emperor (executed)

summary: Deposed Roman emperor Martinian was executed.
text: Martinian, deposed Roman emperor (executed)

summary: Syrian philosopher and writer Iamblichus died.
text: Approximate date – Iamblichus, Syrian philosopher and writer (b. 245)

summary: Constantine the Great ordered the execution of his son Crispus at Pola and subsequently executed his wife Fausta.
text: Emperor Constantine the Great travels to Rome to celebrate the 20th anniversary of his accession to power, but while en route at Pola he orders his older son, Crispus Caesar, to be executed, possibly on charges of adultery. Later, Fausta, second wife of Constantine I, is also executed by being suffocated or boiled in a hot bath.

summary: Helena, mother of Constantine I, discovered the True Cross and the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.
text: September 14 (traditional date) – Helena, mother of Constantine I, discovers the so-called True Cross and the Holy Sepulchre (Jesus's tomb) in Jerusalem. On her pilgrimage, which begins about this year, she pauses on the Aegean island of Patmos, where she is said to found the church of Panagia Ekatontapiliani.

summary: Constantine began construction on Old St. Peter's Basilica in Rome and on the basilica of Golgotha in Jerusalem.
text: Helena tells Constantine that he must atone for executing his son and wife by building churches, and at about this date construction begins on Old St. Peter's Basilica, the first church on the traditional site of Saint Peter's tomb in Rome, and on the basilica of Golgotha on Calvary outside Jerusalem. He also commissions construction of the Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem (dedicated 339).

summary: Saint Nino introduced Christianity to the Kingdom of Iberia.
text: Christianity is introduced to the Kingdom of Iberia (modern-day Georgia) by Saint Nino .

summary: Constantius Gallus, future Roman caesar, was born.
text: Constantius Gallus, Roman consul and statesman (d. 354)

summary: Procopius, Roman general and future usurper, was born.
text: Procopius, Roman general and usurper (executed 366)

summary: Crispus, eldest son of Emperor Constantine I, was executed.
text: Flavius Julius Crispus, son of Constantine I (b. 303)

summary: Roman empress Flavia Maxima Fausta was executed by order of Constantine I.
text: Flavia Maxima Fausta, Roman empress (b. 289)

summary: Licinius II, former Roman caesar, was executed.
text: Licinius II, Roman consul and caesar (b. 315)

summary: Constantine decreed that rural slaves could only be sold within their resident province to alleviate labour shortages.
text: Emperor Constantine the Great decrees that rural slaves can only be sold in the province where they reside, in order to resolve the shortage of labour in the Roman Empire.

summary: Construction began on the Great Church of Antioch.
text: Construction begins on the Great Church of Antioch, which will be completed in 341.

summary: Helena founded Stavrovouni Monastery on Cyprus during her return from the Holy Land.
text: Approximate traditional date – Helena, mother of Constantine, returning from her pilgrimage to the Holy Land, founds Stavrovouni Monastery on Cyprus.

summary: Urban of Langres, future bishop and saint, was born.
text: Urban of Langres, French bishop and saint

summary: Awtel, Christian monk and hermit, died.
text: Awtel, Eastern Christian monk and saint

summary: Saint Cleopatra, a Christian saint, died.
text: Cleopatra, Christian martyr and saint (or 319)

summary: The Christian brothers Jonas and Barachisius were martyred in the Sasanian Empire.
text: Jonas and Barachisius, Persian martyrs

summary: Melitius of Lycopolis, founder of the Melitian sect, died.
text: Melitius of Lycopolis, Christian bishop

summary: The architect Theophilus Patricius officially opened Constantine's Bridge across the Danube between Sucidava and Oescus.
text: Constantine's Bridge, built over the Danube between Sucidava (Corabia, Romania) and Oescus (Gigen, Bulgaria), is officially opened by the Roman architect Theophilus Patricius.

summary: Imru' al-Qays ibn 'Amr, king of the Lakhmids, died.
text: Lakhmid king Imru' al-Qays ibn 'Amr dies. His epitaph, the Namara inscription, is an important source for the Arabic Language.

summary: Athanasius was elected bishop and patriarch of Alexandria following the death of Alexander I.
text: Athanasius is elected pope of Alexandria following the death of Alexander I.
names: Pope of the Coptic Orthodox Church

summary: Valens, future Roman emperor, was born.
text: Flavius Julius Valens, Roman emperor (d. 378)

summary: Alexander I, patriarch of Alexandria, died.
text: Alexander I, pope and patriarch of Alexandria

summary: Papa bar Aggai, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, died.
text: Papa (or Papa bar Aggai), Sassanid bishop

summary: The Roman state initiated legal restrictions on individuals joining the Christian clergy.
text: Roman restrictions on joining the clergy are initiated.

summary: Gregory of Nazianzus, theologian and future Patriarch of Constantinople, was born.
text: Gregory Nazianzus, Greek Patriarch of Constantinople (d. 390)

summary: Constantine the Great dedicated Constantinople as the new imperial capital of the Roman Empire.
text: Emperor Constantine the Great dedicates the Column of Constantine and Constantinople, or Nova Roma (modern-day Istanbul). He had spent four years expanding the city of Byzantium, having chosen the site for its strategic location on the Bosporus. The city became the capital of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: The Goths devastated the city of Tanais in the Don River delta.
text: The Goths devastate the city of Tanais, in the Don River Delta.

summary: Frumentius became the first bishop of the Kingdom of Aksum.
text: Frumentius is the first bishop of Ethiopia .

summary: Constantine the Great banished Eustathius of Antioch to Trajanopolis.
text: Eustathius, Patriarch of Antioch, is banished to Trajanopolis.

summary: Ulfilas translated the Bible into the Gothic language.
text: The Bible is translated into the Gothic language by Wulfila.

summary: Constantine the Great continued construction of a bridge across the Danube for planned campaigns against local tribes.
text: Constantine I continues construction of a bridge (in imitation of Trajan and his architect Apollodorus of Damascus) across the Danube, for forward-staging grounds for planned campaigns against local tribes.

summary: Constantine the Great announced a free distribution of food to citizens in Constantinople.
text: Constantine I announces a free distribution of food to the citizens in Constantinople, similar to the food given out in the city of Rome. The amount is approximately 80,000 rations a day, doled out from 117 distribution points around the city.

text: Emperor Constantine the Great pulls Roman troops out of Britain, and abandons work on Hadrian's Wall.

summary: Calocaerus revolted against Constantine the Great and proclaimed himself emperor on Cyprus.
text: Calocaerus revolts against Constantine I and proclaims himself emperor. Flavius Dalmatius, responsible for the security of the eastern frontier, is sent to Cyprus to suppress the rebellion.

summary: Constantine the Great elevated his youngest son Constans to the rank of Caesar at Constantinople.
text: Constantine I elevates his youngest son Constans to the rank of Caesar at Constantinople.

summary: Saint Monica, mother of Augustine of Hippo, was born in Thagaste.
text: Saint Monica, Christian saint and mother of Augustine of Hippo

text: Flavius Dalmatius puts down a revolt in Cyprus, led by Calocaerus. Calocaerus is brought to Tarsus (Cilicia), and executed.

summary: The Goths protected the Danube frontier against an invasion by the Vandals.
text: The Goths protect the Danube frontier against an invasion by the Vandals.

text: Emperor Constantine the Great reauthorises gladiatorial combat.

text: Constantine the Great campaigned against the Sarmatians.

text: Emperor Constantine I consecrates the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.

summary: Constantine the Great made his nephew Hannibalianus the King of Kings of the Pontic people.
text: Hannibalianus, nephew of Constantine I, is made Rex Regum ("King of Kings of the Pontic people").

summary: Athanasius of Alexandria was banished to Trier on charges of threatening the grain fleet to Constantinople.
text: Athanasius is banished to Trier, on the charge that he prevented the grain fleet from sailing to Constantinople.

text: First Synod of Tyre: Constantine I convenes a gathering of bishops at Tyre to depose and exile Patriarch Athanasius of Alexandria.

summary: Constantine the Great reinstated the Alexandrian priest Arius at a synod in Jerusalem.
text: Constantine I reinstates the Alexandrian priest Arius (declared a heretic at the First Council of Nicaea in 325) in a synod at Jerusalem about a year before Arius' death.

summary: Pope Sylvester I died in Rome after a twenty-one-year reign and was succeeded by Pope Mark.
text: Pope Sylvester I dies at Rome after a 21-year reign. He is succeeded by Mark as the 34th pope.

text: Gregory of Nyssa, Christian bishop and saint

text: Magnus Maximus, Western Roman emperor

text: Theon of Alexandria, director of the Library of Alexandria

text: Sylvester I, pope of the Catholic Church (b. 285)

summary: Constantine the Great reconquered most of Dacia for the Roman Empire.
text: The military successes of Emperor Constantine I result in most of Dacia being reconquered by the Roman Empire.

summary: The first recorded customs tariff came into use in Palmyra.
text: The first recorded customs tariff is in use in Palmyra.

summary: Pope Mark succeeded Pope Sylvester I as bishop of Rome.
text: Pope Mark succeeds Pope Sylvester I as the 34th pope of the Catholic Church.

text: Pope Mark dies at Rome, after an 11-month reign. No successor is immediately found.

summary: The first recorded celebration of Christmas took place.
text: The first celebration of Christmas is recorded.

summary: Pope Mark died.
text: Mark, pope of the Catholic Church

text: Constantine the Great, first Christian Roman emperor of the Western Empire (312–324), and of the Roman Empire (324–337), dies in Achyron, near Nicomedia, at age 65, after he is baptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia.

summary: Descendants of Constantius Chlorus and prominent Roman officials were executed in a dynastic purge.
text: A number of descendants of Constantius Chlorus, and officials of the Roman Empire, are executed in a purge.

summary: King Shapur II of Persia began a war against the Roman Empire, crossing the Tigris to attack Armenia and Mesopotamia.
text: King Shapur II of Persia begins a war against the Roman Empire. He sends his troops across the Tigris to recover Armenia and Mesopotamia.

summary: Shapur II besieged the Roman fortress of Nisibis but was repulsed by Lucilianus.
text: Shapur II besieges the Roman fortress of Nisibis (Syria), but is repulsed by forces under Lucilianus.

summary: Pope Julius I succeeded Pope Mark as bishop of Rome.
text: A 4-month papal vacancy ends; Pope Julius I succeeds Pope Mark, as the 35th pope.

summary: Constantius II announced the restoration of Athanasius as Patriarch of Alexandria.
text: Constantius II announces the restoration of Athanasius, as Patriarch of Alexandria.

summary: Paul I became Patriarch of Constantinople.
text: Paul I becomes Patriarch of Constantinople.

summary: Christianity was declared an official religion in the Kingdom of Iberia.

summary: The three sons of Constantine the Great declared themselves augusti and partitioned the Roman Empire among themselves.
text: Constantine the Great's three sons declared themselves augusti and divided their father's empire into three parts, with Constantine II (emperor) receiving Britain, Iberia, Gaul and Illyria, Constantius II Asia, Syria Palaestina and Egypt, and Constans Italy and Africa. The young Constans was placed under Constantine II's guardianship.

summary: The Romans, allied with the Goths, arrived along the Danube to protect the northern frontier.
text: The Romans, allied with the Goths, arrive in the north of the Roman Empire to protect the Danube frontier.

summary: Emperor Constantius II intervened in Armenia against Persian forces.
text: Emperor Constantius II intervenes against the Persians in Armenia.

summary: Shapur II initiated a widespread persecution of Christians throughout the Sasanian Empire.
text: Shapur II, king of the Persian Empire, begins a widespread persecution of Christians. He orders forcible conversions to the state religion, Zoroastrianism, lest the Christians disrupt his realm while he is away fighting the Romans in Armenia and Mesopotamia.

summary: Construction began on the Church of Santa Costanza in Rome.
text: The Church of Santa Costanza, Rome, starts to be built .

summary: Constantius II hastened to Roman Mesopotamia to counter attacks by King Shapur II of Persia.
text: Emperor Constantius II hastens to his territory in the East, where a revived Persia under King Shapur II is attacking Mesopotamia. For the next 11 years, the two powers engage in a war of border skirmishing, with no real victor.

summary: Pope Julius I gave refuge in Rome to the deposed Alexandrian patriarch Athanasius.
text: Pope Julius I gives refuge in Rome to the Alexandrian patriarch Athanasius, who is deposed and expelled during the First Synod of Tyre (see 335).

summary: Eusebius of Nicomedia was made bishop of Constantinople while Gregory succeeded Athanasius as bishop of Alexandria.
text: Eusebius of Nicomedia is made bishop of Constantinople, while another Arian succeeds Athanasius as bishop of Alexandria, under the name Gregory.

summary: Constantinople surpassed Rome to become the largest city in the world.

summary: Constantine II was ambushed and killed near Aquileia by the troops of his brother Constans.
text: Constantine II, emperor of the western part of the Roman Empire (Britain, Gaul, the Rhine provinces and Iberia), crosses the Alps and attacks the army of his brother Constans I, emperor of the central part of the Roman Empire (Upper Danube, Italy and middle Africa). They clash at Aquileia in northern Italy. Constantine is killed in a skirmish by an ambush of Constans' troops.

summary: Constans became the sole ruler of the Western Roman Empire after the death of Constantine II.
text: Constans is left sole ruler of the Western part of the Roman Empire, with his other brother, Constantius II, emperor of the Eastern portion.

text: The Western Roman Emperor Constans I is in Britain, possibly in a military campaign against the Picts and Scots (the last visit to Britain by a legitimate emperor).

summary: Constantius II campaigned in Adiabene against the Sasanian Persians.
text: The Eastern Roman Emperor Constantius II campaigns in Adiabene, a vassal kingdom of Armenia (Persian Empire).

summary: Pope Julius I convoked the Council of Serdica to unite Western bishops against Arianism.
text: Pope Julius I tries to unite the Western bishops against Arianism by convoking the Council of Serdica, which acknowledges the pope's supreme authority and grants him the right to judge cases involving the legal possession of episcopal sees, but only Western and Egyptian bishops attend, and Arianism remains strong.

summary: Constantius II campaigned in eastern Mesopotamia against the Sasanian Persians.
text: The Eastern Roman Emperor Constantius II campaigns in eastern Mesopotamia, against the Sassanid Persians.

summary: Roman forces under Constantius II defeated Shapur II at the Battle of Singara.
text: Battle of Singara: The Roman army under Constantius wins a close victory, at the strongly fortified city of Singara (Mesopotamia). His enemy, King Shapur II, is forced to lift the siege, and withdraw the Persian army.

summary: Roman forces under Lucilianus repulsed Shapur II's siege of Nisibis.
text: Shapur II, for the second time, besieges the Roman fortress of Nisibis in eastern Mesopotamia, but is repulsed by forces under General Lucilianus.

summary: Bishop Eustorgius I reportedly brought relics of the Three Magi from Constantinople to Milan.
text: Bishop Eustorgius I brings relics of the Three Magi from Constantinople to Milan, according to a 12th century legend.

text: The Council of Philippopolis is held as the result of Eastern bishops leaving the Council of Sardica. In Philippopolis (Bulgaria), they excommunicate Pope Julius, and as a result, the Arian controversy is perpetuated.

summary: Ulfilas escaped religious persecution by Athanaric and settled with his Christian converts near Nicopolis ad Istrum in Moesia.

summary: The Sasanian Empire enrolled women into the army to perform auxiliary services.
text: In Persia, women are enrolled in the army to perform auxiliary services.
