text: Vitalian accepts an agreement and returns with his army to Lower Moesia. After a few inconclusive skirmishes, Anastasius I sends a Byzantine army (80,000 men) under his nephew Hypatius.

summary: Vitalian attacked the fortified Byzantine camp in darkness at Acris and crushed the imperial army.
text: Vitalian defeats the Byzantines at Acris (Bulgaria), on the Black Sea coast. He attacks their fortified Laager in darkness, and in a crushing defeat kills a large part of the imperial army.

summary: Vitalian marched on Constantinople and blockaded the city's harbour with a fleet of two hundred ships.
text: Vitalian, Byzantine general, marches again to Constantinople. A fleet of 200 vessels sails from the Black Sea ports and blockades the entrance of the harbor capital. Emperor Anastasius I is disquieted by riots in the city, which cost many casualties, and decides to negotiate with Vitalian.

summary: Vitalian accepted a ransom in gold to release Hypatius and retreated with his troops to Lower Moesia.
text: Vitalian accepts the receipt of ransom money and gifts worth 5,000 pounds of gold for the release of Hypatius, a nephew of Anastasius I who has been a prisoner since the attack at Acris (see 513). Vitalian retreats to Lower Moesia.

summary: Vitalian advanced on Constantinople and captured the suburb of Sycae across the Golden Horn.
text: Autumn – Revolt of Vitalian: Byzantine general (magister militum) Vitalian mobilises his army, and marches again towards Constantinople. He captures the suburb of Sycae (modern Turkey) across the Golden Horn, and encamps there.

summary: Marinus defeated the rebel fleet at Constantinople using an incendiary chemical substance.
text: Emperor Anastasius I gives Marinus, former praetorian prefect of the East, command over the Byzantine army. He defeats the rebel fleet at the harbor entrance, using a sulfur-based chemical substance, similar to the later Greek fire.

summary: Marinus landed an army at Sycae, routing the rebel force and compelling Vitalian to flee north.
text: Marinus lands with an army on the shore of Sycae and defeats the rebels. Disheartened by the losses suffered, Vitalian flees north under cover of the night.

summary: Emperor Anastasius I celebrated his victory over Vitalian with a procession and thanksgiving service at Sosthenion.
text: As a sign of his victory, Anastasius I leads a procession to Sosthenion, and attends a service of thanks at the local church dedicated to the Archangel Michael.

summary: Empress Ariadne died at Constantinople and was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles.
text: Empress Ariadne, wife of Emperor Anastasius I, dies at Constantinople and is buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles.

summary: Byzantine empress Ariadne died.
text: Ariadne, Byzantine empress
names: List of Roman and Byzantine empresses

summary: Euphemius, deposed patriarch of Constantinople, died in exile.
text: Euphemius, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Pope John II of Alexandria died.
text: John, Coptic Orthodox patriarch of Alexandria
names: List of popes of the Coptic Orthodox Church

summary: Timothy I, patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Timothy I, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Dioscorus II, Coptic Orthodox patriarch of Alexandria, died.
text: Dioscorus II, Coptic Orthodox patriarch of Alexandria
names: List of popes of the Coptic Orthodox Church

summary: Macedonius II, exiled patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Macedonius II, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Emperor Anastasius I died childless at Constantinople and was succeeded by Justin I.
text: Emperor Anastasius I dies childless at Constantinople, age 88, after a 27-year reign in which he has abolished the sale of offices, reformed taxation, and perfected the empire's monetary system, but antagonized some with his heretical Monophysite religious policies. He is succeeded by Justin I (Flavius Justinus), his comes excubitorum, commander of the palace guard. After his death, he leaves the imperial treasury richer by 23,000,000 solidi or 320,000 pounds of gold.

object: Byzantine Empire under the Justinian dynasty
summary: Justin I founded the Justinian dynasty, elevated his nephew Justinian, and had the pretender Theocritus executed.
text: Justin I founds the Justinian dynasty and makes his nephew Flavius Petrus Sabbatius (later Justinian I) his trusted advisor. He becomes the emperor's close confidant and possibly acts as regent. Theocritus, candidate to the throne, is accused of a conspiracy and executed.
names: Byzantine Empire under the Justinian dynasty

summary: An earthquake destroyed the city of Scupi in Moesia Superior.
text: An earthquake destroys the city of Scupi (modern-day Skopje, North Macedonia), in what once was the Roman province of Moesia Superior.

summary: Jabalah IV ibn al-Harith became king of the Ghassanids and invaded Byzantine Palestine, where he was defeated by general Romanus.
text: Jabalah IV ibn al-Harith becomes the king of the Ghassanids. He invades Palestine, but is defeated by a Byzantine army under general (dux) Romanus.

summary: Severus was deposed as patriarch of Antioch by a synod and replaced by Paul the Jew.
text: Severus, patriarch of Antioch, is deposed by a synod for his Monophysitism. Paul the Jew is appointed to replace him.

summary: Byzantine emperor Anastasius I Dicorus died.
text: Anastasius I Dicorus, Byzantine emperor

summary: Theocritus, Byzantine pretender to the imperial throne, was executed.
text: July – Theocritus, Byzantine pretender (executed)

summary: Aeneas of Gaza, Christian Neoplatonist philosopher, died.
text: Aeneas of Gaza, Neoplatonist and Christian philosopher

summary: Flavian II, banished former patriarch of Antioch, died in exile.
text: Flavian II, banished patriarch of Antioch

summary: The Eastern and Western churches reconciled, ending the Acacian Schism.
text: The Eastern and Western churches reconcile their differences, ending the Acacian Schism.

summary: Jacob of Serugh became bishop of Batnan.
text: Jacob of Serugh becomes bishop of Batnan (near modern Diyarbakir, Turkey).

summary: Priscian completed the Institutiones Grammaticae in Constantinople.
text: Priscian, Latin grammarian, writes the Institutiones Grammaticae ("Grammatical Foundations"). In Constantinople, he codifies this manuscript in 18 volumes, which will be widely used through the Middle Ages. It provides the raw material for the field of speculative grammar.

summary: Vitalian became consul and was shortly afterward murdered, likely on the orders of Justinian.
text: July – Byzantine general Vitalian becomes consul, and is shortly later murdered, probably on the orders of Justinian, the nephew and heir-apparent of Emperor Justin I.

summary: Emperor Justin I elected Epiphanius as patriarch of Constantinople.
text: Epiphanius is elected patriarch of Constantinople by Byzantine Emperor Justin I.

summary: Seridus founded his monastery near Gaza.
text: The monastery of Seridus, where Barsanuphius and John the Prophet lived as hermits, is founded in the region of Gaza.

summary: Justin II, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: Justin II, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (d. 578)

summary: John of Cappadocia, patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: John of Cappadocia, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Vitalian, Byzantine general and consul, was assassinated.
text: July – Vitalian, Byzantine general, consul

summary: Isidore of Alexandria, Neoplatonist philosopher, died.
text: Isidore of Alexandria, Neoplatonist philosopher

summary: Justinian was appointed consul by Emperor Justin I.
text: Future Byzantine emperor Justinian, age 39, is appointed consul. He later becomes Commander-in-chief of the Army of the East.

summary: Jacob of Serugh, Syrian poet and theologian, died.
text: Jacob of Serugh, Syrian poet and theologian

summary: Justinian married Theodora in Constantinople.
text: Justinian, later Byzantine emperor, marries in Constantinople his mistress Theodora, who is by profession a courtesan .

summary: Hilderic succeeded Thrasamund as king of the Vandals and Alans.
text: Hilderic succeeds his uncle Thrasamund after a 27-year reign, and becomes king of the Vandals and Alans. He favours Catholicism and grants the inhabitants religious freedom.

summary: Pope Hormisdas died at Rome and was succeeded by John I.
text: Pope Hormisdas dies at Rome after a tenure of 9 years and 17 days, in which he has been instrumental in ending the Acacian Schism. He is succeeded by John I as the 53rd pope.

summary: Pope Hormisdas died.
text: Pope Hormisdas (b. 450)

summary: Syrian theologian Philoxenus of Mabbug died in exile.
text: Philoxenus of Mabbug, Syrian theologian

summary: King Thrasamund of the Vandals died.
text: Thrasamund, king of the Vandals (b. 450)

summary: Emperor Justin I appointed Venantius Opilio as Roman consul for the West.
text: Venantius Opilio is appointed by Byzantium's Emperor Justin to administer the Western Roman Empire as the Roman consul, replacing Anicius Maximus. The Emperor Justin appoints himself as consul for the West, an office vacant since 522, but has Theodorus Filoxenus administering the west.

summary: Emperor Justin I rebuilt the city of Anazarbus and renamed it Justinopolis.
text: Emperor Justin I rebuilds the city of Anazarbus (modern Turkey) and renames it "Justinopolis".

summary: King Theodoric the Great sent Pope John I to Constantinople to negotiate the withdrawal of Emperor Justin's anti-Arian edict.
text: King Theodoric the Great sends Pope John I to Constantinople, to negotiate a withdrawal of Byzantine emperor Justin's edict against Arian Christianity.

summary: The Daisan River flooded Edessa, breaching the city walls and submerging most of the city.
text: The Daisan river, tributary of the Euphrates, floods Edessa, and within a couple of hours fills the entire city except for the highest parts. Eventually the pent-up waters break through the city walls. The Shroud of Turin is allegedly discovered during the rebuilding of the city (see Image of Edessa).

summary: Cosmas Indicopleustes travelled up the Nile on his exploratory voyages.
text: Cosmas Indicopleustes, Alexandrian explorer-geographer, travels up the Nile. He will venture as far to the east as Ceylon, become a monk, and write "Topographia Christiana" to vindicate the biblical account of the world (see 550).

summary: Alexander of Tralles, the Byzantine physician, was born.
text: Alexander of Tralles, physician

summary: John Climacus, Christian monk and ascetic writer, was born.
text: John Climacus, monk and writer

summary: Justin, Byzantine general and aristocrat, was born.
text: Justin, Byzantine aristocrat and general (d. 566)

summary: King Kavad I of Persia invaded the South Caucasus and Upper Mesopotamia with assistance from Al-Mundhir III.
text: Roman–Persian Wars: King Kavad I, assisted by his Arabian vassal, Al-Mundhir III, begins a campaign in the Transcaucasus region and Upper Mesopotamia.

summary: A devastating earthquake struck Antioch and Syria, killing approximately 250,000 people.
text: Probably between May 20 and May 29 – 526 Antioch earthquake: A great earthquake kills approximately 250,000 people in Syria and Antioch.

summary: Theodoric the Great imprisoned Pope John I upon his return to Ravenna from Constantinople.
text: Pope John I returns to Ravenna from Constantinople. Theodoric the Great finds that he has been only partly successful in persuading the Byzantine emperor Justin I to withdraw his edict against Arian Christianity, and throws the pope into prison.

summary: Paul of Edessa, Syriac Orthodox bishop of Edessa, died.
text: Paul of Edessa, Syriac Orthodox bishop of Edessa

summary: Emperor Justin I named his nephew Justinian I as co-emperor of the Byzantine Empire.
text: Emperor Justin I names his nephew Justinian I as co-ruler, as an incurable wound saps his strength.

summary: Justin I died at Constantinople and was succeeded by Justinian I as sole emperor.
text: Justin I, age 77, dies at Constantinople and is succeeded by Justinian I, who becomes sole emperor.

summary: Emperor Justinian I reorganised the command structure of the Byzantine army into a smaller, highly trained force.
text: Justinian I reorganises the command structure of the Byzantine army, and fields a small but highly trained army.

summary: Justinian I appointed Belisarius to command the Eastern Roman army in Armenia and along the Persian frontier.
text: Justinian I appoints Belisarius to command the Eastern army in Armenia and on the Byzantine-Persian frontier.

summary: Justinian I banned pagan religious practices in Egypt and dispatched Christian missionaries southward.
text: Justinian I outlaws pagan religious practices in Egypt, and dispatches Byzantine missionaries to southern territories .

summary: Reconstruction of the Church of the Nativity began in Bethlehem to restore the basilica.
text: The Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem is rebuilt until 565, restoring the architectural tone of the basilica.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Justin I died in Constantinople.
text: Justin I, Byzantine Emperor (b. 450)

summary: Justinian I appointed a commission led by Tribonian to compile Roman laws into the Corpus Juris Civilis.
text: Emperor Justinian I appoints a commission (including the jurist Tribonian) to codify all laws of the Roman Empire that are still in force from Hadrian to the current date; this becomes the Corpus Juris Civilis.

summary: A major earthquake struck Antioch, killing thousands of residents.
text: Natural disaster: A second earthquake strikes Antioch, killing thousands.

summary: Justin, the Byzantine magister militum, was killed fighting the Bulgars along the Danube frontier in Moesia.
text: Justin, Byzantine general (magister militum), dies in battle against the Bulgars on the frontier of the Danubian limes in Moesia. He is succeeded by Constantiolus.

summary: Roman noblewoman and imperial patron Anicia Juliana died in Constantinople.
text: Anicia Juliana, daughter of Olybrius

summary: Patriarch Euphrasius of Antioch died in the earthquake that devastated the city.
text: Euphrasius, patriarch of Antioch (in the earthquake)

summary: King Jabalah IV ibn al-Harith of the Ghassanids died.
text: Jabalah IV ibn al-Harith, king of the Ghassanids

summary: Justin, Byzantine commander in Moesia, fell in battle against the Bulgars.
text: Justin, Byzantine general (magister militum)

summary: Christian rhetorician and sophist Procopius of Gaza died.
text: Procopius of Gaza, Christian sophist and rhetorician

summary: Emperor Justinian I promulgated the Codex Justinianus to reorganize Roman statutory law.
text: Emperor Justinian I issues the Codex Justinianus (Code of Civil Laws), reformulating Roman law in an effort to control his unruly people (see 532).

summary: The Samaritans revolted against Roman rule, and the Church of the Nativity was burned down during the conflict.
text: The Samaritans revolt and are defeated; the Church of the Nativity is burnt down during the Rebellion.

summary: Al-Harith ibn Jabalah became king of the Ghassanids and helped the Byzantine Empire suppress the Samaritan revolt.
text: Al-Harith ibn Jabalah becomes the fifth king of the Ghassanids. He helps the Byzantines to suppress the wide-scale Samaritan Revolt.

summary: Emperor Justinian I ordered the closure of the Platonic Academy in Athens, prompting its pagan philosophers to emigrate eastward.
text: The Academy, originally founded at Athens by Plato around 387 BC, closes down by order of Justinian I, on charges of un-Christian activity. Many of the school's professors emigrate to Persia and Syria.

summary: Monk and monastic founder Theodosius the Cenobiarch died at his monastery near Bethlehem.
text: Theodosius the Cenobiarch, monk and founder of the Monastery of St. Theodosius

summary: Emperor Justinian I appointed a second commission to codify the jurists' writings on Roman law into the Digest.
text: Emperor Justinian I selects a second commission to excerpt and codify the writings of the jurists on Roman law. This becomes the Digest (Pandects).

summary: Tribonian was appointed quaestor sacri palatii and chief editor of the Digest.
text: Tribonian becomes quaestor sacri palatii and chief editor of the compilation of the old Roman lawyers' writings.

summary: Belisarius and Hermogenes defeated a Persian-Arab army at the Battle of Dara.
text: Spring – Battle of Dara: Belisarius and Hermogenes (magister officiorum) defeat a combined Persian-Arab army of 50,000 men at Dara (modern Turkey), by entrenching his infantry in a refused position in the centre line, then carrying out a cavalry envelopment to culminate a classic defensive-offensive battleplan.

summary: Sittas defeated a Persian invasion force in Roman Armenia at the Battle of Satala.
text: Summer – Battle of Satala: A Byzantine cavalry force (30,000 men) under command of Sittas defeats a major Persian invasion into Roman Armenia.

summary: Emperor Justinian I sent an embassy to Carthage to negotiate with Gelimer, who rejected the overture.
text: Justinian I sends an embassy to Carthage to negotiate with Gelimer. Gelimer replies: “Nothing is more desirable than that a monarch should mind his own business.”

summary: The mosaic synagogue floor at Maon in Judea was created.
text: The mosaic synagogue floor from Maon (Judea) is made. It is now kept at the Israel Museum in Jerusalem .

summary: Byzantine empress Sophia was born.
text: Sophia, Byzantine Empress
names: List of Roman and Byzantine empresses

summary: A Persian army defeated Belisarius and the Byzantines at the Battle of Callinicum near Raqqa.
text: Battle of Callinicum: A Byzantine army (20,000 men), commanded by Belisarius, is defeated by the Persians at Raqqa (northern Syria). Emperor Justinian I negotiates an end to the hostilities, and Belisarius is hailed as a hero.

summary: Members of the Blue and Green chariot racing factions were imprisoned for murder in Constantinople.
text: Some members of the Blue and Green chariot racing factions in Constantinople are imprisoned for murder, precipitating the Nika riots the next year.

summary: Khosrow I succeeded his father Kavad I as king of the Sasanian Empire upon Kavad's death.
text: King Kavad I, age 82, dies after a 43-year reign. Khosrau I, his favourite son, is proclaimed successor over his elder brothers.

summary: Kavad I, king of the Sasanian Empire, died.
text: Kavadh I, king of the Persian Empire (b. 449)

summary: Belisarius and Mundus suppressed the Nika riots in Constantinople, killing tens of thousands in the Hippodrome.
text: Nika riots in Constantinople: Anger among the supporters of the most important chariot teams—the Blues and the Greens—escalates into violence towards the emperor. For the next five days the capital is in chaos. The fires that start during the tumult result in the destruction of much of the city. The insurrection is put down a week later by Belisarius and Mundus; 30,000 people are killed in the Hippodrome.

summary: Emperor Justinian I ordered the construction of the Hagia Sophia basilica in Constantinople.
text: Emperor Justinian I orders the building of a new Orthodox Christian basilica in Constantinople – the Hagia Sophia. He chooses Isidore of Miletus and Anthemius of Tralles as architects. The material for the construction is brought from all over the empire, such as large stones from quarries in Porphyry, Egypt. More than 10,000 people are employed.

summary: Justinian I signed the Perpetual Peace treaty with Khosrow I of Persia, concluding the Iberian War.
text: September – Justinian I signs a peace treaty, the "Eternal Peace", with the Persian king Khosrau I, ending the Iberian War (527-531). Both sides agree to return all occupied territories, and Justinian makes a one-off payment of 110 centenaria (11,000 pounds of gold), as a contribution to the defense of the Caucasus passes.

summary: Hypatius, Byzantine nobleman declared emperor during the Nika riots, was executed.
text: Hypatius, Byzantine nobleman (executed)

summary: Pompeius, Byzantine senator, was executed following the Nika riots.
text: Pompeius, Byzantine politician (executed)

summary: Saint Sabbas the Sanctified, monk and founder of Mar Saba monastery, died.
text: Sabbas the Sanctified, monk and saint (b. 439)

summary: King Gelimer dispatched Tzazo to Sardinia to quell a revolt, while Byzantine forces occupied Leptis Magna and Tripolitania.
text: Spring – Vandalic War: Anti-Vandal revolt in Tripolitania and Sardinia; Gelimer, king of the Vandals, dispatches the bulk of the Vandal fleet (120 ships and 5,000 men) under his brother Tzazo to Sardinia. Byzantine forces from Cyrenaica occupy Leptis Magna and Tripolis.

summary: Emperor Justinian I recognized the Bishop of Rome as head of all bishops and the corrector of heretics.
text: In a letter, Emperor Justinian I declares the Bishop of Rome (currently John) to be "head of all Bishops, and the true and effective corrector of heretics."

summary: Emperor Justinian I held a war council in Constantinople and appointed Belisarius to lead an expedition against the Vandals.
text: Summer – Emperor Justinian I holds a war council in Constantinople. His advisers warn him against launching an expedition to North Africa, because of the supply-lines (1,000 miles into Vandal waters) and the huge drain on the imperial treasury. Justinian appoints Belisarius to command the Byzantine army.

summary: Belisarius sailed from Constantinople with an expeditionary fleet of transports and warships to invade Vandal Africa.
text: A Byzantine expeditionary fleet under Belisarius sails in 500 transports, escorted by 92 war vessels (dromons), manned by 20,000 seamen from Constantinople, to attack the Vandals in Africa, via Greece and Sicily. The fleet carries 10,000 infantry, about half Byzantine and half foederati, and 5,000 cavalry, consisting of 3,000 Byzantine horsemen, 1,000 foreign allies (Huns and Heruli) and 1,500 of Belisarius' retainers (bucellarii). On the flagship Belisarius is accompanied by his military secretary Procopius, and his wife Antonina.

summary: Belisarius arrived in Sicily, using the island as a staging area with the permission of Queen Amalasuntha.
text: September – Belisarius arrives at Sicily, which he uses as a staging area, with the permission of the Ostrogoth queen Amalasuntha, daughter of Theodoric the Great and regent of Italy. The Ostrogoths help him with supplies and the fleet is prepared for the final attack.

summary: Belisarius landed the Byzantine army at Caput Vada and began marching northward along the coast toward Carthage.
text: The Byzantine army lands at Caput Vada (modern Tunisia). Belisarius marches his army northwards, towards Carthage (over 140 miles), following the coast, accompanied by the fleet and shadowed by Gelimer. During the march, the Vandal towns fall without a fight.

summary: Belisarius repulsed an ambush by Gelimer at the Battle of Ad Decimum and subsequently captured Carthage.
text: Battle of Ad Decimum: Gelimer attempts to ambush the Byzantines in a defile at the "10th milestone" from Carthage; due to inadequate coordination and the alertness of Belisarius, the attack is repulsed and the Vandals are scattered into the desert. Belisarius enters the capital and orders his soldiers not to kill or enslave the population. The fleet is stationed in the Lake of Tunis.

summary: Belisarius routed Gelimer and the Vandal army at the Battle of Tricamarum, where Tzazo was killed.
text: Battle of Tricamarum: Gelimer assembles an army of about 50,000 men at Bulla Regia (Numidia), and advances towards Carthage. Belisarius moves out to meet the Vandals; he leads the Byzantine cavalry (5,000 men) into battle. Without waiting for his infantry to come up, he charges, despite odds of almost 10-to-1, and throws Gelimer in confusion. Belisarius captures the Vandal camp by storm. Tzazo is killed in an all-cavalry fight, and Gelimer is forced to seek refuge in the mountains of Tunis with the Berbers.

summary: The Digest, a massive compilation of classical Roman legal jurisprudence, was completed.
text: The Digesta or Pandectae, a collection of jurist writings and other sources, is completed (see Corpus Juris Civilis).

summary: King Gelimer surrendered to Belisarius in Numidia, ending the Vandal Kingdom and restoring North Africa to the Roman Empire.
text: March – King Gelimer surrenders to Belisarius, after spending a winter in the mountains of Numidia. He and large numbers of captured Vandals are transported to Constantinople. The Vandal Kingdom ends, and the African provinces return to the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Belisarius appointed Solomon as governor in Africa to pacify the Moors, while Malta became a Byzantine province.
text: April – Belisarius leaves a small force in Africa under the Byzantine general Solomon, to continue the subjugation of the province. He is appointed governor (Exarch) and pacifies the Moorish tribes with success. Malta becomes a Byzantine province (until 870).

summary: Belisarius celebrated a Roman triumph in Constantinople for his conquest of the Vandals, displaying treasures from Jerusalem and Carthage.
text: Summer – Belisarius arrives in Constantinople and is permitted by Emperor Justinian I to celebrate a triumph, the first non-imperial triumph for over 500 years. In the procession the spoils of the Temple of Jerusalem and the Vandal treasure are paraded.

summary: Emperor Justinian I commemorated the victory against the Vandals by minting medals inscribed Gloria Romanorum.
text: Justinian I commemorates the victory against the Vandals by stamping medals in his honor with the inscription "Gloria Romanorum" .

summary: A second and final revision of the Codex Justinianus was published.
text: A second and final revision of the Codex Justinianus is published.

summary: Following Athalaric's death, Amalasuntha elevated Theodahad to co-ruler of the Ostrogoths while he secretly negotiated to surrender Tuscany to Constantinople.
text: King Athalaric dies of tuberculosis, age 18, having dissipated his youth in drink and debauchery. His mother, Amalasuntha, proposes to her cousin Theodahad, the kingdom's largest landowner and her father's last male heir, that he share the throne with her but that he will be king of the Ostrogoths in name only. Theodahad has secret conversations with the Byzantine ambassador, and promises to turn over Tuscany in exchange for a large sum of money, the rank of senator, and permission to live at Constantinople.

summary: Anthemius of Tralles, Greek geometer and architect of the Hagia Sophia, died.
text: Anthemius of Tralles, architect and mathematician

summary: Marcellinus Comes, Latin chronicler and courtier to Justinian, died.
text: Marcellinus Comes, Latin chronicler

summary: Emperor Justinian I used the murder of Queen Amalasuintha as a pretext to launch the Gothic War and invade Italy.
text: The death of Amalasuintha gives Byzantine Emperor Justinian I a pretext to invade Italy and begin the Gothic War.

summary: Emperor Justinian I founded the city of Justiniana Prima in the central Balkans.
text: The Byzantine city of Justiniana Prima is founded, and later becomes a bishop's seat of the Central Balkans.

summary: Emperor Justinian I appointed Belisarius supreme commander and dispatched an expeditionary force to begin the reconquest of Italy.
text: Gothic War: Emperor Justinian I appoints Belisarius commander-in-chief (stratēgos autokratōr), and sends a Byzantine expeditionary force of only 8,000 soldiers (half are heavy East Roman cavalry) to begin the reconquest of Italy.

summary: Belisarius landed in Sicily and besieged Palermo, while Mundus invaded Dalmatia and captured Salona.
text: Summer – Belisarius lands in Sicily and meets little opposition, save for the Gothic garrison of Palermo. Laying siege to the citadel, he blockades the harbour with his ships. Mundus invades Dalmatia and captures its capital, Salona.

summary: Justinian I issued legislation barring wives from bringing criminal adultery charges against husbands, making divorce nearly impossible.
text: Justinian I issues the Lex Julia and declares that a wife has no right to bring criminal charges of adultery against a husband. This makes divorce almost impossible in the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Belisarius completed the conquest of Sicily after defeating the Ostrogothic garrison at Palermo.
text: Belisarius completes the conquest of Sicily, defeating the Gothic garrison of Palermo (Panormos), and ending his consulship for the year.

summary: Solomon defeated Moorish rebels at Mount Mammes and Mount Bourgaon, securing Byzacena for the empire.
text: Spring – Solomon defeats the Moorish rebels at Mount Mammes and Mount Bourgaon. He secures Byzacena (modern Tunisia) and establishes fortifications along the Numidian border.

summary: Justinian I organised Byzantine North Africa into a prefecture centered in Carthage and restored Catholic Church property.
text: April – Justinian I reorganises the province as an African prefecture, centered in Carthage. He restores frontier defences, and returns property to the Catholic Church.

summary: Pope Agapetus I succeeded Pope John II as pope and was sent on an embassy to Constantinople by King Theodahad.
text: Pope John II dies in Rome after a two-year reign, and is succeeded by Agapetus I as the 57th pope. Agapetus is sent by King Theodahad on an embassy to Constantinople.

summary: Byzantine troops expelled Monophysites from Alexandria and installed Theodosius I as patriarch.
text: Byzantine troops drive the extremist Monophysite party out of Alexandria, and establish Theodosius I as patriarch of the Eastern Orthodox Church.

summary: Anthimus I became patriarch of Constantinople.
text: Anthimus I becomes patriarch of Constantinople (535–536).

summary: A Christian basilica was completed at Leptis Magna in North Africa.
text: A Christian basilica is completed at Leptis Magna in North Africa.

summary: Syrian Christian historian Evagrius Scholasticus was born in Syria.
text: Evagrius Scholasticus, Syrian scholar

summary: Epiphanius, patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Epiphanius, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Timothy III, patriarch of Alexandria, died.
text: Timothy III, Coptic Orthodox Patriarch of Alexandria
names: List of popes of the Coptic Orthodox Church

summary: Emperor Justinian I appointed Germanus as military commander to deal with the crisis in Africa, replacing Solomon.
text: Spring – Emperor Justinian I appoints his cousin Germanus as magister militum to deal with the crisis in Africa. He sends a mobile force of comitatenses (mostly cavalry) and an elite guard. Solomon, the previous magister militum, returns to Constantinople.

summary: Belisarius crossed the Strait of Messina into mainland Italy, captured Rhegium, and advanced toward Naples.
text: Summer – Gothic War (535–554): Belisarius crosses the Strait of Messina and invades Italy. He conquers the city of Rhegium and advances to Naples.

summary: Belisarius captured Naples after a month-long siege by infiltrating troops through an abandoned aqueduct.
text: November – Siege of Naples: Belisarius captures Naples after a month's siege, by sending troops into the city through an abandoned Roman aqueduct.

summary: Belisarius entered Rome as the Ostrogothic garrison fled, and began provisioning the city against an impending siege.
text: Belisarius enters Rome through the Porta Asinaria, and the Gothic garrison of 4,000 men flees the city. He sends an urgent request for reinforcements to Justinian I, meanwhile preparing Rome for a siege, by bringing in great quantities of food and other supplies.

summary: Belisarius established headquarters on the Pincian Hill, repaired the Aurelian Walls, and recruited Romans to help defend the city.
text: Winter – Belisarius sets up his headquarters on the Pincian Hill, and repairs the neglected city walls of Rome. He stations a 5,000-man garrison, of whom half are his personal bodyguard (bucellarii). To hold parts of the city, he recruits 20,000 young Romans to man the walls.

summary: Theodahad ceded Provence and upper Alamannia to the Franks, while Gothic forces defeated the Byzantines and killed Mundus at Salona.
text: March – Ostrogothic King Theodahad cedes Provence and upper Alamannia to the Franks, gaining their support in the war. He sends a large Gothic army into Dalmatia. They defeat the Byzantines, Mundus is killed during the fighting at Salona, and the Byzantine army withdraws.

summary: Constantinianus retook Dalmatia and rebuilt the walls of Salona after the Ostrogoths withdrew north.
text: Summer – Constantinianus, magister militum per Illyricum, retakes Dalmatia. The Goths abandon Salona and withdraw to the north. The Byzantines rebuild its walls and reclaim the province.

summary: Vitiges deposed King Theodahad at Ravenna, married Mataswintha, and assumed the Ostrogothic throne.
text: December – Vitiges deposes his rival Theodahad at Ravenna, and marries Mataswintha (daughter of queen Amalasuintha). He becomes king of the Ostrogoths and assembles an army to fight against Belisarius.

summary: Belisarius sailed to Carthage with 1,000 men to relieve the city from mutinous troops led by Stotzas.
text: March – April – Belisarius sails to Carthage with 1,000 men, to suppress a mutiny against Solomon. Meanwhile, Carthage is besieged by 9,000 rebels, including many Vandals, under Stotzas.

summary: Belisarius defeated rebel forces under Stotzas at the Battle of the River Bagradas before returning to Sicily.
text: Battle of the River Bagradas: Belisarius defeats the mutineers, and hurries back to Sicily.

summary: Anthimus I was deposed as patriarch of Constantinople and succeeded by Menas.
text: Before March 13 – Anthimus I is deposed as patriarch of Constantinople in favour of Menas.

summary: Pope Agapetus I died in Constantinople and was succeeded by Silverius as pope.
text: Pope Agapetus I dies in Constantinople, after a reign of just ten months. He is succeeded by Silverius as the 58th pope.

summary: The Council of Constantinople convened to condemn Monophysitism.
text: June 4 – Council of Constantinople.

summary: The Council of Jerusalem convened in Jerusalem.
text: Council of Jerusalem.

summary: The Church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus in Constantinople was completed under Justinian I.
text: The Little Hagia Sophia in Constantinople (begun in 527) is completed as the Church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

summary: Evagrius Scholasticus, church historian, was born in Epiphania.
text: Evagrius Scholasticus, Syrian church historian (or 537) (d. 594)

summary: Mundus, Byzantine general, was killed in action near Salona.
text: unknown date – Mundus, Gepid Byzantine general (killed in action)

summary: King Vitiges and the Ostrogothic army laid siege to Rome as Belisarius mounted a defense outside the Flaminian Gate.
text: Siege of Rome: The Ostrogothic army (45,000 men) under King Vitiges begins the siege of the city. Belisarius conducts a delaying action outside the Flaminian Gate; he and a detachment of his bucellarii are almost cut off.

summary: Vitiges encircled Rome with seven siege camps and cut the Roman aqueducts feeding the city.
text: Vitiges sets up seven camps, overlooking the main gates and access routes to the city, in order to starve it out. He blocks the Roman aqueducts that are supplying Rome with water, necessary both for drinking and for operating the corn mills.

summary: Vitiges assaulted the Aurelian Walls with siege towers but was repulsed at the Praenestine Gate by Byzantine defenders.
text: Vitiges attempts to assault the northern and eastern city walls with four siege towers, but is repulsed at the Praenestine Gate, known as the Vivarium, by the defenders under the Byzantine generals Bessas and Peranius.

summary: The Ostrogoths captured Portus near Ostia, forcing Belisarius to redirect Roman supply ships to Antium.
text: April – The Goths capture the Portus Claudii at Ostia; the harbor is left unguarded by the Romans. Belisarius is forced to unload his supplies at Antium; he sends urgent messages for reinforcements to Constantinople.

summary: Belisarius received cavalry reinforcements and launched sorties against Ostrogothic camps around Rome.
text: Belisarius receives his promised reinforcements: 1,600 cavalry, mostly of Hunnic or Slavic origin and expert bowmen. Despite shortages, he starts raids against the Gothic camps and Vitiges is forced into a stalemate.

summary: Vitiges concluded a three-month armistice with Belisarius to send envoys to Constantinople while famine struck Rome.
text: June – In Rome, famine brings the city to despair; Belisarius sends his secretary Procopius to Naples for more reinforcements and supplies. Vitiges arranges a three-month armistice for Gothic envoys to travel to Constantinople.

summary: Belisarius brought reinforcements and supplies from Ostia into Rome, compelling the Ostrogoths to abandon Portus.
text: November – Belisarius brings his long-awaited reinforcements, namely 3,000 Isaurians and 1,800 cavalry embarked in Ostia, along with a supply convoy, safely to Rome. The Goths are forced to abandon the Portus Claudii.

summary: John the Sanguinary marched into Picenum and was welcomed by the population of Rimini.
text: December – Belisarius sends John "the Sanguinary" with a force of 2,000 men towards Picenum, to plunder the east coast of Italy. He arrives at Ariminum (Rimini), where he is welcomed by the local population.

summary: Justinian I completed the construction of the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.
text: The construction of the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople (begun in 532) is completed.

summary: Germanus defeated the rebel leader Stotzas at the Battle of Scalas Veteres near Carthage.
text: Spring – Battle of Scalas Veteres (6 km south of Carthage, in the Praetorian prefecture of Africa): Byzantine troops under Germanus crush a large-scale mutiny. Stotzas, leader of the rebellion, flees with a handful of followers to Mauretania.

summary: John Cottistis usurped the imperial title at Dara but was killed four days later.
text: John Cottistis starts a short-lived rebellion against Justinian I. He is declared emperor at Dara, but is killed four days later by conspiring soldiers.

summary: The Ostrogoths destroyed the Aqua Virgo while attempting to use its conduit to infiltrate Rome.
text: The Aqua Virgo aqueduct is destroyed by the Goths; they try to use the underground channel as a secret route to invade Rome.

summary: Vigilius became pope after Belisarius deposed Silverius on Justinian I's orders.
text: Pope Vigilius succeeds Silverius as the 59th pope, when the latter is deposed by Belisarius at the order of Justinian I.

summary: Isidore of Miletus, Byzantine architect who designed Hagia Sophia, died.
text: Isidore of Miletus, Byzantine architect

summary: John Cottistis, Byzantine usurper in Dara, died.
text: John Cottistis, Byzantine usurper

summary: The first plague pandemic caused by Yersinia pestis broke out in the Mediterranean world.
text: 541 | |Plague of Justinian: Outbreak of the first plague pandemic caused by Yersinia pestis, which would kill millions of romans all over the empire and afflict the Mediterranean for centuries to come.

summary: Vitiges ended his 374-day siege of Rome and retreated northeast along the Via Flaminia.
text: Siege of Rome: King Vitiges of the Ostrogoths ends his siege (after 374 days) and abandons Rome. He retreats with his Gothic army northeast along the Via Flaminia.

summary: Belisarius attacked the retreating Ostrogoths as they crossed the Milvian Bridge.
text: Belisarius attacks the Goths when they have crossed the Milvian Bridge. After fierce resistance, Vitiges routs in panic, and many are slain or drowned in the river.

summary: Vitiges besieged Ariminum while Byzantine reinforcements under Narses arrived in Picenum.
text: Gothic War: Vitiges strengthens the garrisons of various towns and besieges Ariminum. Byzantine forces under the Armenian general Narses arrive at Picenum.

summary: Belisarius secured Liguria, Mediolanum, and Ariminum, but dissension arose between him and Narses.
text: April – Belisarius secures Liguria, Mediolanum (modern Milan) and Ariminum, but disagreements, especially with Narses, leads to disunity in the Byzantine army.

summary: Theudebert I sent Frankish forces across the Alps and defeated both the Ostrogoths and the Byzantines at the River Po.
text: Summer – King Theudebert I sends a small Frankish force across the Alps, and defeats the Goths and Byzantines at the River Po. Belisarius retreats to Tuscany.

summary: Artabanes killed Byzantine general Sittas during an uprising in Armenia against imperial taxation.
text: Sittas, Byzantine general, suppresses a revolt in Armenia in protest against heavy taxation. During the campaign he is killed by Artabanes, leader of the revolt.

summary: Monophysite Christians established the separate Coptic Church in Alexandria amid persecution by the Byzantine Empire.
text: As a result of persecutions by the Byzantine Empire, Monophysite Christians establish the Coptic Church in Alexandria .

summary: Severus of Antioch, patriarch of Antioch, died in exile in Egypt.
text: Severus of Antioch, patriarch of Antioch

summary: Damascius, Byzantine Neoplatonist philosopher, died.
text: Damascius, Byzantine philosopher

summary: Byzantine general Sittas was killed in Armenia.
text: Sittas, Byzantine general (magister militum)

summary: Ostrogoths and Burgundians recaptured Mediolanum after a prolonged siege, destroyed the city, and massacred its inhabitants.
text: March – Gothic War: The Goths and the Burgundians recapture Mediolanum (modern Milan), after many months of siege, the city reaching the point of starvation. The Byzantine garrison (1,000 men) surrenders and is spared, but the inhabitants are massacred (according to Procopius 300,000 people are murdered), and the city itself is destroyed.

summary: Belisarius blockaded Ravenna by sea and negotiated a treaty with Theudebert I to withdraw Frankish forces to Gaul.
text: Belisarius, still besieging Ravenna, negotiates a treaty with Theodebert I (whose forces are suffering from dysentery), and the Franks retreat to Gaul. The Byzantine fleet controls the Adriatic Sea and blockades the port of the capital from supplies.

summary: Justinian I faced renewed incursions across the Danube frontier by Slavs, Bulgars, Gepids, and Avars.
text: Emperor Justinian I becomes alarmed by renewed barbarian incursions across the Danube frontier from the Slavs, the Bulgars, the Gepids, and the Avars.

summary: An earthquake struck the city of Antioch.
text: Antioch is struck by an earthquake.

summary: Maurice, future emperor of the Byzantine Empire, was born in Arabissus.
text: Maurice, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (d. 602)

summary: Belisarius refused to transmit Justinian I's peace offer to Vitiges and was offered the Western imperial throne by the Ostrogoths.
text: Emperor Justinian I offers to make peace with Vitiges, but Belisarius refuses to transmit the message. The Ostrogoths then offer to support Belisarius as emperor of the West.

summary: Belisarius captured Mediolanum and Ravenna, taking Vitiges and Matasuntha captive to Constantinople.
text: May – Gothic War: Belisarius conquers Mediolanum (modern-day Milan) and the Gothic capital Ravenna. Vitiges and his wife Matasuntha are taken as captives to Constantinople.

summary: Belisarius consolidated Byzantine control in Italy while Ticinum and Verona remained in Gothic hands.
text: Belisarius consolidates Italy and begins mopping-up operations, capturing the Gothic fortifications. The cities Ticinum and Verona north of River Po remain in Gothic hands.

summary: Ildibad succeeded Vitiges as king of the Ostrogoths and recaptured Venetia and Liguria.
text: Ildibad succeeds Vitiges as king of the Ostrogoths, and installs his nephew Totila as commander of the Gothic army. He recaptures Venetia and Liguria in Northern Italy.

summary: Khosrow I broke the Eternal Peace with the Byzantine Empire, invaded Syria, and sacked Antioch.
text: King Khosrow I breaks the "Eternal Peace" treaty with the Byzantine Empire after eight years. Responding to an embassy from the Ostrogoths urging action against Emperor Justinian I's expanding power, he leads the Persian army up the River Euphrates. Extracting tributes from towns along the way, Khosrau I besieges and captures Antioch. He plunders the city extensively, transporting valuable artworks, including marble statues and mosaics, back to Persia.

summary: Solomon captured the Aurès Mountains from the Moors, extending Byzantine authority over Numidia and Mauretania Sitifensis.
text: Solomon captures the Aurès Mountains from the Moors and extends Byzantine authority over Numidia and Mauretania Sitifensis. The city of Theveste (Algeria) is restored and fortified.

summary: Pope Vigilius rejected Monophysitism in letters to Justinian I and Patriarch Menas of Constantinople.
text: Pope Vigilius rejects Monophysitism in letters to Justinian I and patriarch Menas of Constantinople.

summary: Vitiges, deposed king of the Ostrogoths, died in Constantinople.
text: Vitiges, king of the Ostrogoths

summary: Anicius Faustus Albinus Basilius was appointed consul in Constantinople, the last person to hold the ordinary consulship.
text: Anicius Faustus Albinus Basilius is appointed as consul in Constantinople, the last person to hold this office.

summary: The Plague of Justinian appeared in Pelusium before spreading across Alexandria and Constantinople.
text: Plague of Justinian: Bubonic plague appears suddenly in the Egyptian port of Pelusium, spreading to Alexandria and, the following year, to Constantinople. This is the beginning of a 200-year-long pandemic that will devastate Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa.

summary: Belisarius was recalled to Upper Mesopotamia, where he unsuccessfully besieged Nisibis and ravaged the surrounding countryside.
text: Emperor Justinian I recalls Belisarius from Italy to handle the situation in Armenia. He arrives in Upper Mesopotamia and attacks the fortress city of Nisbis. After an unsuccessful siege he ravages the countryside.

summary: Empress Theodora dismissed Praetorian Prefect John the Cappadocian for treason and banished him to Cyzicus.
text: John the Cappadocian, praetorian prefect of the East, is dismissed by the Byzantine empress Theodora for treason. He is banished to Cyzicus, and his estates are confiscated.

summary: Totila was elected king by the Ostrogoths following the death of his uncle Ildibad.
text: Autumn – Totila is elected king by the Ostrogothic nobles after the death of his uncle Ildibad. He wins the support of the lower classes by liberating slaves and distributing land to the peasants.

summary: Totila defended Verona against a superior Byzantine army, securing control over the Po Valley.
text: Winter – Siege of Verona: Totila defends the city of Verona against a numerically superior Byzantine army. He gains control over the Po Valley and prepares a Gothic offensive in Central Italy.

summary: Khosrow I intervened in Lazica and captured the Byzantine fortress of Petra on the Black Sea coast.
text: Lazic War: King Khosrau I intervenes in Lazica (modern Georgia), and supports the weakened king Gubazes II against a full-scale uprising. He sends an expeditionary force under Mermeroes and captures the Byzantine stronghold of Petra, located on the coast of the Black Sea, which provides the Persians a strategic port.

summary: Jacob Baradaeus was consecrated as bishop of Edessa.
text: Jacob Baradaeus becomes bishop of Edessa .

summary: The Persian general Adhurgunbadh died.
text: Adhurgunbadh, Persian general

summary: John Tzibus, Byzantine governor in Lazica, died.
text: John Tzibus, Byzantine governor-merchant in Lazica

summary: Eraric, king of the Ostrogoths, died.
text: Eraric, king of the Ostrogoths

summary: Ildibad, king of the Ostrogoths, died.
text: Ildibad, king of the Ostrogoths

summary: The Plague of Justinian killed hundreds of thousands in Constantinople and millions across the Byzantine Empire, while Emperor Justinian I contracted the disease and recovered.
text: Plague of Justinian: Bubonic plague, spread from Egypt, kills at least 230,000 in Constantinople (modern Istanbul; before counting stops), and perhaps two million or more in the rest of the empire. Emperor Justinian I contracts the disease but recovers.

summary: A Persian force ambushed and routed a Byzantine army of 30,000 men at Dvin in Armenia.
text: Lazic War – Justinian I sends a Byzantine army (30,000 men) to Armenia. The Persians, severely outnumbered, are forced to retreat, but at Dvin the Byzantines are defeated by a force of 4,000 men in an ambush, and are completely routed.

summary: An earthquake struck the Sea of Marmara region, affecting Thrace and the Gulf of Edremit.
text: The 542 Sea of Marmara earthquake takes place in the winter of 542, in the vicinity of the Sea of Marmara. It also affects the coasts of Thrace and the Edremit Gulf.

summary: Totila routed Byzantine forces near Faventia, reviving Gothic resistance in Italy.
text: Spring – Battle of Faventia: King Totila scatters the Byzantine forces near Faventia (modern Faenza) with 5,000 men, beginning the resurgence of Gothic resistance to the reconquest of Italy.

summary: Totila marched into Tuscany and defeated the Byzantines at the Battle of Mucellium near Florence.
text: Battle of Mucellium: Totila marches down into Tuscany and defeats the Byzantines at Florence, in the valley of Mugello. He treats his prisoners well, and many are induced to join his banner.

summary: Totila bypassed Rome, captured Beneventum, and received the submission of Apulia, Lucania, and Bruttium.
text: March – Totila bypasses Rome and begins his expedition in Southern Italy. He captures Beneventum and receives the submission of the provinces of Apulia, Lucania and Bruttium.

summary: Totila besieged Naples, and Gothic warships destroyed a Byzantine relief fleet sent from Sicily.
text: Siege of Naples: Totila besieges the city of Naples in Campania. A Byzantine relief force from Sicily is intercepted and almost destroyed by Gothic warships.

summary: The Byzantine garrison in Naples surrendered to Totila's Ostrogoths following a prolonged siege.
text: Spring – Siege of Naples (542–543): The Byzantine garrison (1,000 men) in Naples surrenders to the Ostrogoths, pressed by famine and demoralized by the failure of two relief efforts. The defenders are well treated by King Totila, and the garrison is allowed safe departure, but the city walls are partly razed.

summary: Khosrow I invaded Syria and advanced toward Edessa to besiege the city.
text: Summer – Khosrow I, Shahanshah of the Sasanian Empire, invades Syria again, and turns south towards Edessa to besiege the fortress city.

summary: A smaller Persian force defeated a Byzantine invasion of Persarmenia at the Battle of Anglon.
text: Battle of Anglon: A Byzantine invasion of Persarmenia is defeated by a much smaller force from the Sasanian Empire.

summary: The Synod of Constantinople condemned the doctrine of apocatastasis.
text: The doctrine of apocatastasis is condemned by the Synod of Constantinople.

summary: Barsanuphius retreated into complete seclusion near Gaza following the deaths of Abbot Seridus and John the Prophet.
text: Barsanuphius, a famous hermit close to Gaza, retreats fully from the world after the death of Seridus, abbot of the nearby monastery, and fellow hermit John the Prophet with whom he wrote over 850 letters to people seeking his advice and guidance. Aelianos follows Seridus as abbot of the monastery.

summary: The Byzantine officer Adolius died at the Battle of Anglon.
text: Adolius, Byzantine officer

summary: The Palestinian hermit John the Prophet died.
text: John the Prophet, Palestinian hermit and Desert Father

summary: Seridus of Gaza, Palestinian abbot, died.
text: Seridus of Gaza, Palestinian abbot

region: The [[Mediterranean]] World, Europe, and the [[Middle East]]
summary: Justinian I sent Belisarius back to Italy with an army to confront the Ostrogoths.
text: Gothic War: Emperor Justinian I sends Belisarius back to the Ostrogothic Kingdom (Italy) with an inadequate Byzantine expeditionary force (4,000 men and 200 ships).

region: The [[Mediterranean]] World, Europe, and the [[Middle East]]
summary: Belisarius relieved Totila's siege of Otranto and marched toward Rome.
text: Belisarius defeats the Gothic army under King Totila, who unsuccessfully besieges the city of Otranto (southern Italy). After their retreat, the Byzantines march towards the city of Rome.

region: The [[Mediterranean]] World, Europe, and the [[Middle East]]
summary: Justinian I issued an edict condemning the Three Chapters, which Pope Vigilius refused to accept.
text: Justinian I issues a new edict condemning the Three Chapters. In Western Europe, Pope Vigilius refuses to acknowledge the imperial edict and is ordered to summon to Constantinople.

region: The [[Mediterranean]] World, Europe, and the [[Middle East]]
summary: Byzantine defenders repulsed Khosrow I's attacks on Dara and Edessa, forcing the Persians into a stalemate.
text: King Khosrau I unsuccessfully attacks the Byzantine fortress city of Dara. The siege of Edessa is repulsed, and the Persians are forced into a stalemate.

region: The [[Mediterranean]] World, Europe, and the [[Middle East]]
summary: Moorish forces defeated a Byzantine army at Cillium on the border of Numidia, and the general Solomon was killed.
text: Battle of Cillium: A medium-sized Byzantine army under Solomon is defeated by the Moors on the border of Numidia. Solomon and his bodyguard are forced to retreat and are later killed.

summary: Jacob Baradaeus consecrated Sergius of Tella as patriarch of Antioch, instigating a lasting schism between the Syriac Orthodox and Eastern Orthodox churches.
text: Jacob Baradaeus consecrates Sergius of Tella as patriarch of Antioch, opening a permanent schism between the Syriac Orthodox Church and the Eastern Orthodox Church.

summary: Solomon, Byzantine general and praetorian prefect of Africa, died in battle against the Moors.
text: Solomon, Byzantine general and prefect of Africa

summary: Justinian I dispatched the general Narses to the Heruli to recruit troops for Byzantine campaigns in Italy and Syria.
text: Emperor Justinian I sends Narses, Byzantine general, to the rulers of the Heruli, to recruit troops for the campaigns in Italy and Syria.

summary: Totila established his military base at Tivoli and prepared a campaign to retake Latium.
text: Gothic War: King Totila establishes his military base at Tivoli (Central Italy), and prepares a campaign to reconquer the region of Latium.

summary: Khosrow I signed a five-year truce with the Byzantine Empire, though warfare persisted in Armenia and the Caucasus.
text: King Khosrau I signs a five year truce with the Byzantine Empire, but war continues to ravage the Caucasus region, especially in Armenia.

summary: Peter, Byzantine general and brother of Emperor Maurice, was born.
text: Peter, Byzantine general (d. 602)

summary: Stotzas, leader of a mutiny against the Byzantine Empire in Africa, died in battle.
text: Stotzas, Byzantine rebel leader

summary: Totila and his Ostrogothic forces plundered Rome after a lengthy siege, dismantled its fortifications, and moved to Apulia.
text: Sack of Rome: After almost a year's siege, the capture of a grain fleet sent by the exiled Pope Vigilius near the mouth of the Tiber, and failure of troops of the Byzantine Empire under Belisarius to relieve the city, the Ostrogoths under King Totila plunder Rome and destroy its fortifications. He then withdraws to Apulia (Southern Italy).

summary: Pope Vigilius arrived in Constantinople to meet with Justinian I, while Pelagius was dispatched by Totila to negotiate.
text: Winter – Pope Vigilius arrives in Constantinople, to meet with Emperor Justinian I. The future Pope Pelagius I is sent by Totila to negotiate with Justinian.

summary: Justinian I granted subsidies to the Lombard king Audoin to prompt him to fight the Gepids in the Carpathians.
text: Audoin receives subsidies from Justinian I, to encourage him to battle the Gepids in the Carpathian Mountains.

summary: Audoin led the Lombards across the Danube into Pannonia and formed an alliance with the Byzantine Empire.
text: Audoin leads the Lombards across the Danube into Pannonia, and becomes an ally of the Byzantines.

summary: Bishop Maximianus completed the construction of the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna.
text: The Basilica of San Vitale (Ravenna) is completed by bishop Maximianus, during the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna.

summary: Belisarius recaptured Rome from the Ostrogoths during the Gothic War.
text: Gothic War: Belisarius recaptures Rome from the Ostrogoths, but his Italian campaign is unsuccessful (he is starved of supplies and reinforcements from Constantinople).

summary: The mosaic panels depicting Justinian I and Theodora were created in the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna.
text: The mosaic panels of Justinian I and Theodora I with attendants, in the Basilica of San Vitale (Ravenna), are made .

summary: Moorish tribes defeated a Byzantine army under John Troglita at the Battle of Marta in Tripolitania.
text: Battle of Marta: The Byzantine army under John Troglita is defeated by Moorish tribes in Tripolitania. He flees to Lunci (9 km south of Mahares), and is forced to withdraw north to the fortress of Laribus (near modern El Kef).

summary: Bishop Maximianus of Ravenna consecrated the Basilica of San Vitale.
text: The Basilica of San Vitale (Ravenna) is consecrated by bishop Maximianus of Ravenna.

summary: Tribonian, Byzantine jurist and principal compiler of the Corpus Juris Civilis, died.
text: Tribonian, Byzantine jurist and author of the Codex Justinianus

summary: Empress Theodora died in Constantinople and was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles.
text: Empress Theodora I dies at age 48, probably of breast cancer (according to Bishop Victor of Tunnuna). Her body is buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles (Constantinople).

summary: Emperor Justinian I relieved Belisarius from military command in favor of Narses.
text: Emperor Justinian I relieves Belisarius from military service, in favour of 70-year-old Byzantine general Narses.

summary: King Gubazes II of Lazica revolted against the Persians and requested military aid from Emperor Justinian I.
text: Lazic War: King Gubazes II revolts against the Persians, and requests aid from Justinian I. He sends a Byzantine expeditionary force (8,000 men) to Lazica (modern Georgia).

summary: Mihr-Mihroe defeated a Byzantine force in the mountain passes and relieved the besieged fortress of Petra.
text: Gubazes II besieges the fortress of Petra, located on the Black Sea. The Persian army under Mermeroes defeats a small Byzantine force guarding the mountain passes, and relieves Petra.

summary: Mihr-Mihroe stationed a garrison of three thousand men in Petra before marching into Armenia.
text: Mermeroes stations a garrison of 3,000 men in the stronghold of Petra, and marches to Armenia. The Persians, lacking sufficient supplies, secure the supply routes and plunder Lazica.

summary: John Troglita led the Byzantine army to crush the Moorish revolt at the Battle of the Fields of Cato in Byzacena.
text: Spring – Battle of the Fields of Cato: The Byzantine army, under John Troglita, crushes the Moorish revolt in Byzacena (Tunisia).

summary: Cosmas Indicopleustes wrote the Christian Topography, detailing Indian Ocean trade routes.
text: Cosmas Indicopleustes, Alexandrian merchant, writes his work Christian Topography. He describes the importance of the spice trade (especially in cloves and sweet aloes) in Ceylon, and the harvesting of pepper in India .

summary: Saint Catherine's Monastery was established in the Sinai Peninsula.
text: Saint Catherine's Monastery is established in the Sinai Peninsula.

summary: Byzantine Empress Theodora died.
text: Theodora I, Byzantine Empress

summary: Carcasan, king of the Ifuraces, was killed at the Battle of the Fields of Cato.
text: Carcasan, king of the Ifuraces (Algeria)

summary: Totila led the Ostrogoths in a third siege of Rome after Justinian I rejected his peace proposals.
text: Siege of Rome: The Ostrogoths under Totila besiege Rome for the third time, after Belisarius has returned to Constantinople. He offers a peace agreement, but this is rejected by Emperor Justinian I.

summary: Totila conquered Perugia, stationed a Gothic garrison, and ordered the execution of Bishop Herculanus.
text: Totila conquers the city of Perugia (Central Italy) and stations a Gothic garrison. He takes bishop Herculanus prisoner, and orders him to be completely flayed. The Ostrogoth soldier asked to perform this gruesome execution shows pity, and decapitates Herculanus before the skin on every part of his body is removed.

summary: Bessas and King Gubazes II defeated Persian forces in Lazica in a surprise attack.
text: Spring – Lazic War: The Byzantine army under Bessas combines forces with King Gubazes II, and defeats the Persians in Lazica (modern Georgia) in a surprise attack. The survivors retreat into Caucasian Iberia.

summary: Roman forces unsuccessfully besieged the Persian-held fortress of Petra in Lazica.
text: The Romans unsuccessfully besiege Petra, Lazica.

summary: The apse mosaic depicting the Transfiguration of Christ was created in Saint Catherine's Monastery.
text: c. 549–564 – Transfiguration of Christ, mosaic in the apse, Church of the Virgin, Saint Catherine's Monastery in Egypt, is made.

summary: Bishop Maximianus of Ravenna consecrated the Basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe.
text: Bishop Maximianus of Ravenna consecrates the Basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe.

summary: Emperor Justinian I appointed Bessas commander of Armenia and entrusted him with the war in Lazica.
text: Emperor Justinian I appoints Bessas commander (magister militum) of Armenia, and entrusts him with the war in Lazica (Georgia).

summary: Byzantine forces laid siege to the fortress of Petra in Lazica.
text: Siege of Petra (550–551)

summary: Totila recaptured Rome after bribing the Isaurian garrison.
text: Gothic War: The Ostrogoths under king Totila recapture Rome after a long siege, by bribing the Isaurian garrison.

summary: Totila plundered Sicily after subduing Corsica and Sardinia, and dispatched a fleet to raid Greece.
text: Summer – Totila plunders Sicily, after he subdues Corsica and Sardinia. He sends a Gothic fleet to raid the coasts of Greece.

summary: Emperor Justinian I sent two Nestorian monks on a mission to Central Asia to spread Christianity.
text: Justinian I sends two Nestorian monks on a mission to Central Asia, to spread Christianity in the East .

summary: The Sasanian Empire under King Khosrow I controlled the silk trade destined for Europe and the Byzantine Empire.
text: The Sassanid Empire, under the reign of King Khosrow I, controls the trade of silk destined for Europe and the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Procopius wrote the Secret History.
text: Procopius writes the Secret History .

summary: The church of Lazica united with the Byzantine church as it split from the Armenian Church.
text: The churches of Lazica (Georgia) and Armenia split. While the Armenian Church remains independent, the Georgian church unites with the Byzantine Empire. This ecclesiastical union deepens political and cultural contact between the two states. As a sign of Lazica's status vis-à-vis Byzantium, Lazic princes are vested with honorific titles of the Byzantine court, including kouropalates, or "minister of the imperial palace" .

summary: John Moschus, a Byzantine monk and hagiographer, was born.
text: John Moschus, Byzantine monk

summary: Peter III of Callinicum, Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch, was born.
text: Peter III of Callinicum, Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch

summary: Germanus, Byzantine general and cousin of Justinian I, died.
text: Germanus, Byzantine general (magister militum)

summary: Justinian I appointed Narses supreme commander in Italy, where Narses assembled an expeditionary force at Salona.
text: After the death of his cousin Germanus, Justinian I appoints Narses new supreme commander, and returns to Italy. In Salona on the Adriatic coast, he assembles a Byzantine expeditionary force totaling 20,000 or possibly 30,000 men and a contingent of foreign allies, notably Lombards, Heruls and Bulgars.

summary: Narses bypassed Gothic-Frank forces along the Adriatic coast, reached Ravenna unopposed, and defeated a Gothic force at Rimini.
text: Gothic War: Narses arrives in Venetia and discovers that a powerful Gothic-Frank army (50,000 men), under joint command of the kings Totila and Theudebald, has blocked the principal route to the Po Valley. Not wishing to engage such a formidable force and confident that the Franks would avoid a direct confrontation, Narses skirts the lagoons along the Adriatic shore, by using vessels to leapfrog his army from point to point along the coast. In this way he arrives at the capital Ravenna without encountering any opposition. He attacks and crushes a small Gothic force at Ariminum (modern Rimini).

summary: An earthquake struck the Malian Gulf area, damaging the cities of Echinus and Tarphe.
text: Spring – The 551 Malian Gulf earthquake takes place in the vicinity of the Malian Gulf; it affects the cities of Echinus and Tarphe.

summary: A major earthquake and tsunami destroyed Beirut, killing roughly 30,000 people.
text: Beirut is destroyed by an earthquake and tsunami. Its epicenter has an estimated magnitude of about 7.2 or 7.6, and according to reports of Antoninus of Piacenza, Christian pilgrim, some 30,000 people are killed.

summary: The Byzantine fleet defeated the Ostrogothic navy off Sena Gallica, ending Gothic sea power.
text: Autumn – Battle of Sena Gallica: The Byzantine fleet (50 warships) destroys the Gothic naval force under Indulf near Sena Gallica (Senigallia), some 17 miles (27 km) north of Ancona. It marks the end of the Gothic supremacy in the Mediterranean Sea.

summary: Bessas led Byzantine and Sabir troops to recapture Petra in Lazica and razed its walls.
text: Spring – Lazic War - Siege of Petra (550–551): The Byzantine army and their Sabir allies (some 6,000 men) under Bessas recapture the strategic Byzantine fortress of Petra, located on the coast of the Black Sea. He orders the city walls razed to the ground.

summary: The Roman bureaucrat Jordanes published Getica on the origins and deeds of the Goths.
text: Jordanes, Roman bureaucrat, publishes "The Origin and Deeds of the Goths" .

summary: Germanus, a future Byzantine Caesar and pretender, was born.
text: Germanus, Byzantine pretender

summary: Narses defeated the Ostrogoths at Taginae, where King Totila was killed, and then entered Rome.
text: Battle of Taginae: Narses crosses the Apennines with a Byzantine army (25,000 men). He is blocked by a Gothic force under King Totila near Taginae (Central Italy). In a narrow mountain valley, Narses deploys his army in a "crescent shaped" formation. He dismounts his Lombard and Heruli cavalry mercenaries, placing them as a phalanx in the center. On his left flank he sends out a mixed force of foot and horse archers to seize a dominant height. The Goths open the battle with a determined cavalry charge. Halted by enfilading fire from both sides, the attackers are thrown back in confusion on the infantry behind them. The Byzantine cataphracts (Clibanarii) sweep into the milling mass. More than 6,000 Goths, including Totila, are killed. The remnants flee, and Narses proceeds to Rome, where he captures the city after a brief siege.

summary: Liberius led a Byzantine army to conquer Cartagena and parts of southeastern Hispania.
text: Emperor Justinian I dispatches a small Byzantine force (2,000 men) under Liberius to Hispania, according to the historian Jordanes. He conquers Cartagena and other cities on the southeastern coast.

summary: Nestorian monks delivered smuggled silkworm eggs from China to Justinian I in Constantinople.
text: Justinian I receives the first silkworm eggs from two Nestorian monks at Constantinople. They were sent to Central Asia (see 550) and smuggled the precious eggs from China hidden in rods of bamboo.
names: Smuggling of silkworm eggs into the East Roman Empire

summary: Teia succeeded Totila as king of the Ostrogoths in Italy.
text: Teia becomes the last king of the Ostrogoths in Italy.

summary: Christian monks smuggled silkworm eggs into the Byzantine Empire, launching its domestic silk industry.
text: Smuggling of silkworm eggs into the Byzantine Empire by monks allows development of the Byzantine silk industry in the Empire.
names: Smuggling of silkworm eggs into the East Roman Empire

summary: Eutychius became the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople.
text: Eutychius becomes patriarch of Constantinople.

summary: John the Merciful, future Chalcedonian Patriarch of Alexandria, was born on Cyprus.
text: John the Merciful, patriarch of Alexandria

summary: Dacius, archbishop of Milan, died while in Constantinople.
text: Dacius, archbishop of Milan

summary: Totila, king of the Ostrogoths, died of wounds sustained at the Battle of Taginae.
text: Totila, king of the Ostrogoths

summary: Anicius Maximus, Roman patrician and former consul, was executed by the Ostrogoths.
text: Anicius Maximus, Roman patrician

summary: Aratius, an Armenian general serving the Byzantine Empire, died in Lazica.
text: Aratius, Armenian general

summary: Menas, patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Menas, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Byzantine forces under Narses defeated the Ostrogoths and killed King Teia at the Battle of Mons Lactarius.
text: Battle of Mons Lactarius: King Teia secretly marches to join forces with his brother Aligern in Campania, to relieve the siege of Cumae. Meanwhile at Mons Lactarius (modern Monti Lattari), Narses lays an ambush. The combined Gothic force is crushed in a hopeless last stand for two days (south of Naples), and Teia is killed in the fighting. Aligern escapes, but surrenders a few months later.

summary: The Ostrogothic Kingdom in Italy was brought to an end after sixty years of rule by the Byzantine conquest.
text: The Ostrogothic Kingdom ends after 60 years of rule in Italy. The Goths are allowed to return to their homes in peace and (re)settle in modern-day Austria. Some 7,000 people retreat to Campsas (Southern Gaul), and resist with minimal help from the Franks against the Byzantines until 554.

summary: Sasanian commander Mihr-Mihroe forced Byzantine forces to retreat from Telephis and Ollaria.
text: The Sassanid commander Mihr-Mihroe force the Byzantines to retreat from Telephis and later Ollaria. (See Battle of Telephis–Ollaria).

summary: A joint Frankish and Alamannic army under Lothair and Buccelin crossed the Alps and defeated a Byzantine force at Parma.
text: Gothic War: Frankish invasion — Two Frankish-Alemanni dukes, brothers Lothair and Buccelin, cross the Alps from Germany with a force of 75,000 men, mostly Frankish infantry. In the Po Valley, they win an easy victory over a much smaller Byzantine force at Parma, and are joined by remnants of the Gothic armies, bringing the total strength of the invaders to about 90,000 men. Narses, gathering his forces as quickly as possible, marches north to harass the Franks, but is not strong enough to engage them in battle. In Samnium (Southern Italy) the brothers divide their forces: Lothaire goes down the east coast, then returns to the north, to winter in the Po Valley. Buccelin follows the west coast into Calabria, where he spends the winter — his army being seriously wasted by attrition and disease.

summary: Emperor Justinian I convened the Fifth Ecumenical Council in Constantinople to condemn the Three Chapters.
text: The Fifth Ecumenical Council is held in Constantinople. In an edict, Emperor Justinian I condemns the Three Chapters, causing further schisms and heresies of monoenergism and monothelitism.

summary: Gelimer, the last king of the Vandals and Alans, died in retirement in Galatia.
text: Gelimer, king of the Vandals and Alans (b. 480)

summary: Teia, the last king of the Ostrogoths, was killed at the Battle of Mons Lactarius.
text: Teia, king of the Ostrogoths

summary: Emperor Justinian I issued the Pragmatic Sanction reorganizing the government of Italy.
text: Byzantine Emperor Justinian I issues a pragmatic sanction reorganizing Italy, and rewards the praetorian prefect Liberius for over 60 years of distinguished service, granting him extensive estates in Italy.

summary: An earthquake struck southwestern Anatolia, causing destruction across the Güllük Gulf and the island of Kos.
text: The 554 Anatolia earthquake takes place in the southwest coasts of Anatolia (Asia Minor). It affects the Güllük Gulf (Mandalya Gulf), and the island of Kos.

summary: Byzantine forces under Narses destroyed a Frankish-Alamannic army at Casilinum in the Battle of the Volturnus.
text: October – Battle of the Volturnus: During the spring Butilinus (Buccelin) has marched north; the Frankish army (infected by an epidemic of dysentery which kills their leader Leutharis (Lothair)) is reduced to about 30,000 men. The Byzantine army, with 18,000 men (including a contingent of Goths under Aligern), marches south to meet them at Casilinum (on the banks of the River Volturno). Byzantine eunuch general Narses sends a cavalry force under Chanaranges to destroy the supply wagons of the Franks. Outmanoeuvring Butilinus, he chooses a disposition similar to that at Taginae. After a frontal assault on the Byzantine centre, the Franks and the Alamanni are annihilated, thus effectively ending the Gothic War (535–554). Narses garrisons an army of 16,000 men in Italy. The recovery of the Italian Peninsula has cost the empire about 300,000 pounds of gold.

summary: Byzantine forces led by Liberius seized Granada and occupied the former province of Baetica.
text: Byzantine forces under Liberius seize Granada (Andalusia) and occupy the old province of Baetica. Justinian I calls Belisarius out of retirement, to complete the consolidation of reconquered regions of Southern Spain.

summary: Athanagild was crowned king of the Visigoths after defeating Agila I with Byzantine aid.
text: Athanagild is crowned as king of the Visigoths and succeeds Agila I. He acknowledges the suzerainty of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Ghassanid forces under al-Harith ibn Jabalah defeated and killed Lakhmid king al-Mundhir III at the Battle of Yawm Halima.
text: Al-Mundhir III ibn al-Nu'man is defeated and killed by the Ghassanids under al-Harith ibn Jabalah, at the battle of Yawm Halima; 'Amr III ibn al-Mundhir succeeds as king of the Lakhmid kingdom.

summary: Cassiodorus founded the monastery of Vivarium on his family estates.
text: Cassiodorus, Roman statesman, founds the Monastery at Vivarium .

summary: Emperor Justinian I permitted Pope Vigilius to return to Rome following the Second Council of Constantinople.
text: Pope Vigilius was allowed to return to Rome after years of pressure from Emperor Justinian regarding the Second Council of Constantinople.

summary: Agila I, king of the Visigoths, died.
text: March - Agila I, king of the Visigoths

summary: Al-Mundhir III ibn al-Nu'man, king of the Lakhmids, died in battle.
text: Al-Mundhir III ibn al-Nu'man, king of the Lakhmid kingdom (Iraq)

summary: The Persian general Mihr-Mihroe died.
text: Mermeroes, Persian general

summary: Liberius, the prominent Roman aristocrat and praetorian prefect, died.
text: Liberius, Roman aristocrat

summary: The Roman Empire under Justinian I reached its height following reconquests in Italy, Dalmatia, Africa, and southern Hispania.
text: By this date, the Roman Empire under Justinian I has reached its height. Justinian I has reconquered many former territories of the Western Roman Empire, including Italy, Dalmatia, Africa and Southern Hispania.

summary: An earthquake devastated the city of Latakia.
text: An earthquake devastates the city of Latakia (modern Syria).

summary: The Byzantine army under Bessas was repulsed from Archaeopolis during the Lazic War.
text: Summer – Lazic War: The Byzantine army under Bessas is repulsed, and forced to retreat out of Archaeopolis (Georgia).

summary: King Gubazes II of Lazica was murdered by Byzantine commanders after criticizing their conduct in the war.
text: King Gubazes II is invited to observe the siege of a Persian-held fortress, and is murdered by the Byzantine military staff after accusing them of incompetence.

summary: The historian Jordanes composed the Getica concerning the origin and deeds of the Goths.
text: Around this time, the historian Jordanes writes several books, among them De origine actibusque Getarum (The origin and deeds of the Goths).

summary: Pope Vigilius died at Syracuse while returning from Constantinople to Rome.
text: Pope Vigilius dies at Syracuse on his journey back home. His body is brought to Rome and buried in the San Martino ai Monti.

summary: Pope Vigilius died.
text: Pope Vigilius

summary: Gubazes II, king of Lazica, was assassinated.
text: September/October - Gubazes II, king of Lazica (Georgia)

summary: The Byzantine general Justin recaptured Archaeopolis and routed the Persian army during the Lazic War.
text: Lazic War: A Byzantine expeditionary force under Justin retakes Archaeopolis (modern Georgia), and routs the Persian army.

summary: Byzantine defenders defeated the besieging Persian army at the town of Phasis in Lazica.
text: Siege of Phasis: The Persians are defeated at the besieged town of Phasis in Lazica, held by the Byzantines.

summary: King Khosrow I opened peace negotiations with Emperor Justinian I, preparing the ground for a fifty-year peace treaty.
text: King Khosrau I opens negotiations with Justinian I, leading to the establishment of a 50 year peace agreement in 562.

summary: Pelagius I, formerly apocrisiarius to Constantinople, was elected Pope of Rome succeeding Vigilius.
text: The diplomatic representative (apocrisiarius) to Constantinople is elected as Pope Pelagius I, succeeding Vigilius as the 60th pope of Rome.

summary: Maximianus, bishop of Ravenna, died.
text: Maximianus, Bishop of Ravenna (b. 499)

summary: Romanos the Melodist, a prominent Syrian hymnographer and poet, died.
text: Romanos the Melodist, Syrian poet

summary: The Avars arrived in the northern Caucasus and sent envoys to Byzantine officials in Lazica.
text: The Avars arrive in the northern region of the Caucasus, between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. They send envoys to the Byzantines in Lazica (modern Georgia). Like the Huns, the Avars are the former elite of a central Asian federation, which has been forced to flee westwards.

summary: A destructive earthquake struck Constantinople, damaging its city walls and public monuments.
text: The 557 Constantinople earthquake occurs.

summary: Cyriacus the Anchorite, a celebrated Christian hermit and centenarian, died in Palestine.
text: Saint Cyriacus the Anchorite, legendary centenarian (b. 448)

summary: Following the collapse of the dome of the Hagia Sophia during an earthquake, Emperor Justinian I ordered it rebuilt.
text: In Constantinople, the dome of the Hagia Sophia collapses due to an earthquake. Emperor Justinian I orders the dome to be rebuilt.

summary: Istämi, ruler of the Western Turkic Khaganate, opened diplomatic relations with the Byzantine Empire.
