text: Istämi, ruler of the Western Turkic Khaganate, establishes diplomatic relations with the Byzantine Empire.

summary: John the Silent died.
text: John the Silent, bishop and saint

summary: Hilary of Galeata died.
text: Hilary of Galeata, Christian monk

summary: Abraham of Cratia died.
text: Abraham of Kratia, Christian monk

summary: Zabergan led Kutrigurs and Huns across the Danube into the Balkans, raiding Thrace and Macedonia before being repulsed near Constantinople by Belisarius.
text: Winter – The Kutrigurs and Huns under Zabergan cross the frozen Danube River, and invade the Balkans. They raid Thracia and Macedonia, but are driven back near Constantinople by a Byzantine force under Belisarius.

summary: Belisarius defeated the invading Kutrigur and Hun forces outside the walls of Constantinople in the Battle of Melantias.
text: Battle of Melantias: Outside the city walls of Constantinople, Belisarius defeats the combined "barbarians" with his veteran cavalry (bucellarii), and a few thousand hastily raised levies.

summary: Constantina, Byzantine empress, was born.
text: Constantina, Byzantine empress

summary: Sophronius of Jerusalem was born.
text: Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem (d. 638)

summary: Dorotheus of Gaza, Christian monk and abbot, died.
text: Dorotheus of Gaza, monk and abbot

summary: Pope John III succeeded Pope Pelagius I in Rome following Pelagius's death.
text: Pope Pelagius I dies in Rome after a five-year reign, and is succeeded by John III as the 61st pope.

summary: Pope Pelagius I died in Rome.
text: Pope Pelagius I

summary: Emperor Justinian I signed a peace treaty with the Sasanian Empire restoring the status quo ante with Lazica in Byzantine control.
text: Emperor Justinian I signs a peace treaty with the Sasanid Empire. The status quo ante is restored, with Lazica (modern Georgia) in Byzantine hands.

summary: Belisarius was put on trial for corruption in Constantinople, found guilty, and imprisoned.
text: Belisarius stands trial for corruption in Constantinople, possibly with Procopius acting as praefectus urbi. He is found guilty and sent to prison.

summary: King Khosrow I recognized Lazica as a Byzantine vassal in the Fifty-Year Peace Treaty, ending the Lazic War.
text: End of the Lazic War: In the Fifty-Year Peace Treaty, King Khosrau I recognises Lazica as a Byzantine vassal state for an annual payment of 5,000 pounds of gold each year.

summary: Emperor Justinian I reconsecrated Hagia Sophia following the rebuilding of its collapsed dome.
text: Justinian I re-consecrates Hagia Sophia after its dome is rebuilt. Paul the Silentiary, Byzantine poet, writes an epic poem (Ekphrasis).

summary: The Byzantine Empire captured the last Ostrogothic strongholds of Verona and Brescia, concluding the Gothic War.
text: The last Ostrogothic strongholds at Verona and Brixia are taken by the Byzantine Empire, ending the Gothic War.

summary: Procopius, Byzantine historian, died.
text: Procopius, Byzantine historian

summary: Emperor Justinian I pardoned Belisarius, released him from prison, and restored his honors and property.
text: Emperor Justinian I pardons Belisarius; he orders his release from prison, and restores his properties and honours. He permits the general to live in obscurity, and gives him a veterans' pension.

summary: The reconstructed Hagia Sophia became the primary monument and center of Eastern Orthodoxy.
text: The new Hagia Sophia (cost: 20,000 pounds of gold), with its numerous chapels and shrines, octagonal dome and mosaics, becomes the centre and most visible monument of Eastern Orthodoxy.

summary: Andreas of Caesarea, Byzantine theologian and bishop, was born.
text: Andreas of Caesarea, bishop and writer (d. 637)

summary: Justin II succeeded Justinian I as emperor of the Byzantine Empire and refused subsidies to the Avars.
text: Justin II succeeds his uncle Justinian I as emperor of the Byzantine Empire. He begins his reign by refusing subsidies to the Avars, who conduct several large-scale raids through the Balkan Peninsula.

summary: Justin II recalled his cousin Justin to Constantinople and placed him under house arrest.
text: Justin II recalls his cousin Justin (pretender to the throne) to Constantinople; after accusations against him, he is placed under house arrest.

summary: Justin II sent Baduarius with a Byzantine army to support the Gepids against the Lombards.
text: Justin II sends his son-in-law Baduarius (magister militum) with a Byzantine army, to support the Gepids in their war against the Lombards.

summary: The Madaba Map mosaic depicting the Holy Land was created in the church of Saint George.
text: The Madaba Map is made in the Byzantine church of Saint George. The floor mosaic contains the depiction of the Holy Land .

summary: Agathias began writing his history continuing from where Procopius had ended.
text: Agathias begins to write a history, beginning where Procopius finished his work.

summary: Justinian I deposed Patriarch Eutychius of Constantinople and replaced him with John Scholasticus.
text: Patriarch Eutychius of Constantinople is deposed as Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople by Justinian I after he refuses the Byzantine Emperor's order to adopt the tenets of the Aphthartodocetae, a sect of Monophysites. From April 12 he is replaced by John Scholasticus.

summary: Justinian I, emperor of the Byzantine Empire, died in Constantinople.
text: Justinian I, emperor of the Byzantine Empire

summary: Byzantine general Belisarius died in Constantinople.
text: Belisarius, Byzantine general ("Last of the Romans")

summary: The Byzantine historian Procopius died in Constantinople.
text: Procopius, Byzantine historian

summary: Emperor Justinian I built Saint Catherine's Monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai.
text: Saint Catherine's Monastery in Mount Sinai, Saint Catherine, South Sinai Governorate, Egypt by Justinian I, which contains the oldest active library, being Ebla tablets (c. 2500–2250 BC) in the city of Ebla, Syria, discovered by Italian archaeologist Paolo Matthiae and his team in 1974–75, the first, if not the oldest, inactive library.

summary: Baduarius led a Byzantine force to defeat the Lombards in Moesia in support of the Gepids, but King Cunimund refused to surrender Sirmium.
text: A Byzantine army, under command of Baduarius, assists the Gepids in their war against the Lombards. The Byzantines win the first battle in the lower Danube (Moesia), but Gepid King Cunimund refuses to hand back the fortress city of Sirmium (modern Serbia), as he had promised.

summary: Emperor Justin II broke the Byzantine treaty with the Gepids amid severe financial strain.
text: Emperor Justin II, facing an empty treasury, breaks the treaty with the Gepids that has existed since 565. King Alboin of the Lombards makes an alliance with the Avars under Bayan I, at the expense of tough conditions. They demand a tenth of the Lombards' cattle and half of the war booty.

summary: Emperor Justin II exiled his cousin Justin to Alexandria, where Justin was subsequently murdered.
text: Justin II sends his cousin Justin to exile in Alexandria, where he is installed as Augustal prefect of Egypt. There he is murdered in his sleep, and his head is cut off and brought to Constantinople (most likely by assignment of Empress Sophia).
names: List of governors of Roman Egypt

summary: The Byzantine general and former consul Justin was murdered in Alexandria.
text: Justin, Byzantine aristocrat and general

summary: Patriarch John Scholasticus organized a theological compromise between Chalcedonians and Monophysites in Constantinople.
text: John III, patriarch of Constantinople, organizes a compromise between the Chalcedonians and Monophysites.

actor: Pope The Yoshis I of Alexandria
summary: Theodosius I, patriarch of Alexandria, died in exile in Constantinople.
text: Theodosius I, patriarch of Alexandria
cast: Pope The Yoshis I of Alexandria
names: Pope The Yoshis I of Alexandria

summary: The Lombards, led by King Alboin, crossed the Julian Alps and invaded Northern Italy, driving displaced populations to establish settlements that became Venice.
text: Spring – The Lombards, led by King Alboin, cross the Julian Alps. Their invasion of Northern Italy is almost unopposed; withered Byzantine forces, that remain in the Po Valley and are based at Ravenna, are no match for the overwhelming Lombard incursion. Residents of the Italian countryside flee at the Lombards' approach. Some retreat to the barrier islands along the shore of the Northern Adriatic Sea, where they establish permanent settlements: the nascent city of Venice.

summary: The Byzantine Empire abandoned Lombardy and Tuscany to the invading Lombards and established a march south of Ravenna.
text: The Byzantines abandon present-day Lombardy and Tuscany, to establish a frontier march in the hills south of Ravenna (still known as Le Marche). Bavarians, Sarmatians, Saxons and Taifali, join the invasion en route. As they advance, the vacuum left behind them on the Balkan Peninsula is filled by Avars, Bulgars and Slavs.

summary: A Turkish khan sent emissaries to the Byzantine Empire.
text: A Turkish khan sends emissaries to the Byzantine Empire .

summary: Emperor Justin II and Empress Sophia sent the Cross of Justin II to Rome to improve relations.
text: Emperor Justin II and his wife Sophia send the Cross of Justin II ("Vatican Cross") to Rome, to improve the relations with the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Emperor Justin II and Empress Sophia sent a relic of the True Cross to Radegund in Poitiers.
text: Emperor Justin II and his wife Sophia send a relic of the "True Cross" to the Frankish princess Radegund, who has founded a monastery at Poitiers.

summary: The Garamantian Kingdom signed a peace treaty with the Byzantine Empire and converted its capital Garama to Christianity.
text: The Garamantian Kingdom (modern Libya) signs a peace treaty with the Byzantine Empire. The capital city of Garama is converted to Christianity.

summary: Byzantine missionaries converted the Nubian kingdom of Alodia to Christianity.
text: The Nubian kingdom of Alodia is converted to Christianity by Byzantine missionaries (according to John of Ephesus).

summary: John of Ephesus completed his Biographies of Eastern Saints.
text: John of Ephesus completes his "Biographies of Eastern Saints" .

summary: Peter IV, Coptic Orthodox patriarch of Alexandria, died.
text: Peter IV, Coptic Orthodox patriarch of Alexandria

summary: Ctesiphon overtook Constantinople as the largest city in the world.
text: Ctesiphon, capital of the Sassanid Empire, becomes the largest city in the world, taking the lead from Constantinople, capital of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Antonina, the widow of the Byzantine general Belisarius, died.
text: Antonina, wife of Belisarius

summary: John Philoponus, an Alexandrian philosopher and Aristotelian commentator, died.
text: John Philoponus, Aristotelian commentator (b. 490)

summary: Visigothic king Liuvigild invaded the Byzantine province of Spania, captured Córdoba, and became sole ruler of the Visigothic Kingdom.
text: The Visigoths under King Liuvigild invade the Byzantine province of Spania (modern Andalusia), and seize the city of Córdoba. After the death of his brother Liuva I, he becomes sole ruler of the Visigothic Kingdom .

summary: Monophysites rejected the Council of Chalcedon, precipitating a renewed schism.
text: The Monophysites again reject the Council of Chalcedon, causing another schism.

summary: Byzantine general Narses died at Domitian's palace in Rome.
text: Narses dies at Domitian's palace in Rome.

summary: Emperor Justin II broke the peace with the Sasanian Empire and sent a Roman army to besiege Nisibis.
text: Byzantine–Sassanid War of 572–591: Emperor Justin II refuses to pay the annual tribute to Khosrau I, putting an end to the 50-year peace treaty established ten years earlier. The Armenians are considered allies to the Byzantine Empire, and Justin sends a Byzantine army into Persian territory, besieging the fortress city of Nisibis (modern Turkey).

summary: King Alboin captured Pavia after a three-year siege and established the city as the capital of the Lombard Kingdom.
text: Siege of Pavia (569–572): King Alboin captures Ticinum (Pavia); after a siege the Byzantine garrison surrenders to the Lombards. The city is of strategic importance, lying at the rivers Po and Ticino, and becomes the capital of the Kingdom of the Lombards.

summary: Alboin was assassinated in his palace at Verona in a plot arranged by Rosamund, after which Cleph became king of the Lombards.
text: Alboin, king of the Lombards, is murdered at Verona in his palace, at the instigation of his wife Rosamund (daughter of the Gepid king Cunimund), and her henchman, Helmechis (the king's squire); both flee to seek Byzantine protection in Ravenna. Alboin is succeeded as king by Cleph, who is not related by blood.

summary: Byzantine epic poet Corippus died.
text: Corippus, Byzantine epic poet

summary: Persian forces under Khosrow I captured the Byzantine stronghold of Dara after a six-month siege, while Adarmahan raided Syria and plundered Apamea and Antioch.
text: Byzantine–Sassanid War: Persian forces under the command of King Khosrau I capture the Byzantine stronghold of Dara, after a six-month siege. Meanwhile, a smaller Persian army under Adarmahan advances from Babylon through the desert, crosses the Euphrates River and ravages Syria. The cities of Apamea and Antiochia are plundered.

summary: Byzantine general Narses died in Rome.
text: Narses, Byzantine general (b. 478)

summary: Byzantine Emperor Justin II abdicated the throne in favor of Tiberius II Constantine, creating him Caesar and adopting him as his son.
text: Emperor Justin II retires due to recurring seizures of insanity; he abdicates the throne in favour of his general Tiberius. Justin proclaims him Caesar and adopts him as his own son.

summary: Empress Sophia and Tiberius agreed to a one-year Mesopotamian truce with the Persians for 45,000 solidi.
text: Winter – Empress Sophia and Tiberius agree to a one year truce with the Persians, at the cost of 45,000 solidi. The truce applies only to the Mesopotamian front; in the Caucasus, war continues.

summary: The Sasanian Empire conquered Yemen, overthrowing regimes allied with Aksum and the Byzantine Empire.
text: The Persian Empire overthrows the Axumite- and Byzantine-affiliated regimes in Yemen (Arabian Peninsula).

summary: Maurice drove the Persians out of Cappadocia and secured the Byzantine position in Caucasian Albania.
text: Byzantine–Sassanid War: A Byzantine army under command of Maurice drives the Persians from Cappodocia (modern Turkey), and strengthens the Byzantine position in Caucasian Albania.

summary: Alexander of Tralles composed his twelve-volume medical work Libri duodecim de re Medica.
text: Alexander of Tralles, Greek physician, writes "Libri duodecim de re Medica" .

summary: Future Byzantine emperor Heraclius was born.
text: Heraclius, emperor of the Byzantine Empire

summary: Justinian defeated Khosrau I near Melitene after the Persian king retreated from raiding Anatolia.
text: Byzantine–Sassanid War: A Persian army under King Khosrau I breaks through the Caucasus into Anatolia (modern Turkey). They attack the cities of Theodosiopolis and Caesarea, but are thwarted. Khosrau is forced to retreat and sacks Sebasteia. On the way home, he is intercepted by a Byzantine force under Justinian (magister militum of the East), and severely defeated near Melitene. The royal baggage is captured, and many Persians drown, while escaping across the Euphrates.

summary: Baduarius mounted an unsuccessful counter-assault against the Lombards in Italy and died shortly thereafter.
text: Baduarius, son-in-law of the Byzantine emperor Justin II, is sent to Italy to resist the Lombard conquest. He leads an aborted counter-assault against the Lombards and dies soon after.

summary: Tardu led the Göktürks across the Cimmerian Bosporus into the Crimea and besieged Panticapaeum.
text: The Göktürks under Tardu cross the Cimmerian Bosporus into the Crimea, and besiege the city of Panticapaeum (Ukraine).

summary: The Byzantine commander and aristocrat Baduarius died.
text: Baduarius, Byzantine aristocrat

summary: Justinian led a Byzantine expeditionary force into Caucasian Albania and raided across the Caspian Sea.
text: Byzantine–Sassanid War: A Byzantine expeditionary force under command of Justinian (magister militum) invades Caucasian Albania, launching raids across the Caspian Sea against the Persians.

summary: Tiberius established a Byzantine naval base at Derbent on the Caspian Sea to construct a fleet.
text: Summer – Tiberius, Byzantine co-ruler (Caesar), establishes a naval base at Derbent on the Caspian Sea to construct a Byzantine fleet .

summary: Maurice was appointed commander-in-chief of the Byzantine army in the East, succeeding Justinian.
text: Winter – Maurice is appointed commander-in-chief of the Byzantine army in the East. He succeeds Justinian, despite complete lack of military experience.

summary: Eutychius was restored as patriarch of Constantinople after twelve years in exile.
text: Eutychius is restored as patriarch of Constantinople, after an exile of 12 years at Amasia (modern Turkey).

summary: John Scholasticus, patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: John Scholasticus, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Maurice invaded Upper Mesopotamia, raided across the Tigris, and deported captives to Cyprus.
text: Byzantine–Sassanid War: A Byzantine army under command of Maurice (magister militum per Orientem) invades Upper Mesopotamia, and raids on both sides of the Tigris. He deports 70,000 captives from Hyrcania to Cyprus, and installs military colonists to guard the strategic locations.

summary: Tiberius II Constantine succeeded Justin II as sole emperor of the Byzantine Empire.
text: Emperor Justin II dies after several periods of insanity. On the advice of his wife Sophia, he has raised his general Tiberius to the rank of co-emperor (Caesar). From December 574 he has ruled jointly with Sophia, and now succeeds them as emperor of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Jacob Baradaeus, bishop of Edessa, died.
text: Jacob Baradaeus, bishop of Edessa

summary: Justin II, Byzantine emperor, died in Constantinople.
text: Justin II, Byzantine emperor

summary: John Malalas, Byzantine chronicler, died.
text: John Malalas, Byzantine chronicler (b. c.491)

summary: Following the death of Khosrow I, Maurice fortified Byzantine borders in Armenia and Syria amid a stalemated front.
text: Byzantine-Sassanid War: King Khosrau I seeks peace, but dies before an agreement can be reached. The Mesopotamian front becomes stalemated, and Maurice (magister militum of the East) fortifies the borders in Armenia and Syria.

summary: Hormizd IV succeeded his deceased father Khosrow I as king of the Sasanian Empire.
text: Khosrau I dies after a 48-year reign, during which he has extended his realm from the River Oxus to the Red Sea. He is succeeded by his son Hormizd IV, who becomes king of the Persian Empire.

summary: Hormizd IV broke off negotiations with the Byzantine Empire, and the Göktürks invaded Khorasan and Hyrcania.
text: Summer – Hormizd IV refuses to give up territories, and breaks off negotiations with the Byzantine Empire. The Türks invade Khorasan and reach Hyrcania on the Caspian Sea.

summary: Pope Pelagius II sent Gregory to Constantinople as his apocrisiarius to seek military aid against the Lombards.
text: Pelagius II sends Gregory as his apocrisiarius (ambassador to the imperial court in Constantinople). He is part of a Roman delegation to ask for military aid against the Lombards.

summary: King Liuvigild exiled Bishop Leander of Seville, who withdrew to Constantinople and wrote against Arianism.
text: Leander, Catholic bishop of Seville, is exiled by Liuvigild and withdraws to Constantinople. At the Byzantine court he composes works against Arianism .

summary: Khosrau I, king of the Sasanian Empire, died.
text: Khosrau I, king of the Persian Empire

summary: The Roman Senate sent an embassy with three thousand pounds of gold to Emperor Tiberius II Constantine pleading for help against the Lombards.
text: The Roman Senate sends an embassy to Constantinople, with a gift (3,000 pounds of gold) to Emperor Tiberius II Constantine, along with a plea for help against the Lombards.

summary: The Avars under Khagan Bayan I invaded the Lower Danube as the Slavs began migrating into the Balkans.
text: The Slavs begin to migrate into the Balkan Peninsula. The Avars, under King (khagan) Bayan I, invade the Lower Danube (modern Bulgaria).

summary: The Avars besieged the Byzantine stronghold of Sirmium on the Sava River.
text: Siege of Sirmium: The Avars march to the right bank of the River Sava, and besiege the Byzantine stronghold of Sirmium (Pannonia).

summary: Fabia Eudokia, future Byzantine empress, was born.
text: Fabia Eudokia, Byzantine empress

summary: Maximus the Confessor, Christian monk and theologian, was born.
text: Maximus the Confessor, monk and theologian (d. 662)

summary: Dorotheus of Gaza, Christian monk and abbot, died.
text: Dorotheus of Gaza, monk and abbot

summary: A Byzantine army commanded by Maurice and supported by the Ghassanids failed to capture the Persian capital of Ctesiphon.
text: Byzantine–Sasanian War: A Byzantine army commanded by Maurice, and supported by Ghassanid forces under King Al-Mundhir III, fails to capture the Persian capital, Ctesiphon, along the Euphrates.

summary: Maurice accused Al-Mundhir III of treason and brought him to Constantinople for trial.
text: Maurice accuses Mundhir III of treason, and brings him to Constantinople to face trial. Emperor Tiberius II Constantine treats him well, and allows Mundhir with his family a comfortable residence.

summary: Al-Nu'man VI and the Ghassanids revolted against the Byzantine Empire after his father was arrested.
text: Al-Nu'man VI, son (de facto) of Mundhir III, revolts with the Ghassanids against the Byzantine Empire, after his father is treacherously arrested.

summary: The Göktürks under Taspar Qaghan besieged the Byzantine city of Chersonesus on the Black Sea.
text: The Göktürks under Taspar Qaghan besiege the city of Chersonesos Taurica (modern Ukraine), located at the Black Sea; their cavalry keep plundering the steppes of the Crimean Peninsula until 590.

summary: Maurice wrote the Strategikon, an encyclopedic military handbook on the science of war.
text: Maurice writes an encyclopedic work on the science of war (the Strategikon), which exercises a major influence on the military system.

summary: Emperor Tiberius II Constantine died at Constantinople and was succeeded by his son-in-law Maurice.
text: Emperor Tiberius II Constantine, age 47, dies (possibly from deliberately poisoned food) at Constantinople, after a 4-year reign during which Thrace and Greece have been inundated by the Slavs. He is succeeded by his son-in-law Maurice, former notary who has commanded the Byzantine army in the war against the Persian Empire.

summary: Maurice appointed John Mystacon as magister militum per Orientem, who then led forces into battle at the Batman River.
text: Autumn – Maurice elevates John Mystacon to magister militum per Orientem. He sends a Byzantine expeditionary force to Arzanene (Armenia), where they fight a pitched battle at the river Nymphius (Batman River).

summary: The Avars under Bayan I captured the Byzantine city of Sirmium after a three-year siege.
text: Siege of Sirmium: The Avars, under their ruler (khagan) Bayan I, aided by Slavic auxiliary troops, capture the city of Sirmium after almost a 3-year siege. Bayan establishes a new base of operations within the Byzantine Empire, from which he plunders the Balkan Peninsula, including Athens.

summary: Gundoald arrived in southern Gaul with Byzantine funding and claimed Poitiers and Toulouse as king.
text: Gundoald, illegitimate son of Clotaire I, arrives with the financial support of Constantinople in southern Gaul. He claims as usurper king the cities Poitiers and Toulouse, part of the Frankish Kingdom .

summary: Byzantine forces defeated and killed Persian general Tamkhosrau when he attacked Constantina.
text: A Persian army under Tamkhosrau crosses the Euphrates River and attacks the city of Constantina (modern Turkey), but he is defeated by the Byzantines and killed.

summary: John Nesteutes became Patriarch of Constantinople.
text: John Nesteutes becomes the 33rd bishop or patriarch of Constantinople.

summary: Eutychius, Patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Eutychius, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Tiberius II Constantine, Byzantine Emperor, died.
text: Tiberius II Constantine, Byzantine Emperor

summary: Agathias, Greek poet and historian, died.
text: Agathias, Greek poet and historian

summary: Justinian, Byzantine general and magister militum, died.
text: Justinian, Byzantine general (magister militum)

summary: Tamkhosrau, Sasanian Persian general, died in battle near Constantina.
text: Tamkhosrau, Sassanid Persian general (marzban)

summary: The Avars captured the cities of Singidunum and Viminacium after Emperor Maurice ended the annual tribute.
text: Emperor Maurice decides to end the annual tribute to the Avars, a mounted people who have swept across Russia and threatened the Balkan Peninsula. They capture the cities of Singidunum (modern Belgrade) and Viminacium (Moesia).

summary: King Liuvigild besieged Seville and allied with the Byzantines against his rebellious son Hermenegild.
text: King Liuvigild lays siege to Seville (Southern Spain), and forms an alliance with the Byzantines. He summons his rebellious son Hermenegild back to Toledo, and forces him to abandon the Chalcedonian Faith.

summary: Refugees fleeing the Slavs and Avars founded the city of Monemvasia in the Peloponnese.
text: The city of Monemvasia (Peloponnese) is founded by people seeking refuge from the Slavs and Avars.

summary: Muhammad accompanied his uncle Abu Talib on trading journeys to Syria.
text: Muhammad, age 12, accompanies his uncle Abu Talib during trading journeys to Syria.

summary: Theodosius, son of Emperor Maurice and Byzantine co-emperor, was born.
text: Theodosius, Byzantine co-emperor

summary: The Byzantine Empire established the Exarchate of Ravenna to organize its Italian possessions under an exarch.
text: The Exarchate of Ravenna is founded, and organised into a group of duchies, mainly coastal cities on the Italian Peninsula. The civil and military head of these Byzantine territories is the exarch (governor) in Ravenna.

summary: The Slavs and Avars invaded the southern Balkans, ravaging Athens and Corinth and threatening the Long Walls of Constantinople.
text: The Slavs push south on the Balkan Peninsula – partly in conjunction with the Avars under their ruler (khagan) Bayan I – ravaging the cities Athens and Corinth, and threatening the Long Walls of Constantinople.

summary: The Persian commander Kardarigan led an unsuccessful siege against the Byzantine fortress of Monokarton.
text: The Persian commander, Kardarigan ("black hawk"), begins an unsuccessful siege of Monokarton (modern Turkey).

summary: Armenian church leader and Syriac historian John of Ephesus died.
text: John of Ephesus, Armenian bishop

summary: Emperor Maurice rejected a Persian peace proposal that demanded renewed Roman payments in gold.
text: Spring – Emperor Maurice rejects a peace proposal of the Persians, in exchange for renewed payments in gold.

summary: A Roman army commanded by Philippicus defeated the Sasanian Persians at the Battle of Solachon near Dara.
text: Battle of Solachon: A Byzantine army under command of Philippicus defeats the Sassanid Persians, near Dara.

summary: The Avars laid siege to Thessalonica, the second city of the Byzantine Empire.
text: The Avars besiege Thessalonica (Central Macedonia), the second city of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: The Vlachs were mentioned for the first time in a Byzantine chronicle.
text: The Vlachs are first mentioned in a Byzantine chronicle .

summary: Slavs advanced to the gates of Thessalonica and penetrated into the Peloponnese.
text: Slavs advance to the gates of Thessaloniki and the Peloponnese.

summary: The Avars destroyed a line of Roman fortifications along the Danubian Limes, including Oescus and Ratiaria.
text: Avars destroy a lien of Roman camps along the Danubian Limes, including Oescus and Ratiaria.

actor: Monastery of St. John in Beth Zagba
summary: The Rabbula Gospels, including the Page with the Crucifixion, was completed at the Monastery of Saint John in Beth Zagba.
text: The Page with the Crucifixion, from the "Rabbula Gospels", at the Monastery of St. John in Beth Zagba (Syria), is completed. It is now kept at the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Florence, Italy.
cast: Monastery of St. John in Beth Zagba
names: Monastery of St. John in Beth Zagba

summary: Emperor Maurice constructed additional fortifications along the Danube frontier against the Avars and Slavs.
text: Emperor Maurice builds more fortifications along the Danube frontier, separating the Byzantine Empire from the realm of the Avars and Slavs .

summary: Byzantine general Comentiolus assembled an army at Anchialus to ambush the Avars in the Haemus Mountains.
text: Comentiolus, Byzantine general (magister militum), assembles an army of 10,000 men at Anchialus (modern Bulgaria). He prepares an ambush for the Avars in the Haemus Mountains.

summary: Byzantine troops mutinied against Priscus, but went on to defeat a Persian offensive led by King Hormizd IV at Martyropolis.
text: Byzantine-Sassanid War: Unpaid Byzantine troops mutiny against Priscus (magister militum per Orientem). King Hormizd IV begins a Persian offensive, but is defeated at Martyropolis (modern Turkey).

summary: Emperor Maurice dispatched Guaram I to Mtskheta, restoring the monarchy of Iberia.
text: Summer – Guaram I of Iberia, Georgian prince in exile, is sent by Emperor Maurice to the city of Mtskheta (Georgia). He restores the monarchy and is bestowed with the Byzantine court title of curopalates.

summary: Bahram Chobin ambushed and defeated the invading Turks at the Battle of the Hyrcanian Rock.
text: First Perso-Turkic War: A Persian army (12,000 men) under Bahrām Chobin, supported by Cataphracts (heavy cavalry), ambush the invading Turks, and win a great victory at the Battle of the Hyrcanian Rock.

summary: A Persian army led by Bahram Chobin captured the Byzantine fortress city of Martyropolis.
text: Byzantine–Sassanid War: A Persian army under Bahrām Chobin captures the fortress city of Martyropolis (modern Turkey).

summary: Emperor Maurice defeated Persian forces under Bahram Chobin at Nisibis and drove them into Armenia.
text: Byzantine–Sassanid War: Emperor Maurice defeats the Persian forces under Bahrām Chobin at Nisibis (modern Turkey), and drives them back into Armenia.

summary: Comentiolus received the deposed Persian king Khosrau II as a refugee at his headquarters in Hierapolis.
text: Comentiolus, commander of the eastern army, receives the legitimate Persian king, Khosrau II, as a refugee in his headquarters at Hierapolis.

summary: Emperor Maurice established the Exarchate of Carthage in Africa, combining civil and military authority.
text: Maurice establishes the Exarchate of Carthage in Africa. He combines the civil authority of a praetorian prefect and the military authority, based at Carthage.

summary: Emperor Maurice proclaimed his eldest son Theodosius co-emperor and heir to the Byzantine throne.
text: Theodosius, eldest son of Maurice, is proclaimed as co-emperor. He becomes his father's heir to the Byzantine throne.

summary: Stephen I succeeded his father Guaram I as ruler of the Principality of Iberia.
text: Stephen I succeeds his father Guaram I as king of Iberia (Georgia) .

summary: Hormizd IV was deposed and assassinated by Persian nobles, and Khosrau II succeeded him as king of the Sasanian Empire.
text: Hormizd IV is deposed and assassinated by Persian nobles. Having ruled since 579, he is succeeded by his son Khosrau II as king of the Persian Empire.

summary: Bahram Chobin defeated the forces of Khosrau II near Ctesiphon and proclaimed himself king of Persia.
text: September – Bahrām Chobin defeats the inferior forces of Khosrau II near Ctesiphon. He seizes the throne and proclaims himself as king Bahrām IV of Persia.

summary: Benjamin I, future Coptic Orthodox Patriarch of Alexandria, was born.
text: Benjamin, Coptic Orthodox Patriarch of Alexandria
names: Pope of the Coptic Orthodox Church

summary: Boran, future queen of the Sasanian Empire, was born.
text: Boran, Queen of Persia (d. 632)

summary: Kavad II, future king of the Sasanian Empire, was born.
text: Kavadh II, king of the Sasanian Empire (d. 628)

summary: Theodore Rshtuni, Armenian general and prince, was born.
text: Theodore Rshtuni, Armenian general

summary: Guaram I, presiding prince of Iberia, died.
text: Guaram I, king of Iberia (Georgia)

summary: Hormizd IV, deposed king of the Sasanian Empire, was murdered.
text: Hormizd IV, king of the Persian Empire

summary: Emperor Maurice dispatched Byzantine forces under Narses to help Khosrow II regain the Persian throne.
text: Byzantine–Sassanid War: Emperor Maurice, seeing an opportunity to end the prolonged war to the advantage of Constantinople, assists Khosrau II to regain the Persian throne. He sends a Byzantine army (35,000 men) under Narses into Mesopotamia, through Syria. At the same time, an expeditionary force in Armenia advances through Caucasian Iberia into Media (modern Azerbaijan).

summary: The Byzantines defeated Bahram Chobin at the Battle of Blarathon near Ganzak.
text: Battle of Blarathon: A Persian army of about 40,000 men under King Bahrām VI is defeated, in the lowlands near Ganzak (northwestern Iran), by the Byzantines. Bahrām flees to seek refuge with the Turks in Central Asia, and settles in Fergana. However, after some time, he is murdered by a hired assassin of Khosrau II.

summary: Emperor Maurice began military campaigns in the Balkans against the Avars and Slavs to secure the Danube frontier.
text: Summer – Maurice begins a series of military expeditions, to defend the Balkan provinces from the Avars and Slavs. He establishes the Danube frontier (Limes Moesiae) from the Delta to the fortress city of Singidunum (Belgrade), and permits the Byzantines to reassert their authority in the interior.

summary: Khosrow II was reinstalled as king of the Sasanian Empire and concluded peace with Emperor Maurice.
text: Khosrau II is reinstalled as king of the Persian Empire. Peace with Constantinople is concluded after a war of almost 20 years. Maurice receives the Persian provinces of Armenia and Georgia. The recognition of the traditional frontiers, and the cessation of subsidies for the Caucasus forts, leaves the Byzantines in a dominant position in their relations with Persia.

summary: John Mystacon, prominent Byzantine general, died.
text: John Mystacon, Byzantine general

summary: Peter III of Callinicum, Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch, died.
text: Peter III of Raqqa, Patriarch of Antioch

summary: Emperor Maurice recaptured the Byzantine stronghold of Singidunum from the Avars.
text: Emperor Maurice regains the Byzantine stronghold Singidunum (modern Belgrade) from the Avars. By counter-invading their homelands on the Balkans, Byzantine troops increase their pay by pillaging in hostile territory.

summary: Priscus defeated Slavic tribes and Gepids south of the Danube and crossed into Wallachia to campaign.
text: Spring – Priscus, commander-in-chief in Thrace, defeats the Slavic tribes and Gepids on Byzantine territory south of the Danube. He crosses the river to fight in the uncharted swamps and forests of modern-day Wallachia.

summary: Priscus disobeyed Emperor Maurice's orders to winter north of the Danube and retreated to Odessus.
text: Autumn – Emperor Maurice orders Priscus to spend the winter with his troops on the northern Danube bank, but he disobeys the emperor's order and retreats to the port city of Odessus (Varna) on the Black Sea Coast.

summary: King Khosrau II defeated the Persian usurper Hormizd V.
text: The Persian usurper Hormizd V (who rises temporarily to power) is defeated by King Khosrau II.

summary: Anastasius I was restored as patriarch of Antioch after the death of Gregory.
text: Anastasius I is restored as patriarch of Antioch, after Gregory dies.

summary: Gregory, patriarch of Antioch, died.
text: Gregory, patriarch of Antioch

summary: Ino Anastasia, Byzantine empress consort, died.
text: Ino Anastasia, Byzantine empress consort

summary: Paul, father of Byzantine Emperor Maurice, died.
text: Paul, father of Maurice

summary: Slavs invaded Moesia and Macedonia, destroying the towns of Aquis, Scupi, and Zaldapa.
text: Balkan Campaign: The Slavs invade the Byzantine provinces of Moesia and Macedonia again; during their pillaging the towns of Aquis, Scupi and Zaldapa in Dobruja are destroyed.

summary: Emperor Maurice replaced general Priscus with his brother Peter as commander-in-chief against the Avars.
text: Autumn – Emperor Maurice replaces general Priscus for disobeying orders. He installs his inexperienced brother Peter, as commander-in-chief in charge of the war against the Avars.

summary: Amos succeeded John IV as the Orthodox Patriarch of Jerusalem.
text: Amos succeeds John IV as Orthodox Patriarch of Jerusalem.

summary: John IV, Orthodox Patriarch of Jerusalem, died.
text: John IV, patriarch of Jerusalem

summary: The Avars plundered Singidunum and retreated to raid Dalmatia as a Byzantine relief force under Priscus approached Novae.
text: Balkan Campaign: A Byzantine relief force under Priscus marches up the Danube River along the southern bank to Novae (modern Bulgaria). The fortress city of Singidunum (Belgrade) is plundered by the Avars, and abandoned after the approach of the Byzantines. The Avars retreat and launch a raid against Dalmatia.

summary: The Lombards sacked the town of Terracina in Central Italy.
text: The Lombards sack the town of Terracina (Central Italy). After they conquer more cities, Terracina remains an important military stronghold of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: John IV the Faster, Patriarch of Constantinople, died after a thirteen-year reign.
text: John IV ("the Faster"), patriarch of Constantinople, dies after a 13-year reign in which he has mediated disputes between the Eastern Orthodox Church and the Monophysites.

summary: John IV the Faster, Patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: John IV, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Emperor Maurice used Marcianopolis as a military base of operations on the lower Danube River against the Slavs in the Balkans.
text: Emperor Maurice uses the city of Marcianopolis (modern Bulgaria) as a military base of operations on the lower Danube River, against the Slavs on the Balkans.

summary: Emperor Maurice composed his last will, designating his son Theodosius to rule the East from Constantinople and Tiberius to rule the West from Rome.
text: Emperor Maurice writes his last will, in which he describes his ideas for governing the Byzantine Empire (his eldest son, Theodosius, will rule the East from Constantinople, and his second son, Tiberius, the West from Rome).

summary: The Avars resumed their Danube campaign and besieged the Byzantine fortress city of Tomis on the Black Sea coast.
text: Autumn – Balkan Campaign: The Avars, strengthened by the tribute of the Franks, resume their campaign along the Danube River, and besiege the Byzantine fortress city of Tomis (modern Romania) on the Black Sea coast.

summary: The Avars lifted their siege of Tomis as Byzantine forces under Comentiolus marched through the Balkan Mountains toward Zikidiba.
text: Balkan Campaign: The Avars lift the siege of the fortress city of Tomis (modern Romania). A Byzantine army under Comentiolus crosses the Balkan Mountains, and marches along the Danube River to Zikidiba.

summary: The Avars routed the Byzantine army under Comentiolus south of the Balkan Mountains and captured Drizipera before being struck by plague.
text: The Avars rout the Byzantine forces of Comentiolus (south of Haemus Mons), and capture Drizipera (Thrace). A large part of their troops are killed by the plague, after many cities are devastated in the Balkan Peninsula.

summary: Emperor Maurice concluded a peace treaty with Avar leader Bayan I and reinforced the Anastasian Wall near Constantinople.
text: Emperor Maurice pays tribute to the Avars and concludes a treaty with their leader Bayan I, allowing Byzantine expeditions in Wallachia. He reorganises his army and strengthens the Long Walls (west of Constantinople).

summary: Emperor Maurice concluded a truce with King Agilulf of the Lombards negotiated by Pope Gregory I, while Agilulf occupied Sutri and Perugia.
text: Maurice makes peace with King Agilulf, conceding northern Italy. Pope Gregory I the Great negotiates a truce, ending 30 years of Lombard terror. Agilulf expands the Lombard Kingdom by occupying Sutri and Perugia.

summary: Avar leader Bayan I ordered the execution of 12,000 Byzantine prisoners of war after Emperor Maurice refused to pay their ransom.
text: Emperor Maurice refuses to pay ransom for 12,000 Byzantine soldiers taken prisoner by the Avars. Their leader Bayan I orders the execution of the prisoners, and slaughters them all. His failure to buy back the captives destroys Maurice's popularity with the Byzantine troops in the Balkan Peninsula.

summary: Byzantine generals Priscus and Comentiolus crossed the Danube and defeated the Avars at Viminacium.
text: Summer – Balkan Campaign: The Byzantine generals Priscus and Comentiolus join their forces at Singidunum (modern Belgrade), and move downstream to the fortress city of Viminacium (Serbia). The Byzantines cross the Danube River and invade Upper Moesia, where they defeat the Avars in open battle.

summary: Priscus pursued retreating Avar forces into Pannonia and devastated their lands east of the Tisza River.
text: Priscus pursues the fleeing Avar tribes and invades their homeland in Pannonia. He devastates the land east of the Tisza River, deciding the war for the Byzantines and ending the Avar and Slavic incursions across the Danube.

summary: Byzantine general Comentiolus reopened the strategic Gate of Trajan mountain pass near Ihtiman.
text: Autumn – Comentiolus reopens the Gate of Trajan pass, near Ihtiman (Bulgaria). This strategic mountain pass, whose fortress "Stipon" defends the border between the provinces Thrace and Macedonia, is not used for decades.

summary: Exarch Callinicus repulsed South Slavic raids into Istria and drove them out.
text: Callinicus, governor (exarch) of Ravenna, repulses attacks of the South Slavs in Istria (Croatia). The region is pillaged, but the Byzantines drive them all out.

summary: Exarch Callinicus broke a truce by kidnapping the daughter of Lombard King Agilulf, triggering war with the Lombards.
text: Callinicus breaks the truce by kidnapping the Lombard daughter of King Agilulf, beginning a war with the Exarchate of Ravenna .

summary: King Khosrau II sent a Persian expedition to South Arabia and conquered Yemen.
text: King Khosrau II sends a Persian expedition to South Arabia and conquers Yemen. He establishes a military base to control the sea trade with the East .

summary: Patriarch Anastasius I of Antioch died.
text: Anastasius I, patriarch of Antioch

summary: Rome remained under Byzantine rule while the rest of the Italian mainland was divided among independent cities and duchies.
text: Rome continues as part of the Byzantine Empire. The Italian mainland is divided into independent cities and duchies.

summary: Venice continued to develop as an independent realm established by coastal refugees.
text: Venice continues as an independent realm, having been built up from fishing villages and settled by fugitives.

summary: Peter led a Byzantine army across the Danube to the Tisza River and defeated the Avars.
text: Balkan Campaign: A Byzantine army under command of Peter, brother of Emperor Maurice, crosses the Danube and advances to the Tisza River, where it defeats the Avars.

summary: King Agilulf expanded Lombard control into Northern Italy and settled relations with the Franks and Rome.
text: The Lombards under King Agilulf expand into Northern Italy, establishing a settlement with the Franks and maintaining intermittent relationships with Rome.

summary: Sophia, Byzantine empress consort and widow of Justin II, died.
text: Sophia, Byzantine Empress consort
names: List of Roman and Byzantine empresses

summary: Phocas led a mutiny of Byzantine troops on the Danube and marched toward Constantinople against Emperor Maurice.
text: Emperor Maurice succeeds in winning over the Avars to Byzantine rule, but his campaigns against the Avars, Lombards, Persians and Slavs drain the imperial treasury, requiring an increase in taxes. He orders the troops to stay for winter beyond the Danube, but a mutiny breaks out under Phocas. He brings the Byzantine forces back over the Danube and marches on to Constantinople.

summary: Phocas entered Constantinople, executed Emperor Maurice and his sons, and was proclaimed Byzantine emperor.
text: A civil war breaks out and Phocas enters Constantinople. Maurice is captured trying to escape; he is forced to witness the slaughter of his five sons and all his supporters, and is then executed (beheaded) after a 20-year reign. His wife, Constantina, and his three daughters are spared, and sent to a monastery. Phocas is proclaimed the new emperor of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Khosrow II launched an offensive against the Byzantine Empire to avenge Maurice as Narses rebelled against Phocas at Edessa.
text: Byzantine–Persian War: King Khosrau II launches an offensive against Constantinople, to avenge Maurice's death, his "friend and father", and tries to reconquer Byzantine territory. Narses, governor of Upper Mesopotamia, rebels against Phocas at the city of Edessa and requests aid from the Persians. Khosrau sends an expeditionary force to Armenia and crosses the Euphrates.

summary: King Liuva II appointed Witteric commander-in-chief of the Visigothic army to expel the Byzantines from Hispania.
text: Spring – Witteric is appointed commander-in-chief of the Visigoth army, and receives orders from King Liuva II to expel the Byzantines from Hispania.

summary: Maurice, emperor of the Byzantine Empire, was executed at Chalcedon near Constantinople.
text: Maurice, Byzantine emperor (b. 539)

summary: Comentiolus, Byzantine general and magister militum, was executed.
text: Comentiolus, Byzantine general (magister militum)

summary: Peter, Byzantine general and kouropalates, died.
text: Peter, Byzantine general (curopalates)

summary: Theodosius, Byzantine co-emperor and son of Maurice, died.
text: Theodosius, Byzantine co-emperor

summary: Tiberius, Byzantine prince and son of Emperor Maurice, died.
text: Tiberius, Byzantine prince

summary: The Roman Senate acclaimed new statues of Emperor Phocas and Empress Leontia, marking its last recorded mention on the Italian mainland.
text: The last mention of the Roman Senate on the Italian mainland is made (according to the Gregorian register). It mentions that the Senate has acclaimed new statues of Emperor Phocas and Empress Leontia.

summary: The future Pope Boniface III was appointed papal legate to Constantinople.
text: The future Pope Boniface III is appointed papal legate to Constantinople.

summary: Avars and Slavs regrouped and pillaged Byzantine provinces south and west of the Danube while Emperor Phocas faced the Persian war.
text: The Avars regroup after they are almost destroyed; together with the Slavs they start pillaging through the Byzantine provinces, west and south of the Danube. Due to the new Persian war, Emperor Phocas has few imperial troops available to defend the Balkan Peninsula.

summary: Khosrau II captured Byzantine positions east of the Euphrates, including the fortress of Dara, and ravaged the Levant.
text: Byzantine–Persian War: King Khosrau II captures the Byzantine positions east of the Euphrates; the Persians destroy many cities in the Levant region, after prolonged sieges such as the Byzantine fortress of Dara (modern Turkey).

summary: Emperor Phocas recognized Agilulf as king of the Lombards, signed a peace treaty, and ceded Orvieto to him.
text: Emperor Phocas recognizes Agilulf as king of the Lombards, and signs a peace treaty. He pays a tribute and cedes Orvieto (Central Italy), among other towns. The Byzantine army is withdrawn from the Balkan Peninsula.

summary: Emperor Phocas executed former empress Constantina and her three daughters at Chalcedon.
text: Phocas has Constantina, empress consort of Maurice, and her three daughters arrested. He accuses her of conspiracy, and has them executed at Chalcedon (Bithynia).

summary: Alexander of Tralles, the Byzantine physician, died in Rome.
text: Alexander of Tralles, physician

summary: Constantina, Byzantine empress consort of Maurice, was executed at Chalcedon.
text: Constantina, Byzantine empress

summary: Cyriacus II, patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Cyriacus II, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Monk and Christian writer John Climacus died.
text: John Climacus, monk and writer

summary: Emperor Phocas bestowed the title of Universal Bishop upon Pope Boniface III to improve relations with Rome.
text: Emperor Phocas bestows the title "Universal Bishop" upon Boniface III, in an effort to improve relations with Rome.

summary: Thomas I was appointed as the sixtieth ecumenical patriarch of Constantinople.
text: Thomas I is appointed as the 60th patriarch of Constantinople.

summary: Emperor Phocas dedicated the Column of Phocas in the Roman Forum.
text: Augustus Phocas dedicated the Column of Phocas in the Roman Forum.

summary: Heraclius the Elder and his son Heraclius launched a revolt from Carthage against Emperor Phocas.
text: Heraclian revolt: Heraclius the Elder, exarch of Africa, and his son (also named Heraclius) revolt against Emperor Phocas, whose regime in Constantinople has become unpopular and violent.

summary: Heraclius the Elder proclaimed himself and his son consuls and claimed imperial authority as Syria and Palaestina Prima rebelled.
text: Heraclius proclaims himself and his son as consuls, claiming the imperial title—and mint coins with the two wearing the consular robes. Syria and Palaestina Prima revolt.

summary: Khosrow II invaded Armenia and raided deep into Byzantine Anatolia through Cappadocia, Phrygia, Galatia, and Bithynia.
text: Byzantine–Persian War: King Khosrau II invades Armenia, and raids deep into Anatolia through the Byzantine provinces of Cappadocia, Phrygia, Galatia, and Bithynia.

summary: The Column of Phocas in Rome was dedicated in honour of Emperor Phocas.
text: The Column of Phocas at Rome is dedicated in honour of Phocas. The Corinthian column has a height of 13.6 m (44 ft).

summary: The Georgian Orthodox Church returned to Chalcedonian Christianity.
text: The Georgian Orthodox Church returns to Chalcedonism .

summary: Nicetas invaded Egypt and defeated the Byzantine forces under Bonus outside Alexandria during the Heraclian revolt.
text: Nicetas, cousin of future emperor Heraclius, launches an overland invasion in Egypt. He defeats a Byzantine army under Bonus (comes Orientis) outside Alexandria, sent from Constantinople.

summary: Heraclius arrived with a fleet at Constantinople, overthrew and executed Emperor Phocas, seized the Byzantine throne, and changed the official language to Greek.
text: Heraclian revolt: Heraclius arrives with a fleet from Africa at Constantinople. Assisted by an uprising in the capital, he overthrows and personally beheads Emperor Phocas. Heraclius gains the throne with help from his father Heraclius the Elder. His first major act is to change the official language of the Byzantine Empire from Latin to Greek (already the language of the vast majority of the population).

object: List of Greek Orthodox patriarchs of Alexandria
summary: John the Merciful became the Greek Orthodox patriarch of Alexandria.
text: John V (the Merciful) becomes patriarch of Alexandria .
cast: List of Greek Orthodox patriarchs of Alexandria
names: List of Greek Orthodox patriarchs of Alexandria

states.entity: List of Greek Orthodox patriarchs of Alexandria

summary: Byzantine Emperor Phocas was overthrown and beheaded in Constantinople.
text: Phocas, Byzantine emperor

summary: Heraclius the Elder, Byzantine general and Exarch of Africa, died.
text: Heraclius the Elder, Byzantine general

summary: The Persian army under Shahrbaraz captured Antioch and Byzantine fortresses in Syria and Mesopotamia.
text: Byzantine–Persian War: The Persian army under Shahrbaraz captures Antioch, and most of the remaining Byzantine fortresses in Syria and Mesopotamia. King Khosrau II is re-establishing a neo-Persian Empire, and intensifies his war effort. The Byzantine army, ruined by defeat and corruption, offers only half-hearted opposition.

summary: Eudoxia Epiphania, daughter of Byzantine Emperor Heraclius, was born.
text: Eudoxia Epiphania, daughter of Byzantine emperor Heraclius

summary: Comentiolus, Byzantine general and brother of Phocas, died.
text: Comentiolus, Byzantine general

summary: Empress Fabia Eudokia died of epilepsy and was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople.
text: Empress Eudokia, wife of Heraclius, dies of epilepsy. She leaves two children, and is buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople.

summary: Sisebut succeeded Gundemar as king of the Visigoths and began campaigning against Byzantine Spania.
text: Sisebut succeeds Gundemar as king of the Visigoths. He begins a campaign against the remains of Byzantine power in Spania.

summary: The Holy Sponge was brought to Constantinople from Palestine.
text: The Holy Sponge is brought to Constantinople from Palestine.

summary: Heraclius Constantine, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: Constantine III, Byzantine emperor (d. 641)

summary: Fabia Eudokia, Byzantine empress consort, died.
text: Fabia Eudokia, Byzantine empress consort

summary: Emperor Heraclius married his niece Martina, who was proclaimed empress of the Byzantine Empire.
text: Emperor Heraclius marries his niece Martina; she becomes empress (Augusta) of the Byzantine Empire. This second marriage is considered to fall within the prohibited degree of kinship, and is approved by the Catholic Church in Constantinople.

summary: Heraclius crowned his infant son Constantine co-emperor and betrothed him to Gregoria.
text: Constantine is crowned co-emperor (Caesar) by his father Heraclius and shortly after betrothed to his cousin, Gregoria, daughter of Nicetas. Only 8 months old, Constantine has no real power and his dynastic title is purely ceremonial.

summary: Heraclius appointed himself and his brother Theodore commanders-in-chief of the Byzantine army.
text: Byzantine–Persian War: Heraclius appoints himself commander-in-chief, along with his brother Theodore (curopalates), to solidify command of the army.

summary: Persian forces defeated Heraclius outside Antioch and captured Damascus, Apamea, and Emesa.
text: Battle of Antioch: Heraclius mobilises a Byzantine expeditionary force to Antioch (Syria), but is completely defeated outside the city by the Persians. Shahin Vahmanzadegan makes further inroads into Central and Western Anatolia. In Syria, Shahrbaraz captures the cities of Damascus, Apamea and Emesa.

summary: Saint Theodore of Sykeon, Byzantine ascetic, died.
text: Saint Theodore of Sykeon, Byzantine ascetic

summary: Priscus, Byzantine general, died.
text: Priscus, Byzantine general

summary: Caesarea Maritima, Arsuf, and Tiberias surrendered on terms to the Sasanians during the Byzantine–Sasanian War.
text: Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628: The Levantine cities of Caesarea Maritima, Arsuf, and Tiberias surrender on terms to the Sasanians.

summary: A Sasanian army commanded by Shahrbaraz captured and sacked Jerusalem, slaughtering tens of thousands and seizing the True Cross.
text: Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628: Sasanian conquest of Jerusalem: A Persian–Judaean army (26,000 men) commanded by Shahrbaraz captures and sacks Jerusalem, after a 20-day siege against the Byzantine Empire. Somewhere between 57,000 and 66,500 citizens are slain; another 35,000 are enslaved, including the Patriarch Zacharias. Many churches in the city (including the "Church of the Resurrection" or Holy Sepulchre) are burned, and numerous relics, including the True Cross, the Holy Lance, and the Holy Sponge, are carried off to the Persian capital Ctesiphon.

summary: The Persians destroyed the Ghassanid Kingdom, a vassal state of the Byzantine Empire.
text: The Persians destroy the Ghassanid Kingdom (Arabia), a vassal state of the Byzantine Empire .

summary: The Avars sacked Salona and damaged Diocletian's Palace in Split.
text: The Palace of Diocletian in Split (Croatia) is damaged by the Avars, who sack the nearby city of Salona. The population flees to the walled palace, which is able to hold out.

summary: The Sudarium of Oviedo was taken from Palestine following the Sasanian invasion.
text: The Sudarium of Oviedo is taken from Palestine, after the invasion of the Sassanid Persians.

summary: Philippicus, a prominent Byzantine general, died.
text: Philippicus, Byzantine general

summary: Slavs overran and settled widely across the Balkans, while Avars raided and settled in the western regions.
text: The Balkans are freely overrun by the Slavs, who settle in large numbers in what is now Bulgaria, Serbia, North Macedonia and parts of Greece. The western territories of modern-day Yugoslavia (Bosnia, Croatia and Dalmatia) suffer raids from the Avars, who settle in this region.

summary: Chatzon led Slavic forces in a combined land and sea assault besieging Byzantine Thessaloniki.
text: The Slavs under Chatzon attack in longboats along the coasts of Thessaly, western Anatolia, and various Greek islands. They besiege the Byzantine city of Thessaloniki in a combined land and sea attack. The Slavs with their families encamp before the city walls.

summary: Avars and Slavic invaders destroyed Epidaurus, prompting refugees to flee and found Dubrovnik.
text: The city of Epidaurus (Dalmatia) is destroyed by the Avars and Slavic invaders. The Illyrian refugees flee to the nearby island Laus, where they found Dubrovnik (Ragusa). The islands of Rab, Krk and Cres become major food suppliers for the surviving cities of the mainland.

summary: Eleutherius succeeded John I as exarch of Ravenna, visited Pope Adeodatus I, and captured Naples from the rebel John of Conza.
text: Eleutherius succeeds John I as exarch of Ravenna. He persecutes those implicated in the murder of John and the judges of the State. After making a courtesy visit to Pope Adeodatus I, Eleutherius captures Naples and kills the rebel leader John of Conza.

summary: Slavic chieftain Chatzon died during the siege of Thessaloniki.
text: Chatzon, chieftain of the Slavs

summary: John I Lemigius, exarch of Ravenna, was killed in Ravenna.
text: John I Lemigius, exarch of Ravenna

summary: John of Conza, an Italian rebel leader against Byzantine rule, died.
text: John of Conza, Italian rebel leader (or 618)

summary: Jewish forces took control of Jerusalem under Sasanian suzerainty, creating an autonomous province and re-establishing the High Priesthood.
text: Byzantine–Sassanid War of 602–628: The Jews of Jerusalem gain complete control over the city; much of Judea and Galilee becomes an autonomous Jewish province of the Persian Empire. The Jewish Temple is rebuilt by Nehemiah ben Hushiel (exilarch of Jerusalem), who establishes a High Priesthood.

summary: Persian general Shahin Vahmanzadegan destroyed the city of Sardis during his campaign through Byzantine Anatolia.
text: The Persian army under Shahin Vahmanzadegan destroys the city of Sardis, including its synagogue. Its importance is due to a highway, leading from the interior to the Aegean coast. Shahin marches through Anatolia, defeating the Byzantines numerous times.

summary: Adaloald succeeded his father Agilulf as king of the Lombards under the regency of Theodelinda and made peace with the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna.
text: Adaloald, age 14, succeeds his father Agilulf as Lombard king of Italy. He reigns under his mother Theodelinda as regent. The Lombard Kingdom gradually begins to convert to Catholicism, and establishes peace with the Exarchate of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Anastasius, Coptic Patriarch of Alexandria, died.
text: Anastasius, Coptic Patriarch of Alexandria
names: Pope of the Coptic Orthodox Church

summary: John the Merciful, Greek Patriarch of Alexandria, died in Cyprus.
text: John the Merciful, Patriarch of Alexandria

summary: Persian general Shahin conquered Chalcedon on the Bosporus, prompting Emperor Heraclius to open peace negotiations before Shahin withdrew toward Syria.
text: Byzantine-Sassanid War: The Persian army under Shahin Vahmanzadegan conquers Chalcedon in Anatolia, and reaches the Bosporus, threatening Constantinople. Emperor Heraclius begins peace negotiations, promising an annual tribute of 1,000 talents of gold and silver. Shahin withdraws with his army to Syria, to focus on the invasion of Egypt.

summary: After failing to capture Emperor Heraclius outside Constantinople, the Avars plundered Thrace and carried off thousands of captives to the Danube.
text: The Avars send envoys to Constantinople for a meeting with Heraclius. He is warned about an ambush, and flees for safety behind the city walls in time. Angry at the failure to capture the Byzantine emperor, the Avars plunder Thrace and return to the Danube River, carrying off 270,000 people.

summary: Persian forces under Shahrbaraz invaded Byzantine Egypt, defeated Roman garrisons, and advanced across the Libyan Desert toward Cyrene.
text: Byzantine–Sassanian War: A Persian expeditionary force under Shahrbaraz invades Egypt, and occupies the province. After defeating the Byzantine garrisons in the Nile Valley, the Persians march across the Libyan Desert as far as Cyrene.

summary: The Persians besieged Alexandria and blockaded its harbor, severing regular grain shipments to Constantinople.
text: The Persians besiege Alexandria; the defence of the city is led by Nicetas (cousin of emperor Heraclius). The Byzantine resistance is undermined by a blockade of the harbor; the usual grain supplies are cut off from Egypt to Constantinople.

summary: John of Conza, rebel leader against the Byzantine exarchate in Italy, died.
text: John of Conza, Italian rebel leader (or 615)

summary: The Persians captured Alexandria, forcing Nicetas and Patriarch John the Merciful to flee to Cyprus.
text: Byzantine–Sasanian War: The besieged city of Alexandria is captured by the Persians. Nicetas, cousin of Emperor Heraclius, and Chalcedonian patriarch, John V, flee to Cyprus. King Khosrow II extends his rule southwards along the Nile.

summary: Emperor Heraclius was persuaded by Patriarch Sergius I to remain in Constantinople rather than relocate to Carthage and began rebuilding the Byzantine army.
text: Heraclius prepares to leave Constantinople and moves the Byzantine capital to Carthage, but is convinced to stay by Sergius I, patriarch of Constantinople. He begins to rebuild the Byzantine army with the aid of funds from church treasures.

summary: The Avars attacked the outskirts of Constantinople while Slavic tribes rebelled against Avar rule in Moravia and Lower Austria.
text: The Avars attack the outskirts of Constantinople. Numerous Slavic tribes rebel against Avar overlordship; they carve out their own sovereign territory in Moravia and Lower Austria .

summary: Kubrat, ruler of the Bulgars, was baptised in Constantinople.
text: Kubrat, ruler of the Bulgars, is baptised in Constantinople.

summary: John Moschus, Byzantine monk and ascetical writer, died in Rome.
text: John Moschus, Byzantine monk and ascetical writer

summary: Khosrow II captured the Byzantine military base of Ancyra during the Byzantine–Sasanian War.
text: Byzantine–Sassanid War: King Khosrau II captures Ancyra, an important Byzantine military base in central Anatolia. After the conquest of Egypt and Palestine, he restores the Persian Empire as it existed in 490 BC under Darius I.

summary: Slavs unsuccessfully besieged Thessaloniki and reduced urban life across the Balkan Peninsula.
text: The Slavs invade the area around Thessaloniki, which is unsuccessfully besieged. The city becomes a Byzantine enclave surrounded by Slavic territory. Urban life disappears and many towns in the Balkan Peninsula become villages.

summary: Eleutherius, Byzantine exarch of Ravenna who rebelled as emperor, was killed by his soldiers.
text: Eleutherius, Byzantine exarch of Ravenna

summary: John the Merciful, Patriarch of Alexandria, died.
text: John the Merciful, Patriarch of Alexandria

summary: Emperor Heraclius concluded a peace agreement with the Avars in exchange for annual tribute.
text: Emperor Heraclius concludes a peace agreement (in exchange for an annual tribute) with the Avars on the Balkan Peninsula, giving him a free hand to assemble Byzantine forces in Asia Minor, for non-military expenditure against the Persian Empire.

summary: The Visigoths conquered the Byzantine city of Málaga in southern Spain.
text: The city of Málaga, in southern Spain in the province of Spania, is conquered by the Visigoths.

summary: Emperor Heraclius sailed from Constantinople and landed near Alexandretta to begin a major counter-offensive against the Sasanian Empire.
text: Byzantine–Sasanian War: Emperor Heraclius sails from Constantinople with an expeditionary force (probably 50,000 men), and starts a counter-offensive against the Persian Empire (his young son, Constantine III, is left behind as regent under the charge of Sergius I, patriarch of Constantinople, and patrician Bonus). He lands a few days later at the junction of Cilicia and Syria, near Alexandretta and ancient Issus.

summary: Emperor Heraclius defeated Persian forces under Shahrbaraz in Cappadocia, recapturing Anatolia before returning to Constantinople.
text: Battle of Issus: Heraclius defeats the Persian forces under Shahrbaraz in Cappadocia. He recaptures Anatolia, but returns to Constantinople to deal with the threat posed to his Balkan domains by the Avars, and puts the Byzantine army into winter quarters in Pontus.

summary: The Western Turks conquered the Oxus valley and captured Khorasan in cooperation with Heraclius against Persia.
text: The Western Turks conquer the Oxus valley and cooperate with Heraclius against Persia, taking Khorasan (modern Afghanistan).

summary: Future Byzantine usurper Mizizios was born.
text: Mezezius, Byzantine usurper (d. 669)

summary: Andronicus, Coptic Orthodox Patriarch of Alexandria, died.
text: Andronicus, Coptic Orthodox Patriarch of Alexandria
names: List of popes of the Coptic Orthodox Church

summary: Emperor Heraclius invaded Armenia, plundered Media, and campaigned against Persian armies while leaving his son Constantine and Bonus to defend Constantinople.
text: Byzantine–Sassanid War: Emperor Heraclius invades Armenia, leaving his son Constantine (age 11) and co-regent Bonus to defend Constantinople against the Persians still at Chalcedon (modern Turkey). He sails with 5,000 reinforcements to join the Byzantine army at Trapezus. Raising additional forces in Pontus, Heraclius strikes through the mountains of Armenia and the northern sub-Caucasian principalities. He plunders Media (Azerbaijan), and avoids the Persian armies who attempt to trap him.

summary: Emperor Heraclius departed Constantinople with Empress Martina and two of his children on campaign.
text: Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium, departs from his capital at Constantinople (now Istanbul in Turkey) with his wife, the Empress Martina, and two of his children, and does not return for more than four years.

summary: Emperor Heraclius advanced through Asia Minor into Armenia and sacked its capital, Dvin.
text: Emperor Haraclius celebrates Easter at Nicomedia (now İzmit) then travels to Caesarea (now Kayseri), proceeding during April to Theodosiopolis. He leads troops into Armenia and sacks its capital, Dvin.

summary: Emperor Heraclius invaded the Sasanian Empire.
text: Heraclius invades the Sassanid Empire (now Iran).

summary: Khosrow II learned of Emperor Heraclius's surprise attack while at Ganzak and recalled General Shahrbaraz from Asia Minor.
text: While at Ganzak at what is now northwest Iran, the Sassanid Emperor Khosrow II (Chosroes) is informed by soldiers who had escaped capture that Emperor Heraclius of Byzantium is preparing a surprise attack. Khosrow dispatches an envoy to inform General Shahrbaraz to abandon a campaign in Asia Minor and to accompany him to face Heraclius.

summary: Emperor Heraclius destroyed Dvin and Nakhchivan, defeated a Persian army at Ganzak, and destroyed the Zoroastrian fire temple at Takht-e Soleymān.
text: Byzantine–Sasanian War: Emperor Heraclius advances with an expeditionary force (40,000 men) along the Araxes River, destroying the fortress city of Dvin, capital of Armenia, and Nakhchivan (modern Azerbaijan). At Ganzak, Heraclius defeats the Persian army and destroys the famous fire temple at Takht-e Soleymān, an important Zoroastrian shrine. He winters his army in Caucasian Albania to gather forces for the next year.

summary: King Khosrow II withdrew most of his troops from Chalcedon to assemble three armies against Emperor Heraclius.
text: Winter – King Khosrow II withdraws most of his troops from Chalcedon (Anatolia); he assembles three armies to trap and destroy Heraclius' forces.

summary: King Suintila led the Visigoths in recapturing Byzantine Spania, ending 70 years of imperial occupation in southern Hispania.
text: The Visigoths under King Suintila recapture the Byzantine territories of Spania (Andalusia), after 70 years of occupation. Only the Balearic Islands stay a part of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Emperor Heraclius routed the Persian forces at Tigranakert and captured the fortresses of Amida and Martyropolis.
text: Byzantine–Sassanid War: Emperor Heraclius marches with his forces westward, through the mountains of Corduene. The Persians go into winter quarters nearby, but Heraclius attacks them at Tigranakert (Kingdom of Armenia), routing the forces of the generals Shahin Vahmanzadegan and Shahraplakan. In less than seven days, he bypasses Mount Ararat and captures the strategic fortresses of Amida along the Arsanias River, and Martyropolis on the upper Tigris. The Persian army in northern Mesopotamia withdraws westward across the Euphrates. Heraclius pursues into Cilicia, accompanied by a great train of booty.

summary: Emperor Heraclius defeated the Persian general Shahrbaraz at the Battle of Sarus near Adana.
text: Battle of Sarus: Heraclius is victorious in a Byzantine assault river crossing. The reinforced Persians under Shahrbaraz are defeated along the Sarus River, near Adana (modern Turkey). Heraclius recaptures Cappadocia and Pontus, and returns to Trapezus to spend the winter. Shahrbaraz retreats in good order, and is able to continue his advance through Asia Minor towards Constantinople.

summary: The Avars and their Slavic allies laid siege to the Theodosian Walls of Constantinople alongside Persian forces.
text: Siege of Constantinople: A horde of Avars, consisting of about 80,000 men (including large contingents of Slavs, Bulgars, and other "barbarians"), attack the walls of Constantinople. A small Persian army arrives on the Bosphorus, on the Asiatic side. The Theodosian Walls are stormed with the most up-to-date siege equipment, in the form of traction trebuchets. The Avars also have mobile armoured shelters (medieval 'sows') and siege towers; the latter are covered in hides for fire protection. The defense of the capital (12,000 well-trained Byzantine troops) is in the hands of Patriarch Sergius I and Bonus (magister militum).

summary: The Byzantine army repulsed the major Avar and Persian assaults on the Theodosian Walls of Constantinople.
text: The Avars and Persian allies under Shahrbaraz launch an attack along the entire length of the Theodosian Walls (about 5.7 kilometres); the main effort is concentrated against the central section, particularly the low-lying mesoteichion. After a fierce infantry battle on the walls, the Byzantine army holds off many assaults on the city. Emperor Heraclius makes arrangements for a new army under his brother Theodore to operate against the Persians in western Anatolia, while he returns to his own army in Pontus.

summary: The Byzantines destroyed the Persian fleet in the Golden Horn and decisively defeated the Avars at Blachernae.
text: In the waters of the Golden Horn, the Persian fleet is destroyed while ferrying reinforcements. The Avars, having suffered terrible losses, running short of food and supplies, burn their siege engines. They abandon the siege and retreat to the Balkan Peninsula. The Byzantines achieve a decisive victory at Blachernae, under the protection of the Church of the Virgin Mary.
names: Church of St. Mary of Blachernae

summary: Heraclius halted Persian operations along the Phasis River in Colchis, enabling his brother Theodore to defeat Shahin in Anatolia.
text: Byzantine–Persian War: Heraclius, his army reduced by campaigning to less than 30,000 men, is on the defensive in Pontus. Apparently he leaves a strong Byzantine garrison in Trapezus, and withdraws north-eastward along the Black Sea into Colchis, where he halts the Persians by aggressive defensive-offensive operations along the Phasis River. By attracting the Persian army under Shahin Vahmanzadegan in Anatolia, he provides Theodore with the opportunity to defeat them. By the end of the summer he threatens the communication of the Persians at Chalcedon (modern Turkey).

summary: Emperor Heraclius invited the Croats and Serbs to settle in Illyricum to clear the province of Avars.
text: Heraclius invites the Croats, a Slavic tribe living in Galicia, Silesia, and Bohemia, to settle in Illyricum. They are given the land between the Drava River and the Adriatic Sea for ridding of Avars. The Serbs are allowed to move from their homeland north of the Carpathians to a territory east of the Croats. Heraclius asks Pope Honorius I to send missionaries to both groups.

summary: Emperor Heraclius concluded an alliance with Tong Yabghu of the Western Turkic Khaganate against the Persian Empire.
text: Winter – Heraclius makes an alliance with Tong Yabghu Qaghan, ruler (khagan) of the Western Turkic Khaganate, for a joint invasion of the Persian Empire the following spring. He promises his daughter Eudoxia Epiphania, age 15, in marriage to Tong Yabghu and sends her under escort with wondrous gifts.

summary: Khosrow II returned to Anatolia with two armies against Constantinople, but one under Shahin Vahmanzadegan was defeated by Theodore.
text: Summer – King Khosrau II plans an all-out effort against Constantinople. He returns to Anatolia with two armies of unknown size, presumably more than 50,000 men each. One of these (possibly commanded by Khosrau himself) is to contain Heraclius in Pontus; another under Shahin Vahmanzadegan is defeated by Theodore.

summary: Future Byzantine emperor Heraclonas was born.
text: Heraklonas, Byzantine emperor (d. 641)

summary: Shahin Vahmanzadegan, Persian general, died after his defeat in Anatolia.
text: Shahin Vahmanzadegan, Persian general

summary: Heraclius swept through Armenia recapturing fortresses, while Persian general Shahrbaraz was cut off in Anatolia and surrendered to Heraclius.
text: Spring – Byzantine–Sasanian War: Emperor Heraclius sweeps through southern Armenia with a 50,000-man expeditionary force, recapturing most of the Byzantine fortresses lost to the Persians ten and fifteen years earlier. The army of Shahrbaraz, still in Anatolia, is now cut off completely. Hearing from Byzantine agents (showing him letters) that King Khosrau II, dissatisfied with his failure to capture Constantinople, is planning to have him executed, he surrenders to Heraclius, refusing to join the Byzantine army against his ungrateful sovereign.

summary: The Göktürks and Khazars captured the Persian fortress at Derbent, while Heraclius marched into the Persian heartland.
text: Third Perso-Turkic War: The Göktürks and their Khazar allies (40,000 men) approach the Caspian Gates, and capture the Persian fortress at Derbent (modern Dagestan). Heraclius marches to the upper Tigris and invades the Persian heartland, leaving the Khazars under Tong Yabghu Qaghan to continue the siege of Tblilisi.

summary: Heraclius defeated the Persian army under Rhahzadh at the Battle of Nineveh, personally killing the Persian general.
text: Battle of Nineveh: Heraclius crosses the Great Zab river and, in a feigned retreat, defeats the Persian army (12,000 men) under Rhahzadh, near the ruins of Nineveh (Iraq). Although wounded, Heraclius refuses to leave the battlefield, and in a final cavalry charge personally kills the Persian general.

summary: Heraclius plundered the Persian royal palace at Dastagird, forcing Khosrow II to flee to Susiana.
text: Winter – Heraclius plunders the city palace of Dastagird and gains tremendous riches (also recovering 300 captured Byzantine flags). He turns northeastward to Caucasian Albania to rest his army. Khosrau II flees to the mountains of Susiana, to rally support for the defense of the Persian capital Ctesiphon.

summary: Bonus, Byzantine general and regent during the siege of Constantinople, died.
text: Bonus, Byzantine general and regent

summary: Rhahzadh, a prominent Persian general, died at the Battle of Nineveh.
text: Rhahzadh, Persian general

summary: King Stephen I of Iberia died during the siege of Tbilisi.
text: King Stephen I of Iberia (Georgia)

summary: Emperor Heraclius concluded a peace agreement with Kavadh II restoring Roman territories and the True Cross, then returned in triumph to Constantinople.
text: Spring – Byzantine–Sassanid War: Emperor Heraclius issues an ultimatum for peace to king Khosrau II, but he refuses his generous terms. The war-weary Persians revolt against Khosrau's regime at Ctesiphon and install his son Kavadh II to the throne. He puts his father to death and begins negotiations with Heraclius. Kavadh is forced to return all the territories conquered during the war. The Persians must give up all of the trophies they have captured, including the relic of the True Cross. Evidently there is also a large financial indemnity. Having accepted a peace agreement on his own terms, Heraclius returns in triumph to Constantinople.

summary: Tong Yabghu Qaghan of the Western Göktürks plundered Tbilisi and executed its Persian defenders.
text: Third Perso-Turkic War: The Western Göktürks under their leader Tong Yabghu Qaghan plunder Tbilisi (modern Georgia). The Persian defenders are executed or mutilated, Tong Yabghu appoints governors (tuduns) to manage various tribes under his overlordship.

summary: Kavadh II overthrew his father Khosrau II to seize the throne of the Sasanian Empire.
text: Khosrau II, the last great king of the Sasanian Empire, is overthrown by his son Kavadh II.

summary: Seven-year-old Ardashir III succeeded his deceased father Kavadh II as king of the Sasanian Empire.
