text: Ardashir III, age 7, succeeds his father Kavadh II as the twenty-fourth king of the Sasanian Empire on the latter's death from plague.

summary: Muhammad sent diplomatic letters to contemporary rulers explaining the tenets of Islam.
text: Muhammad's letters to world leaders explain the principles of the new monotheistic Muslim faith, as they will be contained in his book, the Quran.

summary: John Maron, Syriac monk and first Maronite patriarch, was born.
text: John Maron, Syriac monk and patriarch (d. 707)
names: List of Maronite patriarchs of Antioch

summary: Anastasius of Persia, a Christian monk and martyr, was executed.
text: Anastasius of Persia, monk

summary: Babai the Great, leading theologian of the Church of the East, died.
text: Babai the Great, church father and theologian

summary: Khosrau II, king of the Sasanian Empire, was executed.
text: Khosrau II, king of the Persian Empire

summary: King Kavadh II of the Sasanian Empire died from the plague.
text: Kavadh II, king of the Persian Empire

summary: Shirin, queen and wife of Khosrau II, died.
text: Shirin, wife of Khosrau II

summary: Tong Yabghu Qaghan, ruler of the Western Turkic Khaganate, died.
text: Tong Yabghu Qaghan, ruler of the Göktürks

summary: The Byzantine Empire reconquered Jerusalem from the Sasanian Empire after fifteen years of occupation.
text: September – Jerusalem is reconquered by the Byzantines (after 15 years of occupation), from the Persian Empire.

summary: Emperor Heraclius entered Constantinople in a triumphal ceremonial parade accompanied by the True Cross.
text: Emperor Heraclius enters Constantinople in triumph. In a ceremonial parade, accompanied by the True Cross, he is welcomed by the citizens and his son Heraclius Constantine.

summary: Heraclius adopted the imperial title of Basileus and King of Kings following his victory over Persia.
text: Heraclius styles himself as Basileus, Greek word for "sovereign", and takes the ancient title of "King of Kings", after his victory over Persia.

summary: The Ghassanids repelled a Muslim invasion east of the Jordan River at the Battle of Mu'tah.
text: September – Battle of Mu'tah: The Muslims fail to take the lands east of the Jordan River, and are pushed back near Mu'tah by the Ghassanids.

summary: Shahrbaraz usurped the Sasanian throne from Ardashir III before being deposed forty days later in favour of Borandukht.
text: Shahrbaraz usurps the throne of the Sasanian Empire from Ardashir III, but is himself deposed forty days later by nobility in favour of Borandukht. Khosrow III briefly rules Khorasan in the confusion, until he is assassinated by the governor of the province.

summary: Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, companion of Muhammad, was killed at the Battle of Mu'tah.
text: Jafar ibn Abi Talib, companion of Muhammad and older brother of Ali ibn Abi Talib

summary: Emperor Heraclius returned the True Cross to Jerusalem and attempted to promote Monothelitism.
text: Emperor Heraclius returns the True Cross, one of the holiest Christian relics, to Jerusalem. He tries to promote Monothelitism, which is rejected by the Christians.

summary: Heraclius decreed forced baptism for all Jews, precipitating massacres in Galilee and around Jerusalem.
text: Heraclius issues a decree that all Jews must become Christian; a massacre follows around Jerusalem and in Galilee (Israel), some survivors fleeing to the Daraa area.

summary: Chorpan Tarkhan led Khazar forces into Roman Armenia and defeated a Persian cavalry army.
text: Chorpan Tarkhan, general of the Khazars, invades and devastates Roman Armenia. He defeats a Persian cavalry force (10,000 men) sent by Shahrbaraz to repel the invasion.

summary: Ardashir III was murdered and succeeded as king of the Sasanian Empire by Shahrbaraz.
text: King Ardashir III, age 9, is murdered after an 18 month reign. He is succeeded by Shahrbaraz who becomes ruler (shah) of the Sasanian Empire.

summary: Shahrbaraz was killed and Borandukht ascended the Sasanian throne as queen of Persia.
text: Shahrbaraz is killed and succeeded by Borandukht, daughter of former king Khosrow II. She ascends the throne as 26th monarch of Persia, before being deposed in favour of Shapur-i Shahrvaraz, whose brief reign is then followed by that of her sister Azarmidokht.

summary: Constans II, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: Constans II, Byzantine emperor (d. 668)

summary: Fausta, future Byzantine empress and wife of Constans II, was born.
text: Fausta, Byzantine empress

summary: King Ardashir III of the Sasanian Empire died.
text: Ardashir III, king of the Persian Empire

summary: Shahrbaraz, king of the Sasanian Empire, died.
text: Shahrbaraz, king of the Persian Empire

summary: Emperor Heraclius appointed Cyrus of Alexandria as viceroy and patriarch in Egypt, beginning a persecution of non-Chalcedonian Copts.
text: Emperor Heraclius appoints Cyrus, patriarch of Alexandria, with power to act as viceroy (dioikesis) of Egypt. He begins a 10-year persecution against the non-Chalcedonian Coptic Christians.

summary: Azarmidokht succeeded her sister Boran as monarch of the Sasanian Empire.
text: Azarmidokht (daughter of king Khosrau II) succeeds her sister Borandukht, as monarch of the Persian Empire.

summary: Khosrau IV succeeded Azarmidokht as ruler of the Sasanian Empire.
text: Azarmidokht is succeeded after a few months reign by Khosrau IV, who becomes new ruler (shah) of Persia.

summary: Hormizd VI proclaimed himself king of the Sasanian Empire in Nisibis.
text: Hormizd VI proclaims himself king in Nisibis (Turkey). He seizes the throne and will reign until 632.

object: Monastery of Saint Macarius the Great
summary: Benjamin I, Coptic patriarch of Alexandria, fled persecution and hid in the Monastery of St. Macarius in Upper Egypt.
text: Benjamin I, Coptic patriarch of Alexandria, escapes during the persecutions of his fellow Christians and hides in the monastery of St. Macarius (Upper Egypt).

place.title: Monastery of Saint Macarius the Great

names: Monastery of Saint Macarius the Great
Pope of the Coptic Orthodox Church

summary: Athanasius I Gammolo, Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch, died.
text: Athanasius I Gammolo, Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch.

summary: Boran, queen of the Sasanian Empire, died.
text: Borandukht, queen of the Persian Empire

summary: Caliph Abu Bakr dispatched an expedition under Usama ibn Zayd against Balqa in the Byzantine Empire.
text: June – The first caliph, Abu Bakr, sends an expedition to Balqa, Byzantine Empire, led by Usama ibn Zayd. This expedition is sent based on Muhammad's decision before his death.

summary: Kubrat overthrew Avar rule and founded Old Great Bulgaria across regions from Dacia to Poltava.
text: Kubrat, ruler of the Dulo clan, takes power from the Pannonian Avars and establishes Old Great Bulgaria in the area of Black Cumania. Kubrat's rule stretches from Dacia to Poltava.

summary: Eight-year-old Yazdegerd III ascended the throne as the last ruler of the Sasanian dynasty.
text: Yazdegerd III, age 8, ascends to the throne as king (shah) of the Persian Empire. He becomes the last ruler of the Sassanid Dynasty (modern Iran).

summary: Muhammad, the founder and prophet of Islam, died in Medina.
text: Muhammad, Islamic Prophet (b. 570)

summary: Abu Bakr unified the Arabian Peninsula under the central authority of the Rashidun Caliphate.
text: The Arabian Peninsula is united under the central authority of Abu Bakr. This sets the stage for the Islamic conquest of Persia and the fall of the Sassanid dynasty.

summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid invaded Mesopotamia and won decisive victories at the Battle of Chains and the Battle of the River.
text: April – Battle of Chains (Kuwait) and Battle of River (Iraq): A Muslim army (18,000 men) under Khalid ibn al-Walid invades Mesopotamia, and wins decisive victories.

summary: Rashidun forces under Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated a vastly larger Sasanian army and allied Christian Arabs at the Battle of Walaja.
text: May – Battle of Walaja: The Rashidun Caliphate army under Khalid defeats the Persians and their Arab Christian allies. The Persian army is at least three times the size.

summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated a large Persian army at the Battle of Ullais near the Euphrates.
text: Battle of Ullais: Forces of the Rashidun Caliphate under Khalid defeat an entire Persian army (70,000 men) near the river Euphrates. Khalid besieges the city of Hira.

summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid besieged and captured the fortress city of Al-Hira following brief fighting.
text: Siege of Hira: The Muslim Arabs (15,000 men) under Khalid attack the fortress city of Hira. After a brief fight the citizens surrender, and bring gifts to Khalid.

summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid besieged Anbar until its Persian governor surrendered and withdrew.
text: July – Siege of Anbar: A Muslim Arab army under Khalid besieges the fortress city of Anbar. The Persian governor surrenders and is allowed to retire.

summary: Muslim forces assaulted and captured the Persian frontier post at Ayn al-Tamr south of Anbar.
text: Battle of Ein ut Tamr: The Muslim army attacks a Persian frontier post located south of Anbar. The Arab Christian auxiliaries are overrun and surrender.

summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid coordinated successful night attacks against Christian Arab forces at Muzayyah, Saniyy, and Zumail.
text: November – Battle of Muzayyah, Battle of Saniyy, and Battle of Zumail: Khalid coordinates successful night attacks against the Arab Christians.

summary: Emperor Heraclius sent his brother Theodore to assemble forces against the Muslim conquest of the Levant.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Emperor Heraclius, ill, infirm, and unpopular with the Eastern Orthodox Church, is unable to personally lead the Byzantine army to resist the Muslim conquest of the Levant. He sends his brother Theodore to assemble forces to retake the newly won Muslim territories. Monophysites and Jews throughout Syria welcome the Arab invaders, as they are discontented with Byzantine rule.

summary: Forces of the Rashidun Caliphate defeated a Byzantine army under Theodore at the Battle of Ajnadayn.
text: Battle of Ajnadayn: Byzantine forces (90,000 men according to Muslim sources) under Theodore are defeated by the Rashidun Caliphate near Beit Shemesh (modern-day Israel). Heraclius, who is in Emesa, flees to Antioch upon hearing news of the battle's outcome.

summary: Rashidun forces under Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated a combined Byzantine, Sasanian, and Christian Arab army at the Battle of Firaz.
text: Battle of Firaz: The Rashidun Arabs (15,000 men) under Khalid ibn al-Walid defeat the combined forces of the Byzantine Empire, Persian Empire and Arab Christians (at least 10 times larger than Khalid's army) in Mesopotamia (Iraq).

summary: Rashidun forces under Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan defeated Christian Arabs at the Battle of Dathin near Gaza.
text: Battle of Dathin: Rashidun forces under Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan defeat the Christian Arabs around Gaza. The Muslim victory is celebrated by the local Jews, who have been a persecuted minority within the Byzantine Empire.

summary: The Rashidun Caliphate invaded Byzantine Syria under Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah and Khalid ibn al-Walid.
text: The Rashidun Caliphate starts the Islamic conquest of the Byzantine Empire, when Muslim forces under Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah invade the Levant. Khalid sets out for Syria from Al-Hirah, taking with him half his army, about 8,000 strong.

summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated the Ghassanids and captured Al-Qaryatayn.
text: Battle of al-Qaryatayn: The Muslim Arabs under Khalid defeat the Ghassanids at Al-Qaryatayn, after the inhabitants resist his proposals. His army conquers and plunders the city, before proceeding to capture other towns in the area.

summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated Byzantine forces and their Ghassanid allies at the Battle of Marj Rahit.
text: Battle of Marj Rahit: A Muslim Arab army under Khalid defeats the Byzantine forces (15,000 men) and their Ghassanid allies. After the battle he sends a mounted column to the outskirts of Damascus, to plunder the region.

summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid besieged and captured the Byzantine garrison at Bosra.
text: Battle of Bosra: Muslim forces under Khalid besiege the Byzantine and Christian Arab garrison (12,000 men) at Bosra. After a few days the fortress city surrenders; Khalid imposes a payment of tribute on the inhabitants.

summary: Abu Bakr died at Medina and was succeeded by Umar as the second caliph of the Rashidun Caliphate.
text: Abu Bakr dies at Medina and is succeeded by Umar I, who becomes the second caliph (khalifah) of the Rashidun Caliphate. During his rule, Umar conquers Syria, Persia, and Egypt in a "Holy War".

summary: Muslim Arab forces under Khalid ibn al-Walid conquered Damascus from the Byzantine Empire.
text: Siege of Damascus: Muslim Arabs under Khalid conquer Damascus as the first major city of the Byzantine Empire. Damascan refugees are given a guarantee of safety to retreat to Antioch.

summary: A Muslim army routed and slaughtered a Byzantine convoy of refugees from Damascus near Antioch.
text: Battle of Maraj-al-Debaj: A Byzantine convoy of Damascan refugees (10,000 men) is slaughtered by a Muslim army near Antioch. The Mobile Guard (elite light cavalry) captures a great amount of brocade.

summary: Sophronius became patriarch of Jerusalem and sent synodical letters rejecting Monothelitism.
text: Sophronius becomes patriarch of Jerusalem. He sends synodical letters to Pope Honorius I and the Eastern patriarchs, explaining the Orthodox belief, by renouncing Monothelitism.

summary: Abu Bakr, the first Rashidun caliph, died at Medina.
text: Abu Bakr, Muslim Caliph

summary: Emperor Heraclius concluded an alliance with Khan Kubrat of Great Bulgaria against the Avars.
text: Emperor Heraclius makes an alliance with Kubrat, ruler (khagan) of Great Bulgaria, to break the power of the Avars on the Balkan Peninsula.

summary: Rashidun forces under Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated Byzantine troops at the Battle of Fahl.
text: January – Battle of Fahl: The Rashidun army, (30,000 men) under Khalid ibn al-Walid (known as the "Drawn Sword of God"), defeats the Byzantine forces led by Theodore Trithyrius, at Pella in the Jordan Valley (Jordan).

summary: Muslim Arab forces under Amr ibn al-As conquered Gaza from the Byzantines.
text: Gaza is conquered by the Muslim Arabs under 'Amr ibn al-'As. It becomes the first city in Palestine developed into a centre of Islamic law.

summary: Emperor Heraclius assembled an allied army and established a fortified base near Gadara.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Emperor Heraclius assembles a large army consisting of contingents of Byzantines, Slavs, Franks, Georgians, Armenians, and Christian Arabs. He establishes a base at Yaqusah (near Gadara), close to the edge of the Golan Heights, protecting the vital main road from Egypt to Damascus. The base is protected by deep valleys and precipitous cliffs, well supplied with water and grazing.

summary: Emperor Heraclius held a church assembly at Antioch before departing Syria for Constantinople.
text: Summer – Heraclius summons a church assembly at Antioch, and scrutinises the situation. He accepts the argument that Byzantine disobedience to God is to blame for the Christian disaster in Syria. Heraclius leaves for Constantinople with the words, Peace be with you Syria — what a beautiful land you will be for your enemy.

summary: Muslim forces led by Khalid ibn al-Walid decisively defeated the Byzantine army at the Battle of Yarmouk.
text: 20 – Battle of Yarmouk: In engagements along the Yarmouk River, Muslim forces (25,000 men) of the Rashidun Caliphate, led by Khalid ibn al-Walid, decisively defeat the armies of the Byzantine Empire, effectively completing the Muslim conquest of Syria. It will be regarded as one of the most decisive battles in military history, marking the first great wave of Muslim conquests, after the death of Muhammad.

summary: Byzantine poet George of Pisidia died.
text: George Pisida, Byzantine poet

summary: Byzantine general Theodore Trithyrius died at the Battle of Yarmouk.
text: Theodore Trithyrius, Byzantine general (sacellarius)

summary: Caliph Umar accepted the surrender of Jerusalem from Byzantine forces following a siege.
text: April – Siege of Jerusalem: The Rashidun army (20,000 men), led by 'Amr ibn al-'As, conquers Jerusalem after a six-month siege. The Byzantine garrison surrenders to Caliph Umar I, who is invited by Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, to pray in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Umar declines, fearing that accepting the invitation might endanger the church's status, and turn the Christian holy site into a mosque.

summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated the Byzantine army at the Battle of Hazir near Qinnasrin.
text: Battle of Hazir: Muslim Arab forces (17,000 men) under Khalid ibn al-Walid defeat the Byzantine army near Qinnasrin (Northern Syria). The cities of Beirut and Tyre are captured by Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan after a short siege.

summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid conquered the Byzantine stronghold of Aleppo after a four-month siege.
text: October – Siege of Aleppo: Muslim Arabs under Khalid ibn al-Walid conquer the Byzantine stronghold Aleppo; the large walled city surrenders after a four-month siege. A column of troops under Malik al-Ashtar is sent to take Azaz.

summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated the Byzantine army at the Battle of the Iron Bridge near Antioch, completing the conquest of Syria.
text: Battle of the Iron Bridge: Rashidun forces under Khalid ibn al-Walid defeat the Byzantine army and Christian Arabs near Antioch, at the Orontes River. It marks the complete annexation of Syria into the Rashidun Caliphate.

summary: Bishop and theological writer Andreas of Caesarea died.
text: Andreas of Caesarea, bishop and writer (b. 563)

summary: John Athalarichos, illegitimate son of Emperor Heraclius, died.
text: John Athalarichos, illegitimate son of Heraclius

summary: Byzantine general Menas was killed at the Battle of Hazir.
text: Menas, Byzantine general

summary: Emperor Heraclius created a buffer zone in Anatolia and instituted a system of shadowing guerrilla warfare against Arab invaders.
text: Emperor Heraclius creates a buffer zone (or no man's land) in the heartland of Asia Minor. In the mountainous terrain of Anatolia, the Byzantine forces develop a system of defensive guerrilla warfare. The strategy is known as ‘shadowing warfare’, as it avoids battle with major Muslim invaders, and instead attacks raiding parties on their return when they are laden with booty, captured livestock or prisoners.

summary: Heraclonas obtained the imperial title of Augustus through the influence of his mother Martina.
text: Heraklonas, age 12, son of Heraclius, obtains (through the influence of his mother Martina) the title of Augustus. This brings him in rivalry with his elder half-brother Constantine.

summary: Heraclius issued the Ecthesis, establishing the Monothelite doctrine as official church policy.
text: Heraclius issues his Ekthesis, espousing the Monothelete doctrine (that there is only one will in Christ), and setting it forth as the official doctrine of the Eastern Orthodox Church. The Ekthesis is vigorously opposed, notably by Maximus the Confessor.

summary: Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah captured Caesarea Maritima and Ascalon, and was appointed governor of Syria.
text: Autumn – The Arabian forces under Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah storm Caesarea Maritima, capital of Byzantine Palestine, and effect their final capture of Ascalon (modern Israel). Caliph Umar I stops the Muslim invasion, and appoints Abu Ubaidah governor of Syria.

summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid advanced into Byzantine Anatolia and Armenia, capturing multiple cities.
text: Arab-Byzantine War: The invading Rashidun army under Khalid ibn al-Walid moves into Anatolia, conquering (without strong Byzantine resistance) the cities of Kahramanmaraş, Caesarea Cappadociae, Sebastia, and Malatya (west of the Taurus Mountains). Arab forces march into Armenia, where they capture the cities Edessa and Amida up to the Ararat plain.

summary: Caliph Umar dismissed Khalid ibn al-Walid from command after the conquest of Syria.
text: Umar I dismisses Khalid ibn al-Walid after the conquest of Syria, owing to his ever-growing fame and influence. He wants the Muslims to know that victory comes from God, not his general.

summary: Pope Honorius I died at Rome after a thirteen-year reign and was succeeded by Severinus.
text: Pope Honorius I dies at Rome after a 13-year reign, and is succeeded by Severinus, but the Byzantine emperor Heraclius will delay the new pope's consecration until May 640.

summary: Pyrrhus I became Patriarch of Constantinople following the death of Sergius I.
text: Pyrrhus I becomes patriarch of Constantinople, after the death of Sergius I. He has been an advocate of Monothelitism and a close friend of Heraclius.

summary: Patriarch Sophronius of Jerusalem died.
text: Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem

summary: Patriarch Sergius I of Constantinople died.
text: Sergius I, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Amr ibn al-As led a Rashidun army into Byzantine Egypt and captured the border city of Pelusium.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: The Rashidun army (4,000 men), under the command of 'Amr ibn al-'As, invades Byzantine Egypt. They capture the strategic town of Pelusium (Nile Delta) after a two-month siege. Arab reinforcements led by Zubayr ibn al-Awwam are sent from Medina to assist Amr's army. The losses incurred by the Muslims are ameliorated by Sinai Bedouins, tribes of Rashida and Lakhm; they join the invaders in conquering Egypt.

summary: Exarch Isaac of Ravenna founded the Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta on the island of Torcello.
text: The First Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta is founded by the exarch Isaac of Ravenna on Torcello, confirming the island's importance as a centre of population in Venice at this date.

summary: Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, supreme commander of the Rashidun army in Syria, died during the Plague of Emmaus.
text: Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah, commander of the Rashidun Caliphate (b. 583)

summary: Shurahbil ibn Hasana, general of the Rashidun Caliphate, died during the Plague of Emmaus.
text: Shurahbil ibn Hasana, Rashidun Caliphate general

summary: Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan, general and governor of Damascus for the Rashidun Caliphate, died during the Plague of Emmaus.
text: Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan, general of the Rashidun Caliphate

summary: Byzantine emperor Heraclius sent Christian missionaries to Dalmatian Croatia at the request of Duke Porga.
text: At the request of Porga of Croatia, one of the first dukes or princes (Croatian: knez) of Dalmatian Croatia, the Byzantine emperor Heraclius sends Christian missionaries to the Croatian Provinces .

summary: The Rashidun army laid siege to the Byzantine stronghold of Babylon Fortress in the Nile Delta.
text: May – Siege of Babylon Fortress: The Rashidun army lays siege to Babylon Fortress in the Nile Delta (near Cairo). The next two months' fighting remain inconclusive, the Byzantines having the upper hand by repulsing every Muslim assault.

summary: Amr ibn al-As led the Muslim Arab army to defeat Byzantine forces at the Battle of Heliopolis in Egypt.
text: Battle of Heliopolis: The Muslim Arab army (15,000 men) under Amr ibn al-As defeats the Byzantine forces near Heliopolis (Egypt). Amr divides his troops into three parts, surrounding the Byzantines.

summary: The Rashidun Caliphate captured Babylon Fortress and annexed the Thebaid region of Upper Egypt from the Byzantines.
text: Muslim Arabs capture Babylon after a seven-month siege; during a night assault Arab warriors open the city gates. The Thebaid region (Upper Egypt) is annexed by the Rashidun Caliphate.

summary: The Serapeum of Alexandria was purportedly burned down on the orders of Amr ibn al-As.
text: On orders of the Saracen leader, Amar, the Serapeum of Alexandria, containing works that had survived the destruction of the Library of Alexandria, is burned down, along with its collection of 500,000 manuscripts. This story may be apocryphal.

summary: Pope John IV succeeded Pope Severinus as pope following confirmation by the Exarchate of Ravenna.
text: Pope John IV succeeds Severinus as the 72nd pope. His election is accepted by the Exarchate of Ravenna.

summary: Aretion, Byzantine governor of Jerusalem, died.
text: Aretion, Byzantine governor of Jerusalem

summary: John, Byzantine duke of Barca, died.
text: John, Byzantine duke of Barca

summary: A Rashidun force laid siege to Pelusium during the conquest of Byzantine Egypt.
text: Muslim conquest of Egypt: A Rashidun force laid siege to Pelusium.

summary: The legions of the East Roman army were reorganized into themes.
text: The legions of the East Roman army were reorganized into themes.

summary: Emperor Heraclius died in Constantinople and was succeeded jointly by his sons Constantine III and Heraklonas.
text: Emperor Heraclius, age 65, dies of dropsy at Constantinople after a 31-year reign. He reorganized the imperial administration, but lost Armenia, parts of Egypt, Palestine, Syria and Byzantine Mesopotamia to the Muslim Arabs. Heraclius is succeeded by his sons Constantine III and Heraklonas.

summary: Rashidun forces laid siege to Byzantine Alexandria during the Muslim conquest of Egypt.
text: The Muslim conquest of Egypt continues, with the siege of Alexandria.

summary: Constantine III died after a four-month reign, leaving Heraklonas as sole Byzantine emperor.
text: May – Constantine III, age 29, dies of tuberculosis after a four-month reign, leaving his half-brother Heraklonas sole emperor. Rumors spread that Constantine has been poisoned by Heraclius's second wife (and niece) Martina.

summary: The Byzantine Senate deposed and mutilated Heraklonas and Martina, elevating Constans II to the throne.
text: September – The Byzantine Senate turns against Martina and her son Heraklonas, who are both mutilated, and exiled to Rhodes. Supported by general Valentinus, Constantine's son Constans II, age 10, succeeds to the throne.

summary: Constans II established a new civil-military defensive organisation to protect the Byzantine frontier along the Taurus Mountains.
text: Constans II establishes a new civil-military defensive organisation, based upon geographical military districts. Byzantine forces maintain the frontier, along the line of the Taurus Mountains (Southern Turkey).

summary: The Lombards under King Rothari conquered Genoa and remaining Byzantine territories in the lower Po Valley.
text: The Lombards under King Rothari conquer Genoa (Liguria), and all remaining Byzantine territories in the lower Po Valley, including Oderzo (Opitergium).

summary: Amr ibn al-As captured Alexandria following a six-month siege when Byzantine officials capitulated.
text: Siege of Alexandria: Muslim Arabs under 'Amr ibn al-'As capture Alexandria after a six-month siege. Byzantine officials formally capitulate to Amr, turning the city over to Arab hands.

summary: Asparukh, founder and future khan of the First Bulgarian Empire, was born.
text: Asparukh, ruler (khan) of the First Bulgarian Empire (d. 701)

summary: Byzantine Emperor Heraclius died in Constantinople.
text: Heraclius, Byzantine emperor

summary: Byzantine Emperor Constantine III died in Constantinople.
text: Emperor Constantine III of the Byzantine Empire

summary: Byzantine Emperor Constans II married Fausta.
text: Emperor Constans II marries Fausta.

summary: Cyrus of Alexandria, Byzantine Patriarch of Alexandria and governor of Egypt, died.
text: Cyrus of Alexandria, Patriarch of Alexandria and governor of Egypt

summary: Deposed Byzantine Emperor Heraclonas died in Rhodes.
text: Heraklonas, Byzantine emperor

summary: Emperor Constans II recognised Theodore Rshtuni as ruler of Armenia and commander of the Armenian army.
text: Emperor Constans II recognises Theodore Rshtuni as ruler of Armenia, after his successful campaign against the Muslims. He names him commander (nakharar) of the Armenian army.

summary: Maurikios proclaimed himself dux of Rome and revolted against Exarch Isaac, declaring Rome's independence.
text: Maurikios names himself dux of Rome, and revolts against exarch Isaac (Exarchate of Ravenna). He declares Rome's independence from the Exarchate and from the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Arab forces captured Tripoli from the Byzantine Empire after a one-month siege.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Arab armies continue their military expansion into North Africa and lay siege to Tripoli. The city is captured after one month.

summary: Amr ibn al-As sent a detachment to Sabratha, which surrendered and agreed to pay jizya.
text: 'Amr ibn al-'As sends a detachment to Sabratha (modern Libya). The city puts up feeble resistance, but soon surrenders and agrees to pay Jizya.

summary: Byzantine rebel leader Maurikios Chartoularios was executed.
text: Maurikios Chartoularios, Byzantine rebel leader

summary: General Valentinus attempted to usurp the Byzantine throne from Constans II but was lynched by the populace of Constantinople.
text: Valentinus, Byzantine general, attempts to usurp the throne of his son-in-law Constans II. He appears at the gates of Constantinople with a contingent of Byzantine troops, and demands to be crowned emperor. His claim is rejected, and Valentinus is lynched by the populace.

summary: Byzantine general and usurper Valentinus died in Constantinople.
text: Valentinus, Byzantine general and usurper

summary: Byzantine forces briefly recaptured Alexandria following a local revolt against Arab rule.
text: Alexandria revolts against Arab rule, at the appearance of a Byzantine fleet of 300 ships, and Byzantine forces recapture the city. Abdullah ibn Sa'ad, Arab governor of Egypt, mounts an assault and retakes it. He begins building a Muslim fleet.

summary: Lombard king Rothari defeated Plato, the Byzantine exarch of Ravenna, on the banks of the Panaro River.
text: Plato, exarch (imperial governor) of Ravenna, invades the southern Po Valley. The Lombards under King Rothari defeat him on the banks of the Panaro River (near Modena); 8,000 imperial troops are killed.

summary: Muslim Arab forces retook Alexandria from the Byzantines, bringing an end to almost a millennium of Greco-Roman rule in the city.
text: Arab-Byzantine War: Alexandria is recaptured by the Muslim Arabs, after a Byzantine attempt (see 645) to retake Egypt fails, ending nearly 1,000 years of rule by Greco-Roman states in the city.

summary: Gregory the Patrician, exarch of Africa, revolted against Constans II and declared himself emperor.
text: Gregory the Patrician, Byzantine exarch of Africa, begins a rebellion against Constans II, and proclaims himself emperor; the revolt finds broad support among the populace.

summary: Rashidun forces under Amr ibn al-As defeated Byzantine troops at the Battle of Nikiou.
text: Battle of Nikiou: The Rashidun army (15,000 men) under Amr ibn al-'As defeats a smaller Byzantine force, near the fortified town of Nikiou (Egypt).

summary: Byzantine general Manuel was killed during the Arab reconquest of Egypt.
text: Manuel, Armenian eunuch and general

summary: An Arab army under Abd Allah ibn Sa'd invaded the Byzantine Exarchate of Africa, conquering Tripolitania and Sufetula.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: An Arab army (20,000 men) under Abdullah ibn Sa'ad invades the Byzantine Exarchate of Africa. It conquers Tripolitania and the city of Sufetula, 150 miles (240 km) south of Carthage.

summary: Usurper Gregory the Patrician was defeated and killed by an invading Arab army at Sufetula.
text: Self-proclaimed emperor Gregory the Patrician is killed during the Arab invasion at Sufetula. Africa returns to imperial allegiance after his death, but the foundation of Byzantine rule is fatally undermined.

summary: Gregory the Patrician, rebel Exarch of Africa, was killed at Sufetula.
text: Gregory the Patrician, Exarch of Africa

summary: Emperor Constans II issued an imperial edict forbidding discussion of Monothelitism.
text: Emperor Constans II issues an imperial edict forbidding Monothelitism to be discussed, to quiet the intense controversy caused by the Monothelete doctrine. This edict, distributed by patriarch Paul II in Constans' name, is known as the Typos.

summary: Pope Theodore I excommunicated Patriarch Paul II of Constantinople over the Monothelite controversy.
text: Pope Theodore I excommunicates Paul II of Constantinople.

summary: Arab naval forces under Abd Allah ibn Sa'd conquered Cyprus and sacked Constantia.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Arab naval forces under Abdullah ibn Saad conquer Cyprus, sacking the capital Constantia after a short siege, and looting the rest of the island. The Cypriots agree to pay the same revenue as they have done to Emperor Constans II.

summary: Emperor Constans II ordered Exarch Olympius to arrest Pope Martin I over the condemnation of Monothelitism.
text: Constans II orders Olympius, exarch of the Exarchate of Ravenna, to arrest Pope Martin I on the ostensible grounds that the pope's election has not been submitted to the emperor for approval, but in fact because of the Lateran Council of 649's condemnation of Monothelitism and the Type of Constans. Olympius attempts to gain the support of the citizens of Rome and the bishops, with little success, and perhaps considers the assassination of the Pope.

summary: Mu'awiya I developed an Arab navy in the Levant to confront the Byzantine Empire in the Aegean Sea.
text: Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, governor of Syria, develops an Arab navy in the Levant and uses it to confront the Byzantine Empire in the Aegean Sea. It is manned by Monophysitise Christian, Coptic and Syrian Christian sailors.

summary: The Lateran Council of 649 opened at Rome, condemning Monothelitism and the Type of Constans.
text: The Lateran Council of 649, summoned by Theodore and carried forward by Martin, opens. It strongly condemns Monothelitism and the Type of Constans.

summary: Anastasia, future Byzantine empress and wife of Constantine IV, was born.
text: Anastasia, Byzantine empress

summary: An Arab fleet under Abd Allah ibn Sa'd defeated the Byzantine fleet off Alexandria.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: An Arab fleet under Abdullah ibn Sa'ad defeats the Byzantine fleet (500 ships) off the coast of Alexandria.

summary: Byzantine emperor Constantine IV was born.
text: Constantine IV, Byzantine emperor (d. 685)

summary: Olympius, exarch of Ravenna, died in Sicily.
text: Olympius, exarch of Ravenna

summary: Emperor Constans II surrendered Armenia to the Arabs under Mu'awiya I, who appointed Theodore Rshtuni as ruler.
text: Emperor Constans II voluntarily surrenders Armenia to the Arabs, following a truce with Muawiyah, governor of Syria. Muawiyah grants the Armenians virtual autonomy, and appoints the nakharar Theodor Rshtuni as ruler of Armenia.

summary: Mu'awiya raided Rhodes, carrying off the remains of the Colossus of Rhodes to Syria.
text: Muawiyah leads a raid against Rhodes, taking the scattered pieces of the Colossus of Rhodes (one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World) and shipping it back to Syria, where he destroys the bronze scrap to make coins.
names: Seven Wonders of the Ancient World

summary: Pope Martin I and Maximus the Confessor were arrested at the Lateran in Rome by order of Emperor Constans II and taken to Constantinople.
text: Pope Martin I is arrested in the Lateran in Rome, along with Maximus the Confessor, on the orders of Emperor Constans II, and taken to imprisonment in Constantinople.

summary: Plato, former exarch of Ravenna, died.
text: Plato, exarch of Ravenna

summary: Emperor Constans II appointed his infant son Constantine IV as co-emperor of the Byzantine Empire.
text: Emperor Constans II appoints his son Constantine IV, age 2, co-emperor (Augustus). He is too young to rule as monarch of the Byzantine Empire, and his title remains a given name.

summary: Muawiyah garrisoned Cyprus and conquered the Byzantine island of Kos.
text: Muawiyah, governor of Syria, stations a large garrison on Cyprus. He conquers the Greek island of Kos in the Dodecanese.

summary: Pope Eugene I succeeded the deposed Pope Martin I, who was taken to Constantinople and publicly humiliated by Emperor Constans II.
text: The exiled Pope Martin I is deposed, and succeeded by Eugene I, as the 75th pope of the Roman Catholic Church. On September 17, Martin is taken to Constantinople and publicly humiliated, for having condemned the Byzantine Emperor Constans II in 649.

summary: Pyrrhus, Patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Pyrrhus, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Abd Allah ibn Sa'd led the Arab fleet to victory against Emperor Constans II and the Byzantine navy at the Battle of the Masts.
text: Battle of the Masts: Emperor Constans II personally commands the Byzantine fleet (500 ships), and sets off to challenge the Arab navy. He sails to the province of Lycia (now in Turkey) in the southern region of Asia Minor. The two forces meet off the coast of Mount Phoenix, near the harbour of Phoenix (modern Finike). The Arabs under Abdullah ibn Sa'ad are victorious in battle, although losses are heavy for both sides. Constans barely escapes to Constantinople.

summary: The banished Pope Martin I died in exile in Chersonesus on the Crimean Peninsula.
text: Pope Martin I is banished to Chersonesos Taurica (Ukraine). He dies later in the Crimean Peninsula after a 6-year reign, leaving Eugene I as the uncontested pope (see 654).

summary: Emperor Constans II defeated the Avars in Macedonia and resettled some of them in Anatolia.
text: Emperor Constans II undertakes an expedition to the Balkan Peninsula, and defeats the Avars in Macedonia. He temporarily reasserts Byzantine rule, and resettles some of them in Anatolia to fight against the Rashidun Caliphate .

summary: Emperor Constans II concluded a peace treaty with the Rashidun Caliphate, consolidated control over Armenia, and established the themata system in Anatolia.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Emperor Constans II signs a peace treaty with the Rashidun Caliphate. He uses the pause to strengthen his defences, and consolidates Byzantine control over Armenia. Constans establishes the themata, dividing territorial command in Anatolia.

summary: Emperor Constans II raised his son Heraclius to the rank of co-emperor alongside his brother Tiberius.
text: Constans II elevates his son Heraclius to the rank of co-emperor (Augustus), alongside his brother Tiberius.

summary: Emperor Constans II murdered his brother Theodosius and relocated his imperial court from Constantinople to Syracuse.
text: Emperor Constans II is paranoid about the ambitions of his younger brother, Theodosius, and has him murdered. Having attracted the hatred of the citizens of Constantinople, Constans decides to leave the Byzantine capital and moves to Syracuse (Sicily).

summary: Imperial authorities tried Maximus the Confessor in Constantinople and severed his tongue and right hand.
text: Maximus the Confessor, Christian monk, is recalled from exile in Thrace. He is tried, and sentenced to mutilation. His tongue and his right hand are cut off to prevent his further opposition to the Monothelites.

summary: Byzantine theologian Maximus the Confessor died in exile in Lazica.
text: Maximus the Confessor, Byzantine monk and theologian, dies in exile in Lazica (modern Georgia), on the southeastern shore of the Black Sea.

summary: Byzantine theologian Maximus the Confessor died.
text: Maximus the Confessor, Byzantine theologian

summary: Emperor Constans II landed at Taranto and besieged Lucera and Benevento in an offensive against the Duchy of Benevento.
text: Emperor Constans II launches an assault against the Duchy of Benevento (Southern Italy). Taking advantage of the fact that Lombard king Grimoald I is engaged against Frankish forces from Neustria, Constans disembarks at Taranto, and besieges Lucera and Benevento.

summary: Constans II visited Rome for twelve days, meeting Pope Vitalian and ordering the stripping of ornaments from the Pantheon and other buildings.
text: Constans II visits Rome for 12 days (the only emperor to set foot in Rome for two centuries), and is received with great honor by Pope Vitalian. Constans gives the order to strip buildings, including the Pantheon, of their ornaments, which will be carried back to Constantinople.

summary: Constans II moved the imperial court to Syracuse and stripped sacred vessels from Roman churches.
text: Constans II moves the imperial court from Constantinople to Syracuse. He tries to stop the Arab conquest of Sicily, and restores Rome as seat of the Byzantine Empire. Constans strips sacred altar vessels from churches all over Rome.

summary: Romuald I defeated the Byzantine army under Constans II at the Battle of Forino and captured Taranto and Brindisi.
text: Battle of Forino: The Byzantine army, led by Constans II, is defeated by the Lombards under Romuald I. He seizes Taranto and Brindisi, receiving military aid from the Bulgar Alcek horde, who are settled in the area of Ravenna.

summary: An Arab army advanced through the desert and captured the Byzantine city of Barca in Libya.
text: Muslim Conquest: An Arab army (40,000 men) advances through the desert, and captures the Byzantine city of Barca (Libya).

summary: Emperor Constans II granted Bishop Maurus of Ravenna the right to consecrate bishops without papal approval from Rome.
text: Emperor Constans II grants the request of Bishop Maurus of Ravenna, allowing the city to consecrate its bishop without approval from Rome .

summary: Caliph Muawiyah I launched offensive operations against Byzantine territories in Africa, Sicily, and the East.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Caliph Muawiyah I launches a series of attacks against Byzantine holdings in Africa, Sicily and the East.

summary: Emperor Constans II was assassinated in his bath at Syracuse and was succeeded by his son Constantine IV alongside co-emperors Heraclius and Tiberius.
text: Emperor Constans II is killed under mysterious circumstances in his bath, during a mutiny at Syracuse. The Byzantine court returns to Constantinople after an absence of 5 years, in which the Muslim-Arabs have made annual invasions and devastations of Anatolia. Probably assassinated by his chamberlain after a 27-year reign, Constans is succeeded by his son Constantine IV (the "Bearded"), alongside his brothers Heraclius and Tiberius as co-emperors.

summary: General Mezezius was proclaimed Byzantine emperor by mutinous troops at Syracuse, prompting Constantine IV to prepare a retaliatory expedition.
text: Mezezius, Byzantine general and patrikios ("first patrician"), is proclaimed emperor by the army in Syracuse. Constantine IV organizes an expedition to suppress the military revolt in Sicily.

summary: Caliph Muawiyah I sent an army under his son Yazid against the Byzantine Empire following an invitation from the rebellious commander Saborios.
text: Caliph Muawiyah I receives an invitation from Saborios, Byzantine commander of the troops in Armenia, to help overthrow Constantine IV in Constantinople. He sends a Muslim army under his son Yazid, against the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Yazid reached Chalcedon and captured the strategic Byzantine city of Amorium.
text: Yazid reaches Chalcedon in Bithynia, and takes the important Byzantine center Amorium (modern Turkey).

summary: Future Byzantine Emperor Justinian II was born.
text: Justinian II, Eastern Roman Emperor (d. 711)

summary: Byzantine Emperor Constans II was assassinated in Syracuse.
text: Constans II, Byzantine emperor (b. 630)

summary: Rebel Byzantine general Saborios died after being thrown from his horse.
text: Saborios, Byzantine general

summary: Yazid retreated with his Arab forces to Cyzicus after threatening Constantinople and suffering famine and disease.
text: Spring – Arab forces that have taken Chalcedon, on the Asian shore of the Bosporus, threaten the Byzantine capital Constantinople. The Muslim-Arabs are decimated by famine and disease. Yazid, the Arab commander, retreats to the island of Cyzicus (modern Turkey).

summary: Future Byzantine Emperor Justinian II was born.
text: Justinian II, Byzantine emperor

summary: Byzantine usurper Mezezius was killed in Sicily.
text: Mezezius, Byzantine usurper

summary: The Arab fleet captured Rhodes, Kos, and Chios and seized Cyzicus on the Sea of Marmara to begin a naval blockade of Constantinople.
text: Arab-Byzantine War: The Arab fleet dominates the Aegean Sea and conquers the strategic islands, Rhodes, Cos and Chios. The shore on the southern part of Sea of Marmara is taken, providing an excellent base at Cyzicus to begin the blockade of Constantinople by sea.

summary: Uqba ibn Nafi invaded the Byzantine Exarchate of Africa and established a military base and mosque at Kairouan.
text: Muslim Conquest: A 10,000-man Arab army under the command of general Uqba ibn Nafi invades the Byzantine Exarchate of Africa. He establishes a military base at Kairouan (Tunisia) for further invasions, and founds the Great Mosque, also known as the "Mosque of Uqba".

summary: An Arab fleet entered the Sea of Marmara and initiated a naval blockade of Constantinople.
text: Siege of Constantinople: The Arab fleet enters the Sea of Marmara and appears before the southern walls of Constantinople, in an attempt to blockade the Byzantine capital.

summary: A Muslim expeditionary force landed at Hebdomon and laid siege to the Theodosian Walls of Constantinople.
text: April – A Muslim expeditionary force disembarks on the Thracian shore (near Hebdomon), and lays siege to the massive Theodosian Walls, on the landward side to the west.

summary: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari was killed outside the walls during the Arab siege of Constantinople.
text: Summer – Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, companion and standard-bearer of Muhammad, is killed during the first attempt of the siege of the city .

summary: Arab forces under Yazid retired to Cyzicus for the winter while continuing their blockade of Constantinople.
text: Winter – Arab forces under Yazid (son of caliph Muawiyah I) retire to Cyzicus (Turkey). For the next 4 years the Arab fleet installs a loose blockade around Constantinople.

summary: Arab forces raided Byzantine Crete, killing and enslaving many Roman soldiers.
text: The Muslim-Arabs raid Crete, killing and enslaving many soldiers .

summary: Caliph Muawiyah I sent Yazid with Muslim reinforcements to Constantinople, while the Byzantines faced Slavic and Lombard attacks.
text: Summer – Siege of Constantinople: Caliph Muawiyah I sends his son Yazid with Muslim reinforcements to Constantinople. At the same time, the Byzantines have to face a Slavic attack on Thessaloniki and Lombard attacks in Italy.

summary: Slavic forces launched a major assault against the walls of Thessalonica but were repelled.
text: 25 – 27 July: Climax of the Siege of Thessalonica: Slavic forces launch a large-scale assault on the city walls, but are repelled.

summary: Constantine I, patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Constantine I, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: The Sclaveni withdrew and ended their siege of Thessalonica.
text: The Siege of Thessalonica (676–678) ends, when the Sclaveni withdraw.

summary: Emperor Constantine IV's fleet destroyed the Arab fleet at Sillyon using Greek fire, compelling Yazid to lift the siege of Constantinople.
text: Autumn – Siege of Constantinople: Emperor Constantine IV confronts the Arab besiegers in a head-on engagement. The Byzantine fleet, equipped with Greek fire, destroys the Muslim fleet at Sillyon, ending the Arab threat to Europe, and forcing Yazid (a son of caliph Muawiyah I) to lift the siege on land and sea. The victory also frees up forces that are sent to raise the two-year siege of Thessalonica by the local Slavic tribes.

summary: Agatho succeeded Donus as Pope following Donus's death in Rome and discontinued paying election tribute to the emperor.
text: Pope Donus dies at Rome, after a reign of 1 year and 160 days. He is succeeded by Agatho I, who becomes the 79th pope. He is the first pope to stop paying tribute to Emperor Constantine IV upon election.

summary: Emperor Constantine IV signed a thirty-year peace treaty with Caliph Mu'awiya I, agreeing to pay annual tribute in exchange for Arab withdrawal from Byzantine coastal bases.
text: Emperor Constantine IV signs a peace treaty, of a nominal 30-year duration, with Caliph Mu'awiya I of the Umayyad Caliphate. Constantine pays an annual tribute of 3,000 (nomismata) pounds of gold, 50 horses and 50 slaves. The Arab garrisons are withdrawn from their bases on the Byzantine coastlands, including Crete & Cyzicus.

summary: Emperor Constantine IV led land and sea forces against invading Bulgars under Asparuh and besieged their fortified camp in Dobruja.
text: Byzantine–Bulgarian War: The Bulgars under Asparukh subjugate the country of current-day Bulgaria, north of the Balkan Mountains. Emperor Constantine IV leads a combined land and sea operation against the invaders and besieges their fortified camp in Dobruja.

summary: The Bulgars and their Slavic allies defeated the Byzantine army under Constantine IV at the Battle of Ongal in the Danube Delta.
text: Battle of Ongal: The Byzantine army (25,000 men) under Constantine IV is defeated by the Bulgars and their Slavic allies in the Danube Delta. Bulgar cavalry force the Byzantines into a rout, while Constantine (suffering from leg pain) travels to Nesebar to seek treatment.

summary: King Perctarit made his son Cunipert co-ruler of the Lombard Kingdom and signed a peace treaty with Byzantine Emperor Constantine IV.
text: King Perctarit makes his son Cunipert co-ruler of the Lombard Kingdom. He signs a formal peace treaty with Constantine IV.

summary: The Third Council of Constantinople opened to settle the controversies of monoenergism and monothelitism.
text: The Third Council of Constantinople (Sixth Ecumenical Council) opens in Constantinople to settle the theological controversies of monoenergism and monothelitism, ending September 16, 681.

summary: Constantine IV acknowledged the Bulgar state in Moesia, agreed to pay tribute, and created the Theme of Thrace.
text: Byzantine–Bulgarian War: Emperor Constantine IV is forced to acknowledge the Bulgar state in Moesia, and to pay protection money to avoid further inroads into Byzantine Thrace. Consequently, Constantine creates the Theme of Thrace of the Byzantine Empire (located in the south-eastern Balkans).

summary: The Byzantine army of the Anatolic Theme revolted and marched to Chrysopolis, demanding Constantine IV keep his brothers as co-emperors.
text: Autumn – A military revolt breaks out in the Anatolic Theme (modern Turkey). The Byzantine army marches to Chrysopolis, and sends a delegation across the straits of the Hellespont to Constantinople, demanding that the two brothers should remain co-emperors alongside Constantine IV.

summary: Constantine IV mutilated his brothers Heraclius and Tiberius to disqualify them from rule and removed them from coins and records.
text: September/November – Constantine IV has his brothers Heraclius and Tiberius mutilated, so they will be unable to rule. He orders that their images no longer appear on any coinage, and that their names be removed from official documentation.

summary: Constantine IV lured the leaders of the Anatolic revolt to Constantinople and had them executed at Sycae.
text: Constantine IV agrees to a compromise, and persuades the army to return to their barracks in Anatolia. He invites the leaders of the rebellion to come to Constantinople and consult the Senate as to how to implement the terms. On their arrival, he arrests the leaders and has them hung at Sycae.

summary: Pope Agatho died of plague in Rome after a two-and-a-half-year pontificate.
text: Pope Agatho dies at Rome of plague after a 2½-year reign, in which he has persuaded Constantine IV to abolish the tax heretofore levied at the consecration of a newly elected pope.

summary: The Sixth Ecumenical Council concluded in Constantinople, reaffirming the Council of Chalcedon and condemning Monothelitism.
text: The Sixth Ecumenical Council (see 680) ends at Constantinople. The council reaffirms the Orthodox doctrines of the Council of Chalcedon in 451, and condemns monothelitism.

summary: Romano-Berbers under King Caecilius and their Byzantine allies defeated the Umayyad army at the Battle of Vescera, killing Uqba ibn Nafi.
text: At about this time, Muslim Umayyad Caliphate forces led by Uqba ibn Nafi overrun the south coast of the Mediterranean Sea. He occupies the cities of Tripoli and Carthage, the last Byzantine bases in Africa. In 682 or 683 the Umayyads are ambushed at the Battle of Vescera near Biskra (modern Algeria) by Romano-Berbers of King Caecilius and their Byzantine allies from the Exarchate of Carthage. Uqba ibn Nafi is killed and his army evacuates the city of Kairouan in Tunisia and withdraws to Barca.

summary: Emperor Constantine IV died of dysentery at Constantinople and was succeeded by his son Justinian II.
text: Emperor Constantine IV dies of dysentery at Constantinople after a 17-year reign, and is succeeded by his 16-year-old son Justinian II.

summary: Leo III, future emperor of the Byzantine Empire, was born.
text: Leo III, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (d. 741)

summary: Constantine IV, Byzantine emperor, died.
text: Constantine IV, Byzantine emperor (b. 652)

summary: Emperor Justinian II signed a peace treaty with the Umayyad Caliphate, relocated Maronites from Lebanon, and repositioned imperial military forces.
text: Emperor Justinian II negotiates a peace treaty with the Umayyad Caliphate (resulting in caliph Abd al-Malik paying tribute). He removes 12,000 Christian Maronites, who continually resist the Arabs, from Lebanon. Justinian reinforces the Byzantine navy on Cyprus, and transfers cavalry troops from the Thracesian Theme in Anatolia to the Theme of Thrace in the Balkan Peninsula.

summary: Emperor Justinian II marched through Thrace, restoring Byzantine rule and deporting Bulgars and Slavs to the Opsician Theme in Anatolia.
text: Byzantine–Bulgarian War: Emperor Justinian II carries out a Balkan campaign and marches through Thrace, where he restores Byzantine rule. He establishes a theme administration, and migrates many Bulgars and Slavs to the Opsician Theme (Asia Minor).

summary: Emperor Justinian II signed a treaty with Caliph Abd al-Malik for joint occupation of Cyprus and re-established Byzantine settlement there.
text: Justinian II reestablishes Byzantine settlement on Cyprus, signing a treaty with Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik (and paying an annual tribute) for joint occupation of the island.

summary: Emperor Justinian II defeated the Bulgars in Macedonia, recaptured Thessalonica, and resettled subdued Slavs in Anatolia.
text: Byzantine–Bulgarian War: Emperor Justinian II defeats the Bulgars of Macedonia and recaptures Thessalonica, the second most important Byzantine city in Europe. He resettles the subdued Slavs in Anatolia (modern Turkey), where they are required to provide 30,000 men to the Byzantine army.

summary: Muhammad ibn Marwan defeated the Byzantine army under Leontius at the Battle of Sebastopolis following the desertion of Slavic troops.
text: Battle of Sebastopolis: The Byzantine army under Leontius is defeated at Sebastopolis, (modern Turkey) by Arab forces led by Muhammad ibn Marwan. During the battle, a "special military corps" (some 20,000 Slavs) under Neboulos deserts the Byzantine lines, and goes over to the Muslim Arabs.

summary: The Umayyad Caliphate conquered Armenia, Iberia, and Colchis, forcing Justinian II to agree to joint rule over Cyprus.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Muslims conquer Armenia, Iberia and Colchis, the last remaining Byzantine holdings east of the Taurus Mountains. Emperor Justinian II is forced to agree to joint Byzantine-Arab control of Cyprus, in the Eastern Mediterranean Sea .

summary: Justinian II convened the Quinisext Council in Constantinople and ordered the arrest of Pope Sergius I, which Italian militias refused to execute.
text: The Quinisext Council is held in Constantinople; it lays the foundation for the Orthodox canon law. Justinian II suppresses non-Orthodox religious practices, and orders the arrest of Pope Sergius I; the militias of Rome and the Exarchate of Ravenna refuse, and take the pope's side.

summary: Callinicus I succeeded Paul III as Patriarch of Constantinople.
text: Callinicus I becomes the 71st patriarch of Constantinople, after Paul III.

summary: Paul III, Patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Paul III, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Leontios revolted in Constantinople, deposed and mutilated Emperor Justinian II, and took the Byzantine throne.
text: The population of Byzantium revolts under Leontios, the strategos (military governor) of the Anatolic Theme, and proclaims him emperor. Justinian II is deposed and his nose is cut off (leading to his subsequent nickname of "the Slit-nosed"). He is exiled to Cherson (Crimea), and begins to plot an attempt to retake the throne.

summary: Stephen the Persian, chief eunuch and sakellarios under Byzantine Emperor Justinian II, was executed.
text: Stephen the Persian, chief eunuch and sakellarios of the Byzantine Empire under Justinian II

summary: Paolo Lucio Anafesto was elected the first Doge of Venice.
text: Paolo Lucio Anafesto is elected the first Doge of Venice, which begins its rise as a major power in the Mediterranean Sea. Built up from fishing villages settled by fugitives from the Huns (see 452), the city of Venice occupies some 60 marshy islands (Venetian Lagoon).

summary: Hasan ibn al-Nu'man captured Carthage from the Byzantines, ending Roman rule in North Africa and triggering a fleet revolt that made Tiberios III emperor.
text: Spring–summer – Arab forces under Hasan ibn al-Nu'man capture Carthage, ending Byzantine rule in North Africa. The defeated Byzantine fleet revolts and proclaims Tiberios III, who deposes Leontios after a brief siege of Constantinople, Byzantine Emperor.

summary: Byzantine general Heraclius invaded Cilicia and Syria, defeating an Arab army from Antioch and raiding up to Samosata.
text: Autumn–winter – The Byzantine general Heraclius, brother of Tiberios III, crosses the mountain passes of the Taurus Mountains into Cilicia with an army. He launches a campaign in Syria, defeats an Arab force from Antioch, and raids as far as Samosata (modern Turkey).

summary: Bubonic plague struck Constantinople, Syria, and Mesopotamia, prompting Emperor Leontios to destroy an animal market in the Neorion Harbour.
text: Outbreak of bubonic plague in Constantinople, Syria and Mesopotamia: Theophanes the Confessor reports that the plague lasted four months and describes a large number of deaths in Constantinople. Emperor Leontios orders the destruction of a market in the Neorion cargo port of Constantinople, where animals are sold and which is considered to be the source of infected animals brought from Syria. The Arab army is forced to suspend its military operations. According to Syrian sources, the plague in Syria lasted another two years.

summary: Avar and Slavic tribes conquered Byzantine territories in the Balkans as far south as the Peloponnese.
text: Avar and Slavic tribes conquer Byzantine territories in the Balkans, occupying lands as far south as the Peloponnese peninsula in southern Greece .

summary: Abdallah ibn Abd al-Malik captured the Byzantine stronghold of Theodosiopolis in Armenia.
text: The Umayyad prince Abdallah ibn Abd al-Malik captures the Byzantine stronghold of Theodosiopolis in Armenia.

summary: Muslim general Hassan ibn al-Nu'man died.
text: Hassan ibn al-Nu'man, Muslim emir (general)

summary: Asparuh, founder of the First Bulgarian Empire, died.
text: Asparuh of Bulgaria, founder of the country of Bulgaria

summary: Tervel succeeded his father Asparuh as ruler of the First Bulgarian Empire.
text: Asparuh, founder of the First Bulgarian Empire, dies after a 20-year reign. He is succeeded by his son Tervel, who becomes ruler (khan) of the Bulgarians.

summary: Muhammad ibn Marwan invaded Byzantine Armenia, forcing the surrender of commander Baanes.
text: Arab conquest of Armenia: Umayyad prince Muhammad ibn Marwan invades the Byzantine Armenian provinces east of the Euphrates; local commander Baanes surrenders before a large Arab army, and the population accepts a Muslim governor.

summary: Asparuh, founder of the First Bulgarian Empire, died.
text: Asparuh, ruler of the First Bulgarian Empire

summary: Armenian forces launched a large-scale rebellion against Umayyad rule with Byzantine backing.
text: Arab conquest of Armenia: Large-scale Armenian rebellion against Muslim rule breaks out, with Byzantine support.

summary: Abdallah ibn Abd al-Malik captured Mopsuestia in Cilicia from the Byzantine Empire and refortified it.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: The Umayyad army under Abdallah ibn Abd al-Malik captures Mopsuestia in Cilicia from the Byzantines, and refortifies it, making it the first major Muslim stronghold in the area that will later become the Thughur.

summary: Musa ibn Nusayr built a Muslim fleet in Ifriqiya to harass the Byzantine navy and attack the Balearic Islands.
text: Musa ibn Nusayr, governor of Ifriqiya (western Libya), builds a Muslim fleet to harass the Byzantine navy and conquer the islands of Ibiza, Mallorca, and Menorca .

summary: Duke Faroald II of Spoleto attacked the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna without the support of Lombard King Aripert II.
text: Faroald II, duke of Spoleto, attacks the Exarchate of Ravenna in Italy, after the death of his father Thrasimund I. King Aripert II of the Lombards, desiring good relations with the Byzantine Empire and papacy, refuses to assist him.

summary: Deposed emperor Justinian II escaped from his exile in Chersonesus with help from the Khazar ruler Busir.
text: After spending nearly a decade with the Khazars (a Turkic tribe which controls a Steppe empire), the deposed emperor Justinian II flees from his exile at Cherson (Crimea). He escapes with help from Busir, ruler (khagan) of the Khazars, who marries him to his sister Theodora.

summary: Justinian II escaped an assassination plot backed by Emperor Tiberius III and fled to Bulgaria, securing the support of ruler Tervel.
text: Autumn – Emperor Tiberios III tries to bribe Busir and dispatches two Khazar officials, Papatzys and Balgitzin, to kill Justinian. Warned by his wife, he flees to the Bulgar Khanate, securing the assistance of the Bulgarian ruler Tervel, in exchange for financial considerations.

summary: Heraclius led a Byzantine expeditionary force that defeated and destroyed an Umayyad army at Sisium.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: A Byzantine expeditionary force under Heraclius (brother of Tiberios III) defeats and destroys an Umayyad army (10,000 men) at Sisium (modern Turkey) under Yazid ibn Hunayn, killing most and leading the others off in chains to Constantinople.

summary: Justinian II and an army of Bulgars and Slavs infiltrated Constantinople through an aqueduct, forcing Emperor Tiberius III to flee to Bithynia.
text: Spring – An army of 15,000 Bulgar and Slav horsemen under Justinian II appear before the walls of Constantinople. After three days, his troops discover an unused water conduit under the walls of the city, and enter through the Valens Aqueduct. Hearing that Justinian has taken control of the Blachernae Palace, Emperor Tiberios III flees to Bithynia (modern Turkey), where he evades capture for several months.

summary: Justinian II regained the Byzantine throne and granted the title of Caesar and the region of Zagora to Tervel of Bulgaria.
text: Justinian II ascends to the throne again and rewards his ally Tervel, ruler (khagan) of the Bulgarian Empire, for his assistance with the title of kaisar (Caesar), which makes him second only to Justinian and the first foreign ruler in Byzantine history to receive such a title, and a territorial concession in northeastern Thrace, a region called Zagora in modern-day Bulgaria.

summary: Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan died at Al-Sinnabra after a 20-year reign, and was succeeded by his son Al-Walid I.
text: Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan dies in his winter resort at Al-Sinnabra (Palestine), after a 20-year reign. During his rule, the financial administration of the Umayyad Caliphate has been reorganized. Arab coins have replaced former Byzantine and Sassanian coins, and regular postal service has been established between Damascus and the provincial capitals. Abd al-Malik is succeeded by his son Al-Walid I.

summary: Pope John VI died at Rome and was succeeded by Pope John VII.
text: Pope John VI dies at Rome, after a reign of little more than 3 years. During his rule, he protected the Byzantine exarch Theophylactus, when he invaded the Italian mainland from Sicily. He also induced Gisulf I, Lombard duke of Benevento, to withdraw from Byzantine territory, ransomed captives and ordered the restoration of Wilfrid, as deposed bishop of York. He is succeeded by John VII as the 86th pope of the Catholic Church.

summary: Tiberius, son of Byzantine Emperor Justinian II, was born.
text: Tiberius, son of Justinian II (d. 711)

summary: Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan died.
text: Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, Muslim caliph (b. 646)

summary: Byzantine general Heraclius was executed.
text: Heraclius, Byzantine general (monostrategos)

summary: Callinicus I, patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Kallinikos I, patriarch of Constantinople (or 706)

summary: Justinian II publicly humiliated and executed his predecessors Leontius and Tiberius III in the Hippodrome of Constantinople, and deposed Patriarch Callinicus I.
text: Emperor Justinian II presides over the public humiliation of his predecessors, Leontios and Tiberios III, and their chief associates in the Hippodrome of Constantinople, after which they are executed. Patriarch Kallinikos I is also deposed, blinded and exiled to Rome, and succeeded by Kyros.

summary: Former Byzantine Emperor Leontius was executed in Constantinople.
text: Leontios, Byzantine emperor

summary: Former Byzantine Emperor Tiberius III was executed in Constantinople.
text: Tiberios III, Byzantine emperor

summary: Deposed Patriarch Callinicus I of Constantinople died in exile in Rome.
text: Kallinikos I, patriarch of Constantinople (or 705)

summary: An Umayyad army under Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik invaded Anatolia and laid siege to Tyana.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: An Umayyad army under Maslamah ibn Abd al-Malik invades Asia Minor, and lays siege to Tyana (Cappadocia). The fortress city resists, dragging the siege through the winter and into 708.

summary: Arab Muslims conquered the Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean Sea.
text: The Muslim-Arabs conquer the Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean Sea .

summary: Pope John VII died in Rome, leaving the papal throne temporarily vacant.
text: Pope John VII dies at Rome after a 19-month reign. A prolonged sede vacante exists, until the ratification of the election of Sisinnius by the Exarch of Ravenna, in early 708.

summary: Umayyad forces under Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik captured and sacked the Byzantine city of Tyana after a prolonged siege.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: The Umayyads under Maslamah ibn Abd al-Malik capture and sack the Byzantine city of Tyana (Cappadocia) after a prolonged siege, and following a victory over a Byzantine relief army. Maslamah also leads another expedition in the summer, raiding and conquering Amorium (modern Turkey).

summary: Bulgarian cavalry led by Tervel defeated a Byzantine expeditionary army under Emperor Justinian II at the Battle of Anchialus.
text: Battle of Anchialus: A Byzantine expeditionary force under Emperor Justinian II is defeated near the seaside city of Anchialus, on the Black Sea Coast. The Byzantines are overwhelmed by a surprise attack of Bulgarian cavalry, led by Tervel. Justinian manages to reach the fortress, and escapes to Constantinople on a ship.

summary: Emperor Justinian II dispatched a punitive expedition under Theodore that captured Ravenna and arrested Archbishop Felix.
text: June – Emperor Justinian II sends a punitive expedition to Italy under the patrikios Theodore, to intervene in the dispute between Pope Constantine I and Archbishop Felix of Ravenna, who claims to be independent of the pope's authority. Theodore captures Ravenna, and arrests Felix and other Italian leaders. He deports them to Constantinople, from whence they are exiled to Cherson (Crimea).

summary: Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik raided Byzantine Isauria and was appointed military governor of Armenia and Azerbaijan.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: An Umayyad army under Maslamah ibn Abd al-Malik raids Isauria (modern Turkey). He is appointed military governor of Armenia and Azerbaijan, succeeding his uncle Muhammad ibn Marwan.

summary: The Byzantine city of Cherson rebelled against Emperor Justinian II with Khazar backing, briefly fell to an imperial fleet, and rebelled anew.
text: The Byzantine outpost of Cherson (Crimea) rebels (with Khazar assistance) against Emperor Justinian II. He sends a fleet under the patrikios Stephen, which retakes the city and restores Byzantine control. The fleet, however, is struck by a storm on its way back and loses many ships, while the Chersonites, again with the aid of the Khazars, rebel anew.

summary: The Byzantine general Leo recovered Abkhazia from Arab control for the Byzantine Empire.
text: The Byzantine general Leo (future emperor Leo III) recovers the Abkhazia (Caucasus) for the Byzantine Empire, from the Arabs.

summary: Pope Constantine departed for a year-long visit to Constantinople.
text: Pope Constantine departs for a year-long visit to Constantinople. He will be the last pontiff to visit the capital for more than a thousand years.

summary: Philippicus revolted with Khazar support, seized Constantinople, and had Emperor Justinian II executed.
text: Philippicus incites the inhabitants of Cherson to revolt, with the help of the Khazars. Emperor Justinian II sallies forth from Constantinople to oppose the rebels in the Crimea. Philippicus defeats the Byzantine forces in northern Anatolia, and seizes the capital. He is proclaimed emperor and Justinian is executed, ending the house of Heraclius, that has ruled since 610.
names: Byzantine Empire under the Heraclian dynasty

summary: Henchmen of Philippicus dragged Justinian II's young son Tiberius from St. Mary's Church in Constantinople and murdered him.
text: December – Upon hearing the news of Justinian's death, Anastasia, Justinian's mother, escapes with Justinian's 6-year-old son Tiberius to the sanctuary at the St. Mary's Church (Constantinople). She is pursued by Philippicus' henchmen, who drag the child from the altar and murder him outside the church. It is unknown what became of Justinian's wife, Theodora.
names: Church of St. Mary of Blachernae

summary: Byzantine Emperor Justinian II was executed following his deposition.
text: Justinian II, Byzantine emperor (b. 669)

summary: Co-emperor Tiberius, son of Justinian II, was murdered at the Church of St. Mary of Blachernae in Constantinople.
text: December – Tiberius, son of Justinian II (b. 705)

summary: Bulgars under Khagan Tervel raided Thrace and advanced to the walls of Constantinople.
text: The Bulgars under Tervel, ruler (khagan) of the Bulgarian Empire, raid Thrace and reach the city walls of Constantinople. Skirmishes continue until 716; Emperor Philippicus transfers a Byzantine army from the Opsikion Theme in Asia Minor, to police the Balkan Peninsula.

summary: Conspirators of the Opsikion theme deposed and blinded Emperor Philippicus, elevating Anastasius II to the Byzantine throne.
text: Emperor Philippicus is blinded, deposed, and sent into exile by conspirators of the Opsikion army in Thrace, after a reign of 1 year and 6 months. He is succeeded by Anastasios II, a bureaucrat and imperial secretary, who restores internal order and begins the reorganization of the Byzantine army. He executes the officers who have been directly involved in the conspiracy against Philippicus.

summary: Umayyad forces under al-Abbas ibn al-Walid sacked the Byzantine city of Antioch in Pisidia.
text: Arab–Byzantine wars: The Umayyad Arabs under al-Abbas ibn al-Walid, son of caliph al-Walid I, sack Antioch in Pisidia (modern Turkey), which never recovers.

summary: Stephen the Younger, Byzantine monk and theologian, was born in Constantinople.
text: Stephen the Younger, Byzantine theologian (or 715)

summary: Deposed Byzantine emperor Philippicus died in Constantinople.
text: Philippicus, Byzantine emperor

summary: Theodosius III captured Constantinople, deposed Emperor Anastasius II, and took the Byzantine throne.
text: May – Emperor Anastasios II is deposed in an army mutiny, and succeeded by Theodosius III, a tax-collector from the theme of Opsikion (modern Turkey). After a six-month siege, Theodosius and his troops take Constantinople; Anastasios is forced to abdicate the throne, and retires to a monastery in Thessaloniki (Macedonia).

summary: Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik succeeded his brother Al-Walid I as caliph of the Umayyad Caliphate upon his death in Damascus.
text: Caliph Al-Walid I dies at Damascus after a 10-year reign, and is succeeded by his brother Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik. During his rule the Umayyad Caliphate reaches its greatest height, with successful campaigns undertaken in Transoxiana (Central Asia), Sindh (Pakistan), Hispania and against the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Patriarch Germanus I of Constantinople organised a synod promoting Dyothelitism and sought to improve ties with the Armenian Church.
text: The newly-appointed Patriarch Germanus I of Constantinople organises a council propagating Dyothelitism, and attempts to improve relations with the Armenian Apostolic Church.

summary: Byzantine theologian and iconodule martyr Stephen the Younger was born in Constantinople.
text: Stephen the Younger, Byzantine theologian (or 713)

summary: Caliph Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik began preparations to attack Constantinople, conquering Lycia and advancing land armies to Caesarea.
text: Arab-Byzantine Wars: Umayyad Caliph Sulayman ibn Abd Al-Malik begins the preparations for his campaign on Constantinople; he orders new ships be built in the port-cities in Palestine, Egypt & Ifriqiya. General Umar ibn Hubayra raids southern Anatolia by sea and conquers Lycia, where another Arab fleet joins him, and they spend winter. As the navy advances, Sulayman sends land armies into Anatolia, which settle at Caesarea.

summary: Emperor Theodosius III concluded a treaty with Bulgaria fixing borders, trade terms, and mutual assistance against Arab forces.
text: Emperor Theodosios III concludes a peace treaty with Kormesiy, son of Tervel of Bulgaria, in an effort to secure support against the Arab invasion in Anatolia (modern Turkey). The treaty recognizes the Bulgarian borders, including the newly gained lands of Zagore (see 705). Theodosios agrees to pay annual tribute, and exchange refugees charged with conspiracy against the legal ruler. Goods can only be imported or exported with a state seal. Bulgarian merchants gain official access to the trade market in Constantinople.

summary: Leo III the Isaurian deposed Theodosius III to become Byzantine emperor, ending the Twenty Years' Anarchy.
text: Emperor Theodosios III is deposed after a reign of 1 year and 10 months. He is succeeded by the 32-year-old Leo III the Isaurian, a general (strategos) of the Anatolic Theme (modern Turkey). Theodosios and his son enter the clergy, and he probably becomes bishop of Ephesus. Leo brings an end to the Twenty Years' Anarchy in the Byzantine Empire, which marks the beginning of the so-called Isaurian Dynasty.
names: Byzantine Empire under the Isaurian dynasty

summary: Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik led an army across the Hellespont and constructed siege lines to blockade Constantinople.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Muslim general Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik leads his army of 80,000 men from Pergamum to Abydos, where he crosses the Hellespont. To prevent interference by the Bulgars, or by any Byzantine forces in Thrace, he sends part of his army to a covering position near Adrianople; with his main body, Maslama builds siege lines to blockade Constantinople, which is protected by the massive Theodosian Walls.

summary: Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik began a combined land and sea siege of Constantinople while Leo III prepared the city's defenses.
text: Siege of Constantinople: Maslama begins a combined land and sea effort to capture Constantinople. The capital controls the Bosporus, access between the Mediterranean and Black Sea, and is defended by a garrison of roughly 25,000 men. Leo III orders the granaries be restocked and siege engines installed. The Arab besiegers are suffering immense losses due to disease, and from attrition of siege warfare.

summary: Emperor Leo III ordered the Byzantine fleet to attack the anchored Muslim armada with Greek fire off Constantinople.
text: A Muslim armada, consisting of 1,800 ships commanded by Admiral Suleiman, sails into the Sea of Marmara and drops anchor below the sea walls of Constantinople, to supply their forces ashore. Leo III orders the Byzantine fleet to sally forth from their protected harbors with Greek fire, setting alight the thickly-packed Muslim ships. Many vessels burst into flames, while others collide with each other before sinking.

summary: Basil Onomagoulos declared himself emperor in Sicily but was arrested and executed by forces sent by Leo III.
text: Fall – Basil Onomagoulos, Byzantine official, declares himself rival emperor in Sicily after the news arrives that Constantinople has fallen to an Arab siege. Leo III dispatches a chartoularios named Paul, with imperial instructions for the Byzantine army on the island. Basil is arrested and executed; his head is sent to Leo, while the other rebels are mutilated and exiled.

summary: Byzantine usurper Basil Onomagoulos was executed.
text: Basil Onomagoulos, Byzantine usurper

summary: Emperor Leo III sent the Byzantine navy to destroy a Muslim supply fleet in the Sea of Marmara and ambushed an Arab army near Nicomedia.
text: Spring – A Muslim supply fleet of 760 ships under Sufyan arrives from Egypt and North Africa, concealing itself along the Asiatic shore. The Byzantines learn of the fleet's location from defecting Christian Egyptian sailors. Emperor Leo III sends the Byzantine navy again; his Greek fire ships destroy the enemy vessels in the Sea of Marmara and seize their supplies on shore, denying the sieging army vital provisions. On land the Byzantine troops ambush an advancing Arab army, and destroy it in the hills around Sophon, south of Nicomedia (modern Turkey). The Arab besiegers are still suffering from hunger and pestilence.

summary: A Bulgar relief force attacked Umayyad siege lines at Constantinople, forcing Caliph Umar II to lift the thirteen-month siege.
text: Siege of Constantinople: A Bulgar relief force attacks the siege lines at Constantinople, on the west side of the Bosporus. Contemporary chroniclers report that at least 22,000–32,000 Arabs are killed during the Bulgarian attacks. Caliph Umar II is forced to lift the siege after 13 months; the Muslim army attempts to withdraw back through Anatolia, while the rest escapes by sea in the remaining vessels. The Arab fleet suffers further casualties to storms, and an eruption of the volcano of Thera. According to Arab sources 150,000 Muslims perish during the campaign.
