summary: Constantine V, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: Constantine V, Byzantine emperor (d. 775)

summary: Emperor Leo III executed former emperor Anastasios II after his Bulgarian-backed rebellion against Constantinople failed.
text: Ex-Emperor Anastasios II starts a revolt against Leo III with considerable support, including auxiliaries provided by Tervel, emperor (khagan) of the Bulgarian Empire. His attack on Constantinople fails; Anastasios is captured and is put to death (by beheading), on the orders of Leo.

summary: The Church of Nubia transferred its allegiance from the Eastern Orthodox Church to the Coptic Church.
text: The Church of Nubia transfers its allegiance, from the Eastern Orthodox Church to the Coptic Church .

summary: Anastasius II, deposed Byzantine emperor, was executed following a failed attempt to retake the throne.
text: Anastasios II, Byzantine emperor

summary: Emperor Leo III settled Slavs in the Thracesian Theme and crowned his infant son Constantine V as co-emperor.
text: Summer – Emperor Leo III secures the Byzantine frontier, by inviting Slavic settlers into the depopulated districts of the Thracesian Theme (western Asia Minor). He undertakes a set of civil reforms, and reorganizes the theme structure in the Aegean region. Leo's 2-year-old son Constantine V is associated on the throne, and married to Tzitzak, daughter of the Khazar ruler (khagan) Bihar.

summary: Emperor Leo III ordered the forced baptism of all Jews and Montanists in the Byzantine Empire.
text: Emperor Leo III enforces the baptism of all Jews and Montanists in the Byzantine Empire.

summary: A Muslim fleet raided the Byzantine Balearic Islands, Byzantine Sardinia, and Lombard Corsica.
text: A Muslim fleet raids the Byzantine-ruled Balearic Islands, as well as Byzantine Sardinia and Lombard Corsica.

summary: Felix, archbishop of Ravenna, died.
text: Felix, archbishop of Ravenna

summary: King Liutprand placed Byzantine Corsica under Lombard control to defend it against Muslim raids.
text: King Liutprand puts Corsica, nominally under Byzantine authority, under Lombard government, defending it from Muslim raids .

summary: Emperor Leo III issued edicts banning the veneration of images, initiating the Byzantine iconoclastic controversies.
text: Emperor Leo III issues a series of edicts banning the veneration of images (726–729), and launching the iconoclastic controversies. Most of the clergy – particularly in Italy and Greece – are opposed to these edicts with uncompromising hostility, and in the western parts of the Byzantine Empire the people refuse to obey his religious reforms.

summary: Muslim forces under Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik raided Anatolia and plundered the Byzantine fortress city of Caesarea.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Muslim forces under Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik resume their expedition against Anatolia (modern Turkey). In a large-scale raid they plunder the fortress city of Caesarea.

summary: Marcello Tegalliano, second Doge of Venice, died.
text: Marcello Tegalliano, second Doge of Venice, dies after a 9-year reign.

summary: Venetians revolted against Emperor Leo III's iconoclastic decrees, elected Orso Ipato as Doge, and later helped restore Byzantine power in Ravenna.
text: Uprising in Venice against Byzantium: The cause of mass unrest is the iconoclastic decrees of Emperor Leo III. A few days later, political demands are put forward for wide autonomy within the Byzantine Empire and the right to appoint the ruler of the region (Doge). The rebels elect Orso Ipato the Doge of Venice. Desiring to preserve the proceeds of the treasury from the second most important port of the Byzantine Empire, and not having the resources to cope with a well-fortified and armed region, Byzantium agrees with all the requirements put forward. Orso Ipato is recognised by Leo III, who gives him the title hypatos. The Venetian fleet, led by Orso Ipato, frees Ravenna from the Lombards and restores the power of the Byzantine governor there.

summary: The volcanic island of Thera erupted and Jerash suffered a major earthquake.
text: Seismic activity in the Mediterranean Sea: The volcanic island of Thera erupts, while the city of Jerash (in present-day Jordan) suffers a major earthquake.

summary: Marcello Tegalliano, doge of Venice, died.
text: Marcello Tegalliano, doge of Venice

summary: Smbat VI Bagratuni, prince of Armenia, died.
text: Smbat VI, Armenian prince

summary: A rebel fleet under Agallianos Kontoskeles bound for Constantinople was destroyed by the Byzantine navy using Greek fire.
text: A revolt breaks out in Greece against the religious policies of Emperor Leo III (see 726). A rebel fleet under Agallianos Kontoskeles sets out for Constantinople with Kosmas, an anti-emperor, but is destroyed by the Byzantine fleet through the use of Greek fire.

summary: Umayyad forces under Mu'awiya ibn Hisham sacked Gangra and unsuccessfully besieged Nicaea.
text: Siege of Nicaea: Muslim forces under Mu'awiya ibn Hisham (son of Umayyad caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik) penetrate deep into Asia Minor, and sack the fortress city of Gangra, but unsuccessfully lay siege to Nicaea (northwestern Anatolia).

summary: A revolt against iconoclasm in Italy led to the Exarchate of Ravenna repulsing imperial forces and breaking away from Byzantine control.
text: A revolt breaks out in Italy against Leo's Iconoclasm; this results in the independence of the Exarchate of Ravenna, after part of a Byzantine invasion force is lost in a storm in the Adriatic Sea, and the remainder of Byzantine troops are repulsed.

summary: King Liutprand conquered Bologna, captured the port of Classis, and overran the Pentapolis.
text: King Liutprand takes advantage of the anti-imperial turmoil. He conquers Bologna and other cities beyond the Po River (Northern Italy). The Lombards take "Classis", the strategic seaport of Ravenna, and overrun the Pentapolis.

summary: Pope Gregory II condemned Byzantine iconoclasm at Rome, precipitating a political break between central Italy and the empire.
text: July – Pope Gregory II condemns iconoclasm at Rome, causing Italy to break with the Byzantine Empire. He becomes the virtual temporal ruler of most Byzantine possessions.

summary: Agallianos Kontoskeles, Byzantine commander and rebel leader, died when his fleet was destroyed.
text: Agallianos Kontoskeles, Byzantine commander and rebel leader

summary: Paul, exarch of Ravenna, was killed during an uprising.
text: Paul, exarch of Ravenna

summary: King Liutprand signed the Donation of Sutri with Pope Gregory II, transferring parts of Latium to the papacy.
text: King Liutprand of the Lombards occupies all of the Exarchate of Ravenna. He advances towards Rome along the Via Cassia, and is met at the city of Sutri by Pope Gregory II, near the borders of the Duchy of Rome. Liutprand signs the Donation of Sutri, by which parts of Latium are given to the papacy (the first extension of papal territory in Italy). This marks the historical foundation of the Papal States.

summary: Italian forces raised by Pope Gregory II defeated Byzantine troops under Exarch Eutychius at the Battle of Ravenna.
text: Battle of Ravenna: Byzantine troops under Eutychius, exarch of Ravenna, are defeated by an Italian force, raised by Gregory II, in opposition to iconoclasm.

summary: King Liutprand of the Lombards allied with Exarch Eutychius of Ravenna against Rome while subjugating Spoleto and Benevento.
text: King Liutprand contracts an alliance with Eutychius, exarch of Ravenna, and agrees to support him in his attack on Rome, while subjugating the independent southern Lombard duchies of Benevento and Spoleto.

summary: Exarch Eutychius defeated and killed the usurper Tiberius Petasius at Monterano with the support of Pope Gregory II.
text: Tiberius Petasius proclaims himself emperor in Tuscia. Eutychius defeats him with the support of Pope Gregory II, and Tiberius is killed in Monterano, with his head sent to the Byzantine emperor Leo III as a gift.

summary: Umayyad forces sacked the Byzantine fortress of Charsianon in central Anatolia.
text: September–October – Umayyad forces sack the Byzantine fortress of Charsianon in central Anatolia (modern Turkey), which remains a contested stronghold during the next century of Byzantine–Arab warfare.

summary: Emperor Leo III ordered the destruction of all religious icons, initiating the Byzantine Iconoclasm.
text: Leo III of the Byzantine Empire orders the destruction of all icons, beginning the First Iconoclastic Period. Many monks flee to Greece and Italy (taking smaller icons with them, hidden in their clothing); others flee to the caves of the Cappadocian desert.

summary: Future Patriarch Tarasios of Constantinople was born.
text: Tarasios, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Byzantine usurper Tiberius Petasius was killed at Monterano.
text: Tiberius Petasius, Byzantine usurper

summary: Pope Gregory III succeeded Pope Gregory II as bishop of Rome following the latter's death.
text: Pope Gregory II dies at Rome after a 16-year reign, in which he has fought Iconoclasm. He is succeeded by the Syrian-born cleric Gregory III, as the 90th pope of the Catholic Church.

summary: Pope Gregory III convened a synod at Saint Peter's in Rome, which formally condemned Iconoclasm as a heresy.
text: Synod of Rome: Gregory III summons a council at the shrine of Saint Peter. All western bishops participate, including the Roman nobility. Gregory condemns Iconoclasm as a heresy.

summary: Telets, future khagan of the First Bulgarian Empire, was born.
text: Telets, ruler (khagan) of the Bulgarian Empire

summary: Barjik, prince of the Khazar Khaganate, died.
text: Barjik, prince of the Khazar Khaganate

summary: Emperor Leo III married his son Constantine to Tzitzak, daughter of the Khazar khagan Bihar, strengthening the alliance between Byzantium and the Khazars.
text: Byzantine Emperor Leo III marries his 15 year old son Constantine to Tzitzak (later baptised as Irene), the daughter of the Khazar Khagan Bihar, as a sign of diplomatic unity between the Byzantine Empire and the Khazar Khaganate.

summary: Emperor Leo III confiscated papal estates in Sicily and Calabria and transferred ecclesiastical jurisdiction over Illyricum to the patriarch of Constantinople.
text: Emperor Leo III confiscates the papal territories in Sicily and Calabria (Southern Italy), from which Pope Gregory III derives most of his income tax. He transfers ecclesiastical jurisdiction in the former Praetorian prefecture of Illyricum to Anastasius, patriarch of Constantinople. Gregory begins his support of a revolt in Italy against iconoclasm. By now the break between the papacy and the Byzantine Empire is almost complete.

summary: Arab forces under Mu'awiya ibn Hisham penetrated deep into Anatolia and captured the Byzantine cities of Antalya, Dorylaeum, and Afyonkarahisar.
text: Arab-Byzantine Wars: Arab forces under Mu’awiya ibn Hisham penetrate deep into Anatolia and conquer the cities of Antalya, Doralyum and Afyonkarahisar. These conquests differ from previous ones, as Arab military settling occurs in them, making them a base to raid Byzantium.

summary: Kardam, future ruler of the Bulgarian Empire, was born.
text: Kardam, ruler (khan) of the Bulgarian Empire

summary: Plato of Sakkoudion, Byzantine abbot and religious figure, was born in Constantinople.
text: Plato of Sakkoudion, Byzantine abbot

summary: Doge Orso Ipato of Venice was murdered at the instigation of Exarch Eutychius of Ravenna, and Domenico Leoni was elected magister militum.
text: Orso Ipato is murdered at the instigation of Eutychius, exarch of Ravenna. He is succeeded by Domenico Leoni, who is elected magister militum of Venice.

summary: Mu'awiya ibn Hisham, Umayyad general, died.
text: Mu'awiya ibn Hisham, Muslim general

summary: Orso Ipato, Doge of Venice, died.
text: Orso Ipato, doge of Venice

summary: Kormesiy was deposed by the Bulgarian nobility and replaced on the throne by his son Sevar.
text: Kormesiy, ruler (khagan) of the Bulgarian Empire, is deposed by the nobility. He is replaced on the throne by his son Sevar, who is a descendant of the royal Dulo clan.

summary: Felice Cornicola was appointed hypatos and magister militum of Venice.
text: Felice Cornicola is appointed hypatos (Byzantine consul) and magister militum of Venice.

summary: Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik, Umayyad prince and general, died.
text: Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik, Arab general

summary: Liutprand sacked the Exarchate of Ravenna and threatened Rome, prompting Pope Gregory III to seek Frankish assistance before negotiating a peace accord.
text: The Lombards under King Liutprand sack the Exarchate of Ravenna, and threaten Rome. Pope Gregory III asks Charles Martel, Merovingian mayor of the palace, to help fight the Lombards (he also requests assistance in fighting the Byzantines and the Arabs). Liutprand signs a peace accord, and pulls back his forces to Pavia. After the pope's appeal to the Franks, a relationship begins that will continue as the Frankish Kingdom gains power.

summary: Teodato Ipato was appointed hypatos and magister militum of Venice.
text: Theodatus Ursus is appointed hypatos (Byzantine consul) and magister militum of Venice.

summary: Byzantine forces under Emperor Leo III and Constantine V defeated an invading Umayyad army at Akroinon.
text: Battle of Akroinon: Following the disastrous Battle of Sebastopolis (see 692), Emperor Leo III has largely confined himself to a defensive strategy, while the Umayyad armies regularly launch raids into Byzantine-held Anatolia. Caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik assembles an expeditionary force (90,000 men) under his son Sulayman ibn Hisham. One of these armies, 20,000 men strong under Abdallah al-Battal, is defeated at Akroinon (modern-day Afyon) by the Byzantines, led by Leo and his son, the future emperor Constantine V. About 6,800 Muslim Arabs, however, resist and manage to conduct an orderly retreat to Synnada (Phrygia).

summary: A major earthquake struck Constantinople, damaging its defensive walls and public buildings.
text: 740 Constantinople earthquake. An earthquake strikes Constantinople and the surrounding countryside, causing destruction to the city's land walls and buildings.

summary: Arab fleets sent from Ifriqiya raided Sicily, Sardinia, Provence, and Greece, returning with extensive plunder.
text: Sicily, Sardinia, Provence, and Greece are raided by a fleet of Arab Muslim ships sent by the governor of Ifriqya, the ones raiding South Western Europe are led by Habīb Ibn Abi ‘Ubayda Al-Fihrī, while the fleet raiding Greece is led by Mu’awiya ibn Hishām. All of them are successful, submitting the Islands and returning with much wealth from the spoils of war.

summary: Theoktiste, Byzantine noblewoman and mother of Theodore the Studite, was born.
text: Theoctista, politically influential Byzantine woman (d. 802)

summary: Umayyad military commander Abdallah al-Battal was killed at the Battle of Akroinon.
text: Abdallah al-Battal, Arab general

summary: Anna, Byzantine princess and wife of Artabasdos, died.
text: Anna, Byzantine princess and empress, wife of Artabasdos

summary: Emperor Leo III died at Constantinople and was succeeded by his son Constantine V.
text: Emperor Leo III ("the Isaurian") dies of dropsy at Constantinople, after a 24-year reign that has saved the Byzantine Empire and delivered Eastern Europe from the threat of an Arab conquest. He is succeeded by his son Constantine V.

summary: Artabasdos defeated Constantine V, entered Constantinople, and was crowned Byzantine emperor.
text: Artabasdos, Byzantine general (strategos) of the Armeniac theme, defeats Constantine V and advances on Constantinople, where he is crowned emperor. He secures the support of the themes of Thrace and Opsikion, and abandons Leo's religious policy of iconoclasm. Constantine seeks the support of the Anatolic theme.

summary: Leo III, emperor of the Byzantine Empire, died.
text: Leo III, emperor of the Byzantine Empire

summary: Sulayman ibn Hisham led Arab forces on a raid across Anatolia reaching Heraclea Pontica.
text: Arab-Byzantine Wars: Arab forces under Sulayman ibn Hisham invade Anatolia, reaching as far as Herakleia, and return with much wealth and livestock.

summary: Teodato Ipato succeeded his father as doge of Venice and moved the capital from Heraclea to Malamocco.
text: Teodato Ipato succeeds his father Orso Ipato, as the fourth doge of Venice. He moves the capital from Heraclea to Malamocco.

summary: Constantine V defeated the usurper Artabasdos, recaptured Constantinople, and blinded Artabasdos and his son Niketas.
text: Summer – Emperor Constantine V defeats his brother-in-law Artabasdos, who has led a two-year insurrection in an attempt to usurp the Byzantine throne. He heads for Constantinople, and captures the capital three months later. Artabasdos and his son Niketas are publicly blinded, and relegated to the monastery of Chora. Constantine renews his policy of Iconoclasm.

summary: Constantine V reformed the Imperial Guard of Constantinople into elite military units known as tagmata.
text: Constantine V reforms the old Imperial Guard of Constantinople into new elite cavalry and infantry units, called tagmata (Greek for 'the regiments'). He uses these troops against a rebellious theme in north-west Anatolia (modern Turkey), and later for offensive campaigns against Arab Muslim raiders and Bulgars.

summary: A bubonic plague epidemic killed one-third of the population of Asia Minor before sweeping into the Peloponnese.
text: Bubonic plague in Asia Minor kills 1/3 of the population, and subsequently sweeps through the Peloponnese (Balkan Peninsula) .

summary: Emperor Constantine V invaded Syria, captured Germanikeia, and resettled part of the local Christian population in Thrace.
text: Arab–Byzantine Wars: Taking advantage of discontent among the Muslim Arabs, Emperor Constantine V invades Syria, and captures Germanikeia (modern Turkey). He organises the resettlement of part of the local Christian population in Thrace.

summary: The Byzantine navy decisively defeated the Umayyad Egyptian fleet at the Battle of Keramaia.
text: Arab–Byzantine Wars – Battle of Keramaia: The Byzantine navy scores a crushing victory over the Umayyad Egyptian fleet.

summary: Emperor Constantine V, aided by Italian ships, destroyed the Umayyad fleet off Cyprus.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Emperor Constantine V destroys the Arab fleet off Cyprus, with the aid of ships from the Italian city-states, breaking the naval power of the Umayyad Caliphate.{{citation

summary: An outbreak of bubonic plague struck Sicily, Calabria, and Monemvasia.
text: Bubonic plague breaks out in Sicily, Calabria (Southern Italy), and Monemvasia (modern Greece).

summary: The future Byzantine emperor Leo IV was born.
text: Leo IV, Byzantine emperor (d. 780)

summary: Eastern Orthodox saint Basil the Confessor died.
text: Basil the Confessor, Eastern Orthodox saint

summary: Byzantine empress Irene of Khazaria died.
text: Irene of Khazaria, Byzantine empress

summary: Emperor Constantine V crowned his young son Leo IV as co-emperor in Constantinople.
text: June – Leo IV, son of Emperor Constantine V, is crowned co-emperor at Constantinople. Only a year or so after his mother Irene died, Constantine's second wife Maria dies, at approximately the same time as Leo's coronation.

summary: King Aistulf of the Lombards captured Ravenna, terminating the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna.
text: King Aistulf of the Lombards captures Ravenna and the Romagna, ending the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna. The last exarch Eutychius is killed by the Lombards. Aistulf threatens Rome, claiming a capitation tax. Pope Zachary, alarmed, appeals for aid from the Byzantine Empire, but his request is declined.

summary: Byzantine empress Maria, second wife of Constantine V, died in Constantinople.
text: June – Maria, Byzantine empress

summary: Eutychius, the last Byzantine exarch of Ravenna, was killed when the Lombards captured Ravenna.
text: Eutychius, Byzantine exarch of Ravenna

summary: Abd al-Rahman ibn Habib al-Fihri raided Sardinia and attempted an invasion of Byzantine Sicily.
text: Abd al-Rahman ibn Habib al-Fihri launches an assault on the island of Sardinia, perhaps the beginning of the occupation of the island by the Muslim Arabs that lasts until 1005. He also attempts to invade Sicily, but finds the defenses too strong.

summary: Future Byzantine empress Irene of Athens was born.
text: Irene of Athens, Byzantine empress

summary: Byzantine theologian Joannicius the Great was born in Bithynia.
text: Joannicius the Great, Byzantine theologian (d. 846)

summary: Emperor Constantine V convened the Council of Hieria, which endorsed Iconoclasm and intensified the persecution of Byzantine monasteries.
text: February – Council of Hieria: Emperor Constantine V summons a Christian council in the palace of Hieria in Constantinople. The council, under the presidency of Bishop Theodosius of Ephesus, supports the policy of Iconoclasm and condemning the use of religious images (icons) in the Byzantine Empire. Constantine increases the persecution of the monasteries; hundreds of monks and nuns are mutilated or put to death.

summary: Emperor Constantine V fortified the Danube frontier and settled Armenians and Syrians in Thrace, prompting Bulgar raids up to the Anastasian Wall.
text: Byzantine–Bulgarian War: Emperor Constantine V builds a series of fortifications along the Byzantine frontier on the Danube, and starts settling Christian Armenians and Syrians in the Thracesian Theme. In response, Kormisosh, ruler (khagan) of the Bulgarian Empire, demands the payment of tribute. Constantine refuses, and the Bulgars raid into Thrace, reaching the Anastasian Wall stretching between the Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara (near the outskirts of Constantinople).

summary: Constantine V defeated the Bulgars at the Battle of Marcellae, forcing Kormisosh to make peace before being deposed by Vinekh.
text: Battle of Marcellae: Constantine V sends a Byzantine expeditionary force (500 ships and 6,000 cavalry) to Thrace, and defeats the Bulgars around the Danube Delta and near the fortress city of Markeli (modern Bulgaria). Kormisosh is forced to accept a peace treaty, and confirms the existing frontier. Due to the constant political crisis, the Bulgarian Empire is on the verge of destruction. Kormisosh is deposed during a palace coup and succeeded by Vinekh, a member of the Vokil clan.

summary: Pepin the Short defeated King Aistulf of the Lombards and issued the Donation of Pepin, creating the Papal States under Pope Stephen II.
text: King Aistulf of the Lombards again threatens Rome with a view to making it his capital, but the Franks under Pepin III ("the Short") arrives with his sons Charles and Carloman, defeats Aistulf, and confers the Donation of Pepin, which establishes the Papal States (including the lands of Ravenna and the Pentapolis). Pepin has taken territory that legally belongs to the Byzantine Empire; he gives it to Pope Stephen II.

summary: Nikephoros, son of Emperor Constantine V, was born.
text: Nikephoros, son of Constantine V (or 758)

summary: Pope Stephen II died in Rome and was succeeded by his brother Pope Paul I.
text: Pope Stephen II dies at Rome after a 5-year reign, in which he has freed the papacy from Byzantine rule. Stephen allies with Pepin III against the Lombards, and becomes the first temporal sovereign of the Papal States. He is succeeded by his brother Paul I, as the 93rd pope of the Catholic Church.

summary: Nikephoros, son of Byzantine Emperor Constantine V, was born.
text: Nikephoros, son of Constantine V (or 756)

summary: Nikephoros I, future patriarch of Constantinople, was born.
text: Nikephoros I, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Theophanes the Confessor, a Byzantine monk and chronicler, was born.
text: Theophanes the Confessor, Byzantine monk (or 760)

summary: Bulgarian forces under Vinekh ambushed and defeated Byzantine Emperor Constantine V at the Battle of the Rishki Pass.
text: Battle of the Rishki Pass: Emperor Constantine V invades Bulgaria again, but his forces are ambushed and defeated while crossing the Rishki Pass, near Stara Planina (modern Bulgaria). The Bulgarian ruler (khagan) Vinekh does not exploit his success, and begins peace negotiations.

summary: Theodore the Studite was born in Constantinople.
text: Theodore the Studite, Byzantine abbot (d. 826)

summary: Byzantine monk and chronicler Theophanes the Confessor was born in Constantinople.
text: Theophanes the Confessor, Byzantine monk (or 758)

summary: Byzantine military commander Thomas the Slav was born.
text: Thomas the Slav, Byzantine general

summary: Emperor Constantine V defeated Telets and the Bulgars at Anchialus and returned to Constantinople in triumph.
text: June – Battle of Anchialus: Emperor Constantine V sends a Byzantine expeditionary force (800 ships and 9,600 cavalry) to Thrace, to defend the fortress city of Anchialus on the Black Sea Coast. Meanwhile, Telets, ruler (khagan) of the Bulgarian Empire, blocks the mountain passes and takes positions on the heights near Anchialus. During a desperate cavalry charge, the Bulgars are defeated and many are captured; Telets manages to escape. Constantine enters Constantinople in triumph, and kills all the prisoners.

summary: Byzantine troops allied with Lombard king Desiderius invaded the Papal States, prompting mediation by Frankish king Pepin the Short.
text: August – Byzantine troops invade the Papal States, in alliance with King Desiderius of the Lombards. King Pepin III ("the Short") intervenes, and begins negotiations between the Lombards and Pope Paul I. Desiderius promises to end the hostilities, but on condition that Pepin sends back Lombard hostages held by the Franks.

summary: Theophanes the Confessor recorded icebergs floating past Constantinople from the Black Sea.
text: According to the historian Theophanes the Confessor, icebergs float past Constantinople from the Black Sea .

summary: Stephen the Younger, Byzantine iconodule monk and theologian, was martyred.
text: Stephen the Younger, Byzantine theologian (or 765)

summary: Iconodule theologian Stephen the Younger was martyred in Constantinople.
text: Stephen the Younger, Byzantine theologian (or 764)

summary: Emperor Constantine V publicly humiliated nineteen conspirators in the Hippodrome of Constantinople and executed Constantine and Strategios Podopagouros.
text: Emperor Constantine V publicly humiliates 19 high-ranking officials in the Hippodrome of Constantinople, after discovering a plot against him. He executes the leaders, Constantine Podopagouros and his brother Strategios, and blinds and exiles the rest.

summary: A Byzantine relief army defeated Abbasid forces under al-Hasan ibn Qahtaba at Kamacha, forcing them to retreat into Armenia.
text: Autumn – Siege of Kamacha: Abbasid forces under al-Hasan ibn Qahtaba are defeated at the fortress city of Kamacha, in eastern Cappadocia (modern Turkey). A Byzantine relief army (12,000 men) forces the Abbasids to retreat into Armenia.

summary: Sabin, ruler of Bulgaria, fled to Mesembria and escaped to Constantinople, where Emperor Constantine V welcomed him.
text: Sabin, ruler (khagan) of Bulgaria, flees to the Byzantine fortress city of Mesembria, from where he escapes to Constantinople. Constantine V arranges for the transfer of Sabin's family from Bulgaria.

summary: Emperor Constantine V deposed Patriarch Constantine II after discovering a conspiracy, appointing Nicetas I in his place.
text: Summer – Patriarch Constantine II is deposed and jailed, after the discovery of Constantine Podopagouros' plot against Constantine V. Nicetas I is appointed patriarch of Constantinople.

summary: Byzantine official Constantine Podopagouros was executed in Constantinople for plotting against Emperor Constantine V.
text: August 25: Constantine Podopagouros, Byzantine official

summary: Byzantine general Strategios Podopagouros was executed in Constantinople for conspiring against Emperor Constantine V.
text: August 25: Strategios Podopagouros, Byzantine general

summary: Emperor Constantine V invaded Bulgaria, burnt settlements around Pliska, and concluded a peace treaty with Khan Pagan.
text: Byzantine–Bulgarian War: Emperor Constantine V invades Bulgaria across the Balkan Mountains, setting afire some settlements around the Bulgarian capital of Pliska. Constantine accepts a peace agreement with Pagan, the Bulgar ruler (khagan), whose land is in anarchy.

summary: King Pepin III received a Byzantine delegation at Gentilly to discuss Italian politics and iconoclasm.
text: Pepin III receives a Byzantine delegation at his court in Gentilly (southern suburbs of Paris). They discuss foreign policy regarding Italy, and Byzantine Iconoclasm.

summary: Pope Paul I died in Rome, after which Duke Toto of Nepi orchestrated the election of his brother Constantine II as pope.
text: Pope Paul I dies at Rome after a 10-year reign, in which he has protested against Constantine V's revival of Iconoclasm at Constantinople. He gives refuge to Greek monks who were expelled from the Byzantine Empire, and moves the relics of many saints from the catacombs to Roman churches. Duke Toto of Nepi has his layman brother elected to succeed Paul, under the name Constantine II.

summary: Constantine II, deposed Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, was executed in Constantinople.
text: Constantine II, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Pope Stephen III convened the Lateran Council in Rome to reform papal election procedures and condemn iconoclasm.
text: 15 – Pope Stephen III holds a Lateran Council: the papal election procedure (abuse of which has led to the election of antipopes) is changed, and the iconoclasm of the Council of Hieria is anathematized.

summary: Michael I Rangabe, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: Michael I, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (d. 844)

summary: Michael II, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: Michael II, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (d. 829)

summary: Prokopia, future Byzantine empress, was born.
text: Prokopia, empress of the Byzantine Empire

summary: Constantine VI, future emperor of the Byzantine Empire, was born.
text: Constantine VI, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (d. 797)

summary: Adrian I succeeded Pope Stephen III as the bishop of Rome.
text: Pope Stephen III dies after a 3½-year reign, in which he has approved the acceptable reverence of icons in the Eastern Church. On February 1 he is succeeded by Adrian I (also referred to as Hadrian) as the 95th pope of Rome.

summary: Charlemagne besieged King Desiderius in Pavia, while Adalgis fled to Emperor Constantine V in Constantinople and the Franks captured Verona and Mortara.
text: Siege of Pavia: Charlemagne besieges Pavia, which is poorly stocked with food. King Desiderius remains in the capital, and orders his son Adalgis to defend Verona to guard Gerberga, and the children of Carloman I. After a short siege, Adalgis flees to Constantinople, where he is received by Emperor Constantine V. Meanwhile, the Franks capture the cities of Verona and Mortara.

summary: Byzantine abbot and saint Peter of Atroa was born.
text: Peter of Atroa, Byzantine abbot and saint (d. 837)

summary: Byzantine Emperor Constantine V ambushed and decisively defeated a Bulgarian raiding force in southwestern Macedonia.
text: Battle of Berzitia: The Bulgarian ruler (khagan) Telerig sends a small raiding army (12,000 men) to strike into the southwest of Macedonia, and capture Berzitia. Emperor Constantine V is informed about this raid by his spies in Pliska, and assembles an enormous force (80,000 men). He surprises the Bulgarians, who did not expect to find a Byzantine army there, and defeats them decisively. The Bulgars suffer heavy losses.

summary: Bulgarian ruler Telerig deceived Constantine V into identifying Byzantine agents in Pliska and executed them all.
text: Telerig sends a message to Constantine V, stating that he is going to flee in exile to Constantinople. In exchange, he asks the emperor to reveal the spies to his associates in Pliska for their own safety. Constantine sends the Bulgarian government a list of the spies; however, Telerig executes them all, and eliminates the Byzantine spy network within his government.

summary: Leo IV succeeded his father Constantine V as Byzantine emperor after Constantine died on campaign in Bulgaria.
text: Emperor Constantine V dies while on a campaign in Bulgaria. In his 34-year reign he has suppressed monasticism and image worship, restored aqueducts, revived commerce, and repopulated Constantinople. He is succeeded by his 25-year-old son Leo IV ("the Khazar"), who continues Constantine's campaigns against the Bulgars and Muslim Arabs.

summary: The Abbasid Caliphate crushed an Armenian uprising at the Battle of Bagrevand, driving several noble families into Byzantine territory.
text: Battle of Bagrevand: The Abbasids put an end to an Armenian rebellion. Muslim control over Transcaucasia is solidified, while several major Armenian nakharar families, notably the Mamikonian, lose power and flee to the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Leo V the Armenian, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: Leo V, Byzantine emperor (d. 820)

summary: Theodosia, future Byzantine empress, was born.
text: Theodosia, Byzantine empress

summary: Theophanes the Branded, Byzantine monk and hymnographer, was born.
text: Theophanes the Branded, Byzantine monk (d. 845)

summary: Byzantine Emperor Constantine V died while campaigning against the Bulgarians.
text: Constantine V, Byzantine emperor (b. 718)

summary: Leo IV the Khazar crowned his five-year-old son Constantine VI as co-emperor and suppressed a subsequent rebellion led by his half-brother Caesar Nikephoros.
text: Emperor Leo IV ("the Khazar") appoints his 5-year-old son Constantine VI co-ruler of the Byzantine Empire. This leads to an uprising, led by one of Leo's half-brothers, Caesar Nikephoros, the second son of former emperor Constantine V. The revolt is quickly suppressed. Fortunately for Nikephoros, his only punishment is to be stripped of his titles, while the rest of the conspirators are blinded, tonsured, and exiled to Cherson (southern Crimea) under guard.

summary: Saint George the Standard-Bearer, archbishop of Mitylene, was born.
text: Saint George the Standard-Bearer, archbishop (d. 821)

summary: Michael Lachanodrakon repulsed an Abbasid invasion by defeating Arab forces at Germanikeia and resettling captives in Thrace.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Emperor Leo IV ("the Khazar") repulses an Abbasid invasion in Anatolia. A Byzantine expeditionary force under Michael Lachanodrakon, military governor (strategos) of the Thracesian Theme, defeats the Muslim-Arabs at the fortress city of Germanikeia in Cilicia (modern Turkey). He plunders the region and takes many captives, mostly Jacobites, who are resettled in Thrace.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Leo IV died and was succeeded by his young son Constantine VI under the regency of Empress Irene and Staurakios.
text: Emperor Leo IV ("the Khazar") dies after a 5-year reign, in which he has been dominated by his wife Irene of Athens, an iconodule. He is succeeded by his 9-year-old son Constantine VI; due to his minority, Irene and her chief minister Staurakios exercise a regency over him.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Leo IV died in Constantinople.
text: Leo IV, Byzantine emperor (b. 750)

summary: Harun al-Rashid led an Abbasid invasion into Byzantine Asia Minor and captured the fortress of Magida.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Arab forces (95,000 men) under Harun al-Rashid, son of the Abbasid caliph Al-Mahdi, cross the Taurus Mountains and capture the Byzantine border fortress of Magida. Harun leaves his lieutenant Al-Rabi' ibn Yunus to besiege the city of Nakoleia (Phrygia), while another force (30,000 men), probably under Yahya ibn Khalid, is sent to raid the western coastlands of Asia Minor. Harun himself, with the main army, advances to the Opsician Theme.

summary: Empress Irene agreed to a three-year truce and tribute payment to Harun al-Rashid after Abbasid forces reached Chrysopolis.
text: Summer – Harun al-Rashid reaches as far as Chrysopolis, across the Bosporus Straits from the Byzantine capital, Constantinople. After the defection of the Armenian general Tatzates, Empress Irene accepts a three-year truce, including the annual payment of a tribute of 70,000 or 90,000 gold dinars, and the handing over of 10,000 silk garments. Harun releases all his captives (5,600 men), including chief minister Staurakios and other hostages.

summary: Emperor Constantine VI was betrothed to Rotrude, the daughter of Charlemagne.
text: Emperor Constantine VI is betrothed to the 6-year-old Rotrude, daughter of Charlemagne; Irene sends a scholar monk called Elisaeus to educate her in Greek language and manners.

summary: Staurakios led a Byzantine expedition through Greece and the Peloponnese, subduing Slavic communities and collecting tribute.
text: A Byzantine expeditionary force under Staurakios, chief minister (logothete), begins a campaign against the communities (Sclaviniae) of Greece. Setting out from Constantinople, the imperial army follows the Thracian coast into Macedonia, and then south into Thessaly, Central Greece and the Peloponnese. Staurakios restores a measure of Byzantine authority over these areas, and collects booty and tribute from the locals.

summary: Paul IV abdicated as patriarch of Constantinople.
text: Paul IV abdicates as patriarch of Constantinople.

summary: Tarasios was elected patriarch of Constantinople.
text: Tarasios is elected patriarch of Constantinople.

summary: Paul IV, former patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Paul IV, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Višeslav became ruler of Dalmatian Croatia with the backing of Pope Adrian I and the Byzantine Empire.
text: Prince (or duke) Višeslav, with the support of Pope Adrian I and the Byzantine Empire, becomes ruler of Dalmatian Croatia .

summary: Byzantine saint Antony the Younger was born.
text: Antony the Younger, Byzantine saint (d. 865)

summary: Tatzates, a Byzantine general, died.
text: Tatzates, Byzantine general

summary: Prince Arechis II of Benevento signed a peace agreement with the Duchy of Naples to counter the Frankish threat.
text: King Charles the Younger, son of Charlemagne and ruler of Aquitaine, visits Monte Cassino and Capua, both in Beneventan territory. Prince Arechis II, feeling threatened by the Franks, decides that he needs to stop quarrelling with the Byzantine Duchy of Naples so he can focus on the Frankish foe. Prince Arechis II therefore signs a peace agreement, or 'pactum', with the Duchy of Naples.

summary: Frankish and Beneventan forces defeated an invading Byzantine expeditionary army in southern Italy.
text: Empress Irene sends a Byzantine expeditionary army to invade southern Italy, but it is defeated and driven out (at Pope Adrian I's urging) by the Frankish army, allied with the forces of Benevento. She breaks off the engagement (see 782) between her son Constantine VI and the Frankish princess Rotrude, daughter of King Charlemagne.

summary: Empress Irene restored the veneration of icons at the Second Council of Nicaea, ending the first iconoclastic period.
text: Second Council of Nicaea: Empress Irene restores the veneration of icons (images of Christ and saints). This is a major victory of the monks, who will advance extensive claims to complete freedom for the Eastern Orthodox Church in religious matters. This ends the iconoclastic period in the Byzantine Empire.

summary: An Abbasid expeditionary force defeated two Byzantine armies at the Battle of Kopidnadon in Cappadocia.
text: September – Battle of Kopidnadon: An Abbasid expeditionary force crosses the Cilician Gates into the Anatolic Theme (modern Turkey). It is confronted by two Byzantine armies at Podandos in Cappadocia, who are defeated.

summary: The Franks defeated an invasion of southern Italy led by Adalgis and annexed Chieti into Spoleto.
text: Byzantine troops led by Adalgis, son of former Lombard king Desiderius, invade southern Italy. His attempts are thwarted by the Franks, who attack territories in Benevento, obtaining notably the annexion of Chieti (Spoleto).

summary: Methodios I, Patriarch of Constantinople, was born.
text: Methodios I, patriarch of Constantinople (or 800)

summary: Pepin of Italy conquered Istria and established a tributary march despite Byzantine protests.
text: King Pepin of Italy conquers Istria on the Adriatic, ignoring Byzantine protests. He establishes a tributary march, and sends missionaries.

summary: Leo of Catania, bishop of Catania and Christian saint, died.
text: Leo of Catania, saint and bishop of Catania (b. 709)

summary: The Armeniac Theme revolted against Empress Irene and proclaimed Constantine VI sole ruler of the Byzantine Empire, leading to Irene's confinement at Constantinople.
text: September – The Armeniac Theme, located in northeastern Asia Minor (modern Turkey), revolts against Empress Irene, and declares the 19-year-old Constantine VI sole ruler of the Byzantine Empire. Other themes follow its example, and imprison their strategoi. Constantine sends his iconoclast general Michael Lachanodrakon, to ensure that the Armeniacs (his closest supporters) take an oath. Irene is confined and imprisoned in her palace at Constantinople; all her eunuchs are exiled.

summary: Athanasia of Aegina, Byzantine noblewoman, monastic founder, and saint, was born.
text: Athanasia of Aegina, Byzantine noblewoman, adviser and saint

summary: Emperor Constantine VI suppressed a rebellion and restored his mother Irene of Athens as co-empress of the Byzantine Empire.
text: Spring – Emperor Constantine VI suppresses a rebellion, and restores his mother Irene to her former position as co-empress of the Byzantine Empire. The rival factions in Constantinople continue their intrigues against Constantine.

summary: Bulgarian forces under Kardam defeated the Byzantine army led by Emperor Constantine VI at the Battle of Marcellae.
text: Battle of Marcellae: Constantine VI leads a Byzantine expeditionary force into northern Thrace. At the border castle of Marcellae, near the modern town of Karnobat (Bulgaria), the Bulgarians under Kardam defeat the Byzantines.

summary: Michael Lachanodrakon, Byzantine general, died at the Battle of Marcellae.
text: Michael Lachanodrakon, Byzantine general (strategos)

summary: Theophylact, future Byzantine co-emperor, was born.
text: Theophylact, Byzantine co-emperor

summary: Empress Irene organized a conspiracy against her son Constantine VI, had him blinded and exiled, and assumed sole rule of the Byzantine Empire.
text: April 19 or August 19 – Empress Irene organizes a conspiracy against her son Constantine VI. He is captured and blinded; Irene exiles him to Principo, where he dies shortly thereafter of his wounds. Irene begins a 5-year reign, and calls herself basileus ("emperor") of the Byzantine Empire. (Sources and historians conflict on whether this was in April or August.)

summary: Ignatios, future patriarch of Constantinople, was born.
text: Ignatius I, patriarch of Constantinople (or 798)

summary: Constantine VI, deposed Byzantine emperor, died of his wounds on the island of Principo.
text: Constantine VI, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (b. 771)

summary: Future Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople Ignatius I was born.
text: Ignatius I, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne Emperor of the Romans at Old Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome.
text: Charlemagne, king of the Franks, is crowned Holy Roman Emperor by Pope Leo III as Charles I, with the title "Emperor of the Romans". The coronation takes place during Mass at the Basilica of St. Peter in Rome, on Christmas Day. The Frankish Empire is formed in Western Europe, which is not recognized by Empress Irene at Constantinople. This triggers a series of disputes with the Byzantines around who is officially ruling the former Western Roman Empire.

summary: Future ecumenical patriarch Methodios I of Constantinople was born.
text: Methodios I, patriarch of Constantinople (or 788)

summary: Byzantine chief minister Staurakios died.
text: Staurakios, Byzantine chief minister

summary: Empress Irene was deposed and banished to Lesbos, and Nikephoros I was crowned Byzantine emperor.
text: Empress Irene is deposed after a 5-year reign, and banished to Lesbos. High-ranking patricians place Nikephoros, the minister of finance (logothetes tou genikou), on the throne. He is crowned in the Hagia Sophia at Constantinople, by Patriarch Tarasios, as emperor of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Caliph Harun al-Rashid established the line of succession during the hajj to Mecca, naming al-Amin as his primary heir.
text: The Mecca Protocol: Caliph Harun al-Rashid and the leading officials of the Abbasid Caliphate perform the hajj to Mecca, where the line of succession is finalized. Harun's eldest son al-Amin is named heir, but his second son al-Ma'mun is named as al-Amin's heir, and ruler of a broadly autonomous Khurasan. A third son, al-Qasim, is added as third heir, and receives responsibility over the frontier areas with the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Influential Byzantine noblewoman Theoktiste died.
text: Theoctista, politically influential Byzantine woman (b. 740)

summary: Nikephoros I and Charlemagne settled imperial boundaries in the Adriatic Sea through the Pax Nicephori.
text: Emperors Nikephoros I and Charlemagne settle their imperial boundaries in the Adriatic Sea, and sign the Pax Nicephori ("Peace of Nikephoros"). The Byzantines retain control of the coastal cities and islands in Dalmatian Croatia, while Frankish rule is accepted over Istria and the Dalmatian hinterland. Venice is recognized as independent by the Byzantine Empire.
names: Byzantine Empire under the Nikephorian dynasty

summary: General Bardanes Tourkos was proclaimed emperor by Anatolian themes and marched on Chrysopolis before negotiating peace.
text: Summer – Bardanes Tourkos, Byzantine general (strategos), is proclaimed emperor by the troops of the Anatolic, Opsikion, Thracian and Bucellarian themes. The 'rebel' army marches to Chrysopolis, a suburb of Constantinople. After the defection of two of his trusted aides, future emperors Leo the Armenian and Michael the Amorian, Bardanes negotiates peace.

object: Byzantine Empire under the Nikephorian dynasty
summary: Khan Krum of the Bulgarian Empire began expanding his territory and raided the northern Byzantine frontier.
text: May – Krum, ruler (khan) of the Bulgarian Empire, begins his territorial expansion and raids the Byzantine northern frontier. He leads his warriors — mostly Bulgars, Slavs, Thracians and Macedonians — across the Carpathian Mountains, over the Danube River, and throughout Transylvania, Thrace, and Macedonia.
names: Byzantine Empire under the Nikephorian dynasty

summary: Former Byzantine empress Irene of Athens died in exile.
text: Irene of Athens, Byzantine empress

summary: An Abbasid expeditionary force defeated Byzantine Emperor Nikephoros I at the Battle of Krasos in Phrygia.
text: Battle of Krasos: Emperor Nikephoros I refuses to pay the tribute imposed by Caliph Harun al-Rashid of the Abbasid Caliphate. A Muslim-Arab expeditionary force invades Asia Minor. During a surprise attack, Nikephoros suffers a major defeat against the Saracens at Krasos in Phrygia. According to Arabian sources, the Byzantines lose 40,700 men and 4,000 pack animals, while Nikephoros himself is almost killed, but saved by the bravery of his officers.
names: Byzantine Empire under the Nikephorian dynasty

summary: Emperor Charlemagne completed the conquest of Saxony and re-established the diocese of Bremen while Venice aligned with Pepin of Italy.
text: Summer – Emperor Charlemagne finishes the conquest of Saxony. The Carolingian administration in the north is restored and the diocese of Bremen is re-established. Venice, torn by infighting, switches allegiance from Constantinople to King Pepin of Italy, son of Charlemagne.

summary: A Byzantine relief army under Skleros defeated besieging Slavic tribes and retook Patras.
text: Siege of Patras: Local Slavic tribes of the Peloponnese lay siege to the city of Patras (modern Greece), with aid from an Arab fleet. A Byzantine relief army under Skleros, military governor (strategos) from Corinth, is sent and retakes the city. The captured Slavs in Patras are made slaves, and a church is dedicated to St. Andrew.

summary: Harun al-Rashid led an invasion into Cappadocia and captured, sacked, and razed Heraclea Cybistra.
text: Arab–Byzantine wars: Caliph Harun al-Rashid leads a huge military expedition, assembling men from Syria, Palestine, Persia, and Egypt. The invasion army (reportedly 135,000 men) departs from Raqqa, residence of Harun, and enters Cappadocia through the Cilician Gates, sacking several Byzantine fortresses and cities. Heraclea is captured after a month-long siege (August/September). The city is plundered and razed; its inhabitants are enslaved and deported to the Abbasid Caliphate.

summary: Humayd ibn Ma'yuf al-Hajuri raided Cyprus and captured sixteen thousand inhabitants as slaves.
text: Arab–Byzantine wars: An Abbasid fleet under Humayd ibn Ma'yuf al-Hajuri raids Cyprus, carrying off 16,000 inhabitants as slaves.

summary: Nikephoros I was elected patriarch of Constantinople, succeeding Tarasios.
text: Nikephoros I is elected patriarch of Constantinople, succeeding Tarasios.

summary: Tarasios, patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Tarasios, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Emperor Nikephoros I was forced to sue for peace with Caliph Harun al-Rashid, agreeing to pay tribute and dismantle border fortifications.
text: Emperor Nikephoros I is forced to sue for peace, on condition of paying 50,000 nomismata to Caliph Harun al-Rashid, and agrees to a yearly tribute. Nikephoros promises not to rebuild the dismantled forts. Rashid recalls his forces from various sieges, and evacuates Byzantine territory.

place.title: Byzantine Empire under the Nikephorian dynasty

names: Byzantine Empire under the Nikephorian dynasty

summary: Humayd ibn Ma'yuf al-Hajuri led an Abbasid fleet raiding the Peloponnese, Rhodes, and Myra.
text: An Abbasid fleet under Humayd ibn Ma'yuf al-Hajuri raids the Peloponnese, Rhodes and Myra.

actor: Byzantine Empire under the Nikephorian dynasty
summary: The Byzantine relief of the Siege of Patras brought an end to independent South Slavic rule in the Peloponnese.
text: Siege of Patras: This marks the end of independent rule by the South Slavs in the Peloponnese (or 805).
cast: Byzantine Empire under the Nikephorian dynasty
names: Byzantine Empire under the Nikephorian dynasty

states.value: Byzantine Empire under the Nikephorian dynasty

summary: Krum, ruler of the Bulgarian Empire, captured the fortress of Serdica after a siege, razing its walls and slaughtering the Byzantine garrison.
text: Spring – Siege of Serdica: Krum, ruler (khan) of the Bulgarian Empire, captures the fortress of Serdica (modern Sofia), after a long siege. According to Byzantine sources, he massacres the garrison (supposedly 6,000 men), sacks the city, and razes the city walls, before returning with much loot to Bulgaria. In the following years (and centuries), Serdica will serve as a base for the expansion of the Bulgars to the south of the Balkans.

summary: A Frankish flotilla at Comacchio defeated an attacking Byzantine fleet in the Venetian Lagoon.
text: A Byzantine fleet lands in the Venetian Lagoon, and attacks a Frankish flotilla at Comacchio, but is defeated. Doge Obelerio degli Antenori marries a Frankish bride, Carola; she becomes the first dogaressa of Venice.
cast: Carola, wife of Obelerio degli Antenori
names: Carola, wife of Obelerio degli Antenori

summary: Charlemagne recognized Byzantine dominance over Venice and Dalmatia following the expulsion of Frankish forces.
text: Spring – The Venetian dukes change sides again, submitting to King Pepin, under the authority of his father Charlemagne, who then proceeds to take Venice. Emperor Nikephoros I sends a Byzantine fleet to Dalmatia, prompting Pepin to withdraw to the mainland. A legate is dispatched to Venice, where he deposes the turncoat dukes, before continuing on to Aachen, to negotiate a peace with Charlemagne. Charlemagne recognises Byzantine dominance over Venice and Dalmatia in the Adriatic Sea.

summary: Kassia, Byzantine abbess, poet, and composer, was born.
text: Kassia, Byzantine abbess and hymnographer

summary: Photios I, ecumenical patriarch of Constantinople, was born.
text: Photius I, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Emperor Nikephoros I rejected Bulgarian peace terms and led a large Byzantine expeditionary force into Bulgaria.
text: Byzantine–Bulgarian War: Emperor Nikephoros I organises a new campaign against the Bulgarian Empire, gathering an expeditionary force (most of the Roman army) from all parts of the empire. He is accompanied by high-ranking officials and aristocrats, including his son Stauracius and brother-in-law Michael I Rangabe (both later emperors temporarily). Krum, ruler (khan) of Bulgaria, sends envoys to sue for peace. Nikephoros refuses to accept the terms and marches through the Balkan passes towards Pliska, the Bulgarian capital.

summary: Nikephoros I destroyed Bulgarian armies, captured and sacked the capital Pliska, and plundered Krum's treasury.
text: Nikephoros I reaches Pliska, and destroys a Bulgarian army of 12,000 elite soldiers who guard the stronghold. Another hastily assembled relief force of 50,000 soldiers suffers a similar fate. The Byzantines capture the defenseless capital. Nikephoros plunders the city and captures Krum's treasury. He burns the countryside, slaughters sheep and pigs, as he pursues the retreating Bulgars southwest towards Serdica (modern-day Sofia).

summary: Krum defeated the Byzantine army in the Battle of Vărbitsa Pass and killed Emperor Nikephoros I, fashioning his skull into a silver drinking cup.
text: Battle of Vărbitsa Pass: Nikephoros I is trapped (probably in the Vărbitsa Pass) and defeated by the Bulgars, who use the tactics of ambush and surprise night attacks to immobilize the Byzantine forces. Nikephoros himself is killed; Krum has the emperor's head carried back in triumph on a pole, where it is cleaned out, lined with silver and made into a jeweled skull cup, which he allows his Slavic princes (archons) to drink from with him.

summary: Staurakios was crowned emperor of the Byzantine Empire at Adrianople while paralyzed from wounds suffered at the Battle of Pliska.
text: Stauracius is installed as emperor at Adrianople (the first time a Byzantine emperor is crowned outside Constantinople). Because of a sword wound near his neck (during the Battle of Pliska), Stauracius is paralyzed. The imperial court is split between the noble factions of his wife Theophano and his sister Prokopia.

summary: Michael I was declared emperor of the Byzantine Empire, forcing the incapacitated Staurakios to abdicate and retire to a monastery.
text: Michael I is declared emperor of the Byzantine Empire; Stauracius is forced by senior officials to retire to a monastery.

summary: Basil I, future emperor of the Byzantine Empire, was born.
text: Basil I, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (d. 886)

summary: Byzantine Emperor Nikephoros I was killed at the Battle of Pliska fighting the Bulgars.
text: Nikephoros I, emperor of the Byzantine Empire

summary: Former Byzantine emperor Staurakios died in a monastery in Constantinople from wounds received at Pliska.
text: Ex-emperor Staurakios, a son of Nikephoros I, dies of putrefaction in his wounds (see 811) in a monastery. He has reigned only two months and eight days, before being exiled by senior officials in Constantinople.

summary: Emperor Michael I recognized Charlemagne as emperor of the Frankish Empire in exchange for the return of Venice to the Byzantine Empire.
text: Emperor Michael I re-opens peace negotiations with the Franks, and recognizes Charlemagne as emperor (basileus) of the Frankish Empire. In exchange for this recognition, Venice is returned to the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Bulgarian forces under Krum invaded the Byzantine Empire and captured the fortress cities of Develt and Mesembria.
text: Byzantine–Bulgarian War: The Bulgars, led by Krum, ruler (khan) of the Bulgarian Empire, launch an invasion against the Byzantines. They capture the fortress cities of Develt and Mesembria, near the Black Sea.

summary: The Republic of Amalfi dispatched galleys to assist the Byzantine strategos of Sicily against Aghlabid invaders.
text: The Republic of Amalfi sends galleys to support the Byzantine general (strategos) of Sicily, Gregorio, against the Aghlabid invaders. It is one of the earliest evidences of the independence of the city.

summary: Byzantine nun and saint Theodora of Thessaloniki was born on Aegina.
text: Theodora of Thessaloniki, Byzantine nun and saint (d. 892)

summary: Former Byzantine emperor Staurakios died in exile in Constantinople.
text: Staurakios, Byzantine emperor

summary: Nikephoros, Caesar and son of Byzantine emperor Constantine V, died in exile.
text: Nikephoros, son of Constantine V

summary: Krum of Bulgaria defeated Byzantine Emperor Michael I Rangabe at the Battle of Versinikia near Edirne.
text: Battle of Versinikia: The Bulgars, led by Krum, ruler (khan) of the Bulgarian Empire, defeat Emperor Michael I near Edirne (modern Turkey). The Byzantine army (26,000 men) is destroyed by a counter-attack of Bulgarian heavy cavalry, while trapped in the valley. Krum captures the Byzantine camp and a rich prize, including gold and weaponry.

summary: Michael I Rangabe abdicated as Byzantine emperor in favor of Leo the Armenian and entered a monastery.
text: Michael I, under threat by conspiracies, abdicates in favor of his general Leo the Armenian, and becomes a monk (under the name Athanasius). His sons are castrated to prevent them succeeding the Byzantine throne, and relegated into monasteries. One of them, Niketas (renamed Ignatius), eventually becomes a patriarch of Constantinople.

summary: Krum escaped a Byzantine ambush outside the walls of Constantinople and ravaged Eastern Thrace in retaliation.
text: Krum reaches Constantinople, and sets his camp outside the walls. He is given an invitation, and a promise of safe conduct, to meet Leo V. Krum sets out unarmed for the capital with only a small escort, but is ambushed and manages to escape. After this unsuccessful Byzantine murder attempt, the Bulgars ravage much of Eastern Thrace.

summary: Krum captured Adrianople after a siege and deported around ten thousand inhabitants to Bulgarian territory north of the Danube.
text: Autumn – Siege of Adrianople: Krum captures Adrianople—one of the most important Byzantine fortresses in Thrace—after being attacked with siege engines. The garrison is forced to surrender, due to starvation. On the orders of Krum, the population of the surrounding area (numbering about 10,000) is transferred to Bulgarian territory, north of the Danube.

summary: Ashot I became the first Bagratid presiding prince of Iberia under Byzantine protection.
text: Ashot I ("the Great") becomes the first Georgian Bagratid prince of Iberia, under Byzantine protection.

summary: Theophilos, future emperor of the Byzantine Empire, was born.
text: Theophilus, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (d. 842)

summary: Soldiers broke into the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople and appealed to the tomb of Constantine V, marking the start of the second Byzantine Iconoclasm.
text: A group of soldiers broke into the Church of the Holy Apostles and pleaded with the body of the iconoclast basileus Constantine V to restore the Empire, marking the beginning of the second Byzantine Iconoclasm.

summary: Krum, ruler of the Bulgarian Empire, died of a stroke and was succeeded by his son Omurtag.
text: Byzantine–Bulgarian Wars: Over the winter Krum, ruler (khan) of the Bulgarian Empire, had assembled a huge army (including Slavs and Avars), for a campaign against the Byzantine Empire. But before he sets out for a major attack on Constantinople, he dies of a stroke. Krum is succeeded by his son Omurtag.

summary: Leo V the Armenian clashed over iconoclasm with Patriarch Nikephoros I of Constantinople, who was excommunicated.
text: Byzantine Iconoclasm: Conflict erupts between Emperor Leo V and Patriarch Nikephoros, on the subject of iconoclasm. The latter is excommunicated.

summary: Byzantine abbot Plato of Sakkoudion died.
text: Plato of Sakkoudion, Byzantine abbot

summary: Emperor Leo V the Armenian signed a thirty-year peace treaty with Khan Omurtag in Constantinople.
text: Byzantine–Bulgarian Treaty: Emperor Leo V the Armenian signs a 30-year peace agreement in Constantinople with Omurtag, ruler (khan) of the Bulgarian Empire. The Rhodope Mountains become the Byzantine border again, and Leo regains its lost Black Sea cities, after the Bulgars have them demolished.

summary: A council led by Patriarch Theodotus I at the Hagia Sophia reinstituted Byzantine iconoclasm.
text: Synod of Constantinople: A council led by patriarch Theodotus I, in the Hagia Sophia, reinstitutes iconoclasm.

summary: Sicilian abbot Leoluca was born in Corleone.
text: Leoluca, Sicilian abbot

summary: Byzantine missionary and bishop Methodius was born in Thessalonica.
text: Methodius, Byzantine missionary and bishop (d. 885)

summary: Future Byzantine empress Theodora was born in Paphlagonia.
text: Theodora, Byzantine empress

summary: Byzantine monk and chronicler Theophanes the Confessor died in exile on Samothrace.
text: Theophanes the Confessor, Byzantine monk (or 818)

summary: Michael the Confessor, bishop of Synnada, died.
text: Michael the Confessor, bishop of Synnada

summary: Theophanes the Confessor, Byzantine chronicler and monk, died in exile on Samothrace.
text: Theophanes the Confessor, Byzantine monk (or 817)

summary: Leo V the Armenian was assassinated by conspirators in the Hagia Sophia at Constantinople and succeeded by Michael II.
text: Emperor Leo V (the Armenian) is assassinated by conspirators in the Hagia Sophia, at Constantinople. Though unarmed, he fights back fiercely but dies of his wounds. He is succeeded by Michael II, the commander of the palace guard (excubitores). Leo's family (including his mother and his wife Theodosia) are exiled to monasteries in Princes' Islands.

summary: Emperor Leo V the Armenian died in Constantinople.
text: December 25, Leo V, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (b. 775)

summary: Thomas the Slav rebelled against Michael II, gained control of Anatolian themes, made peace with Caliph Al-Ma'mun, and blockaded Constantinople.
text: Byzantine general Thomas the Slav leads a revolt, and secures control over most of the Byzantine themes (provinces) in Anatolia. He gets recognition from the Abbasid Caliphate, and concludes a peace treaty with Caliph al-Ma'mun. Thomas crosses with his fleet from Abydos to Thrace, and blockades Emperor Michael II in Constantinople; but Thomas' first attack on the capital fails.

summary: Abbasid forces conducted border skirmishes and raids deep into Byzantine Anatolia.
text: By the time Al-Ma'mun becomes caliph, the Arabs and the Byzantines have settled down into border skirmishing, with Arab raids deep into Anatolia to capture booty.

summary: George the Standard-Bearer, archbishop of Mytilene, died.
text: George the Standard-Bearer, archbishop of Mytilene (b. c. 776)

summary: Thomas the Slav unsuccessfully besieged Constantinople, where his fleet was destroyed by Emperor Michael II using Greek fire.
text: Byzantine general and usurper Thomas the Slav continues his revolt against Emperor Michael II. He unsuccessfully besieges Constantinople, while his fleet is destroyed by Michael's fleet, using Greek fire.

summary: Omurtag of Bulgaria sent a relief army and defeated the Byzantine rebel forces at Kedouktos near Heraclea.
text: Battle of Kedouktos (near Heraclea): Khan Omurtag of Bulgaria sends a relief army, and defeats the Byzantine rebels.

summary: Gregory Pterotos, Byzantine general, died.
text: Gregory Pterotos, Byzantine general (strategos)

summary: Emperor Michael II defeated the rebel forces of Thomas the Slav in Thrace and executed him after a five-month siege of Arkadiopolis.
text: Emperor Michael II defeats the rebel forces under Thomas the Slav in Thrace. He and his supporters are forced to seek refuge in Arkadiopolis (modern Turkey). After five months of blockade, Thomas surrenders and is delivered to Michael, seated on a donkey and bound in chains. He pleads for clemency and prostrates before Michael, but is executed.

summary: Thekla, Byzantine empress and wife of Michael II, died.
text: Thekla, Byzantine empress

summary: Thomas the Slav, rebel leader and rival claimant to the Byzantine throne, was executed.
text: Thomas the Slav, Byzantine general and usurper

summary: A major earthquake damaged the city walls of Panion and Heraclea Perinthus, prompting both rebel-held cities to surrender to Emperor Michael II.
text: February – A major earthquake strikes Byzantium in Asia Minor (now part of western Turkey) and part of Greece, damaging the city walls of Theodosiopolis (now Barbaros in Turkey) and Heraclea Perinthus at the same time that the forces of Byzantine Emperor Michael II the Amorian are suppressing the rebellion by Thomas the Slav. Both cities surrender after the natural event.

summary: Emperor Michael II celebrated a Roman triumph in Constantinople after defeating the rebellion of Thomas the Slav.
text: May – In Constantinople and throughout the Byzantine Empire, Michael II celebrates the festival of Triumph to mark his return to the capital after defeating the rebellion of Thomas the Slav

summary: Euphemius organized an uprising against Emperor Michael II, proclaimed himself emperor in Syracuse, but was defeated and driven out to North Africa.
text: May – Euphemius, Byzantine admiral, organises an uprising in Sicily against Emperor Michael II. He proclaims himself Emperor (with the title of basileus) in Syracuse, independent from Constantinople. In turn, Euphemius is defeated by Byzantine troops (reinforcements from the East), and is driven out to North Africa.

summary: Cyril, Byzantine missionary and linguist, was born in Thessalonica.
text: Cyril, Byzantine missionary and bishop (d. 885)

summary: Theodore the Studite, Byzantine monk and abbot, died in exile.
text: Theodore the Studite, Byzantine abbot (b. 759)

summary: Emir Ziyadat Allah I sent an Aghlabid Muslim expeditionary force under Asad ibn al-Furat to support Euphemius, landing at Mazara del Vallo in Sicily.
text: Euphemius, exiled Byzantine admiral, asks for the help of North African Arabs, to retake Sicily and Malta from the Byzantines. Emir Ziyadat Allah I of Ifriqiya promises to return the islands to Euphemius, in exchange for a yearly tribute, and sends an Arab Muslim expeditionary force of 10,000 men under the 70-year-old Asad ibn al-Furat, which lands at Mazara del Vallo in Sicily.

summary: Muslim forces led by Asad ibn al-Furat besieged Syracuse in support of the rebel Byzantine army.
text: Fall – Siege of Syracuse: Muslim forces under Asad ibn al-Furat, in support of the rebel Byzantine army, besiege Syracuse, Sicily.

summary: Cyril, Byzantine scholar and missionary to the Slavs, was born in Thessalonica.
text: Cyril, Byzantine missionary and bishop (d. 869)

summary: Muslim forces under Asad ibn al-Furat defeated a Byzantine relief army at Syracuse, but were later forced by disease and starvation to break off the siege.
text: Siege of Syracuse: The Muslims under Asad ibn al-Furat defeat a Byzantine relief army sent from Palermo, and backed by a Venetian fleet led by Giustiniano Participazio. Al-Furat decides to break off the siege at Syracuse, as his forces suffer greatly from lack of food. Later he dies during an outbreak of an epidemic.

summary: Emissaries from the besieged Byzantine garrison at Castrogiovanni murdered the rebel Byzantine admiral Euphemius.
text: Summer – Euphemius, Byzantine admiral, is murdered by emissaries from the Byzantine garrison at Castrogiovanni, which is besieged by the Muslims. Threatened by Byzantine reinforcements arriving from Constantinople, the survivors burn their ships and retreat overland westward to Mazara del Vallo.

summary: Saracen pirates destroyed the ancient city of Kydonia on the northwest coast of Crete.
text: Kydonia, on the northwest coast of Crete, is destroyed by Saracen pirates .

summary: Rebel Byzantine admiral Euphemius was assassinated at Castrogiovanni.
text: Euphemius, Byzantine admiral and usuper

summary: Nikephoros I, former Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople and defender of icon veneration, died.
text: Nikephoros I, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Theophilos succeeded his father Michael II as sole emperor of the Byzantine Empire following Michael's death in Constantinople.
text: Emperor Michael II dies after an 8-year reign in Constantinople, and is succeeded by his 16-year-old son Theophilos, as sole emperor of the Byzantine Empire. He continues his father's ideology of iconoclasm.

summary: The Saracens of Crete defeated the Byzantine fleet at the Battle of Thasos and raided islands throughout the Aegean Sea.
text: October – Battle of Thasos: Saracens from the newly founded Emirate of Crete almost annihilate the Byzantine fleet at Thasos, close to the coast of Thrace. The Cyclades and other islands in the Aegean Sea are pillaged.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Michael II died in Constantinople and was succeeded by his son Theophilos.
text: Michael II, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (b. 770)

summary: Emperor Theophilos married the Armenian noblewoman Theodora in Hagia Sophia at Constantinople.
text: Emperor Theophilos, 16, marries the Armenian noblewoman Theodora, in the Hagia Sophia at Constantinople. He chooses her during a representation of a bride-show; she becomes empress (Augusta) of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Muslim reinforcements from Ifriqiya and Al-Andalus defeated Byzantine forces in Sicily before retreating to Mazara del Vallo due to plague.
text: Byzantine–Arab War: Muslim reinforcements from Ifriqiya and Al-Andalus (modern Spain) defeat Byzantine forces under Theodotus in Sicily, but a plague once again compels them to retreat to Mazara del Vallo, and evacuate to North Africa.

summary: Emperor Theophilos invaded Abbasid dominions and sacked Tarsus before suffering defeat in Cappadocia.
text: Byzantine–Arab War: Emperor Theophilos invades the Abbasid dominions, and reaches the Euphrates River in north-eastern Syria. He captures and sacks the city of Tarsus, but is defeated in Cappadocia.

summary: Caliph Al-Ma'mun invaded Anatolia and captured Heraclea Cybistra and Tyana from the Byzantine Empire.
text: Summer – Muslim Arabs under Caliph Al-Ma'mun launch an invasion into Anatolia (modern Turkey), and capture a number of Byzantine forts. Heraclea Cybistra and Tyana fall to the Arabs.

summary: Muslim Arabs besieged Palermo, and Byzantine commander Symeon surrendered the city.
text: Fall – Muslim Arabs reinvade Sicily, and lay siege to Palermo. Symeon, Byzantine commander of the imperial bodyguard (spatharios), surrenders the city in exchange for a safe departure.

summary: Euthymius of Sardis, Byzantine monk and bishop, died.
text: Euthymius of Sardis, Byzantine monk and bishop

summary: Caliph Al-Ma'mun captured the Byzantine fortress of Loulon after a lengthy siege.
text: Byzantine–Arab War: The Byzantine fortress of Loulon (modern Turkey) is captured by the Abbasids. Its garrison surrenders to Caliph Al-Ma'mun, after a lengthy siege.

summary: Emperor Theophilos promulgated an edict banning the usage of icons in the Byzantine Empire.
text: Emperor Theophilos promulgates a new edict against the usage of icons in the Byzantine Empire. He establishes strict punishments against idolators, and persecutes violators.

summary: Emperor Theophilos offered an armistice and tribute to the Abbasid Caliphate in exchange for Byzantine prisoners.
text: Byzantine-Arab War: Emperor Theophilos signs an armistice for peace with the Abbasid Caliphate. He offers Caliph Al-Ma'mun 100,000 gold dinars, in return for 7,000 Byzantine prisoners.

summary: Future Ecumenical Patriarch Euthymius I of Constantinople was born.
text: Euthymius I, Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople (d. 917)

summary: Byzantine official Nicetas the Patrician died.
text: Nicetas the Patrician, Byzantine official

summary: Emperor Theophilos led a Byzantine army into Mesopotamia, sacked Arsamosata and Sozopetra, and forced Melitene to pay tribute.
text: Byzantine–Arab War: Emperor Theophilos leads a massive Byzantine expeditionary force into Mesopotamia. He sacks the cities Arsamosata and Sozopetra — which some sources claim as the birthplace of Abbasid caliph Al-Mu'tasim — and forces Melitene to pay tribute.

summary: Slavs around Thessaloniki revolted against the Byzantine Empire, leading Emperor Theophilos to evacuate captives to trans-Danubian Bulgaria.
text: The Slavs in the vicinity of Thessaloniki revolt against the Byzantine Empire. Theophilos undertakes an evacuation of some Byzantine captives, who are settled in trans-Danubian Bulgaria.

summary: Bulgarian forces under minister Isbul campaigned along the Aegean coast and captured Philippi along with much of Thrace and Macedonia from the Byzantine Empire.
text: Presian I, ruler (khan) of the Bulgarian Empire, sends his prime-minister Isbul against the Smolyani (a Slavic tribe in Byzantine territory near the Struma River). The Bulgarian army campaigns along the Aegean coasts, and conquers most of Thrace and Macedonia, including the fortress city of Philippi, as recorded in the Presian Inscription.

summary: Peter of Atroa, a Byzantine abbot, died.
text: Peter of Atroa, Byzantine abbot (b. 773)

summary: Antony I, ecumenical patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Antony I, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Abbasid forces defeated Byzantine Emperor Theophilos at the Battle of Anzen.
text: Battle of Anzen: Caliph al-Mu'tasim launches a major punitive expedition against the Byzantine Empire, targeting the two major Byzantine fortress cities of central Anatolia (Ancyra and Amorium). He mobilises a vast army (80,000 men) at Tarsus, which is divided into two main forces. The northern force, under commander al-Afshin, invades the Armeniac Theme from the region of Melitene, joining up with the forces of the city's emir, Umar al-Aqta. The southern, main force, under al-Mu'tasim, passes the Cilician Gates into Cappadocia. Emperor Theophilos attacks the Abbasids, inflicting 3,000 casualties, but is heavily defeated by a counter-attack of 10,000 Turkish mounted archers. Theophilos and his guard are encircled, and barely manage to break through and escape.

summary: Abbasid forces breached, captured, and sacked the Byzantine fortress city of Amorium.
text: August – Siege of Amorium: The Abbasids besiege the Byzantine fortress city of Amorium, which is protected by 44 towers, according to the contemporary geographer Ibn Khordadbeh. Both besiegers and besieged have many siege engines, and for several days both sides exchange missile fire. However, a Muslim prisoner defects to al-Mu'tasim, and informs him about a place in the wall which has been badly damaged by heavy rainfall. The Abbasids concentrate their hits on this section, and after two days manage to breach the city wall. After two weeks of repeated attacks, the Byzantine defenders surrender. The city is sacked and plundered, 70,000 inhabitants are slaughtered, and the survivors are sold as slaves.

summary: The Hungarians raided the Lower Danube against Byzantine insurgents at the request of the Bulgarian Empire.
text: The Hungarians (also known as Magyars) who until this time have lived east of the Carpathians, raid the Lower Danube at the request of the Bulgarian Empire against the Byzantine insurgents.

summary: Michael III was born in Constantinople.
text: January – Michael III, Byzantine emperor ( 867) (most probable date: 839 is also possible)

summary: Eudokia Ingerina was born in Constantinople.
text: Eudokia Ingerina, Byzantine empress

summary: Byzantine general Constantine Kontomytes defeated Cretan Saracens near Mount Latros.
text: Constantine Kontomytes, Byzantine general (strategos) of the Thracesian Theme, inflicts a severe defeat on the Cretan Saracens. He leads a Byzantine expeditionary force, to raid the monastic community near Mount Latros (modern Turkey).

summary: A Venetian fleet failed to assist the Byzantines against the Arabs at Crotone, and Muslim forces captured Brindisi.
text: Venice sends a fleet of 60 galleys (each carrying 200 men) to assist the Byzantines in driving the Arabs from Crotone, but the attack fails. Muslim troops conquer the city of Brindisi .

summary: Byzantine Emperor Theophilos died of dysentery at Constantinople and was succeeded by his infant son Michael III with Empress Theodora as regent.
text: Emperor Theophilos dies of dysentery at Constantinople, after a 12-year reign in which he expended much effort defending the eastern frontier against the invading Muslim Arabs. Theophilos is succeeded by his 2-year-old son Michael III, with his mother Theodora as regent and the 'temporary' sole ruler of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: A council in Constantinople formally reinstated the veneration of icons, ending the Byzantine Iconoclastic Controversy.
text: The Medieval Iconoclastic Controversy ends, as a council in Constantinople formally reinstates the veneration of icons in the churches.

summary: Byzantine emperor Theophilos died at Constantinople.
text: Theophilus, Byzantine emperor (b. 813)

summary: A Byzantine expedition led by Theoktistos captured Crete, but the troops were slaughtered by Arab forces after Theoktistos abandoned them.
text: Summer – A Byzantine expedition, led by Theoktistos, conquers Crete from the Saracens. After initial success, he is forced to abandon his army, due to political intrigues in Constantinople. The troops are left behind and slaughtered by the Arabs.

summary: Empress Theodora II restored the veneration of icons throughout the Byzantine Empire, ending Byzantine Iconoclasm.
text: Feast of Orthodoxy – Official end of Iconoclasm: Empress Theodora II restores the veneration of icons in the Orthodox churches in the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Empress Theodora II ordered the persecution of the Paulicians across Anatolia, leading to the massacre of approximately 100,000 followers.
text: Theodora II orders a persecution against the Paulicians throughout Anatolia; about 100,000 followers in the Byzantine theme of Armenia are massacred.

summary: Anthony the Confessor, Byzantine archbishop of Thessalonica, died.
text: 2 November – Anthony the Confessor, Byzantine bishop of Thessalinike

summary: Abbasid Arab forces defeated a Byzantine army led by Theoktistos at the Battle of Mauropotamos in Anatolia.
text: Spring – Battle of Mauropotamos: A Byzantine expedition under Theoktistos is sent to Anatolia (modern Turkey), against the Muslim Arabs of the Abbasid Caliphate, who have raided the Byzantine themes of Cappadocia, Anatolikon, Boukellarion, and Opsikion. The Byzantines are defeated, and many of the officers defect to the Arabs.

summary: Michael I Rangabe, former Byzantine emperor living as a monk, died.
text: Michael I, former Byzantine emperor
