summary: The Byzantine Empire and the Abbasid Caliphate conducted a ten-day prisoner exchange at the River Lamos in Cilicia.
text: Byzantine–Arab War: A prisoner exchange occurs between the Byzantine Empire and the Abbasid Caliphate, at the River Lamos in Cilicia (modern Turkey). The exchanges last for 10 days, and the Byzantines recover 4,600 prisoners.

summary: The Abbasid Caliphate executed forty-two captured Byzantine officials from Amorium at Samarra after they refused to convert to Islam.
text: 42 captured Byzantine officials from Amorium are executed at Samarra, then the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate, after they repeatedly refuse attempts to convert them to Islam.

summary: Theophanes the Branded, a Byzantine monk and hymnographer, died.
text: Theophanes the Branded, Byzantine monk (b. 775)

summary: Bulgarian forces invaded Byzantine Macedonia along the Struma River, devastating Serres and Philippi.
text: Byzantine–Bulgarian War: The Bulgarians violate the peace treaty (see 815), and invade Macedonia along the River Struma. The cities of Serres and Philippi are devastated.

summary: Byzantine theologian and hermit Joannicius the Great died on Mount Olympus in Bithynia.
text: Joannicius the Great, Byzantine theologian (b. 752)

summary: Saracens under the Berber leader Kalfun captured Byzantine Bari and founded the Emirate of Bari.
text: The Saracens, under the Berber leader Kalfun, capture the Byzantine city of Bari (Southern Italy). He becomes the first ruler of the Emirate of Bari, and expands his influence on the Italian mainland with raids.

summary: Patriarch Methodios I of Constantinople died.
text: Methodius I, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Saracens conquered Ragusa in Sicily after starving its Byzantine garrison and razing the city.
text: The Saracens conquer Ragusa (Sicily), after its Byzantine garrison is forced by severe famine to surrender. The city and its castle are razed to the ground.

summary: Former Byzantine co-emperor Theophylact died in exile.
text: Theophylact, Byzantine co-emperor (b. c.793)

summary: Nicholas I Mystikos, later ecumenical patriarch of Constantinople, was born.
text: Nicholas I Mystikos, Byzantine patriarch (d. 925)

summary: A Byzantine fleet sacked and destroyed the Egyptian port city of Damietta, seizing supplies intended for Crete.
text: A Byzantine fleet (85 ships and 5,000 men) sacks and destroys the port city of Damietta, located on the Nile Delta in Egypt. A large quantity of weapons and supplies intended for the Emirate of Crete are captured.

summary: Emperor Michael III ordered the murder of his co-regent Theoktistos.
text: Theoktistos, co-regent of the Empire on behalf of 15-year old Emperor Michael III, is murdered on the orders of Michael.

summary: Saints Cyril and Methodius created the Slavic alphabet.
text: The Slavic alphabet is created by Saints Cyril and Methodius.

summary: Theoktistos, chief minister of the Byzantine Empire, was murdered.
text: Theoktistos, Byzantine chief minister

summary: Emperor Michael III overthrew the regency of his mother Theodora and appointed his uncle Bardas as de facto regent.
text: Emperor Michael III overthrows the regency of his mother Theodora. He appoints his uncle Bardas as the de facto regent and co-ruler of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: An earthquake struck Corinth in the Byzantine Empire, killing an estimated 45,000 people.
text: November – An earthquake in Corinth, Greece kills an estimated 45,000 people.

summary: Emperor Michael III banished his mother Theodora to the Gastria Monastery in Constantinople.
text: Emperor Michael III, under the influence of his uncle Bardas, banishes his mother Theodora to the Gastria Monastery. Bardas, the de facto regent, becomes the most powerful person in the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Emperor Michael III imprisoned Patriarch Ignatios I of Constantinople and replaced him with Photios I.
text: Ignatios I, patriarch of Constantinople, is imprisoned by orders of Emperor Michael III, and replaced by the layman Photius I.

summary: A Rus' fleet entered the Bosporus and pillaged the suburbs of Constantinople and the Princes' Islands.
text: Byzantine–Rus' War: A fleet of about 200 Rus' vessels sails into the Bosphorus, and starts pillaging the suburbs of Constantinople. The raiders set homes on fire, and drown and kill the citizens. Unable to do anything to repel the invaders, Patriarch Photios I urges his flock to implore the Theotokos to save the Byzantine capital. Having devastated the suburbs, the Rus' Vikings pass into the Sea of Marmara and attack the Isles of the Princes, plundering the local monasteries.

summary: Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius arrived on an embassy to Khazaria.
text: Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius arrive in Khazaria.

summary: Byzantine noblewoman and monastic founder Athanasia of Aegina died.
text: Athanasia of Aegina, Byzantine noblewoman

summary: Byzantine general Constantine Kontomytes died.
text: Constantine Kontomytes, Byzantine general

summary: The Council of Constantinople confirmed Photios the Great as patriarch and passed seventeen canons.
text: Spring – The Council of Constantinople, attended by 318 fathers and presided over by papal legates, confirms Photius the Great as patriarch, and passes 17 canons.

summary: Constantine the Philosopher invented the Slavonic alphabet to help convert the Moravians to Christianity.
text: Constantine the Philosopher (alias Saint Cyril) invents the 42-letter Slavonic alphabet (Cyrillic script) as a tool for converting the Moravians to Christianity .

summary: The Council of Shirakavan convened Armenian, Byzantine, and West-Syrian church representatives to discuss union and agreed on peaceful coexistence.
text: During the Council of Shirakavan representatives of the Armenian, Byzantine and West-Syrian Churches convenes to discuss church union. Though this is not achieved, an agreement is formulated which allows for the peaceful co-existence of Orthodox and non-Chalcedonians in the Byzantine-Armenian borderlands.

summary: A Byzantine army under Petronas annihilated invading Muslim forces led by Umar al-Aqta at the Battle of Lalakaon.
text: Battle of Lalakaon: A Byzantine army confronts an invasion by Muslim forces, led by Umar al-Aqta, Emir of Malatya. The Muslims raid deep into Byzantine territory, reaching the Black Sea coast at the port city of Amisos. Petronas annihilates the Arabs near the River Lalakaon, in Paphlagonia (modern Turkey).

summary: The Christianization of Kievan Rus began, ending the dominance of the Rus' Khaganate.
text: The Christianization of Kievan Rus begins, ceasing the 63-year-long dominance of the Rus' Khaganate .

summary: The Byzantine Empire invaded Bulgaria to impose Orthodox Christianity on Boris I.
text: The Byzantine Empire invades Bulgaria in order to impose Orthodox Christianity on Boris I.

summary: Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius arrived in Great Moravia at the request of Prince Rastislav.
text: The Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius arrive with a few disciples in Moravia, by request of Prince Rastislav.

summary: Pope Nicholas I excommunicated Patriarch Photios I of Constantinople.
text: Nicholas I excommunicates Patriarch Photios I of Constantinople.

summary: Muslim governor Ali ibn Yahya al-Armani was killed in battle against the Byzantines.
text: Ali ibn Yahya al-Armani, Muslim governor

summary: Karbeas, leader of the Paulicians, died.
text: Karbeas, leader of the Paulicians

summary: Umar al-Aqta, Emir of Melitene, died in battle against the Byzantines.
text: Umar al-Aqta, emir of Melitene

summary: Orso I Participazio succeeded the deceased Pietro Tradonico as Doge of Venice.
text: Pietro Tradonico dies after a 28-year reign. He is succeeded by Orso I Participazio, who becomes doge of Venice.

summary: Boris I converted to Orthodox Christianity at Pliska, initiating the Christianization of Bulgaria.
text: The Christianization of Bulgaria begins: Boris I, Knyaz of the Bulgarian Empire, is converted to Orthodox Christianity. His family and high-ranking dignitaries accept the Orthodox faith at the capital, Pliska - from this point onwards the rulers of the Bulgarian Empire are known as ‘Tsars’ rather than ‘Khans’.

summary: Simeon I, future ruler of the First Bulgarian Empire, was born.
text: Simeon I, ruler (tsar) of the Bulgarian Empire (or 865)

summary: Pietro Tradonico, Doge of Venice, died.
text: Pietro Tradonico, doge of Venice

summary: Boris I of Bulgaria suppressed a revolt and executed 52 leading boyars and their families.
text: Boris I, ruler (knyaz) of the Bulgarian Empire, suppresses a revolt, and orders the execution of 52 leading boyars, along with their whole families.

summary: Kassia, a Byzantine abbess, poet, and hymnographer, died.
text: Kassia, a Byzantine abbess and hymnographer, dies. She is one of the first Early Medieval composers of many hymns.

summary: Simeon I, future ruler of the Bulgarian Empire, was born.
text: Simeon I, ruler (khan) of the Bulgarian Empire (or 864)

summary: Petronas, a leading Byzantine general and uncle of Emperor Michael III, died.
text: Petronas, Byzantine general

summary: Antony the Younger, a Byzantine governor and monk, died.
text: Antony the Younger, Byzantine governor and saint (b. 785)

summary: Kassia, a Byzantine abbess and hymnographer, died.
text: Kassia, Byzantine abbess and hymnographer

summary: Basil the Macedonian murdered Byzantine regent Bardas at Miletus during an expedition against Crete.
text: Bardas, the regent of the Byzantine Empire, is murdered by Basil the Macedonian at Miletus, while conducting a large-scale expedition against the Saracen stronghold of Crete.

summary: Emperor Michael III adopted Basil the Macedonian and crowned him co-emperor of the Byzantine Empire.
text: Basil the Macedonian is crowned co-emperor of the Byzantine Empire, and is adopted by the much younger Michael III.

summary: Boris I of Bulgaria sent a diplomatic mission led by the nobleman Peter to Rome to renew ties with the West.
text: Boris I, ruler (knyaz) of the Bulgarian Empire, sends a diplomatic mission, led by the Bulgarian nobleman Peter, to Rome, in an effort to renew ties with the West.

summary: Future Byzantine Emperor Leo VI was born in Constantinople.
text: Leo VI, Byzantine emperor (d. 912)

summary: Byzantine chief minister and regent Bardas died when he was assassinated at Miletus.
text: Bardas, Byzantine chief minister and regent

summary: Emperor Michael III was murdered on the orders of co-emperor Basil I, who became the sole ruler of the Byzantine Empire and founded the Macedonian dynasty.
text: Emperor Michael III is murdered, by order of his co-emperor Basil I. Basil becomes sole ruler (basileus) of the Byzantine Empire, and founds the Macedonian Dynasty (until 1056). Basil rebuilds the Byzantine army and navy, in an effort to restore the empire.

summary: The Council of Constantinople anathematized Pope Nicholas I and the use of the Filioque clause in the Creed.
text: The Council of Constantinople is held (presided over by Patriarch Photius), which anathematizes the use of the Filioque clause in the Creed, and also Pope Nicholas I, for his attacks on the work of Greek missionaries in Bulgaria.

summary: Basil I removed and banished Patriarch Photius I and reinstated Ignatius as patriarch of Constantinople.
text: September – Photius I ("the Great"), patriarch of Constantinople, is removed from office and banished. Ignatius is reinstated as patriarch by Basil I.

summary: Stephen I, future patriarch of Constantinople, was born.
text: Stephen I, patriarch of Constantinople (d. 893)

summary: Lazarus Zographos, a Byzantine monk and painter, died.
text: Lazarus Zographos, Byzantine monk and painter

summary: Michael III, emperor of the Byzantine Empire, died.
text: Michael III, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (b. 840)

summary: Aghlabid forces under Muhammad II conquered Malta and conducted raids into mainland Italy.
text: Muslim Arab forces under Muhammad II, emir of the Aghlabid Dynasty (modern Tunisia), conquer the island of Malta and raid into the mainland of Italy.

summary: Emperor Basil I allied with Frankish Emperor Louis II and dispatched a Byzantine fleet to support the siege of Bari.
text: Summer – Emperor Basil I allies with the Frankish emperor Louis II against the Saracens. He sends a Byzantine fleet of 400 ships (according to the Annales Bertiniani), under the command of Admiral Niketas Ooryphas, to support Louis (who is besieging the city port of Bari) and to clear the south of the Adriatic Sea of Muslim raiders.

summary: An earthquake severely damaged the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, collapsing its eastern half-dome, which Basil I ordered repaired.
text: The Hagia Sophia Basilica (church) in Constantinople suffers great damage during an earthquake, which makes the eastern half-dome collapse. Basil I orders it to be repaired.

summary: Emperor Basil I and Pope Adrian II convened the Fourth Council of Constantinople, which deposed Patriarch Photios I and reinstated Ignatios.
text: The Fourth Council of Constantinople, called by Basil I and Pope Adrian II, opens. The council will condemn Photius I and depose him as patriarch, reinstating his predecessor Ignatios.

summary: Byzantine missionary Cyril died in Rome.
text: Cyril, Byzantine missionary and bishop

summary: Muslim forces led by Halaf al-Hadim conquered Malta, ending Byzantine rule on the island.
text: Byzantine–Arab War: A Muslim expeditionary force, led by Halaf al-Hadim, Arab governor of Sicily, conquers Malta. He is welcomed by the local Christian inhabitants as liberator of the agonizing Byzantine yoke. The Muslims sign a treaty with the Christians to live in peace after liberating the island from the Byzantines.

summary: The Fourth Council of Constantinople concluded, granting the Bulgarians an autocephalous archbishopric seated at Pliska.
text: The Fourth Council of Constantinople ends. The Bulgarians are granted an autocephalous archbishopric. with its seat in the capital of Pliska.

summary: Future Byzantine emperor Alexander was born.
text: Alexander III, Byzantine emperor (d. 913)

summary: Romanos I Lekapenos, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: Romanos I, Byzantine emperor (d. 948)

summary: Salih ibn Wasif, Turkish military commander of the Abbasid Caliphate, died.
text: Salih ibn Wasif, Muslim general

summary: Al-Muhtadi, caliph of the Abbasid Caliphate, was deposed and killed in Samarra.
text: Al-Muhtadi, Muslim caliph

summary: Future Doge of Venice Pietro II Candiano was born.
text: Pietro II Candiano, doge of Venice

summary: Chrysocheir, leader of the Paulicians, died.
text: Chrysocheir, leader of the Paulicians (or 878)

summary: Abbasid general Muhammad ibn Ali al-Armani was killed along the frontier by Byzantine forces.
text: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Armani, was killed at the Caliphate - Byzantine border in 873.

summary: Muslim general Muhammad ibn Ali al-Armani was killed.
text: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Armani, Muslim general

summary: The remains of Patriarch Nikephoros I were interred in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople.
text: The remains of Saint Nikephorus I are interred in the Church of the Holy Apostles, in Constantinople.

summary: An Arab fleet from Taranto sacked Comacchio and attacked Grado, where they were repelled by the Venetians.
text: Fall – An Arab fleet from Taranto sails up the Adriatic Sea and sacks Comacchio, putting it to flames. They attack Grado (bishopric of the Venetian Republic), but are repelled by the Venetians.

summary: Ibrahim II succeeded his brother Muhammad II as emir of the Aghlabid dynasty in Ifriqiya.
text: Muhammad II, emir of the Aghlabids, dies and is succeeded by his brother Ibrahim II. Towards the end of his reign, a caravan of pilgrims from Mecca introduces the plague in Ifriqiya (Tunisia).

summary: Mary the Younger, Byzantine saint, was born.
text: Mary the Younger, Byzantine saint (d. 902)

summary: Muhammad II, emir of the Aghlabids, died.
text: Muhammad II, emir of the Aghlabids

summary: Byzantine forces occupied Bari in southern Italy, and Emperor Basil I made it the capital of the new Theme of Longobardia.
text: At the invitation of Benevento, the newly-restored Byzantine fleet appears in the waters off Otranto. On the orders of Emperor Basil I, the Byzantines sail up the Adriatic Sea and reconquer part of southern Italy. The city of Bari is occupied in the name of the Byzantine Empire. Instead of holding it for his 'ally' Adelchis of Benevento, Basil makes it the capital of the new Byzantine Theme of Longobardia.

summary: The Aghlabids invaded Byzantine Sicily and laid siege to Syracuse.
text: August – Siege of Syracuse: The Aghlabids begin raiding the Byzantine territories, in the east of the island of Sicily. They besiege Syracuse, and blockade the fortress city by sea and land.

summary: Photius I was reinstated as Patriarch of Constantinople following the death of Ignatios.
text: Photius I is reinstated as patriarch of Constantinople, after the death of Ignatius.

summary: Ignatios, Patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Ignatius, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: The Aghlabids captured the Byzantine fortress city of Syracuse after a nine-month siege.
text: Siege of Syracuse: The Aghlabids capture the Byzantine fortress city of Syracuse, after a nine-month siege. Most of the population is massacred by the Arabs.

summary: Bardas Phokas the Elder, a Byzantine general, was born.
text: Bardas Phokas the Elder, Byzantine general (d. 968)

summary: Emperor Basil I convened the Fourth Council of Constantinople and reinstated Photius I as patriarch of Constantinople.
text: Fourth Council of Constantinople: Emperor Basil I calls for a synod, and reinstates Photius I as patriarch of Constantinople.

summary: Byzantine admiral Nasar defeated an Aghlabid fleet in a night engagement off Cephalonia.
text: Battle of Cephalonia: A Byzantine fleet, under Admiral Nasar, is sent by Emperor Basil I to the Ionian Islands. Nasar defeats the Aghlabids in a night battle near Cephalonia (modern Greece).

summary: Patriarch Photius I inaugurated the Nea Ekklesia church in Constantinople.
text: The Nea Ekklesia is inaugurated in Constantinople, by Patriarch Photius I, setting the model for all later cross-in-square Orthodox churches.

summary: Eudokia Ingerina, Byzantine empress, died.
text: Eudokia Ingerina, Byzantine empress

summary: Abbasid governor Yazaman al-Khadim of Tarsus routed a Byzantine army under Kesta Styppiotes in a night attack.
text: Yazaman al-Khadim, Abbasid governor of Tarsus, routs a Byzantine army under general Kesta Styppiotes, in a night attack. According to Arab chroniclers, 70,000 out of 100,000 Byzantine troops are killed.

summary: Byzantine general Kesta Styppiotes was killed in battle against Yazaman al-Khadim.
text: Kesta Styppiotes, Byzantine general

summary: Methodius, Byzantine missionary and bishop who helped Christianize the Slavs, died in Great Moravia.
text: Methodius, Byzantine missionary and bishop (b. 815)

summary: A wide-ranging conspiracy against Byzantine Emperor Basil I, led by John Kourkouas, was uncovered.
text: March – A wide-ranging conspiracy against Emperor Basil I, led by John Kourkouas, is uncovered.

summary: Basil I died and was succeeded as sole Byzantine emperor by Leo VI the Wise, who subsequently reburied Michael III in Constantinople.
text: Emperor Basil I the Macedonian dies from a fever, contracted after a hunting accident. He is succeeded by the 19-year-old Leo VI, officially Basil's son, but reputedly a son of former emperor Michael III, as sole ruler (basileus) of the Byzantine Empire. After his coronation Leo reburies the remains of his reputed father Michael, with great ceremony in the imperial mausoleum, within the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople.

summary: Emperor Leo VI dismissed Patriarch Photios I of Constantinople and replaced him with his own brother Stephen I.
text: December – Emperor Leo VI dismisses Patriarch Photius I, who has been his tutor, and replaces him with his own brother Stephen I.

summary: The First Bulgarian Empire adopted the Glagolitic alphabet devised by Cyril and Methodius.
text: The Glagolitic alphabet, devised by Cyril and Methodius, missionaries from Constantinople, is adopted in the Bulgarian Empire.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Basil I died from a fever contracted after a hunting accident.
text: Basil I, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (b. 811)

summary: The Aghlabids scored a crushing victory over a Byzantine fleet at the Battle of Milazzo off Sicily.
text: October – Battle of Milazzo: The Aghlabids score a crushing victory over a Byzantine fleet off Sicily.

summary: The Magyars moved into the Balkans under Árpád, became entangled in a Byzantine-Bulgarian war, and settled in Great Moravia.
text: The Magyars, an Ugric tribe from the steppe of Central Asia, move west under the leadership of Árpád. They are pushed by their rivals, the Pechenegs, into the Balkan Peninsula, and become entangled in a war between Bulgaria and the Byzantine Empire. The Magyars head north and settle in Great Moravia.

summary: The Byzantine Empire captured Benevento, deposed Prince Orso, and made the city the capital of the theme of Longobardia.
text: Summer – Orso, Lombard prince of Benevento, is deposed after the capture of Benevento by the Byzantines. Benevento becomes the capital of the thema of Longobardia.

summary: Vladimir of Bulgaria signed a military alliance with King Arnulf of Carinthia against the Byzantine Empire.
text: Vladimir, ruler (knyaz) of the Bulgarian Empire, signs a military alliance with Arnulf of Carinthia of the East Frankish Kingdom. This alliance works against the pro-Byzantine policy of his father.

summary: Byzantine nun and saint Theodora of Thessaloniki died.
text: Theodora of Thessaloniki, Byzantine nun and saint (b. 812)

summary: Boris I of Bulgaria dethroned and blinded Vladimir, raised Simeon I to the throne, moved the capital to Preslav, and Simeon allied with the Pechenegs.
text: Vladimir, ruler (khan) of the Bulgarian Empire, is dethroned by his father Boris I, with help from loyal boyars. He is blinded, and succeeded by his brother Simeon I, as prince of Bulgaria; the capital is moved from Pliska to Preslav. Simeon makes an alliance with the Pechenegs (or Patzinaks), a semi-nomad Turkic tribe from the Central Asian steppes.

summary: The Council of Preslav expelled the Byzantine clergy from Bulgaria and replaced Greek with Old Church Slavonic as the official language.
text: Council of Preslav: The Byzantine clergy is expelled from Bulgaria, and the Greek language is replaced with Old Bulgarian (also known as Old Church Slavonic), as an official language.

summary: Stephen I, patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Stephen I, patriarch of Constantinople (b. 867)

summary: Photios I, former Patriarch of Constantinople, died in exile.
text: Photius I, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Theophano Martinakia, Byzantine empress and wife of Emperor Leo VI, died.
text: Theophano Martiniake, Byzantine empress

summary: After Stylianos Zaoutzes convinced Leo VI to move the Bulgarian market to Thessaloniki, Simeon I of Bulgaria invaded Byzantine territory.
text: Byzantine–Bulgarian War: Stylianos Zaoutzes, leading minister and basileopator, convinces Emperor Leo VI (the Wise) to move the Bulgarian market from Constantinople to Thessaloniki. This affects the commercial importance of Bulgarian trade. Simeon I, ruler (khan) of the Bulgarian Empire, mobilizes his Bulgarian forces and invades Byzantine territory, ravaging the countryside.

summary: Michael Maleinos, Byzantine nobleman and monastic leader, was born in Cappadocia.
text: Michael Maleinos, Byzantine nobleman and monk (d. 963)

summary: The Magyars entered the Carpathian Basin and crossed the Danube on Byzantine ships to ravage Bulgarian territory for Emperor Leo VI.
text: The Magyars are expelled from western Siberia, and settle in the Carpathian Basin, under the leadership of Árpád (the traditional date of 896 held during the 20th century has proved to be erroneous). Emperor Leo VI (the Wise) seeks aid from the Magyars, and after crossing the Danube on Byzantine ships, they ravage Bulgarian territory.
names: Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin

summary: Simeon I of Bulgaria sought refuge in the fortress of Drastar and called for a truce, prompting Emperor Leo VI to send Leo Choirosphaktes to negotiate.
text: Simeon I (the Great), ruler (khan) of the Bulgarian Empire, seeks refuge in the fortress of Drastar, while the Magyars reach the outskirts of the capital Preslav. Facing a difficult situation with war on two fronts, Simeon calls for a truce. Leo VI sends the diplomat Leo Choirosphaktes to Bulgaria, to negotiate the terms.

summary: Guy IV of Spoleto conquered Benevento from the Byzantines and proclaimed himself prince.
text: Guy IV, duke of Spoleto, conquers Benevento (after the Byzantines have moved the capital of Byzantine Italy from Benevento to Bari). Guy makes himself prince, thereby uniting the two Italian states. The Byzantines attempt to retake Benevento, but are defeated by Lombard troops.

summary: Bulgarian forces under Simeon I decisively defeated the Byzantine army at the Battle of Boulgarophygon in Thrace.
text: Summer – Battle of Boulgarophygon: Simeon I invades the Theme of Thrace (in the southeastern Balkans). The Byzantines transfer a new army to Europe, to deal with the Bulgarian threat. The armies clash at Boulgarophygon (modern Turkey); the Byzantines are completely destroyed in battle.

summary: Byzantine official and chief minister Stylianos Zaoutzes died in Constantinople.
text: Stylianos Zaoutzes, Byzantine official and minister

summary: Byzantine empress Zoe Zaoutzaina, consort of Emperor Leo VI, died in Constantinople.
text: Zoe Zaoutzaina, Byzantine empress consort of Leo VI

summary: Emperor Leo VI launched an offensive against Abbasid forces in Cilicia, Upper Mesopotamia, and Armenia.
text: Arab–Byzantine wars: Emperor Leo VI ("the Wise") begins an offensive against the Abbasid army in Cilicia, Upper Mesopotamia and Armenia. He also continues the war against the Muslims in Sicily and southern Italy.

summary: Atenulf I of Capua conquered Benevento, deposed Duke Radelchis II, and allied with the Byzantine Empire against the Saracens.
text: Spring – Atenulf I, Lombard prince of Capua, conquers the Duchy of Benevento. He deposes Duke Radelchis II and unites the two southern Lombard duchies in Mezzogiorno (Southern Italy). The Byzantines offer a strategic alliance to Atenulf who directs a campaign against the Saracens. They establish themselves on the banks of the Garigliano River. From here, Arab warbands launch frequent raids in Campania.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Leo VI married Eudokia Baïana following the death of his wife Zoe Zaoutzaina.
text: Summer – After the death of his wife Zoe Zaoutzaina, the Byzantine emperor Leo VI marries Eudokia Baïana.

summary: Abdallah, son of the Aghlabid emir Ibrahim II, suppressed a Muslim revolt and attacked the remaining Byzantine strongholds in Sicily.
text: August – Abdallah, son of the Aghlabid emir Ibrahim II, represses a revolt of his Muslim subjects, and then initiates a campaign against the last Byzantine strongholds in Sicily.

summary: Abu Abbas Abdallah resumed his Aghlabid campaign against Byzantine Sicily, dispatching his fleet toward Messina and bombarding Damona.
text: March – Abu Abbas Abdallah resumes his Aghlabid campaign against the Byzantine enclaves of Sicily. He dispatches his fleet towards Messina, while bombarding the town walls of Damona.

summary: Abu Abbas Abdallah crossed the Strait of Messina and took Reggio Calabria after its Byzantine garrison fled.
text: Abu Abbas Abdallah crosses the Strait of Messina and proceeds to Reggio Calabria. Appearing before its walls, the Byzantine garrison flees, surrendering the city to the Aghlabids.

summary: Abu Abbas Abdallah defeated a Byzantine relief navy at Messina and dismantled the city's fortifications.
text: Summer – Abu Abbas Abdallah defeats a relief Byzantine navy dispatched from Constantinople at Messina. He dismantles the fortifications of Messina and transfers his booty to Palermo.

summary: Arethas of Caesarea was appointed court rhetor at Constantinople and nominated Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia.
text: January – Arethas of Caesarea speaks on the occasion of the Epiphany. He becomes the official rhetor at the Byzantine court of Emperor Leo VI (the Wise) at Constantinople, and is nominated as Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia.

summary: Nicholas Mystikos became the Patriarch of Constantinople.
text: Nicholas Mystikos, a layman close to Photios, becomes Patriarch of Constantinople.

summary: Patriarch Antony II of Constantinople died.
text: Antony II, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Byzantine Empress Eudokia Baïana, wife of Leo VI, died.
text: Eudokia Baïana, Byzantine empress and wife of Leo VI

summary: Ibrahim II landed in Sicily and crushed a reinforced Byzantine army at Giardini.
text: June – Ibrahim II lands with an Aghlabid expeditionary force in Trapani, and proceeds to Palermo. He crushes the reinforced Byzantine army at Giardini.

summary: The Aghlabid army captured Taormina, the last Byzantine stronghold in Sicily.
text: Taormina, the last Byzantine stronghold in Sicily, is captured by the Aghlabid army. After nearly 75 years, all of Sicily is in Aghlabid hands.

summary: Ibrahim II crossed the Strait of Messina into Calabria and laid siege to Cosenza.
text: September – Ibrahim II crosses the Strait of Messina into Calabria. He begins his march to conquer the rest of Italy, and lays siege at Cosenza.

summary: Ibrahim II died of dysentery near Cosenza, leading Ziyadat Allah to lift the siege.
text: Ibrahim II dies of dysentery in a chapel near Cosenza. His grandson, Ziyadat Allah, takes over the army, but lifts the siege.

summary: Byzantine saint Mary the Younger died in Bizia.
text: Mary the Younger, Byzantine saint (b. 875)

summary: A Saracen fleet under Leo of Tripoli stormed and sacked Thessalonica, taking thousands of captives.
text: Sack of Thessalonica: A Muslim fleet, led by the Greek renegade Leo of Tripoli, appears outside Thessalonica and begins its attack after a short and silent inspection of the fortification of the city. After attacks from the sea for two days, the Saracens are able to storm the city walls, overcome the Thessalonians' resistance and capture the city. The sacking continues for a full week, before the raiders depart for their base in the Levant. Having freed 4,000 Muslim prisoners and captured 60 ships, gaining a large loot, they carry off 22,000 men and women as slaves.

summary: Byzantine generals Andronikos Doukas and Eustathios Argyros defeated the Abbasid garrisons of Mopsuestia and Tarsus near Marash.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: The Byzantines under Andronikos Doukas, along with Eustathios Argyros, campaign against the Abbasids and defeat the Muslim garrisons of Mopsuestia and Tarsus, near Marash (modern Turkey).

summary: Emperor Leo VI signed a peace treaty ceding Macedonian and southern Albanian territories to Simeon I of Bulgaria.
text: Emperor Leo VI (the Wise) is forced to sign a peace treaty with Simeon I, ruler (knyaz) of the Bulgarian Empire. All Slavic-inhabited lands of Macedonia and southern Albania are ceded to the Bulgarians.

summary: Byzantine emperor Constantine VII was born.
text: Constantine VII, Byzantine emperor (d. 959)

summary: Abbasid commander Ahmad ibn Kayghalagh launched a raid against the Byzantine Empire from Tarsus and reached the Halys River.
text: Abbasid commander Ahmad ibn Kayghalagh leads a raid against the Byzantine Empire from Tarsus, joined by the governor Rustam ibn Baradu. He reaches the Halys River and takes 4,000–5,000 captives.

summary: Varangian prince Oleg of Novgorod led the Kievan Rus' against Constantinople and secured a commercial treaty.
text: Rus'–Byzantine War: Varangian prince Oleg of Novgorod leads the Kievan Rus' in a campaign against Constantinople, concluded by the Rus'–Byzantine Treaty (in which the city of Chernihiv in Ukraine is first mentioned). He lays siege to the Byzantine capital with some 2,000 ships (dugout boats), and secures trading rights from the world's leading center of commerce.

summary: Nicholas I Mystikos was deposed as Patriarch of Constantinople following a dispute with Emperor Leo VI and was replaced by Euthymius I Syncellus.
text: Nicholas I Mystikos is deposed as Patriarch of Constanstinople, (having fallen out with the Byzantine Emperor Leo VI), and is replaced by Euthymius I Syncellus.

summary: Three-year-old Constantine VII was crowned co-emperor of the Byzantine Empire by Patriarch Euthymius I at the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.
text: The three-year-old Constantine VII, the son of Emperor Leo VI (the Wise), is crowned as co-emperor of the Byzantine Empire by Patriarch Euthymius I at Constantinople. The ceremony is held in the Hagia Sophia. After the rituals, Constantine is crowned (symbolically) and becomes Leo's successor.

summary: Byzantine monk and missionary Blaise of Amorion died in Constantinople.
text: Blaise of Amorion, Byzantine monk and missionary

summary: Byzantine saint Thomais of Lesbos was born on Lesbos.
text: Thomais of Lesbos, Byzantine saint (d. ca. 947)

summary: Byzantine empress Helena Lekapene was born.
text: Helena Lekapene, Byzantine empress

summary: Byzantine abbot Nilus the Younger was born in Rossano, Calabria.
text: Nilus the Younger, Byzantine abbot (d. 1005)

summary: Byzantine general Andronikos Doukas died in exile in Baghdad.
text: Andronikos Doukas, Byzantine general

summary: Byzantine general Eustathios Argyros died.
text: Eustathios Argyros, Byzantine general

summary: Following the death of Emperor Leo VI, Alexander became Byzantine emperor alongside young Constantine VII and exiled Empress Zoe Karbonopsina.
text: Emperor Leo VI (the Wise) dies after a 26-year reign, in which he has completed the Byzantine code of laws (Basilika). He is succeeded by his brother Alexander III as emperor (basileus) alongside Leo's 6-year-old son Constantine VII. Alexander becomes de facto ruler of the Byzantine Empire and expels Empress Zoe Karbonopsina, the mother of Constantine, from the palace and exiles her to a nunnery.

summary: Orso II Participazio became the doge of Venice and dispatched his son Pietro to Constantinople to re-establish relations with Emperor Alexander.
text: Orso II Participazio becomes the doge of Venice. He sends his son Pietro to Constantinople in order to re-establish the relationship with Alexander III.

summary: Nicholas Mystikos was restored as Patriarch of Constantinople after Euthymius I was deposed.
text: Euthymius I is deposed as Patriarch of Constantinople, and Nicholas Mystikos is restored.

summary: Nikephoros II Phokas, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: Nikephoros II, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (d. 969)

summary: Emperor Leo VI the Wise died in Constantinople and was succeeded by Alexander.
text: Leo VI, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (b. 866)

summary: Emperor Alexander died of exhaustion after playing polo, and was succeeded by his nephew Constantine VII under a regency council.
text: Emperor Alexander III dies of exhaustion while playing the game tzykanion (Byzantine name for polo). He is succeeded by his 8-year-old nephew Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos ("born in the purple"), a son of the late emperor Leo VI (the Wise). The government is administered by a regency council composed of Constantine's mother, Empress Zoe Karbonopsina, Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos and his guardian John Eladas.

summary: Simeon I of Bulgaria led an army to Constantinople and besieged the Byzantine capital.
text: August – Byzantine–Bulgarian War: Simeon I (the Great), ruler (knyaz) of the Bulgarian Empire, launches a campaign at the head of a large Bulgarian army, and reaches Constantinople unopposed. The Bulgarians besiege the Byzantine capital and construct ditches from the Golden Horn to the Golden Gate at the Marmara Sea.{{cite book | ref=

summary: Constantine Doukas attempted to usurp the Byzantine throne from Constantine VII but was killed by the imperial guard in Constantinople.
text: Summer – Constantine Doukas, a Byzantine general (magister militum), tries, unsuccessfully, with the support of several aristocrats to usurp the throne from the young Constantine VII. He is killed in a clash by the soldiers of the Hetaireia guard, assembled by John Eladas. His head is cut off and presented to Constantine.

summary: Sicilian lords declared independence from the Fatimid Caliphate, pledged allegiance to the Abbasids, and acclaimed Ahmed ibn Khorob as emir.
text: Caliph Abdullah al-Mahdi Billah of the Fatimid Caliphate replaces the unpopular governor Ibn Abi Khinzir with Ali ibn Umar al-Balawi. But the Sicilian lords find this unacceptable and decide to declare independence of Sicily. They acknowledge allegiance to the Abbasid caliph Al-Muqtadir and acclaim an Aghlabid prince, Ahmed ibn Khorob, as emir of Sicily. The Sicilians re-launch their conquest of Byzantine Calabria, while Ahmed ibn Khorob in Sicily leads a successful assault against the North African cities of Sfax and Tripoli.

summary: Shabbethai Donnolo, Jewish physician and scholar, was born in Oria.
text: Shabbethai Donnolo, Jewish physician (d. 982)

summary: Byzantine Emperor Alexander died in Constantinople.
text: Alexander III, Byzantine emperor (b. 870)

summary: Constantine Doukas, Byzantine general and usurper, was killed in Constantinople.
text: Constantine Doukas, Byzantine general

summary: Empress Zoe Karbonopsina led a palace coup in Constantinople and overthrew Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos as regent over Emperor Constantine VII.
text: Spring – Empress Zoe Karbonopsina leads a palace coup at Constantinople and, with the support of the magistros John Eladas, overthrows Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos as regent over her son, Emperor Constantine VII. She allows Nicholas to remain as patriarch, repudiates the title granted to Simeon I of Bulgaria (see 913) and nullifies the marriage plans (with a Bulgarian princess) made for her son by Nicholas.

summary: Simeon I of Bulgaria invaded Byzantine Thrace and captured Adrianople, which the Byzantines promptly ransomed back.
text: Summer – Byzantine–Bulgarian War: Simeon I, with the Bulgarian army, invades the themes of Thrace and Macedonia. Simultaneously, the Bulgarian troops penetrate into the regions of Dyrrhachium and Thessalonica to the west. Thrace's largest and most important city, Adrianople (modern Turkey), is besieged and captured. However, the Byzantines promptly regain the city in exchange for a huge ransom.

summary: John Eladas, member of the Byzantine regency council, died.
text: John Eladas, Byzantine regent

summary: A Christian coalition led by Pope John X and supported by the Byzantine navy defeated the Saracens at the Battle of Garigliano.
text: Summer – Battle of Garigliano: The Christian League, personally led by Pope John X, lays siege to Garigliano (a fortified Arab camp in the area of Minturno), which is blockaded from the sea by the Byzantine navy. After three months of siege, plagued by hunger, the Saracens decide to break out of Garigliano and find their way back to Sicily by any means possible. Christian hunting parties fall on the fleeing Arabs, and all are captured and executed.

summary: Clement of Ohrid, Bulgarian scholar and bishop, died and was buried at the monastery of Saint Panteleimon in Ohrid.
text: Clement of Ohrid, Bulgarian scholar, writer and enlightener of the Slavs, dies. He is regarded as the first bishop of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church and the founder of the first Slavic Literary School. Clement is buried in his monastery, Saint Panteleimon, in Ohrid (modern North Macedonia).
names: Church of Saints Clement and Panteleimon

summary: Clement of Ohrid, Bulgarian scholar and bishop, died.
text: Clement of Ohrid, Bulgarian scholar

summary: Bulgarian forces under Tsar Simeon I routed a Byzantine army led by Leo Phokas at the Battle of Achelous near Anchialos.
text: Battle of Achelous: A Byzantine expeditionary force (62,000 men) under General Leo Phokas (the Elder) is routed by the Bulgarians at the Achelous River near the fortress of Anchialos (modern Pomorie) on the Black Sea coast. Phokas flees to Mesembria (modern Nesebar) and escapes by boarding a ship. Tsar Simeon I (the Great) becomes de facto ruler of the whole Balkan Peninsula, except the well-protected Byzantine capital of Constantinople and the Peloponnese.

summary: The Bulgarian army under Simeon I defeated Byzantine forces under Leo Phokas in a surprise night attack at Katasyrtai near Constantinople.
text: Fall – Battle of Katasyrtai: The Bulgarian army under Simeon I marches southwards to Constantinople. Leo Phokas, who survived at Anchelous, gathers the last Byzantine troops to intercept the Bulgarians before they reach the capital. The two armies meet near the village of Katasyrtai, just outside Constantinople. After a surprise night attack, the Byzantines are completely routed from the battlefield.

summary: Bulgarian commanders seized Petar Gojniković during peace talks and installed Pavle Branović as the ruler of Serbia.
text: Bulgarian–Serbian War: Simeon I sends a Bulgarian expeditionary force under Theodore Sigritsa and Marmais to Serbia. The two persuade Petar Gojniković, a Serbian prince who formed an anti-Bulgarian coalition, to meet for a peace agreement. They seize him and send the rebellious prince to the Bulgarian capital of Preslav, where he dies in prison. Simeon replaces Petar with Pavle Branović, a grandson of prince Mutimir, who lives in Preslav. Serbia becomes a puppet state until 921.

summary: The future patriarch of Constantinople Theophylactus was born.
text: Theophylactus, patriarch of Constantinople (d. 956)

summary: Former patriarch of Constantinople Euthymius I died.
text: Euthymius I, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: The Byzantine admiral Constantine Lips died.
text: Constantine Lips, Byzantine admiral

summary: The Byzantine general Nicholas Picingli died.
text: Nicholas Picingli, Byzantine general

summary: Prince Petar Gojniković of Serbia died in Bulgarian captivity in Preslav.
text: Petar Gojniković, Serbian prince

summary: Romanos Lekapenos seized the Boukoleon Palace in Constantinople, assumed high imperial titles, and became regent for Constantine VII.
text: Romanos Lekapenos, admiral (droungarios) of the Byzantine navy, seizes the Boukoleon Palace in Constantinople. He is named megas hetaireiarches (head of the imperial guard). Lekapenos consolidates his position and becomes regent of Emperor Constantine VII. He marries his 9-year-old daughter Helena Lekapene to Constantine and assumes the new title of basileopator (one of the highest offices in the Byzantine Empire).

summary: The Bulgarian Orthodox Church was declared autocephalous and elevated to a patriarchate at an ecclesiastical council.
text: The Bulgarian Orthodox Church is declared as autocephalous and elevated to the rank of patriarchate at an ecclesiastical council.

summary: Romanos I Lekapenos was crowned co-emperor of the Byzantine Empire alongside Constantine VII and assumed effective rule.
text: Romanos I has himself crowned co-emperor of the Byzantine Empire. He shares the throne with the 15-year-old Constantine VII (his son-in-law), and constructs an alternative palace at Constantinople with an adjoining monastery near the Great Palace. Though Constantine retains his formal position as first on the protocol list, Romanos becomes sole ruler.

summary: Byzantine monk Athanasius the Athonite was born in Trebizond.
text: Athanasius the Athonite, Byzantine monk

summary: Lombard historian and bishop Liutprand of Cremona was born in Pavia.
text: Liutprand of Cremona, Lombard bishop (d. 972)

summary: Bulgarian forces under Theodore Sigritsa defeated the Byzantine army at the Battle of Pegae outside Constantinople and devastated the area around the Golden Horn.
text: March – Battle of Pegae: Bulgarian forces under kavhan (first minister) Theodore Sigritsa defeat the Byzantine army at the outskirts of Constantinople. After the battle, the Bulgarians burn the palaces in Pegae ("the Spring"), and devastate the area north of the Golden Horn.

summary: Landulf I of Benevento supported an anti-Greek revolt across Apulia and was recognized as strategos of Longobardia.
text: Landulf I, prince of Benevento, supports an anti-Greek Apulian rebellion, ravaging several Byzantine strongpoints as far as Ascoli. The Apulian nobility, professing loyalty to the Byzantine Empire, appoints Landulf as stratego of the Theme of Longobardia.

summary: Byzantine admiral Alexios Mosele died.
text: Alexios Mosele, Byzantine admiral

summary: Bulgarian forces defeated the Byzantine army outside Constantinople in the Battle of Constantinople.
text: Summer – Battle of Constantinople: Emperor Romanos I sends Byzantine troops to repel another Bulgarian raid at the outskirts of Constantinople. The Byzantines storm the Bulgarian camp, but are defeated when they are confronted by the main Bulgarian forces. Having won the battle, the Bulgarians lack the maritime power to conduct a successful siege of Constantinople.

summary: Byzantine empress Theodora died.
text: Theodora, Byzantine empress

object: Church of St. Mary of the Spring (Istanbul)
summary: Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria burned the Church of St. Mary of the Spring outside Constantinople.
text: Byzantine–Bulgarian War: Tsar Simeon I, ruler (knyaz) of the Bulgarian Empire, leads the burning of the Church of St. Mary of the Spring in Constantinople.

place.title: Church of St. Mary of the Spring (Istanbul)

names: Church of St. Mary of the Spring (Istanbul)

summary: Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria met with Byzantine Emperor Romanos I Lekapenos on the Golden Horn to arrange a truce.
text: After pillaging the suburbs of Constantinople, Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria meets with the Byzantine Emperor Romanos I Lekapenos on the Golden Horn to arrange a truce, according to which Byzantium will pay the Bulgarians an annual tribute in exchangefor the return of some cities on the Black Sea coast.

summary: Byzantine co-emperor Romanos I Lekapenos concluded a treaty with Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria, providing him with ornate weapons.
text: Byzantine co-Emperor Romanos I Lekapenos concludes a treaty with the Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria and provides the Bulgarian monarch with "gold and silver shields and lances."

summary: Stephen Lekapenos and Constantine Lekapenos were elevated to co-emperors of the Byzantine Empire alongside Constantine VII, Romanos I, and Christopher.
text: Stephen Lekapenos and Constantine Lekapenos are promoted to the position of co-Emperors of Byzantium, joining Constantine VII, Romanos I and Christopher, creating a pentarchy with five monarchs.

summary: Prince Zaharija of Serbia ambushed and defeated a Bulgarian punitive force led by Theodore Sigritsa and Marmais.
text: Fall – Bulgarian–Serbian War: Tsar Simeon I sends a punitive expedition force against Serbia, led by Theodore Sigritsa and Marmais, but they are ambushed and defeated. Zaharija, prince of the Serbs, sends their heads and armour later to Constantinople .

summary: Muslim governor and commander Damian of Tarsus died.
text: Damian of Tarsus, Muslim governor

summary: Bulgarian commander Marmais died in battle in Serbia.
text: Marmais, Bulgarian nobleman

summary: Bulgarian minister Theodore Sigritsa died in battle in Serbia.
text: Theodore Sigritsa, Bulgarian minister

summary: Zaharija, Prince of the Serbs, died.
text: Zaharija, prince of Serbia

summary: Nicholas I Mystikos, Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, died at the age of seventy-three.
text: Nicholas I Mystikos, twice the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople and having reigned a second time since 912, dies at the age of 73.

summary: Stephen II became the new Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, succeeding Nicholas I Mystikos.
text: Stephen II becomes the new Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople and head of the Eastern Orthodox Church, succeeding Nicholas I.

summary: A Fatimid expedition overran Apulia, defeated Byzantine garrisons, and destroyed Oria, capturing Shabbethai Donnolo before his family ransomed him.
text: At the age of 12, Shabbethai Donnolo, who will become one of the most prominent physicians in Italy and the doctor to the Byzantine court, is kidnapped by Arab slavers as a Fatimid expeditionary force, led by Jafar ibn Obeid, lands in Abruzzo in southern Italy and overruns Apulia and the city of Otranto. After defeating the Byzantine garrisons, the Arabs lay siege to the castle of Oria and destroy it, killing the defenders and taking the women and children as slaves back to North Africa. Donnolo's family pays a ransom and the Fatimid Amir Abu Ahmad Ja'far ibn 'Ubaid sets him free.
names: History of slavery in the Muslim world

summary: The Fatimid chamberlain Ja'far ibn Ubayd returned to Mahdia after a seventeen-month raid of Byzantine Sicily.
text: September — The Chamberlain Ja'far ibn Ubayd of the Fatimid Caliphate returns to the Fatimid capital of Mahdiya (now in Tunisia) after a successful 17-month campaign to pillage the Byzantine-ruled island of Sicily.

summary: Emperor Romanos I deposed the chief minister John Mystikos and appointed the chamberlain Theophanes as his leading adviser.
text: October — In Byzantium, John Mystikos, chief minister (paradynasteuon), is deposed by the Emperor Romanos I, flogged, and sent into exile in a monastery. He is replaced by the chamberlain (protovestiarios) Theophanes, who becomes the closest adviser of Emperor Romanos I. At this time the Byzantine Empire has been embroiled in a protracted and disastrous war with Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria.

summary: Duke Tomislav was crowned King of Croatia and established an alliance with the Byzantine Empire against Bulgaria.
text: Tomislav, duke of the Croatian duchies of Pannonia and Dalmatia, is crowned as king of Croatia. He forges an alliance with the Byzantines during the struggle with the Bulgarian Empire .

summary: Basil Lekapenos, later a prominent Byzantine chief minister, was born.
text: Basil Lekapenos, Byzantine chief minister (d. 985)

summary: John I Tzimiskes, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: John I Tzimiskes, Byzantine emperor

summary: Nicholas I Mystikos, Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Nicholas I Mystikos, Byzantine patriarch (b. 852)

summary: Peter I succeeded Simeon I as emperor of the Bulgarian Empire and concluded a peace treaty with the Byzantine Empire.
text: Simeon I, emperor (tsar) of the Bulgarian Empire, dies of heart failure in his palace at Preslav after a 34-year reign. He is survived by four sons and succeeded by his second son Peter I, who signs a peace treaty with the Byzantine Empire. The peace is confirmed by Peter's marrying Maria Lekapene (the daughter of Christopher Lekapenos, son and co-emperor of Romanos I). The treaty restores the borders to those established by several treaties (thus recognizing Bulgaria's possession of Macedonia).

summary: Fatimid forces led by Sabir al-Fata captured and destroyed Taranto, enslaving much of its population.
text: Led by the Slavic Sabir, the Fatimids from Sicily, capture and destroy Taranto. They enslave much of the population.

summary: The Byzantine Empire and the Bulgarian Empire ratified the Treaty of Constantinople, formally recognizing Bulgarian imperial status.
text: October/November - Treaty of Constantinople. The Bulgarian Empire solidifies its status as a great power.

summary: The Patriarchate of Constantinople recognized the Bulgarian Orthodox Church as autocephalous.
text: The Bulgarian Orthodox Church is recognised as autocephalous, by the Patriarchate of Constantinople.

summary: Simeon I, emperor of the Bulgarian Empire, died at Preslav.
text: Simeon I, emperor (tsar) of the Bulgarian Empire

summary: A Fatimid fleet commanded by Sabir al-Fata raided Byzantine southern Italy, sacking Taranto and Otranto and enslaving their inhabitants.
text: Summer – A Fatimid fleet under Sabir al-Fata raids Byzantine southern Italy. It captures a locality named ('the caves') in Apulia and sacks the cities of Taranto and Otranto. The inhabitants are carried off to North Africa as slaves.

summary: Tryphon succeeded Stephen II as patriarch of Constantinople.
text: Tryphon succeeds Stephen II as patriarch of Constantinople (until 931).

summary: Stephen II, patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Stephen II, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: The Slavic-Arab leader Sabir defeated a Byzantine fleet and captured Termoli before returning to North Africa.
text: Summer – The Slavic-Arab leader Sabir defeats a small Byzantine fleet and seizes Termoli (in Molise, on the Adriatic coast). He returns to Africa laden with booty and slaves.
names: History of slavery in the Muslim world

summary: Nikon the Metanoeite, a Byzantine Eastern Orthodox monk and preacher, was born in Pontus.
text: Nikon the Metanoeite, Byzantine monk (d. 998)

summary: Boris II, future ruler of the Bulgarian Empire, was born.
text: Boris II, ruler (tsar) of the Bulgarian Empire (d. 977)

summary: Byzantine co-emperor Christopher Lekapenos died.
text: Christopher Lekapenos, Byzantine co-emperor

summary: Tryphon, former patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Tryphon, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: The Hungarians allied with the Pechenegs and raided through Thrace to Constantinople.
text: Spring and Summer – The Hungarians make an alliance with the Pechenegs, and fight their way through Thrace to Constantinople.

summary: The Hungarians and Pechenegs defeated the Byzantine and Bulgarian armies at the Battle of W.l.n.d.r, compelling Romanos I to sign a peace treaty and pay tribute.
text: Battle of W.l.n.d.r: The Hungarians and Pechenegs kill Constantinople's inhabitants, inflict severe damage on the countryside, and defeat both the Byzantine Empire and Bulgaria, forcing them to pay tribute. Emperor Romanos I signs a peace treaty with the Hungarians.

summary: Abdullah al-Mahdi Billah, founder and caliph of the Fatimid Caliphate, died.
text: Abdullah al-Mahdi Billah, Fatimid caliph (b. 873)

summary: Melias, an Armenian prince and Byzantine general, died.
text: Melias, Byzantine general (strategos)

summary: Byzantine holy fool and saint Andrew of Constantinople died.
text: Andrew of Constantinople, Byzantine saint

summary: Romanos II, future Byzantine emperor, was born in Constantinople.
text: Romanos II, Byzantine emperor (d. 963)

summary: Byzantine general and governor Damian Dalassenos was born.
text: Damian Dalassenos, Byzantine governor

summary: Igor of Kiev led a Rus' invasion fleet against the Byzantine Empire, reaching Constantinople before being repelled by Byzantine forces using Greek fire and destroyed in Thrace.
text: May – September – Rus'–Byzantine War: The Rus' and their allies, the Pechenegs, under the Varangian prince Igor I of Kiev, cross the Black Sea with an invasion fleet of 1,000 ships (40,000 men) and disembark on the northern coast of Asia Minor. While the Byzantine fleet is engaged against the Arabs in the Mediterranean, the Rus' forces reach the gates of Constantinople. Emperor Romanos I organizes the defense of the capital and assembles 15 old ships (equipped with throwers of Greek fire) under the chamberlain (protovestiarios) Theophanes. The Byzantines repel the Rus' fleet (nearly annihilating the entire fleet) but can not prevent the invaders from pillaging the hinterland of Constantinople, venturing as far south as Nicomedia (modern-day İzmit). In September, John Kourkouas and Bardas Phokas ("the Elder"), two leading generals, destroy the Rus' forces in Thrace. Igor manages, with only a handful of boats, to escape to the Caspian Sea.

summary: Hugh of Provence besieged the Moorish stronghold of Fraxinetum with Byzantine naval assistance and Hungarian auxiliary troops.
text: Battle of Fraxinet: King Hugh of Provence launches an attack on Fraxinet, the Moorish fortress on the Côté d'Azur that had taken control of the Piedmontese valleys. With the assistance of a Byzantine fleet sent by Emperor Romanos I, Hugh lays siege to the Moorish fortress with the help of Hungarian auxiliary troops (Kabars).

summary: Hugh of Provence made a truce with the Moors of Fraxinetum, prompting the Byzantine Empire to terminate its alliance with him.
text: Fall – Hugh of Provence makes a truce with the Moors of Fraxinet, after hearing the news that a Swabian army is about to descend on Italy. He allows the Moors to attack the Alpine passes for his own political ends in his struggle with Berengar of Ivrea. The Byzantines cry foul and end their alliance with Hugh.

summary: Emperor Romanos I Lekapenos bought peace from raiding Hungarians with annual tribute and sent Byzantine forces under John Kourkouas to invade northern Mesopotamia.
text: Spring – Allied with the Rus', a Hungarian army raids Moesia and Thrace. Emperor Romanos I buys peace, and accepts to pay a yearly tribute (protection money) to the Hungarians. His frontiers now 'protected' on the Balkan Peninsula, Romanos sends a Byzantine expeditionary force (80,000 men) led by general John Kourkouas (his commander-in-chief) to invade northern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq).

summary: Sayf al-Dawla defeated Byzantine forces and captured the city of Aleppo.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Byzantine forces are defeated by Sayf al-Dawla. He captures the city of Aleppo, and extends his control over the Al-Jazira–Upper Mesopotamia region. Al-Dawla's rule is recognized by the Ikhshidids. With the recovery of Edessa, the Greeks also obtain the fabled Image of Edessa.

summary: The Byzantine Empire received the Image of Edessa in Constantinople with a triumphal entry.
text: The "Holy Mandylion" (a cloth with the face of Jesus) is conveyed to Constantinople, where it arrives on the feast of the Dormition of the Theotokos. A triumphal entry is staged for the relic in the capital.
names: Dormition of the Mother of God

summary: Stephen Lekapenos and Constantine Lekapenos deposed their father, Emperor Romanos I Lekapenos, exiling him to the Princes' Islands.
text: Emperor Romanos I is arrested and deposed after a 14-year reign by his own sons, the co-emperors Stephen and Constantine. He is carried off to the Prince Islands and forced to become a monk.

summary: Constantine VII overthrew co-emperors Stephen and Constantine Lekapenos to become the sole ruler of the Byzantine Empire.
text: The co-emperors Stephen and Constantine are overthrown barely a month after deposing their father, Romanos I. With the help of his wife, Constantine VII becomes sole emperor of the Byzantine Empire. He appoints to the highest army commands four members of the Phokas family, which have been in disgrace under Romanos.

summary: Constantine VII concluded a trade treaty with Kievan Rus' regulating Rus' merchants in Constantinople.
text: Constantine VII concludes a Rus'–Byzantine treaty in which Rus' merchants are to conduct their trade in Constantinople. While many Rus' make their fortunes in trade with the Arab Muslims, the Rurik Dynasty of Kiev grows rich from Byzantine commerce.

summary: Theodora, Byzantine princess and later empress consort, was born.
text: Theodora, Byzantine empress consort

summary: Thomais of Lesbos, a Byzantine saint, died.
text: Thomais of Lesbos, Byzantine saint (b. ca. 909)

summary: Leo Phokas the Younger led Byzantine reprisals against Sayf al-Dawla's raids, taking captives and razing the walls of Hadath.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Hamdanid forces under Sayf al-Dawla raid into Asia Minor. The Byzantines respond with reprisals led by Leo Phokas the Younger, taking captives and razing the walls of Hadath (modern Turkey).

summary: Deposed Byzantine Emperor Romanos I Lekapenos died in exile.
text: Romanos I, Byzantine emperor (b. c. 870)

summary: Theophilos Kourkouas captured Erzurum for the Byzantine Empire after a seven-month siege while Byzantine forces raided Lykandos and Antioch.
text: Arab-Byzantine War: Hamdanid forces under Sayf al-Dawla raid into the theme of Lykandos, but are defeated. The Byzantines counter-attack and seize Germanikeia, defeating an army from Tarsus, and raiding as far south as Antioch. General (strategos) Theophilos Kourkouas captures Theodosiopolis (modern-day Erzurum) after a 7-month siege.

summary: The Emirate of Crete routed the Byzantine expeditionary force under Constantine Gongyles in a surprise attack.
text: A Byzantine expeditionary force under Constantine Gongyles attempts to re-conquer the Emirate of Crete from the Saracens. The expedition ends in a disastrous failure; the Byzantine camp is destroyed in a surprise attack. Gongyles himself barely escapes on his flagship.

summary: Symeon the New Theologian, a Byzantine monk and poet, was born.
text: Symeon (the New Theologian), Byzantine monk and poet (d. 1022)

summary: Leo Phokas heavily defeated Sayf al-Dawla in an ambush after a Hamdanid raid into the Anatolic Theme.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: A Hamdanid army (30,000 men) led by Sayf al-Dawla raids into Byzantine theme Anatolia. He defeats Bardas Phokas, but is then ambushed on his return and heavily defeated by Leo Phokas.

summary: A page from the Joshua Roll depicting Joshua leading the Israelites was created in Constantinople.
text: Page with Joshua Leading the Israelites, from the Joshua Roll, is made in Constantinople. It is now kept at the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana in Rome .

summary: Al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Kalbi led Kalbid forces from Sicily to invade Byzantine Calabria, attacking Gerace and Cassano.
text: Summer – Kalbid forces under Al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Kalbi (an aristocratic member of the ruling Fatimid Caliphate) sail from Sicily and invade Byzantine Calabria. He attacks several towns, including Gerace and Cassono.

summary: Sayf al-Dawla defeated a Byzantine army led by Bardas Phokas near Marash and captured his son Constantine Phokas.
text: Battle of Marash: Emir Sayf al-Dawla marches north into the Byzantine Empire and ravages the countryside of Malatya (modern Turkey). On his way back, he crosses the Euphrates and intercepts a Byzantine army led by Bardas Phokas (the Elder), near Marash. The Byzantines are defeated; Bardas himself barely escapes through the intervention of his attendants. His son Constantine Phokas, governor of Seleucia, is captured and held prisoner in Aleppo, until his death from an illness some time later.

summary: Theophanu, Byzantine princess and future Holy Roman Empress consort, was born.
text: Theophanu, empress consort of the Holy Roman Empire (d. 991)

summary: Emperor Constantine VII appointed Nikephoros Phokas as Domestic of the Schools in the East to prepare a campaign against Sayf al-Dawla.
text: Summer – Emperor Constantine VII appoints Nikephoros Phokas to commander of the Byzantine field army (Domestic of the Schools) in the East. He gives him order to prepare a campaign against the Hamdanid emir Sayf al-Dawla. Constantine makes treaties with neighbouring rulers, to seek military aid.

summary: A Byzantine fleet under Basil Hexamilites decisively defeated the Hamdanid fleet at Tarsus in Cilicia.
text: September - October – A Byzantine fleet under Basil Hexamilites deals a crushing defeat to the Hamdanid fleet at Tarsus in Cilicia (modern Turkey).

summary: Patriarch Theophylact of Constantinople died.
text: Theophylact, Byzantine patriarch (b. 917)

summary: Olga of Kiev, regent of Kievan Rus', converted to Eastern Orthodox Christianity during a visit to Constantinople.
text: Olga of Kiev, ruler and regent of Kievan Rus', converts to the Eastern Orthodox Church, from paganism .

summary: Byzantine forces commanded by John Tzimiskes defeated the Hamdanids at the Battle of Raban.
text: October / November – Battle of Raban: The Byzantines under John Tzimiskes defeat the Hamdanid forces in northern Syria. Emir Sayf al-Dawla is forced to retreat – many of his court companions and ghilman fall in pursuit, while over 1,700 of his Turk cavalry are captured and paraded in the streets of Constantinople.

summary: Future Byzantine Emperor Basil II was born.
text: Basil II (Bulgar Slayer), Byzantine emperor (d. 1025)

summary: A Hungarian army led by Apor raided Thrace and Macedonia up to Constantinople, but was defeated on its return by Byzantine forces.
text: April - May – The Byzantines refuse to pay the yearly tribute. A Hungarian army, led by Apor, invades Macedonia and Thrace. He plunders its territories until reaching Constantinople. On his way back, Apor is defeated during a night attack by Byzantine forces.

summary: Constantine VII died at Constantinople and was succeeded as Byzantine emperor by his son Romanos II.
text: Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos ("born in the purple") dies at Constantinople after a 46-year reign. He is succeeded by his 21-year-old son Romanos II as ruler of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Romanos II appointed Leo Phokas the Younger as Domestic of the Schools in the West.
text: Winter – Romanos II appoints Leo Phokas (the Younger) to be commander of the Byzantine field army (Domestic of the Schools) in the West. The Phokas clan becomes one of the leading families in Constantinople.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Constantine VII died.
text: Constantine VII, Byzantine emperor (b. 905)

summary: Nikephoros Phokas landed an expeditionary force on Crete and laid siege to Chandax.
text: Summer – Siege of Chandax: A Byzantine fleet with an expeditionary force (comprising about 50,000 men) under Nikephoros Phokas lands on Crete. Nikephoros defeats the Muslim resistance and begins a siege at the capital of Chandax. He decides to blockade the city for the winter, while his engineers begin to construct siege engines. Emir Abd al-Aziz ibn Shu'ayb sends for aid by the Fatimids in Ifriqiya and the Caliphate of Córdoba (modern Spain).

summary: Leo Phokas the Younger ambushed and routed Sayf al-Dawla's Hamdanid army at the Battle of Andrassos.
text: Battle of Andrassos: The Byzantines under Leo Phokas the Younger defeat the Hamdanid army (30,000 men) in an ambush in the passages of the Cilician mountains, in south Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey). Emir Sayf al-Dawla barely manages to escape, and returns to Aleppo with only 300 horsemen. The Hamdanids can no longer afford to raid in Anatolia, which is a turning point in the Arab-Byzantine wars in the East.

summary: Constantine VIII was born in Constantinople.
text: Constantine VIII, Byzantine emperor (d. 1028)

summary: Nikephoros II Phokas captured Chandax after an eight-month siege, ending the Emirate of Crete and converting the island into a Byzantine theme.
text: Siege of Chandax: Byzantine forces under Nikephoros II Phokas capture and pillage Chandax after an 8-month siege. Nikephoros massacres the population without mercy and carries them off into slavery, returning to Constantinople with Emir Abd al-Aziz ibn Shu'ayb and his family as prisoners. The island Emirate of Crete is converted into a Byzantine theme and the remaining Muslims are converted to Christianity.

summary: Byzantine empress Helena Lekapene died in Constantinople.
text: Helena Lekapene, Byzantine empress

summary: A Byzantine force commanded by General Nikephoros Phokas invaded northern Syria and sacked Aleppo.
text: December – Arab–Byzantine wars – Sack of Aleppo: A Byzantine expeditionary force under General Nikephoros Phokas invades northern Syria, and sacks Aleppo, capital of the Hamdanid emir Sayf al-Dawla. In late December Aleppo is taken by storm, with the population killed or enslaved; the city is razed. The Byzantine army takes possession of 390,000 silver dinars, 2,000 camels and 1,400 mules.

summary: Pandulf Ironhead intercepted letters revealing that Pope John XII was plotting with Berengar II and the Byzantine Empire against Otto I.
text: Fall – Otto I receives news that John XII has betrayed him and entered into intrigues with Berengar II, but also with the Byzantine Empire. The letters are intercepted by Pandulf I (Ironhead), Lombard prince of Benevento.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Romanos II died, leaving his infant sons Basil II and Constantine VIII under the regency of Empress Theophano.
text: Emperor Romanos II dies at age 39, probably of poison administered by his wife, Empress Theophano. He is succeeded by his infant son Basil II. Theophano becomes regent and de facto ruler, naming her other son Constantine VIII (only 3 years old) as co-emperor of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Nikephoros II Phokas was proclaimed emperor by his troops in Caesarea and took control of the Bosporus.
text: Nikephoros II Phokas is proclaimed emperor by his troops in Caesarea. He sends a fleet to secure the Bosphorus Strait against his enemies. Chief minister Joseph Bringas gathers support and closes the gates of Constantinople. General Marianos Argyros is killed in a riot, forcing Bringas to flee.

summary: Nikephoros II Phokas entered Constantinople in triumph and was crowned emperor in Hagia Sophia.
text: Nikephoros II makes a triumphal entry in Constantinople and is hailed as 'the conqueror'. He is crowned emperor in Hagia Sophia.

summary: Emperor Nikephoros II married Empress Theophano, widow of Romanos II, bolstering his legitimacy.
text: Nikephoros II marries the former Byzantine consort Theophano, the widow of Emperor Romanos II, bolstering his legitimacy.

summary: Athanasius the Athonite founded the Monastery of Great Lavra at Mount Athos.
text: The Monastery of Great Lavra at Mount Athos (northeastern Greece) is founded by the Byzantine monk Athanasius the Athonite.

summary: Anna Porphyrogenita, Byzantine princess and later Grand Princess of Kiev, was born.
text: Anna Porphyrogenita, Grand Princess of Kiev (d. 1011)

summary: Romanos II, Byzantine emperor, died.
text: Romanos II, Byzantine emperor (b. 938)

summary: Stephen Lekapenos, deposed Byzantine co-emperor, died in exile.
text: Stephen Lekapenos, Byzantine co-emperor

summary: Marianos Argyros, Byzantine general, died.
text: Marianos Argyros, Byzantine general

summary: Michael Maleinos, Byzantine monk, died.
text: Michael Maleinos, Byzantine monk

summary: Emperor Nikephoros II recaptured Cyprus and took Anazarbus and Adana during his Cilician campaigns.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Emperor Nikephoros II continues the reconquest of south-eastern Anatolia (modern Turkey). He recaptured Cyprus through Niketas Chalkoutzes, and reorganizes the conquered lands into new themes. In the summer, they take the fortress cities of Anazarbus and Adana. Byzantine troops under General John Tzimiskes besiege Mopsuestia, but with the coming of winter he is forced to retreat to Caesarea.

summary: Muslim forces under Al-Hasan ibn Ammar defeated a Byzantine relief army sent by Nikephoros II at the Siege of Rometta.
text: 25 – Siege of Rometta: Nikephoros II sends an expedition to Sicily. The Byzantine army (40,000 men) is sent to break the Muslim siege at Rometta, and to regain Sicily for the Byzantine Empire. For two days a battle takes place in the area between the beach and the besieged citadel of Rometta. The Saracens (under Al-Hasan ibn Ammar) manage to defeat the Byzantine relief force.

summary: Emperor Nikephoros II completed the conquest of Cilicia while Byzantine forces reoccupied Cyprus.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Emperor Nikephoros II conquers the fortress cities of Tarsus and Mopsuestia. The Muslim residents abandon the defense and flee into Syria. Nikephoros completes the conquest of Cilicia; Muslim raids into Anatolia (modern Turkey) permanently cease. Byzantine troops under General Niketas Chalkoutzes occupy Cyprus, liberating the Greek population from Muslim domination.

summary: The Fatimids destroyed the Byzantine fleet and took Rometta, completing their conquest of Sicily.
text: Battle of the Straits: The Byzantine attempt to recover Sicily fails, when the Byzantine fleet is annihilated by the Fatimids. The last Byzantine stronghold on the island, Rometta, surrenders. The population is massacred, and the survivors are sold into slavery. Caliph Al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah completes the conquest of Sicily, and establishes naval superiority in the Western Mediterranean.
names: History of slavery in the Muslim world

summary: Joseph Bringas, Byzantine court eunuch and chief minister, died in exile.
text: Joseph Bringas, Byzantine eunuch and official

summary: Emperor Nikephoros the Second and Sayf al-Dawla conducted a prisoner exchange at Samosata.
text: Arab–Byzantine wars: A prisoner exchange occurs at the border between the Byzantine Empire and the Emirate of Aleppo at Samosata, headed by Emperor Nikephoros II and Sayf al-Dawla, the Emir of Aleppo. The Emirate receives 3,000 captured prisoners from the region of Cilicia, after its conquest by the Byzantine Emperor, as well as the poet Abu Firas al-Hamdani, who has previously been held prisoner by the Byzantines.

summary: The Hungarians invaded the Bulgarian Empire and compelled Tsar Peter the First to grant them passage toward Byzantine lands.
text: The Hungarians invade the Bulgarian Empire and force Peter I, emperor (tsar) of the Bulgarians, to conclude a peace treaty with them. He lets them cross to attack the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Patriarch John the Seventh of Jerusalem was burned at the stake by a mob after appealing to Emperor Nikephoros the Second.
text: John VII, patriarch of Jerusalem, is burned at the stake by a Muslim mob after writing to Emperor Nikephoros II, pleading him to intervene in Palestine and retake it from the Fatimid Caliphate.

summary: Otto the Great granted the vacant Duchy of Spoleto to Pandulf I at Capua and received the homage of neighboring Lombard rulers.
text: Otto I goes on a tour of the Lombard duchies of southern Italy. In Capua he grants Pandulf I (Ironhead) the vacant Duchy of Spoleto and Camerino and charges him with prosecuting the war against the Byzantine Empire. In Benevento, Otto receives the homage of Pandulf's brother and co-ruler Landulf III. In Salerno he receives also the support of Gisulf I.

summary: Otto the Great dispatched an imperial delegation to Constantinople seeking the Byzantine princess Theophanu for his son Otto II.
text: Otto I dispatches an imperial delegation (led by a Venetian named Domenico) to Constantinople with assurances of his friendship and a request for Princess Theophano (a daughter of the late Emperor Romanos II) for his 12-year-old son Otto II. As dowry Otto demands the Byzantine holdings in southern Italy.

summary: Sviatoslav I of Kiev defeated Bulgar forces in the Balkans at the behest of Byzantine Emperor Nikephoros II.
text: Summer – Sviatoslav I, Grand Prince of Kiev, defeats Bulgar forces in the Balkans at the behest of Emperor Nikephoros II (who pays him 1,500 pounds of gold to invade the Bulgarian Empire).

summary: Emperor Nikephoros II met Otto the Great's delegation in Macedonia and rejected Otto's territorial claims in Byzantine Italy.
text: The imperial delegation arrives in Macedonia, but goes nowhere with Nikephoros II. Far from offering Byzantine Italy as dowry for Theophano, Nikephoros refuses to accept the claims of Otto I.

summary: Emperor Nikephoros II received a Bulgarian embassy seeking aid against Kievan Rus' and incited the Pechenegs to attack Kiev.
text: Emperor Nikephoros II receives a Bulgarian embassy led by Prince Boris (the son of Tsar Peter I of Bulgaria), with a plea for help against the invading Kievan Rus'. Nikephoros, occupied in the East, is unable to support him. Instead he sends envoys to summon the Pechenegs to aid Boris. They besiege Kiev, but Grand Prince Sviatoslav I (on campaign in Bulgaria) returns with a Kievan relief force, and defeats the Pechenegs. He drives them out into the Steppe, and sets up viceroys to rule his Rus' territory.

summary: Emperor Otto I invaded Byzantine Langobardia and assaulted Bari, but Byzantine resistance forced him to withdraw.
text: Spring – Emperor Otto I (the Great) travels to Capua to meet there with ambassadors of Nikephoros II, who again reiterate their friendship, but refuse to consent to his dowry demands (see 967). Otto invades the Byzantine Theme of Langobardia with a Lombard expeditionary force. With the assistance of Benevento-Capua and naval support from Pisa, Otto attempts to take Bari by assault, but Byzantine resistance is stiff, and Otto withdraws back to Ravenna.

summary: Future Byzantine emperor Romanos III Argyros was born.
text: Romanos III Argyros, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (d. 1034)

summary: Byzantine general Bardas Phokas the Elder died.
text: Bardas Phokas (the Elder), Byzantine general

summary: Byzantine forces captured Antioch from the Hamdanids and advanced into Syria to capture Aleppo.
text: Siege of Antioch: Byzantine general Michael Bourtzes (during a night attack) seizes part of Antioch's fortifications. The capture of the city from the Hamdanids is completed three days later, when reinforcements under the stratopedarches Peter Phokas arrive. The Byzantine army then moves deeper into Syrian territory — besieging and taking the city of Aleppo.

summary: John I Tzimiskes became Byzantine emperor after Nikephoros II Phokas was murdered in the Boukoleon Palace at Constantinople.
text: Emperor Nikephoros II is murdered in the royal palace of Boukoleon at Constantinople after a 6-year reign. Former friends have acted on the instructions of his wife Theophano. Nikephoros is succeeded by his nephew John I Tzimiskes, who becomes co-emperor and regent. He sends Theophano into exile to the island of Prinkipo (Prince Islands).

summary: Peter I abdicated the Bulgarian throne in favour of his eldest son Boris II after suffering a stroke.
text: Peter I, emperor (tsar) of the Bulgarian Empire, suffers a stroke and abdicates the throne in favour of his eldest son Boris II. He arrives (after being an honorary hostage at Constantinople) in Preslav and is proclaimed as the new ruler. Boris regains lost territory from the Kievan Rus' and recaptures Pereyaslavets, an important trade city at the mouth of the Danube.

summary: Byzantine forces captured Pandulf Ironhead at the siege of Bovino and imprisoned him in Constantinople.
text: Pandulf Ironhead, duke of Benevento and Capua, leads the siege of Bovino. He is captured by the Byzantines and taken in chains to Bari, and jailed in Constantinople. Neapolitan forces under Marinus II, duke of Naples, invade Benevento-Capua, capture the city of Avellino and then lay siege to Capua.

summary: Pope John XIII convened a synod at Rome and raised the bishopric of Benevento to an archbishopric.
text: Summer – Pope John XIII convenes a synod at Rome. He raises the bishopric of Benevento to Archbishopric of Benevento. The city is made a metropolitan see over 10 bishoprics in Byzantine Capitanata (Southern Italy).

summary: Byzantine Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas was assassinated and died in Constantinople.
text: Nikephoros II, emperor of the Byzantine Empire

summary: A Kievan Rus' force sacked Philippopolis and marched through Thrace toward Constantinople as Byzantine commanders gathered an army.
text: Emperor John I delegates the war in the Balkans to his brother-in-law, the Domestic of the Schools Bardas Skleros, and to the eunuch general Peter Phokas, who begin to gather a Byzantine army in Thrace. At the news of this, a powerful Kievan expeditionary force (30,000 men), along with many Bulgarians and a Pecheneg contingent, is sent south over the Balkan Mountains.
