After sacking the Bulgarian stronghold of Philippolis (modern-day Plovdiv), they bypass the heavily defended city of Adrianople, and turn towards Constantinople.

summary: Byzantine troops under Bardas Skleros routed Kievan and Bulgarian forces at Arcadiopolis, expelling Sviatoslav I from Thrace.
text: Battle of Arcadiopolis: John I dispatches an elite force (10–12,000 men) to delay the Kievan Rus'. The Byzantines under Bardas Skleros successfully ambush the Kievan-Bulgarian invaders at Arcadiopolis (modern Turkey). The battle turns into a complete rout, killing thousands. Grand Prince Sviatoslav I is driven out of Thrace and withdraws his forces to the fortress city of Silistra.

summary: Bardas Skleros extinguished the rebellion of Bardas Phokas the Younger in Caesarea and sent the rebels into exile on Chios.
text: Summer – Bardas Phokas (the Younger) and his family rebel against their own cousin, John I. Bardas is proclaimed 'emperor' by his troops at Caesarea, but the rebellion is extinguished by Bardas Skleros. Phokas and his relatives are captured and exiled to the island of Chios (Aegean Sea).

summary: Holy Roman Emperor Otto the Great concluded a peace treaty with John I Tzimiskes at Bari, securing the release of Pandulf Ironhead.
text: Summer – Byzantine-Imperial truce: Emperor Otto I (the Great) meets with John I at Bari and accepts a permanent peace agreement. Pandulf I (Ironhead) is released from captivity in Constantinople (see 969).

summary: Polyeuctus, Patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Polyeuctus, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Byzantine forces under Emperor John I captured Dorostolon after a three-month siege and renamed it Theodoropolis.
text: Battle of Dorostolon: A Byzantine expeditionary army (possibly 30–40,000 men) attacks the Bulgarian frontier, personally led by Emperor John I. He lays siege to the fortress city of Dorostolon (located on the Lower Danube), and is reinforced by a fleet of 300 ships equipped with Greek fire. The Kievan Rus' and their Bulgarian allies are reduced to extremities by famine. After a 3-month siege, Grand Prince Sviatoslav I agrees to sign a peace treaty with the Byzantines, whereby he renounces his interests towards Bulgarian lands and the city of Chersonesos in Crimea. Sviatoslav is allowed to evacuate his army to Berezan Island, while the Byzantines enter Dorostolon. John renames the city Theodoropolis (named after the reigning Empress Theodora).

summary: John I celebrated a triumph in Constantinople with the captive Bulgarian tsar Boris II and annexed Bulgarian lands in Thrace and Moesia into the Byzantine Empire.
text: John I returns in triumph to Constantinople. He brings along Boris II, ruler (tsar) of the Bulgarian Empire, and his family, together with the contents of the Bulgarian imperial treasury. Boris is given the Byzantine 'court title' of magistros as compensation. The Bulgarian lands in Thrace and Lower Moesia become part of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Byzantine forces defeated a Fatimid army near Alexandretta, forcing the Fatimids to lift their siege of Antioch.
text: Battle of Alexandretta: The Byzantines defeat a Fatimid force (4,000 men) near Alexandretta (modern Turkey), while the main Fatimid army is besieging the fortress city of Antioch. Coupled with news of an advance against Damascus of the Qarmatians, the Fatimids are forced to lift the siege and withdraw to Egypt.

summary: Byzantine army commander Anemas died during the Siege of Dorostolon.
text: Anemas, Byzantine (Muslim) army commander

summary: Byzantine patrician and pretender Kalokyros was captured and executed.
text: Kalokyros, Byzantine patrician and pretender

summary: John I Tzimiskes divided Bulgarian lands into six themes, redeployed troops to Macedonia and Philippopolis, and invaded Upper Mesopotamia.
text: Spring – Emperor John I Tzimiskes divides the Bulgarian territories, recently held by the Kievan Rus', into six new themes. He turns his attention to the East against the Abbasid Caliphate and its vassals, beginning with an invasion of Upper Mesopotamia. John transfers Byzantine troops to Macedonia, and the region of Philippopolis in Thrace, to dilute the Slavs.

summary: John I resettled Bulgarian boyars in Constantinople and Anatolia, conferring high titles and lands upon them.
text: John I removes various Bulgarian boyars from their homes, and settles them in Constantinople and Anatolia (modern Turkey), where they are given high titles and lands.

summary: John I granted a charter establishing the Monastic Republic of Mount Athos in Greece.
text: John I grants a charter for the Monastic Republic of Holy Mount Athos, in Greece.

summary: The Pechenegs ambushed and killed Grand Prince Sviatoslav I at the Dnieper rapids, and Yaropolk I succeeded him in Kiev.
text: Spring – Grand Prince Sviatoslav I is ambushed by the Pechenegs (possibly in the service of the Byzantines) and killed during his attempt to cross the Dnieper rapids (modern Ukraine). His skull is made into a drinking cup. Sviatoslav is succeeded by his eldest son Yaropolk I as ruler of Kiev, which leads to a civil war with his brother Oleg.

summary: Otto II married Byzantine princess Theophanu in Rome, where Pope John XIII crowned her empress.
text: Otto II (the Red), joint-ruler and son of Otto I (the Great), marries the Byzantine princess Theophanu (niece or granddaughter of John I). She is crowned empress by Pope John XIII at Rome. Creating an alliance between the Ottonian Dynasty and the Byzantine Empire (called the Tzimiscian Peace).

summary: Grand Prince Sviatoslav I of Kiev died.
text: Sviatoslav I (Igorevich), Grand Prince of Kiev

summary: The Byzantine army under Melias conducted military operations in Upper Mesopotamia.
text: Spring – The Byzantine army, led by General Melias (Domestic of the Schools in the East), continues the operations in Upper Mesopotamia.

summary: Arab forces attacked and routed the Byzantine army under Melias during the siege of Amida.
text: July: Melias moves against Amida (modern Turkey). He defeats the Arabs outside the walls, and begins to lay siege to the city. After a few days, a violent wind and a thick dust spreads over the Byzantine camp. Covered by the dust, the Arabs attack and rout the Byzantines. Many of them are slaughtered and some, including Melias, are taken prisoner. Previous Byzantine gains in the area are lost. The wounded Melias dies later in captivity.

summary: Byzantine general Melias died.
text: Melias, Byzantine general

summary: Antipope Boniface VII was expelled to Constantinople, and Benedict VII was elected pope.
text: Fall – Boniface VII is expelled by order of Otto II and flees to Constantinople, taking the Church treasury of the Vatican Basilica along with him. He is succeeded by Benedict VII as the 135th pope of the Catholic Church.

summary: Emperor John I Tzimiskes raided Mesopotamia and conquered several Syrian cities, pressing south toward Tripoli.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Emperor John I raids Mesopotamia and invades Syria, using the Byzantine base at Antioch to press southwards to Tripoli. He conquers the cities of Baalbek, Damascus, Sidon, Tiberias and Caesarea, but fails to take Jerusalem.

summary: Caliph Al-Mu'izz died in Egypt and was succeeded as ruler of the Fatimid Caliphate by his son Al-Aziz Billah.
text: Caliph Al-Mu'izz dies in Egypt after a 22-year reign in which he has extended his realm from Sicily to the Atlantic. He is succeeded by his son Al-Aziz Billah as ruler of the Fatimid Caliphate.

summary: Fatimid caliph Al-Mu'izz died in Cairo.
text: Al-Mu'izz, Fatimid caliph (b. 932)

summary: Byzantine Emperor John I Tzimiskes died at Constantinople and was succeeded as sole ruler by Basil II.
text: Emperor John I Tzimiskes dies at Constantinople, after returning from a second campaign against the Abbasids in Syria. He is buried in the Church of Christ Chalkites, and succeeded by his 18-year-old nephew Basil II, who becomes sole ruler of the Byzantine Empire. The administration remains in the hands of Basil Lekapenos (an illegitimate son of the late Emperor Romanos I).

summary: Emir Abu'l-Qasim launched a raiding expedition into Byzantine southern Italy from Sicily, imposing tribute on Cosenza and besieging Gravina.
text: June – Emir Abu'l-Qasim launches a raiding expedition into Byzantine Italy from Sicily. He imposes a tribute on the cities of Cosenza and Cellere. Meanwhile, a Fatimid fleet assaults the Apulian coast and raids the surrounding countryside. Abu'l-Qasim sends an army to Otranto and besieges Gravina, before returning to Sicily – bringing home hundreds of captives and slaves.

summary: A Venetian rebellion burned the doge's palace and killed Pietro IV Candiano and his family.
text: Summer – Pietro IV Candiano, doge of Venice, demands Venetian assistance to put down a revolt in his personal fiefs around Ferrara. The Venetians also revolt against Candiano and assault the doge's palace. Repelled by mercenary forces, they burn the neighborhood – bringing the palace down with it. Candiano and his family escape, but are killed by the mob.

summary: Byzantine Emperor John I Tzimiskes died.
text: John I Tzimiskes, Byzantine emperor

summary: Bulgarian nobleman Aron died.
text: June 14: Aron, Bulgarian nobleman

summary: Bulgarian nobleman David was killed.
text: June 14: David, Bulgarian nobleman

summary: Bulgarian nobleman Moses died during the siege of Serres.
text: June 14: Moses, Bulgarian nobleman

summary: Pietro IV Candiano, doge of Venice, was killed by an enraged mob.
text: Pietro IV Candiano, doge of Venice

summary: Roman was crowned ruler of Bulgaria after escaping Byzantine captivity, though General Samuel retained military control following Boris II's death.
text: May – Boris II, dethroned emperor (tsar) of Bulgaria, and his brother Roman manage to escape from captivity in Constantinople. They reach the Bulgarian border, but Boris is killed by mistake by the border guards. Roman is crowned as new ruler, although leadership and the control of the army remain in the hands of General Samuel (a member of the Cometopuli Dynasty).

summary: Buyid ruler 'Adud al-Dawla expelled the Hamdanids from Mosul, forcing Abu Taghlib to flee to Byzantine Antzitene.
text: Summer – 'Adud al-Dawla, ruler (shah) of the Buyid Dynasty, drives the Hamdanids out of Mosul and tries to unify the country. Abu Taghlib is forced to flee to the Byzantine city of Antzitene.

summary: King Ashot III of Armenia died.
text: Ashot III (the Merciful), king of Armenia

summary: Boris II, former emperor of Bulgaria, was killed near the Bulgarian border while escaping Byzantine territory.
text: Boris II, emperor of the Bulgarian Empire

summary: Byzantine eunuch general Peter was killed in battle against rebel forces in Anatolia.
text: Peter, Byzantine eunuch general

summary: General Bardas Phokas defeated the rebel forces of Bardas Skleros at the Battle of Pankaleia.
text: Battle of Pankaleia: Rebel forces under General Bardas Skleros are defeated by the Byzantine army loyal to Emperor Basil II, commanded by General Bardas Phokas (the Younger), near Pankaleia (modern-day Hisarköy). Phokas regroups his forces and continues his march to the East, drawing Skleros away from Constantinople.

summary: Vitale Candiano succeeded Pietro I Orseolo as Doge of Venice after Pietro fled to France.
text: Pietro I Orseolo, doge of Venice, escapes from Venice and travels to the Benedictine abbey of Michel-de-Cuxa (Southern France). He is succeeded by Vitale Candiano (not the bishop of Grado) as doge of Venice.

summary: Yaroslav the Wise, future grand prince of Kiev, was born.
text: Yaroslav I (the Wise), Russian grand prince (d. 1054)

summary: Zoe Porphyrogenita, future empress of the Byzantine Empire, was born.
text: Zoë, Byzantine empress consort

summary: Bardas Phokas the Younger defeated rebel general Bardas Skleros at the Second Battle of Pankaleia near Sarvenis.
text: Second Battle of Pankaleia: An Ibero-Byzantine expeditionary force, under General Bardas Phokas (the Younger), inflicts a crushing defeat on the rebels of General Bardas Skleros, at Sarvenis (modern Turkey). Skleros manages to escape, and finds shelter with his Muslim allies. The rebellion is subdued without difficulty.

summary: Vitale Candiano abdicated as doge of Venice and was succeeded by Tribuno Memmo.
text: Vitale Candiano, doge of Venice, abdicates for health reasons after a 14-month reign, and retires to a monastery. He is succeeded by Tribuno Memmo, a son-in-law of the murdered Pietro IV Candiano. Tribuno declares a general amnesty for everyone complicit in the plot against Pietro.

summary: Ya'qub ibn Killis replaced Jawhar as-Siqilli as vizier of Egypt.
text: Jawhar as-Siqilli is dismissed as vizier of Egypt after an unsuccessful campaign in Syria (near Damascus). He is replaced by Ya'qub ibn Killis.

summary: Hamdanid emir Abu Taghlib died near Ramla.
text: Abu Taghlib, Hamdanid emir

summary: Vitale Candiano, doge of Venice, died.
text: Vitale Candiano, doge of Venice

summary: Vladimir the Great consolidated the Kievan realm and was proclaimed ruler of all Kievan Rus'.
text: Vladimir I (the Great), grand prince of Kiev, consolidates the Kievan realm from modern Ukraine to the Baltic Sea. Vladimir is proclaimed ruler (knyaz) of all Kievan Rus'.

summary: Sviatopolk I, future Grand Prince of Kiev, was born.
text: Sviatopolk I, Grand Prince of Kiev

summary: Future Byzantine empress Theodora Porphyrogenita was born in Constantinople.
text: Theodora Porphyrogenita, Byzantine empress (d. 1056)

summary: Emperor Otto II moved the imperial court to Rome, making it his capital and receiving western European nobles.
text: Spring – Emperor Otto II (the Red) leads the imperial court to Rome, making the city his imperial capital, and receives nobles from all parts of Western Europe. Otto makes plans to conquer Byzantine Italy.

summary: Otto II departed Rome and invaded Apulia to campaign against the Saracens.
text: Fall – Otto II departs with an expeditionary force from Rome, and invades Apulia (Southern Italy) to punish the Saracens. He demands a fleet from Pisa, and imposes a trade embargo against Venice.

summary: Venetian nobleman Giovanni Orseolo was born.
text: Giovanni Orseolo, Venetian nobleman (d. 1006)

summary: Future Byzantine empress Theodora Porphyrogenita was born.
text: Theodora, Empress of the Byzantine Empire (d. 1056)

summary: Otto II assembled an imperial army at Taranto and advanced into Calabria against the forces of the Kalbid Emirate of Sicily.
text: Summer – Emperor Otto II (the Red) assembles an imperial expeditionary force at Taranto, and proceeds along the gulf coast towards Calabria. In the meantime, Emir Abu'l-Qasim (Kalbid) of the Emirate of Sicily declares a Holy War (jihad) against the Germans, but his forces retreat when he notices the unexpected strength of Otto's troops (not far from Rossano).

summary: Kalbid Muslim forces defeated Emperor Otto II at the Battle of Stilo, despite the death of Emir Abu'l-Qasim in the battle.
text: July 13 (or 14) – Battle of Stilo: Abu'l-Qasim is cornered by the imperial German forces led by Otto II at Cape Colonna (south of Crotone). After a violent clash, the German heavy cavalry destroys the Muslim centre, killing al-Qasim in the initial fighting. The Saracens hold together and draw Otto into a trap, encircling and defeating his forces (killing around 4,000 men).

summary: Buyid ruler Adud al-Dawla concluded a ten-year peace treaty with the Byzantine Empire.
text: 'Adud al-Dawla, emir (king of kings) of the Buyid Dynasty, concludes a 10-year peace treaty with the Byzantine Empire. He establishes what will soon become the most important hospital of Baghdad.

summary: The Battle of Stilo was fought in Byzantine Calabria between the Holy Roman Empire and the Kalbid Emirate of Sicily.
text: July 13 (or 14) – Battle of Stilo:

summary: Abu'l-Qasim, Kalbid emir of Sicily, was killed at the Battle of Stilo.
text: Abu'l-Qasim, Kalbid emir of Sicily

summary: Shabbethai Donnolo, Jewish physician and scholar from Byzantine Southern Italy, died.
text: Shabbethai Donnolo, Jewish physician (b. 913)

summary: At the Diet of Verona, Emperor Otto II declared war against the Byzantine Empire and the Emirate of Sicily, while Otto III was elected king.
text: Summer – Diet of Verona: Emperor Otto II (the Red) declares war against the Byzantine Empire and the Emirate of Sicily. He assembles a large expeditionary force for a renewal of an invasion in Calabria (Southern Italy). Otto gifts the Rheingau ("Rhine District") to the Archbishopric of Mainz during the 'Veronese donation'. Otto III is elected king of Germany and Italy.

summary: Bakjur attacked Aleppo with Fatimid troops but was repulsed by Byzantine forces under Bardas Phokas the Younger.
text: Fall – Fatimid troops under the defecting Hamdanid governor of Homs, Bakjur, attack Aleppo (modern Syria), but are repulsed through the intervention of the Byzantine army. Bardas Phokas (the Younger) sacks the city, while Bakjur flees to Fatimid territory in Egypt.

summary: Antony III, Patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Antony III (the Studite), patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Antipope Boniface VII returned to Rome with Crescentii support and seized the papal throne.
text: Anti-Pope Boniface VII returns from Constantinople and gains support from the powerful Roman Crescentii family. He takes hold of the papal throne.

summary: Amalfitan Benedictines founded a Latin Christian monastery on Mount Athos with the support of John the Iberian.
text: Amalfitan Benedictines found the only Latin Christian monastery on Mount Athos with the support of John the Iberian. The monastery will last until 1287.

summary: Basil Lekapenos, Byzantine chief minister, died.
text: Basil Lekapenos, Byzantine chief minister (b. 925)

summary: Georgian general and monk John Tornike died.
text: Tornike Eristavi, Georgian general and monk

summary: Bulgarian forces under Tsar Samuel ambushed and defeated Emperor Basil II and his Byzantine army at the Gates of Trajan.
text: Battle of the Gates of Trajan: Emperor Basil II leads a Byzantine expeditionary force (30,000 men) against the Bulgarians to capture the fortress city of Sredets. After a siege of 20 days, Basil is forced to retreat from the Sofia Valley towards the town of Ihtiman (through a passage known as the Gate of Trajan). The Bulgarians under Tsar Samuel ambush and defeat the Byzantine forces. Only the elite Varangian Guard escapes with heavy casualties and leads Basil to safety through secondary routes.
names: Battle of the Gates of Trajan

summary: Bardas Phokas the Younger and Bardas Skleros rebelled against Emperor Basil II and overran Anatolia.
text: Bardas Phokas (the Younger) and Bardas Skleros, two members of the military elite, begin a wide-scale rebellion against Emperor Basil II. They overrun Anatolia, and Phokas declares himself Emperor. Basil applies for military assistance from Prince Vladimir the Great, ruler of Kievan Rus', who agrees to help him and sends a Varangian army (6,000 men).
names: Rebellion of Bardas Phokas the Younger

summary: The population of Bari revolted against Byzantine rule.
text: The population of Bari revolts against the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Emperor Basil II led an attack with his Varangian guard across the Bosporus, defeating and executing the rebel commander Kalokyros Delphinas at Chrysopolis.
text: Fall – Emperor Basil II, supported by a contingent of 6,000 Varangians (the future Varangian Guard), organizes the defences of Constantinople to meet a threat from the insurgents, Bardas Phokas the Younger and Bardas Skleros. Basil crosses the Bosphorus, and leads a surprise attack on the rebel camp of Kalokyros Delphinas, at Chrysopolis. Delphinas is captured and executed, either by crucifixion or by impalement .

summary: Vladimir the Great was baptized at Chersonesus, married Anna Porphyrogenita, and initiated the Christianization of Kievan Rus'.
text: Grand Prince Vladimir the Great, ruler of Kievan Rus', marries Anna Porphyrogenita (sister of Basil II) and converts to Christianity. He is baptized at Cherson in the Crimea, taking the Christian name of Basil (in honor of his brother-in-law). Vladimir returns in triumph to Kiev, and begins the Christianization of Kievan Rus' to the Eastern Orthodox Church.

summary: Metropolitan Michael I of Kiev founded the Mezhyhirskyi Monastery with Greek monks from Constantinople.
text: The Mezhyhirskyi Monastery (located on the Dnieper River) is founded by Michael I, first metropolitan bishop of Kiev. He arrives with Greek monks from Constantinople.

summary: Byzantine general Kalokyros Delphinas died.
text: Kalokyros Delphinas, Byzantine general (or 989)

summary: Emperor Basil II defeated Bardas Phokas the Younger at Abydos with the aid of Varangians, ending the rebellion against Constantinople.
text: Emperor Basil II uses his contingent of 6,000 Varangians to help him defeat Bardas Phokas (the Younger), who suffers a seizure during the siege of Abydos (threatening to blockade the Dardanelles). Phokas dies, ending the revolt and threat to Constantinople. Upon Phokas' death, the other rebel leader Bardas Skleros (who is captured and blinded) yields to Basil's superior forces.

summary: An earthquake struck Constantinople, collapsing the western dome arch of the Hagia Sophia.
text: The Hagia Sophia at Constantinople is struck by a great earthquake, causing the collapse of the western dome arch. Basil II asks the Armenian architect Trdat, the creator of the Cathedral of Ani, to direct the repairs.

summary: Byzantine general and rebel Bardas Phokas the Younger died at the Battle of Abydos.
text: Bardas Phokas, Byzantine general

summary: Rebel Byzantine general Kalokyros Delphinas was executed at Chrysopolis.
text: Kalokyros Delphinas, Byzantine general (or 988)

summary: Jovan Vladimir, future Prince of Duklja, was born.
text: John Vladimir, Serbian prince

summary: Nicodemus of Mammola, an Italian monk and saint, died.
text: Nicodemus of Mammola, Italian monk and saint

summary: Theophanu, Holy Roman Empress and regent, died.
text: Theophanu, Holy Roman Empress and regent

summary: Byzantine Emperor Basil II began a military campaign against the First Bulgarian Empire.
text: Spring: Byzantine Emperor Basil II begins a campaign against the Bulgarians.

summary: Pietro II Orseolo became Doge of Venice and established a protectorate along the Dalmatian islands.
text: Pietro II Orseolo becomes the 26th Doge of Venice. Venice establishes a protectorate on the coast of the Dalmatian Islands.

summary: Sicilian Arab forces besieged the city of Taranto.
text: Taranto is sieged by Sicilian Arabs.

summary: Bardas Skleros, a Byzantine general and rebel leader, died.
text: Bardas Skleros, Byzantine general

summary: Ashot-Sahak, king of Vaspurakan, died.
text: Ashot-Sahak, king of Vaspurakan (Armenia)

summary: Hamdanid mercenary and governor Bakjur was executed near Aleppo.
text: Bakjur, Hamdanid mercenary and governor

summary: Sa'd al-Dawla, Hamdanid emir of Aleppo, died.
text: Sa'd al-Dawla, Hamdanid emir (b. 952)

summary: Pietro II Orseolo, Doge of Venice, concluded a treaty with Byzantine Emperor Basil II granting Venice trade privileges in Constantinople in exchange for military transport.
text: Spring – Pietro II Orseolo, doge of Venice, concludes a treaty with Emperor Basil II to transport Byzantine troops, in exchange for commercial privileges in Constantinople. Venetian ships are exempted from customs duties at Abydos (mostly foreign goods are carried on Venetian ships). Venetian merchants in Constantinople are placed directly under the Grand Logothetes (Minister of Finance).

summary: Fatimid general Jawhar al-Siqilli died in Cairo.
text: Jawhar al-Siqilli, Fatimid general

summary: Michael I, Metropolitan of Kiev, died.
text: Michael I, Kievan metropolitan bishop

summary: Prince David II of Tao-Klarjeti died.
text: David II, prince of Tao-Klarjeti (Georgia)

summary: Fatimid forces under Manjutakin defeated a Byzantine relief army commanded by Michael Bourtzes at the Battle of the Orontes.
text: Battle of the Orontes: Fatimid forces, under Turkish general Manjutakin (also the governor of Damascus), besiege Apamea (modern Syria). Emperor Basil II sends a Byzantine expeditionary army, led by Dux Michael Bourtzes, to relieve the city in alliance with the Hamdanid Dynasty. Manjutakin defeats the Hamdanids with his forces and attacks the Byzantine force in the rear. The Byzantine army panics and flees, losing some 5,000 men in the process.

summary: Emperor Basil II led an expedition to Syria, lifted the Fatimid siege of Aleppo, and secured the Orontes Valley for the Byzantine Empire.
text: Arab–Byzantine War: Emperor Basil II launches a counter-campaign against the Fatimid Caliphate. He leads a Byzantine expeditionary army (13,000 men) to aid the Hamdanid emir Sa'id al-Dawla, and crosses Asia Minor in only sixteen days. Basil lifts the siege of Aleppo, and takes over the Orontes Valley. He incorporates Syria into the Byzantine Empire (including the larger city of Antioch) which is the seat of its eponymous Patriarch.

summary: Caliph Al-Aziz Billah died at Bilbeis and was succeeded by his son Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah as ruler of the Fatimid Caliphate.
text: Caliph Al-Aziz Billah dies at Bilbeis in Egypt after a 21-year reign in which he has expanded his Shiite caliphate at the expense of the Byzantines, using Turkish mercenaries (Mamelukes). He is succeeded by his 11-year-old son Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah as ruler of the Fatimid Caliphate (until 1021).

summary: Nikephoros Ouranos defeated the Bulgarian army of Samuel of Bulgaria at the Battle of Spercheios.
text: Battle of Spercheios: Byzantine forces, under General Nikephoros Ouranos, defeat the Bulgarians at the Spercheios River in Greece. During a night battle, the Bulgarian co-ruler Samuel is wounded; he and his son Gavril Radomir evade capture, by feigning death among the bodies of their slain soldiers. Samuel sets off to Bulgaria, and retreats with the remnants of his army, into the Pindus Mountains. Ouranos returns to Constantinople, with 1,000 heads of Bulgarian soldiers and 12,000 captives.

summary: Samuel of Bulgaria succeeded his brother Roman of Bulgaria as tsar of the Bulgarians following Roman's death in Constantinople.
text: Summer – Roman of Bulgaria dies in captivity in Constantinople. He is succeeded by his brother Samuel (a member of the Cometopuli dynasty) who takes the Bulgarian title of tsar. He possibly receives his 'imperial crown' from Gregory V .

summary: Roman, tsar of the Bulgarian Empire, died in captivity in Constantinople.
text: Roman, ruler (tsar) of the Bulgarian Empire

summary: Emperor Samuel of Bulgaria invaded the Kingdom of Croatia and seized Dyrrachium before withdrawing after besieging Zadar.
text: Croatian–Bulgarian War: Emperor Samuel launches a military campaign against the Kingdom of Croatia to prevent an alliance between the Serbian principality and the Byzantines. He seizes Dyrrachium (modern-day Durrës in Albania) and advances along the Dalmatian coast. The Bulgarian army is forced to withdraw into Croatian hinterlands (now part of Bosnia and Herzegovina), after the Siege of Zadar.

summary: Forces of the Fatimid Caliphate stormed Tyre and defeated a Byzantine relief squadron.
text: Summer – Revolt of Tyre: The city of Tyre (modern Lebanon) is stormed by forces of the Fatimid Caliphate. A Byzantine squadron attempts to reinforce but is repulsed by the Fatimid navy. The defenders are massacred or taken captive to Egypt. The Byzantine captives are executed.

summary: A Fatimid relief army defeated the besieging Byzantine forces under Damian Dalassenos at the Battle of Apamea.
text: Battle of Apamea: Byzantine forces under governor (doux) Damian Dalassenos besiege the fortress city of Apamea for control over northern Syria. The Fatimids send a relief army from Damascus – and defeat the Byzantines, Dalassenos is killed by a Kurdish officer in battle.

summary: Byzantine dux Damian Dalassenos died in battle at Apamea.
text: Damian Dalassenos, Byzantine governor (doux)

summary: Sisinnius II, patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Sisinnius II, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Byzantine monk and preacher Nikon the Metanoeite died in Sparta.
text: Nikon the Metanoeite, Byzantine monk and preacher

actor: Byzantine Empire under the Macedonian dynasty
summary: Byzantine commanders Theodorokanos and Nikephoros Xiphias captured the former Bulgarian capitals of Pliska and Great Preslav.
text: The Byzantine Empire under the Macedonian dynasty was engaged in a long and hard war with the First Bulgarian Empire. The Byzantine generals, Theodorokanos and Nikephoros Xiphias captured the former Bulgarian capitals of Pliska and Great Preslav, along with Little Preslav, extending Byzantine control over the northeastern portion of the Bulgarian state (Mysia and Scythia Minor). At the same time, Byzantium was instrumental in the Christianization of Kievan Rus' and of other medieval confederations of Slavic states.
cast: Byzantine Empire under the Macedonian dynasty
names: Byzantine Empire under the Macedonian dynasty

states.value: Byzantine Empire under the Macedonian dynasty

summary: Argyrus, future Byzantine general and Catepan of Italy, was born in Bari.
text: Argyrus, Byzantine general

summary: Constantine IX Monomachos, future Byzantine emperor, was born in Constantinople.
text: Constantine IX, Byzantine emperor (d. 1055)

summary: John Mauropous, Byzantine hymnographer and metropolitan bishop of Euchaita, was born.
text: John Mauropous, Byzantine hymnographer (d. c.1070/1092)

summary: Michael I Cerularius, future Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, was born in Constantinople.
text: Michael I, Byzantine patriarch

summary: The Byzantine Empire annexed the Tao/Tayk region as the Theme of Iberia.
text: The Tao/Tayk region is annexed by the Byzantines, as the Theme of Iberia.

summary: Sergius II became Patriarch of Constantinople.
text: July – Sergius II becomes Patriarch of Constantinople.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Basil II attempted to reconquer Bulgaria.
text: Byzantine Emperor Basil II attempts to reconquer Bulgaria.

summary: David III of Tao, Georgian prince of Tao-Klarjeti, died.
text: David III of Tao ("the Great"), Georgian prince

summary: Future Byzantine Emperor Nikephoros III Botaneiates was born.
text: Nikephoros III, Byzantine emperor (d. 1081)

summary: Sa'id al-Dawla, Hamdanid emir of Aleppo, died.
text: Sa'id al-Dawla, Hamdanid emir of Aleppo (Syria)

summary: Byzantine forces invaded the First Bulgarian Empire.
text: Byzantine conquest of Bulgaria: Byzantine forces invaded Bulgaria.

summary: Byzantine monk and monastic founder Athanasius the Athonite died on Mount Athos.
text: Athanasius the Athonite, Byzantine monk (b. 920)

summary: King Gurgen-Khachik of Vaspurakan died.
text: Gurgen IV, king of Vaspurakan (Armenia)

summary: Byzantine Emperor Basil II defeated Bulgarian forces under Samuel at the Battle of Skopje.
text: Battle of Skopje: Emperor Basil II defeats the Bulgarian forces near Skopje (modern North Macedonia). Leaving his army behind, Samuel of Bulgaria manages to escape. Basil continues his campaign and besieges the fortress of Pernik. By the end of the year Basil has reconquered about half of the Bulgarian Empire.

summary: Allied Venetian and Byzantine forces relieved Bari from a three-day Saracen siege.
text: Fall – Venetian-Byzantine forces defeat the Saracens at Bari. The citadel is on the brink of capitulation after a 3 day siege. Giovanni, a son of Doge Pietro Orseolo II, is married to the Byzantine princess Maria Argyra.

summary: The future Fatimid caliph al-Zahir li-I'zaz Din Allah was born in Cairo.
text: al-Zahir li-i'zaz Din Allah, Fatimid caliph of Egypt (d. 1036)

summary: Italo-Byzantine monk and abbot Nilus the Younger died near Rome.
text: Nilus the Younger, Byzantine abbot (b. 910)

summary: Future Byzantine emperor Constantine X Doukas was born.
text: Constantine X, Byzantine emperor (d. 1067)

summary: Venetian nobleman Giovanni Orseolo died.
text: Giovanni Orseolo, Venetian nobleman (b. 981)

summary: Future Byzantine emperor Isaac I Komnenos was born.
text: Isaac I Komnenos, Byzantine emperor

summary: Melus led a Lombard revolt in Bari against the Byzantine Catepanate of Italy and mobilised an army with Dattus to invade southern Italy.
text: Lombard Revolt: Lombard forces led by Melus, an Italian nobleman, revolt in Bari against the Catepanate of Italy (a province of the Byzantine Empire). He and his brother-in-law Dattus (or Datto) mobilise a large army and invade southern Italy.

summary: Otto Orseolo succeeded his father Pietro II Orseolo as the Doge of Venice.
text: Doge Pietro II Orseolo dies after an 18-year reign in which he has started the expansion of Venetia by conquering the islands of Lastovo and Korčula along the Dalmatian coast. Pietro is succeeded by his 16-year-old son Otto Orseolo as sole ruler of Venice.

summary: Fatimid caliph Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah ordered the destruction of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.
text: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem is destroyed by the Fatimid caliph Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah.

summary: Georgian calligrapher and monk George the Hagiorite was born.
text: George the Hagiorite, Georgian calligrapher (d. 1065)

summary: Lu'lu' al-Kabir, emir of Aleppo, died.
text: Abu Muhammad Lu'lu' al-Kabir, emir of Aleppo (Syria)

summary: Pietro II Orseolo, Doge of Venice, died.
text: Pietro II Orseolo, doge of Venice (b. 961)

summary: Future Byzantine emperor Michael IV the Paphlagonian was born.
text: Michael IV the Paphlagonian, Byzantine emperor (d. 1041)

summary: John Kourkouas, Byzantine catepan of Italy, died.
text: John Kourkouas, Byzantine catepan

summary: Mahmoud the Fat rose against the Lombard rebels and delivered Bari to Byzantine catepan Basil Mesardonites.
text: Lombard Revolt: Mahmoud the Fat of Bari rises up against the Lombard rebels, led by Melus, and delivers the city to Basil Mesardonites, Byzantine governor (catepan) of the Catepanate of Italy. Melus is forced to flee to Salerno, and his brother-in-law Dattus escapes to Monte Cassino, but their families are taken captive, and carted off to Constantinople.

summary: Basil Mesardonites secured the cooperation of Guaimar III of Salerno and had Abbot Atenulf expel Dattus from Monte Cassino.
text: Autumn – Basil Mesardonites visits Guaimar III of Salerno to secure his cooperation. Melus is forced to flee again. Basil proceeds to Monte Cassino – and persuades Abbot Atenulf to expel Dattus. Pope Sergius IV supports Dattus with papal troops, to garrison the tower on the Garigliano River, a fortified complex in the territory of the Duchy of Gaeta.

summary: Anna Porphyrogenita, Grand Princess of Kyiv and Byzantine imperial princess, died.
text: Anna Porphyrogenita, Grand Princess of Kiev

summary: Byzantine governor Theophylact Botaneiates defeated Bulgarian forces near Thessaloniki during Basil II's expedition.
text: Summer – Battle of Thessalonica: Emperor Basil II launches a raiding expedition against Bulgaria. From Western Thrace via Serres he reaches the valley of the Strymon River, near Thessaloniki (modern Greece); the local Byzantine governor Theophylact Botaneiates defeats the Bulgarians.

summary: Basil II crushed the Bulgarian forces at the Battle of Kleidion, ordering thousands of captured soldiers blinded.
text: Battle of Kleidion: Basil II defeats the Bulgarian forces, between the mountains of Belasitsa and Ograzhden, near the town of Kleidon. By order of Basil, almost 15,000 prisoners are blinded; Tsar Samuel survives the battle, but dies of shock. Basil earns the nickname "Bulgar-Slayer".

summary: Bagrat III, the first king of a unified Georgia, died.
text: Bagrat III, king of Abkhazia (Georgia)

summary: Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria died shortly after the catastrophic defeat of his army at the Battle of Kleidion.
text: Samuel, emperor (tsar) of the Bulgarian Empire

summary: Abu'l-Abbas ibn al-Furat, vizier of the Fatimid Caliphate, died.
text: Abu'l-Abbas ibn al-Furat, Fatimid vizier (or 1015)

summary: Byzantine general and governor Theophylact Botaneiates died in an ambush near Strumica.
text: Theophylact Botaneiates, Byzantine general and governor

summary: Vladimir the Great died at Berestove and was succeeded as Grand Prince of Kiev by his son Sviatopolk I.
text: Vladimir the Great dies at Berestove after a 35-year reign. He is succeeded by his son Sviatopolk I as Grand Prince of Kiev.

summary: John Komnenos, Byzantine aristocrat and military commander, was born.
text: John Komnenos, Byzantine aristocrat (d. 1067)

summary: Michael V Kalaphates, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: Michael V Kalaphates, Byzantine emperor (d. 1042)

summary: Vladimir the Great, Grand Prince of Kiev, died at Berestovo near Kiev.
text: Vladimir the Great, Grand Prince of Kiev

summary: Gavril Radomir, Emperor of Bulgaria, was murdered during a hunting expedition by his cousin Ivan Vladislav.
text: Gavril Radomir, emperor (tsar) of Bulgaria

summary: Irene of Larissa, Empress consort of Bulgaria, was murdered alongside Emperor Gavril Radomir.
text: Irene of Larissa, empress (tsarina) of Bulgaria

summary: Melus of Bari launched a second revolt against Byzantine rule in southern Italy with Norman mercenaries.
text: Melus of Bari makes a second attempt against Byzantine-held Southern Italy. To support his cause, he hires Norman mercenaries, unwittingly triggering the rise of Norman rule over southern Italy.

summary: A combined Byzantine and Kievan Rus' force captured Georgius Tzul, effectively ending Khazaria's existence.
text: Georgius Tzul, ruler of Khazaria, is captured by a combined Byzantine Empire–Kievan Rus' force, which effectively ends Khazaria's existence.

summary: Jovan Vladimir, ruler of Duklja, was executed in Prespa.
text: Jovan Vladimir, Serbian prince. (b. 990)

summary: Melus of Bari and his Norman mercenaries defeated a Byzantine army along the Fortore River.
text: Summer – Melus of Bari, a Lombard nobleman, revolts and is supported by Norman mercenaries at Capua. He marches into Apulia to catch the Byzantine army off-guard. Melus defeats the Byzantines on the banks of the Fortore River and ravages the territory in Apulia.

summary: Emperor Basil II appointed Basil Boioannes as catapan of Italy and dispatched reinforcements from Constantinople.
text: Winter – Emperor Basil II ("the Bulgar Slayer") replaces Leo Tornikios with the new catapan Basil Boioannes and sends him reinforcements (including a detachment of the elite Varangian Guard) from Constantinople.

summary: Byzantine general Leo Passianos died.
text: Leo Passianos, Byzantine general

summary: Eustathios Daphnomeles blinded and captured Ivats, ending the final resistance to the Byzantine conquest of Bulgaria.
text: Ivats, Bulgarian nobleman and rebel leader, is treacherously blinded and captured by strategos Eustathios Daphnomeles, ending the last resistance to the Byzantine conquest of Bulgaria by Basil II.

summary: Basil Boioannes decisively defeated Melus of Bari and his Norman mercenaries at the Battle of Cannae.
text: October – Battle of Cannae: The Lombard adventurer Melus of Bari and his Norman mercenaries are decisively defeated by the Byzantine army, led by the Catepan Basil Boioannes.

summary: Byzantine monk and philosopher Michael Psellos was born.
text: Michael Psellos, Byzantine monk and philosopher

summary: Norman nobleman Gilbert Buatère was killed fighting the Byzantines at the Battle of Cannae.
text: October 1: Gilbert Buatère, Norman nobleman

summary: Norman nobleman Osmond Drengot was killed fighting the Byzantines at the Battle of Cannae.
text: October 1: Osmond Drengot, Norman nobleman

summary: Ivan Vladislav, Emperor of Bulgaria, was killed while besieging the Byzantine fortress of Dyrrhachium.
text: Ivan Vladislav, emperor (tsar) of Bulgaria

summary: The Bulgarian boyars surrendered to Byzantine Emperor Basil II at Ohrid, establishing the Byzantine theme of Bulgaria.
text: Byzantine conquest of Bulgaria: The Bulgarian boyars accepted the establishment of the theme of Bulgaria on the territory of the former Empire, with significant autonomy for themselves.

summary: Sergius II, Patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Sergius II (the Studite), patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Byzantine troops commanded by Catepan Basil Boioannes and allied with Prince Pandulf IV of Capua captured the fortress of Troia.
text: Byzantine troops under Catepan Basil Boioannes (supported by his ally Prince Pandulf IV) capture the fortress of Troia.

summary: Filarete of Calabria was born in Palermo.
text: Filarete of Calabria, Sicilian saint

summary: Lombard rebel leader Dattus died after being captured by the Byzantines.
text: Dattus (or Datto), Lombard rebel leader

summary: Lombard nobleman and rebel leader Melus of Bari died.
text: Melus of Bari, Lombard nobleman and rebel leader

summary: Senekerim-Hovhannes Artsruni surrendered the Kingdom of Vaspurakan to the Byzantine Empire in exchange for Sebasteia and governorship of Cappadocia.
text: Senekerim-Hovhannes Artsruni, Armenian king of Vaspurakan, surrenders his kingdom to the Byzantine Empire. In return, he receives Sebasteia and becomes governor of Cappadocia.

summary: The Byzantine army under Basil II defeated George I of Georgia at the Battle of Shirimni.
text: Battle of Shirimni, the Byzantine Empire under Basil II defeats the Kingdom of Georgia under Giorgi I at Shirimni, at the Lake Palakazio, modern Lake Çıldır, Turkey

summary: Future Byzantine empress Eudokia Makrembolitissa was born.
text: Eudokia Makrembolitissa, Byzantine empress (d. 1096)

summary: The Byzantine army under Basil II defeated George I of Georgia at the Battle of Svindax, ending the war.
text: Spring – Battle of Svindax: The Byzantine army under Emperor Basil II defeats the Georgians at Svindax (modern Turkey). King George I is forced to negotiate a peace treaty, ending the Byzantine–Georgian wars.

summary: Nikephoros Xiphias assassinated Nikephoros Phokas Barytrachelos after their joint rebellion against Basil II collapsed.
text: Summer – Nikephoros Phokas Barytrachelos conspires with the Byzantine general Nikephoros Xiphias against Basil II. The rebellion collapses and Xiphias assassinates Phokas.

summary: Emperor Henry II descended through Rome onto Capua after southern Lombard states allied with the Byzantines.
text: Spring – Emperor Henry II divides his army into three columns and descends through Rome onto Capua after the Lombard states of Southern Italy had switched their allegiance to the Byzantinians in the wake of the battle of Cannae four years earlier. The bulk of the expeditionary force (20,000 men) led by Henry, makes its way down the Adriatic coast.

summary: Byzantine public servant and historian Michael Attaleiates was born.
text: Michael Attaleiates, Byzantine historian (d. 1080)

summary: Byzantine monk and Christian mystic Symeon the New Theologian died.
text: Symeon the New Theologian, Byzantine monk (b. 949)

summary: Byzantine aristocrat and rebel Nikephoros Phokas Barytrachelos was killed in Cappadocia.
text: Nikephoros Phokas, Byzantine aristocrat

summary: Byzantine general Basil Boioannes sailed from Bari to invade Croatia, taking King Kresimir III's wife hostage.
text: Basil Boioannes, Byzantine general and governor of the Catapanate of Italy, sails from Bari across the Adriatic Sea to begin an invasion of Croatia, ruled by Krešimir III. He later takes Kresimir's wife as a hostage, transporting her to Bari and then to Constantinople as a hostage.

summary: A Byzantine expedition threatened Sicily, prompting an appeal to the Zirids whose relief fleet was wrecked off Pantelleria.
text: Byzantine expedition to invade Sicily: Governor Ahmed al-Akhal appeals to the Zirids of Ifriqiya for help. They dispatch a fleet, but these are caught up in a storm and destroyed near Pantelleria.
names: History of Islam in southern Italy

summary: A Byzantine fleet destroyed a band of Kievan Viking raiders at the Battle of Lemnos.
text: Battle of Lemnos: Kievan Viking raiders (800 men) sail through the straits at Abydos to the Aegean Sea. From there they make for the island of Lemnos, but are defeated by a Byzantine fleet of the Cibyrrhaeot Theme.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Basil II died in Constantinople and was succeeded by his brother Constantine VIII.
text: Byzantine Emperor Basil II ("Bulgar Slayer") dies in Constantinople after a 50-year reign. Never married, he is succeeded by his brother and co-emperor Constantine VIII, who becomes sole ruler of the Byzantine Empire. Constantine calls the Sicilian invasion off. Catapan Basil Boioannes diverts the Byzantine expeditionary force already assembled on Calabria, to join the siege of Capua.

summary: Byzantine noblewoman and future regent Anna Dalassene was born.
text: Anna Dalassene, Byzantine empress and regent

summary: Byzantine philosopher John Italus was born.
text: John Italus, Byzantine philosopher (d. 1090)

summary: Byzantine Emperor Basil II died after a nearly fifty-year reign.
text: Basil II, Byzantine emperor (b. 958)

summary: Patriarch Eustathius of Constantinople died.
text: December – Eustathius of Constantinople, Byzantine patriarch

summary: Emperor Constantine VIII died at Constantinople after arranging the marriage of his daughter Zoë to Romanos III Argyros.
text: Emperor Constantine VIII dies at Constantinople after a 3-year reign. On his deathbed, and without a male heir, Constantine arranges that his eldest daughter, Zoë Porphyrogenita, succeeds him and marries the Byzantine nobleman, Romanos III (Argyros).

summary: Romanos III Argyros and his wife Zoë Porphyrogenita took the throne of the Byzantine Empire.
text: Zoë Porphyrogenita takes the throne as empress consort. Her husband, Romanos III (age 60) becomes emperor of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Constantine VIII died in Constantinople.
text: Constantine VIII, Byzantine emperor (b. 960)

summary: Emperor Romanos III Argyros led a Byzantine army toward Aleppo and encamped near Azaz, where his forces were encircled by Mirdasid Bedouin troops.
text: Emperor Romanos III Argyros decides to retaliate upon the incursions of the Muslims on the eastern frontier. He leads a Byzantine expeditionary force (20,000 men) to secure Antioch. The Mirdasid emir Shibl al-Dawla Nasr of Aleppo sues for peace, but Romanos refuses to negotiate and leads his army against Aleppo, against the advice of his generals. The Byzantine army encamped near Azaz, where they were encircled by the Mirdasids' Bedouin troops, who cut off the Byzantines from food and water.

summary: Emperor Romanos III Argyros retreated toward Antioch after suffering a defeat near Azaz, though Byzantine forces subsequently repulsed a Fatimid assault on Maraclea and recaptured Azaz.
text: Romanos orders a retreat to Antioch. As the army is exhausted from the heat and the lack of supplies, the retreat soon turns into a flight in panic. Romanos returns to Constantinople in humiliation, but his generals on the eastern frontier manage to salvage the situation: a Fatimid attack on Maraclea is repulsed, and Azaz itself is captured in December after a brief siege. In April/May 1031, Emir Nasr of Aleppo agreed to vassal and tributary status with Byzantium.

summary: Romanos IV Diogenes, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: Romanos IV, emperor of the Byzantine Empire (d. 1072)

summary: Byzantine general George Maniakes captured Edessa from Arab forces, stabilizing the empire's eastern border.
text: The Byzantine general George Maniakes captures Edessa from the Arab Muslims and stabilizes the eastern frontier.

summary: Emperor Romanos III Argyros sent a Byzantine expeditionary army under Michael Protospatharios to reinforce Calabria.
text: Spring – Emperor Romanos III (Argyros) sends a Byzantine expeditionary army under General Michael Protospatharios, which includes Western auxiliaries and elite troops of Asia Minor, to reinforce the Byzantine position in Calabria (Southern Italy).

summary: Constantine Diogenes, Byzantine general, died by suicide in Constantinople to avoid implicating his fellow conspirators.
text: Constantine Diogenes, Byzantine general

summary: John VIII bar Abdoun, Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch, died while detained by Byzantine authorities.
text: John VIII bar Abdoun, patriarch of Antioch (b. 944)

summary: Emperor Romanos III Argyros was murdered in his bath at the instigation of Empress Zoe, who married Michael IV the Paphlagonian and elevated him to the Byzantine throne.
text: Emperor Romanos III (Argyros) is drowned in his bath, at the urging of his wife Zoë, who marries her chamberlain, and elevates him to the throne of the Byzantine Empire, as Michael IV. Romanos is buried in the Church of St. Mary Peribleptos in Constantinople.
names: Church of St. George of Samatya

summary: Byzantine Emperor Romanos III Argyros died in Constantinople.
text: Romanos III (Argyros), Byzantine emperor (b. 968)

summary: Byzantine general George Maniakes landed in Sicily and defeated the Zirids to begin the reconquest of the island.
text: Summer – A Byzantine expeditionary force under George Maniakes lands at Sicily, and defeats the Zirids. Maniakes begins his campaign to reconquer the island.

summary: John of Debar, Bulgarian archbishop of Ohrid, died.
text: John of Debar, Bulgarian clergyman and bishop

summary: Lombard rebels murdered Nikephoros Dokeianos, the Byzantine catepan of Italy, at Ascoli Satriano.
text: Spring – Nikephoros Dokeianos, Byzantine governor of the Catepanate of Italy, is murdered by Lombard rebels at Ascoli. He is replaced by Michael Dokeianos, who arrives in November with a Varangian army.

summary: Peter Delyan led a rebellion against the Byzantine Empire and was proclaimed tsar at Belgrade.
text: Peter Delyan leads a rebellion against the Byzantine Empire and is proclaimed by the Bulgarian nobles as emperor (tsar) Peter II in Belgrade.

summary: Byzantine general and Catepan of Italy Nikephoros Dokeianos died.
text: Nikephoros Dokeianos, Byzantine general

summary: Following the death of Emperor Michael IV, Empress Zoë elevated her adoptive son Michael V Kalaphates to the Byzantine throne.
text: Emperor Michael IV the Paphlagonian dies after a 6-year reign. His wife, Empress Zoë, elevates (on the advice of her lover John the Orphanotrophos) her adoptive son to the throne of the Byzantine Empire, as Michael V Kalaphates. Shortly after, Michael comes into conflict with his uncle John, and banishes him to a monastery.

summary: Norman and Lombard forces led by William Iron Arm defeated the Byzantines at the Battle of Olivento near Monte Vulture.
text: Battle of Olivento: Norman troops and their Lombard allies, led by William Iron Arm, are victorious against the Byzantines at the feet of the Monte Vulture, near the River Olivento in Apulia.

summary: Lombard-Norman rebel forces led by William Iron Arm defeated a Byzantine army at the Battle of Montemaggiore.
text: Battle of Montemaggiore: Lombard-Norman rebel forces, led by William, are again victorious, and defeat a Byzantine army (18,000 men) on the hill of Montemaggiore, near the River Ofanto.

summary: Lombard-Norman rebel forces led by William Iron Arm defeated the Byzantines at Montepeloso and captured Catepan Exaugustus Boioannes.
text: Battle of Montepeloso: Lombard-Norman rebel forces, led by William, defeat the Byzantines at Montepeloso. During the battle, Boioannes, governor of the Catepanate of Italy, is captured.

summary: Byzantine forces, aided by the Varangian Guard under Harald Hardrada, defeated Bulgarian troops at the Battle of Ostrovo.
text: Winter – Battle of Ostrovo: The Byzantines, with the help of the Varangian Guard, led by Harald Hardrada (future king of Norway), defeat the Bulgarian troops, near Lake Ostrovo in Greece.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Michael IV the Paphlagonian died in Constantinople.
text: Michael IV the Paphlagonian, Byzantine emperor (b. 1010)

summary: Bulgarian rebel leader and tsar Petar Delyan died.
text: Peter Delyan, Bulgarian rebel leader and ruler (tsar)

summary: Emperor Michael V Kalaphates banished his adoptive mother and co-ruler Zoë to Principo, triggering a revolt.
text: Emperor Michael V Kalaphates banishes his adoptive mother and co-ruler Zoë, for plotting to poison him, to the island of Principo. His announcement as sole emperor leads to a popular revolt.

summary: Zoë and her sister Theodora were proclaimed co-ruling empresses at Hagia Sophia as Michael V was overthrown and blinded.
text: Zoë is proclaimed as empress at an assembly in Hagia Sophia, along with her sister Theodora, as co-ruler. Michael V flees to the monastery of Stoudios, but is arrested, blinded and castrated.

summary: Empress Zoë replaced Synodianos with George Maniakes as governor of the Catepanate of Italy.
text: Zoë recalls Synodianos, governor of the Catepanate of Italy, and replaces him with George Maniakes (the disgraced head of the Sicilian campaign). All of Apulia is in the hands of the Lombard rebels.

summary: Constantine IX Monomachos married Empress Zoë and ascended the Byzantine throne as co-emperor in Constantinople.
text: Zoë marries her third husband, a Byzantine bureaucrat who ascends as co-emperor Constantine IX at Constantinople. Theodora agrees to surrender her co-emperorship.

summary: George Maniakes marched through Apulia and plundered rebel towns before being recalled to Constantinople by Constantine IX.
text: Summer – George Maniakes goes on a march through Apulia, plundering the towns that have declared for the Lombard rebels. Constantine IX recalls Maniakes to Constantinople.

summary: George Maniakes revolted against Emperor Constantine IX and captured Catepan Pardos at Otranto.
text: George Maniakes revolts against Constantine IX and is declared emperor by his troops. He captures Pardos who has landed with an army at Otranto to take over his command.

summary: Byzantine forces reconquered the fortress city of Edessa, returning it to Christian control.
text: Byzantine–Arab War: The Byzantines reconquer the fortress city of Edessa (modern Turkey), returning it to Christian hands, after 400 years of Islamic rule .

summary: Duklja secured its independence from the Byzantine Empire.
text: Duklja secures its independence from the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Harald Hardrada left Byzantine service as leader of the Varangian Guard and returned to Norway.
text: Harald Hardrada, leader of the Varangian Guard in the Byzantine Empire, returns to Norway, possibly because of his involvement in Maniakes' revolt.

summary: Deposed Byzantine emperor Michael V Kalaphates died.
text: Michael V Kalaphates, Byzantine emperor

summary: Pardos, Byzantine catepan of Italy, died.
text: Pardos, Byzantine governor (catepan) of Italy

summary: Constantine IX Monomachos's forces defeated the rebellious general George Maniakes near Thessaloniki, where Maniakes was killed.
text: Spring – Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos sends a Byzantine expeditionary force to the Balkans against the rebellious George Maniakes, governor of the Catepanate of Italy. The two armies meet near Thessaloniki in northern Greece. The rebel army – better organized, seasoned and with superior leadership – is initially successful, but Maniakes is killed by an arrow at the moment of his triumph. After this, his army is routed.

summary: A Kievan Rus' naval fleet under Vladimir Yaroslavich launched an unsuccessful assault against Constantinople.
text: Rus'–Byzantine War: A Kievan Rus' naval raid, led by Grand Prince Vladimir Yaraslavich, unsuccessfully attacks Constantinople. A 6,000-strong Kievan contingent under Vyshata is also defeated and deported to the capital.

summary: Alexios Stoudites, patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Alexios Stoudites, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Byzantine general and rebel George Maniakes died in battle.
text: George Maniakes, Byzantine general and governor

summary: The Bagratid Kingdom of Armenia surrendered to the Byzantine Empire, ending the kingdom.
text: The Bagratid Kingdom of Armenia is surrendered to the Byzantine Empire, ending the Kingdom.

summary: Harald Hardrada returned to Scandinavia through Sigtuna in Sweden after fleeing the Byzantine Empire.
text: Harald Hardrada returns to Scandinavia through Sigtuna in Sweden, after escaping from the Byzantine Empire with a fortune.

summary: Maria Skleraina, Byzantine noblewoman and political adviser, died in Constantinople.
text: Approximate date – Maria Skleraina, Byzantine Imperial political adviser

summary: Leo Tornikios rebelled and besieged Constantinople, but was repelled by Emperor Constantine IX and later captured and blinded.
text: 28 – Rebel general Leo Tornikios (a nephew of Emperor Constantine IX) proclaims himself emperor at Adrianople, and besieges Constantinople. Byzantine troops personally led by Constantine repel him, and re-occupy the walls. Tornikios is forced to withdraw, while his followers start to abandon him. Finally, he is captured at a church in Boulgarophygon (modern Turkey), and is publicly blinded.

summary: Emperor Constantine IX permitted the Pechenegs to cross the Danube and settle permanently within Byzantine territory as allies.
text: Winter – Constantine IX allows the Pecheneg tribes to cross the Danube and settle permanently in Byzantine territory. He buys their alliance with presents, using them to attack his enemies (Bulgars and Magyars) in the rear, and so to prevent any southward advance of the Kievan Rus'.

summary: Byzantine and Georgian forces confronted the invading Seljuks at the Battle of Kapetron, where Seljuk general Ibrahim Inal captured the Georgian duke Liparit IV and withdrew safely with spoils.
text: Battle of Kapetron: A combined Byzantine-Georgian army, under Byzantine generals Aaronios and Katakalon Kekaumenos (supported by the Georgian duke Liparit IV), confronts the invading Seljuk Turks, led by Ibrahim Inal (a half-brother of Sultan Tughril), at Kapetron (near modern-day Pasinler). The Byzantines defeat their opposing Turkish forces in the flanks, but in the centre Ibrahim Inal captures Liparit, and can safely withdraw from Byzantine territory, laden with spoils and captives, including Liparit.

summary: Emperor Constantine IX sent an embassy with gifts and ransom to Sultan Tughril to secure the release of Liparit IV.
text: Winter – Emperor Constantine IX sends an embassy with gifts and a ransom, to release Liparit IV to Tughril. However, the sultan sets Liparit free, on the condition that he will never again fight the Seljuks.

summary: Pecheneg warriors turned back from the Bosporus, marched through Bulgaria to Serdica, and launched a revolt in Thrace against Emperor Constantine IX.
text: Spring – Pecheneg Revolt: Emperor Constantine IX decides to transfer 15,000 Pecheneg warriors from their positions in the Balkans to the eastern front. Upon approaching the Bosporus, the Pechenegs decide to turn back, and march through Bulgaria, until they reach the Byzantine city of Serdia. Later, joined by followers, the Pecheneg tribes raise the banner of revolt in Thrace.

summary: Michael VII Doukas, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: Michael VII Doukas, Byzantine emperor

summary: Constantine Arianites, Byzantine general, died.
text: Constantine Arianites, Byzantine general

summary: Michael Dokeianos, Byzantine general, died.
text: Michael Dokeianos, Byzantine general

summary: Empress Zoë of the Byzantine Empire died in Constantinople.
text: Zoë, empress of the Byzantine Empire

summary: Drogo of Hauteville met Pope Leo IX in southern Italy before being assassinated near Bovino.
text: Summer – Drogo of Hauteville, count of Apulia and Calabria, meets Pope Leo IX in southern Italy – who has been sent by Emperor Henry III (the Black) to re-establish the "freedom of the Catholic Church". Drogo is forced to promise Pope Leo to stop the Normans from pillaging the Lombard countryside. On his way back (August 10), Drogo is assassinated near Bovino by a Byzantine conspiracy.

summary: Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos concluded peace with the Pechenegs to end the Pecheneg revolt.
text: End of the Pecheneg Revolt: Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos makes peace with the Pechenegs. However, Pecheneg raids do not cease; they not only damage the economy by plundering, but Constantine is also forced to buy protection or peace from them by gifts, land grants, privileges and titles.

summary: Maria of Alania, future Byzantine empress consort, was born.
text: Maria of Alania, Byzantine empress consort (d. 1118)

summary: Lazaros of Mount Galesios, Byzantine monk and stylite, died.
text: Lazaros, Byzantine monk and stylite

summary: Sultan Tughril led a Seljuk army into Armenia and captured the fortress city of Artchesh after an eight-day siege.
text: Sultan Tughril leads a large Seljuk army out of Azerbaijan into Armenia, possibly to consolidate his frontier, while providing an incentive to his Turkoman allies in the form of plunder. Tughril divides his army into four columns, ordering three to veer off to the north to raid into central and northern Armenia, while he takes the fourth column towards Lake Van. The Seljuk Turks capture and sack the fortress city of Artchesh, after an 8-day siege.

summary: Pope Leo IX sent Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida on a legatine mission to Constantinople to negotiate with Patriarch Michael I Cerularius.
text: Spring – Pope Leo IX sends a legatine mission, under Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida, to Constantinople, to negotiate with Patriarch Michael I Cerularius, in response to his actions concerning the church in Constantinople. Leo becomes the first pope directly to invoke the forged Donation of Constantine, citing a large portion in a letter to Michael, believing it genuine.

summary: Papal legate Humbert of Silva Candida placed a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael I Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia.
text: East–West Schism: The papal legate Humbert of Silva Candida laid on the altar of Hagia Sophia a document proclaiming the excommunication of Michael I Cerularius, the patriarch of Constantinople.

summary: Following the death of Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos, Theodora was proclaimed empress of the Byzantine Empire.
text: Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos dies after a 12½-year reign at Constantinople. He is succeeded by Theodora (a sister of the former Empress Zoë), who is proclaimed by the imperial guard (with strong opposition from the council) as empress of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos died.
text: Constantine IX, Byzantine emperor

summary: Byzantine governor Theodore Aaronios died.
text: Theodore Aaronios, Byzantine governor

summary: Michael VI succeeded Empress Theodora upon her death in Constantinople, ending the Macedonian dynasty.
text: Empress Theodora (a sister of the former Empress Zoë) dies after a 18-month reign, by a sudden illness at Constantinople. She is succeeded by Michael VI Bringas ("the Old"), who had served as military finance minister under the former Emperor Romanos III. Michael is appointed through the influence of Leo Paraspondylos, Theodora's most trusted adviser. This ends the Macedonian dynasty.

summary: Theodosios Monomachos attempted to seize the throne in Constantinople but was arrested and exiled to Pergamon.
text: Theodosius, a nephew of the former Emperor Constantine IX, tries to usurp the Byzantine throne, and liberates all the prisoners who flock to his banner. With their support, he marches through the streets of Constantinople to the Palace. There, the Varangian Guard forms outside to stop him. Theodosius loses heart and heads for Hagia Sophia. Later he is captured, and exiled to Pergamon.

summary: Byzantine Empress Theodora died in Constantinople, ending the Macedonian dynasty.
text: August 31: Theodora, empress regnant of the Byzantine Empire

summary: Leo of Ohrid, Archbishop of Ohrid and Byzantine theologian, died.
text: Leo of Ohrid, Byzantine archbishop and theologian

summary: General Isaac Komnenos proclaimed himself emperor in Paphlagonia and revolted against Emperor Michael VI.
text: General Isaac Komnenos proclaims himself emperor in Paphlagonia (modern Turkey), and starts a civil war against Emperor Michael VI. He advances with a Byzantine expeditionary force towards Constantinople. At the same time, Michael sends an army against the rebels – western regiments and eastern ones (those from the Anatolic Theme and Charsianon) – to stop him.

summary: Rebel forces under Isaac Komnenos defeated the imperial army of Emperor Michael VI at the Battle of Petroe near Nicaea.
text: Battle of Hades: Rebel forces under Isaac Komnenos defeat the Byzantines on the plains of Hades (near Nicaea). General Katakalon Kekaumenos routs the imperial right flank, and reaches the enemy's camp. He destroys the tents and supplies, which leaves the way open to Constantinople.

summary: Michael VI abdicated following riots in Constantinople, and Isaac I Komnenos was crowned emperor of the Byzantine Empire.
text: A riot in favor of Isaac Komnenos breaks out in Constantinople. Patriarch Michael I convinces Michael VI to abdicate the throne, and Isaac is crowned as emperor of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Former Byzantine Emperor Michael VI Bringas died.
text: Michael VI, Byzantine emperor

summary: Byzantine Emperor Isaac I Komnenos deposed Patriarch Michael I Cerularius and exiled him to Marmara Island.
text: Byzantine Emperor Isaac I Komnenos deposes Michael I Cerularius, patriarch of Constantinople, and has him exiled to Prokonnessos (until 1059).

summary: Emperor Isaac I Komnenos abdicated the Byzantine throne due to illness and appointed Constantine X Doukas as his successor.
text: Emperor Isaac I Komnenos falls ill on a hunt and retires to a monastery after a 2-year reign. He abdicates the Byzantine throne and appoints Constantine X, a Paphlagonian nobleman, as his successor.

summary: The Magyars and Pecheneg tribes crossed the Danube River into Byzantine territory but were halted by Byzantine forces.
text: Fall – The Magyars cross the Danube River, together with several Pecheneg tribes, but are halted by Byzantine forces .

summary: Peter Krešimir IV was crowned King of Croatia and Dalmatia and was confirmed as ruler of the Dalmatian cities by the Byzantine Empire.
text: Peter Krešimir IV is crowned king of Croatia and Dalmatia. His coronation is recognised by the Byzantine Empire who confirm him as the supreme ruler of the Dalmatian cities, i.e. over the Theme of Dalmatia – excluding the theme of Ragusa and the Duchy of Durazzo.

summary: Alp Arslan crossed the Halys River with a Seljuk expeditionary force and plundered the Byzantine Theme of Sebasteia.
text: In Seljuk Empire Alp Arslan succeeds his father Chaghri Beg as governor of Khorasan. He crosses with a Seljuk expeditionary force the upper Halys River and plunders the Theme of Sebasteia (modern Turkey).

summary: Michael I Cerularius, former Patriarch of Constantinople, died in exile.
text: Michael I Cerularius, Byzantine patriarch

summary: Former Byzantine emperor Michael VI Bringas died.
text: Michael VI Bringas, Byzantine emperor

summary: Robert Guiscard led Norman forces in invading Apulia and capturing Taranto and Brindisi from the Byzantine Empire.
text: Summer – Norman forces under Duke Robert Guiscard invade Apulia, and capture the cities of Taranto and Brindisi (under control of the Byzantine Empire). Guiscard prepares a Sicilian expedition against the Saracens and returns to Calabria (Southern Italy), where his brother Roger Bosso waits with siege engines.

summary: Byzantine emperor Konstantios Doukas was born.
text: Constantius Ducas, Byzantine emperor (d. 1081)

summary: Byzantine emperor Isaac I Komnenos died.
text: Isaac I (Komnenos), Byzantine emperor

summary: Byzantine statesman and historian Nikephoros Bryennios the Younger was born in Adrianople.
text: Nicephorus Bryennius, Byzantine statesman (d. 1137)

summary: Byzantine aristocrat Nikephoros Komnenos was born.
text: Nicephorus Komnenos, Byzantine aristocrat

summary: Constantine Leichoudes, Patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Constantine III, Byzantine patriarch

summary: Seljuk forces under Alp Arslan captured and sacked the Byzantine city of Ani after a 25-day siege.
text: The Seljuk Turks under Alp Arslan invade Anatolia, and capture Ani after a siege of 25-days. He sacks the city and slaughters its citizens.

summary: Byzantine empress Irene Doukaina was born.
text: Irene Doukaina (or Ducaena), Byzantine empress (d. 1138)

summary: Byzantine Christian historian Yahya of Antioch died.
text: Yahya of Antioch, Byzantine historian

summary: Following the death of Emperor Constantine X Doukas, Empress Eudokia Makrembolitissa became co-regent of the Byzantine Empire alongside Caesar John Doukas.
text: Emperor Constantine X dies after a 7-year reign at Constantinople. His wife, Empress Eudocia Macrembolitissa, is crowned Augusta and becomes co-regent for her two sons (Michael VII and Konstantios) along with Constantine's brother John Doukas, who rules as Caesar of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: The Seljuk Turks invaded Cappadocia, sacked the Byzantine city of Caesarea, and raided the territory around Antioch.
text: Spring – The Seljuk Turks make incursions into Mesopotamia, Cilicia and Cappadocia. They sack the Byzantine city of Caesarea, move south through the Cilician Gates and raid the region around Antioch in Syria.

summary: Byzantine aristocrat and future governor John Taronites was born.
text: John Taronites, Byzantine governor

summary: Byzantine Emperor Constantine X Doukas died at Constantinople after a reign of seven years.
text: Constantine X, Byzantine emperor (b. 1006)

summary: Byzantine general John Komnenos died.
text: John Komnenos, Byzantine general

summary: Empress Eudokia Makrembolitissa married Romanos Diogenes, who was proclaimed co-emperor as Romanos IV of the Byzantine Empire.
text: Empress Eudokia Makrembolitissa, wife of the late Emperor Constantine X, marries General Romanos Diogenes (a member of a prominent Cappadocian family) – who is proclaimed co-emperor as Romanos IV of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Emperor Romanos IV campaigned against the Seljuks and recaptured the fortress city of Hieropolis in northern Syria.
text: Autumn – Romanos IV begins a campaign against the Seljuk Turks, leading a Byzantine expeditionary force (which is in poor condition). He is successful in recapturing the fortress city of Hieropolis (modern-day Manbij) near Aleppo in northern Syria.

summary: A Seljuk raiding party penetrated Byzantine territory and sacked the city of Amorium while Romanos IV campaigned in Syria.
text: Winter – Romanos IV leaves a portion of his army as a rearguard at Melitene. The Byzantine garrison fails to check a Seljuk raid that manages to sack Amorium (penetrating deep in Byzantine territory). Romanos winters near Aleppo before returning to Constantinople.

summary: Norman forces under Robert Guiscard laid siege to the Byzantine city of Bari in southern Italy.
text: Norman conquest of southern Italy: Norman forces under Robert Guiscard (duke of Apulia and Calabria) lay siege to the Byzantine city of Bari.

summary: Byzantine general and catepan Abulchares died.
text: Abulchares, Byzantine general and catepan

summary: Emperor Romanos IV campaigned against the Seljuk Turks across the Euphrates and captured the strategic fortress city of Chliat.
text: Spring – Emperor Romanos IV begins a campaign against the Seljuk Turks, and marches towards the Euphrates via Melitene. He crosses the river at Romanopolis (modern Turkey), and captures the strategic fortress city of Chliat on the north-western shore of Lake Van. Romanos leaves a Byzantine rear guard on the upper Euphrates under General Philaretos Brachamios with orders to defend the Mesopotamian frontier.

summary: Alp Arslan defeated the Byzantine rear guard, plundered Cappadocia, and captured Manzikert, Chliat, and Van.
text: Seljuk forces under Alp Arslan defeat the Byzantine rear guard and advance deep into Cappadocia and Lycaonia. They plunder at will, but fail to capture the city of Iconium. Romanos retreats and returns to Constantinople. Alp Arslan takes advantage of Romanos' retreat and captures Manzikert. He recaptures the strategical fortress cities of Chliat and Van, consolidating his control over the Lake Van region.

summary: Norman forces under Robert Guiscard defeated a Byzantine relief force near Bari and occupied Gravina and Obbiano in Apulia.
text: Spring – Romanos IV sends a Byzantine fleet (supported with an army) to relieve the siege of Bari. The Normans under Robert Guiscard defeat the Byzantines, and occupy the cities of Gravina and Obbiano in Apulia.

summary: Byzantine co-emperor Leo Diogenes was born.
text: Leo Diogenes, Byzantine co-emperor (d. 1087)

summary: A Byzantine counter-attack drove the Seljuq Turks across the Euphrates.
text: A successful Byzantine counter-attack drives the Seljuq Turks across the Euphrates.

summary: John Komnenos was born in Constantinople.
text: John Komnenos, Byzantine aristocrat and official

summary: Alp Arslan defeated the Byzantine army at the Battle of Manzikert and captured Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes.
text: Battle of Manzikert: The Byzantine army (35,000 men) under Emperor Romanos IV meets the Seljuk Turk forces of Sultan Alp Arslan near the town of Manzikert. Although the armies are initially evenly matched, as the Byzantines advance, the Seljuk Turks withdraw before them, launching hit-and-run attacks on the Byzantine flanks. While attempting to withdraw, the Byzantine army falls apart, either through treachery or confusion; the battle ends in a decisive defeat for the Byzantine Empire. Romanos is captured (though released by Alp Arslan within a week) and much of the elite Varangian Guard is destroyed; this will prove catastrophic for the Byzantine Empire.

summary: John Doukas and Michael Psellos deposed Romanos IV Diogenes in Constantinople, crowning Michael VII Doukas.
text: Romanos IV is deposed by John Doukas (Caesar) and his political advisor Michael Psellos after his return to Constantinople. Michael VII Doukas is crowned co-emperor and his mother Eudokia is forced to retire to a monastery.

summary: The Kingdom of Hungary invaded Byzantine territory and captured the border fortresses of Belgrade, Sirmium, and Taurunum.
text: The Kingdom of Hungary launches a campaign against the Byzantine Empire. They besiege and capture the border fortress of Belgrade, along with Sirmium and Taurunum.

summary: Robert Guiscard captured Bari after a 32-month siege, bringing an end to the Byzantine Catepanate of Italy.
text: Siege of Bari: The capital of Bari, the last Byzantine-controlled city in the Catepanate of Italy, is captured by Italo-Norman forces under Duke Robert Guiscard after a 32-month siege.

summary: Byzantine aristocrat and general Manuel Komnenos died.
text: Manuel Komnenos, Byzantine aristocrat

summary: Deposed Byzantine Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes was blinded and exiled to the Monastery of the Transfiguration on Proti.
text: Romanos IV Diogenes, deposed ruler of the Byzantine Empire, is blinded and sent into exile to the island of Proti (in the Sea of Marmara) at the Monastery of Transfiguration. A few days before his death, he receives a letter from Michael Psellos (his political advisor), congratulating him on the loss of his eyes.

summary: Hungarian forces plundered the Balkans en route to Niš before their campaign against Byzantium ended due to internal conflict.
text: Byzantine–Hungarian War (1071–1072): the Hungarians plunders the Balkans on their route to Niš. The war ends with the emerging internal conflict between Solomon, King of Hungary and his cousin, Duke Géza.

summary: Former Byzantine Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes died in exile on Proti after being blinded.
text: Romanos IV Diogenes, ruler of the Byzantine Empire

summary: Roussel de Bailleul rebelled against the Byzantine Empire, defeated an imperial army under Caesar John Doukas, and sacked Chrysopolis.
text: Spring – Emperor Michael VII Doukas sends a Byzantine army to deal with Seljuk raiding in Cappadocia, supported with a mixed force of Norman and French mercenary heavy cavalry under Roussel de Bailleul. Roussel re-conquers some territory in Galatia and declares it an independent Norman state. Michael, enraged, sends another army led by his uncle, Caesar John Doukas and the veteran General Nikephoros Botaneiates to deal with the rising of the Norman threat in Asia minor. But the Byzantines are defeated and John is captured. Roussel marches with a force (3,000 men) across Bithynia to the Bosporus and sacks Chrysopolis, near Constantinople.

summary: Seljuk Turks allied with Michael VII Doukas ambushed and defeated Roussel de Bailleul and the rebel John Doukas in Anatolia.
text: Spring – Norman mercenaries, led by Roussel de Bailleul, proclaim John Doukas emperor of the Byzantine Empire. His nephew, Emperor Michael VII Doukas, forms an alliance with Seljuk chieftain Suleiman ibn Qutulmish, who is raiding in the eastern regions of Anatolia. The Seljuk Turks ambush the Norman forces; Roussel and John are defeated and captured; but a ransom, raised by Roussel's wife, allows him to return to Amaseia.

summary: Byzantine general Joseph Tarchaneiotes died.
text: Joseph Tarchaneiotes, Byzantine general

summary: The future emperor Alexios Komnenos captured the Norman rebel Roussel de Bailleul in Amaseia.
text: The future Emperor Alexios Komnenos captures the Norman rebel Roussel de Bailleul in Amaseia. Roussel had established a principality in eastern Anatolia in 1073 after rebelling against Emperor Michael VII Doukas, basing his power on his western mercenaries and local support in exchange for protection against invading Turkmen.

summary: John VIII, Patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: John VIII, patriarch of Constantinople

summary: Byzantine historian John Xiphilinus died.
text: John Xiphilinus, Byzantine historian

summary: Nikephoros Bryennios and Nikephoros Botaneiates were proclaimed emperors by their troops, and Bryennios marched toward Constantinople after rejecting Michael VII's offer of caesar.
text: Fall – Nikephoros Bryennios the Elder, governor (doux) of the Theme of Dyrrhachium in the western Balkans, and Nikephoros Botaneiates, a general (strategos) of the Theme of Anatolics (modern Turkey), are proclaimed emperors by their troops. Emperor Michael VII Doukas offers Bryennios the title of caesar (co-emperor) if he submits to his rule, but Bryennios refuses. He sets out from Dyrrhachium, and marches towards Constantinople.

summary: Suleiman ibn Qutulmish united the Oghuz Turks in Anatolia and founded the Sultanate of Rum.
text: Suleiman ibn Qutulmish, a cousin of late Sultan Alp Arslan, consolidates his leadership over the Oghuz Turks and founds the Sultanate of Rum (modern Turkey).

summary: Byzantine aristocrat and governor Alexios Komnenos was born.
text: approximate date – Alexios Komnenos, Byzantine aristocrat and governor

summary: Byzantine nobleman Andronikos Doukas died.
text: Andronikos Doukas, Byzantine nobleman

summary: Norman warrior and mercenary leader Roussel de Bailleul was executed.
text: Roussel de Bailleul, Norman warrior and military leader
