summary: Nikephoros Botaneiates revolted against Emperor Michael VII Doukas, marched on Nicaea with Seljuk support, defeated the imperial army, and proclaimed himself emperor.
text: Spring – Nikephoros Botaneiates, a Byzantine general (strategos) of the Theme of the Anatolics, revolts against Emperor Michael VII Doukas. With the support of the Seljuk Turks who provide him with troops, Nikephoros marches upon Nicaea (modern Turkey). He defeats the imperial army and proclaims himself emperor.

summary: Nikephoros Botaneiates entered Constantinople in triumph and was crowned emperor as Nikephoros III while Michael VII resigned to enter a monastery.
text: Nikephoros Botaneiates enters Constantinople in triumph and is crowned by Patriarch Cosmas I as emperor Nikephoros III of the Byzantine Empire. Michael VII resigns his throne after a 7-year reign and retires into the Monastery of Stoudios.

summary: Alexios Komnenos defeated the rebel general Nikephoros Bryennios the Elder at the Battle of Kalavrye.
text: Battle of Kalavrye: The imperial forces of General Alexios Komnenos are victorious over the rebellious army (12,000 men) under Nikephoros Bryennios the Elder, governor (doux) of the Theme of Dyrrhachium. Bryennios is captured and later blinded.

summary: Philaretos Brachamios abandoned his claim to the imperial throne upon being appointed governor of Antioch.
text: Philaretos Brachamios abandons his claim to the Byzantine throne, on being appointed governor of Antioch, a foundation of the later Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia.

summary: Byzantine eunuch official and chief minister Nikephoritzes died under torture.
text: Nikephoritzes, Byzantine governor

summary: Seljuk forces led by Suleiman ibn Qutulmish reached and occupied Ionia on the western coast of Asia Minor.
text: The Seljuk Turks under Sultan Suleiman ibn Qutulmish reach and occupy the western coast of Asia Minor, an area known since the Archaic Period (c. 800–c. 500 BC) as Ionia (modern Turkey).

summary: Nikephoros Melissenos seized Byzantine Asia Minor, allied with Suleiman ibn Qutalmish, and proclaimed himself emperor against Nikephoros III Botaneiates.
text: Autumn – Nikephoros Melissenos, a Byzantine general and aristocrat, seizes control of what remains of Byzantine Asia Minor (modern Turkey), and proclaims himself emperor against Nikephoros III Botaneiates. Melissenos makes an alliance with Sultan Suleiman ibn Qutulmish and recruits many Turkish mercenaries to his army.

summary: Ruben I established his authority in mountainous Cilicia, founding an independent Armenian principality.
text: The Rubenid Principality of Cilicia gains independence after its founder, Ruben I, succeeds in establishing his authority in the mountainous regions of Cilicia.

summary: Michael Attaleiates, a Byzantine public official and historian, died.
text: Michael Attaleiates, Byzantine historian and writer

summary: Alexios I Komnenos forced Emperor Nikephoros III Botaneiates to abdicate and was crowned emperor of the Byzantine Empire.
text: Emperor Nikephoros III is forced to abdicate the throne, and retires to the Peribleptos monastery. He is succeeded by Alexios I Komnenos, who is crowned on April 5, as ruler of the Byzantine Empire. His brother-in-law Nikephoros Melissenos supports Alexios as new emperor, in exchange for the title of Caesar (co-emperor), and is appointed as commander of the Byzantine armies in the West.
names: Church of St. George of Samatya

summary: Duke Robert Guiscard sailed from Italy with an army and fleet and landed at Avalona to campaign against the Byzantine Empire.
text: May – A Norman fleet of 150 ships (including 60 horse transports), led by Duke Robert Guiscard, sets off towards the Dalmatian coast. An army of 15,000 men (including about 1,300 Norman knights) sails to the city of Avalona (modern Albania); they are joined by several ships from Ragusa, a republic in the Balkans who are enemies of the Byzantines.
names: Horse transports in the Middle Ages

summary: Robert Guiscard defeated Alexios I Komnenos and his Byzantine army at the Battle of Dyrrhachium.
text: Battle of Dyrrhachium: After taking the island of Corfu, Robert Guiscard advances to Dyrrhachium (modern-day Durrës), and lays siege to the city. Alexios I Komnenos attempts to defend Illyria from the Normans (the first recorded mention of Albania), but is defeated by Guiscard, outside Dyrrhachium, the Byzantine capital city of Illyria.

summary: Chaka Bey conquered Smyrna from the Byzantine Empire and established an independent maritime principality.
text: Seljuk emir Tzachas (or Chaka Bey) conquers Smyrna (modern-day İzmir) and founds a short-lived independent state, which emerges as the first sea power in Turkish history.

summary: Konstantios Doukas, Byzantine co-emperor, was killed at the Battle of Dyrrhachium.
text: October 18: Konstantios Doukas, Byzantine emperor (b. 1060)

summary: Nikephoros Palaiologos, Byzantine general, died at the Battle of Dyrrhachium.
text: October 18: Nikephoros Palaiologos, Byzantine general

summary: Former Byzantine emperor Nikephoros III Botaneiates died in Constantinople.
text: Nikephoros III, Byzantine emperor

summary: Alexios I Komnenos, with Seljuk Turkish support, expelled the Normans under Bohemond from Thessaly after their capture of Dyrrhachium.
text: Spring – The Normans under Duke Robert Guiscard take Dyrrhachium (modern-day Durrës) in Illyria and advance inland, capturing most of Macedonia and Thessaly. Robert is forced to leave Greece to deal with an uprising in Italy. He leaves his son Bohemond in charge of the army, who lays siege to the city of Larissa. Emperor Alexios I Komnenos mobilizes a new army, and with the support of 7,000 Seljuk Turks he clears Thessaly from the Normans.

summary: Alexios I granted the Republic of Venice extensive trading privileges and tax exemptions across the Byzantine Empire in exchange for naval defense against the Normans.
text: Byzantine–Venetian treaty: Alexios I signs a trade and defence pact with Venice, in the form of an imperial Golden Bull. He grants the Venetians a commercial colony in Constantinople, as well as free trading and exemption from taxes, throughout the Byzantine Empire in return for their defense of the Adriatic Sea against the Normans.

summary: Emperor Alexios I Komnenos recaptured Kastoria and surrounding territory from the Normans.
text: October – While Robert Guiscard is in Italy, emperor Alexios I Komnenos retakes territory previously lost to the Normans, including the town of Kastoria. Several Normans, including Peter Aliphas, switch sides to the Byzantines.

summary: Byzantine princess and historian Anna Komnene was born in Constantinople.
text: Anna Komnene, Byzantine princess (d. 1153)

summary: Byzantine general Basil Apokapes died.
text: Basil Apokapes (or Apocapes), Byzantine general

summary: Theodora Doukaina Selvo, Byzantine princess and dogaressa of Venice, died.
text: Approximate date – Theodora Doukaina Selvo, Venetian dogaressa (b. 1058)

summary: Robert Guiscard sailed to Illyria and occupied Corfu and Cephalonia.
text: Robert Guiscard returns with 150 warships in Illyria (modern Albania), and occupies Corfu and Kefalonia with the support of Ragusa and the Dalmatian city-states.

summary: Seljuk forces under Sultan Malik-Shah I conquered Antioch from Philaretos Brachamios.
text: The Seljuk Turks under Sultan Malik-Shah I conquer Byzantine Antioch, held by Philaretos Brachamios, an Armenian general, who seizes power as a usurper.

summary: Robert Guiscard died of fever after being carried ashore on Cephalonia.
text: Summer – Robert Guiscard heads for the Ionian Islands despite an epidemic among troops on Corfu. His son, Roger Borsa, lands on Cephalonia but Guiscard falls sick as his ship approaches the northernmost headland and is carried ashore, where he dies of fever (on July 17).

summary: Byzantine princess Maria Komnene was born.
text: Maria Komnene, Byzantine princess

summary: Byzantine aristocrat Constantine Komnenos was born.
text: Constantine Komnenos, Byzantine aristocrat

summary: Norman duke Robert Guiscard died on the island of Kefalonia while campaigning against the Byzantine Empire.
text: Robert Guiscard, Norman warrior and nobleman

summary: Byzantine general Gregory Pakourianos was killed in battle against the Pechenegs near Philippopolis.
text: Gregory Pakourianos, Byzantine politician and general, killed in battle

summary: Suleiman ibn Qutalmish, ruler of the Sultanate of Rum, was killed in battle near Antioch.
text: Suleiman ibn Qutulmish, ruler of the Sultanate of Rum, killed in battle

summary: Sailors from Bari seized the relics of Saint Nicholas from his church in Myra and brought them to Italy.
text: The relics of Saint Nicholas, patron saint of seafarers, are stolen by Italian sailors from his church in Myra (modern Turkey) and transported to Bari in southern Italy.

summary: Future Byzantine emperor John II Komnenos was born in Constantinople.
text: John II Komnenos, Byzantine emperor (d. 1143)

summary: Leo Diogenes, Byzantine co-emperor, was killed in battle against the Pechenegs near Dristra.
text: Leo Diogenes, Byzantine co-emperor (b. 1069)

summary: Irene of Hungary, future Byzantine empress consort of John II Komnenos, was born in Esztergom.
text: Irene of Hungary, Byzantine empress consort (d. 1134)

summary: Byzantine prince and future archbishop John IV of Ohrid was born in Constantinople.
text: John IV, Byzantine prince and archbishop

summary: Byzantine statesman and Caesar John Doukas died.
text: John Doukas, Byzantine usurper

summary: A church council in Constantinople discussed relations between Eastern and Western Christianity.
text: September: A church council, held in Constantinople, discuses relations between Eastern and Western Christianity.

summary: Tzachas established an independent maritime state in Smyrna and allied with the Pechenegs to blockade Constantinople.
text: Spring – Tzachas, a Seljuk Turkish military commander, establishes an independent maritime state centred in the Ionian coastal city of Smyrna (modern-day İzmir). He proclaims himself emperor (basileus), and concludes an alliance with the Pechenegs in Thrace. Tzachas uses his fleet to blockade Constantinople by sea, while the Pechenegs besiege the capital by land.

summary: Emperor Alexios I Komnenos and his Cuman allies decisively defeated and slaughtered the Pechenegs at the Battle of Levounion.
text: Battle of Levounion: Emperor Alexios I, supported by his allies, defeats 80,000 of Pechenegs (including women and children) at the Evros River, near Enos (modern Turkey). The Cumans and Byzantine forces fall upon the enemy camp, slaughtering all in their path. The Pechenegs are butchered so savagely, that this people is almost wiped out.

summary: Byzantine prince and general Andronikos Komnenos was born.
text: Andronikos Komnenos, Byzantine prince and general

summary: Emperor Alexios I Komnenos recovered Sinope through bribery and defeated the Seljuk fleet off Cius.
text: Summer – Emperor Alexios I Komnenos bribes one of Kilij Arslan's (sultan of the Sultanate of Rum) officials to recover Sinope (the capital of Paphlagonia), and neighbouring coastal regions. He uses the Byzantine fleet to defeat the Seljuk navy off the coast of Cius in Bithynia.

summary: Abu'l-Qasim, Seljuk governor of Nicaea, died.
text: Abu'l-Qasim, Seljuk general and governor

summary: Isaac Komnenos, Byzantine co-ruler and son of Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, was born.
text: Isaac Komnenos, Byzantine co-ruler

summary: Kilij Arslan I killed the Seljuk general and usurper Tzachas.
text: Tzachas, Seljuk general and usurper, killed

summary: Emperor Alexios I Komnenos repulsed a Seljuk advance on Nicaea and forced Abu'l-Qasim to conclude a truce.
text: Spring – Emperor Alexios I Komnenos sends a Byzantine expeditionary force under General Tatikios to Nicaea, in an attempt to re-capture the city from the Seljuk Turks. However, the arrival of Barkiyaruq's army en route stops the Byzantines. Alexios sends reinforcements; short of supplies, the Seljuk Turks retreat. Abu'l-Qasim, Seljuk governor of Nicaea, is defeated and forced to conclude a truce with Alexios.

summary: Byzantine princess Eudokia Komnene was born.
text: Eudokia Komnene, Byzantine princess (d. 1129)

summary: Emperor Alexios I Komnenos sent envoys to Pope Urban II at the Council of Piacenza, appealing for military aid against the Seljuk Turks.
text: March – Emperor Alexios I Komnenos send envoys to Pope Urban II at the Council of Piacenza and appeals to the Christian states of Western Europe for military aid against the Seljuk Turks. Urban responds favourably, hoping to heal the Great Schism of 40 years earlier, and to reunite the Catholic Church under papal primacy by helping the Eastern churches.

summary: The Cumans crossed the Danube and invaded Thrace to support pretender Constantine Diogenes, occupying Paristrion.
text: Summer – The nomadic Cumans cross the River Danube and invade Thrace, to support the pretender Constantine Diogenes (son of the late Emperor Romanos IV). The Cumans occupy the province of Paristrion (located in the Lower Danube). Emperor Alexios I places Byzantine detachments to guard the passes over the Balkan Mountains, but they are bypassed.

summary: Walter Sans Avoir led French crusaders across the Sava into Byzantine territory at Belgrade before marching to Niš.
text: French members of the People's Crusade led by Walter Sans Avoir enter Hungary, without incident they arrive at Semlin, and cross the Sava into Byzantine territory at Belgrade. Meanwhile, Walter demands food but he is refused entry, and the crusaders are forced to pillage the countryside. Eventually Walter is allowed to carry on to Niš, where he is provided with food.

summary: Peter the Hermit and his followers crossed the Sava, pillaged Belgrade after its citizens fled, and continued to Niš.
text: The People's Crusade (some 30,000 men) led by Peter the Hermit crosses the Sava (stealing boats from the local fishermen) but are attacked by Pechenegs and Hungarian forces. The citizens of Belgrade flee and the crusaders pillage and burn the city. Peter travels for seven days, and arrives at Niš.

summary: The Byzantine army defeated the People's Crusade near Niš, capturing Peter the Hermit's supply train and treasury.
text: July – The People's Crusade led by Peter the Hermit is defeated by the Byzantine army (mostly Hungarian and Bulgar mercenaries) in battle near Niš. The crusader supply train of some 2,000 wagons and Peter's treasury chest is captured by the Byzantines. About a quarter of the People's Crusade is lost.

summary: Peter the Hermit's crusaders reached Sofia and Philippopolis, where local Byzantine authorities and populations provided them with supplies.
text: The People's Crusade led by Peter the Hermit reaches Sofia, where they meet envoys from Constantinople with orders to keep them supplied along the road. At Philippopolis the Greeks are so deeply moved by the suffering of Peter and his followers that the locals give them money, food and horses.

summary: Emperor Alexios I Komnenos received Peter the Hermit outside Constantinople and provided financial assistance to his forces.
text: The People's Crusade led by Peter the Hermit arrives at Constantinople. He is received by Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, who gives him financial support. The crusaders commit endless thefts in the suburbs. Peter combines his forces with Walter Sans Avoir and camps outside Constantinople.

summary: The Byzantine fleet transported the People's Crusade across the Bosporus to Civetot.
text: 6 – The People's Crusade reorganize their forces and gather supplies. Alexios I advises Peter the Hermit to wait for reinforcements but he ignores the advice. The People's army (some 30,000 men) is transported across the Bosporus – by the Byzantine fleet to Civetot (modern Turkey).

summary: Hugh, Count of Vermandois departed for the First Crusade, traveling through Rome and Bari before being shipwrecked near Epirus.
text: August – Hugh ("the Great"), count of Vermandois (a brother of King Philip I), departs to join the First Crusade. He travels with a small army via the Alps to Rome. While sailing the Adriatic Sea from Bari to Dyrrachium his fleet is reduced by shipwreck. Hugh's own ship is stranded on the shore near Epirus.
names: Army of Hugh the Great on the First Crusade

summary: Crusaders led by Geoffrey Burel raided villages in the suburbs around Nicaea, committing atrocities against the local inhabitants.
text: September – French forces (7,000 infantry and 300 knights) led by Geoffrey Burel raid around Nicaea (the capital of the Rum Seljuk Turks), plundering livestock and villages in the suburbs. They commit atrocities against local Christian peasants. Children are tortured and dismembered by the crusaders.

summary: German crusaders led by Rainald of Breis assaulted and captured the castle of Xerigordos near Nicaea.
text: September – German forces (5,000 infantry and 200 knights) led by Rainald of Breis raid the region of Nicaea. They advance eastward and assault the Seljuk garrison in the castle of Xerigordos. They manage to capture; and, find it well stocked with provisions. The Greek Christians inside are spared.

summary: Kilij Arslan I sent a Seljuk force that besieged and recaptured Xerigordos, killing or enslaving Rainald of Breis's crusaders.
text: Siege of Xerigordos: Sultan Kilij Arslan I sends a Seljuk expeditionary force to assault and recapture the castle of Xerigordos. They cut off the water supply, and Rainald of Breis is forced to surrender. Many of the crusaders are killed but others convert to Islam and become slaves.

summary: Raymond IV of Toulouse set out with his army for the First Crusade, traveling through Provence and the Balkans toward Thessaloniki.
text: October – Raymond IV ("Saint-Gilles"), count of Toulouse, sets off to join the First Crusade. He travels with his army, accompanied by his wife Elvira and Bishop Adhemar of Le Puy, via Provence through the Balkan route (along the coast of Croatia). He arrives at Dyrrachium to march to Thessaloniki.
cast: Elvira of Castile, Countess of Toulouse
names: Elvira of Castile, Countess of Toulouse

summary: Bohemond I sailed from Brindisi across the Adriatic Sea to join the First Crusade, landing in Albania.
text: October – Bohemond I, Italo-Norman prince of Taranto (the son of Duke Robert Guiscard), departs to join the First Crusade. He crosses the Adriatic Sea from Brindisi with his army (some 4,000 men), and arrives in Vorë. While traveling, Bohemond gives strict orders not to plunder Byzantine villages.

summary: Seljuk forces led by Kilij Arslan I defeated and destroyed the People's Crusade at the Battle of Civetot.
text: Battle of Civetot: The Seljuk Turks led by Kilij Arslan I defeat the People's army (20,000 men) near Nicaea. The crusaders are slaughtered, and the camp at Civetot is captured. Only children are spared and sent into slavery. Around 3,000 manage to escape back to Constantinople.

summary: The last of the four main crusader armies arrived at Constantinople, bringing the total crusader force to 60,000 men.
text: December – The last of the four planned Crusader armies arrives at Constantinople, bringing the total numbers to 60,000 infantry and knights. Curiously there isn't a single king among the Crusaders' leaders. At this time Philip I, William II, and Henry IV are all under excommunication by Urban II.

summary: Godfrey of Bouillon was appointed leader of the First Crusade and agreed to swear an oath of loyalty to Emperor Alexios I Komnenos.
text: Godfrey of Bouillon is appointed the primary leader of the First Crusade, making it a largely French war in practice and causing the inhabitants of the Holy Land to refer to Europeans generally as "Franks". Godfrey and the other leaders agree to take an oath of loyalty to Alexios I.

summary: Theodora Komnene, daughter of Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, was born.
text: Theodora Komnene, Byzantine princess

summary: Former Byzantine empress Eudokia Makrembolitissa died.
text: Eudokia Makrembolitissa, Byzantine empress and regent

summary: Crusaders led by Godfrey of Bouillon attacked the Byzantine imperial palace at Blachernae and were joined by Bohemond I.
text: Spring – The Crusaders under Godfrey of Bouillon attack the Byzantine imperial palace at Blachernae. Norman forces led by Bohemond I join the Crusaders – he is not welcome in Constantinople because his father, Robert Guiscard, has invaded Illyria (territory belonging to the Byzantine Empire), and captured the cities of Dyrrhachium and Corfu (see 1084).

summary: The Crusaders began the siege of Nicaea, defeating an advance force of Seljuk Turks.
text: Siege of Nicaea: The Crusaders begin their campaign with the siege of Nicaea (the capital of the Sultanate of Rum), assigning their forces to different sections of the walls, which are well-defended with 200 towers. Towards the end, an advance party of the Seljuk Turks is defeated by troops of Raymond IV of Toulouse ("Saint-Gilles") and Robert II.

summary: The Seljuk Turks surrendered Nicaea to the Crusaders and the Byzantine Empire occupied the city.
text: The Seljuk Turks surrender Nicaea to the Crusaders after a month siege. The Byzantines occupy the city; their commander Manuel Boutoumites is named by Emperor Alexios I Komnenos as doux of Nicaea. In the consternation the Crusaders are not allowed to plunder the city and are forced (again) to pledge their allegiance to Alexios.

summary: The Crusaders defeated a Seljuk army led by Kilij Arslan I at the Battle of Dorylaeum.
text: Battle of Dorylaeum: The Crusaders defeat a Seljuk army led by Kilij Arslan I, ruler of the Sultanate of Rum, who wants revenge for the capture of Nicaea. During the battle many Crusaders are killed but the Seljuk Turks are forced to flee and abandon their tents and treasure after being surprised by the arrival of a second Crusader army.

summary: Crusaders arrived outside Antioch and initiated a siege of the city.
text: Siege of Antioch: The Crusaders arrive outside the city and begin the siege. They can not impose a complete blockade on Antioch. The Seljuk garrison comes out of the city to harass Crusader siege-lines and intercept supply convoys (supported by a Genoese fleet of 12 galleys) from Saint Symeon and Alexandretta (modern Turkey).

summary: Crusaders commanded by Bohemond I and Robert II defeated Seljuk relief forces from Aleppo at Harenc.
text: Battle of Harenc: The Crusaders under the command of Bohemond I and Robert II defeat Seljuk forces from Aleppo, which try to relieve besieged Antioch.

summary: Crusaders under Bohemond I ambushed and routed a Seljuk relief force led by Fakhr al-Mulk Radwan at the Lake of Antioch.
text: Battle of the Lake of Antioch: The Crusaders under Bohemond I defeat a Seljuk relief force (some 12,000 men) led by Sultan Fakhr al-Mulk Radwan of Aleppo. Bohemond gathers 700 knights, and marches in the night to ambush the Seljuk Turks at the Lake of Antioch (modern Turkey). After several successful cavalry charges the Crusaders rout the Seljuk army, forcing Radwan to retreat to Aleppo.
names: Battle of the Lake of Antioch

summary: Baldwin of Boulogne took control of Edessa and established the County of Edessa as the first Crusader state.
text: Baldwin of Boulogne enters Edessa, and is welcomed as liberator by the Armenian clergy. The local population massacres the Seljuk garrison and officials – or forces them to flee. Baldwin is acknowledged as their ruler (or doux). He assumes the title of count and establishes the first crusader state. Baldwin marries Arda of Armenia, daughter of Lord Thoros of Marash, and consolidates his conquered territory.

summary: Crusaders under Bohemond I captured Antioch after an Armenian guard opened the gates, establishing the Principality of Antioch.
text: Siege of Antioch: The Crusaders under Bohemond I capture Antioch after a 8-month siege. He established secret contact with Firouz, an Armenian guard who controlled the "Tower of the Two Sisters". He opened the gates and Bohemond entered the city. Thousands of Christians are massacred along with Muslims. Bohemond is named Prince of Antioch (under protest) and creates the Principality of Antioch.

summary: Kerbogha of Mosul besieged the Crusaders inside Antioch, while Emperor Alexios I Komnenos turned back his Byzantine relief army.
text: Battle of Antioch: Emir Kerbogha, ruler (atabeg) of Mosul, arrives at Antioch with a Seljuk army (35,000 men) to relieve the city. He lays siege to the Crusaders who have just captured the city themselves (although they do not have full control of it). A Byzantine relief force led by Emperor Alexios I Komnenos turns back after Count Stephen of Blois convinces them that the situation in Antioch is hopeless.

summary: Crusaders under Bohemond I sortied from Antioch, defeated Kerbogha's besieging army, and secured the city.
text: Following the Holy Lance discovery by Peter Bartholomew in Antioch, the Crusaders under Bohemond I (leaving only 200 men) sortie from the city and defeat the Seljuk army. Kerbogha is forced to withdraw to Mosul, the garrison in the citadel surrenders to Bohemond personally (who raises his banner above the city) and the Crusaders occupy Antioch. The Crusade is delayed for the rest of the year.

summary: Bohemond I granted commercial privileges and warehouse rights in Antioch to the Republic of Genoa.
text: Donation of Altavilla: Bohemond I grants commercial privileges and the right to use warehouses (fondaco) to the Republic of Genoa. This marks the beginning of Italian merchant settlements in the Levant.

summary: Adhemar of Le Puy, papal legate and spiritual leader of the First Crusade, died of typhus in Antioch.
text: Adhemar of Le Puy (or Aimar), French bishop and nominal leader of the First Crusade, dies during an epidemic (probably typhus). With this, Rome's direct control over the Crusade effectively ends.

summary: Fatimid forces under Caliph Al-Musta'li recaptured Jerusalem and occupied Palestine.
text: August – Fatimid forces under Caliph Al-Musta'li recapture Jerusalem and occupy Palestine. The Crusaders threaten the borders of the Fatimid Caliphate which already has lost the Emirate of Sicily (see 1091).

summary: Crusaders captured the city of Ma'arra after a month-long siege and massacred many inhabitants.
text: Siege of Ma'arra: The Crusaders capture the city of Ma'arra after a month's siege and massacre part of the population. Short of supplies, the army is accused of widespread cannibalism.

summary: Pope Urban II presided over the Council of Bari to discuss theological issues with the Greek Orthodox Church.
text: October – The Council of Bari presided by Pope Urban II discusses relations between the Western and the Eastern Church.

summary: Raymond IV of Toulouse led the Crusaders south from Antioch toward Jerusalem, crossing the Orontes River.
text: The Crusaders, under Raymond IV, count of Toulouse (Raymond of Saint-Gilles), leave Antioch, and head south towards Jerusalem. They are joined by forces of Tancred (a nephew of Bohemond I) and Robert II, duke of Normandy. Raymond is given free passage and supplies, and accepts guides from the Emir of Shaizar (modern Syria), who conducts the army (6,000 men) across the Orontes River (between Shaizar and Hama).

summary: Raymond IV of Toulouse made a treaty at Masyaf and captured the strategic fortress of Hosn al-Akrad.
text: The Crusaders, under Raymond IV, reach Masyaf, where a treaty is agreed to. They decide to continue the march, rather than to capture or destroy the town. The next day the Crusaders enter the deserted town of Rafaniyah, that provides them with much-needed supplies. Raymond moves into the Buqaia Valley, and takes the strategic Kurdish fortress of Hosn al-Akrad (the future Krak des Chevaliers castle).

summary: Godfrey of Bouillon and Robert II of Flanders besieged Jabala until its emir submitted to Crusader suzerainty.
text: February – The Crusaders under Godfrey of Bouillon set out from Antioch to Latakia. They are joined by forces of Bohemond I and Robert II, count of Flanders. On their arrival, Bohemond decides to turn back to consolidate his power in Antioch. Godfrey and Robert move on to besiege the small sea-port of Jabala. After two weeks, the Emir of Jabala makes a truce, and accepts the suzerainty of the Crusaders.

summary: Raymond IV of Toulouse lifted the three-month siege of Akkar and resumed marching south toward Tripoli.
text: The Crusaders under Raymond IV besiege the fortified town of Akkar – whose garrison is loyal to Jalal al-Mulk Abu'l-Hasan, emir of Tripoli (modern Lebanon). On May 13 after a 3-month siege the investment of Akkar is raised and Raymond orders the camp to be struck. The Crusader host, finally joined by the forces of Godfrey of Bouillon and Robert II, resumes his march southwards to Tripoli.

summary: Raymond Pilet captured the port of Tortosa after tricking its garrison into fleeing by sea.
text: Raymond IV sends a small part of his army under Raymond Pilet to attack the port of Tortosa on the Syrian coast. The Crusaders led many fires around the port to make believe their number is greater than it is. Fooled by the deception, the governor and the garrison flees by sea in the night leaving the port open for the Crusaders to capture. The port becomes strategically important for supplies.

summary: The Crusaders marched past Tripoli and crossed the Dog River into Fatimid territory north of Beirut.
text: May – The Crusaders march past Tripoli, accompanied by guides provided by the emir who lead them safely through the towns of Batroun and Byblos. On May 19 they cross the Dog River north of Beirut into Fatimid territory. There local governors supply the Crusaders with tribute and food in return for no damage to the agricultural area. The Fatimids keep no large troops in the north, except for small garrisons.

summary: The Fatimid garrison of Sidon attacked the Crusaders while they were looting local villages but was repulsed.
text: The Fatimid governor of Sidon refuses to cooperate and his garrison attacks the Crusader host while they are looting local villages. The Fatimids are repulsed, the towns further south generally follow the example of Beirut. The Crusaders move on to Tyre – Raymond IV decides to wait for two days to allow a force under Baldwin of Le Bourg (supported by knights from Antioch) to catch up with him.

summary: The Crusaders marched past Haifa and Mount Carmel to Caesarea, where they rested for four days.
text: The Crusaders march to Haifa and along the coast under Mount Carmel to Caesarea (modern Israel), where they rest for four days in order to celebrate Whitsun (Whit Sunday).

summary: The Crusaders occupied Arsuf and turned toward Ramlah, while Tancred liberated Bethlehem.
text: 6 – The Crusaders occupy Arsuf and turn inland towards Ramlah, where they reorganise for the march against Jerusalem. A Crusader force under Tancred liberates Bethlehem.

summary: The Crusaders reached the outskirts of Jerusalem and began besieging the city after rejecting a peace offer.
text: Siege of Jerusalem: The Crusaders reach the outskirts of Jerusalem, and begin the siege of the Holy City. Iftikhar al-Dawla offers a peace agreement but this is refused.

summary: Crusaders under Godfrey of Bouillon assaulted Jerusalem at the Damascus Gate but were repelled.
text: The Crusaders under Godfrey of Boullion launch their first assault on Jerusalem, while the Fatimid garrison and Jewish militia defend the northern wall at the Damascus Gate.

summary: Guglielmo Embriaco brought six Genoese supply ships into Jaffa, where most were trapped by a Fatimid fleet.
text: A naval squadron of six Genoese ships led by Guglielmo Embriaco (loaded with military materials) enters the port of Jaffa; all except one are trapped by a larger Fatimid fleet.

summary: The Crusaders were repulsed in an assault on Jerusalem and marched around the walls in a religious procession.
text: The Crusaders attempt to take Jerusalem by storm but are repulsed. In a procession they walk around the walls under leadership of priests in the hope the city would surrender.

summary: The Crusader army launched an assault against the northern and southern walls of Jerusalem but failed to establish a foothold.
text: The Crusader army (some 12,000 men) launch a final assault on Jerusalem. The attacks against the northern and southern wall are repulsed without establishing a foothold.

summary: Raymond IV of Toulouse sailed to Constantinople to obtain the support of Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos for his attempt to capture Tripoli.
text: May or June – Count Raymond IV of Toulouse (Saint-Gilles) sails to Constantinople to obtain the support of Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos in his attempt to seize Tripoli.

summary: Seljuk forces under Sultan Kilij Arslan I defeated a second wave of European crusaders at Heraclea Cybistra.
text: Crusade of 1101 – A second wave of European crusaders attempts to cross Anatolia, to reach the Kingdom of Jerusalem. They are defeated by the Seljuk troops under Sultan Kilij Arslan I, at Heraclea. A handful of crusaders under Raymond IV of Toulouse manage to reach the Byzantine port of Bafra, at the mouth of the River Halys.

summary: Byzantine admiral Eustathios recaptured western Cilician ports and occupied Tarsus, Adana, and Mamistra.
text: Summer – The Byzantine fleet under Admiral Eustathios recaptures the ports of western Cilicia, Seleucia and Corycus. Eustathios extends his power over Cilician territory (belonging to Bohemond I) further east – occupying Tarsus, Adana and Mamistra.

summary: Anna Dalassene, mother of Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, died in Constantinople.
text: Anna Dalassena, Byzantine noblewoman

summary: Tancred attacked the Byzantine Empire and recaptured Tarsus, Adana, and Mamistra in Cilicia, while Bohemond I was ransomed from Seljuk captivity.
text: Spring – Bohemond I, Norman prince of Antioch, is released from Seljuk imprisonment at Niksar, after a ransom is paid of 100,000 gold pieces. During his absence, Tancred (Bohemond's nephew) attacks the Byzantines, and re-captures the cities of Tarsus, Adana and Mamistra in Cilicia. Tancred is deprived of his lordship by Bohemond's return, and is rewarded with a small fief within the Principality of Antioch.

summary: Raymond IV of Toulouse invaded the Beqaa Valley, captured Tortosa, and began constructing a castle to besiege Tripoli with naval support from Byzantine Emperor Alexios I.
text: The Crusaders under Raymond IV invade the Beqaa Valley and capture Tortosa to isolate Tripoli. Raymond expands towards the Orontes River, and begins to build a castle on the Mons Peregrinus which helps in the Siege of Tripoli (see 1102). Emperor Alexios I supports the Crusaders by sending a Byzantine fleet (ten ships) to blockade the port of Tripoli.

summary: The Byzantine military re-occupied Tarsus, Adana, and Mamistra, chased a Genoese fleet, and captured the port of Latakia.
text: Summer – The Byzantines re-occupy the Cilician cities of Tarsus, Adana and Mamistra. A naval squadron, under Admiral Cantacuzenus, pursues in Cypriot waters a Genoese raiding fleet, and sails on to Latakia, where they capture the harbour and the lower city. Bohemond I reinforces the garrison in the citadel.

summary: Bohemond I left Antioch for Italy to raise an army against Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, leaving Tancred as co-ruler.
text: Autumn – Bohemond I departs to Italy for reinforcements. He takes with him gold and silver, and precious stuff to raise an army against Emperor Alexios I Komnenos. Tancred becomes co-ruler over Antioch – and appoints his brother-in-law, Richard of Salerno, as his deputy.

object: Constance of France, Princess of Antioch
summary: Bohemond I of Antioch married Constance of France in Chartres and prepared a campaign against Alexios I Komnenos.
text: Spring – Bohemond I, prince of Antioch, marries Constance of France (daughter of King Philip I) in the cathedral of Chartres. Philip agrees to marry his second daughter, the 9-year-old Cecile of France, to Tancred (nephew of Bohemond). Meanwhile, Bohemond mobilises an expeditionary force (some 30,000 men) to begin a campaign against Emperor Alexios I.
cast: Constance of France, Princess of Antioch
names: Constance of France, Princess of Antioch

summary: Bohemond I of Antioch returned to Apulia with an expeditionary force to prepare an invasion of the Byzantine Empire.
text: Autumn – Bohemond I returns to Apulia (Southern Italy) with an expeditionary force to prepare an offensive against the Byzantines. He is accompanied by his newlywed wife Constance (who is pregnant by him) and followers.

summary: Alexios Komnenos, Byzantine co-emperor, was born in Balabista.
text: Alexios Komnenos, Byzantine co-emperor (d. 1142)

summary: Bohemond I of Antioch landed an army near Avlona in the Byzantine Empire and plundered the countryside.
text: Bohemond I, prince of Antioch, lands with his army (some 34,000 men) in Epirus near Avlona. He plunders the countryside and marches to Dyrrhachium (modern Albania).

summary: Bohemond I began the siege of the Byzantine port city of Dyrrhachium, defended by Alexios Komnenos.
text: November – Siege of Dyrrhachium: Bohemond I begins the siege of the Adriatic port city of Dyrrhachium held by its doux Alexios Komnenos.

summary: Crusaders led by Tancred of Galilee recaptured Tarsus, Adana, and Mamistra from Byzantine control.
text: The Crusaders under Tancred, prince of Galilee, recover the Cilician cities of Tarsus, Adana and Mamistra conquered by Emperor Alexios I 3-years ago (see 1104).

summary: Byzantine general Stephen Kontostephanos was born.
text: Stephen Kontostephanos, Byzantine general (d. 1149)

summary: Bohemond I lifted the siege of Dyrrhachium and signed the Treaty of Devol, becoming a vassal of the Byzantine Empire.
text: September – Siege of Dyrrhachium: Italo-Norman forces under Bohemond I lift the siege due to illness and lack of supplies. Bohemond becomes a vassal of the Byzantine Empire by signing the Treaty of Devol.

summary: Andronikos Komnenos, Byzantine prince and son of Emperor John II Komnenos, was born.
text: Andronikos Komnenos, Byzantine prince (d. 1142)

summary: John Tzetzes, Byzantine poet and grammarian, was born.
text: John Tzetzes, Byzantine grammarian

summary: Crusaders led by Baldwin I besieged Tyre while refusing an alliance with a Byzantine embassy against Tancred of Galilee.
text: Winter – Crusaders, led by Baldwin I, besiege Tyre, without a supporting fleet. During the siege, a Byzantine embassy arrives in the Crusader camp. The Byzantines try to persuade Baldwin to join a coalition against Tancred, Italo-Norman prince of Galilee, but he refuses.

summary: Malik Shah of Rum invaded Anatolia and marched on Philadelphia, where he was halted by the Byzantine governor Constantine Gabras.
text: Spring – Malik Shah, Seljuk ruler of the Sultanate of Rum, begins incursions into Anatolia. He marches on Philadelphia with his army, but is halted by the Byzantines under Gabras, governor of the Theme of Chaldia.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos relieved the siege of Nicaea and defeated the forces of Malik Shah near Cotyaeum.
text: Spring – Siege of Nicaea: Malik Shah, Seljuk ruler of the Sultanate of Rum, sends an expedition through Bithynia to the very walls of Nicaea. Seljuk forces raid Abydos on the Hellespont, with its rich custom-houses. Malik Shah attacks and captures Pergamum. Emperor Alexios I Komnenos sets out to meet the Seljuk invaders. He lifts the siege at Nicaea and wins a complete victory near Cotyaeum (modern Turkey).

summary: Byzantine archbishop and scholar Eustathius of Thessalonica was born.
text: Eustathius of Thessalonica, Byzantine archbishop (d. 1195)

summary: Byzantine clergyman Euthymios Malakes was born.
text: Euthymios Malakes, Byzantine bishop

summary: Alexios I Komnenos repulsed and routed the Seljuk army under Sultan Malik Shah near Philomelium, forcing him to accept a peace treaty.
text: Autumn – Battle of Philomelion (1116): Emperor Alexios I Komnenos leads an expedition into Anatolia and meets the Seljuk army under Sultan Malik Shah (near Philomelium). The Byzantines introduce a new battle formation of Alexios' devising, the parataxis (a defensive formation, consisting of a hollow square, with the baggage in the centre). During the battle, the Seljuk Turks mount several attacks on the formations, but all are repulsed. The Byzantine cavalry makes two counterattacks; the first is unsuccessful. But a second attack, led by Nikephoros Bryennios the Younger, breaks the Seljuk forces, who then turn to flight. The following day Malik Shah again attacks, his army completely surrounding the Byzantines from all sides. The Seljuk Turks are once more repulsed, with many losses. Alexios claims the victory, and Malik Shah is forced to accept a peace treaty, in which he promises to respect the frontiers of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Emperor Alexios I Komnenos died after a thirty-seven-year reign and was succeeded by his son John II Komnenos.
text: Emperor Alexios I Komnenos dies after a 37-year reign, in which he has regained control over western Anatolia (modern Turkey). He stabilizes his frontiers against the wars with the Normans in the western Balkans, and the Seljuk Turks in the East. Alexios is succeeded by his 30-year-old son, John II Komnenos (the Good), as ruler of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: The Byzantine general Philocales captured Sardis from the Sultanate of Rum.
text: The Byzantine general Philocales captures Sardis, from the Seljuk Sultanate of Rûm.

summary: Manuel I Komnenos, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: Manuel I Komnenos, Byzantine emperor (d. 1180)

summary: Andronikos I Komnenos, future Byzantine emperor, was born.
text: Andronikos I Komnenos, Byzantine emperor (d. 1185)

summary: Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos died.
text: Alexios I Komnenos, Byzantine emperor

summary: Basil the Physician, Bogomil leader, was executed.
text: Basil the Physician, Bogomil religious leader

summary: Maria of Alania, former Byzantine empress, died.
text: Maria of Alania, Byzantine empress (b. 1053)

summary: Byzantine forces under Emperor John II Komnenos conquered Sozopolis from the Sultanate of Rum.
text: Siege of Sozopolis: Byzantine forces under Emperor John II Komnenos conquer Sozopolis in Pisidia, from the Sultanate of Rum. The Seljuk garrison is defeated while they are trapped between the Byzantine cavalry and the army (which is besieging the fortress).

summary: Emperor John II Komnenos recovered southwestern Anatolia from the Seljuk Turks and reinforced the Danube frontier against the Pechenegs.
text: Emperor John II Komnenos recovers southwestern Anatolia (modern Turkey) from the Seljuk Turks and then hastens to the Balkans, where the Pechenegs are continuing their incursions. He transfers Byzantine troops to the Danube frontier at Paristrion.

summary: Emperor John II Komnenos and the Varangian Guard decisively defeated the Pechenegs at the Battle of Beroia.
text: Battle of Beroia: Emperor John II Komnenos transfers the Byzantine field army from Asia Minor (where it has been engaged in fighting the Seljuk Turks) to the Balkans. The Pechenegs who have set up their camp (defended by a circular formation of wagons) near Beroia (modern Bulgaria) are defeated. John orders the Varangian Guard (some 480 men), the elite Palace Guard to hack their way through the Pecheneg circle of wagons, causing a general rout in their camp. Pecheneg survivors are taken captive and enlisted in the Byzantine army.

summary: A Venetian fleet commanded by Doge Domenico Michiel laid siege to the Byzantine island of Corfu.
text: A Venetian fleet under Doge Domenico Michiel with well over a hundred ships sets sail from Venice, carrying an army of around 15,000 men and siege-material on the Venetian Crusade. The fleet departs for Palestine – but the Venetians pause to attack Corfu (this in retaliation for the refusal of John II to renew exclusive trading privileges). For six months, throughout the winter of 1122–23, the Venetians lay siege to the Byzantine island.

summary: War broke out between the Republic of Venice and the Byzantine Empire after Emperor John II Komnenos refused to renew trading privileges.
text: War with Venice begins: Over the non-renewal of trading privileges by John II Komnenos.

summary: The Republic of Venice pillaged Rhodes, ravaged Samos and Lesbos, and occupied Byzantine Chios.
text: The Republic of Venice pillages the islands of Rhodes, ravages Samos and Lesbos, and occupies Chios (controlled by the Byzantine Empire). The Republic of Florence sacks and conquers the neighboring independent republic of Fiesole in Italy.

summary: Emperor John II Komnenos re-confirmed the treaty of 1082 with Venice, securing Braničevo and recovering Sirmium.
text: Summer – Emperor John II Komnenos re-confirms the treaty of 1082. This ends the hostilities with Hungary and Venice. John secures Braničevo, and recovers the region of Sirmium on the Danube, but is forced by Venice to renew the exclusive commercial privileges.

summary: Hungarians invaded the Byzantine Empire, advancing south as far as Philippopolis.
text: Hungarians invade the Empire: Invaders go far south as Philippolis.

summary: Emperor John II Komnenos defeated Hungarian forces and their Serbian allies at Haram.
text: Byzantine–Hungarian War: Emperor John II Komnenos defeats the Hungarians and their Serbian allies at the fortress of Haram (or Chramon), which is modern-day Nova Palanka.

summary: Byzantine governor John Doukas Komnenos was born.
text: John Doukas Komnenos, Byzantine governor (d. 1176)

summary: Byzantine aristocrat John Kontostephanos was born.
text: John Kontostephanos, Byzantine aristocrat

summary: Byzantine forces repelled an invasion by the Hungarians.
text: Invading Hungarins are repelled

summary: Dobrodeia of Kiev, Byzantine princess, died.
text: Dobrodeia of Kiev, Byzantine princess

summary: Andronikos Komnenos, Byzantine prince, died.
text: Andronikos Komnenos, Byzantine prince (or 1130)

summary: Byzantine aristocrat Andronikos Kontostephanos was born.
text: Andronikos Kontostephanos, Byzantine aristocrat (or 1133)

summary: Byzantine aristocrat Andronikos Doukas Angelos was born.
text: Andronikos Doukas Angelos, Byzantine aristocrat

summary: Byzantine aristocrat Andronikos Kontostephanos was born.
text: Andronikos Kontostephanos, Byzantine aristocrat

summary: Byzantine empress Irene Doukaina died.
text: Irene Doukaina, Byzantine empress (b. 1066)

summary: Robert of Ketton and Herman of Carinthia travelled through France, the Byzantine Empire, and the Crusader States.
text: Robert of Ketton and Herman of Carinthia travel throughout France, the Byzantine Empire, and the Crusader States.

summary: Leo Styppes was enthroned as Patriarch of Constantinople.
text: Leo Styppes becomes Patriarch of Constantinople.

summary: Neophytos of Cyprus, Orthodox monk and writer, was born.
text: Neophytos of Cyprus, Cypriot Orthodox priest (d. 1214)

summary: Byzantine Empress Irene of Hungary died.
text: Irene of Hungary, Byzantine empress (b. 1088)

summary: John IX Agapetos, Patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: John IX (Agapetos), Byzantine patriarch

summary: Emperor John II Komnenos sent an embassy offering subsidies to Lothair III for a campaign against Roger II of Sicily.
text: Lothair III receives a Byzantine embassy at his court, on behalf of Emperor John II Komnenos. It offers large financial subsidies for Lothair to start a campaign against Roger II. The negotiations will last for some months.

summary: Emperor Lothair III invaded southern Italy in response to Emperor John II Komnenos and conquered Apulia from King Roger II of Sicily as Duke Grimoald of Bari rebelled.
text: Summer – Emperor Lothair III invades southern Italy in response to the appeal of Emperor John II Komnenos (see 1135) and conquers Apulia from King Roger II of Sicily. Duke Grimoald of Bari, supported by Lothair III, rebels against Roger.

summary: Emperor John II Komnenos launched his first major military campaign in the east from Constantinople.
text: John II launches his first serious campaign in the east.

summary: Emperor John II Komnenos captured Mersin, Tarsus, Adana, Mamistra, and Anazarbus, subduing Armenian Cilicia.
text: Spring – Emperor John II (Komnenos) leads a Byzantine expeditionary force into Cilicia (the Byzantine fleet guards his flank). He defeats the Armenians under Prince Leo I ("Lord of the Mountains"), and captures the cities of Mersin, Tarsus, Adana and Mamistra. Leo retreats to the great fortifications of Anazarbus – where its garrison resists for 37 days. The Byzantine siege engines batter down its walls, and the city is forced to surrender. Leo escapes into the Taurus Mountains, while the Byzantine forces march southward into the plain of Antioch.

summary: Emperor John II Komnenos besieged Antioch and forced Raymond of Poitiers and Joscelin II of Edessa to become Byzantine vassals.
text: John II appears before the walls of Antioch, and encamps with the Byzantine army on the north bank of the Orontes River. For several days he besieges the city, Raymond of Poitiers (prince of Antioch) is forced to surrender. He recognizes John as his suzerain and becomes with Joscelin II (count of Edessa) a vassal of the Byzantine Empire.

summary: Byzantine statesman and general Nikephoros Bryennios the Younger died.
text: Nicephorus Bryennius, Byzantine statesman (b. 1062)

summary: Byzantine Emperor John II Komnenos invaded Syria, advanced on Aleppo, and took multiple regional fortresses by assault.
text: Byzantine Emperor John II Komnenos, having led an expeditionary force into Syria, arrives before the walls of Aleppo. The city proves too strong to attack, but the fortresses of Biza'a, Athareb, Ma'arrat Nu'man and Kafartab are taken by assault. While the Byzantines besiege the city of Shaizar, the Crusader allies Prince Raymond of Poitiers of Antioch and Count Joscelin II of Edessa remain in their camp playing dice.

summary: John II Komnenos besieged Shaizar until Emir Abu'l Asakir Sultan agreed to pay an indemnity and become a Byzantine vassal.
text: Siege of Shaizar begins. The Byzantines under John II besiege the capital of the Munqidhite Emirate. They capture the lower city on May 20, but fail to take the citadel. John negotiates with Emir Abu'l Asakir Sultan who sends him an offer to pay a large indemnity and become a vassal of the Byzantine Empire. John, disgusted by his Crusader allies, accepts the terms and raises the siege on May 21.

summary: Byzantine empress consort Irene Doukaina died in Constantinople.
text: Irene Doukaina, Byzantine empress

summary: Byzantine Emperor John II Komnenos compelled the Principality of Antioch to submit to imperial suzerainty.
text: John II vassalizes the Principality of Antioch.

summary: Leo I, Prince of Armenia, died in captivity in Constantinople.
text: February 14: Leo I, prince of Armenia

summary: Emperor John II Komnenos led an expedition across Anatolia to Antalya, repelling Seljuk forces, and forged an alliance with Conrad III of Germany.
text: Spring – Emperor John II Komnenos and his sons lead a Byzantine expeditionary force across Anatolia to Antalya. He drives back the Seljuks and Turcomans – who again are trying to invade Phrygia. John strengthens the frontier defences in northern Syria and sends an embassy to Germany – to seek an alliance against King Roger II of Sicily. To seal the alliance, the emissaries request that King Conrad III send a princess of his family to be married to the emperor's son, Manuel. Instead, Conrad selects his sister-in-law, Bertha of Sulzbach, and sends her to the Byzantine Empire escorted by Emicho, bishop of Würzburg.

summary: Emperor John II Komnenos advanced to Turbessel against Cilician Armenia after his eldest sons Alexios and Andronikos died of illness.
text: Late Summer – John II establishes a supply base for his further campaigns at Antalya. While waiting for reinforcements, his eldest son Alexios and appointed heir, falls ill and dies. His other two sons, Andronikos and Isaac are tasked to escort the body, but during the voyage Andronikos also dies. John continues his campaign against the Armenian kingdom of Cilicia – to re-conquer the fortresses that the Danishmends have taken. He appears by forced marches at Turbessel in mid-September. Meanwhile, Isaac brings the corpses of his two brothers back to Constantinople, where they are entombed in the Pantokrator Monastery.

summary: Byzantine forces under Emperor John II Komnenos failed to capture Antioch.
text: Autumn – Imad al-Din Zengi, Seljuk governor (atabeg) of Mosul, continues his campaign against the Kurds in southeastern Anatolia (since 1141). Byzantine forces under John II fail to take Antioch.

summary: Byzantine co-emperor Alexios Komnenos died of fever in Attalia.
text: Alexios Komnenos, Byzantine co-emperor (b. 1106)

summary: Byzantine prince Andronikos Komnenos died while conveying his brother's body.
text: Andronikos Komnenos, Byzantine prince (b. 1108)

summary: Manuel I Komnenos succeeded John II Komnenos as Byzantine emperor after John died from a hunting accident on Mount Taurus.
text: Emperor John II Komnenos Komnenos dies of a poisoned arrow wound while hunting wild boar on Mount Taurus in Cilicia. He is succeeded by his 24-year-old son Manuel I, who is chosen as his successor, in preference to his elder surviving brother Isaac. Manuel dispatches John Axouchos, his commander-in-chief (megas domestikos), to Constantinople ahead of him – with orders to arrest Isaac in the Great Palace.

summary: Patriarch Leo of Constantinople died in Constantinople.
text: Leo of Constantinople, Byzantine patriarch

summary: Byzantine Emperor John II Komnenos died following a hunting accident in Cilicia.
text: John II Komnenos, Byzantine emperor (b. 1087)

summary: Byzantine princess Maria Komnene was born.
text: Approximate date – Maria Komnene, queen consort of Hungary and Croatia (d. 1190)

summary: Raymond of Poitiers travelled to Constantinople and accepted the suzerainty of Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos.
text: Raymond of Poitiers, prince of Antioch, travels to Constantinople to ask Emperor Manuel I Komnenos for help to support his campaign against the Seljuks. When he arrives, Raymond is forced to accept the suzerainty of the Byzantine Empire. Manuel treats him graciously, gives him gifts and promises him a money subsidy.

summary: Merv surpassed Constantinople to become the most populous city in the world.
text: Estimation: Merv (in the Seljuk Empire) becomes the largest city in the world, surpassing Constantinople.

summary: Maria of Antioch, future Byzantine empress and regent, was born.
text: Maria of Antioch, Byzantine empress and regent (d. 1182)

summary: Manuel Komnenos, son of future Byzantine emperor Andronikos I, was born.
text: Manuel Komnenos, son of Andronikos I (d. 1185)

summary: Byzantine princess and future Queen of Jerusalem Theodora Komnene was born.
text: Theodora Komnene, queen of Jerusalem

summary: Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos ordered the sack of Philomelion and relocated its Christian population.
text: Sack of Philomelion: Under the orders from Manuel I, before relocating the Christian population.

summary: Conrad III led a German crusader army across Hungary into the Byzantine Empire and reached Sofia, where Michael Palaiologos Doukas welcomed him.
text: May – July – A German expeditionary force (some 20,000 men) under King Conrad III leaves Regensburg and passes into Hungary. The German nobility is headed by Conrad's nephew and heir, Frederick I, duke of Swabia. On July 20, Conrad crosses into the Byzantine Empire, and reaches Sofia – where Michael Palaiologos (a nephew of Emperor Manuel I) gives Conrad an official welcome and provides the Crusaders with food.

summary: Louis VII led a French crusader force from Metz through Bavaria and Hungary toward the Byzantine frontier.
text: June – A French expeditionary force (some 18,000 men) led by King Louis VII departs from Metz and travels through Bavaria. Louis is accompanied by the French nobility and his wife, Queen Eleanor of Aquitaine, heiress of France. At Regensburg, where the force arrives on June 29, the Crusaders journey peaceably for fifteen days through Hungary and reach the Byzantine frontier at the end of August.

summary: After suffering a flash flood in their camp, Conrad III and his crusaders rejected Emperor Manuel I's advice to cross at the Hellespont and pushed toward Constantinople.
text: The German crusaders suffer a natural disaster near Constantinople, when part of their encampment is swept away by a flash flood with considerable loss of life. Emperor Manuel I Komnenos orders the Crusaders to cross to Asia Minor by the Hellespont. Conrad III ignores the advice of Manuel and after some minor clashes with the Byzantines, pushes towards Constantinople.

summary: Conrad III arrived at Constantinople and camped at Galata, prompting Emperor Manuel I to order the German crusaders transported across the Bosporus.
text: The German crusaders under Conrad III reach Constantinople, where there is a frosty exchange of letters between Conrad and Manuel I. The German forces make camp at Galata on the northern shore of the Golden Horn. Manuel orders that a full-scale effort must be made to transport the Germans, who are causing troubles by sacking the Philopatium, across the Bosporus.

summary: Conrad III crossed the Bosporus to Nicomedia and divided his crusader forces, sending knights across Seljuk territory and pilgrims along the Aegean coast.
text: Autumn – Conrad III decides not to wait for the French and crosses the Bosporus into Asia Minor. He leads the German crusader army to Nicomedia, and divides his forces into two divisions. Conrad takes the knights and his professional soldiers across Seljuk central territory while the baggage train, pilgrims and a defending force under Bishop Otto of Freising travel along the Aegean coast.

summary: Louis VII arrived at Constantinople, crossed into Asia Minor, and arranged to meet Conrad III at Uluabat after learning of the German defeat.
text: 5 – Louis VII arrives at Constantinople and joins with forces from Savoy under Amadeus III (his uncle) – who have taken the land route through Italy. Louis crosses the Bosporus, and leads the French crusader army into Asia Minor – where he hears in Nicaea of Conrad's defeat at the end of October. Louis sends a military escort for Conrad and agrees to rendezvous at Lopardium. The German crusaders under Otto of Freising follow the coastal road before turning inland, up the Gediz River valley to Philadelphia. Otto's force is ambushed by the Seljuk Turks, just outside Laodicea, losing many men killed or taken prisoner. Otto and the survivors struggle on to Adalia, from where they sail for the Holy Land. Others attempt to continue along the southern coast of Anatolia.

summary: Louis VII and Conrad III combined their crusader forces at Uluabat and marched down the Aegean coast to Ephesus.
text: November – The combined forces of Louis VII and Conrad III meet at Lopardium and march along the coastal road via Pergamon and Smyrna to Ephesus, where they celebrate Christmas. Conrad, still suffering from his wounds, sails back to Constantinople to be placed under the care of Manuel's own physicians. Meanwhile, the Crusader camp is attacked by Turkish raiders near Ephesus.

summary: Louis VII and the French crusaders repelled a Turkish ambush outside Ephesus in the Meander Valley.
text: Battle of Ephesus: The French crusaders under Louis VII leave Ephesus, and ascend the Meander Valley. Louis is warned by messengers of Manuel that Seljuk and Danishmendid forces are assembling west of Adalia. Louis ignores the advice and successfully fends off an ambush just outside Ephesus.

summary: George of Antioch captured Corfu for Sicily and pillaged Corinth, Athens, and Thebes, initiating an eleven-year war with the Byzantine Empire.
text: A Sicilian fleet (some 70 ships) under George of Antioch attacks Corfu, the island surrenders and welcomes the Normans as their liberators. Leaving a garrison of 1,000 men, George sails to the Peloponnesus. He pillages the cities of Corinth, Athens and Thebes. King Roger II begins an 11-year war between Sicily and the Byzantine Empire.

summary: King Conrad III recovered from his wounds and departed Constantinople with funds and a fleet provided by Emperor Manuel I Komnenos to sail to Palestine.
text: King Conrad III recovers from his wounds and leaves Constantinople with his household. He is well supplied with money by Emperor Manuel I Komnenos and uses these funds to recruit pilgrims to augment the forces that remain to him. Conrad and his re-equipped Crusaders sail with a Byzantine fleet to Palestine. The fleet is scattered by storms and lands in different ports.

summary: Conrad III sailed to Thessaloniki and concluded an alliance with Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos against Roger II of Sicily.
text: Conrad III sails from Acre to Thessaloniki and forms an alliance with Manuel I against King Roger II of Sicily. During his visit Henry II, Duke of Austria ('Jasomirgott') marries Manuel's niece, Theodora Komnene.

summary: Anna Komnene wrote the Alexiad, a biography of her father Emperor Alexios I Komnenos.
text: Anna Komnene writes the Alexiad, a biography of her father, the late Emperor Alexios I Komnenos.

summary: Roger II established a silk industry in Palermo using silk workers brought from Greece.
text: An Italian silk industry is started at Palermo by Roger II, who takes numbers of silk workers back from Greece.

summary: Emperor Manuel I Komnenos recovered Corfu from the Normans with Venetian naval assistance.
text: Spring – Emperor Manuel I Komnenos recovers Corfu with the help of the Venetians, who defeat the Sicilian fleet. During the three-month siege, Byzantine admiral Stephen Kontostephanos is killed by a stone thrown by a catapult. Manuel prepares an offensive against the Normans; King Roger II sends a fleet (some 40 ships) under George of Antioch, to pillage the suburbs of Constantinople.

summary: The Byzantine navy attacked the French fleet returning around the Peloponnese, capturing several ships and taking them to Constantinople.
text: April – King Louis VII and Queen Eleanor of Aquitaine sail homeward in separate Sicilian ships. While the fleet rounds the Peloponnese (southern Greece) it is attacked by ships of the Byzantine navy. Louis gives orders to raise the French flag and is allowed to sail on. But the ships containing many of his followers and his possessions are captured and taken as a war-prize to Constantinople.

summary: Stephen Kontostephanos, Byzantine aristocrat and megas doux, died during the siege of Corfu.
text: Stephen Kontostephanos, Byzantine aristocrat (b. 1107)

summary: The Byzantine army defeated a combined Serbian-Hungarian force near the Tara River, compelling Uroš II to accept a peace agreement.
text: Battle of Tara: The Byzantines defeat the Serbian-Hungarian army under Grdeša, count (župan) of Travunija, near the snow-covered Tara River. The Serbs are overpowered, and Grand Prince Uroš II is forced to accept the peace agreement made by Emperor Manuel I Komnenos. Uroš is succeeded by his brother Desa, who becomes co-ruler of the Principality of Serbia (until 1153).

summary: Byzantine painter Theodore Apsevdis was born in Constantinople.
text: Theodore Apsevdis, Byzantine painter (d. 1215)

summary: Byzantine princess Maria Komnene was born in Constantinople.
text: Maria Komnene, Byzantine princess (d. 1182)

summary: Nicholas IV, Patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Nicholas IV, patriarch of Constantinople (b. 1070)

summary: Manuel I Komnenos imprisoned Andronikos I Komnenos in the imperial palace in Constantinople for conspiring against him.
text: Spring – Andronikos I Komnenos, son of Isaac Komnenos, is imprisoned in the imperial palace for conspiring against his uncle, Emperor Manuel I (Komenenos) at Constantinople.

summary: Constantinople surpassed Merv to become the most populous city in the world.
text: Estimation: Constantinople, capital of the Byzantine Empire, becomes the largest city of the world, taking the lead from Merv in the Seljuk Empire.

summary: Future Byzantine emperor Alexios III Angelos was born in Constantinople.
text: Alexios III (Angelos), Byzantine emperor (d. 1211)

summary: Byzantine princess and historian Anna Komnene died in Constantinople.
text: Anna Komnene, Byzantine princess and historian (b. 1083)

summary: Bari rebelled against King William I of Sicily and recognized Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos as overlord.
text: The city of Bari rebels against King William I ("the Bad") of Sicily and recognizes the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos as its overlord.

summary: Raynald of Châtillon allied with Thoros II and brutally plundered Byzantine Cyprus.
text: Spring – Raynald of Châtillon, prince of Antioch, makes an alliance with Thoros II (the Great), ruler of Armenian Cilicia. He invades Cyprus and conducts a widespread plundering of the Byzantine island. The Crusaders and the Armenian forces march up and down the island robbing and pillaging every building, church and convent as well as shops and private houses. The crops are burnt; the herds are rounded up – together with all the population – and driven down to the coast. The massacre lasts about three weeks; on the rumor of a Byzantine fleet in the offing, Raynald gives the order for embarkation. The Crusader ships are loaded with booty, and every Cypriot is forced to ransom himself.

summary: William I of Sicily defeated the Byzantine army at Brindisi and recaptured Bari.
text: King William I (the Bad) lands with a Sicilian expeditionary force in Apulia. He defeats the Byzantine army at Brindisi and recaptures Bari.

summary: Future Byzantine emperor Isaac II Angelos was born in Constantinople.
text: Isaac II Angelos, Byzantine emperor (d. 1204)

summary: Emperor Manuel I Komnenos led a surprise invasion of Cilicia, forcing Thoros II to flee into the mountains and occupying the region.
text: Autumn – Emperor Manuel I Komnenos sets out from Constantinople at the head of an expeditionary army. He marches to Cilicia; and while the main army follows the coast road eastwards Manuel hurries ahead with a force of only 500 cavalry. He manages to surprise Thoros II "the Great", lord of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, who participated in the attack on Cyprus in 1156. Thoros flees into the mountains and Cilicia is occupied by the Byzantines.

summary: Empress Bertha of Sulzbach, consort of Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos, died in Constantinople.
text: Bertha of Sulzbach, Byzantine Empress (b. 1110s)

summary: Emperor Manuel I Komnenos sent an embassy led by John Kontostephanos to Jerusalem to seek a bride from the Crusader states.
text: Spring – Emperor Manuel I Komnenos sends an embassy led by John Kontostephanos to Jerusalem, to ask King Baldwin III to nominate one of the princesses of the Crusader states, as a bride for the widowed emperor. Their two candidates are 15-year-old Maria of Antioch, and Melisende of Tripoli. Baldwin suggests Melisende, and her brother Count Raymond III sets about gathering an enormous dowry. The ambassadors are not satisfied, and delay the marriage for over a year. They hear rumours about Melisende's birth, based on her mother's (Countess Hodierna of Jerusalem) infidelity, and therefore Melisende's possible illegitimacy. In the end, the Emperor marries Maria in 1161 and Melisende eventually enters a convent.

summary: Byzantine princess Eudokia Komnene was born in Constantinople.
text: Eudokia Komnene, French noblewoman (d. 1203)

summary: Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos married Maria of Antioch at Hagia Sophia.
text: The widowed Emperor Manuel I Komnenos marries Maria of Antioch, aged 16, at Hagia Sophia.

summary: Renier of Montferrat, future Byzantine political figure, was born.
text: Renier of Montferrat, Byzantine politician (d. 1183)

summary: Manuel I Komnenos formed an alliance with the Republic of Venice against Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa.
text: Spring – Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos makes an alliance with Venice against Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, who takes an oath at the Diet of Würzburg to support Antipope Paschal III against Pope Alexander III.

summary: Andronikos I Komnenos escaped from prison in Constantinople and took refuge with Yaroslav Osmomysl in Kyiv.
text: Andronikos I Komnenos, a cousin of Manuel I, escapes from prison at Constantinople. After passing through many dangers, he reaches Kiev and seeks refuge at the court of Prince Yaroslav Osmomysl.

summary: Emperor Manuel I Komnenos granted trade quarters in Constantinople to Genoa and Pisa after Venice refused to pay a subsidy.
text: Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos asks Venice to help pay the costs of defending Sicily, whose Norman rulers have had good relations with Venice. Doge Vitale II Michiel refuses to pay the requested subsidy. Manuel begins to cultivate relationships with the main commercial rivals of Venice: Genoa and Pisa. He grants them their own trade quarters in Constantinople, very near the Venetian settlements.

summary: Byzantine forces under Andronikos Kontostephanos defeated the Hungarians at the Battle of Sirmium.
text: Battle of Sirmium: Byzantine forces (15,000 men) under General Andronikos Kontostephanos defeat the Hungarians at Sirmium. Emperor Manuel I (Komnenos) consolidates his control over the western Balkans.

summary: Stefan Nemanja defeated Byzantine forces at the Battle of Pantina and became Grand Župan of Serbia.
text: Probable date – Battle of Pantina: The Byzantines intervene on behalf of Grand Prince Tihomir of Serbia against his rebellious brother, Prince Stefan Nemanja, who defeats the Byzantine forces and becomes Grand Župan of Serbia.

summary: King Amalric I of Jerusalem and Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos negotiated an alliance against Fatimid Egypt.
text: Summer – King Amalric I of Jerusalem and Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos negotiate an alliance against Fatimid-Egypt. Archbishop William of Tyre is among the ambassadors sent to Constantinople to finalize the treaty.

summary: Manuel I Komnenos demanded tribute from Egypt and dispatched a fleet under Andronikos Kontostephanos that defeated Fatimid ships near Cyprus.
text: Late Summer – Emperor Manuel I Komnenos sends an embassy to Egypt to demand tribute, and threatens the country with war when they refuse to pay it. The Byzantine fleet under Admiral Andronikos Kontostephanos sets out from the Hellespont; 60 war galleys are sent to Palestine with money for "the knights of Jerusalem". Andronikos with the rest of the fleet sails to Cyprus, at which he defeats a patrolling squadron of 6 Fatimid ships.

summary: Saladin defeated a joint Crusader and Byzantine force under King Amalric I besieging Damietta.
text: Winter – Saladin supported by reinforcements from Nur al-din, defeats a Crusader-Byzantine force under Amalric I near Damietta. During the 3-month siege, the Crusaders are forced to retreat to Palestine.

summary: Future Byzantine emperor Alexios II Komnenos was born in Constantinople.
text: Alexios II Komnenos, Byzantine emperor (d. 1183)

summary: Luke Chrysoberges, Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, died.
text: Luke Chrysoberges, Byzantine patriarch

summary: Emperor Manuel I Komnenos ordered the arrest of all Venetians within the Byzantine Empire and the seizure of their ships and property.
text: Emperor Manuel I (Komnenos) orders the arrest of all Venetians in his empire, and seizes their ships and goods.

summary: Doge Vitale II Michiel led a Venetian fleet to capture Trogir and Dubrovnik before plague decimated the force.
text: September – Doge Vitale II Michiel leads a Venetian fleet (120 ships) against the Byzantines, conquering the cities of Trogir and Dubrovnik. But the plague takes a heavy toll among the fleet's crewmen; half the ships have to be burned to keep them from falling into enemy hands. A plague also breaks out in Venice, when the remaining ships return.

summary: King Amalric of Jerusalem visited Constantinople and signed a treaty recognizing Emperor Manuel I Komnenos as his suzerain.
text: King Amalric I of Jerusalem departs with a large staff for Constantinople. At Callipolis he is met by his father-in-law, John Doukas Komnenos, military governor (doux) of Cyprus. Amalric enters the Byzantine capital and is welcomed by Manuel I. In June, a treaty is signed, Amalric recognizes Manuel's suzerainty over Jerusalem.

summary: Agnes of France, future Byzantine empress, was born in Paris.
text: Agnes of France (or Anna), Byzantine empress (d. 1220)

summary: Emperor Frederick Barbarossa laid siege to Alessandria, opposed by the Lombard League joined by Venice, Sicily, and Constantinople.
text: Emperor Frederick I (Barbarossa), on his fifth Italian campaign, begins the siege of Alessandria in northern Italy. He is opposed by the Lombard League (now joined by Venice, Sicily and Constantinople).

summary: Margaret of Hungary, future Byzantine empress, was born.
text: Margaret of Hungary, Byzantine empress (d. 1223)

summary: Theodore I Laskaris, future Byzantine emperor of Nicaea, was born in Constantinople.
text: Theodore I, emperor of Nicaea (d. 1221)

summary: Byzantine scholar and metropolitan Nicholas Hagiotheodorites died.
text: Nicholas Hagiotheodorites, Byzantine scholar and official

summary: Emperor Manuel I Komnenos marched a Byzantine expeditionary force toward Iconium while the Seljuks harassed his advance.
text: Summer – Emperor Manuel I (Komnenos) assembles a Byzantine expeditionary force, and marches towards Iconium, the Seljuk capital. Meanwhile, hordes of Seljuk Turks destroy crops and poison water supplies, to make Manuel's march more difficult, and harass the Byzantine army, in order to force it into the Meander Valley. Kilij Arslan II, ruler of the Sultanate of Rum, hears of the expedition, and sends envoys to ask for peace.

summary: Seljuk forces ambushed and defeated Emperor Manuel I Komnenos and his Byzantine army at the Battle of Myriokephalon near Lake Beyşehir.
text: Battle of Myriokephalon: The Seljuk Turks defeat the Byzantine forces led by Manuel I, who are ambushed when moving through a narrow mountain pass near Lake Beyşehir. The Byzantines are dispersed and surrounded. They suffer heavy casualties and their siege equipment is destroyed. Manuel flees in panic and is forced to sign a peace treaty with Kilij Arslan II.

summary: Anna Komnene Angelina, future Empress of Nicaea, was born in Constantinople.
text: Anna Komnene Angelina, Nicene empress (d. 1212)

summary: Byzantine general John Kantakouzenos was killed at the Battle of Myriokephalon.
text: September 17: John Kantakouzenos, Byzantine general

summary: Byzantine governor John Doukas Komnenos died.
text: John Doukas (Komnenos), Byzantine governor (b. 1128)

summary: Byzantine general Michael Aspietes died.
text: Michael Aspietes, Byzantine nobleman and general

summary: Thirty-three Armenian bishops held a synod at Hromkla to discuss union with the Byzantine Church.
text: A synod of thirty-three Armenian bishops in Hromkla discusses the conditions for union with the Byzantine Church and sends a profession of faith to emperor Manuel I Komnenos who dies before receiving it.

summary: Alexios II Komnenos succeeded Manuel I Komnenos as Byzantine emperor under the regency of Maria of Antioch.
text: Emperor Manuel I Komnenos dies in Constantinople after a 37-year reign. He is succeeded by his 11-year-old son, Alexios II Komnenos, who will reign briefly as emperor of the Byzantine Empire under the regency of his mother, Maria of Antioch. Maria assumes power as regent (until 1183) and takes as her advisor and lover, Alexios Komnenos (protosebastos), a nephew of Manuel I, which causes scandal and unrest among the Byzantine populace.

summary: Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos died in Constantinople.
text: Manuel I (Komnenos), Byzantine emperor (b. 1118)

summary: Byzantine poet and scholar John Tzetzes died in Constantinople.
text: John Tzetzes, Byzantine poet and grammarian (b. 1110)

summary: Byzantine princess and future queen consort Irene Angelina was born.
text: Irene Angelina, queen of Germany and Sicily (d. 1208)

summary: Eastern Orthodox inhabitants of Constantinople massacred the Venetian, Genoese, and other Latin residents.
text: April – Massacre of the Latins: The Eastern Orthodox inhabitants of Constantinople massacre the Venetian, Genoan, and other Latin officials and traders who rule as agents of Empress Maria of Antioch. She is the mother and regent of 12-year-old Emperor Alexios II.

summary: Andronikos I Komnenos entered Constantinople, had Maria of Antioch imprisoned, and was proclaimed co-emperor.
text: August – Andronikos Komnenos, a cousin of Maria's late husband, Emperor Manuel I (Komnenos), raises an army and enters the city, representing himself as the 'protector' of Alexios. He is proclaimed as co-emperor under the name Andronikos I, and has Maria imprisoned and later condemned to be strangled – forcing a signature from Alexios to put his mother to death.

summary: King Béla III of Hungary ravaged Belgrade and Braničevo while allied with Serbia against the Byzantine Empire.
text: May – June – Béla III, king of Hungary, ravages the region of Belgrade and Barancs (modern-day Braničevo). Meanwhile, Serbia allies itself with Hungary to gain independence.

summary: Alexios I, future founder and emperor of the Empire of Trebizond, was born.
text: Alexios I (Megas Komnenos), emperor of Trebizond (d. 1222)

summary: Future Byzantine emperor Alexios IV Angelos was born.
text: Alexios IV (Angelos), Byzantine emperor

summary: Byzantine general John Komnenos Vatatzes died during his rebellion against Andronikos I Komnenos.
text: John Komnenos Vatatzes, Byzantine general

summary: Byzantine princess Maria Komnene was poisoned and died in Constantinople.
text: July – Maria Komnene, Byzantine princess (poisoned) (b. 1152)

summary: Renier of Montferrat was poisoned and died in Constantinople alongside his wife Maria Komnene.
text: July – Renier of Montferrat (the Caesar John), Italian husband of Maria Komnene (poisoned) (b. 1162)

summary: Maria of Antioch, empress and former regent of the Byzantine Empire, was executed on the orders of Andronikos I Komnenos.
text: Maria of Antioch, Byzantine empress (b. 1145)

summary: Andronikos I Komnenos was proclaimed Byzantine Emperor at the Chalke gate and ordered the murder of Alexios II Komnenos.
text: Alexios II is compelled to condemn his own mother to death. In September, Andronikos Komenos is formally proclaimed Byzantine Emperor before the crowd on the terrace of the Church of Christ of the Chalke. By the end of the month, Andronikos orders Alexios' assassination; the young emperor is strangled in secret with a bow-string and his body thrown in the Bósporos.

summary: Andronikos I Komnenos married the young widow Agnes of France.
text: Andronikos I marries Alexios II's widow, the 11-year-old Agnes of France.

summary: Andronikos I Komnenos agreed to pay annual indemnities to the Republic of Venice for losses suffered during the Massacre of the Latins.
text: November – Andronikos makes a treaty with Venice, in which he promises a yearly indemnity as compensation for Venetian losses, during the Massacre of the Latins.
